If thou shalt do this thing, and God command thee so, then thou shalt be able to endure, and all this people shall also go to their place in peace.*

God blesses this arrangement, and Moses takes to it and does as Jethro advised. 

We see other times, in other places throughout the Bible that God approves of delegation of authority. He wants the people to know His ways and laws and the ordinances of remembrance, that in what they do they know the next right choice to make. 

We are to know the word of God that we can know ourselves what His will is. Without needing someone micromanaging and interpreting scripture, to constantly make decisions for us on normal matters. 

God then sets up captains over people, to judge matters for their people. By 10s, 100s and 1,000s. And a leader who answers to God, for the tougher matters of judgment. Thus will it be in the Millennium. Those who showed judgment and did great things for the Lord will be given much in the Kingdom. Those good and faithful servants will be made rulers, as Jesus described in the parable of the servants. 

We see the wisdom in this arrangement. The way it maximizes the ability to serve God and edify people. And this exists today through God's word; the priesthood of believers, the husband/father of the home, the local pastor, his helpers the decons or elders, all answering to Jesus. It is the form of Christian nationalism that we should seek.

It is also worth mentioning that God can use unsaved people, people who are wrong on doctrine but in position of authority, to do His will. 

Jethro as Moses' father-in-law was to be honored. His advice, considered and heeded. We sometimes see brothers and sisters in Christ struggle with that, where their parents are unsaved, sometimes wicked. Occasionally reprobate. And how does one honor them and honor God? 

The same question comes up with husbands with wives who won't submit to Christ or to their husbands, godly wives with unsaved husbands who treat them poorly, and other hierarchical conflicts, such as submitting to government when it is wicked. 

God's word is clear and consistent. That we are to as much as possible live peaceably with all men. To submit to the higher authority with meekness and faith, always keeping God as the head, that we don't cater to evil ourselves or join in another man's sin. 

People hate to hear that. They want to rebel constantly and be in open defiance of the order of things in this world. Only refusing to budge on the clear fundamental teachings of God, but also giving honor to whom honor is due, and paying tribute to whom tribute is due, and trusting God in all.

*I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.*

*And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.*

But if we walk in the Spirit, continuing in prayer and studying the word to be approved by God, faith grows, and with that faith, judgment and discernment which all work together to keep us from being afraid and reactionary.

Aside from the obvious symbolism of Christ in the blood and burnt offerings, the bread waved before the Lord, the sanctification rituals for Aaron and his sons, the detailed ordinances given to Moses from God is also a perfect example of worldly religion, given as much as a schoolmaster as the rest of the law. 

Let me explain my thoughts on this, and by no means is this authoritative but it's how it strikes me at this time, so soon after our study on Hebrews. Like all Biblical teachings, the depth of meaning is great and often multiple meanings can be found in the symbolism that are all correct in their own way. God's word is that deep. 

But when we see all these things laid out, a complex series of vestments, offices, specific and detailed sacrifices and the times and days to be honored, we see God giving to the children of Israel the most well thought out and complete ritualistic religion, the outward practices of faith, that the world has ever seen. Natural man may have pantheons and priests, ceremony and holiday and sacrifices, but they seem almost random and simple, obvious traditions of men.  

God here provides the ultimate in worship practices along those traditions of men, refined by His mind and reflecting patterns in Heaven, and symbols of the Christ to come. Kept holy by a holy God that there is no sin within it, but still outwardly worldly compared to the spirit of the New Testament.

The Children of Israel were always a stiff-necked people, prone to mischief. And of them were smote 3,000 by the sons of Levi at the order of Moses, and the Lord's promise to plague those in sin for the idol they made. 

God sought to destroy them utterly and from Moses make a new nation to carry the promise and blessing of the seed, that is Christ Jesus. To make of him a new Abraham. But the Lord repented of the evil He sought to do, and allowed Moses to execute judgment, rather than wipe out all of Israel. 

Now Moses with the tablets carved by God's own hand returned from the mountain, and seeing the sin of Israel, he smashed God's laws to the ground, the people not worthy of such a gift.

This is who God is. We who are saved seek to know Him and throughout scripture we are given many names and descriptions that allow us to understand the holy God. Here is the quality of God that is judgment. He is merciful and longsuffering. He forgives. But He does not clear the guilty, and he visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third or fourth generation. 

That is not to say they are punished for the sins of the father, but rather their inequities being judgment upon their people for generations. God is about to declare a genocide of the people in the way towards the promised land. The wickedness they have done in His sight. The groves and high places, molten gods and altars. God tells Moses that they are to destroy these people that their wickedness doesn't infect the children of Israel, through practice, through marriage, or in any way including eating meat sacrificed to idols. 

We learn a name for God and it is Jealous. He is a jealous God. Jealousy is not envy or covetousness. It is fiercely protecting that which one owns. God is saying in this covenant He owns them, they are His people. And if they go whoring after strange gods because they were snared by covenant to make peace with the people He has judged be destroyed, He will have vengeance upon the children of Israel.

The feast of unleavened bread that begins immediately after Passover, which is the sabbaths of Christ when He is 3 days and 3 nights in Hell for our sins. And because His only begotten Son is a sacrifice for us, and because the firstborn sons of the children of Israel were spared in passover, even if their cattle, they belong to God and must be attoned through a substitutionary sacrifice. All a picture of Christ. 

The sabbath, again a picture of Christ. 

The feast of weeks, which leads to the Pentecost. The firstfruits of the harvest. 

Then the feast of the harvest at years end. 

All a picture of the time to come, and a memorial for the children of Israel that they may know Jesus. 

*Thou shalt not offer the blood of my sacrifice with leaven; neither shall the sacrifice of the feast of the passover be left unto the morning.*

The unleavened bread and unfermented wine of the Lord's supper. Taking Jesus down from the cross before sunset on Passover. 

The first of the firstfruits are God's under this Mosaic law. All a picture of Christ.

*Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk.*

What does this mean? Why do Jews forbid the mixing of dairy with meat entirely from this passage? 

The act of seething, a form of boiling meat, in this case in milk, was a way of cooking, even basting in butter that which is roasted. It's a wonderful way to enjoy the food that God has blessed us with, but even the idea of using the actual mother's milk to cook her kid seems cruel. But why prohibit it? 

The logic of man says that the traditions of the people they were to drive out included this form of cruel sacrifice to their pagan gods. That may be. It could also be symbolism of Christ and a prohibition of the cooking method that they keep it a burnt offering. 

But what it does not do is ban dairy with meat generally. The "kosher" practices are just more of the vain traditions of the judaizers. And these dietary laws are done away with for Christians in the New Testament anyway. But it is an interesting verse to chew upon, no pun intended.

The first several chapters of Leviticus, which lays out the Levitical priesthood and its ordinances and practices, deal with the subject of sacrifice for atonement and oblations, gifts given to the Lord of meats, which in Biblical terms is foodstuffs, not just flesh of an animal. 

As we see in chapter 1, this is the holocaust or burnt offering of the lamb without blemish. The blood carrying the atonement. The sweet savour of the fire roasted fats and meats being pleasing to the Lord. 

And this is a picture of Christ. Just as are the meat offerings in chapter 2. Everything in the Old Testament does. 

Here we see the gift offering of fine flour, anointing oil and frankincense. The bread, representing Jesus, made without leaven, leaven representing sin.  Note that it was both raw ingredients baked by Aaron and his sons. Or finished cakes and wafers. Cooked or baked. And the priests eat thereof what is left over. The frankincense consumed completely, all anointed with oil, as befitting a King. 

*And the priest shall take from the meat offering a memorial thereof, and shall burn it upon the altar: it is an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the Lord.*

Showing the Israelites the truth of their savior in these ordinances. As a memorial to Him that was to come. All burnt upon the fire. 

But the oblations of the firstfruits shall not be burnt in the altar. And all the meat offerings of the first fruits are to be salted generously. To season it completely as it is the salt of the covenant with God. 

This represents the saved, the firstfruits of the harvest. The salt, the holy Spirit. 

*Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men*.

Salt is a seasoning, increasing the savour of the food, enhancing it. But it is also a preservative, keeping food fresh, longer. In this way, the Spirit acts in the believer. It isn't burned in the fire, just as believers are spared Hell. 

God makes a provision for the corn given in a meat offering to be as the flour or unleavened bread, anointed with oil and frankincense, to be burned as the other flours, as a cornmeal, that there be no confusion.

The people were not to eat the fat or the blood. The ban on blood predates the Levitical law and goes back to Adam being taught of God how to sacrifice, and the laws given to Noah after the flood.

**1 John 1:9** 
*If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness*

Confession, the act of admitting guilt, of revealing your own faults and iniquities, is a fundamental act of humility in the Christian life. It is the realization that leads to repentance towards the Gospel, the understanding that yes, we have sinned before God and His standards are just and right, for He is holy, and we ask for mercy and salvation knowing in our hearts that we deserve death, for we have earned it. The wages of sin. 

A soul that sins and doesn't confess their trespass to God, can't avail themselves of the sacrifice. You can't get saved without this acknowledgment. You can't accept salvation without knowing you need to be saved. 

And as we covered in Romans; all men know. By the wrath of God revealed from heaven upon the ungodly. By the conviction of the holy Spirit, reproving the world. By the conscience we have, the law written in our hearts. So that we have no excuse. Everyone knows. 

But few confess. 

It is humiliating to be found out. It is one of the first sins we commit affirmatively, lying about something we have done. We seek to avoid punishment, but more so, our pride has us seek to avoid being exposed. Especially since so many sins are petty and embarrassing. Coveting. Lusts. All come from selfish and disgusting places. Admission that we aren't "good" is a hard nut to crack. 

This pride and dishonesty, lying about sin to God, to others, even lying to ourselves, is the biggest stumbling block to accepting the Gospel. 

Either a person will deny that God is real, that His judgments are right, that they aren't absolved by technicality, that the Bible doesn't *really* say that. 

*Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?*

It is that lie that Satan uses to tempt us, from Eve on. And like Adam and Eve, hiding in the bushes from God, covering their sin with their own works, blaming someone else, even blaming God, as Adam did, we see the cope humans will cling to to avoid that humiliation of confession. Even before the eyes of God, in His presence. 

This pride against confession is what draws people to a works-based false religion. 

The idea that they are "good people" because they keep ordinances and receive sacraments, even the false half-hearted "confession" to a "priest," being absolved not by faith but by vain repetitions of prayer, given as punishment. 

People seek to be absolved in any way possible short of actually acknowledging their sin. 

And we see in our study of Leviticus, God provided the framework in the law that if anyone could follow it without falling short, they could theoretically be saved. It is the ultimate works religion, the only one God endorsed, and He did it to show that we need salvation in Christ. That all will fall short. 

Even in the paradise of Eden, with one commandment only, man sinned. 

We are given the law as a schoolmaster to bring us to the understanding that we need Jesus. And by the law, the understanding that to receive Christ we have to admit we need saving. That our righteousness is as filthy rags. That we sin, and God's judgment is just and right. 

And so we must confess we are guilty under the law to be saved, and once saved, we confess our sins that God may work through the Spirit indwelling us to remove those thorns in our hearts. 

We study the scriptures, and often learn that things we have done in the past were actually sinful. And like the Hebrews, once we have that knowledge we need to confess and seek atonement in faith through the Lord. 

**Proverbs 28:13** 
*He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.*

**James 5:16** 
*Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.*

Brothers and sisters in Christ should edify one another, being of one mind in Christ. And that includes admitting our faults, confessing our trespasses with each other, and seeking prayer to help us overcome the flesh. 

This is natural, normal and good. 

The very act of a sincere confession to God is often enough to bring us out of the delusional rationalizing we do to cover our sins. And to tell others of our sin, knowing that it could be humiliating but for their love and grace, and their own humility in being an admitted sinner, is freeing. Knowing others are praying for your growth. These things provide a bulwark against sin. If your heart isn't deceiving you, it becomes more humiliating to stay in a sin than it is to fear being exposed. 

True confession is a wonderful tool given by God that we may become separated unto the Gospel and better vessels fitted to His purpose. 

False confession, anything that seeks to be given excuse or justification for our sin that we may remain in it, or that we can work it off in some way of penance, is wicked as Hell and leads people further and further into sin.

The heave and wave offerings were a form of free will offering given in peace to God, in thanksgiving, and in supplication or to a vow, with the understanding that a portion went to feed the Levite priests. 

Heave and wave, the motions done with the portion that was given the priests. Literally lifting up or waving above their heads, signifying that portion that was theirs. 

Some interpretations hold that the wave offerings signify the resurrection of Christ, while the heave as either His being lifted up on the cross or, more commonly His assent into Heaven on Pentecost. I don't know, or really have a strong opinion on it. It is sufficient to know that Christ is the propitiation, the sacrifice, by which we make peace with God and Whom we give thanks through. Blessing all we do in Jesus' name.

I generally avoid commentaries when doing a study, seeking to allow the Bible to explain itself. They have a purpose, my own thoughts recorded here are a commentary, but reliance on them often keeps us from allowing the Spirit to give us the knowledge and wisdom, directly from the word. 

But, for these Levitical ceremonial laws and ordinances, sometimes I lean on them. I try to make sense of it myself from scripture first, then go to them to see what others may have to offer. 

In his commentary on Exodus 29:27, Clarke wrote this regarding the heave and wave offerings: “As the *wave-offering* was agitated *to* and *fro*, and the *heave-offering up* and *down*, some have conceived that this twofold action represented the *figure of the cross*, on which the great *Peace-offering* between God and man was offered in the personal sacrifice of our blessed Redeemer.” For this idea, Clarke cited the work of Charles Houbigant, a French Bible scholar of the 18th century.

Seems as likely as my own interpretation. Your mileage may vary.

Over the course of 9 chapters we have seen the detailed instructions from the Lord to Moses, telling the Levitical priesthood of Aaron and his eldest two sons with great specificity, what they were to do regarding purification and sacrifice, where and how and when, and to what portion was God's, the blood, the burnt offering, the wave and the heave offerings, all of it. 

And despite these clear and explicit teachings of the word of God, the first thing the newly anointed sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, do is add their own works to it. 

They light incense with a "strange fire," that is not the fire the Lord provided within the Tabernacle, but fire they made themselves. Their intentions seem to be good; they offered this strange fire before the Lord. They were seeking to praise Him, perhaps. Glorifying God with their own invention of religious expression, which the Lord commanded them not. 

*And there went out fire from the Lord, and devoured them, and they died before the Lord.* 

Aaron, chosen to be the first high priest of the Levitical priesthood, honored by his sons being chosen with him, to lead the congregation and perform the propitiations and oblations, to instruct the people in the ways of salvation through Christ by their adherence to the commands of God, in sanctification, showing the judgment of God that all the people may glorify Him. And he watches his sons burn to death, seeking their own righteousness. 

The error of Cain is a natural impulse for man. To add our own works or to place new and strange ways of worship upon the things of God that His word instructs, is something we see throughout the Bible. And we see God's judgement upon those who seek their own sanctification, their own means of being holy. Who add to His word. Who brings their own works to the table of the Lord. 

And yet, it continues. 

Just as Judaizers and those teaching strange doctrines of men were creeping in unawares to the early New Testament churches. Just as heretics and apostates twisted the word of God, bringing another gospel, so too did *Nadab and Abihu*. 

Those who claim that the "church fathers" were correct when they deviated from scripture and that there were hidden traditions, passed down from apostles, are the same as those who Jude wrote about in his epistle;

*Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Core.*

They bring strange fire before the Lord.

This is the reason why Biblical fundamentalism is the only way. What is derisively called "sola scripta" by those seeking to mock the word of God, is taught throughout scripture, Leviticus 10 being another example in a long list of them. 

Most people who mock the idea are not only unsaved, natural men who cannot understand the things of God, but worse; they place themselves above God. Their pride in thinking they know better, have secret knowledge, conceits about their own righteousness, makes them not only go astray, but lead others along with them. 

As Jesus says;

*Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves.*

Woe unto them. 

These special boys are in for a rude awakening, just as Aaron's sons.

After having kin remove the remains, Moses calls Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons, and instructs them to do as the Lord commanded, to eat the sin offering, cooked by the same fire that killed their brothers, that came from the Lord. To eat it beside the altar, because this is a holy thing, designed to teach the congregation of the separation of holy from unholy. From clean and unclean. 

But later, Moses sees their portion of the offering burnt without the camp. Likely in fear of divine retribution, Moses seeks out the sons to rebuke them, but Aaron says it was his own fault. That he couldn't bear to do it given the events of the day and the loss of his eldest two sons. Aaron admits the error, but appeals to the fact that it wouldn't have been done in the spirit of God's command had he gone along and ate it, and that it wouldn't have been acceptable given his state. This excuse is acceptable to Moses. 

It is important to make this distinction, that while we must obey God's commands and seek to diligently follow what His word tells us is right, there are times where our heart isn't in it. Our spirit is low. And unlike those who seek to add their own works to the glory of God, kindling His wrath, the Lord is understanding of our own weakness and longsuffering in His mercy. 

Aaron held his peace. He had accepted the judgment of God. But he was still grieved. He was on God's program but it was too bitter that day. Aaron resumed his duties following this, but it was too much to bear at the time. 

God is merciful and loves us. He is understanding that sometimes the truth of His word is bitter to us, in the flesh. His judgments may seem harsh to us at the time, and we may need a little time to come to acceptance. We must not use that occasion to curse God or to backslide. But He is patient.

Note that Moses instructs the priests should remain sober. And that if they drink alcohol and enter into the Tabernacle, they will die. 

*Do not drink wine nor strong drink, thou, nor thy sons with thee, when ye go into the tabernacle of the congregation, lest ye die: it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations*...

This instruction coming on the heels of the devastating loss of two sons, may have been directed at Aaron in his grief, but it's a standing command from the Lord for those who are called His priests. We who are saved are of the royal priesthood. We are a Tabernacle of the Spirit of God. 

Just as **Proverbs 31** states;

*It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine; Nor for princes strong drink: Lest they drink, and forget the law, And pervert the judgment of any of the afflicted.*

We who are saved are joint heirs to the kingdom. We are princes. 

As priests and princes, we should abstain from intoxicants. We are called to be sober. To refrain from the appearance of evil. To be holy because He is holy. 

It is incredibly difficult to read these scriptures and come to the conclusion that it's ok to drink booze. 

And it is gravely heretical to claim, as the Romans do, that the priests they appoint should drink alcohol as part of their false sacrifice at the altar they claim is holy. Blasphemously calling it the blood of Christ.

I have covered the symbolism and importance of the law of leprosy, and the atonement offered at the cleansing of one who is cured in another post [here](https://t.me/HouseOfWews2/9168).

It is fascinating to me that an incurable disease is given a process by God for ritual cleansing in the case of a leper who is cured.   

There were cases in the OT of leprosy being "cured." In **Numbers 12**, after Aaron and Miriam gainsay Moses for marrying an Ethiopian, God curses Miriam with leprosy for 7 days. 

The other instance is in **2 Kings** 5, where a captain of the Syrian guard, Naaman contracts the disease, and the Syrian King sends him to the king of Israel asking him to heal his servant. 

*And it came to pass, when the king of Israel had read the letter, that he rent his clothes, and said, Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man doth send unto me to recover a man of his leprosy? wherefore consider, I pray you, and see how he seeketh a quarrel against me.*

As we see, it was as if he had asked him to raise the dead. An impossible task and the king worried that it was a provocation for war with Syria. But the prophet Elisha heard of it and said;

*And it was so, when Elisha the man of God had heard that the king of Israel had rent his clothes, that he sent to the king, saying, Wherefore hast thou rent thy clothes? let him come now to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel.*

It's a wonderful story of faith and shows the power of God, highly recommend reading it. 

But we can see that the idea that one could be healed from leprosy would have been something that the Israelites would have thought impossible save by God. 

And yet an entire chapter is devoted to this unlikely thing, filled with imagery of the sacrifice of Christ. A picture of Jesus saving sinners from death. And the purpose of the practical application, as we see Elisha say, is to let people know there is a prophet of God among them. 

Jesus heals the leper and sends him to the temple to perform this ritual, as a testimony unto the priests, that the Son of God was here.

As I wrote about it in the study of **Luke 5**;

"The bird in the earthen vessel, the clay that man is made from, as a substitutionary sacrifice, its blood upon wood, like the wood of the cross. On the scarlet, as the garments of Christ were so stained. On the hyssop, like the sprig dipped in vinegar, given to Jesus on the cross. And this blood of atonement then cleanses the man, and the living bird, like the risen Christ ascends to the heavens." 

Jesus Christ is in an earthen vessel, made manifest in the flesh. There is running water, the baptismal washing that came with the carnal ordinances, the law of the clean and unclean. 

Everything points to Jesus.

We don't figure out what's right and wrong from circumstances, we aren't called to be superstitious. God doesn't instruct us to place our faith in rituals or washings, ordinances and observations. He calls us to serve others and to study His word. 

There are blessings and judgments and promises and curses, God's wrath revealed against the workers of iniquity, His mercy revealed by those who believe on Jesus and are saved. 

**Matthew 5:44-45**
*But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.*

The Bible tells us that sometimes circumstances happen for no other reason that God willed it. That we may not know His purpose and it isn't our place to question Him. (Read **Job** to see how God views our second guessing Him!)

But man has the gift of pattern recognition, and it is hard not to see that the fates that befall others must be in answer to their sin. Jesus rebuked the people doing this;

Some things are just chance. Some times things happen, and we can't say why. 

**Ecclesiastes 9:11**

We need to have peace with this. It isn't all about us. We aren't special boys. We may get reproved and chastened by God for our sin. We may receive unexpected blessings because we walk in the spirit and do the things of God with a meek heart. Loving others the way Christ loves us. Nations might be judged for their wickedness. But sometimes things happen that God may be glorified. 

Keep that in mind, that the Christian life's entire purpose is to give all glory to God, and reveal His grace and mercy from Heaven, to help the lost. To heal the brokenhearted.

Flowing with milk and honey, a land taken by those who failed to fear and serve the living God, but set about to establish their own righteousness. And then sanctified by the Lord to His purpose. 

This historical and physical story is a picture of the spiritual, and the individual salvation of us who believe and are adopted by God as His people. 

And so we should notice the order of things; salvation is front loaded and found only by faith. For the salvation of Israel from bondage and death came by faith alone, by the blood. 

The Isralites in Egypt were not told to change their ways first. To become holy first. To repent of their sins and throw themselves before God crying for mercy because of how wicked they were. 

God decided in His grace to offer them mercy if they believed Moses and Aaron, and trusted in the blood of the lamb. 

And so all Israel was saved. 

Then they were baptized together. Then they were given God's law. Then they were told to sanctify themselves, for their own good and to better serve God's will. 

Those who place the giving of the law before the acceptance of faith are in error. Those telling others they must turn from their sins first before they can believe are entangling them in bondage. Placing the yoke upon those who should be set free.

This same pattern is seen in Abraham. Abraham was given the word of God by His promises, and in faith alone was given those blessings.

*Abraham believed God and it was counted unto him for righteousness*.

Not by the law. Not by circumcision, for Abraham was saved decades before God gave circumcision as an ordinance. But by believing God. 

Abraham didn't repent of his sins, follow the law, or grovel for mercy. God in His amazing grace, offered salvation unto him, and out of free will, Abraham accepted. 

His faith was such that Abraham willingly offered his only begotten son upon the altar, knowing God would keep His word, and by this act, his faith was made perfect. That one may look upon that and see Abraham justified by men. 

But not before God. It was faith alone that saved him. If it were his willingness to obey God, then Abraham would have the glory. 

But all the glory is God's. He did it all. We just have to trust Him as Abraham did. That while we are yet sinners, Christ died for us.

I know I am bringing two lines of thought together; the study of Leviticus and its ordinances and statutes for sanctification, and the current heresy that I have been hammering against with scripture. And forgive me if I failed to fit the two pieces together elegantly enough. But I think it is a complimentary study to see how God looks at things, rather than man, and how consistent He is in how He extends His mercy to us while we are yet sinners, His grace to those that believe, and the precious salvation that comes from His Son. That all glory is his. Not of ourselves, least any man should boast. That by understanding this, we may be conformed to His purpose, without being holier than thou scolds and hypocrites, lacking mercy and judgment. But in the Spirit, a light to the lost and a comfort to the broken hearted. That God may have the increase.

Repentance, or metanoia, having a change of heart, coming to a new understanding that is (by grace, led of the Spirit); discernment. 

We gain discernment regarding the will of God and the state of ourselves and man in relation to Him, when we repent. When we believe the scriptures that say God would offer a sacrifice of His own making to free us from death and Hell. That that sacrifice is the Son of God, Jesus Christ. 

That discernment, if the new man created at salvation is fed, leads to a change in attitude towards sin. It becomes less desirable. The lusts of the flesh can lose their appeal. Even disgusting us. 

If that new man isn't fed, and they continue walking in the flesh, they are still saved by the knowledge of the truth, but that discernment is dulled and God may have to chasten the person to work godly sorrow in their heart. If they remain backslidden, God may call them home. 

But they are still saved. 

Saying "real repentance WILL mean you turn from sin, and WILL walk in the Spirit," is false. We must pick up our cross daily. It is a choice to engage in sanctification. But salvation is of Christ, not ourselves. It is by grace, not of ourselves.

Chapter 21 contains more of the Levitical priesthood laws regarding the holiness of the priests, the sons of Aaron. That they may not defile themselves by touching or being around a corpse other than close kin. 

That they should be the husband of one wife, just as pastors must be, and their wives must be virgins. Not a widow or divorced, or profane. 

1 Timothy 3:2-12
*A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach; Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous; One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity; (For if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?) Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil. Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre; Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless. Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well.*

While the holiness of a Levitical priest is unique, the cleanliness rituals both practical and ceremonial, and can be mirrored in the qualifications for pastor, it is important to recognize that we who are believers are part of a holy priesthood too. And for us, we should seek to be as separated spiritually as they were in the flesh.

There are further provisions against a priest acting as a pagan priest, with rending of clothes, cutting the corners of their beard or hair in the fashion of the Egyptian and Canaanite priests. Acting in a profane way, desecrating the temple of God. 

This holiness extended to not allowing the halt, lame, deaf and blind, broken, crippled or birth defects enter into the holy places or to offer the sacrifice. God does say they may eat of the portion given to the Levitical priests and their families. This isn't a eugenic command, simply relating to the office itself.

And may point to the current time, that in Christ we are healed and allowed to boldly go before the Father, but those who haven't been made righteous in the blood of Christ may not, not being spiritually made without blemish.

Now we are here in Leviticus chapter 23, and in it God provides the basic terms of the sabbaths and holy days to be kept by the children of Israel. 

Understanding that sabbaths means rest, and that the prohibition of doing work on the sabbath is a picture of Christ Jesus, and the rest we enter into in Him. That we are saved by the rest given to us by the Lord and not our own works. That if a child of Israel works on these days, he is cut off, just as anyone trusting in their works for salvation is likewise cut off from the Kingdom of God. It is an undeniable truth that is repeated over and over again throughout the Bible, from the creation through Revelation. We are saved by Christ's perfect work, not our own. Not by being a "good person" or contrite or "trying to avoid sin" or how well we make "Jesus the Lord of our life."

Jesus paid it all in full, and the Spring feasts of Passover, unleavened bread and Pentecost all serve as ordinances to the Isralites as a picture of Christ. 

I covered much of this in the Gospel studies, recently in [a study of Luke](https://t.me/HouseOfWews2/9753).

It is fascinating and amazing how God set this before the people and thousands of years later, we see it pay off with Jesus, the Passover lamb, slain on a sabbath, in Hell for 3 days and nights, all sabbaths, and risen again, only to ascend into Heaven on Pentecost, the feast of the first fruits held 50 days after Passover. The day in which the disciples went out to the multitude of gathered Jews preaching the Gospel in every tongue. The 5,000 saved that day being the first fruits of the spring harvest.

Then we see the [Fall feasts](https://t.me/HouseOfWews2/7743) (which I touch on in this study of Revelation). Which with the trumpets and gathering of the harvest, is a picture of the day of the Lord. The second coming of Jesus Christ, to gather the elect, the dead first reborn to glorified bodies, then those who are alive and remain, changed in a twinkling of an eye, all to meet the Lord in the sky, caught up together in the clouds. The day of our redemption. Amen.

The details and how each of the ordinances given by the Lord unto the people corresponding to and a picture of the things to come, is fun to study out, but the knowledge of His giving us these things that we may know Him and build in faith, that He is true to His word and His word is consistent, over thousands of years and many authors, given by the Spirit and preserved by God for all time. We can trust His word because He has shown us in it a singular voice, and the theme that is Christ. Everything points to Him. Jesus is found in every book of the Bible. The faith of the Old Testament saints was the same as New; believing on the Lord to save us, a gift given in grace from our Father because He so loved us. That while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Amen

**Leviticus 24** begins with the command to have the lamps of the Tabernacle burn continually, dusk to dawn. A statute for ever. That there is light in the place of God. 

And God commands that there be bread baked as a memorial, continually, as an offering before the Lord, and eaten by the Levitical priests. This is called the shewbread, concentrated by the Lord. 

The light symbolizes the truth of God throughout the Bible, and so it is never dark before Him. The bread is both the life given the people by God's grace and His word. 

This shewbread becomes a means of feeding David and his men as they flee Saul, who was in a murderous rage against the future king. Even as it was offered to God and holy, but to the Lord's purpose, it fed His favored in a time of need. 

Likewise, as Jesus rebukes the Pharisees when He and His disciples gleaned corn on the Sabbath to eat, Jesus points to how these things are the Lord's, and not just blind tradition and meaningless ritual. That He is the Lord of the sabbath.

Often religion becomes rote practices, that forget the meaning behind them as the Pharisees had. Using these things to condemn. Jesus says had they understood who He was, that He was present for mercy in His death and resurrection to come, that the sacrifices of the temple were a picture of Him who had come not to condemn but to save, that they'd understand why it was acceptable for them to eat of their work, as the Levites were allowed on the sabbath. Because they did the work of God.

The second half of the chapter begins with a narrative of a child of Egyptian heritage born into the Tribe of Dan, blaspheming God, and God's instructions to take him without the camp and those who heard the blasphemy to stone him to death. 

God reiterates that even strangers among them are under His law, both to their good, and to their punishment for violating it. 

He says His law is justice, that a murderer be put to death. That blemish, or physical harm, be answered in a like manner; breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth.

This concept of God's law has been understood for millennia, preserved for all time, but in 1901 a Babylonian relic was found that contained what is called Hammurabi's Code, a list of laws credited to the ancient king by archeologists, which included the eye for an eye form of justice. 

During the 20th century, what was part of God's perfect law (repeated from **Exodus 21:24-25**
*Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot*, *Burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe*) began to be credited to a man, and after it had permeated culture that the concept of an eye for an eye actually originated from Hammurabi's Code, people began to mistakenly think it wasn't God's perfect law. And once they'd managed to mislead people with that, they then began to discredit the concept as barbaric, a remnant of ancient Babylon and not the commandments of God. 

And so by the close of the 20th Century, most people had no idea that this was found in scripture, and were taught to think of it as a savage injustice.

If the concept was raised by Christians at all, it was in the context of **Matthew 5:38-39**; *Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.* And this was taught as somehow Jesus contradicting the concept, as if He wasn't the author of it. When Jesus says love thy neighbor, The same people pretend it was a new commandment when it comes from Leviticus as well.

But Jesus calling those who are saved by faith in Him to love even our enemies, to pray for them, to not answer violence with violence, but to show mercy and love to them, isn't saying that the law itself is unjust, for it will be the law in the Millennial Kingdom. He's talking about our hearts storing up wrath, vengeance, and hatred. 

Before a magistrate, the eye taken for an eye would still be justice. 

**1 Timothy 1:9-11**
*Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers, For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine; According to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.*

But we who are righteous should forgive those who wronged us and show mercy to those in need. These two concepts aren't contradictory but complimentary. 

Our mercy doesn't upend the law. Our being at liberty from the law spiritually means we should be more circumspect in how we view our enemies. Our trust in God for vengeance taking priority over our executing our own wrath. 

But if the law demands restitution, so be it. The sword is not wielded in vain.

What those who seek to undermine confidence in scripture do is trust that Christians won't be able to rightly divide the word of God, and this higher level concept would escape us, and lead us to showing perverse judgment. 

If you notice, by abandoning the law for the unrighteous, instead of mercy and love and limited restitution to a like-for-like code, we have a "justice system" that either punishes the wrong doer far exceeding what is right in the eyes of God, or not doing anything to rightly punish the wicked and protect the innocent. Those that deserve death still live, often freed to offend again.

Those who deserved perhaps the loss of a tooth, or to pay restitution for damages end up incarcerated for years to no one's profit. It is skewed and unjust and it encourages vengeance, hatred and variance, instead of mercy and love.

The nuance required to understand these differences, The worldly application of biblical principles with people who aren't believers versus how believers should respond personally. This causes confusion for many in other applications such as application of Romans 13 and 14. 

Christians are called to be meek, to be peacemakers, to be humble in realizing that our condition is by the grace of God and not of ourselves. To be understanding of our enemies that by love, we may overcome it and bring them to the same peace that we have found in the grace of God. 

But that doesn't mean that in this world, God's law shouldn't be upheld. And if we were to stone to death, someone for a capital violation, We should not do so gleefully and with vengeance but with understanding. And after applying just mercy. 

By not walking this line, we have a society wherein there is no justice and there is no mercy. 

We have courts that are grossly unfair. We have a criminal justice system that can't decide between rehabilitation and punishment and so attains neither. 

We don't put to death those who have their own blood upon them. And we lock up people who could have simply worked off the harm they caused. The application of the law becomes arbitrary and capricious rather than circumspect and done with discernment.

I don't know if I'm explaining this concept well, and I myself struggle with the seeming dichotomy. But we have to understand that it isn't God's law that is imperfect, it is us.

We want vengeance and God wants justice. We want mercy when it applies to us but deny it to others, Just as God's mercy is extended to us by His grace, but the wages of sin is a debt we all owe. And a person's blood is upon themselves when they violate God's law. 

This I think is why it's so important to stay in God's word, to feed the new man. These concepts become clearer and we begin to see the nuances and glory in how perfect God's judgment is.

Leviticus chapter 25 brings us the law of Jubilee, a perpetual sabbatical observation of the 7th year, in the land of Canaan which the Lord brought the children of Israel, culminating in the 49th year, 7 times 7, a jubilee, a proclamation of liberty, wherein all God's children shall be redeemed. 

Of course this parallels with Christ, and the redemption from the bonds of sin He makes for us, as the near kin, the Son of man, setting us free. 

The particulars of this law, which wouldn't take effect for the Isralites until they had settled the land, driving out the former inhabitants and dividing by lot the tribes and the habitations thereof, showed not only the foresight of God's providence, but His terms as the actual owner, the land Lord so to speak, of the land He gives them. 

And so, 6 years the fields are sown and the vineyards dressed, but in the 7th, there was no work to be done in the land. God promises them that the 6th year will be bountiful enough to tide them over to the 9th year, that they could live off their stores, because God provides all. Not of their own works. 

The timing of the jubilee, which was marked in the 49th year, 7 sabbaths, was marked at the end of the fall feasts by the trumpets at the end of the day of atonement. 

Just as Pentecost is celebrating the 7th sabbath after Passover, the spring feasts, represent Christs work here at His first coming, then the Jubilee is marked by the fall feast, which is emblematic of His second, and the day of redemption for believers. The trumpet sounds to announce the victory of the Lord, the atonement bought with blood, the redemption from bondage and the liberty given all, rich or poor.

And so, the land given to the people by lot would return to them, and if it had been sold during the proceeding years to be worked by another, it would be redeemed back to the inheritors. Thus the price must be fair, and match the nearness of the jubilee; less time, less expensive. 

By this God provided that no family ever be perpetually destitute. And while being sold into servitude, it was always to be released in the jubilee. Not as bondsmen, or chattel slaves. 

No usury given to a brother, either. And no defrauding them in buying or selling. 

The Lord gives these things as a soft reset that allows for everyone to partake in His bounty and that none becomes rich by the accumulation of land and houses. (Except in the cities, where this didn't apply, being hubs of commerce and safety, not home.)

**Isaiah 5:8**
*Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!*

God hates unfair dealings, taking advantage of others for profit, especially in their poverty. Unjust weights and measures. Mistreatment of servants. Usury among His people and the accumulation of property and capital, to the exclusion of others. 

Basically, Capitalism. 

But that is not to say He endorsed Communism, either. But fair and righteous trade and checks on over accumulation of wealth, or subjugation of His people. Productive enterprise and free markets (little f, little m), were the way He provided. 

This system was fair and just and kept in remembrance of God being who we rely on, who provides for all. Rich or poor, servant or free. 

The right of return to their own place, the inheritance they claim, enabled the genealogies to be recorded, and kept the tribes separated as He had ordained through the lots when it was eventually divided. 

It kept the integrity of nations, as a people, as kin. 

The genealogies also then served a purpose, bringing us to Christ's human family being perfect in its generations as it is given in the Gospel. And the real jubilee being the ultimate sabbath, which is Jesus. 

The elegance and perfection of this law shouldn't be lost in the allegory or spiritual application, however. It really is the way that we should live, even today.

Ultimately, the ordinances of jubilee serve as a sobering reminder that we are servants of God, and we cannot be given or taken in bondage to any other master. 

We may work and toil for another, to pay our way and support our family, but not as slaves, because we are bought for a price already, by the blood of Christ. And so, even as we work here on this earth, we answer to Him. The last chapter of Leviticus, the law of the vow, offering and tithe. These are the general conditions for the sake of clarifying what goes into the surety of  a vow or, rather the amount held until completion of the vow, that could be redeemed upon completion, or the case of land and other things offered to the priesthood outside of what is proscribed earlier, for the sake of a special promise to God. 

It is an idea later corrupted, where we see Jesus in the Gospels call out the Pharisees for allowing an adult son to place his things in such a vow, to avoid his responsibility to honor his father and mother, caring for them in their old age, or "Corban." 

*But ye say, If a man shall say to his father or mother, It is Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; he shall be free.*

The idea of temporarily giving or using collateral to ensure keeping of a vow before God, and redemption, is reflected in salvation, where Jesus is offered, the vow made, the Spirit serving as surety until the day of redemption.

In **Numbers 2**, the Lord commands Moses to organize the camp of Israel around the Tabernacle. First the Levites divided into four smaller camps, to the South, West, North and East of the Tabernacle. With the tent of worship at its heart, the entrance facing East, that the morning sun would shine into it. 

God then told them to make four camps; to the East, the standard of Judah. To the South, the standard of Reuben. To the West, the standard of Ephraim. To the North, the standard of Dan. Each banner with the ensign, the emblem of that tribe. 

And within each camp, the other tribes would muster. In the East, first camped Judah, then next to them the tribe of Issachar, then the tribe of Zebulun. 186,400 of the armies total of the three tribes. 

And when the camp would go out and move, they would fall in ranks in that order. Leading the march. 

Next, to the South, first came Ruben. And those that pitched by them, Simeon. Then next to Simeon, Gad. 151,450 men. 

And when they marched, the camp of Ruben would fall in behind the camp of Judah. And the disassembled Tabernacle and the Levites, behind them, in the midst of the march. 

On the West, in the camp of Ephraim camped according to their armies, with Manasseh camped next to them, with Benjamin then next. 108,100 men. 

On the North, under the standard of Dan fell their tribe, then by him was the tribe of Asher, followed next by Naphtali. 157,600. 

The camps of Ephraim and Dan following in line when the camp of the children of Israel were on the move.

Now, to the point. What **Numbers 2** lays out is a picture of the camp, surrounding the Tabernacle, the heart of the camp where the Spirit of God appears as a cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. The Levites to each direction, serving the 4 camps. 

The rectangular tent of the Tabernacle facing East would see the camp of Judah. Larger than the others. West, a bit smaller. North and South, almost equal. 

There are two schools of thought on this, presented above. One school teaches that each camp surrounded the Tabernacle in a square, the tribes each side by side. 

The other sees the camp laid out in a nearly perfect cross. With the camps laid out by one tribe, next to them another, and then another. 

A cross with the heart being the holy place of God. Where the blood was shed for sacrifice, a picture of Christ. Facing East, looking towards Judah. Jesus being the morning star.

**Revelation 22:16**
*I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star.*

While we cannot know with 100% certainty that the layout was a cross, it certainly is what is described in my opinion. I cannot see it any other way, and Numbers has many references to Jesus, as we will see. The idea it would just be an uneven box-shaped camp seems absurd. 

Not to get to any spoilers, consider this passage from **Numbers 24;**

*And Balaam lifted up his eyes, and he saw Israel abiding in his tents according to their tribes; and the spirit of God came upon him. And he took up his parable, and said, Balaam the son of Beor hath said, and the man whose eyes are open hath said: He hath said, which heard the words of God, which saw the vision of the Almighty, falling into a trance, but having his eyes open: How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, and thy tabernacles, O Israel!*

Balaam, a character we shall encounter soon enough, is looking down at the camp of Israel and the Spirit of God came upon him and he marveled at the layout of the camp. 

I don't believe that he was viewing a rough square. I believe he was looking towards the cross.

The debate over this is definitely tertiary doctrine. No one has to believe one way or another about it. But the picture of Christ should inform everything we read in the Old Testament. Themes Numbers teaches throughout. 

The next few chapters can be rough. But all scripture is given for our profit. It was written for our edification and to build faith in us. Things like the layout of the camp builds faith that God's plan was always, from everlasting. Jesus the same yesterday today and forever. Amen

Chapter 5 of Numbers is divided into three sections, highlighted by God restating or clarifying previous commands given in Exodus and Leviticus, and adding another, the law of jealousy. 

First, God reiterates the law of the unclean, those with leprosy, issues which means blood issues, sores or boils, or other kinds of sickness that causes the body to release fluids, and those unclean having come in contact with the dead. That these people be put without the camp that their uncleanliness doesn't affect others. 

We have already read these things and the timing of the exile. Leprosy being contagious and generally incurable, the person would be permanently removed, although a ritual with the Levites and a method for determining they be clean if healed was laid out in **Leviticus 14:1-9** (covered [here](https://t.me/HouseOfWews2/9168) and [here](https://t.me/HouseOfWews2/11251))

Issues potentially carrying some kind of contagious disease, withdrawn until it has cleared or they are healed. We see a woman with blood issues her whole life healed by simply touching the hem of Jesus' cloak in **Luke 8:43-48**.

The law about being unclean by the touching of a carcase was given against the Levites with general instructions and is mentioned here, with mose specific rules given in **Numbers 19:11**;
*The one who touches the corpse of any person shall be unclean for seven days.*...With purification rituals attached. 

Physically they are instructions to keep diseases from spreading. To stop outbreaks of illness that could spread from person to person. Spiritually, all are a picture of sin, and the exile similar to church discipline, the removal of leaven that can spoil a whole lump. 

It also pictures the removal of our own sin in our lives, that can grow and metastasize until we are castaway in our backslidden state. Useless to the Lord. 

You can also see how it pictures separation from the world, keeping the unclean from that which is holy, the temple of God within us, where the holy Spirit dwells; that *shall ye put out, without the camp shall ye put them; that they defile not their camps, in the midst whereof I dwell.*

We should be mindful of these applications, understanding that the physical revelation of the Old Testament carries with them the spiritual applications for our lives as Christians today.

I'm am always struck by the very nature of creation and the things we experience and witness, all serve as a parable to bring us understanding of the spiritual things of God. 

Even death and disease serve as a method for God to teach His people about the nature of sin, or the need for cleansing in Christ. The world is the way it is for our benefit. God is revealed from Heaven that we may better understand Him. That it is all to His purpose. Amen

Next is the law of recompense for trespasses against another. That when a man or woman commit any sin (which is transgression of the law), they trespass against the Lord, and if guilty, they must confess the trespass and pay the person it was against whatever it cost them in damages, plus 20% for their trouble. And if it could not be paid to the person, then paid to their kin. And without kin, brought to the priest and offered to the service of God that atonement may be made for them. 

Note the recompense is due God, and for every sin. God demands payment plus the fifth, which when you consider the sins of man in a given day, if all were to be covered, even a righteous and godly man could be bankrupt by the end of a few days. 

But the redemption is covered in Christ. God's recompense for our sin paid for by the blood of Jesus, a propitiation for our sin, atonement given that we may be justified in that reckoning. 

The concept of the ledger and the debt incurred by sin is given that we may know we can never do enough to offset it. Our only hope is in Christ.

**Numbers 5:9-10** touches on that which a man reserves for the priests, a holy gift given independently of a sin or trespass offering. For the holy service of God. Also called 'corban.'

Given the context here, I think it was an understanding that the offered thing, money or wealth, or animal, which would be given the Levites at an appointed time or in death or when an animal reached age to be sacrificed, was set aside and belonged to the priest and not to be used as recompense. **Exodus 34:13-14**
*But ye shall destroy their altars, break their images, and cut down their groves: For thou shalt worship no other god: for the Lord, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God*...

The law of jealousy, outlined here in chapter 5 of Numbers, refers to the Biblical meaning of holding that which is yours as precious and sacred. Loving that which is yours. 

A name of God is Jealous, and in and of itself it is good and holy. And the infidelity of the Israelites with false gods and idols demonstrated that they did not regard God's jealousy, and instead held it in contempt.

It is not the same as envy, which our modern vernacular has added to the word, and the negative connotations that come with it, which is covetousness. It also is not the obsessive overprotection of something that isn't rightly yours, like some use it. 

But it is a godly emotion, which all of us can have. And like wrath and love itself, it is a good thing when appropriate, but that can be made toxic and lead us to sin because we are flesh. 

 And so, in seeking to give man the perfect law, God instituted a way for a husband who may be jealous for his wife, to determine if that were warranted, and for women dealing with an obsessive husband to have protection. 

God says that if a woman has a secret affair and is defiled by adultery, and the husband doesn't have any actual proof, but suspicion, he is to take her to the priest with an offering of plain barley. The priest will then prepare water set aside for the altar and dust of the ground of the Tabernacle, and mix it. Then he shall shave the woman's head, give her the barley to hold, with the water in his hand, have her swear an oath that she has been faithful. 

But if she lies and is guilty the water will be bitter, causing her thighs to rot and her belly to swell. And the woman was to say amen, amen to this and drink. 

The curse written down and blotted out with the water. It was left for God to judge. The priest offered the offering upon the altat. And the water was left to either curse or clear. 

Verse 28 indicates to me that the lying unfaithful woman may have been left barren by the experience, as the cleared wife "shall conceive seed." 

So we can see that by having an outlet for this gave both spouses a form of protection and an incentive to be both chaste in their dealings, never leading their husbands to jealousy, even falsely as a manipulation, and to keep husbands from inordinately accusing their wives. 

The wife's head was shorn and uncovered regardless of the outcome. The shame of it would be for both to bear. The woman would become a curse and a warning to others. The man, a cuckold, or potentially one, bringing him shame as well. 

Thus the perfect law of God always sought to discourage wrong doing, even as it punished those that did transgress the law.

**Numbers 6** gives the vow of the Nazarite, the law of the vow and the consecration into service unto the Lord. 

Not to be confused with Nazarene, someone from Nazareth as Christ Jesus was, the Nazarite was someone, male or female, who took a vow for a time to dedicate themselves to special service for the Lord. The rules laid out are simple, no wine or fermented wine, "strong drink," nor vinegar or wine vinegar, or grape or seed or skin. Nothing from the vine. (This is the clearest indication in scripture that "wine" means unfermented juice, as the distinction with wine vs strong drink or liquors indicates)

They were not to take a razor to their hair, but let it grow out during the period of service. 

They had to avoid being unclean, especially the uncleanliness of being near or touching the dead. 

We get very little in scripture by way of the why someone would take the vow, the specific time it would last, if any, or the details of that service. 

What we do know from the special cases of Samson, Samuel and John the Baptist, who were dedicated at infancy to this vow that the separation was made to be in great service to the people and to God. 

Were the lifelong Nazarites long-haired or just simply not shorn with a razor? Did Sampson have to offer numerous sacrifices for the dead he had slain? Why was his gift great strength when Samuel and John were not? While they showed great fear of God and meekness, Samson was bold and given to women and wrath. I don't know.

Vows were made for various purposes and reasons, just as the Nazarites. People vowed special offerings, gifts to the priests of money and items, fasting was often accomplished by vow. And vows to God should always be taken seriously and not haphazardly. 

**Ecclesiastes 5:4-6**
*When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.*

**Numbers 30:2**
*If a man vow a vow unto the LORD, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth.*

Even in the New Testament, there were some who swore vows, and the expectations of the grave nature of it was the same. 

We see in **Acts 5** the vow made by Ananias and his wife to offer the price of a sold property to the church at Jerusalem, only to withhold a portion for themselves. 

*But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession, And kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles' feet. But Peter said, Ananias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep back part of the price of the land? And Ananias hearing these words fell down, and gave up the ghost: and great fear came on all them that heard these things. And the young men arose, wound him up, and carried him out, and buried him.*

The Bible says 3 hours later, Sapphira was confronted with the same dereliction of their vow, and suffered the same fate as her husband. 

The Bible shows Paul taking various vows, as in **Acts 18:18** which appears to be Nazarite;
 
*And Paul after this tarried there yet a good while, and then took his leave of the brethren, and sailed thence into Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila; having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow.*

And Paul takes a vow in **Acts 21** at the behest of James, the brother of Jesus, that results in his arrest at Jerusalem. 

As we see throughout Acts and the early epistles, Paul sought to bridge the gap between the believing Jews and Gentiles, with the Gospel of grace, because of his love for his brothers after the flesh, and his disentanglement from the practices of the Jews came over time, mainly through his opposition to Judaizers.

But should we as New Testament Christians take vows?

We are already called to live consecrated lives in service of the Lord. Separated unto the Gospel. And as such, are supposed to be dedicated to the purposes of God without vow, but as His. 

And in doing so, we see that the more important thing is that our testimony be without question or ill repute. Blameless. Honest in our dealings that when we say to someone the reason for our hope, we are a good witness for the Gospel that they might be saved.

We are in **Numbers 9**, and we see this the 3rd Passover, held in the wilderness and the Lord tells Moses not to forget the ordinance that He has established, using the Passover in Egypt and the physical salvation of Israel as a picture of Christ and the individual salvation of man. I've done larger studies on the parallels and processes [before](https://t.me/HouseOfWews2/9752). But it is always good to note that it was a reminder of Christ to come, just as the Lord's supper is a reminder of Christ for us now. 

Here, God provides Moses with a few guidelines given circumstance. That the ceremonially unclean and those sojourning participate in Passover just the same, that strangers among them that wish to are invited, and those that don't participate are cut off and bear their own sin. 

The parallels are pretty clear as to how this corresponds to individual salvation in Jesus. Anyone. Even the unclean. Even those afar off from God, get to participate in the sacrifice and the blood. Even the stranger among them. The sinner, the worldly, the Gentile...all are invited to take part in the salvation by the blood, in the faith of Jesus Christ. 

And those who don't are cut off and made to pay for their sin. 

It is that simple. People try to overcomplicate salvation because they want to make it about themselves or to make it a sensual experience that they can "feel," or see. Because they lack faith, which is the evidence of things unseen. 

And then we are called to follow Him. 

Just as the movement of the Tabernacle and the camps was dictated by the movement of God upon them, the pillars of smoke and fire. At the commandment of the Lord they moved. At His command they rested. 

And so it is to be in our lives, that after salvation we follow the Lord.

It is right and good to follow the Lord, moving to His commandments. And accepting His will for our lives. 

But again, people conflate or confuse the order of things. The salvation out of sin of Egypt had already taken place, with the shedding of blood of the Passover lamb. The baptism of the waters of the sea followed. The understanding of the law given. The sanctification of the people. The continuous atonement with burnt offerings and blood of the sacrifices. The command to follow where God takes us after that. Being led into the promised land. 

The order of things is given that there can be no misunderstanding. God is not the author of confusion. People want to add and mix things based on their own ideas, not the word of God.

With **Numbers 11**, we enter into the more narrative-driven portion of the book. Less difficult to get through, no less full of doctrine. 

Here we see the children of Israel as they are typically shown throughout the exodus and wandering in the wilderness, complaining and in disfavor of the Lord. 

They and the mixed multitudes among them, begin to lust. To put their carnal desires above their love of God. To look back to Egypt as better than their miraculous salvation. To miss the life they had and the things of the world they fared on, and resenting the heavenly bread which God provided. 

The like picture of our salvation today, the longing for the old ways of our sinful lives. Nostalgia for the wickedness of the world and the various temptations available in it. 

The separation and sanctified life of the Christian can often feel like this. Working, reading scripture, praying, church...a routine that sees little variance, and if we aren't careful, can become stale and boring. 

When I first read through Exodus and Numbers, as a younger babe in Christ, I would be angry at the Israelites and look down on them, saying "no wonder God is so angry with them. He's providing them food from heaven and they still complain!" Now, as a more mature Christian, I feel more sympathetic, and see how my own walk with God has likely angered Him, as I have gone after lusts of the world. It has strengthened my walk to see myself in them, and made me more understanding for those struggling. 

Give us this day our daily bread...live by every word of God. Be hungry for the manna. Don't be distracted from the word with the temptations of the worldly. Appreciate that God has inspired and preserved His word for all generations. The privilege we have to study it day and night. 

And that we are called to prophesy, preaching His word to every creature. That the Spirit is upon our hearts. It isn't just manna to feed us, but to feed others.

In that spirit, we can appreciate God's chastisement of the Hebrews, giving them the meat they crave, in abundance. 

*Ye shall not eat one day, nor two days, nor five days, neither ten days, nor twenty days; But even a whole month, until it come out at your nostrils, and it be loathsome unto you: because that ye have despised the Lord which is among you, and have wept before him, saying, Why came we forth out of Egypt?*

If you have experienced this, where you backslide and fall away from walking in the spirit, longing for the old life you left behind when you were born again, and starve the new man to feed the old, you've witnessed this same thing. 

Phonecalls or texts from an old drinking buddy. A woman at work suddenly seems interested in you. The gang from high school wants to get together. The dealer you used to score from you run into unexpectedly. It is more than a test. It's often a lesson of excess in the thing you were lusting after, and you find if you should stumble back into sin, that it doesn't hold the same appeal. That you can't enjoy it. Even if you run greedily after whatever it is you missed about spiritual Egypt, your time in bondage, in short order you'll see it as repulsive and gross. You will have it coming out of your nostrils. 

Some prefer that misery. Even eating the metaphorical quail long after it has spoiled and sickened them. But for many Christians it is a wakeup call and a reminder of how good we have it walking with the Lord. 

*For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.*

Thank God for His love and correction.

If they still have the kingdom because "All Israel shall be saved" then why would they care if Gentiles were grafted in, to the point where they persecuted and murdered people in multiple countries across half a continent? 

Why are the Jews the villain?

So, we are here in **Numbers** chapter 12, and we have a story of the brother and sister of Moses, Aaron and Miriam, and their sedition against Moses because of his marriage to an outlandish woman, an Ethiopian. 

Claiming they were on par with Moses, having had the Spirit of the Lord upon them and having then preached His word through them, they presumed to speak with authority over the appointed man of God. 

Moses in his meekness didn't speak against them, but the Lord in His anger did, saying that His inspiration to prophecy given men in visions and dreams wasn't the same thing as His relationship with Moses which was direct and personal, speaking mouth to mouth. Not in "dark speeches," or dark sayings as parables and metaphors used to teach doctrine are called in the New Testament. But directly. Frankly. In person. God asks why they are not afraid to speak out against Moses given that obvious position of favor and authority that had been granted him. 

And His wrath was kindled, and Miriam became leprous, skin as white as snow. Aaron seeing this begged for forgiveness to Moses, who then intercedes on Miriam's behalf. But the Lord, to show Miriam and others who might rise in sedition a lesson, has her put without the camp for 7 days of shame. 

This chapter has been used to justify or argue something about mixed marriages with other nations, races, kindred, religion...to justify miscegenation, and to condemn those who oppose taking a stranger as a spouse. The "Ethiopian wife" and the "white as snow" punishment of Miriam, has added to this debate. 

But it's not what the chapter is about. 

It is literally about sedition and setting yourself up as better than or worthier than the man of God that He has placed over you in His hierarchy. 

That even if you disagree with their own life choices and resent them for whatever reason, you still must respect God's choice, giving honor to those who should be honored. Tribute to those due tribute. 

**1 Samuel 15:23**
*For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king.*

The reason behind their rebellion is incidental. They used a flaw in Moses to seek to undermine him. That's the essence of the story. If that's who God puts in place of power, given the spirit of leadership over the people, then that's who God chose. Render honor to them, and fear the Lord. 


It doesn't change the fact that there are several prohibitions and warnings against taking outlandish women as wives. That taking a stranger for a wife leads to children who fall away from the faith of their fathers and chase idols. It is a punishment on a nation to be bred out of existence, and it begins by the acceptance of mixed marriage. It was especially true in the idea that Israel was a means of getting from Abraham to David to Christ Jesus. And it remains true in a spiritual sense today, and being unequally yoked, and the judgment against nations being ethnically erased still exists, and will unto the day of redemption. 

God sets the boundaries and habitations thereof. The nations will rejoice in that day. And we will be one people in the resurrection. Until then, it isn't prudent to be accepting culturally of miscegenation.

We have to be very careful in letting the Bible tell us what's being discussed, to understand the context and not wrestle something else out of it. And it angers a lot of people who have settled into one side or another on a secondary or tertiary doctrine, and seek justification from scripture for it, to make dogmatic statements. 

I have noticed that so many of these dogmas, and the binaries that form from them, are carnal and incidental to the larger point being made. And so people miss the forest for the trees. 

When I have applied this form of exegesis to pet theories in scripture, even when I agree with the theory in whole or in part, people get angry. "Both sides" foam at the mouth over this. Labels of heresy and compromise abound. But in my view the Bible is very clear on doctrine and things that have to be forced out of the text aren't worthy of being dogmatic. Simple as. 

The Bible is not for our eisegesis to win fights online. Especially about carnal things. It is for the winning of souls.
