**Numbers 13** presents the turning point in the children of Israel under Moses. They had been camped at Mt Sinai, Horeb in the south of the Arabian Peninsula for over a year. There God had communed with Moses, the Law given, the Tabernacle built. The camps made, and their order given. The sanctification of the people performed. 

So now was their time to enter into the promised land. 

We read in the account in Numbers that God authorized the sending of 12 spies, one of each tribe, into the land to report back what the Israelites would be encountering there. But we see in **Deuteronomy 1** that the initial idea to send someone wasn't God's, but the people's. 

Though God promised them He would scatter and destroy the inhabitants before them, and promised that the land was full of richness, a land of milk and honey. And God said to Moses go in to possess it, yet the people said "We will send men before us and bring us word." 

Moses agreed and God allowed it and told Moses the makeup of the spies, authorizing them to go into Canaan. 

The Bible tells us that among the 12 men chosen were Oshea the son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, who is also known as Joshua, a key figure, as well as bold Caleb, son of Jephunneth of the tribe of Judah. 

Moses instructs them to simply go and report back; of the people there be few or many, strong or weak, walled cities or tents. And the nature of the land, if it be fat or lean. And to return with examples of the fruit of the land, as it was Spring and the first fruits of the vine would be ripe. 

And so the men spied out the land and returned after 40 days with the famous grapes of Eshcol, a cluster so large two men had to carry it. 

Reporting to Moses and Aaron and the assembly of the people, they confirm what God had promised, a land flowing with milk and honey. 

Then the men reported of the people who dwelt in the land and it dismayed the children of Israel. 

*Nevertheless the people be strong that dwell in the land, and the cities are walled, and very great: and moreover we saw the children of Anak there. The Amalekites dwell in the land of the south: and the Hittites, and the Jebusites, and the Amorites, dwell in the mountains: and the Canaanites dwell by the sea, and by the coast of Jordan*.

Caleb, apparently seeing the fear come on the people immediately tried to calm them down before Moses, saying Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it. 

Caleb showed faith in God's promise. 

But the other men answered in doubt and fear. 

*We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we. And they brought up an evil report of the land which they had searched unto the children of Israel, saying, The land, through which we have gone to search it, is a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof; and all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature. And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.*

Their fear spread to all the people, and the faith in the God who had led them from Egypt and promised to deliver them, faded. And God's anger was kindled. 

*Yet in this thing ye did not believe the Lord your God...And the Lord heard the voice of your words, and was wroth, and sware, saying, Surely there shall not one of these men of this evil generation see that good land, which I sware to give unto your fathers.*

The exceptions to this curse were Caleb and Joshua. The lack of faith and questioning the word of God led to having the Israelites shut out for a generation. Left to wander 40 years in the wilderness.

There are lessons in these stories that are for our benefit as  Christians. Here we see how doubt can lead to disputations, and even when assurances of the bold in faith come, many people cling to fear and would rather believe a bad report than trust in the Lord and His word. For this cause, many who seek salvation turn away. 

Probably the biggest stumbling block people get caught on is the idea of eternal security. That once we are saved, we are always saved. That our faith in Christ is unto redemption. Not only that He exists. Not only that He is the Son of God. Not only that He lived, died for us and was raised again from the dead, but that the earnest of our redemption is given us, the Spirit that indwells and quickens us, sealing us, and that in no way shall we be cast out. That we may know we have eternal life. 

*And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father's hand. I and my Father are one.*

This is the promise made by Jesus. That we are given the Kingdom of Heaven by faith in Him. The promised land. 

Speaking in the spirit of Caleb, Paul boldly testifies;

*For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.*

Yet, those seeking the truth may need our testimony. They may need us to spy out the land and confirm to them from scripture exactly what God said that they may believe. To boldly proclaim His Gospel. 

But there will be many, including those who claim to be of God, who give a bad report. Who tell people that their problems are insurmountable. That their sins are like giants and they are as grasshoppers. That to enter the promised land would be death. 

And so fear and doubt spread and keep people from accepting the truth. From trusting in the Lord to deliver them. 

This is the spirit of fear and doubt that uses the lie that eternal security doesn't exist. That you can lose your salvation. That because you are small and weak, you won't make it. You won't "persevere to the end." That you must "Repent-of-your-sins!" That if you fail to produce "fruit" by the judgment of men that you cannot make it to Heaven. 

But we see here, God was providing the fruit, in a size and abundance that they could not even imagine. Joshua and Caleb showed them the fruit that comes from trusting in the Lord. 

And yet they saw their fears as bigger than their God.

We should be reminded by these Old Testament stories that God was going to deliver all of the children of Israel to the promised land, that He would do all the work. Going out before them. They merely had to trust in Him and He would do the rest. The picture of individual salvation is the same. 

Never let others tell you you need to do works of your own to be saved, that it isn't a free gift paid for by Jesus, that grace isn't grace. Never make your sins or tribulations and problems to be a cause not to trust God. Never let your shame or fear keep you from turning towards Him. 

When you do, you will see your faith grow. You will witness miracles. You will be led of God to places you can't imagine, and be given the opportunity to do great things for the Lord. To harvest fruit more abundantly. To have your faith quiet other people's fears. To counter those who give a bad report with the peace that passes all understanding. Be bold in Christ.

The budding of Aaron's rod, a dead branch, brought to life, as an image of the chosen High Priest of the people is a clear and obvious picture of Christ Jesus. A rod out of the stem of Jesse, a Branch that grew out of his roots. Who was dead and was risen, and, like the almonds that Aaron's rod brought forth, Jesus gave forth fruit for all time, those that believe on His holy name. 

Aaron's rod is added to the Ark with the manna and the tablets, in the Tabernacle of testimony. They literally were carrying God's word made manifest, in the heart of their camp. The testimony that His word was true.

The law of the water of separation is given by the Lord. That those that become unclean by contact with a dead person could be purified, and the things of the tent where in the person died, and their sin be covered, a purification ritual. 

The law requires a red heifer, without blemish, be brought without the camp and slain and burned. In the fire was required cedar, hyssop and scarlet. This is a holocaust, a burnt offering, that is an explicit picture of Christ. The cedar wood of the cross, the hyssop dipped in vinegar, the scarlet of His blood. 

The ash mixed with water to be used on the 3rd day for purification, that on the 7th day the unclean may be clean. The parallel with Jesus 3 days and nights, and our redemption at his eventual return.

Whatever prophecy this ritual foresaw was filled in Christ. The burnt offering for our sin, and the water of life given us to purify ourselves.

**Exodus 17:6** 
*Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it, that the people may drink. And Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.*

**Numbers 20** begins like most stories about the children of Israel, complaining and carrying on with a lack of faith or fear of the Lord. 

They have witnessed triumphant miracles, seen the hand of the Lord strike down their enemies by the sea they passed through. Been guided through the desert by a pillar of flame. Had their bellies filled with bread made from manna of heaven. And have had water come from out from a rock to drink. 

They have seen punishment of the Lord, His wrath revealed from Heaven, taking out thousands of their people. By fire. Plague. Venom. The earth swallowing up those that rebelled against the Lord. 

His mercy and His wrath, the same revelations which Paul writes about in Romans, that no man has an excuse to not know and fear the Lord. 

And yet they complain. 

And so here, having been condemned for a generation to wander the wilderness for their unbelief in the promise of God to deliver them into the promised land, and fresh off of the rebellion that had the Lord had slain so many by plague, they once again complained to Moses. "Wherefore have ye made us to come up out of Egypt?" Lacking faith that God would provide.

Moses and Aaron go to the Lord in prayer with their problem. The correct thing to do, of course. 

*And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, Take the rod, and gather thou the assembly together, thou, and Aaron thy brother, and speak ye unto the rock before their eyes; and it shall give forth his water, and thou shalt bring forth to them water out of the rock: so thou shalt give the congregation and their beasts drink.*

Similar to the event that happened earlier in Exodus, the people murmering in complaint, and God had Moses strike the rock and brought forth water. So the people knew it was possible and Moses knew to follow the word of the Lord. And yet, in his anger or frustration, Moses disobeyed the word of God, and instead of speaking to the rock, he struck it with his rod. Not once, as at *Meribah* in Exodus, but twice. 

Speaking to the rock is a picture of calling upon Christ for salvation; *If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.* God wishes to be sanctified by the people from this miracle. (Not that He needs man to make him holy, in this use it means to acknowledge that He is holy.)

And because Moses disobeyed His word, God keeps Him and Aaron from ever stepping foot in the land He had promised them. 

But the water came forth and the people and their cattle drank, and they sanctified the Lord anyway, despite that great cost.

Now the people wandering came to the boundaries of Edom, their brothers after the flesh, and not wishing to battle, Moses sent word that they would pass along the king's highway, and not take of the fields of vineyards. Only asking for safe passage through in the name of the God their mutual fathers knew. 

And the Edomites denied them passage, and threatened to come put them to the sword. 

And again, Moses entreated them to allow them passage, even offering to pay for any incidental water their cattle may drink. And again Edom said no, coming down to war against the Israelites. A contentious relationship that would ultimately see Edom destroyed and her people scattered, as they'd no longer followed the Lord. 

And so to avoid war, Moses turned his people back into the wilderness.

You can see comparing this story to the incident in **Exodus 17**, where Moses sent Joshua against the Amalek shortly after bringing forth the water from the rock, and they were victorious against their oppressors. 

Obedience to the word of God, and they received the water and later victory against their enemies by the power of the Lord. 

And here, in disobedience, slinking away in fear. 

In the Christian life, we may go through phases like this. Where despite being delivered for so much early in our salvation, and despite seeing the blessings that come from obeying God, we may backslide. Become disillusioned. No longer listen to what His says, and do our own thing. Striking the rock, twice even. And when it comes time for battles against the world, turning in fear, unsure without faith. 

It can be difficult to get back on track. To turn to God in humility and ask forgiveness. But if we do, He is merciful to forgive and forget. He wants to do things for His children that we may sanctify His holy name.

Finally, we are told of the death of Aaron and the Lord passing the mantle of High Priest to his son, Eleazar.

Moses' sister Miriam passes earlier in the chapter, but to little notice. Aaron however is given 30 days of honor in mourning by all Israel. Worth noticing.

Chapter 27 of **Numbers** covers two cases of inheritance, one by the law and one by election. 

When the daughters of Zelophehad come to ask that their father's portion fall on them, as he had no sons, Moses seeks the council of the Lord. 

The establishment of the law of inheritance, the idea that each family have its place, and the generational wealth of the land God gave them to possess being passed down by the law, is set as a statute of judgement, a precedent set by the Lord. 

Of course this idea always was, that the eldest inherits by law. But, as we see played out with Ishmael and Isaac, Esau and Jacob, even with Israel and Joseph, giving the second youngest of 12 the double portion usually reserved  for the eldest, that some are elect, or chosen, to receive that inheritance over the one legally entitled to it. 

We see that as Moses is commanded by God to climb one last mountain, Abarim, to see the promised land, his thoughts are with who shall inherit his role as leader of the people. And it doesn't fall on his own sons, Gershom and Eliezer, who by law it could be expected, but to Joshua, the son of Nun. God chooses to elect Joshua in place of the children after the law.

The idea that there is a legal inheritance, for earthly matters and yet an inheritance and blessing of election for spiritual things of God, is found continuously in scripture, starting with Cain the elder, and Abel the younger. And it all pictures the adoption of the Gentiles in the seed of Abraham, who is Christ Jesus over Abraham's children after the flesh. The first children of God, circumcised of the flesh, rejected, reorobate, for the adoption of children of God, circumcised of the heart. 

The entire Bible teaches this. What is derisively called "replacement theology," is simply the understanding that the eldest may receive the inheritance of earthly things, but the Kingdom of Heaven is only inherited by faith. 

Just as the daughters of Manasseh were given the land promised their father in the absence of brothers by law, and Joshua was given leadership of the children of Israel by the election of faith.

Here in **Numbers 29** and **30**, we have the Lord again reestablishing commandments and ordinances of the law. We will have a second giving of the law when we go through the book of Deuteronomy as well. God repeats each thing as important, for the edification of the children of Israel, and to our own edifying as Christians in our life and as judges in the Millennium to come. 

The fall feasts, as we have covered elsewhere, signifying the second coming of Christ. The feast of trumpets, as in Revelation. 

The law of vows, especially concerning fathers and husbands, over their women, reflecting the order of hierarchy given by the Lord. It makes what is often done flippantly and in vain today, seem far more grave and serious. But as Jesus said, better to not vow at all. 

We are nearing the end of **Numbers**, God willing by the end of this week. These recaps are necessary as constant reminders that the Israelites were not left to rely on tradition, but on the word of God given them. The books of Moses kept to be read by the priests and the sacrifices made continually that they may not forget what they are a picture of.

Another straight narrative in **Numbers 31**, a telling of the slaughter of the Midianites, who had tried to curse the Israelites through Balaam, and who had managed through whoredoms to bring many to worship Baal. We see the deaths of their kings and of Balaam, their priest. The spoil taken, which included male children and adult women, whom Moses insists be put to the sword, least they lead men astray again and another plague is sent by God in judgment. 

The spoils then left are divided up, each man of war his own, and the people their own, and to the Levites a share, and to God, His. Further the men of war offer of their own share a portion to honor God, as a memorial.

We see that the law of the unclean being purified by the manner laid out in **Numbers 19** is applied here. Each man who had slain or touched a body, their captives and the spoil, all things that could not be purified by fire were taken without the camp for 7 days, with the washings done on the 3rd day. 

When you consider all the pestilence that had been brought against them in the wilderness, adherence to this practice makes sense, pleasing God and also isolating any contaminated person or item. 

The things that could be purified by fire were passed through the fire. Gold and silver and other metals. It reminds me of 1 Corinthians 3:12-15;

Here in **Numbers 32**, we find the tribes of Ruben, Gad and Manasseh, entreating Moses that they be allowed to set their tribes homelands east of the Jordan, rather than cross over into Canaan. 

They had much cattle, especially after the spoil of the nations God had driven out before them, and those He had them put down by the edge of the sword. This land was good for cattle, they argued. A familiar theme of those choosing the easier path in this world;

Settling for the land, east of the Jordan because of having much cattle and the land being good for the herds, ended poorly for just Lot.

For the sons of Ruben, the first born who was denied his inheritance by law, and told his people should not excel, perhaps the idea of the bird in the hand appealed to them more than their lesser status and inheritance would be in the promised land. 

Gad as well, of Jacob and his first wife Zipporah, were not favored among the tribes, but were warriors. They sought the frontier surrounded by enemies of Israel. 

Manasseh, also the eldest of Joseph, like Ruben to Israel. Like Edom to Jacob, who was destined to be great, but Ephraim the younger was the elect, given the greater blessing. 

These tribes sought to receive what they felt was good enough, rather than seek that which the Lord had allotted them. 

And Moses, afraid of a repeat of the 12 spies and the sowing of fear among the people by their bad report, which cursed the children of Israel with 40yr wandering in the wilderness, tells them no, least their not crossing over brings a similar fear to the people, and kindles God's wrath.

In **Numbers 35**, God gives the law of sanctuary cities and the judgments against murderers and the allowance for cases of manslaughter. Read through it and you really can appreciate how perfect God's law is. 

With the granting of the land to the tribes of Israel, given by lot, the Levites who have no inheritance are to be given land within the tribes, cites and suburbs for living among them. To minister and serve. 

And on top of that, given cities to serve as refuge for those that accidentally slay a man, that someone seeking revenge not slay them in return. 

All to minimize the blood shed in the land, which cannot be cleansed. Multiple times in **Numbers**, the laws for cleansing those who were exposed to death or bloodshed. But the land itself cries out over bloodshed, as we saw in the murder of Abel;

**Genesis 4:8-10**
*And Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him. And the Lord said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?*

*And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.*

It was this curse of Canaan, made by Noah when Ham had uncovered his father's nakedness, and so by the time of **Exodus**, the Canaanites land was polluted by the blood shed and offerings to idols. God's judgment upon them that they be dispossessed and slain to give the land to Israel. 

But it was polluted again, even by the wickedness of the Israelites who turned to whoredoms and killed their own children to idols as the people there before them;

**Psalm 106:37-40**
*Yea, they sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto devils, And shed innocent blood, Even the blood of their sons and of their daughters, Whom they sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan: And the land was polluted with blood. Thus were they defiled with their own works, And went a whoring with their own inventions. Therefore was the wrath of the LORD kindled against his people, Insomuch that he abhorred his own inheritance.*

And so the idea of having a city of refuge, where the innocent of murder could flee and live, so long as they were found to have done it by accident, until the death of the high priest. 

That the revenger catching them outside the city was innocent of the blood. And that the murderer be put down upon the testimony of witnesses, their own blood being upon them. It's an elegant system that prevents the people from falling into tribal warfare, especially given the Levitical priests being among all the tribes.

*And the chief fathers of the families of the children of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, of the families of the sons of Joseph, came near, and spake before Moses, and before the princes, the chief fathers of the children of Israel:*

*2 And they said, The Lord commanded my lord to give the land for an inheritance by lot to the children of Israel: and my lord was commanded by the Lord to give the inheritance of Zelophehad our brother unto his daughters.*

*3 And if they be married to any of the sons of the other tribes of the children of Israel, then shall their inheritance be taken from the inheritance of our fathers, and shall be put to the inheritance of the tribe whereunto they are received: so shall it be taken from the lot of our inheritance.*

*4 And when the jubile of the children of Israel shall be, then shall their inheritance be put unto the inheritance of the tribe whereunto they are received: so shall their inheritance be taken away from the inheritance of the tribe of our fathers.*

*5 And Moses commanded the children of Israel according to the word of the Lord, saying, The tribe of the sons of Joseph hath said well.*

*6 This is the thing which the Lord doth command concerning the daughters of Zelophehad, saying, Let them marry to whom they think best; only to the family of the tribe of their father shall they marry.*

*7 So shall not the inheritance of the children of Israel remove from tribe to tribe: for every one of the children of Israel shall keep himself to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers.*

*8 And every daughter, that possesseth an inheritance in any tribe of the children of Israel, shall be wife unto one of the family of the tribe of her father, that the children of Israel may enjoy every man the inheritance of his fathers.*

*9 Neither shall the inheritance remove from one tribe to another tribe; but every one of the tribes of the children of Israel shall keep himself to his own inheritance.*

*10 Even as the Lord commanded Moses, so did the daughters of Zelophehad:*

*11 For Mahlah, Tirzah, and Hoglah, and Milcah, and Noah, the daughters of Zelophehad, were married unto their fathers brothers' sons:*

*12 And they were married into the families of the sons of Manasseh the son of Joseph, and their inheritance remained in the tribe of the family of their father.*

*13 These are the commandments and the judgments, which the Lord commanded by the hand of Moses unto the children of Israel in the plains of Moab by Jordan near Jericho.*

The final chapter of **Numbers**, and one last bit of housekeeping for Moses and the law, revisiting the command of God that land inheritance in a family that has no sons should go to the daughters. The worry being that their daughters marry of another tribe and this dilutes the inheritance when those sons take possession of the land. Moses gives the command of the Lord that the inheritance remains in the tribe, so as the daughter must marry those of her father's family. 

Recall that at jubilee, there is a right of return, that any land sold or let to outsiders is returned to the family that had owned it, keeping the boundaries and habitations thereof as given by God. Now daughters could marry outside the tribe, but not carry with them rights to property inherited. The Lord had need that the tribes remain separated as much as possible, leading to the birth of Christ.

And with that commandment, we come to the end of the study of **Numbers**. Difficult in some places, wonderful picture of Jesus in others, and wisdom and doctrine throughout, well worth the effort.

Here in **Deuteronomy 2**, Moses continues his retelling of the time in the wilderness, the 40 years recounted in part in the **Book of Numbers**. There are some perspective changes and details added that broaden the underlying history, and containing details that flesh out the story. 

A few things that stand out to me in this reading; the promises of land to Lot and Edom, and the nature of the giants that were in many of these lands. 

Modern "Jews" and their Zionist pets will make quite a big deal about the conditional covenant made in the wilderness to deliver the land to Israel, which had been promised to Abraham and his seed, which is Christ. But the promises to Lot and Easau were to the nations they spawned, by the blessings of God, and yet those nations were destroyed in time, and the land taken as spoil, after the wickedness of the people. The same as Israel. The same as the remnant in Judah. God judges nations on this earth and their bounds and habitations are His to give and take away.

As for the giants, the men who were of such stature they frightened the spies sent to scout the promised land, whose reports caused fear and doubt among the children of Israel, leading to the banishment of that generation of men, precipitating the 40 years of wandering, we learn that there were such giants in the other lands, too.

**Deuteronomy 16** opens with a recitation of the Three Pilgrimage Festivals, the ordinances set forth by God in the wilderness. 

*Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God in the place which he shall choose*

The first Passover and the feast of unleavened bread, then the Feast of Weeks, known as Pentecost, and finally the fall feast of the Tabernacle. While there are details as to their keeping of the feasts, the primary reason for their retelling here, as in previous chapters regarding the sacrifices and such, were to let the Israelites know that they were to go to the place He would designate. The place the Lord would put His name. 

These feasts being a picture of Jesus, and the mandate to return to the place God elected to set up His Tabernacle or Temple, set up events in the Gospels. There was a purpose to Jesus of Nazareth returning to Jerusalem for Passover, and the Jews gathered there, just as on Pentecost there were Jews from all over the world returned to mark the feast. Just as at the return of Christ, there will be a gathering of His children.

*And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast, thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy manservant, and thy maidservant, and the Levite, the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, that are within thy gates.*

*Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the Lord thy God which he hath given thee.*

What a concisely phrased explanation of the Christian life, and God's expectations for us. He blessed us, His children. He asks in return that we give to Him as we are able, according to those blessings. 

The giving isn't required for the blessing. But the blessing asks for the giving. And we know that there are two main ways the Lord asks us to give unto Him; winning souls and right judgment. 

What a day when we are bringing in the sheaves! When the fullness of man has come in, and to the Lord is given the increase. 

As the parables of the sower, the wise servant, and others told by Jesus, picturing the Kingdom of God and the fruit that we are called to bring forth, after our kind. The winning of souls through the gospel. 

And in judgement, knowing; *Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted.*

It's no coincidence that the reminder of keeping the feasts, bringing the gifts, remembering the blessings given by the Lord to us, is followed immediately by;

*Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the Lord thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment.*

That we are to be unspotted, blameless in our judgement. Not being a respecter of persons. Not showing favor to one over another, but executing right judgment. Not taking bribes, which would pervert out judgment. That we be just in our ways that we may live. 

The two things we are separated unto God's ministry in the Gospel to do, linked forever in the feasts that are Christ's.

*Thou shalt not plant thee a grove of any trees near unto the altar of the Lord thy God, which thou shalt make thee. Neither shalt thou set thee up any image; which the Lord thy God hateth.*

This warning again, as was so frequently given in previous chapters, against the planting of groves for worship around the altar that will be set up, is to avoid it falling away over time to the practices of the heathen. The pagan Canaanites driven from the land. It doesn't bring blessings. It doesn't bring gratitude and gifts of the calling. It doesn't bring right judgment. It brings wickedness of the reprobate mind. 

God could not be clearer; Do not set up an image to bow and serve. God HATES idols. The Lord hates the setting up of an image for worship. 

Note he doesn't say "of false gods." There are no caveats given. Yes, His concern is that over time they will be worshipped in the flesh rather than kept in the Spirit. But He is firm that He hates them entirely. 

Catholics and Orthodox who have set up idols, graven images and icons, God hates them. 

God hates them. 

This can't be ignored or rationalized away. It isn't "different when we do it." God doesn't make an allowance for your sincerity or your zeal. He doesn't care about your intentions, or the fig leaf of "veneration." God hates your images. 

And the worship of those graven images, regardless of who you believe they portray, brings harsh judgement upon the people who kneel before them in prayer. Who light candles and incense to them. Who hold vigils and pray in vain repetitions before them. 

*Neither shalt thou set thee up any image; which the Lord thy God hateth.*

He shall not multiply horses to himself, meaning not breed horses that he would eventually use for chariots of war. Verse 1-9 of **Deuteronomy 23** provides instruction on those who are not to be allowed to meet with the men of Israel gathered for war or governance. It is the assembly as seen in Numbers and again later in Judges, the representatives of the tribes that are gathered to fight for Israel or to judge matters therein. 

It is often confused with the assembly *for* the Lord, whereby they meet for the Sabbath or the whole host of Israel, as in Leviticus. 

The castrated, eunuch, bastards because their father could be a Moabite or Ammonite, for example, the strangers of those nations who marry into the tribes of Israel. God makes allowance for the Edomites as their brothers, and Egyptians, because as a stranger in their lands, many of the Hebrews had Egyptian lineage and of the mixed multitude that came out of Egypt with them. The Lord says by the 3rd generation they are indistinguishable from the other Hebrews.

There is a loyalty issue to this, and a preventative against corruption of the blood lines or usurpation of authority by a foreigner or someone with no children as a legacy.

Next is a clarification for the rules of uncleanliness, that if it occurs at night, you gotta go sleep outside the camp of people, until the purging and washing in the evening is done. 

Next is a provision that is topical; proper disposal of human waste. Even here in ancient times, the Lord tells them to carry a shovel to bury their feces, that no uncleanliness is found among them as He walks through the camp, being with them. Some pagan cultures still have not learned this lesson.

*Thou shalt not deliver unto his master the servant which is escaped from his master unto thee: He shall dwell with thee, even among you, in that place which he shall choose in one of thy gates, where it liketh him best: thou shalt not oppress him.*

This statute to defend those escaped from servitude seems straightforward but counterintuitive, but remember they were in bondage in Egypt, set free by the Lord. The same grace and mercy should be shown.

If they have repented, and asked to be forgiven, we are to treat them as if they'd never sinned. It's not on us to remind them or judge them on those things they've left behind. For we were once bondmen in Egypt.

The life of Moses, to whom the law was given, nears its end, and Joshua, a picture of Christ, is given power to lead the children of Israel into the promised land. 

Like John, a voice crying out in the wilderness, Moses cleared the way, making the paths straight for the one who would come to bring deliverance. 

The book of the law is written, and placed in the Ark that is in the heart of the camp. Done to bear witness of the sins and iniquity of the people. Like the law written in the hearts of man, a conscience, pricked of the Spirit to lay bare our transgressions. To let us know when we have gone astray. As a testimony of the Lord against them who were given the oracles of God. To remind them of their need for His salvation. 

An ordinance is given, that in the jubilee year, at the fall feast of Tabernacles, the feast of tents, the people shall gather and hear the reading of the Law. The story of God and His people. His Commandments and His love for them that believe on His name. How he rescued them from bondage and delivered on the promises He made. Every 7 years the people will be reminded. And so the Lord teaches Moses a new song. One to teach the children of Israel that they may know that God knows, they will break the covenant.

The people forsake the God who delivered them, and chase after other gods. God promises to forsake them in turn, for all the evils that they wrought. 

Moses, delivering this all to the people before the congregation, reiterates his own knowledge that they will turn aside. That they will utterly corrupt themselves. 

Once again, proving dispensationalism to be unbiblical heresy.

And so we are here in **Joshua** chapter 2, and the newly anointed leader of the Hebrews is about to lead the people over the Jordan and into the promised land. 

His first act is to send 2 spies to spy out the walled city of Jericho. This is similar to an earlier appearance of Joshua, in **Numbers 13**, where Moses sent 12 spies into the land, and 10 spies were bad and 2 were good.

Joshua and Caleb were the good men, who had faith in God to deliver the land to them. The 10 cast doubt and fear. 

Not wishing a repeat, apparently, Joshua sends only 2, and these men make their way into Jericho by way of the home of the harlot, Rahab. There she lodges them and hides the spies when the king of Jericho sends out men to find them. The harlot hides the men upon her roof and sends the kings men on a fruitless search back towards Jordan. 

She tells the Hebrew spies that she has done this because the whole land knows that the Lord God is with them, and are friegtened of them, considering the miracles of the Red Sea and the defeat of the other Canaanite kings. She has faith that the same Lord God will bring them victory in Jericho. The spies thank her, and she asks that they swear her family will be protected in their eventual siege of the city. The spies grant her an oath. That if she places the scarlet thread she had let them down on in her window, that all within her household will be saved. 

Her faith in God to deliver the Israelites, and her faith in the promise of the spies, will lead to her salvation, as we will see in a few chapters. And the same faith serves as a picture of Christ. The scarlet thread, like the blood on the door frames on the first Passover. The same scarlet thread of the blood of Christ that runs throughout the Bible. 

And Rahab is part of that bloodline of Christ Jesus, as we see during the genealogy of Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew;

**Matthew 1:5-6**
*And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse; And Jesse begat David the king; and David the king begat Solomon of her that had been the wife of Urias*

The Greek spelling of 'Rachab,' is Rahab. She birthed Boaz of Judah, who eventually begets David, in the human lineage of Christ. A scarlet thread. 

And she is saved by her faith, we know. Despite being a harlot. Despite her sinful life. She is redeemed, and honored with a mention in the Hall of Faith found in **Hebrews 11**, in the company of great Old Testament believers;

**Hebrews 11:31**
*By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace*.

She is also used by James, alongside Abraham, in his examples of those whose actions demonstrated to others the faith she had in her heart;

**James 2:25**
*Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way?*

Given as an example of faith by God, to show us that He may use anyone for His purpose, and redeem anyone who holds the faith.

Notice the spies, upon hearing her declaration of faith in the Lord, never told her to repent of harlotry. Never placed a condition of her being contrite and sorry for her sin before agreeing to save her from the sword. Just her trust in that scarlet thread, that by the word of God she and her family would be delivered. 

Repenters and other works-based false prophets would judge her in unrighteousness, despite her profession of faith. And while she clearly cleaned up her life, was married and produced godly children, as part of the human lineage of Jesus, it was her faith that saved her. Amen

Here in **Joshua 3**, we see Joshua commanding the priests and people, with God's word. The Lord tells him, *This day will I begin to magnify thee in the sight of Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee.* 

Now, prior to these events, Joshua was a man of renown among the children of Israel. Moses chose him to lead the fighting men of Israel for their first battle after the exodus from Egypt, against the Amalekites in Rephidim. Joshua went with Moses to the Mount where Moses received the 10 commandments from God, and was with him when they returned to the reveling of the golden calf. And of course Joshua was one of the 12 spies sent to scout Canaan. He had a name for himself. He secured the Tabernacle of meeting, during Moses speaking with God;

*And the Lord spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend. And he turned again into the camp: but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, departed not out of the tabernacle*.

All this, and anointed by Moses upon his death to lead them, but it was this day that the Lord began to magnify him before the children of Israel. For it was this day that, by the command of God, the people crossed the Jordan as the Lord parted the waters, holding back the flow of the river in the late rains of the harvest, at its peak levels. Held back in a heap of water while the Levites with the Ark stood on dry ground and the people passed over, clean. 

It was a miracle of God, whose word Joshua carried to the people, and his obedience and faith that magnified him before the people. Not his own work. Not his previous deeds. Not his station. But his faith and obedience to the living God.

The Lord, the captain of the Hosts, Jesus Christ Himself IMO, appeared before Joshua and He commanded the new leader of Israel in the manner that God would deliver the city of Jericho to them. 

And Joshua, carefully explained the plan to the people, and they believed, following all the Lord's words given to Joshua. Circling the city with the Ark. Blowing the horns. Giving a shout on the 7th time on the 7th day. And a miracle occurred, the walls came tumbling down. 

Joshua not only conveyed the word of God, but cautioned the people to be silent, least they feel the need to shout at another time, and in doing so disobey the word of God. And while God hates it when we add our own works or deeds to His plan for us, He appreciates diligence in our honoring His command. To take the spirit of His word and apply it to how we live our Christian life. 

This is a key point of separation. Taking not just the letter of the commandments and statutes God has provided us, but honoring the Spirit of it and not leaving ourselves open to temptation. Some professing Christians call this "legalism." But Joshua wasn't being legalistic in his telling the people to remain silent in their performance of God's command until the final day and appointed time. He was safeguarding them against temptation.

*And the city shall be accursed, even it, and all that are therein, to the Lord: only Rahab the harlot shall live, she and all that are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers that we sent. And ye, in any wise keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest ye make yourselves accursed, when ye take of the accursed thing, and make the camp of Israel a curse, and trouble it. But all the silver, and gold, and vessels of brass and iron, are consecrated unto the Lord: they shall come into the treasury of the Lord.*

Joshua learns of the trespass when an easy victory for the children of Israel against the Amorites, turns into an embarrassing defeat. Rending his clothes in torment, the Lord chastises him and reveals that there has been sin that has turned Him against the Israelites. He gives Joshua instruction to find out who has taken the accursed things of Jericho into the camp. 

By tribe, family and house, Joshua inquired, and finally Achan confesses; *When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight, then I coveted them, and took them; and, behold, they are hid in the earth in the midst of my tent, and the silver under it.*

The items, Achan, his children and possessions, are all led without the camp. They are stoned and it all burned in the valley of Achor, or "troubles," and a cairn of stones was heaped upon the remnants as a reminder to the children of Israel. A memorial to what happens when one brings sin among them.

The spiritual application of this story, like much of the accounts of Israel from Egypt though the promised land, can be applied to our lives as saved Christians. Sometimes, even as we are delivered by God from our enemies, or having received blessings by our obedience and reward, our hearts turn to covetousness. We are given a temptation to sin. The devil loves to bring a test before us when God is in the process of rewarding our faith in Him. When we are the most comfortable. 

Many times in the Christian life, you will find that you've made it through something by walking in the Spirit and trusting in God, only to stumble at the finish line because the relief turns to complacency. Satan looks for ways to accuse us and what better time than victory? 

The lesson of Achan can be a valuable one, to not depart from the path God laid out for us, even in victory, because it can undo all the good God has done in our life, and lead to our destruction. The devil hides temptations even in the smallest victories of our lives. How much more the temptation when the odds seem overwhelmingly against you, and yet you persevere in the Lord.

Beware of the sin of Achan. Don't let the devil snatch defeat from victory.

Continuing the narrative of the taking of Canaan by Joshua and the Israelites, we see that the kings of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites have begun to ally against the invasion of the Hebrews, led by the Lord God that performed miracles in Egypt and destroyed the kings beyond Jordan. 

And the people of Gibeon, seeing the power of God at work in Jericho and Ai, decide a different strategy; they offer a truce by deception. Wearing old and tattered clothing and supplies, they pretend they are from a far land, afraid of the Lord God, and get Joshua to swear an oath that they would not be harmed. But Joshua discovered their city is just 3 days away, neighbors to the camp at Gilgal. 

In punishment for the deception, Joshua commands they agree to be servants of Israel in perpetuity. Bondsmen, hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God. Serving the congregation and the altar for the Levites. The Ark finding a home there for a while in the time of the Kings. 

King Saul, in his zeal, will attempt to wipe them out during his reign. And for this betrayal of the oath, David his successor will deliver up the sons of Saul to the city of Gibeon for execution.

**Joshua 10** is one of the greatest battles of the history of man, where Joshua and the Israelites, the Lord fighting for them, fought the battle of the 5 Kings at Gibeon, where more men were slaughtered by the hailstones rained on them by God than the edge of the sword. 

Joshua commanded the sun and moon to stand still so that they could destroy the enemies of God in the light. And the Lord granted it. The Bible says this miracle was told of in the Book of Jasher, what seems to be a lost book of the history of the Hebrews, called the "book of the righteous." Many forgeries have been produced, and Jewish fables surround this mention, but we have the inspired preserved word of God in Joshua to tell us of His glory that day. 

As the armies of Israel pursued the 5 Kings, the sought refuge in a cave. Joshua has stones rolled in front of the entrance, to deal with them later. 

The nature of this battle, the miracles, the wrath of God, kings hiding in mountains to escape, is a picture of the end times. The Day of the Lord. Where instead of standing still, the Sun and Moon darken. The stars fall from the heavens. And the kings and mighty men of the earth are cut down by the coming of Christ Jesus, with ten thousands of His saints. 

With the kings trapped, Joshua leads his armies against the nearby city of Makkedah, killing its king and all the people. Following this, he executes the 5 Kings, hanging them all from trees, cursed (*for he that is hanged is accursed of God*). He proceeds to then raid and slaughter city after city, killing king after king, until all these kingdoms were taken in one campaign, because the Lord God of Israel fought for Israel.

*And there was no day like that before it or after it, that the Lord hearkened unto the voice of a man: for the Lord fought for Israel.*

The glory and power of the Lord to execute His fierce wrath and deliver enemies, is the promise for the second coming of Christ as well. It is the prayers of the saints, asking for His wrath to be poured out. That every knee bow and tongue confess, He is Lord. That our enemies be made to know He loved us. 

As wicked and awful the world may seem, we as Christians have this sure hope of being delivered. That the Lord will repay. So stand fast in the faith of Christ. Unafraid.

Wherefore comfort one another with these words.*

*Therefore let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober. For they that sleep sleep in the night; and they that be drunken are drunken in the night. But let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation. For God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation by our Lord Jesus Christ, Who died for us, that, whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him. *Now we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by our gathering together unto him, That ye be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand. Remember ye not, that, when I was yet with you, I told you these things?And now ye know what withholdeth that he might be revealed in his time. For the mystery of iniquity doth already work: only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way. And then shall that Wicked be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming: Even him, whose coming is after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders, And with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved. *But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.*

*Therefore I will look unto the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me.*

*Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain.*

*Simeon and Levi are brethren; instruments of cruelty are in their habitations. In **Genesis 49**, as Jacob blesses each son, the children of Israel, he places  Levi and Simeon together. Note that for their wrath their nations are cursed. Levi to be scattered throughout Israel, as the Levitical priesthood was, having no inheritance of their own, and dividing Simeon into Judah, where they eventually fade away. 

There are some accounts of Simeon left to come. But minor mentions. Their numbers dwindled by half between the census in the wilderness, from the beginning of the 40 years to the end. In Judah they remained, until a mention in **1 Chronicles 4**;

*These mentioned by their names were princes in their families: and the house of their fathers increased greatly. And they went to the entrance of Gedor, even unto the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks. And they smote the rest of the Amalekites that were escaped, and dwelt there unto this day.*

This is prior to the Babylonian captivity, and it is assumed they being within Judah, were carried away captive, and by the return, lost as an individual tribe. 

Of course, 12,000 saved believers from Simeon will be among the 144,000 in the wrath, according to **Revelation 7:7**.

*Zebulun shall dwell at the haven of the sea; and he shall be for an haven of ships; and his border shall be unto Zidon.*

The territory allotted Zebulon was at the southern end of the Sea of Galilee, with its eastern border, the western border being the Mediterranean, the south bordered by the Tribe of Issachar, and the north by Asher on the western side and Naphtali on the east. It isn't quite near Zidon/Sidon which is by Tyre, in the northern part of Asher, but it is entirely possible that by their central location along the river Kishon, between two seas, that as a seafaring people had made ports along the coast of the Mediterranean. 

Their tribe has very little mention, other than again to say they'd be part of the north kingdom of Israel, and scattered away by Assyria during their conquest of the kingdom (and their part of the 144K). But their territory is where Christ Jesus was raised, as a Galilean in Samaria. Not as a Jew in Judea.

They may have to wait until tomorrow, but for the most part, their stories are similar and their dates the same. Other than the remnants of saints among their people, each falls to Idolatry and the same abominations of the people who God drove out before them, and so were scattered or bred out of existence, some returning to Christ during His ministry. Most never retaining any of the blessings of God having been unfaithful.

Here in **Joshua 22**, the first half of the chapter, we find the children of Israel victorious in the promised land, delivered to them by the power of God, who had driven out the kingdoms and left them cities and fields and vineyards, a land flowing with milk and honey. 

But not all the tribes of Jacob wished to settle there. Before they'd crossed over into the land west of the Jordan, the tribes of Gad, Ruben and half the tribe of Manasseh had petitioned the Lord through Moses that they may have the land to the east of the river, which was good for cattle, being they had much and were ranchers. Just as Lot saw the plains of Jordan, and saw it was good for herding his flocks, there in the east, and separated himself from Abraham, pitching his tent towards Sodom. This was the same land. 

And Moses became indignant at their request, because he felt they were abandoning the brethren to do their own thing, just as the battle was about to be truly met. That it would discourage the remaining Israelites from crossing into the promised land, just as their fathers who spied out the land had 40 years earlier, causing God to curse them to wander in the wilderness. 

But, they said not so, while they would build cities for their children and pens for their cattle, the Gaddites and Rubenites and half tribe of Manasseh vowed that their men of war would go before the people across the Jordan and fight with them until Canaan was theirs, and they had peace. 

So, here in Joshua, having kept their word and fought with their brethren, they are given permission to enter into rest in the lands Moses had given them. And Joshua warns them to follow in the commandments of God and then blesses them further, as they departed;

*Return with much riches unto your tents, and with very much cattle, with silver, and with gold, and with brass, and with iron, and with very much raiment: divide the spoil of your enemies with your brethren.*

These men had let their yea mean yea, their promise kept. They believed God and kept His will, but asked in return to have that which they sought on the east of the Jordon, and the Lord gave it to them.

We know the Lord is faithful, and keeps His word. We know the Father answers our prayers and fulfils our needs, and allows us that which is in our hearts as long as it doesn't conflict with His larger plans. If we ask, it shall be given. We may have confidence as believers that if we ask anything according to His will, that our petitions that we desire will be granted. And blessings given for our obedience to His will. 

The lesson for believers today is that our promises and blessings are related. Our willingness to do as He commands of us grants us not only reward for our obedience, but He will accommodate that which we seek in this life, so long as it is according to His will. God is flexible, and a good Father;

**Luke 11:11-13**
*If a son shall ask bread of any of you that is a father, will he give him a stone? or if he ask a fish, will he for a fish give him a serpent? Or if he shall ask an egg, will he offer him a scorpion? If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?*

These men risked their lives for their brothers, they obeyed the will of God. They let their actions speak to their vow, and we're not only given that which they sought for themselves and their families, but were blessed on top of it all for their faith and obedience. 

Following this example, being willing and able to do the will of God, as His sons, adopted by our faith in Christ, allows us to enter boldly before the throne, and ask Him and receive. 

**Hebrews 4:16**
*Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.*

In my own life, I know with certainty that when I first seek the things of God, when I turn to His word, and pray for His will to be done, to be used as He sees fit, that I am blessed beyond measure and the things I seek are given unto me. 

This isn't a prosperity gospel. It is the promise of God. Seeking His will first will find you asking for ways to please Him, to be a blessing to others, rather than riches. Asking for patience or understanding and wisdom. Asking to be able to lead others to Christ. 

The material blessings will follow, usually just enough to satisfy your needs. Just enough to keep you from trouble, in my case. But the spiritual blessings of helping others to the truth or even just being in the right place at the right time to affect someone positively, they are endless and wonderful. And you receive a good name, as these men did. Amen.

*Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way.*

**Proverbs 18:13**
*He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.*

In the second part of **Joshua 22**, we see that time has passed and the men of war from Gad, Ruben and half tribe of Manasseh have returned east, across the Jordan to their inheritance. Their land bordering Ammonites and Moabites, the places the children of Israel had come through to reach the promised land. And word makes it back to Shiloh, at the Tabernacle of the Lord that the Israelites across the Jordan had set up an altar for themselves. 

The Israelites fear the worst. That these men who had helped liberate the land for their brethren had turned from the Lord and began worshiping the gods of the people who had been driven out and slain. 

We see again Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron, who had ended the plague of God sent against the Israelites for joining the fornication and worship of Baal at Mt. Peor in Moab by slaying with a javelin a man of Israel and a Midianite woman flagrantly fornicating within the camp. A plague which slew 23,000 in one day, 24,000 over all;

**1 Corinthians 10:8**
*Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand.*

Phinehas journeys out with the princes of Israel to inquire about the altar. Confronting the Gaddites, Rubenites and men of Manasseh, he asks if they've rebelled against God. He reminds them of the matter of Baal-Peor, and of Achin, who had kept the cursed thing from Jericho to his own destruction ans his family's as well as the defeat of the armies of Israel, and the deaths of untold numbers of men in that defeat. He begs them, that if the land they possessed was too wicked for them, that they not resist the call to worship false gods, to bring their people back over the Jordan to be with the other tribes. To get right with God. 

But the tribes east of the Jordan explain that it is nothing like this. That their intentions were pure. They say may God judge their hearts, and punish them if they're lying, but that they simply set it up as a witness to their fellowship with the God of Israel and their brethren. To serve as a reminder for their children, that even though a river separate them, they are of Israel. They named it Ed which means 'witness.' This answer satisfied everyone, and so there was a happy ending all around.

But the story has applications that we can learn from, as does the entire Bible. But here we see the tendency of distance and absence from among one another often leads to misunderstanding. 

We can see it in our own experiences, where a sibling moves away to the city, or a brother from church takes a job in another state, or even coworkers who don't share an office or a site, but question the ethic of those working remotely...distance and absence stir up questions, and an innocent act by one can spark a potential conflict between the two. 

Godly parents worry about whether their children who leave the nest are living godly themselves. For example we see Job offering sacrifices for his children, just in case they weren't;

**Job 1:5**
*And it was so, when the days of their feasting were gone about, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all: for Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts. Thus did Job continually.*

It is a natural feeling to have, but it can also lead to paranoia and rash action. 

Phinehas, who in his zeal for the Lord acted decisively in Moab, taking a spear and ending the judgment against his people with the deaths of the fornicator and the whore, shows discernment, judgment and mercy here, at Ed. Rather than impulsively allowing his hatred of every false way lead to violence, he asks of them the altars purpose. And rather than accuse, he reminds them of why he has concerns. That not only would this be bad for them if they'd fallen away to Baal, but that God's judgment is upon nations, and all of Israel could suffer. Phinehas asks them to return cross the Jordan if it meant repenting of their possible sin, a chance to get right. And, most importantly, he listens to their answer, not deciding the matter before hearing them out. 

This is a pattern we can all learn from. Especially in situations where we don't know the intent of the heart. The same right judgment he showed in Peor, he shows here. 

And of course there's an innocent explanation. And the explanation made by men of the 2.5 tribes who had just demonstrated their honor by keeping their word in settling Canaan is accepted. And all of Israel rejoiced at the news. Crisis averted.

Now, the other application is that we should hate every false way, and there is no harm in asking someone professing to be Christian to explain their apparent behavior or statements that seem contrary to the Gospel. 

As we see online especially, there are many who hold damnable heresies and doctrines of devils, claiming to be of Christ. There is no profit in blind ecumenicalism, and accepting everyone calling themselves Christian regardless of their beliefs. But we should trust someone who claims to be a believer, giving them the benefit of the doubt unless there is a sign that concerns us. And then, remembering Phinehas, inquire what they meant, meekly and with care. It could simply be a misunderstanding or a different way of phrasing something, perfectly innocent. 

Yes, if they announce their beliefs in a false gospel or a different god, or some vain traditions and dead works, we should confront them with scripture and rebuke them. But there are times brothers as set at variance, when the truth is there are only surface differences caused by distance and absence of fellowship. 

Thankfully, God's word has a shortcut to finding out if we share a common foundation; asking "What must one do to be saved?" Paul repeatedly uses the gospel as a way of assurance of common mindedness with the churches he writes to. That we all share the same foundational belief. As Jesus says of testing the spirit of a teacher, we shall know them by their fruits, by the beliefs of their followers. If they are saved by the gospel or if they believe some false way. 

We need to meekly and humbly seek to know, before either grabbing a javelin or declaring peace, and always ready to provide a way out should they prove to be going the way of Balaam, and heading to the destruction of Baal-Peor. By giving them the true gospel in love. Amen

**Judges 1 & 2** sets the stage for the next era of Israel, following the death of Joshua. The various tribes failed to utterly destroy the Canaanites in the land God had given them to possess, and instead made tributaries of them. Valuing their gold more than God. Keeping these people among them, that they become thorns in their sides.

The corruption of the following generations, who turned from the deliverance of God and His covenant, was sown in the remnants of the heathen among them. They turned to worship Baal and Asteroth, 'the queen of heaven." They were beset and spoiled constantly by the remnants of the nations. The children of Israel were even taken as slaves. 

And periodically, when the complaints of the Israelites were heard by God, he sent a judge. A deliverer to save them from their plight. And when the judge was dead, they returned to corruption and adultery with idols, following other gods. 

The picture of Christ, the judge who delivers us from death and bondage, but who never dies, living forever the first fruits of the resurrection. Who will judge the quick and the dead at the judgment seat of Christ for saints, the great white throne for the unregenerate. 

It is Christ Jesus, the angel of the Lord who appears before them to let them know that He would no longer drive the heathen from them, because they had not thrown down their altars and slain the people. The covenant He would never break was broken, *finding fault with them.*

Christians in the world, delivered by the most High Judge, Christ Jesus will see, their children and grandchildren fall away to the world, just as the tribes of Judah did. But the promise of His deliverance remains forever, that they may turn to Him and call upon His name and be saved. 

We will see this patterned for us in **Judges**, again and again.

Just to recap the theme going into the **Book of Judges**; God having delivered the people into the promised land commanded them to utterly destroy the inhabitants and to smash down their altars to the false gods they worshipped. The Lord had been with them in every battle (save one, thanks to the abomination of Achan). He had driven out the people that Joshua and his armies went against. He delivered 33 Kings into their hands. The Lord God rained hail the size of boulders, drove men out with hornets, felled the walls of cities with the shout and trumpets of the Israelites. 

But yet they did not fully eradicate the Canaanites and others in the land. They resorted to allowing them to stay in tribute. Valuing their gold more than the commandments of God. 

They had the knowledge of the will of the sovereign God, and *chose*, of their own will, to ignore His word, to do as they saw was right in their own eyes. Despite all their valiant deeds and the miracles they witnessed while obeying Him, they slacked off in their duty to do that which was comfortable. Easy. To leave the work unfinished. 

By their choice. By free will. 

And God responded by removing the hedge of protection around them. By allowing them to feel the consequences of their actions. By using these nations as a thorn in the side of Israel, to prove her that they may learn the ways of war, rather than peace. To be a snare with their false gods, so that the glory of God could be known. That in their tribulation they would call out to the Lord for salvation, and He would place His Spirit on a judge He would raise up to deliver them. 

The Bible is the record of God's will for man, in Christ Jesus. And it demonstrates that He gave His word as a testimony, that man should believe Him. The Godhead being three persons, that the witness be true, just as the law requires. Jesus appeared resurrected to witnesses that others believed their report. The Spirit indwells believers, that it testify to them they have eternal life, that they may **know**. The Bible exists, inspired and preserved, that we may hear the word and have faith that it is true, and obey His commandments beginning with the gospel of Christ.

It is always a choice. And God uses our choices to His purpose, even when we are disobedient. Even when some don't believe the report. Even when people fall away from the truth.

Calvinism demands that a sovereign God removes that choice, the need for His word as testimony, the Spirit to believe, and makes all of man's shortcomings God's responsibility. It denies the power of God to see His will done **despite** our failings. To use our sins as a means of shaping the clay as a Potter. 

The covenants become worthless, because why make promises and give blessings for man's obedience when the obedience is given to them? 

The Israelites failed to harken to the commandments of God, and lost those blessings and protections. Just as the covenant with Moses in the wilderness established as terms; I will be your God, and ye shall be My people. But if they took up the gods and abominations of those in the land, it would be a curse, and they would be troubled until they turned back to the Lord. 

The covenant was glorious, but the fault was with them. 

None of this makes sense in a Calvinistic world view. There is no lesson to learn from it. If they were predestinated to disobey, then the punishment they received wouldn't be to prove them and provoke them to repentance. God's decision to let them suffer the consequences to teach them their need for salvation in Him wouldn't make any sense. There's no need for the law to be a schoolmaster if faith and obedience is handed down by the good will of a sovereign Lord, on whomever He will. 

And it limits God, showing He needs total control of man's actions in order to have the outcome He desires, rather than the glory and power of His will being done despite man's disobedience. 

And it makes Christ's obedience to the Father's will unto death meaningless, for if man's obedience is forced upon them, why would the Son saying "not my will, but the Father's" mean anything at all to us? How would that perfect obedience save us? How is it an inspiration to strive for that perfection? 

The gospel of the Calvinist is a hopeless thing, and their false god is weak and capricious.

*28 And he said unto them, Follow after me: for the Lord hath delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand. And they went down after him, and took the fords of Jordan toward Moab, and suffered not a man to pass over.*

*31 And after him was Shamgar the son of Anath, which slew of the Philistines six hundred men with an ox goad: and he also delivered Israel.*

The pattern of falling away, turning to God for deliverance, and God sending a judge to free the children of Israel begins. 

We see that God determines that the heathen in the land that they had failed to utterly remove will serve as a means to test the people, to keep them ready for war, to humble them, to tempt them to marry their outlandish woman and worship their false gods. 

And when they suffered the fruit of their adultery, and came to see their need for God's salvation, repented towards Him, and called upon His name, He would send a deliverer. 

In the same way, tribulation and sin in the world serve to test man, and as a schoolmaster, bring people to be humbled before God and seek His help. To call upon the name of Christ, the judge of all, to deliver us. 

The Jews, who say they are but are not and do lie, exist in this world for the same reason these Canaanites do. The same with every evil organization of men. 

They are here to keep us spiritually equipped for war. To tempt us into sin and worship of false gods. To test us and try us. To bring us to Him. 

You can almost hear an ancient Israelite saying "of God real, why bad things happen? Why Chushanrishathaim attack us?" 

Here in Judges we see exactly why. And it is to glory God.

Now in the narrative we see the early history of the Israelites in the promised land. The 5 lords of the Philistines, Sidonians, Hivites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Moabites, Jebusites, and Canaanites in general, are both bordering and among the land inherited by each tribe. 

The king of Mesopotamia, Chushanrishathaim comes against them and leads them as captives 8 years, and Caleb's nephew Othneil has the Spirit of the Lord come up on him, and he as judge delivers the Mesopotamian into his hands. And for 40 years they knew peace. And Othneil dies. 

The 40 year pattern is a generational cycle used by God throughout history. The wandering in the wilderness. The cycle of judges and kings. The time between Pentecost and the ascension of Jesus to the destruction of the temple and Jerusalem in 70AD...God provides a span of these generations to allow man to get right, as He judges nations. 

Next we see Moab come up against Israel as the agent of God's wrath for Israel for falling away again. The children of Ammon and Amalek, who take possession of Jericho, the city of palm trees. And for 18 years the children of Israel serve under Eglon. 

And when Israel cried unto the Lord for deliverance, Ehud, a Benjamite was raised up by the Lord as judge. And Ehud, the left-handed judge slays Eglon in God's name, in one of the most gruesome deaths of the Bible. 

Judges has some of the best narratives ever, better than those Netflix and HBO could ever imagine. 

And after the destruction of the Moabites under Ehud, the land knows rest for 80 years. 

Then we learn of Shamgar son of Anath, who slew 600 Philistines with an ox goad, an unimaginable feat, yet relegated to a single verse. (We will see another mention of Shamgar in a few chapters, in the song of Deborah)

But we see the pattern. The harder the times, the more likely the people turn to the Lord. The better the times, the quicker they fall away. 

In our Christian life, we may see similar patterns. There's a tendency towards leaning on God, turning to prayer more often, reading the Bible more, increasing church attendance, maybe even fasting...but when the deliverance comes, many begin to shirk those things. And rather than walk in the Spirit, backslide towards walking in the flesh. 

God uses tribulation to prove us. That we may learn to trust Him more, to increase our faith. To learn mercy and judgement. To increase patience. 

We see it throughout the Epistles. 

**Romans 5:1-5**
*Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.*

It's the same pattern, spiritual rather than physical, but similar. A picture of our Christian life.

**Judges 4** begins with the generation following the death of Ehud the judge, and the Israelites falling once again into sin. The Lord sells them into the hand of Jabin, king of Canaan, and his captain Sisera. For 20 years he oppressed the children of Israel.

**Isaiah 3:12**

Deborah was righteous in the sight of the Lord and wise by her understanding of His word. There is no indication that her judgment was wrong, and matters brought before her must have been answered satisfactorily to the parties, or all Israel wouldn't seek her out, there beneath the palms. 

But it was not God's intention that a woman shall rule. It is a sign of weak and faithless men where they feel the need to. 

Happy international women's month. 

Now this prophetess goes to a man named Barak, asking him why he had not harkened to a command by God to rise an army of 10,000 men from Nephatali and Zebulon, to go against Sisera, which presumably Barak was aware of, that God had promised to deliver the Canaanite army into Barak's hand. 

*And Barak said unto her, If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go.*
