Barak saw the Lord was with Deborah, and in his own way, needed reassurance from the Lord that He was with him and his men, setting out to do this seemingly impossible thing. 

Fear is a lack of faith. Barak did not know the Lord was with him, but knew He was with Deborah. For his lack of faith, Deborah prophesied *the Lord shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.* The honor of victory would go to a woman, since the man lacked faith. And Deborah went with him. 

Next, we are introduced to Heber the Kenite, descended from Moses father in law, who separated himself from his people, who had allied themselves with Sisera, and who told the captain of Barak's plan to attack. 

Sisera prepares his armies and their chariots of iron, and lay in wait for Barak and his men. The odds of defeating him even worse now that he was prepared. 900 iron chariots. Horsemen and infantry, against the 10,000 Israelites. Hopeless but for the Lord. 

To God's glory, the opposing armies were discomfited, set in disarray and scattered, and they fell by the sword before Barak. Sisera fled the battle on foot, as the Israelite army slew all of his men. 

And finding the tent of Heber, the Kenite, and presuming their allegiance, Sisera sought refuge from Jael, Heber's wife. And Jael took him in, and gave him comfort. Milk and a mantle to keep warm by. Promising to hide him from any seeking him. And lulling Sisera to sleep. 

Then the goodly woman took a tent stake and hammer, and drove it through his temple to the ground. 

Barak, in pursuit of Sisera, finds Jael who shows him what had become of the oppressor of Israel. 

And the glory was God's, who *subdued on that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel*, ultimately leading to his defeat at the hands of the children of Israel. Amen.

Women in the word of God are not as some haters of God would claim. Weak, and incidental. But godly women are used mightily by Him, for the Lord's purpose. Yes they are called to be submissive to their fathers and husbands, but submission isn't total helplessness. It is just the order of delegation of authority, God, lords, husband, wife, children, each with a role to play. Each requiring both sacrifice and responsibility. It isn't a lack of agency, but an acknowledgement of the proper order of things, that it be well with the people. 

Deborah setting up a place of judgment, as someone who knew the law and understood His word, in the absence of men stepping up wasn't rebellion, it was of necessity. But even so she didn't seek to usurp authority over the man. She didn't raise an army to lead it. She didn't travel the land to be its queen. She sat beneath a palm tree, and her God given wisdom brought people to her. 

Barak was a leader of men, but weak in faith. He needed Deborah to goad him into action and trust in the Lord. Still, Deborah went to him, to lead. But God reveals to Deborah that a woman will be given the honor of victory, to the shame of Barak. 

God wants strong men, full of faith, to take their role seriously, gravely. To be the leader of their home, loving their wives as an extension of themselves. To turn away from temptation and chasing adultery, fornication and false gods. 

But women play a role, in supporting and encouraging men. Being keepers at home, instructing their children in the right paths. And like Jael, honoring their husband's decisions, leaving their people for the plains of Zaanaim, even when it means brutally killing a man who her husband had given up family to reject allegiance with. 

That's the strength that comes from submission. How God uses the weak to destroy the strong. How He reveals His mighty hand, in impossible situations. It is why we are called to submit to whatever higher authority is in our lives, knowing that in doing so we are serving God. Not in rebellion. That the Lord will reward us for our faith, and use us in our weakness to confound the mighty. Amen.

**Judges 6**, in which we meet one of the most doubting men chosen of God in the Bible. Gideon is not as well known as Thomas, but his need for reassurance and signs of God being with him, because his faith was weak, is matched only by the great things God uses him for. 

A simple farmer in his father's house, under oppression of the Midianites and surrounded by Baal worship, even in his own family. The story of Gideon shows even the weakest of faith is stronger than dead idols and great armies.

The angel of the Lord appears to Gideon, and the Lord speaks to him saying *Surely I will be with thee, and thou shall smite the Midianites as one man.*...*Thou shalt save Israel from the hands of the Midianites: have I not sent thee?* 

What I believe is an OT appearance of Jesus, the angel of the Lord speaks to Gideon, the word of God either way, and yet the poor farm boy needs more. He says, "show me a sign."

How often in our lives, when we know the right thing to do, but are afraid, do we delay doing it and place the burden on the Lord to show us a sign? To put the ball in God's court as a means of procrastinating, allowing fear to overwhelm our faith? I believe every Christian has had a moment like this. 

A clear path, the word of God unmistakable, understanding what must be done of His will, and rather than answering the call of "Have I not sent thee?" with "Show me a sign that you are with me oh Lord?"

We may not have an angel or Jesus appear to us, tell us directly, and then even consume a sacrifice on an altar with fire to convince us the next right thing the Lord has for us to do. It may be a Bible reading, a sermon we hear, subtle and not so subtle answers to prayers, divine appointment...God speaks to us every day if we are listening. And He has works for each of us who hear the call. 

But fear, doubts, comfort in our own situations, may keep us from doing what we should. By asking for a sign, we put it off, when the sign of God actually speaking to us and presenting the task or challenge should be sign enough. But man is stubborn and often needs the carrot and the stick. Fear the stick and give praise for the carrot is what I have learned, begrudgingly over time. As God does here for Gideon, He will do for us to shape us into the vessels He needs. And the sooner we go with the flow, usually the better it works out. 

Be not afraid and trust in the Lord.

Gideon, the son of Joash, from the Abiezrite clan, was of the tribe of Manasseh, living in Ophrah, which is on the promised land side of the Jordan, where the western half tribe of Manasseh resided. The Midianites, on the eastern side of the Jordan south of Edom and Moab. This is how extensive the reach of the Midianites were, as they rated Israel to take as spoil everything they planted. God sent them against Israel for their falling away and worship of Baal. 

And to drive home the point of how extensive that abomination was, We see that all of the people living in Ophrah including his own father, worshiped at an altar and a grove dedicated to the Canaanite god. 

Gideon was clearly a believer in the Lord, though he questioned why they suffered so. But he knew why, He was surrounded by it. It was punishment for their adultery. 

Today many Christians, especially those of us who may have gotten saved from a Bible way to heaven video, or through talking to people online, or by a door-knocker on a missions trip or soul-winning marathon. They believe in the Lord and call upon Jesus name and are saved, yet they are surrounded by people who believe in a false god. It can be very difficult in those situations to stand up for the Lord against the popular opinion of those around us. Including our families. It can be hard to do the right thing. 

But we see Gideon instructed to tear down the altar and burn the wood of the grove, and he does so. And when the men come inquiring who did it, Gideon's active faith in service to the Lord. Reveals the dead idol that they had been worshiping, his wayward father leading his defense. 

Often that is all it takes to bring other people to the understanding of the Lord. To just stand up and do the next right thing as He is presented it to you. Our faithful obedience can convince people far more than our words. And often the only hindrance to doing something great for the Lord that brings others around to the truth is our own fear.

*And Joash said unto all that stood against him, Will ye plead for Baal? will ye save him? he that will plead for him, let him be put to death whilst it is yet morning: if he be a god, let him plead for himself, because one hath cast down his altar. Therefore on that day he called him Jerubbaal, saying, Let Baal plead against him, because he hath thrown down his altar.*

This rebuke by Joash against the Baal-worshipping lynch-mob that had come against his son is such a perfect illustration of how empty paganism and idolatry are compared to serving the living God. "Let Baal plead against him." Jerubbaal becomes one of Gideon's names. Our God destroys those who come against Him, without need of an unruly mob insulted by the exposure of their vanity.

*Then all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the children of the east were gathered together, and went over, and pitched in the valley of Jezreel.*

*But the Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon, and he blew a trumpet; and Abiezer was gathered after him. And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh; who also was gathered after him: and he sent messengers unto Asher, and unto Zebulun, and unto Naphtali; and they came up to meet them.*

A battle looms in the fertile plains of Meddigo, in the heart of Israel. The armies of the East camped there, and the Spirit of the Lord comes upon Gideon, who gathers his kin, and sends word to the surrounding tribes for men. Amassing his own army to go and fight. 

And yet Gideon doubts that the Lord is with him. And again, seeks a sign, dew on a piece of wool, and God grants him the sign, not only dew upon the flax, but soaking it. But doubtful Gideon, afraid, asks for another. Dew on everything else but the wool, and God grants him his sign. 

God is longsuffering and willing to work with us, but ultimately we have to accept on faith the word of God and do the right thing. Even when it is scary and uncertain by man's wisdom, it is to the glory of God that he uses the weak to defeat the strong. Amen

*The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.*

Continuing the story of Gideon, AKA Jerubbaal, who the Lord has chosen to deliver Israel from the hands of the Midianites. We read in **Judges 6** that Gideon had assembled men for war against the camp of the Midians in the valley of Meggado. There Gideon asked the Lord for not one, but two signs that He was with them and would deliver the host into his hands, and the Lord granted him these signs. 

Gideon's doubt was great but with a sign (or two), he turned his fear into faith. It is the same for us as believers. We may have all the faith we think we need, but when tried, fear comes. We are saved, we know His word is true, we know through Him all things are possible. And yet...

I often think about the father in Mark 9, who came to Jesus to have his son healed of the dumb spirit that possessed him. The father thought Jesus could save him, but still he feared there was no hope for his son. He was conflicted between fear and faith. 

**Mark 9:23-24**
*Jesus said unto him, If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth. And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.*

In the same way, we often search for faith in our tribulation, not because we doubt God, but we have doubts about ourselves. Our own weakness. The impossible odds we seem to face. 

*But with faith, all things are possible*. 

And while the signs Gideon had asked for were given him, the dew on the wool and the ground, and Gideon's believed that God would deliver the enemy, God wasn't through increasing his faith. Helping his unbelief. 

The host of Midianites were as a sea of grasshoppers in the valley, Israel had only mustered 32,000 men, and were outnumbered. The Lord says to Gideon that he has too many men. They would credit themselves for the victory, and so He instructs Gideon to send home those too scared to fight, and immediately 22,000 depart. 

But the 10,000 are still too many, says the Lord, and He instructs Gideon to take them to water, and the men who vow down to the water to drink, send home. Keeping only those that lapped the water from their cupped hand. 300 remained. 

When you ask God for assurance in faith, be prepared to have that faith come by testing it mightily. For whom much is given, much is expected. 

Gideon wanted a sign that the Lord, Who was speaking to him, whose Spirit had come over him, who had brought Gideon to this place and God answered his need for signs, was now telling Gideon that the hosts of Midianites that were as sand, too numerous to count, we're going to be delivered into his hands with a force of 300. You wanted faith, here it is. 

God not only uses the weak to confound the strong, He makes us weaker that we may become strong.

Having purged the army of Israel down to the 300, the Lord tells Gideon to get down to the enemy's camp that he may know God has already won the victory for him. And, knowing Gideon is sometimes afraid, tells him to take his servant Phurah with him if he's afraid. (Phurah goes, so that answers that)

There the pair hear the men of the camp discussing a dream that when interpreted reveals they are afraid of Gideon, knowing the Lord was with him. 

Gideon understanding their state of, probably relating to it, returns to his camp and the 300, with a plan. 

Dividing the men into groups, surrounding the camp on three sides, Gideon tells the men to do as he does. Each with a trumpet, and a clay pot with a lamp inside, Gideon tells them when he blows his trumpet, shout *The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon.*

The judge who needed signs to turn his fear into faith was preying upon the fears of his enemy. 

And so just after midnight, they follow Gideon's lead and blow the trumpets and smash the pitchers and hold up the lamps and shout, *The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon!*

And they stood their ground. 

And the sound and the sight and the battle cry all worked on the fear of the Lord in them, and they not only scattered and retreated but in panic slaughtered one another with their own swords.

And as the remnant of the Midianites and Amalek host fled East, towards the Jordan, men from throughout Israel joined Gideon in pursuit, killing two princes, and bringing their heads to Gideon.

Sometimes Christians get the mistaken idea that tribulations and temptations and attacks by adversaries are sent by God to test our faith, to prove ourselves worthy of His love. And so they will try to go it alone to show God how strong they are. 

This is a mistake. 

**Romans 5:6-8**
*For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly. For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die. But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.*

God loves us so much, despite our weakness, that He sent His only begotten Son. That Jesus so loves us, He died for us while we were yet sinners. 

Yes, God wishes us to grow in faith, and shapes us by our experiences to be better vessels for His purpose. But increased faith doesn't mean relying more and more upon yourself, but rather leaning more and more upon Him to deliver us. 

Like Gideon, we may have fears and doubts, and require signs. But the Lord knows and understands, and will surely provide us with a way out. He will provide us with a Phurah, to go with us into the breach. Like Barak needed Deborah with him. 

He will ask for our trust, and to stand firm and do as He commands, but the battles are already won by Him. The Lord delivered us already. We have overcome. This is how He increases our faith. How He helps our unbelief. 

God uses the weak. He uses foolish things to confound the wise. No one would think that 300 men blowing trumpets and smashing pots and shouting could rout tens of thousands. What a foolish plan! But they had already been delivered into Gideon's hands by the Lord. 

Just as the Israelites were delivered from Egypt. Just as Jericho fell. Just as Jael the housewife had victory over Sisera. Just as the giants were destroyed and the land was delivered, and 33 Kings were toppled in a single campaign. 

Just as death and Hell have been conquered. By the mighty hand of God.

When we are tempted, tested and tried, remember this, God has already given us victory. We just have to obey His word, be watchful and ready to act on the opportunities He will provide.

Chapter 8 of **Judges** begins abruptly, carrying the narrative of chapter 7, where as Gideon and the 300 pursued the host of the Midianites back east, across the Jordan, he sent messengers to the tribes of Israel in the area to join in the pursuit, and we saw the men of Ephraim capture two princes of the Midianites. 

Here, the chapter opens with the the men of Ephraim angry that Gideon had not called them to the initial battle. Of course of all the men Gideon gathered, God dismissed most before He used the acts of the 300 to drive the army from the land. 

Gideon answers them tactfully and with humility; *What have I done now in comparison of you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?* Abiezer being the family of Manasseh Gideon belonged to, the men of Ephraim in "gleaning" or opportunistically had subdued two princes of the host, God delivering them to their hands. This simple acknowledgement of their role stayed their resentment, allowing the forces to continue their chase of the armies of the East. 

**Proverbs 15:1**
*A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.*

As Gideon and his men continue to go after them, they pass through Succoth, a place in the wilderness that Israel had passed through, and Gideon as captain asks them for bread to feed his men, and they refuse. 

*I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian. And the princes of Succoth said, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army?*

The men of the next community, Penuel respond the same way. 

Gideon vows that when he returns, he will take thorns as scourges against the men of Succoth and tear down the tower of Penuel. A vow he fulfilled after he and his men capture the fleeing princes, Zebah and Zalmunna, whipping and killing the men and razing the tower. 

Gideon tells his captives, Zebah and Zalmunna, that had they spared lives of those at Tabor, an apparent raid they'd conducted in Israel, he would have spared their lives.

Gideon asks his young son to take the heads of the princes, but by his youth he can't do it. Gideon takes them instead, after Zebah and Zalmunna mock him. 

So the armies were defeated and the children of Israel took the spoil and returned back across the Jordan, hailing Gideon for delivering them out of the hands of the Midianites. 

They call for Gideon to be made king and his son and future sons to rule over them. But Gideon meekly declined, giving glory to God.

However, he does ask for tribute. The gold earrings of the men slain, which when taken together was a substantial weight of gold. And while judging Israel the rest of his days, back in Ophrah of Manasseh, he takes the gold of his spoil and makes himself an ephod. A golden vestment of the office of the high priest. 

This is the snare of Gideon. This causes the children of Israel to go a whoring. 

Some interpretations of this make the ephod an idol that is worshipped, but it seems unlikely that Jerubbaal, aka Gideon, a smasher of idols, "the accused of Baal," would set up an idol and there's no indication that they worshipped the ephod itself. 

It is more likely in my opinion to mean that Gideon, despite his declining to be a king, allowed his popularity and fame to make him seek to usurp the place God chose, Shiloh, and the office of the high priest to whom the Ephod crafted by Moses belonged. And rather than go to Shiloh for spiritual matters, many in Israel came down to Ophrah and Gideon. 

The number of wives and sons he produced showed that he did take advantage of his glory, despite deferring the glory of the victory to God. The spoils he took as tribute became a snare, and caused the Israelites to go whoring, away from the commandment of the Lord. 

So we see, even Gideon, full of fear. Requiring signs. Witnessing the miracle of their defeat of a troop of over a hundred and fifty thousand with 300 men, let his success go to his head. Leading him to sin. 

This is a trap some very successful Christians fall in to. Who have been used mightily for God, and done great works for Him. For all their humility and understanding that it was not of them, pride eats away at their character. God's success begins to seem to them to be a partnership. And their *idea* of what God wants take the place of what God actually wills for them. 

We can apply this to great modern preachers of the word, who have won thousands of souls to Christ, and then, building an empire from the success, sow the seeds their own downfall. 

And the people who they helped forget these men, after they've died. And their children turn to wickedness. Worshiping Baal as the Israelites do. The children of these great soldiers for God not turning out to be godly men, but wicked, like Gideon's son, Abimelech.

**Judges 8:33-34**
*And it came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baalberith their god. And the children of Israel remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side*

Here in **Judges 9** we are given the story of Abimelech, one of the 70 sons of Gideon, also known as Jerubbaal, and his brief, violent and wicked time as king over Shechem. 

Shechem is a city north of Jerusalem and south of Samaria, in the center of Canaan, on the west Bank of the Jordan. It is where Abraham built an altar to God upon the covenant he received, and where Jacob pitched his tents. It is where his sons, Levi and Simeon killed all the men, after their sister Dinah was raped. 

Shechem is where Joshua assembled the children of Israel and asked them to choose this day whom they would serve, the gods of Babylon , beyond the Euphrates; Baal and Asteroth who were the gods of the Canaanites or the living God Who had led them from Egypt and given them the promised land. It became a Levitical city in Ephraim, a city of refuge. 

Gideon had taken a concubine from among the people of Shechem, from among the ruling families, and her son was Abimelech. 

And so, after the death of Gideon, with the people of Israel forgetting the Lord God and worshiping Baal-Berith, they had built a temple to the false "god of the covenant" there, and it is in Shechem Abimelech goes to seek power. 

Not content to share the diminishing power of being a son of Gideon with his 70 brothers, Abimelech curries favor with his mother's kin in Shechem, and in exchange for a piece of silver from the temple of Berith, one per brother, gathers a gang of base fellows, vain and light, to set about slaying them. 

They succeeded in murdering them all up on a rock, save one, Jotham. Jotham curses Abimelech and the men of the city for their treachery, saying by allegory that Israel had great men before it that refused to be king, represented by the olive, the fig and the vine, and yet they chose the worst, a briar. The bramble. And that by doing so Abimelech would destroy them by fire. 

Jotham then flees, hiding in Beer.

And so for 3 years, the cruel king rules in Shechem, and the men of the city grow disillusioned by their choice because *God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem*. Their trust was diminished, and they sought to deal with their king treacherously. They hired a band of men to lay in wait for him in the mountains, men who robbed all who passed by, and Abimelech was made aware of their plans. 

The bandits failing them, the men turned to one of their own, Gaal son of Ebed. Gaal, his men and the men of the city get drunk, and Gaal curses Abimelech, Zebul his chief officer and ruler of the city, and promises to rule in place of the king after overthrowing the son of Jerubbaal. 

Zebul hears of it and informs Abimelech, and they plot to surround the city and take it to put down the rebellion. 

When Gaal sees the companies of men surrounding the city, Zebul at first taunts him, questioning his senses, saying he is afraid of shadows. But then tells Gaal that here is his chance, go out and fight Abimelech the same who he had cursed. Abimelech defeats the men, and they flee into the city but Zebul throws the rebels out. Abimelech's men slay them and turn towards the city and take it. Slaughtering the men and burning down the tower and the temple and salting the earth, Jotham's curse fufiled.

Not satisfied with the destruction of Shechem, Abimelech moves on the city of Thebez, which too has a strong tower, a keep in the center of the city. The last refuge for siege in the walled cities. And like the tower of Shechem, Gideon's son begins to light fire to the door, to burn the tower down with the people inside. 

And a woman throws down a piece of millstone, that grinds the wheat to flour, and it hit Abimelech in the head, breaking his skull. And the wicked wannabe king calls his armourbearer and begs him to run him through with a sword, so no one could say he was killed by a woman. Reminiscent of the death of Sisera by the hand of Jael. 

*And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they departed every man unto his place.* 

The brief civil war was over. 

*Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren: And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads: and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.*
The book of Judges is better than any Hollywood blockbuster or Netflix series. The Sopranos has nothing on Jerubbaal, Abimelech and the rest of these men. I love God's word.

Abimelech serves as a picture of a type found throughout scripture, and the pattern we see even today. Mighty man of the Lord does great works and has a son that's prodigal or worse, wicked. Some misguided, some reprobate. 

The children of Jacob, to varying degrees. The sons of Aaron. Gideon and Abimelech. David and Absolom. 

Ultimately, it is a picture of God and fallen man. The Good King and his wayward or wicked son. The pastor and the pastor's son. 

It seems that great men of God, who do good and mighty works for the Lord, often produce a child or two who openly rebel against them. Who become prodigal. And at times the father is unable to handle the truth and enables their offspring's wickedness. And others who do the right thing, choosing God over their own, and casting them out to be destroyed by their own wickedness. 

We as parents have an obligation, a Godly duty, to be a picture of God's unconditional love and grace, forgiving our children's sins without enabling them. Chastening them when needed, but like the father of the Prodigal, rushing to meet them when they come home. To not be hypocrites. To live the example that we hold them to.

To be strong enough to cast out the reprobate. To bring an unruly son to the gates to be stoned. 

Our behavior as parents is how children learn about God. It is an awesome responsibility, and one even the most separated fathers can fail at. Even as we, knowing God, fall away to sin, children will ultimately choose their way. 

And so you have examples of men like Jack Hyles, who built an ephod of the spoils given him by God. A Bible college. A high school. Bus ministries and other things he took pride in, put his name on, along with the fame and respect that came with it. 

And he had a son, David, who was wicked as Hell. An Abimelech. 

But these things do not detract from the great works of the Lord, who uses men to do His will. They just show the weakness of the vessel. Jack Hyles was a mighty preacher, won hundreds of not thousands to the Lord. But the snare of pride led to the downfall of what he built.

It's tragic and sad. But it does not undo the mighty works done by God, just as Abimelech didn't change the deliverance of Israel under his father. 

If you know any pastors who may be struggling with an unruly son or daughter, pray for them. Use discernment. Keep the works of God separate from the failures of men. God will repay.

We are here in **Judges 11**, and the story of Jephthah the Gileadite, son of a whore and the eponymous patriarch of Gilead. We are told he was a mighty man of valor, who by the jealousy and resentment of his half-brothers, was cast out of the community. He went to the wasteland, the land of Tob, and there he formed a gang of vain men, outlaws. 

But when the children of Ammon came and made war against them, the elders of Gilead called for him to return and to be captain of their troops. Jephthah agrees so long as they pledge to make him their ruler, and they vow to God they will if he delivers them from the Ammonites. 

Now, we know Jephthah is a man of faith, who *uttered all his words before the Lord*, taking on the responsibility of leadership in His name. He also is given honorable mention in the 'Hall of Faith' in **Hebrews 11:32-34**;

*And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets: Who through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions. Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.*

And so, after his own pledge and profession of his faith, he rode out with men of Gilead and confronted the king of Ammon. Jephthah asks why they are attacking Israel, and the king responds that it is retribution for the taking of their land 300 years prior, as the children of Israel approached the promised land. 

Jephthah, showing knowledge of their history, reminds them that the Ammonites brought it up on themselves, attacking the Israelites as they sought to pass between their coasts. That in the centuries since, the Ammonite kings accepted their loss of land. He says that since the Lord God had given the children of Israel the land by driving out the previous inhabitants, it was theirs. And he taunts their false god Chemosh, saying wouldn't they accept any land as their possession of it drove out the people? 

And after this history lesson, Jephthah calls on the Lord the Judge to judge between them. And the Spirit of the Lord comes down, He delivers the Ammonites into the hands of Israel.

The Spirit of the Lord was upon him. He was definitely a man of faith. But yet, as Barak needed Deborah with him, and Gideon needed the dew upon the flax, Jephthah vowed a vow unto the Lord to assure his victory over the children of Ammon. That he would sacrifice whatsoever crossed his doorway when he returned from battle victorious, if the Lord delivered the enemy into his hands. 

Returning victorious, he came to Mizpeh and his house, and there was his only child, his young daughter come to meet him. He rent his clothes and cried; *Alas, my daughter!* 

His daughter tells him he must honor his vow to the Lord. Especially now that He had delivered victory and given him his enemies in vengeance. 

She only asks to have 2 months to travel the mountains lamenting her death in virginity, which he grants. Sacrificing her as he vowed to do. Her story creating a custom in Israel among her daughters, that 4 days a year they lamented her plight.

As Jesus says, *Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black.*

God does not need our vows, our promises to do good or to perform works in order to deliver us. He simply asks we trust in Him and let our *yea mean yea.* 

Jephthah would have won victory over the children of Ammon by the power of the Lord. He did not need to add his own works as part of God's plan. But God holds us to vows;

**Ecclesiastes 5:4**
*When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.*

So it should not be done in an idle fashion. But if possible, a vow to God in exchange for His favor should not be done at all. Godly living and honest character do not require such a thing. It is by God mighty hand that we are delivered. Not of works of ourselves. 

Jephthah paid a price he needn't have, because he placed a portion of his faith in his own hands.

After Jephthah's tragic victory in **Judges 11**, he finds himself in a similar situation as Gideon had a century earlier, back in **Judges 8**;

*And the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not, when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? And they did chide with him sharply.*

Here in **Judges 12**, rather than deescalate the conflict with the men of Ephraim with kind words as Gideon had, Jephthah chooses conflict and he and his men smite the men of Ephraim, driving them back across the Jordan. 

It is here we get the term 'Shibboleth,' a word that the Ephraimites struggled to pronounce as the Gileadites did. By asking the fleeing men to say it, knowing it would betray them as of Ephraim, Gilead put them to the sword. 

This shows that even just a few hundred years since Moses and the settling of the land by Israel, that distinct dialects and regional accents had occurred. The tribes of Israel were themselves nations. And subgroups like Gilead, which was the name of part of the land settled by Gad, on the east bank of the Jordan, had grown to be its own thing. God sets boundaries and habitations, dividing nations by blood and language, shifting over time as He judges them. 

We often see the term 'Shibboleth' used today as a derogatory way of describing a longstanding belief that a group of people may share that separates them from others. A way of gatekeeping looked down upon by those with modernist views, seeking to infiltrate and influence the older group.

There have been those who have accused fundamentalists of maintaining Shibboleths, from matters of separation to the sole use of the KJB, and even to the nature of the gospel...All have been attacked as 'archaic' means of resisting change in the modern era, and to that we should say "Amen!" 

Scripture tells us repeatedly of how we can recognize false teachers and warns of those creeping in privily, unawares, to spy out our liberty and to lead believers astray. The main shibboleth being the gospel of grace and reconciliation through faith in Christ. If someone brings a false gospel, we know they are not of God but accursed.

Samson begins the story by going into the cities of the Philistines, down from Dan to Timnath, and a Philistine girl there catches his eye. He returns to his parents and tells them to get her for him to wife. 

Naturally, his parents are upset at this, that he would want an outlandish woman, unclean, to wed. They ask why not a woman from their tribe or from Israel, a fellow believer, a daughter of the circumcision. He insists and they relent, not knowing that this was of the Lord. That it was an opportunity for Samson to get in with the Philistines who were oppressing Israel. 

As he makes his way back to Timnath, he encounters a young lion and tears it apart with his bare hands, by the power of the Spirit of the Lord. It is a supernatural act of strength, as an unarmed man rends a lion apart as a normal man could a baby goat. Samson, having touched an unclean thing, tells not his father or mother. 

Samson talks with the woman, and she pleases him. Time passes, and on his way back to take her as a wife, he notices the carcass of the lion and that a bee hive has set up in it, producing honey. He reaches into this dead, unclean carcass and takes of the honey with his bare hands, and eats it and gives it to his parents to eat, without telling them where it came from. 

The wedding is arranged and Samson makes a feast lasting 7 days, and having no groomsmen among the people, 30 Philistine men are made his companions. Samson offers them a bet in the form of a riddle, the stakes, 30 sheets and 30 sets of clothes. 

The men agree, and Samson says *Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness*, referring to the lion and the honey. An impossible riddle that even his parents would be unable to solve. 

And after 3 days of fruitless guessing, the 30nmen threaten the would-be bride and her family to pry the answer from Samson. She begs and pleads for the next several days and on the final day of the feast, Samson tells her the answer. His physical strength is mighty, but his weakness, as we will see throughout his story, is women. 

The 30 companions tell Samson the answer, and he knows they cheated. *If ye had not plowed with my heifer, ye had not found out my riddle.* 

And the Spirit of the Lord comes upon him, and he travels to a neighboring city and slays 30 Philistines in Ashkelon, taking from their unclean dead bodies the spoils of 30 sheets and sets of raiment, to pay of his bet.

Samson then returns to his father unmarried, and the girl is given to one of the 30 Philistine men who served as his companions.

It is always interesting to me when I read the story of Samson, how often he violated the vow of separation he was meant to live by. His being with unclean women and unclean carcasses, even eating from one, and yet the Spirit of the Lord remained on him. He was used for mighty works. But his temper and his love of women would be his undoing.

*16 And Samson said, With the jawbone of an ass, heaps upon heaps, with the jaw of an ass have I slain a thousand men.*

*17 And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking, that he cast away the jawbone out of his hand, and called that place Ramathlehi.*

*18 And he was sore athirst, and called on the Lord, and said, Thou hast given this great deliverance into the hand of thy servant: and now shall I die for thirst, and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised?*

*19 But God clave an hollow place that was in the jaw, and there came water thereout; and when he had drunk, his spirit came again, and he revived: wherefore he called the name thereof Enhakkore, which is in Lehi unto this day.*

*20 And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.*

Continuing the story of Samson, **Judges 15** picks up some time later, where he decides to visit his betrothed Philistine woman with a baby goat, and discovered that her father had married her off to another. 

Samson then, feeling vindictive as the one who was "wronged," captures and sets loose 300 foxes with torches between their tied-together tails, destroying the corn fields of the Philistines. 

When they learn of this and why, the Philistines burn to death the girl and her father, Timnite. Not satisfied, Samson slaughters many of them, then leaves for Lehi in Judah, upon the rock of Etam. 

The armies of Philistine camp against Judah, and the men of the tribe come to Samson and are wroth with him. They have submitted to being ruled over by the heathens, and Samson is causing problems. He asks if they are there to slay him, and they say no. But to be bound and delivered. 

So tied up in cords, they bring him to the camp of men, and there the Spirit of the Lord comes upon him, the bands snap like burnt cotton. Freed, the Nazarite picks up a freshly dead jawbone of an ass and slaughters 1000 men. *Heaps upon heaps.* And casting the jawbone aside, he names the place Ramathlehi, the hill of the jaw-bone. 

After the slaughter, Samson thirsts and cries out to the Lord; *Thou hast given this great deliverance into the hand of thy servant: and now shall I die for thirst, and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised?*

And out of the hollow of the jawbone sprung up a fountain, named Enhakkore, the fountain of the crier, and from this dead thing in the midst of a thousand corpses, Samson drank and was revived.

Again, we see Samson, under a lifetime vow of cleanliness and separation, using unclean things to cause havoc, and consuming that which sprung up from death. Like the honey from the lion, now the water from the jawbone of an ass. 

And yet the Spirit of the Lord still came up on him. His strength hadn't failed. He judged Israel for 20 years in the days of the Philistines. The secret of his strength not yet revealed.

Samson's story ends with a bang. His weakness revealed; Women. 

He is nearly caught because of his visit to a harlot in Gaza. And just as his riddle was given away to the daughter of Timnath for her pleading, Delilah the Philistine manages to get Samson to tell her his heart, and his belief that the Lord was with him due to his hair, kept unshaved due to his lifelong vow. 

Women, and their persistence with him, was Samson's undoing. 

The lifelong vow of the Nazarite that he violated so often, being unclean with dead bodies, eating from carcasses, drinking from bloody bones, and laying with harlots, included not taking a razor to his hair. And that's where he drew the line. 

Many times as Christians, we do the same thing. We know what we ought to do and that which we should not. And we set an arbitrary line around one particular thing, that we fool ourselves into thinking we are right with God so long as that one thing isn't violated, even as we sin all around it. 

And God is patient and longsuffering. 

But when our heart, our trust, is in that one thing, especially under a vow, and not Christ, He will punish us when we break it. Delilah was the means. The hair she shaved, the 7 locks he had, was just the thing, the vow, he used as a fig leaf. Once gone, the Spirit given strength he had was gone. 

Samson was made blind. Tied to posts and mocked. And even with stubble growing back, was still weak. Led around by a boy. 

But Samson called upon the Lord for deliverance. *O Lord God, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes*.

And the Lord answered his prayers, and sacrificing himself, Samson killed 3,000 Philistines including their lords, gathered to offer sacrifices to their false god. 

In the end it was faith that delivered Samson. In the end God was the source of his strength. Amen

*12 And Micah consecrated the Levite; and the young man became his priest, and was in the house of Micah.*

**Judges 17** begins the story of Micah, not to be confused with the later prophet, but here, a young Ephraimite in the time of the judges; *In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes*.

Micah had stolen 11,000 shekels of silver from his mother. Apparently conflicted by this, he confesses to her and returns the money, saying he had sought to bring it to a founder in order to make a graven image. A molten image. 

His mother, rather than be offended at his theft or his Idolatry, blesses the endeavor by giving 200 of the shekels to the founder herself, and commissions the graven image and the molten image to satisfy her son. 

Micah and his mother both were of Israel and recognize the Lord as their God, but had fallen so far from His way for them that they sought after idols of silver. 

The Bible says Micah had an house of gods, a church full of graven and molten images. He made an ephod, the priestly garment, and teraphim, which we would call icons, or relics. Items of worship. Micah even consecrated his young son to serve as a priest. 

Micah was an Ortho-bro, setting up a shrine. 

But an unnamed Levite, out of Judah strikes out on his way to find a place to serve. Coming to noubt Ephraim, he finds Micah, and stays with him. Micah offers the Levite the role of spiritual father, to be his priest for hire. Paying him ten shekels a year, and clothing and food. The Levite agrees and takes on the role of house priest. 

Micah says *Now know I that the Lord will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to my priest.*
(Pictured: Micah's house of gods, colorized)

Micah, doing what seems good in his eyes, thinking in some way he is following the Lord, has sought to establish his own religion, his own church, even as the Tabernacle is in Shiloh. 

His family appears to be wealthy, his mother's riches and her spoiling of her son, catering to his whims even after his theft is revealed, shows that in many ways, Micah is blessed. Born into a peaceful area, with silver enough to make idols, and even to hire a priest to legitimize his endeavor. Naturally, not knowing better, having a zeal for the Lord but not after knowledge, Micah believes his efforts are blessed of the Lord. He thinks by his accumulating idols and images, an ephod and teraphims, and even a genuine Levite to be his priest, to call "father," that the Lord will do him good. 

Micah creates a building full of gods, a priest called "father." A place of worship to the Lord that violates the commands set forth by the word of God, because it seemed right in his own eyes.

Even when our cause is righteous, and even when the right thing is to oppose the wicked, if we aren't right with God ourselves, we cannot expect His help.

Seek ye first the kingdom of God. Walk in the Spirit. Sanctify yourself, knowing that God is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.

In the final chapter of **Judges**, we see how fallen the children of Israel have come, doing only what is right in their own eyes. 

We have seen them fail to drive the Canaanites out of the land, worshiping their idols, being led by women, their holiest man under a lifetime vow, whoring and eating unclean things. Setting up their own churches and establishing their own priesthood with idols and images. Wicked stuff. 

And then, Benjamin wiped out down to 600 men, because they harbored and protected reprobate sodomites in the land, commiting abominations. Raping a woman to death because the man they sought was refused them. 

And that man, horrifyingly sending parts of her corpse to the tribes, seeking vengeance. And those tribes in turn being smitten by the sword, until they finally got right enough with God to win their over their own brethren, Benjamin. 

**Judges** is a wicked period in the history of Israel, and yet it is also a common thing in all nations that do not seek after the Lord or have Him as King over them. Even with the perfect law, a comprehensive religion and the underlying promise of salvation by faith in Him, calling upon His name, Israel are lost without a strong human leader. 

While there were undoubtedly saved believers in Israel, and they were meant to be a light to all nations, their own brethren fell away to apostasy and sin.

Here in **Judges 21**, we see even when trying to do the right thing, men left to their own heart still do that which is wicked. 

The men who went up to war from all of Israel, repented of their slaughter of Benjamin. Note, God had ultimately approved of it, giving them victory and delivering Benjamin to them. 

But they then second guess themselves. They change their mind and lament that they've put out one of the tribes, condemning it to death, because even with the remnant of 600 men, hiding out in the rock Rimmon, they had no wives or children. And the men of Israel who had gathered in the assembly at Mizpeh had sworns an oath to God that none would give their daughters to Benjamin to wife. 

Faxed with this quandary of their own making, they seek out a solution that would be right in their own eyes. 

Of course, God teaches us about vows. That we shouldn't vow at all. But if we do, follow through. 

Realizing that of all the assembly, the men of Jabeshgilead failed to come down to Mizpeh. They had foresaken the assembly, and thus had not made the vow about wives for Benjamin. And the men at Mizpeh had additionally vowed to slay any who forsook the assembly. 

And so the gathered army turned on Jabeshgilead, killing all the men and women who had lain with men, kidnapping 400 virgins, and offering them to the remnant of Benjamin. And understanding they were 200 short, strike a deal with the Benjamites that they would allow them to go to a feast at Shiloh and take 200 daughters who they could capture while they danced in the fields. Their fathers and brethren would not be held to the vow, for they weren't given but taken by force.

A wicked solution to a wicked situation.

None of this was from God. And when we Seek to do that which is right in our own eyes, error compounds error. Sin begets worse sin. 

Had everyone kept to the law, obeying the commandments of God, heeding His ways, it would have been well with them. Israel would have been a light to the world, leading the nations to God. 

Instead they fell short. They put themselves in terrible positions, and constantly needed a deliverer to save them when doing what seemed right in their own eyes failed them.

And so Judges ends with the oft-repeated admonition to us at the ends of the world; *In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.*
The greatest rebuke against Libertarianism is the Book of Judges.

The book of Judges is a difficult one, detailing the history between the settling of Israel under Joshua, and before the era of kings that begins with Saul. There are great heroes in the book, like Gideon and Sampson, but the key lesson throughout is that not everyone in the Bible behaves righteously. Many are wicked and sinful. The key to understanding is found in the often-repeated verse; *In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.*

That's the larger context. That even when the people turn to the Lord and do the right thing, it isn't always for the right reasons and many times they just do what they think is right in their own eyes. 

All this to say the story told in Judges 19-21, of the sodomites protected within the tribe of Benjamin, and God's command to smite the tribe, He giving the others of Israel victory over them for their condoning and protecting these wicked sons of Belial, is very illustrative of the times we live in today, where people do what is right in their own eyes. **Matthew 1:1-17**
*The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren; And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar; and Phares begat Esrom; and Esrom begat Aram; And Aram begat Aminadab; and Aminadab begat Naasson; and Naasson begat Salmon; And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse*...

It is interesting that the grandmother and great-grandmother of David were a Moabite and a Canaanite harlot of Jericho. That Jesus' human lineage is not one of ethnic purity. Jacob married Leah, a woman of Mesopotamia, and sired Judah. Abraham was a Chaldean. The genetic claim of Jews, so-called, to the kingdom comes through intermarrying with other nations and people. 

Also worth pointing out they are the only two women mentioned by name in the genealogy given by Matthew.

In the narrative, we see this is set during the period of Judges, where as we know, men did that which was right in their own eyes. And so we find a man of Judah, Elimelech and his wife, Naomi, deciding to leave the promised land during a famine, and seek their fortune sojourning for a season in Moab. They are there long enough for their sons Mahlon and Chilion to wed Moabite woman, Orpah and Ruth. 

And in the course of time, Elimelech and his sons die in Moab, and Naomi, hearing the famine had ended in Israel, seeks to return to her people. The decision to leave the promised land seeking bread turned out tragically for her. Her husband doing what was right in his own eyes left her bitter and feeling cursed by God for their bad choices. 

So, Naomi sets out to return to Judah, and tells her tearful daughters-in-law they are free to return to their people and their gods. Orpah does. Ruth refuses, vowing to return with Naomi, to make Israel her people, and the Lord God her God. Till death do they part. 

So, returning to Bethlehem and created by those who recognize Naomi, she tells them to call her Mara, meaning "bitter," because she says, *The Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.*

**Ruth 1** serves as a prelude for the remaining story, establishing Ruth and how she came to be in Bethlehem.

*So Naomi returned, and Ruth the Moabitess, her daughter in law, with her, which returned out of the country of Moab: and they came to Bethlehem in the beginning of barley harvest*.

A tale not quite as depressing as the descent into evil that the books of the **Judges** portrayed.

As Ruth vowed before the Lord, *for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God*. Gleaning is God's method of feeding the poor and the stranger. That they work to eat from the leftovers in the field after the harvest. A kindness, and effective means of maintaining the welfare of the people, and a picture of the blessings that fall unto the stranger by being around a group of godly believers, who in their faith are blessed beyond their needs. Ruth catches the eye of Boaz, who has come from the city to see the harvest. The servants tell him of her diligence in gleaning, her hard work, and her service to Naomi is known to him. 

Boaz tells her to stay with his maidens and servants, to glean no other field. To take freely the water his servants had drawn. That she will be safe with them. He even feeds her supper, until she is fully sufficed.

 *Then she fell on her face, and bowed herself to the ground, and said unto him, Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I am a stranger?*

It reminds me of **Psalm 8** the psalmist talking to God; *What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?*

Ruth found grace in the eyes of the lord of the harvest. The salvation imagery is so powerful here. 

As Boaz says to Ruth; *The Lord recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the Lord God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.* Her trust is in the Lord, and so her works receive recompense.

Believers are rewarded for diligently seeking the Lord. For putting their trust in Him, their works receive recompense.

The salvation of God by faith in Him was always available to all men. Even a Moabite woman. It was never exclusive to "the Jews." Israel was to be a light to the world to bring them to repentance. 

Boaz is a Godly man, following the law. He recognized Ruth by her chaste conversation, her behavior. And by extending his grace on her, that she may live off his bounty, she is thankful. 

So she cleaned until even, and brought home to Naomi a bushel of barley flour that she had ground out of her gleaning, telling Naomi it was of Boaz. 

*And Naomi said unto her daughter in law, Blessed be he of the Lord, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead.*

The bitter "Mara" seeing that God is blessing her. That His kindness to His children is eternal. To the living and the dead in Him. 

And so, Ruth kept fast to the maidens of Boaz until the end of the wheat harvest.

But when told it is a package deal, and he would have to redeem Ruth as well, the wife of the dead, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, he balks. *I cannot redeem it for myself*, he says. *Redeem thou my right for thyself; for I cannot redeem it*. 

And passing the right to the next nearest of kin, the man removes his shoe, as was custom, and tells Boaz to buy it for himself. Done before the elders, a testament in front of witnesses of all the people.

The laws of the right of redemption, and the process of securing a means of redeeming a property to keep it as part of the inheritance of the extended family, and more importantly, the redemption of the childless widow, to keep the dead man's name, to raise the dead to its inheritance, are a like picture of Christ. 

In this case, you see the nearer kinsman offered the right to redeem the parcel of land, and his willingness to do so, but his inability to redeem the person, Ruth, and raise the name of the dead. This is a picture of the Law itself.

By the Law the people could maintain their land, to keep the inheritance within the family. But the Law is unable to redeem the person, and raise their name from the dead unto their inheritance. 

Boaz, picturing Christ Jesus, desires to, and is able, to do both. 

And Ruth, a figure of the believer who has called upon the Lord to save her, bearing fruit and building up Israel, the Israel of God, that are other believers.

Beginning the book of **1 Samuel**, we are given the origin of the prophet. His father, a Levite originally from Bethlehem (also known as an Ephrathite), named Elkanah is introduced. Having two wives, Hannah, who he loved and who was without child, and Peninnah, who had children by him, and who was the adversary of Hannah, who provoked her for being barren. 

Being devout, Elkanah took his family to the Tabernacle in Shiloh to offer sacrifices, during the time of Eli as High Priest, which was during the life of Samson the judge. Eli had two sons serving as priests under him, Hophni and Phinehas. 

And so, setting herself before the Lord during this pilgrimage, Hannah weeping asks the Lord to open her womb and bear her a son, vowing to dedicate him to the Lord from birth, never to see a razor taken to his head. 

Eli witnessing her silent prayers, seeing her lips move, presumed she was drunk. But she says;

*No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the Lord. Count not thine handmaid for a daughter of Belial: for out of the abundance of my complaint and grief have I spoken hitherto.*

Eli answers that she may go in peace and the God of Israel may grant her her petition. 

They returned home, and Elkanah knew his wife, and the Lord remembered her and opened her womb, giving her a son. She names him Samuel, because he was asked of the Lord. 

And she kept him at home until Samuel had weaned, and then took him to Shiloh and made an offering to the Lord in thanksgiving, bringing the child to Eli. There she reminds the High Priest of her prayer and it being answered in her son, and her vow that he shall be lent to the Lord all his life.

The Lord uses many seemingly barren women to birth those He uses for great things. There are none truly barren in the Bible. All who are mentioned, God grants them a child. The fervent prayer of the faithful avails much, and the misery of a childless woman moves the Lord to give them a son, time and again. 

It is the weak things of this world that He uses for His purpose. 

It is important to recognize that God determines when a woman has a child or not. He opens the wombs and closes them. Children are a blessing from God, born innocent. 

**Psalm 127:3-5**
*Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: And the fruit of the womb is his reward. As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man; So are children of the youth. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them: They shall not be ashamed, but they shall speak with the enemies in the gate.*

Today, the world uses chemicals and artificial means to keep women sterile, or to create embryos to place inside them. And killing them like burdens instead of blessings. 

They seek to play God and become daughters of Belial, as Eli presumed Hannah was. They pass their children through the fire. They sacrifice them to Moloch, the god of this world. 

Even IVF, which has given many barren women a child, produces thousands of embryos that are destroyed, lives of infants sacrificed to achieve one selfish wish. They are like Hagar the bondwoman being used by Sarah to circumvent God's will. 

But the faith of women like Hannah is rewarded, and so enduring the insults of her adversary, and patiently petitioning the Lord, He blessed her.

They placed the golden images on the same fire, all while the lords of the Philistines spied this play out, having followed the cart on its way.

Now, of course the jewels of gold the Philistines used as their trespass offering is not what the Lord had established. While He had handed down specifics to Moses for a trespass offering which may not be known to these heathen priests, the knowledge of the offerings acceptable unto God was with man since Abel. 

But absent the word and not having an understanding of the spiritual things of God, they just made things up like the golden emerods and mice. Superstitiously sending the unguided cart out from them on the hopes it was near happenstance that the plague fell upon them. Seeking a sign from their own understanding. 

Ironically, they had the word of God present before them inside the ark that carried the tablets of Moses. 

They had the right God, the understanding of who He was, and His power, even acknowledging His power over the idols they worshipped. But with all that they still had no idea how to please Him, not having faith in His word. 

In much the same way we see how apostate churches, filled with idols and a priesthood that lacks understanding, makes up foolish rituals and rites, seeking after superstitious signs, despite acknowledging the true God, even the Son and holy Spirit. 

They invent sacraments, meat and drink offerings to idols, rites and practices like blessing against choking on fishbones by holding unlit candles to their throats, wearing scapulas of leather and prayer beads for luck. Burying images of men upsidedown to sell property. Calling upon spirits of house gods to find their lost items. Wishing upon these same spirits to bring them fortune. 

All of these vain traditions of men are as profane and offensive as the idea of casting golden images of a hemorrhoid and offering it to the Lord.

*And he smote the men of Bethshemesh, because they had looked into the ark of the Lord, even he smote of the people fifty thousand and threescore and ten men: and the people lamented, because the Lord had smitten many of the people with a great slaughter.*

While it is unclear how many Philistines died during the seven months of plague and evil done by the Lord, we know that of the city of Bethshemesh God slew 50,070 men for the temerity of looking inside the ark. They should have known better, who had the oracles of God and the Levites among them, to whom much had been given, but they allowed their own curiosity to get the best of them and so they were sorely punished. 

**Luke 12:48**
*But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more.*

We spend a lot of time rebuking false ways and warning those caught up in these apostate cults and damnable heresy of the Hell that awaits them if they don't repent, but it should also be a warning to us that know better. That our knowledge and understanding means that should we stray from the goodness of God, we should expect a much worse punishment for it. 

**Hebrews 12:6-7**
*For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not?*

One could argue that the ignorance of the Philistines was a pain in their ass, but the willful sin of the men of Judah in Bethshemesh was far worse because of the expectation of understanding the Lord held against them. 

A valuable lesson on obeying the commandments of God for a Christian.

Ashtaroth being the "queen of heaven" fertility goddess that the Catholics worship to this day, every bathtub-"Mary" in front yards and small groves all over America, an image to *Ashtaroth*, cursing the land. Baalim her lord.

One of the greatest revivals of all time.

The Philistines were subdued, and cities they had captured returned to Israel, and during the days of Samuel the hand of the Lord remained against them. 

And Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life, traveling the land.

**1 Samuel 13** is part one of a story regarding a particular battle with the Philistines, introducing Jonathan, King Saul's son, a faithful believer and mighty man of valor. It also continues to establish Saul as having questionable judgement when it comes to certain decisions, especially here in chapter 13. Decisions that have long lasting ramifications.

There are skirmishes with the Philistine garrisons and spoilers, or raiding parties, had been plaguing Israel. Saul with his 2,000 men and Jonathan with a thousand had gone against them and smote some, and the Philistines gathered to fight with 30,000 chariots and 6,000 horsemen and people as the sand which is on the sea shore. Their occupation has brought with it abomination in the land. 

And the people of Israel his themselves from this fierce army. In rocks and caves and thickets of wood. Some fled to Gad over Jordan. 

And Saul remained with his men, who were afraid. And Samuel had instructed Saul, telling the king to tarry 7 days for him that he would make an offering unto the Lord. But, the king, impatient at Samuel being late, and seeing the people scattered and afraid decided to wait no longer. He took it up on himself to do burnt offerings to the Lord. 

As he does, Samuel arrives and Saul goes to greet him. Samuel asks, What have you done?

*Because I saw that the people were scattered from me, and that thou camest not within the days appointed, and that the Philistines gathered themselves together at Michmash; Therefore said I, The Philistines will come down now upon me to Gilgal, and I have not made supplication unto the Lord: I forced myself therefore, and offered a burnt offering.*

Samuel rebukes the king, saying;
*Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the Lord thy God, which he commanded thee: for now would the Lord have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever. Spoilers; we know this man after God's own heart is David.

This also is a prophecy of Christ Jesus, who, like David would fulfil all the Father's will. 

And unlike Saul, Jesus is both King of kings, but also a high priest, forever. And unlike Saul His sacrifice being as the Father had ordained, and fully acceptable. 

**Hebrews 4:14-16**
*Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession. And so Saul in his haste, acting as a priest and not king, showed in his zeal a lack of judgement and faith. And sowed further seeds of his own destruction.

As we saw in chapter 12 when Samuel told the people of Israel that God had appointed them a king, despite that not being His will, that the people convicted of this sin asked for forgiveness and the sacrifices were offered and the Lord reiterated His promise to them for salvation. That if they simply turn to Him and appreciate what He's done, He will be their God and they will be His people. 

And so the Philistines which had occupied parts of Israel setting up garrisons, were afflicted by the small standing army Saul had assembled. Jonathan and Saul each liberating cities from the garrisons which had been set up in them by the enemy. Small victories that then provoked the Philistines into assembling a mighty army. 

In a similar way, Christians who have sinned and gotten right with the Lord may experience small victories and regained ground in their Christian life. God may have us live with the consequence of our sin, but He does help us to win battles against the things that had led us there. 

But like the Philistines who rallied a great army, our spiritual enemies often do the same. Their garrisons may be removed from places in our heart, but that doesn't mean that the battle is won. It's times like that where we have to be more vigilant to obey God's word and to trust in Him. 

Saul didn't learn that lesson. He leaned on his own understanding. After having provoked the Philistines into a massive retaliatory response, and seeing the fear of the people under him, Saul disobeyed the word of God doing what seemed right in his own eyes. 

We have to be careful not to undercut whatever progress God has given us. In a like manner we need to be even more vigilant as we see success given us by God.

Sometimes we get a false confidence in our own abilities, giving ourselves more credit that we deserve. Not understanding that a battle isn't the war. That we need to wait on Christ Jesus, our high priest, rather than making our own way. Often we can fall further and cause more trouble for ourselves in the long run. Sowing seeds of failure in our haste. Backsliding further than we had when God last delivered us. A cautionary tale.

*50 And the name of Saul's wife was Ahinoam, the daughter of Ahimaaz: and the name of the captain of his host was Abner, the son of Ner, Saul's uncle.*

*51 And Kish was the father of Saul; and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel.*

*52 And there was sore war against the Philistines all the days of Saul: and when Saul saw any strong man, or any valiant man, he took him unto him.*

A long chapter for a quick story; Jonathan, the son of Saul, takes his armourbearer and goes up to spy out the garrison a Bethaven, and there, seeing a choke point between two rocks, senses an opportunity for the Lord to deliver his enemies to him. 

Trusting in the Lord, Johnathan says if the Philistines call us down, we shall meet them because the Lord has delivered them to our hands. And by faith he allows them to see him, and of course they call him out. And Jonathan proceeds to smite them with his armourbearer behind, finishing them off. Twenty men fall at the first. 

And the Philistines react in the camp and the vibrations and noise reach Saul who is sitting beneath a pomegranate tree, miles away. 

Saul's watchmen tell him of the battle and he numbers his troops and realizes it is his son, faithful Jonathan. 

First Saul asks for the ark of God, but the noise increased and so Saul says to the priest, "stay thy hand."

Where Jonathan went out by faith, Saul leaned on the ark, and it failed him. And so assembling his men, and the men disorderly came together, including the Hebrews among the Philistines and those in hiding, rallying to the battle Jonathan had begun. 

Jonathan by faith showed leadership and courage that became infectious. And Saul, who had remained behind struggled to find the faith and leadership his son had displayed. Courage that brought out of hiding the fearful Israelites to attack the enemy camp. 

Despite the success, Saul commanded the men not eat until evening, a fast he decided to decree after the victory had already begun. The Lord had already saved Israel that day. By faith, not of their own works. But Saul had commanded a fast. 

And the men of Israel, exhausted obeyed. But Jonathan who hadn't heard his father's order, dipped his spear in honey that had by chance fallen on the ground, and ate it, the rush of it lighting up his eyes. Enlightened. 

While the men all looked on with fear knowing the vow Saul had foolishly made, Jonathan points out how even the taste he had of it had enlightened him, say; *How much more, if haply the people had eaten freely to day of the spoil of their enemies which they found? for had there not been now a much greater slaughter among the Philistines?*

A picture of the Spirit that quickens those who eat freely of Christ, how much greater the victory had they gone by faith and Saul had not taught for commandments the doctrines of men. 

And so they smote the Philistines and yet were faint with hunger, and so when they fell upon the spoils of sheep, ox and cow, they ate them straight away, with the blood. 

And so Saul's foolish vow, adding works of righteousness to what was won by faith alone, led the men of Israel to sin.

And so King Saul commands the spoil be brought to him and he again sets up an altar and offers the meat that it be drained of blood and the men may eat thereof. But again, this wasn't his place to do it, and so again Saul does wrong trying to do right. 

Afterwards Saul sought council of the Lord as to whether to continue through the night to spoil the Philistines, yet God does not answer. 

Saul assembled the men and asks the current high priest, Ichabod who was the grandson of Eli, to cast the lots to separate the men and find the sin that he felt was preventing the Lord's blessing. The Thummim and Urim of the High Priest's ephod. 

And so, by lot the men are separated until it is revealed that it was Jonathan who had broken Saul's foolish vow. Saul had made a big show of it during the casting of the lots, that even if it were his very own son, they would be out to death. And when it is, Saul is convinced that he must slay Jonathan. 

But the people stand with Jonathan and say as God lives they would defend his life. And so Saul forgets about it and leaves off following the Philistines, allowing them to go back to their place. 

Yet again, Saul compounds his error without admitting to it, and rather than repent or ask forgiveness, he just lets it go. 

Just as when Samuel tells him in chapter 13 that his impatient sacrifice had cost him the kingdom, the blessing and inheritance, Saul just went and numbered his men and did what he was going to do anyway. 

Christians can often be stubborn in this way. Knowing they've sinned and having been called out on it and consequences compounding, and yet they seek not forgiveness nor admit they were wrong. 

Saul keeps allowing the will of the people to decide for him as well. To please them he offered that sacrifice. To please them he reneges his vow. Saul is a weak leader and his faith is not always enough to keep him from folly, because he does what he thinks is right rather than follow the word of God.

Saul may have had the victory over the Philistines that day, but his error and his making everything worse meant he had to deal with Philistines until his death. They were a garrison in his heart. The sin that undoes so many of the faithful.

He won many great victories, he delivered Israel from enemies. He smote the Amalekites. He had sons and daughters and a wife. But the Philistines remained a threat. 

And, as Samuel had warned the people, when Saul found a strong or valiant young man, he drafted them. Bringing them into his army. Leading them off to war.

It really can be difficult to recognize that Saul was saved. He believed on the Lord. It becomes harder and harder to keep that perspective going forward, as we read through **Samuel**. But Saul was certainly saved by grace through faith in the Lord. 

His victories, the times the Lord used him for good for His people, where he was blessed personally, all show that even a less than perfect Christian can still have a great impact. But there are pitfalls and snares that we all face. And our end can be as tragic as Saul's if we allow ourselves to forget the word of God and to stay on the path He leads us. If we lean on our own understanding. If we don't recognize our error when chastised, and ask for forgiveness. The longsuffering of God has limits and He will take from us blessings and eventually even call us home if we bo longer can be useful to His works that He has crafted us to do.
