Chapter 15 of **1 Samuel**, and the tragic story of King Saul continues. The first king over Israel is given yet another chance to do the will of God, and again leaning on his own understanding, Saul does not obey God's word. 

Told to wipe out all Amalak, from the king to the infants, and all the livestock, Saul allows the men with him to spoil the best sheep and other livestock, and keeps king Agag of the Amalak alive as a captive. 

Samuel had told Saul clearly the word of God, and all he had to do was obey. And God repents of His choice of Saul as king, because he did not follow His commandments. Samuel grieves all night at the word of the Lord, and sets out to meet Saul in the morning. 

Saul greets the prophet saying *I have perform the commandment of the Lord,* yet Samuel points to the noise of the sheep and oxen, asking what is it, knowing full well. 

And Saul said they were the best of the Amalekites, taken in spoil and how he plans on offering them as sacrifice to the Lord. Seemingly oblivious to the fact that it contradicted the word of God. 

Samuel recounts what the Lord had commanded, and this was not part of it. 

*Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord?*

And the king begins to argue why his disobedience was actually righteous, and in doing so admits the problem; the people took of the spoil, and to please them Saul compromised between them and the word of God. 

Saul acknowledges his sin, that because he feared the people, he obeyed their voice not the Lord's. And full of regret, Saul begs for forgiveness and that Samuel remain with him, but Samuel breaks fellowship, telling Saul the Kingdom had been rent from him the way Saul had rent his clothes in anguish at the truth of his cowardice and compromise, when he was told he'd been rejected as king. 

*And also the Strength of Israel will not lie or repent: for He is not a man that He should repent*.

Samuel allows Saul to worship God. Saul slays the king of Amalak. And Samuel departs the company of Saul not to see him again until the day of his death. And Samuel mourns Saul: and the Lord repented that He had made Saul king over Israel.

This chapter contains some key scripture and doctrines, but the primary message for Christians here is the understanding God will give us multiple chances to be used by Him for His purpose, if we harken to His word. Follow His commandments. And every time we turn rather to what seems right in our own eyes, or add too or diminish His word, or compromise to please men, He is grieved. 

Saul, His anointed remains king until his death. But the Lord is no longer with him. The word of the Lord taken away with Samuel. Saul was castaway. He never stopped believing, never lost his salvation, but he no longer would receive the blessings and benefits, and he would backslide into vanity and wickedness. Pride and paranoia, until he lost everything including his own life. 

People who doubt the gospel will often slanderously report that we teach a license to sin. But in truth, we who are saved are held to a higher standard. To whom much is given, much is expected. The chastisement of God is fierce against our sin. 

Obedience to the Lord is not for our spiritual salvation, but rather that it be well with us and we may be His workmen doing great things for the Lord. When we compromise with the world, seek approval from men, we are dealt with more harshly.

When God sent Saul to slay the Amalak, he and the people had no problem with the genocide to be carried out when it was against things that were vile and refuse. But when they saw nice things, *the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good,* they stayed their hand and thought better of themselves than what God commands. 

Christians do this too. It is easy to eliminate many sins in our lives. To stop doing vile things, while in the Spirit. But the sin that is appealing, that seems good and profitable in our eyes. That we struggle with eliminating. 

And sometimes, like Saul, we even convince ourselves God can use it to His glory. That by not eliminating it from our lives we are actually doing right. Rationalizing evil by calling it good. 

But God will not be impressed with our rebellion.

The familiar story of David and Goliath. How a shepherd boy slew the giant with one smooth stone. It is one of the most well known stories in the world, a feat everyone has heard of and a byword for overcoming impossible odds. But the world doesn't see the lesson; that it wasn't David who overcame Goliath, but the Lord. David's faith wasn't in himself, or his weapon of choice, but the power of God to deliver him. 

*The Lord that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine*...

...*Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied. This day will the Lord deliver thee into mine hand; and I will smite thee, and take thine head from thee; and I will give the carcases of the host of the Philistines this day unto the fowls of the air, and to the wild beasts of the earth; that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. And all this assembly shall know that the Lord saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the Lord's, and he will give you into our hands.*

It is not by works we have done. It is not by our own cunningly made devices and armor. Our sword or our strength, but His. 

And all the earth knows there is a God in Israel, that our God is true and delivered David. That God doesn't save by sword and spear but He wins the battle and delivers salvation into our hands. 

The parallel with the spiritual things of God, the Christian life of trusting in the Lord. Our victories are His, that the assembly may know that it is the Lord that delivers us. The battle is His.

David believed God and it was counted for righteousness. He was anointed to be king. He had been to Saul to play the harp, be an armourbearer for the troubled king. Yet he remained a humble shepherd. Obedient to his father, he leaves to provide provision for his brothers who had been drafted into the kings service (as Samuel had warned), and to bring honor to their captain, that he may bring back word to Jesse. 

Goliath taunting the men of Israel is as the scoffers of this world. Mocking them and putting them to open shame. 

When David hears this he is angered that all the army, including his brothers, have been cowardly, allowing Goliath to humiliate them and by extension the power of God. 

His brothers, rather than be stirred by his faith, instead question David's motives. Make light of it. Just as we as Christians have family members who do just the same. Who are ashamed by our faith and their doubts, and rather than be strengthened, turn to resent us. To impune our intentions. 

David remains steadfast, and word reaches the king. Saul, once again, is far from battle. He hears our David and naysays against him; You are too young and small, with no experience fighting. 

David replies that God had already delivered unto him a bear and a lion, and that He will deliver David out of the hand of the Philistine.

Saul hearing his testimony tells David to go, and may the Lord be with him. Saul, as appointed leader, as a king who stood literally head and shoulders above all other men in Israel, who had years of battle experience, sends off a youth to do what should have been his responsibility. 

Goliath may have been 9ft tall and mighty, but Saul probably was a physical match, with the best coat of mail and helmet of brass, and a sword. Fully equipped. But he sent other men's sons out to battle. 

In typical Saul fashion, he attempts to fit David with his kit, giving him the armour and sword, but David refuses the king, saying he cannot trust those things, having not proved them. Saul's trust was in those things, David's in God. God who had proved to the shepherd that He was with him.

And so the future king, David, confronts the Philistine champion, and with his faith, slays the giant with one blow. And using Goliath's own sword, slays him and decapitates him. The Philistines flee, the emboldened Israelites pursue and slaughter them and spoil their camp. 

David returns to the king, with the trophy of his victory with him. 

Earlier in the story, when David learned of Goliath, the men of the camp had rumoured that whosoever slay the giant would be rewarded by the king;

*Have ye seen this man that is come up? surely to defy Israel is he come up: and it shall be, that the man who killeth him, the king will enrich him with great riches, and will give him his daughter, and make his father's house free in Israel.*

This is a picture of the victory Christ gives us, the reward we are elected into for allowing God to deliver us in Him, by faith. We are rewarded with eternal life, and are made His sons. And we become free, that is are set at liberty. In David's case, the family of Jesse would live tax free in the kingdom. In ours, we live free of the tax on our sin, the wages of death. 

And so with the victory won, David brought the head of the giant to Jerusalem, but kept the armor as spoil. 

Saul, as he sent off David, asks his captain of the host, Abner, *whose son is this youth?* Abner doesn't know but seeks to find out. Saul, who had known David, been soothed by the boy's harp and psalms, who had offered to bear his armor, hadn't bothered to know anything of him. 

After the fact, Abner brings David and his trophy before the king, who asks "whose son are you?" David answered Jesse of Bethlehem, but this is a picture of Jesus Christ. There's an echo of Jesus being brought before Herod, accused of the Jews for saying truthfully that He was the son of God.

Here in chapter 20 we find Jonathan, the son of the king and presumed heir torn between his loyalty to his father and to his friend, David, whom he loved like a brother. 

Saul had previously vowed before Jonathan that "as the Lord liveth he would not harm David." Unbeknownst to Jonathan, Saul broke that vow and tried to kill David in his sleep, and then at Naioth, where he'd fled with Samuel. 

Jonathan believes his father wouldn't do such a thing without telling him, but as David says, Saul knows their bond. Jonathan had already pledged his sword and bow to David. 

David makes a similar vow, swearing *truly as the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth, there is but a step between me and death.* A very similar oath as made by Saul. But unlike Saul, David and Jonathan aren't so easily swayed from keeping their word. 

While Saul is a saved believer, an evil spirit had come on him from the Lord as recompense for his constant wavering between keeping the word of God and pleasing others. Between being in faith and not fear. Now all the king knew was fear. And from that fear came envy and worry. 

David and Jonathan are also brothers in the faith, believing on the living God. 

They hatch a plan. The king would host a feast for the new moon, and when David failed to be there, Jonathan would tell his father that David was gone to Bethlehem for a family sacrifice, and had asked permission of Jonathan who'd granted him leave. 

If Saul was unperturbed by the news, all was well. But if he were to react in anger, Jonathan would know his heart and David's life was threatened. To communicate this, David would hide in a field, 3 days, and Jonathan would come with his bow and shoot arrows toward the hiding place. Jonathan devised a code; when he'd tell his young squire to fetch the arrows, of all were well, then he'd say "Behold the arrows are in this side of thee" and if Saul was wroth, he would say "Behold, the series are beyond thee." 

At the first night of the feast, Saul looked for David but made assumptions that his son-in-law must have been unclean. That he wouldn't knowingly miss the feast of the king. But the second night, he sought David and Jonathan told him their planned alibi. 

Saul instantly knows Jonathan has betrayed him for David, and shouts obscenities as his own son, calling him a son of a whore, saying that as long as David lives, Jonathan will not be established. That he will not inherit the kingdom of Israel. He then throws his javelin at his own heir, to smite him. 

Jonathan has his answer, and knows that David was correct. Saul seeks His friend's life. 

On the 3rd day, Jonathan goes to the field and fires his arrows and gives the signal that David must flee as his lad fetches the arrows. Giving his bow and quiver to the lad and sending him back to the city, Jonathan finds David and they make a tearful and tragic goodbye. 

And, as they had pledged to one another a covenant before in the name of the Lord, Jonathan reminds that David had swore not to kill Jonathan or his children when he comes to power. Jonathan reiterates this oath;
*Go in peace, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the Lord, saying, The Lord be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever*.

It is impossible to read this chapter, and miss the number of times both Jonathan and David appeal to the Lord in their communication with each other. 

*God forbid; thou shalt not die*...

*David sware moreover...truly as the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth, there is but a step between me and death.*

*And Jonathan said unto David, O Lord God of Israel, when I have sounded my father about to morrow any time, or the third day, and, behold, if there be good toward David, and I then send not unto thee, and shew it thee; The Lord do so and much more to Jonathan: but if it please my father to do thee evil, then I will shew it thee, and send thee away, that thou mayest go in peace: and the Lord be with thee, as he hath been with my father. And thou shalt not only while yet I live shew me the kindness of the Lord, that I die not...But also thou shalt not cut off thy kindness from my house for ever: no, not when the Lord hath cut off the enemies of David every one from the face of the earth.*

*So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, Let the Lord even require it at the hand of David's enemies...*

*If I expressly say unto the lad, Behold, the arrows are on this side of thee, take them; then come thou: for there is peace to thee, and no hurt; as the Lord liveth. But if I say thus unto the young man, Behold, the arrows are beyond thee; go thy way: for the Lord hath sent thee away. And as touching the matter which thou and I have spoken of, behold, the Lord be between thee and me for ever...*

*And Jonathan said to David, Go in peace, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the Lord, saying, The Lord be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever.*

The parallel with salvation, calling upon the living God, the Lord God of Israel, literally of the seed of David, and these paths sworn between Jonathan and David are obvious. Saul, like the remnant of unbelieving Jews, having the kingdom taken from him, and given to another, and so he seeks the son of Jesse's life. Just as they sought Christ's.

But Jonathan loves David more than his own father, more than his own earthly reward, more than even inheriting a kingdom of man. No greater love. We should love our brothers in Christ this much. We should love Jesus like this and more.

And when thou hast stayed three days, then thou shalt go down quickly, and come to the place where thou didst hide thyself when the business was in hand, and shalt remain by the stone Ezel.

From what I gather, Ezel may mean separation/departure, and the stone may have marked the way away from the city, a place where travelers would say goodbye to those departing on the way. But In the margin notes made by the KJV translators, they note Ezel is the stone "that showeth the way." 

Just as Jesus is the rock and the way. It is where Jonathan and David call upon the name of the Lord. Where Jonathan vows to love David's seed forever. Where they both speak of the living God, and make a covenant.

I don't know, I wondered about it and this is what I found and how it seems to me.

**Luke 6**
*And it came to pass on the second sabbath after the first, that he went through the corn fields; and his disciples plucked the ears of corn, and did eat, rubbing them in their hands.*

*2 And certain of the Pharisees said unto them, Why do ye that which is not lawful to do on the sabbath days?*

*3 And Jesus answering them said, Have ye not read so much as this, what David did, when himself was an hungred, and they which were with him;*

*4 How he went into the house of God, and did take and eat the shewbread, and gave also to them that were with him; which it is not lawful to eat but for the priests alone?*

*5 And he said unto them, That the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath.*

*6 And it came to pass also on another sabbath, that he entered into the synagogue and taught: and there was a man whose right hand was withered.*

*7 And the scribes and Pharisees watched him, whether he would heal on the sabbath day; that they might find an accusation against him.*

*8 But he knew their thoughts, and said to the man which had the withered hand, Rise up, and stand forth in the midst. And he arose and stood forth.*

*9 Then said Jesus unto them, I will ask you one thing; Is it lawful on the sabbath days to do good, or to do evil? to save life, or to destroy it?*

*10 And looking round about upon them all, he said unto the man, Stretch forth thy hand. And he did so: and his hand was restored whole as the other.*

*11 And they were filled with madness; and communed one with another what they might do to Jesus.*

Here in **1 Samuel 21** we find the story referenced by Jesus in **Luke 6**, where David fleeing Saul seeks food from the priest at Nod. All that is present is the shewbread, sanctified and hallowed. He asks that David than those with him are clean, and acquiesces to give it to them. And David, lying to say he was on urgent business of the king, asks if there be a weapon there, and providentially enough, there is the sword of Goliath whom he had slain. 

Doeg the Edomite, chief over Saul's herdsmen sees David. This comes into play in the next chapter. But it's interesting that David, son of Jacob who is Israel, the good shepherd who will be king, is betrayed by a son of Esau who is Edom, the evil shepherd, whom Saul trusted over his flocks. 

Fleeing from Nob, David crosses to the land of the Philistines, his sworn enemies, and seeks sanctuary from Saul at Gath, and their king Achish. 

The men at the gate recognize David, and even acknowledge what Saul feared, that David was truly the king of Israel, having the love of the people. But David's fame is a problem, and he fears the king will have him taken. And so he changes his behavior to that of a mad man, pounding on the gate. The king chastised the guards saying not to bring a madman into his house. 

Another interesting parallel with **Luke 6** is that the Jews become stricken with madness, determined to seek the life of Jesus, who heals the man with the withered hand in their house on a Sabbath. 

The rulers of the Jews, like Saul, understood that the Son of Jesse was a threat to their power, like David to Saul. And like Saul, they had an evil spirit fall on them and knowing they were rejected of God, they sought Jesus' life.

David, on the run from King Saul, who is seeking his life, continued to write psalms, songs of worship and praise, thanksgiving and faith in the Lord to deliver him, even while hiding in a cave in the wilderness. His trust in the Lord giving him hope, even as all of Saul's resources are turned against him. 

We see David return to Judah and seek refuge for his father and mother in Moab. Once safe there, his brothers other men gathered to join him in hiding, about 400 men. 

*And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him*.

This is a picture of Christ, gathering the distressed and discontent, those carrying the debt of sin unto Him. Despite persecution. Knowing that He shall deliver us. 

Saul hears of David's movements and those that went to him, the king *abode* *in Gibeah under a tree in Ramah, having his spear in his hand*, surrounded by his kinsmen the Benjamites, his servants. He implied that David would not treat them as well as he has, that they have land and power through Saul, appealing to their own greed. And chastising them out of paranoia for not telling him that Jonathan had betrayed him with David, aiding his escape. 

It is in this setting that Doeg the Edomite enters the court to approach the king, having witnessed David at Nob, seeking aid from the priest there, Ahimelech the son of Ahitub. Saul calls for the all the priests of Nob to come before him. 

*Saul said unto him, Why have ye conspired against me, thou and the son of Jesse, in that thou hast given him bread, and a sword, and hast enquired of God for him, that he should rise against me, to lie in wait, as at this day?*

David received holy bread and a mighty sword from the priest while calling upon the Lord. An image of the bread of life that is come down from Heaven, Christ Jesus, and His word, sharper than any two-edged sword, which is given us who seek after God. 

The priests tell the king that they had no reason to suspect David was anything but an honored servant to Saul, his very son-in-law. Despite their plea of ignorance, the king said, *Thou shalt surely die, Ahimelech, thou, and all thy father's house.* 

Saul orders his footmen, his personal guard made up of Israelites, and tells them to execute the priests, but they all refuse the kings orders. They feared God more than Saul. 

And so Saul turned to Doeg to do it for him, which the Edomite gladly did, killing 85 men that day, and then leading a sack of Nob, killing man, woman, child and beast. 

Saul like many today, turned to spiritual Edom. Away from Israel and the things of God.

*And one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped, and fled after David. And Abiathar shewed David that Saul had slain the Lord's priests.*

David realizes that he was betrayed by Doeg, knowing the Edomite would tell Saul. Taking blame for the deaths of his father's house, David promises safety to Abiathar. 

It may be Doeg David writes about in **Psalm 52**, who loves evil more than good. And lying more than righteousness. And in his tribulation, David again sang unto the Lord;

David and his men repel the Philistines successfully, and Saul hearing of it gathers his men to go up against the city thinking he could trap David there. Having a priest there with the ephod, which has the Urim and Thummim, David inquires of the Lord what he should do. Saul however acts of his own accord. 

David asks of God if the people he just saved will betray him to the king, and the answer is yes. David even shows further concern for the city that would betray him, Saul would destroy it simply to get at him. So David and his men flee. 

And so we see a cat and mouse game develop between Saul and David. And the people who David hides among, offer him up to be killed despite his heroism. Again, another picture of Christ Jesus in David. 

Jonathan again seeks out. David and the friends again strengthen their commitment, Jonathan pledging that when David is king he will serve by his side. Trusting the person whom God sent.

The pursuit of David continues, Saw getting close with his befores to David and his men. They circle around a mountain seeking escape and David is delivered when Saul is called away with his forces to another battle with the Philistines. They call that place *Selahammahlekoth,* which means the rock of escape, or the rock of separation. 

David's time in the wilderness being sought after by the enemies of the world is similar to the life of a Christian as they go from Ezel, The rock of the way, to Selahammahlekoth, the mount of separation. These subtle details are included to not only provide a narrative that we can follow and understand but contain the deeper things of God. His word really is beautiful.

The living God is the God of judgment and vengeance, delivering His sons and bringing his wrath on our enemies. As followers of Christ, we are called to love our enemies and give them a chance to repent of the evil they seek to do to us. Even to support them in their need, and to forgive them if they turn away from their anger. 

**Matthew 5:44-48**
*But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same? And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the publicans so? Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.*

This is one of the hardest doctrines to accept for many Christians. It can be the thing that snares them and keeps them from being perfect, complete, in their faith. 

Of course, to be saved, we must have trust in God's promise of salvation and eternal life in Christ Jesus. We have to believe that He can deliver us from wrath. 

We may believe that He can heal us of our sins, removing thorns from our heart and conforming us to His purpose. We will pray for our physical well-being and the safety and health of our loved ones, trusting His tender mercies and that He will help us in our affliction. 

We might even develop faith deep enough to not fear when hard times come, when money is tight, when we need food or clothing or shelter. That He will provide. 

But when we are wronged by another, when we are unfairly persecuted, or others hold us in contempt and seek our harm, it is often difficult to trust in the Lord to deliver us. To bring to nothing their schemes. We want to fight back, answer railing for railing, to protest and proclaim our righteousness loudly, to all who will listen, so they know that our enemies cause is not just. 

But what sayeth scripture?

When David has the opportunity to end this one-sided feud with King Saul, he chooses to let God judge. To allow the Lord to deliver him. 

By his kindness to Saul, humiliating the paranoid king by showing that mercy and his good intentions to all the men present, Saul was left no choice but to withdraw. David's faith in God and the righteousness of obedience to His word, not only saves his life and the life of his men, but heapes coals upon his enemy's head. 

And as we know, God's vengeance against Saul is coming, his destruction is assured. Saul knows it too, and asks favor from David, to spare his seed after David is king, a covenant David had already made with Jonathan. 

By trusting in the Lord, without a single blow, David has been delivered and his enemy made weak. Saul, with 4,000 men surrounding the cave, could have easily turned and destroyed the upstart and his small band. Instead he slunk away in defeat. 

This is the kind of faith that makes us perfect, Jesus says. The lack of fear, trusting in the righteousness established in us by Christ, testified of by the Spirit, knowing the power of the Father to deliver us. With that sure knowledge, loving your enemies becomes our strength. It is a mercy given them by victors, even if that victory hasn't been seen yet. A victory we have already received in Jesus, having overcome the world.

*And the men of David said unto him, Behold the day of which the Lord said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good unto thee.*

We may have friends and family that don't have the faith to understand this strength. They may see the opportunity to exact vengeance as a sign from God, as David's men did. They may be afraid, and look for the easiest way out, and push you into taking it with the best of intentions.

It can be hard to do the right thing in the presence of that kind of peer pressure. 

It is notable that while Saul consistently bowed to that sort of pressure, choosing to please man rather than do as God said, David does the right thing and silences his men by keeping to the principles of righteousness as God has given us. 

Had he done as they thought best, doing what seemed good to him, rather than what is good to the Lord, who knows what may have happened, but it's a good bet that they'd be in worse straits, surrounded and outnumbered and without the protection of God, having not trusted in Him. 

So take heart. Faint not. Trust in the Lord. Do what's right in His eyes. The rest takes care of itself.

Here in chapter 25 of **1 Samuel**, with several more chapters left, and a whole **2nd Samuel** to come, the titular prophet himself dies. Even with all he had done for the Lord and the 40 years he'd judged Israel and stood as its moral compass, his death is a paragraph. His life is not wasted, his eternity secure, and the impact of his work for the Lord reverberating even now, to us today, but his death is hardly a mention. 

It is a fitting way to view things for the saved Christian. We will all die physically, but that's just a moment in time. We are dead to the flesh as it is, and sealed by the Spirit unto redemption and eternity awaits in Christ. So we should live as Samuel, while we draw breath and not worry about the moment God takes us home to be with Him. 

And with the prophet's death, David goes down to Paran, still hiding in the wilderness, 600 men with him in his band. And while staying there, they were near a wealthy man's fields near Carmel, where this man, Nabal had his flocks. 

And Nabal was married to a beautiful, believing woman named Abigail. But Nabal was mean and greedy, a son of Belial according to his servants. Churlish and evil in his doings. 

David, hearing Nabal had come down to sheer his flock, sent 10 young men to see the rich man, and to ask of him some food and supplies, seeing as how David's men had helped guard the area and protect his herds and herdsmen from harm. He sends them in peace, reiterating this three times. 

And Nabal, hearing their plea mocks David, railing against him that he was in rebellion to the king, an obvious lie. He tells the young men to leave with nothing, saying he doesn't know them or owe them anything. 

David, hearing this, is outraged. He tells 400 of his men to girde up and grab their swords, for to go an slay Nabal and all his servants, the menfolk, those who pisseth against the wall. 

Now one of the servants of Nabal makes an appeal to Abigail, telling her the circumstances and fearing for his life. She puts together a fitting tribute of provisions, sending it before her, and sets out an ass to see David and plead her case. 

David, still angry at being used and railed against by her husband, meets up with her, and she bows before him, begging his forgiveness in the name of the living God. 

Nabal, the very name meaning foolish, has acted rashly, she says. Abigail says that her meeting him is a divine appointment, an act of the Lord, staying David's hand from shedding blood and taking vengeance for himself. 

She prophesies that surely David is the Lord's anointed, that the spirit is upon him, and soon enough he would be king and his enemies would be destroyed. And when that surely comes to pass, the insults of Naban will mean nothing to him. 

*And David said to Abigail, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me: And blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand.*

David takes her gifts and sends her away in peace. 

Abigail finds Nabal drunken, holding a feast fit for a king, his heart merry within him, so she holds off on telling him what she had done. His reveling showing his greed, that if he had that much food and drink to waste at a party, it would have been nothing to him to spare what David had asked for. 

But in the morning, when his wife tells him, the Bible says, *his heart died within him.* If he wasn't a reprobate, a true son of Belial, before, he was now. And ten days later, the Lord smote Nabal and he died. Vengeance is His.

David, upon hearing the news that the Lord had avenged him, immediately sends for Abigail to wife. But least we think this was a good and proper thing, or see some romance in it, the Bible also mentions immediately after that David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel to wife. But Saul had gave Michal his daughter, wife of David, away to another man, Phalti, which will come into play later on.

It is interesting that just a chapter after David had trusted in the Lord, by passing on the opportunity to slay Saul and end his exile, showing great faith and patience, David reacts so strongly to the railing of Nabal. 

Not only had David humiliated the king, heaping coals on his head, and gained more favor in the eyes of the Lord by not rebelling against the appointed leader over him, despite Saul's murderous heart, David had shown the Christian spirit to his men who wanted him to kill the king. Being a great example to them, and by extension to all of us who have read this. 

But sometimes, especially after a victory in the Christian's life, we face temptations. The world turns harder against us. We become less guarded against our own sins, and fall victim to our flesh, just as we should be growing more in the Spirit. 

Sometimes it feels like we are determined to sabotage what God has wrought in us, and the Devil is all too happy to give us the opportunity to stumble and fall, that he can accuse us before the Lord. 

Sometimes we catch ourselves. Other times our passions run so hot, we need another saved person to act as our better angel, advising us against the evil we are set to do, as Abigail does here for David. 

And often, even if we turn from the worst that we might do, we settle on a lesser sin to scratch that itch within our flesh. The thorn in our hearts. 

Abigail, a godly woman and beautiful, was loyal to her wicked husband. She didn't betray Nabal or allow David to take him off her hands, rather she saved his life. She did right by the Lord and by her husband and it worked out for her that the Lord destroyed Nabal. 

But David is married, and yet seeks her for his wife. While Abigail does nothing wrong. Being a window, David falls into sin. And not only with Abigail, which may have been a great love story, but with yet another woman, making Abigail a sister wife to Ahinoam. David's sin affects her, and will lead him to greater sin with Bathsheba, and eventually will serve as a bad influence on his son Solomon, who will have a thousand wives and concubines. 

This is why we can't rest on our victories, we can't become complacent just because we have done the right thing, and God has blessed us for it. We should always keep in mind **1 Peter 5:8;**

*And when Saul enquired of the Lord, the Lord answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets.*

The Lord has left him to his fear. 

Now Saul was not the best leader, and wasn't the most dedicated believer, but he had the decency to cast out and kill the abominable; the mediums and necromancers and wizards from the land. *And Samuel said to Saul, Why hast thou disquieted me, to bring me up? I believe this is the first time the familiar actually has seen the spirits of the dead. I believe that, as most sorcery and divinations, are scams that prey on people's weaknesses, fear and depression. And are satanic in their practice because of it. But every so often, they are used by evil spirits, or even allowed a glimpse of the spirit world by God, to His purpose, as was the case here. 

Samuel upbraides Saul, and reminds him of the prophecy Samuel had already told the king; the kingdom was lost to him and would be David's. 

 *Because thou obeyedst not the voice of the Lord, nor executedst his fierce wrath upon Amalek, therefore hath the Lord done this thing unto thee this day*.

The spirit of Samuel goes on to say the Philistines will be victors, and that in a day, Saul and his sons will lose their lives to the heathen. 

Saul is devastated, and already fasting, refused food. But the witch convinces the doomed king to eat, finally, a fattened calf and unleavened bread, and sends the king to meet his fate.
Sometimes, I feel as though Christians may say that they feel like David. But for the most part I think most act more like Saul.

Now, David had gone to Ziklag originally out of fear of Saul. Unlike the doomed king, David had the word of God, the ephod with the Urim and Thummim, the blessing of the prophet Samuel, and the Spirit of the Lord upon him. The Lord had delivered David multiple times, and rewarded him for his faithful service to Him and to his king, despite Saul's persecution. David had all those, but in the midst of tribulation, he fled to his enemies the Philistines, and took up residency in Ziklag. 

There, he and his men and their wives and children, along with the priest Abiathar lived for over a year, spoiling the Amelekites and other heathens, giving a portion to King Achish of the Philistines, claiming he was taking it from Judah. Living a lie, in deception out of fear. 

That lie nearly cost he and his men everything, as they went up with Achish and his legions to invade Israel, setting them against their own brethren. But God had another plan for him, and the princes of the Philistines told the king they didn't trust him, and so the king sent David and his band home.  

There's a time when we are tried that we may do what seems right in our eyes. Where our faith isn't perfect, and our trust in the Lord to deliver us is overwhelmed by fear, and we make bad choices. We sin. We fall back into the world. We hide our faith to fit in with the world, and tell ourselves that we are still doing the work of the Lord, even though we are hiding it from the unsaved around us. Lying to them and ourselves. 

The Lord may still save us from the worst consequences of our actions, but He may also let us twist in the wind a little bit, to help us develop the faith we should have had in the first place. 

This is true of David, as the Amelekites had raided their town, and taken captive their wives, sons and daughters, spoiling the village and burning it to the ground. 

The men with David are distraught, some seek to stone him, blaming his poor leadership for bringing this desolation to their door. 

They weep and wait until they cannot anymore, David with them, his wives gone into captivity as well. 

In their despair, David encouraged himself in the Lord his God. Doing what he should have done 16 months before. Determined, he seeks the Lord's council and calls for the ephod, enquiring what he should do. The Lord tells him to go and overtake the spoilers, and they will recover all without fail. 

So David and his 600 men head out, but partway there, by the brook of Besor, 200 men, exhausted fall out and remain behind. But David and the 400 pursued the raiders, and finding an Egyptian boy, a servant to the captors, they play him with food and water and he agrees to take them to their camp. 

There David and his men smite the Amelekites from dusk through dawn and into the next evening, sparing none but 400 camel riding men who fled. All of their families were safe and sound. Their possessions accounted for plus spoils beside. 

As they return to Ziklag, they reunite with the 200 who had stayed behind, and some of the men with David, reprobates, sons of Belial, tried to deny those who hadn't made it to the camp any portion. But David insisted that they be compensated as much as the rest. The blessings of God had been given them by His grace, and would be shared throughout. Blessings so abundant, David had enough to send forth to Judah and his friends, saying; *Behold a present for you of the spoil of the enemies of the Lord.*

Having learned a hard lesson, nearly losing everything, David turned again to the Lord and the Lord delivered him, and with more than he had feared he had lost. 

Keep this in mind when you fear the worst. When you want to flee to Ziklag. When you want to seek your own way, better the way of the Lord. 

*And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.*

So keep the faith.

And so we come to the end of Saul, a Benjamite, son of Cis, or Kish as it is in the Old Testament. A man head and shoulders above the other men of Israel. Anointed by God to be their first king. 

And while Saul was most assuredly saved, his life as king was not the example of a Christian walk that we aspire too. 

We see him developing from a loyal son, seeking the lost donkey of his father, to an unsteady and uncertain leader, plucked from the least tribe of Israel, just a generation removed from their decimation for harboring sodomites. Every bit the part of king, but with none of the heart to lead. 

Saul spends his time as King worrying about what others think of him, what they may do or say. Caring about the world over the word of God. Indecisive. Prone to bad choices. And ultimately paranoid and wrathful, knowing the Lord had repented of his kingship and had chosen another to take his place. David, the apple of God's eye. A man after the Lord's own heart. 

Now to Saul and his sons would have been the promises given to David. But his transgressions against the Lord were too great. And even with warning after warning, Saul back slid further and further. 

Had this Saul repented, and confessed his sin and asked for forgiveness, he may have been restored. But he was blinded by the evil spirit given him by God for his disobedience. Seeking the witch of Endor was the final straw, and God gave him an ignoble death, and a fitting end, along with his sons. 

It is fitting that of all the people God could choose to use to spread the gospel to the Gentiles, He found a man of Benjamin named Saul, also known as Paul (his Roman name), the name and the tribe redeemed by Paul's dedication to the word of God.

We see that, following his conversion on the road to Damascus, where he was blinded by God but restored by His word, when he sought out Ananias and was healed, Saul/Paul did his best to keep the word of God, and to not be castaway. Mortifying his flesh against sin. Preaching hard against backsliding and for separation from the world. A man who risked being rejected by his own people, being tortured, stoned, persecuted, arrested, held in bonds for years, and likely died for the cause of Christ. 

The two Sauls of Benjamin couldn't have been more different. But both were the anointed of God.

The men of the camp rend their clothes and David mourns the loss of the king, and especially his son Jonathan, who was closer than a brother to him. 

*Also he bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow, behold, it is written in the book of Jasher.*

This verse is mildly controversial, referencing a lost, deuterocanonical book, the Book of the Righteous, transliterated from *Jasher*. In the King James, this verse has *use of the* added before the bow to make it easier to understand. The bow being the preferred weapon of Jonathan, David instructed that the sons of Judah be instructed in it, to be proficient archers like his slain friend.

Without having this apocryphal book, the preserved and inspired word of God gives us the only information we need about what it contains. Many forgeries claiming to be *The Book of Jasher* have been passed off over the years, but the important content is preserved by God for all ages. 

I personally believe there is a double meaning here, and that *the Bow* is also the name of the song David wrote to honor the mighty who have fallen, King Saul and Jonathan, lamenting their deaths, celebrating his friendship and calling all Israel to mourn.

*How are the mighty fallen* is yet another wildly used phrase in popular culture, that comes from the beauty of the King James Bible translation. As an idiom, it has come to mean that someone once in power has been toppled. 

The song of David's mourning is far more valuable and insightful than just this poetic turn of phrase. 

We see David demonstrate true sadness at the loss of Saul. Forgiveness that he extended to someone who had been his bitter enemy for years. Someone who had tried to kill him multiple times. We expect the future king to mourn the loss of his beloved friend Jonathan, but his kind remembrance of the fallen first King of Israel, recalling his valiance and goodness to the daughters of Israel, shows the forgiveness that Christians should have towards one another. Especially in death, knowing that we ourselves will be transformed as fully new men, and our past sins forgotten and forgiven by the Lord. 

David strived to make peace with Saul while the king was alive. And in death, honored the Lord's anointed. No resentment or bitterness. 

But more; In the death of those who've hurt us, or were against us, we should also offer this spirit of forgiveness and let go of any enmity to those who may not have been saved. To our unsaved parents who've wronged us, to family we've felt betrayed us. To friends and neighbors and coworkers who may have done us wrong, without cause. We should let go of the animosity and hurt feelings we may have had, because we know that they have their punishment. That God is just and He will repay. We should only lament that they weren't won to Christ in life, and let go of the pain of the past. 

This attitude of forgiveness is one of the key aspects of Christian life. It is part of what allows us to live peacefully with all men. To have a productive life filled with love, joy and longsuffering. Building our faith. 

If you have animosity towards a brother or sister in Christ, let it go. And if they've passed on, joyfully look for them in the resurrection. 

And if it be that they never believed, rest easy knowing that the Lord is just.

I hope those who skim my channel, the 100 or so daily visitors, stop for a moment and read that last post, and take it to heart. When you see the forgiveness of David, a man after God's own heart, you can learn from it and find peace.

Following the death of Saul, when Judah made David King over them, and a Benjamite captain, Abner made one of Saul's sons, Ishbosheth, king over the rest of Israel. 

David at first appealed to the men of Gilead, and others, but they followed after Abner. And eventually to rectify the matter, the two camps met at the pool of Gibeon, and agreed to allow a small battle of their respective camps to determine the matter. Twelve each, in what became known as the 'land of sharp blades,' Helkathhazzurim. 

David's men were victorious, and Abner beaten, fled. We hear of the hero Asahel, fleet of foot, who pursued the Benjamite captain. And Abner repeatedly sought to deter Asahel, wishing to spare him. But in the end Abner slew his pursuer, and made it to Benjamin to seek refuge. 

Seeing that the only resolution in this was an all out battle between Judah and Benjamin, Abner asked for peace and Joab, that captain of David's men held back from attacking. They returned to David and buried their Asahel as a hero. David lost 19 men total, Abner's men lost 360.

First, we see David, a man after God's own heart, inquire of the Lord if he should go unto Judah, into Hebron. And the Lord answered saying yes. 

David further sought peace with the men of Israel, specifically Jabeshgilead who had honored Saul by retrieving his body from the enemy, and informing them all that Judah had anointed him king. A peaceful offer to do the same. Letting them all know he was willing to honor them. 

We see even though Abner's plans were different, that he took sought an outcome that was as peaceful as possible. They agree to a battle of champions, 12 vs 12. When that doesn't go his way, and he flees, Abner seeks peace with the one pursuing him. When the men of Judah arrive and see the gathered forces of Benjamin, again he cries out for peace. 

There is an honor in being a peacemaker. Regardless of the righteousness of the cause or the bitterness of the disagreement, or whatever else has been done to wrong the different parties. Especially between brothers.

The most peaceful solution should always be sought, even when that solution is rejected and more forceful action is required. Even if peace creates an uneasy result, it is preferable than brothers going to war with one another.

And while the conflict between Judah and Benjamin wore on, David grew stronger and Saul's house grew weaker. And so the loyal servant grew determined to make peace and place David as King throughout all of Israel. He sent word to David and promised to deliver him the support of the elders of Israel. The theme of the last few chapters of 1st Samuel, and these opening chapters of 2nd, continues to be the right place for wrath and the importance of forgiveness.

But his love for God and trust in the Lord to carry him through, seeking peace with his enemies and leaving vengeance to the Lord made him a man after God's own heart. 

That kind of leadership pleased the people far more than the fear of Saul, who acted impulsively trying to please everyone but God.

King David's first thought at being anointed over all Israel was the restoration of the ark of God, and so he sought to return it from where it has been since being recaptured from the Philistines. During Saul's reign, he apparently never thought to do so. 

And they take it down to Jerusalem, singing praise and playing instruments and dancing before the Lord. But the oxen stumble, and Uzzah falters and touches the ark, disrupting the peace, and is struck down by God then and there. 

Was Uzzah's sin not trusting in the Lord to deliver His ark to the house of David? I think so. But his death set David back, and the king questioned his own wisdom in brining the ark down. Fearing God he sought a sign and left the ark with the house of Obededom, the Gittite. 

It always makes me laugh thinking about how Obededom must have felt about that. But the grace of God was upon him, and his house blessed, and David knew it was God's will to finish the journey and bring the ark to His city. Where God had placed His name. Where Abraham had offered tithes to Melchizedek, to the Lord. Where Abraham offered Isaac. Where Christ would one day suffer and rise again in glory.

David's first wife, Saul's daughter Michal, who had loved David, now despises him. And in her hatred she mocks the king for his celebration of God before the ark. Trying to shame him for his behavior. In the end her bitterness costs her a chance to bear an heir. She dies childless. Consumed by resentment towards her one time love, and the failures of her father. It's tragic, but all too common in this world today. 

Many women find themselves like Michal. Facing adversity and tribulation, they turn to misery and not to God. It is a sad, lonely life. Often ending in reprobation. 

It is important for fathers and mothers to show their daughters the love of Christ early and often, that they may believe and in faith accept what ever comes. Blessings and temptations. Having a solid foundation in Jesus.

Having been made king over all Israel, David establishes an empire, conquering the surrounding areas, from the city of Gath of the Philistines, where David had sought refuge, up to the Syrians and the border of the Euphrates River, and down to the Moabites and the Edomites over the Jordan, making all the surrounding nations into vassals paying tribute to Israel. Critics of the Authorized Version of the King James Bible, and nonbelievers alike, will point to an apparent discrepancy in the telling of these events taken from **2 Samuel 8** and its parallel in **1 Chronicles 18**, a matter of horsemen and chariots. 

*David smote also Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates. And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: and David houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved of them for an hundred chariots.*

vs 

*And David smote Hadarezer king of Zobah unto Hamath, as he went to stablish his dominion by the river Euphrates. And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: David also houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved of them an hundred chariots*.

The difference between the two numbers is "corrected" in many modern versions, while others leave it but attempt to change the wording in a way to square the seeming contradiction. 

But is there a contradiction? The number of chariots and horses, 100, remains consistent, as David cut the hamstrings of the other horses taken, and only kept 100 chariots. 

To me it reads that David did the same with the horsemen themselves, decimating them and reserving 700 out of 7000, for the hundred chariots and horses he reserved. 

Matthew Henry agrees with the King James reading and offers this explanation: "The horsemen are here said to be 700, but 1 Chronicles 18:4 they are said to be 7000. If they divided their horse by ten in a company, as it is probable they did, the captains and companies were 700, but the horsemen were 7000."

The fact that God inspired the retelling of much of these histories in two places written years apart, for our own knowledge and admonition, is a blessing. That they have been preserved for us is a providential miracle. Seeming discrepancies that can be explained by simple understanding, comparing the two accounts, should be understood to be a different view of the same event, not in error but giving an additional detail not given in the other. Or a clarification of a point God wished us to have. 

That modern versions use these to cast doubt or to inject their own words is a mistake that comes from a lack of faith in the preservation of the word.

And how do we know we can trust the KJV? If there's a discrepancy like this, could it be wrong? 

Thankfully, we can compare scripture with scripture;

**2 Samuel 10:18**
*And the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew the men of seven hundred chariots of the Syrians, and forty thousand horsemen, and smote Shobach the captain of their host, who died there.*

**1 Chronicles 19:18**
*But the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew of the Syrians seven thousand men which fought in chariots, and forty thousand footmen, and killed Shophach the captain of the host.*

And so we see that for 1000 chariots we have 7000 men, and so with the decimation of the company of chariots and horsemen, a 7-1 ratio, both accounts in Samuel and Chronicles are correct.

Here in **2 Samuel 9**, we see David, now King of Israel, honoring the covenant made with Jonathan, the son of Saul. He extends not only mercy and forgiveness to Mephibosheth, but provides him with his inheritance, servants to care for him, and that he shall eat at the king's table, forever. 

Mephibosheth is a picture of a sinner, seeking grace in the eyes of the King, who is a picture of Christ. He was crippled in youth, as we are in sin, and custom would have the heirs of the previous king killed, yet David not only pardons him that fate, but sets him up as an adopted son, welcome at his table. 

This is the mercy and grace we are to show to people. David, unlike the paranoid Saul, does this kindness and keeps his oath and is rewarded by the loyalty of Mephibosheth later during an uprising, when the young lord is betrayed by the servant, Ziba, who David had placed under him. 

(Ziba is a picture of the Jews who were unfaithful servants, as we will see in chapter 19)

The world today would see David's actions as weak and foolish, but as we see again and again his faith in the Lord and willingness to forgive and make peace has led to David being strong, bringing the whole region under his control. Blessed by God, his enemies destroyed before him. 

This lesson, to be as David, to show the mercy and grace God showed us on others, is a lesson in faith.

*Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the Lord do that which is good in his sight.*

This encouraging message of faith given by Joab before what could have been a haplessly outnumbered battle, with his forces split and surrounded, should be a mantra for Christians, especially Christian men. 

Too often today, professing Christian men come off as afraid, behave with no honor or duty to their people, and do not trust in the Lord to do what He sees as right.   

We see it daily, especially among the "conservatives," and even the more right-wing. Men, who seeing the odds and thinking that it's "so over," that the "West has fallen," either cower in fear, retreat from the world to hide, or take up blindly reactionary causes to "do something!" and force outcomes without any faith in the Lord to provide victory. 

But the Bible tells us again and again to have no fear. In the life of David we see that he behaved like a man, valiantly. Having the morality of God to guide him and following His word. Trusting in the Lord to deliver him and his people. And in his leadership, King David's faith and attitude trickled down to his captains, and from them to their men. And eventually to all Israel, rising up to put an end to the threats facing them, when God delivered victory against their enemies. 

That's the secret to winning. To win souls and obey God, live righteously and trust in Him when the battle comes.

The famous story of David and Bathsheba, and the King's gravest sins. Coveting, adultery, lying and murder.

 David not being with his men in battle during the time for war left him opportunity for sin. Idle hands are the devil's tools. His gaze falling on another man's wife and her nakedness, compounded by the covetous nature of the lust it stirred in him. His use of his station to bring her in unto him to lay with her. All stemming from that initial dereliction to his duty. 

A Christian who sins often finds themselves in that situation by a similar set of circumstances. We are to crucify our flesh daily and walk in the Spirit. The Bible tells us that we should wake in the morning in prayer. Beginning the day getting right with the Lord. 

But David tarried in bed, rather than in battle. And rather than refresh himself in the Spirit, thinking of the things of the Lord, he wandered. 

When we do that, blow off our commitments, "take a day off" from prayer or study, we often wander, too. 

Temptations that we would not normally experience present themselves, and with our minds not on the spiritual things of God, we can give in to them. 

Of course David's actions have consequences. Our Father often lets those consequences of our willful sin have repercussions that are for our admonition and instruction. A chance to make it right. And yet often our sinful nature leaves us making it worse. 

David seeks to cover up Bathsheba's pregnancy by sending for her husband, Uriah. Hoping the Hittite would take the opportunity of coming from the front lines to Jerusalem to visit his wife and lay with her, covering up the pregnancy. 

But Uriah has more honor than that, and refuses the comfort of home while his fellows are encamped for war. His commitment to his duty contrasting with David's initial dereliction. 

David tries again, all but ordering Uriah to his home, sending a feast from his own royal kitchen, and still Uriah stays with the guards and servants. 

David's attempts to get Uriah to do the wrong thing fail, so the King takes more desperate measures to cover for his sin. He orders his general, Joab, to send Uriah into the hottest of battles, that he may be smitten dead. David goes from a momentary lapse in duty and honor to premeditated murder. 

This is how Christians backslide. This is how sin compounds.

Of course, David takes Bathsheba as his wife, one of many. He lives with his sin and the poor decisions he has made. But the Lord is displeased and David's actions won't remain hidden for long.

Here in **2 Samuel 12** the prophet Nathan is sent by the Lord to expose David's sin in taking another man's wife and doing it dishonestly through murder. 

Nathan speaking the words of God tells David a parable of a rich man with abundant flocks who takes the poor man's only ewe. David is outraged at the story and demands the rich man be put to death for his lack of mercy, only to be told by the prophet that the rich man is the King. 

The Lord knows our secret sin, and the things we are ashamed of will be revealed in due time. But God is also merciful, in that while we may sin and while we may face temporal punishment for it, He will not impute our sin against us, because we are justified in Christ. 

*And David said unto Nathan, I have sinned against the Lord. And Nathan said unto David, The Lord also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die.*

We who are saved in Christ shall not die. Our sin has been put away by the washing of the regeneration given to us by the Spirit, by trusting in the blood of the Lamb. 

But in this life we will be punished, that we may learn and the glory of God be known, not just by His mercy but His wrath. As an example for others. 

And so the prophet tells the king that David's wives will be taken from him, and what he did in darkness will be done to him in broad daylight. That the Lord would raise up evil against him from his own house. And finally, that the son Bathsheba gave him will surely die. 

David acknowledges his sin and understands his plight is of his own making, and ultimately accepts God's judgment against him. This is a model for us to follow. This is how we get right with God.

And so David's son is stricken with illness, and for seven days the king refuses to eat or any comfort, hoping that God may repent and spare his son. But on the 7th day, his infant child dies. The servants are hesitant to tell the king, but David sees their whispering and asks is the child dead, and they say yes. 

David arises from his mourning and asks for food, and the servants are amazed that he took the news so well. But David says, while the boy lived he hoped that the Lord might turn from his judgement, but now that he's dead he knows he will someday see him again. 

This is the comfort we have in the death of a young child. That they are with Christ in Heaven. 

It is curious that many professing Christians teach the lie of original sin condemning infants, innocents who have not sinned themselves, and will often use **Psalm 51** to do it, while the Psalm was written by David during his despair, saying he himself was wicked beyond measure, using hyperbole to describe his own condition in this very matter, not to condemn his own child.

And so in time the Lord blessed David and Bathsheba with a son they name Solomon, telling Nathan to tell them to call him Jedidiah, because *the Lord loved him*. 

Solomon is the Lord showing them that they are forgiven, a sign of His grace towards them. Reconciled by a son, born to a king, whom the Lord loves. A sort of picture of Jesus.

Meanwhile, the war against Ammon continued, and Joab has their capital in hand. He sends word to the absent King David to come with his armies to finish the job, lest Joab takes it and the crown himself. This is a jab at David for his dereliction that led to the sin with Bathsheba. And David does as Joab says, taking the city.  

Unlike previous conquests which were led by David and given victory by the Lord, where David took the spoil of gold and silver and dedicated to God, here he takes the golden crown for himself and places it upon his own head after a victory he played no real part in. And then subjecting the Ammonities to be servants of Israel, enslaving them, so soon after being forgiven by God.

After all the mercy and grace God showed him, and for all his regret for what he had done, David seems to still not be fully right with the Lord.

It is important to note that God primarily punished David for *given great occasion to the enemies of the Lord*. 

We who are professing believers are supposed to live like it. To be blameless before others. Not sinless, which is an impossible standard while we live in the flesh, but blameless. Trying to do the right thing, being a good example. Living like we have eternal life. Princes of the Kingdom. 

Keeping that perspective can be difficult at times. But forgiveness, mercy and grace, charitable love, meekly displaying the joy we have in the hope of Christ, goes a long way towards bringing others to the truth of Jesus. His light shining through us. 

And so when we wilfully sin, and bring shame on the gospel, giving *great occasion to the enemies of the Lord* *to blaspheme,* do not be shocked when you are chastened by the Lord.

The continued consequences for David's sin and his poor example as father have begun to compound, just as Nathan prophesied. 

His multiple wives have led to near siblings lusting after another. David's growing comfort as King has led to his being soft with his sons, and esteeming their feelings and his feelings for them over the love of God and His commands. 

And so David's son Amnon is sick with desire for his half sister Tamar. Tamar is sister of Absalom, both children of David and his 4th wife Maacah, the daughter of Tamil, the king of Geshur. 

Under the subtle provocation of his cousin, Jonadab, who tells Amnon to fake like he's sick and ask for Tamar to come prepare food for him, he enacts the plot and takes the opportunity to rape his half-sister, who the Bible tells us was a virgin. 

As he begins to force her, she says to stay his hand and simply ask the King to give her as wife, a request she says David would grant. This, to me, says a lot about how spoiled David had made his sons. But it may have just been a desperate attempt by the princess. 

And as soon as Amnon has raped her, his feelings of lust are replaced by hate, hating her more than the love he'd previously felt. 

Often in sin, we crave what we ought not and then despise the thing we'd craved. It is the nature of sin. Pleasure for a moment and pain for a lifetime. 

The prince casts her out of his house, further compounding her shame. In anguish and no longer a virgin, Tamar rends her colorful dress that marked her chastity and returns to her brother's house. 

This thing done in secret is known throughout the kingdom. Absolom is furious and promises revenge. David hears and is angry, but does nothing. 

Had he followed the law of God, there were remedies. He could have had his son executed. He could have forced their marriage. But he did nothing for fear of his children more than the Lord. This sets in motion a series of terrible events. 

After two years of inaction, Absolom devises a plot for revenge. He calls all the brothers and even the King to the shearing of his flocks. David declines but the princes agree and go to the feast prepared as a trap for Amnon. And there, when Amnon was drunken, Absolom ordered his servants to murder the prince. 

The other brothers flee, Absolom as well, going north to his grandfather's Kingdom of Geshur. 

David at first hears that all his sons are dead, and suffers this anguish before the wicked cousin Jonadab tells him the news that it was only Amnon. The rest returned and mourned with David. 

And despite it all, David longed to reunite with Absolom, which would be soon enough.

Parents do their children no favors by withholding punishment from them. God the Father scourges every son He receives. It should always be done in love, and appropriately, not to frustrate the child but to edify and bring them to understanding.

And so, Absolom, having been forgiven and embraced by his father David for murdering his brother, begins to plot a coup. With vanity and flattery, he captures the hearts of Israel. He builds himself a small army, with horsemen and chariots. He subverts the judgment of the King by intercepting those come to seek judgment, and disingenuously pronouncing everyone who comes seeking resolution to a conflict as being right and just, while insinuating his father David is failing them. All under David's nose. 

With this support established, Absolom tells his father that he had vowed a vow to God for his 40th birthday, to return to his place of birth in Hebron to offer himself to the Lord. And so, blessed by David, the prince begins his seditious plan. 

Sending spies throughout Israel, he tells them when the trumpets sound, to announce that Absolom has been anointed king in Hebron. 

David's chief councilor, Ahithophel goes with Absolom as part of the conspiracy, and to grow the upstarts support. 

Eventually, David is informed of the plot and it's progress, and to protect the lives of the people of Jerusalem, he evacuates the city to the wilderness, to the mount of Olives, where Jesus so often went to preach and pray. 

David's humility and faith, and his concern for the bloodshed that would come up on Israel is contrasted with his son's disregard for the people, only seeking power. Lying about an oath to the living God, and misleading 200 men to accomplish it. 

David does leave behind some people. 10 of his concubines to keep the house. He sends the priest Zadok and his sons and the ark back to Jerusalem, saying it is where it belongs regardless of God's judgment upon him. 

Loyal servants follow David, and a testimony of one who had just arrived under David's house refused to leave him, even as the King gave him permission to flee and not face their fate. Ittai the Gittite, in my opinion, is a picture of a new believer in Christ, who comes to believe during tribulation. The messianic imagery of the loyal servants following the king into the wilderness to praise God during peril, a picture of the great tribulation. Especially that Gentiles like the Gittite are among them, while disloyal men of Judah plot the murder of the King. 

Hushai the Archite came to meet David, another council of his house. David says to return to the city and spy on Absolom and pass information on to the Zadok and Abiathar, to relay it to the king. And Absolom came into Jerusalem without a fight.

David continues his exile in the wilderness, passing through Benjamin. There he encounters Ziba, servant of Saul to whom David commanded keep watch over the lame son of Jonathan, Mephibosheth. Ziba has brought asses to ride and food and provisions for the king and his party. 

David enquires why, and Ziba claims Mephibosheth has gone to claim the throne in Jerusalem, but Ziba declares loyalty to David. This is a ploy by the servant to become master over the inheritance of Saul, and for now, it works. David grants Ziba control over the holdings, purchased by lies and a few hundred loaves of bread. 

Again Ziba represents the unbelieving Jews, who are bad servants seeking to steal the inheritance for themselves. Mephibosheth the sinners saved by the King. A picture of things to come. 

Then Shimei, of the house of Saul comes out and begins cursing David as he and his party pass. Throwing rocks and dust and shouting "*Come out, come out thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial!"* Blaming David for the downfall of Saul. 

David's men seek permission to behead him for his insolence, but David humbly accepts this as God's doing, and says if he suffers it perhaps God would bless him for it. 

 *It may be that the Lord will look on mine affliction, and that the Lord will requite me good for his cursing this day.*

Again, the meekness of allowing God to judge and repay, holding to His esteem rather than the esteem of men is what we as Christians are called to do.

Then we see Absolom in Jerusalem has fallen under the sway of Ahithophel, who had advised his father before him, and now saw opportunity to have power through the rebellion of the son.

Absolom not only does so, but sets up a tent on the roof that all Israel may see his sin. This fulfilling the prophecy given by Nathan that while David took a man's wife in secret, his would be taken before all Israel, in the sight of the sun. And more, on the same roof where David first coveted Bathsheba. 

Of course this is an abomination to the Lord and a grave sin under the law, but this was the sway Ahithophel held over the would-be king.

Chapter 20 of **2 Samuel** picks right up from the end of 19; where the other tribes of Israel come down to Judah to complain they were not called to bring King David back from his exile;

*And, behold, all the men of Israel came to the king, and said unto the king, Why have our brethren the men of Judah stolen thee away, and have brought the king, and his household, and all David's men with him, over Jordan? But all Israel had backed Absolom in his coup attempt and their heart was not with him, despite their claim to having more part in David than Jidah. Here in chapter 20, when the reprobate Sheba, of Benjamin comes and says "*We have no part in David*," the men of Israel depart to follow Sheba. 

It is interesting to note that Sheba, a son of Belial, a reprobate says also "*Neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse,"* which is, ultimately Jesus Christ. He is the inheritance, the root of Jesse, promised to David by the Lord. 

David returns to his house, and put the concubines defiled by Absolom away, as widows. Cared for but no longer David's to go in unto.

David calls to Amasa, the general Absolom had elevated over Joab during the insurrection. When David returned across the Jordan, Amasa had begged for mercy and David diplomatically kept him as a captain, and here tells him to pursue after Sheba, to nip this new civil war in the bud. The king orders Amasa to make haste to prevent the rebel from reaching a fortified city, giving him three days to muster and depart. 

But Amasa took his time, and delayed and likely was giving Sheba time to get away. And so David orders Abishai to gather Joab and his men to take off after Sheba. Amasa joins them, going to the front to lead them, and Joab comes to him subtly and pretends to be greet his rival, and when Amasa leans in, Joab stabs him and leaves him to die. Yet another murder by Joab. Yet another time where Joab's doing right in his own eyes led to his second guessing the King.

Joab is a faithful servant to the King, but he leans on his own understanding and executed his own judgement repeatedly. Like many believers, he would choose what was expedient over what his master willed. Taking matters into our own hands, we may think what sins we do are justified by the outcome we are seeking, that the ends justify the means. But the Bible teaches us faith and patience, especially in trouble, temptation and tribulation.

After the murder of Amasa, the men choose to follow after Joab, to finish their mission. And finding Sheba in the city of Abel, they set to besiege them. But a wise woman of the city calls to Joab and asks if he is willing to slaughter them to do it, and Joab says he would rather not. Aho she strikes a bargain with him, and after consulting with the people of Abel, they kill Sheba and throw his head over the wall to Joab, in peace. And Joab retires his men and returns to Jerusalem, captain of the guard again. And David's government is reestablished.

As we move into the final chapters of **2 Samuel**, the narrative is no longer a chronological telling, but a sort of summary of events that occurred outside the main narrative, given by God for example and instruction. 

The first half of chapter 21 deals with a crime of Saul that has had lingering repercussions for Israel. Saul had gone and killed men of Gibeon. 

The Gibeonites were the city of Canaan that had tricked Joshua into a vow of non-aggression back in **Joshua 9**. Joshua swore before God without consulting the Lord, that no harm would come to them after they presented themselves as impoverished strangers from a far land, rather than their near neighbors, afraid of the Israelites. Joshua, upon finding out their trickery kept the vow, but made them be laborers for Israel.

Now, years later, Saul in his zeal had gone to smite them and drive them from the land. 

David, now king, faced a famine that had lasted years. He inquired of the Lord, and He said it was due to the blood shed by Saul against the Gibeonites. 

To make peace with God and repay the blood debt, David offers up 7 sons of Saul, including the five sons of his first wife, Michal, daughter of Saul who had been given to another man during David's exile. She had despised David in the end and this likely did nothing to improve that relationship. He also took two sons of Rizpah. David spared Mephibosheth because of his vow to Jonathan. 

The Gibeonites hanged the men, and as the harvest began, Rizpah mourned in sackcloth upon the rocks of the field, from the beginning of the harvest to the later rain. David, moved by her mourning went and gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabeshgilead, and the seven sons, and delivered them to the sepulchre of Kish, that they may sleep with their fathers. And this pleased the Lord and the famine ended.

The second half of the chapter deals with wars against the Philistines, and David's eventually being too old to go out to battle, falling faint. The sons and brother of Goliath sought to slay David and the Israelites, and all were killed by the hand of David and his servants.
