The end of David's life is come, and the final words of the King are recorded, and they begin with a beautiful recitation of faith and doctrine.

David, the anointed of God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel, acknowledges that he was inspired by God, Who spoke through him in the Psalms. In case there was any doubt about the inspiration of the Psalms of David, which were quoted throughout the New Testament by Jesus and the Apostles. *The Spirit of the Lord spake by me, and His word was in my tongue*.

David goes further to say the God of Israel, the Rock of Israel, spake to him and advised that he as King must be just, ruling in the fear of God. This is the truth, and a standard that David, being human didn't always achieve.

But it is undeniable as we read his life story that he strove to rule as a God fearing judge, with mercy and faith. An example in patience and longsuffering for Christian believers. He tried to be as the light of the morning, which is how Jesus is described in scripture, that the people of Israel would be as the tender grass covered in dew springs forth at the light. Putting the profit of others before himself, something we are commanded to in scripture;

**Philippians 2:3-5**
*Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus*

David is a picture of the king as servant. A picture of Christ, and an example for us who follow after Jesus.

David then says; *Although my house be not so with God; yet he hath made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things, and sure: for this is all my salvation, and all my desire, although he make it not to grow.*

What a wonderful description of salvation! Although his house was not always right with God, his sin and the sin of his sons, still God had made a covenant with David in Jesus, the everlasting Kingdom to come of his seed. His salvation, and all David wanted. The Lord delivered regardless of David's worthiness and his own humble acknowledgement that it was undeserving, but for the grace of God. 

David says that despite God delivering him and all he desired, all the good things that came from God, the Lord kept him from coveting more. Leaving him satisfied. We know that wasn't always true, but it wasn't of God when David coveted Bathsheba, but his sin was punished in this life, and David is looking at his eternal life to come, where his sin is remembered no more.

**2 Samuel 23:5** is such a wonderful testimony of the grace of God and the underserved favor of His promises and salvation, that of course modern perversions twist it to mean the opposite; a picture of salvation by grace and not of works changed to make grace no more grace. To make the blessings, promises and covenant David received, including his salvation, into something he worked to deserve. 

Only the KJB renders this verse properly, in the context of David's life and without any contradiction of the gospel of grace.

David then begins to give praise and honor for his mighty men, the Thirty, (although there are 37 named, and one hinted at but left out), providing a form of immortality that even today thousands of years later, we know their name, their people and their exploits. 

Again, David humbly giving credit where it is due, rather than to himself. 

The list is extensive, and some we know from other places in the Bible, and others only appear here and in **1 Chronicles 11**, where a similar list is given. 

One noticeably absent name, although he is mentioned several times, but never given honor himself; Joab. I suspect Joab was one of the second three, who is skipped over in the telling. Likely due to his eventual betrayal of David, but his absence is something that stands out. 

The rest of these men of valor, who slew multitudes of the enemies of Israel, giants and hosts of men, all in service to the King, were clearly dear to David. And the most tragic of all, is the final mention of Uriah the Hittite, whom David had murdered after committing adultery with his wife.

*25 And David built there an altar unto the Lord, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. So the Lord was intreated for the land, and the plague was stayed from Israel.*

The final chapter of **2 Samuel** tells a tale from some point in King David's reign, where God is angry with the people of Israel, and in His anger he allows Satan to tempt David into sin that they may be punished. And so David comes to desire a census of the people, ordering Joab and his captains to number the people. 

David as king wants to know the number of men for his own purpose, and neglects to do it in accordance with the word of God. The Lord requires a tithe of a half shekel at the numbering, to support the tabernacle and His priests. Something the sweet psalmist of Israel should know, as David writes in the Psalms, *O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day.* And yet...

So with the numbering done the wrong way and the punishment in Exodus being a plague against Israel, the means and reason for punishment are established because David did not resist Satan in this thing. 

God sends a prophet named Gad to tell David of His displeasure, and the Lord offers David a choice of punishment, (though we know from Exodus how this will end up going) and David throws himself and all Israel on the mercy of the Lord. 

The angel of death comes upon them, and 70,000 men are slain. But as the destroyer came to Jerusalem, the Lord repents and stays the angel's hand, by the threshing floor of Araunah. 

This is similar in a way to the Great Tribulation; 

**Matthew 24:21-22**
*For then shall be great tribulation, such as was not since the beginning of the world to this time, no, nor ever shall be. And except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved: but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened.*

Jesus tells us that for the sake of the believers on earth midway through the Tribulation, before the Rapture and the wrath to follow, God cuts short the works of the beast, least no flesh remain. 

And David as a picture of Christ, takes on the sin of Israel and asks the Lord to punish him alone for the sake of his "sheep." 

God through the prophet Gad, speaks to David and tells him to set up an altar at the threshinghouse, and David buys the place and the animals for sacrifice which Araunah had offered to give, knowing that David must pay for the sins of the people that the plague may be stayed. Just as Jesus paid it all that we be spared Hell.

This is a pretty deep story, and it can be confusing because it relies on knowledge of scripture to discern what exactly is going on. Especially when the sin of David is not spelled out and the account in **1 Chronicles 21** adds Satan into the mix. 

But like anything else in the Bible, the answer to our confusion is found by comparing scripture with scripture. Too often, Christians can be led away with foolish doctrine because they don't know the word of God. 

Satan will tempt us when God allows it, and often our reaction is used by God to get our attention, to show us our error. To give us a chance to get right, as in this case. God always provides a means of escape;

**1 Corinthians 10:13**
*There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.*

And the means of Satan's testing begins with making us either question the word of God (*Ye, hath God said?*) or taking advantage of our ignorance that we may be led into sin;

**Hosea 4:6**
*My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me: seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children.*

The law of God is perfect. It serves a wonderful purpose. It allows us to have knowledge and understanding of the mind of the Lord, and His will for us. 

People get bogged down in theology and vain philosophy of men, and lose sight of the purpose of the word. Christians should study to be approved before God, reading His word daily, our daily bread. The words of eternal life given to us by the inspiration of God.

Wrapping up **2 Samuel** is bittersweet. The story of David is told again in **1 Chronicles**, but it is for a different purpose and while equally important, there's something about the humanity of David in Samuel that resonates with me. 

I hope everyone takes the time to read through the scripture I have presented, even if you scroll past my commentary.

1 Kings begins with a other son in rebellion against an elderly, dying David, this time Adonijah the son of Haggith, who begins to behave as Absolom and takes advantage of David being bedridden to declare himself King of Israel. 

We see Joab, who was left out of David's praise of his mighty men, has joined in the sedition, along with Abiathar the priest. 

But the mighty men, and Nathan the prophet and Zadok the priest and others remained loyal to David and the kingdom. They tell Bathsheba to go inform the King of this treachery, for her life and the life of Solomon, the promised heir. 

So while the upstart and his coconspirators feast outside the city, David commands that Solomon be anointed king, and Zadok and Nathan do as he commands, and all Jerusalem praises King Solomon. Adonijah and the others at the feast gear the commotion and Jonathan son of Abiathar comes to tell them of the news. The men scattered and Adonijah fears, gripping the horns of the altar he had set up for the feast, where the beasts were slain. His guests abandoned him, he fears for his life, but Solomon promises his halfbrother peace if he shows himself worthy. So he sends for Adonijah, who comes and bowed before King Solomon is spared and allowed to go to his house.

The image of David giving the kingdom to Solomon, putting all beneath his feat, David's anointed riding on a donkey, while the child in rebellion clings to the altar, is to me an echo of The Father putting all in subjection under the Son, Christ Jesus. And the betrayal of the Jews pictured in Adonijah and the altar. The mercy of Solomon to him, as the mercy of Christ that all men may bow before Him and proclaim that He is Lord. 

This allegory plays out more, as we shall see in the next chapter.

We finally come to the death of King David, and before he passes on he has words for his son, Solomon. 

He reminds Solomon to walk in the ways of the Lord that it be well with him and his kingdom. A walk with God that David mostly kept, despite a few times of his own lusts getting the better of him. 

David has unfinished business with Joab and Shimei, and leaves it to Solomon in his wisdom to do that which is right. Having Joab executed for the blood on his head, for the murders of righteous men, having participated in the attempted sedition of Adonijah. 

And Shimei,  the Benjamite who cursed David and coaxed a reprieve from the King when David returned from exile during the Absolom coup. Shimei, Solomon judges to remain in Jerusalem for the rest of his life, and when Shimei leaves to retrieve two runaway servants, Solomon has him put to death. A fitting end for those that despised the anointed of the Lord.

Now Adonijah, who had been spared after he bent the knee to Solomon comes to the King's mother, Bathsheba, with a request. He asks for Abishag a Shunammite to be his wife. In 1 Kings 1 we are told that the sick and dying David took young and fair Abishag to lay with him for warmth. And although they never consummated their relationship, she was as a concubine to the King. 

Adonijah asks Bathsheba saying that because of her relationship with Solomon, the king couldn't refuse her. Perhaps flattered, Bathsheba does as he asks and approaches the king, and is even given honor of sitting at his right hand, and she asks this thing for the halfbrother of Solomon. 

Solomon, in his wisdom, recognizes what this entails, for an elder son to take for wife the concubine of the former king, solidifying Adonijah's false claim to the throne. Solomon correctly ignores his mother's petition and orders the upstart's death. 

Roman Catholicism will sometimes point to a truncated version of this story to paint a picture of Mary as "queen" and mediatrix between man and Christ Jesus. They will include the flattery of Adonijah, saying "*for he will not say thee nay*" anything Mary asks of Him. As if this were some sort of cheat code to get around the will of God by appealing to the mother of Christ. 

They will say that Solomon's response to his mother is the same response of Jesus to Mary, "*Ask on, my mother: for I will not say thee nay.*"

They will ignore that Solomon not only said nay, but had Adonijah killed for his attempt to make an endrun around the anointed of the Lord. 

There is one mediator between God and man. The man Christ Jesus.

Joab, knowing he was to be executed for the blood he had shed and his betrayal of the king, flees to the tabernacle, and grabs hold of the altar and refuses to budge, thinking that this will save him. But Solomon knows that the blood Joab shed remained on David's kingdom, and by extension his own, and must be repaid to get right with God. Again, like Adonijah who had done the same thing in the previous chapter, Joab's desperation to escape the just punishment for his sin by clinging to the altar, rather than to the mercy of the King, is an image of the unbelieving Jews clinging to their dead works and vain traditions, rather than repentance towards Christ.

We read that *Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee.* And that these cities, near the border of Hiram's nation of Tyre, which is Lebanon, pleased him not.

The area was filled with remnants of Canaanites who had not been purged from the land. They are called Cabul by the Phoenician King, which according to the context, means unpleasing or not desired. 

This area in the Northwest of Galilee is where the Decapolis, the ten cities mentioned in the Gospels is located. An important part of Christ's early ministry. Where the fame of His works went out throughout Syria and Galilee and down to Judea and beyond the Jordan River. 

I don't know if it was meant as a gift to the king of Tyre or surety on loans given to Solomon for the vast wealth provided to build the Temple and his palace and all the improvements and cities built up in this time, but it seems odd that Solomon would, in his wisdom, give a gift that would insult his friend and benefactor. All we really know is Solomon eventually built them up himself and filled them with men of Israel.

He also built ships for trade on the Red Sea, sending them out to places like Ophir, which is believed to be on the Indian subcontinent, famous for gold and other precious materials. 

The cities mentioned in the proceeding verses are along a trade road through southern Palestine, in the wilderness that the Israelites had wandered. A road connecting the port of Eziongeber to Jerusalem, and likely continuing through to Solomon's allies in Egypt and Tyre. 

We are told how he built up his armies by making the men of Israel soldiers of war, and multiplying horses and chariots. And by subjugation of the Canaanite tribes as bondsmen. 

The wealth and power of Israel reached its peak in this time. And Solomon went to the Temple and made sacrifices to God three times a year, and burnt incense to the Lord.

With King Solomon dead, his son Rehoboam goes up to Shechem, the place Abraham talked to God when he entered Canaan, where Joseph was buried, and where Israel had dwelt. And there he went to be anointed king. 

But Jeroboam, son of Nebat, to whom the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite spoke the word of God, that he should be king over the 10 tribes in Israel, came with the men of Israel to challenge the heir of David. 

Ahijah had told Jeroboam, a mighty man who was put in charge over the children of Joseph, (Manassas and Ephraim) by Solomon, that God had ordained that the kingdom be rent as a garment. And gave the covenant that God would bless him as king over Israel, excluding Judah; *if thou wilt hearken unto all that I command thee, and wilt walk in my ways, and do that is right in my sight, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did; that I will be with thee, and build thee a sure house, as I built for David, and will give Israel unto thee.*

Solomon hearing this, sought to have Jeroboam killed, and so he had fled to Egypt. 

Returning from that exile he led the men to confront Rehoboam, saying that his father Solomon had made the men of Israel to carry a heavy yoke. To perform grievous service for the King. 

In **1 Samuel 8**, when the people went to Samuel demanding a king, the Lord spoke through Samuel warning the people that a king would take their sons for chariots and horsemen and manservants, and their daughters to be cooks, and their vineyards for himself and their income by tax. Solomon had indeed done all this. 

Was it unfair, given they demanded a king over Israel and were warned? Maybe. Though Solomon also brought them great wealth, and rest in the land, and made Israel great among nations. 

Obviously, Jeroboam had ulterior motives as well, seeking the approval of Israel that he may be king, and making Rehoboam look weak; Either relent and pledge to lighten the yoke, deny their claims and look uncaring to the people, or to react angrily and rash. 

This difficult situation was one the Lord had caused, *that He might perform His saying which the Lord spoke by Ahijah*. Ironically, this was one that the wisdom of Solomon would perhaps have been able to navigate. But lacking that wisdom, Rehoboam asks for 3 days and he sought counsel from his father's elder advisors and from his own young men in his court.

The elder gave moderate advice; speak good words and promise to serve them, and the people will be yours. The younger gave harsh advice, that as King he would increase the burden. That his little finger would be thicker than his father's loins against them. 

There is debate among Christians as to which advice was right, and if the men of Israel had a valid complaint. Should we heed the hoary head of experience, or the brash and young? But really, the scripture tells us the Lord had made this a no win situation to begin with. Rehoboam was going to lose the 10 northern tribes regardless of what he did.

He could have shamed his own father by conceding their complaints, and been shown to be weak as Saul, seeking after the approval of the masses. The advice of the elders wasn't much better than that of the young men that he chose to follow. 

And so he answered them roughly and Jeroboam speaks for Israel and says they will have nothing making them loyal to Judah and the throne of David. They depart, every man for their tents and leave the Kingdom divided. Rent as a garment, never to be united again.

*And it came to pass, when all Israel heard that Jeroboam was come again, that they sent and called him unto the congregation, and made him king over all Israel: there was none that followed the house of David, but the tribe of Judah only.*

Once this occurs, Rehoboam assembles his men, including the remnant of Benjamin that remained inside the territory of Judah, and sought to go out to war against Israel. But the Lord speaks through the prophet Shemaiah, saying not to do this thing, and slay brothers. That the divided kingdom had come from Him. And so they stand down. 

Meanwhile, in the North, Jeroboam realizes that with the Temple in Jerusalem, and the pilgrimages the men were required to take under the ordinances of God, three times a year, plus all the sacrifices and services of the Levites there, that eventually he would lose the hearts of the people and they would turn towards Rehoboam because of the Lord. 

And so, forsaking the word of God given him by Ahijah the Shilonite, the King sets up altars to golden calves, one in Bethel, and the other in Dan. In the South and one in the far north. He set up high places and created his own feasts and made requirements for worship at the same time as those given by the Lord. 

And further, he made priests of the lowest of people, not of the Levites. Generally in scripture what is being described are reprobates. Sodomites and the worst manner of people. Sons of Belial. 

Creating his own false religion, claiming to be worshiping the "god that took them out of Egypt," while worshiping the golden calf, idolatry. Setting up his own feast days. Using an unqualified priesthood made up of the lowest people, all for political power...This is a picture of the apostate Roman Catholic Church. 

It will eventually lead to the utter destruction of Israel.

In **1 Kings 17** we are introduced to the great prophet of the Northern Kingdom, Elijah the Tishbite. Elijah is a key figure in scripture, having been prophesied as coming in the day of the Lord, a voice crying out in the wilderness, fulfilled by John the Baptist. He appeared with Moses at the transfiguration of Christ Jesus. 

Some believe he is one of the two witnesses to come after the Tribulation and the Rapture, during the pouring out of the wrath of God. The witnesses having the power to shut up the heavens from rain, as we see Elijah do in the name of the Lord in this chapter. 

Prophesying the word of God to King Ahab, declaring a drought upon the land for their wickedness, God sends His prophet to hide beyond Jordan. 

At the brook of Cherith, the Lord feeds him by ravens, quenched by the brook as long as it flows. When even the brook is dried up, the Lord sends him down to Zidon, and to a widow and her son. 

Arriving there, he sees the widow and asks for water and bread. The widow confesses that she had just enough grain and oil to make a final meal for her and her son. Elijah tells her that by the word of the Lord God of Israel that the barrel of meal and cruse of oil will not run out until the end of the drought. And this miracle plays out just as he had said. And so during the wrath of God upon the wicked, so are we kept alive by His grace. 

The word of God is like the meal and oil, the bread that never spoils or wastes. Never depleted. The promise of life by faith, that we will always be provided for. That we have eternal life in His word. 

And even as her son becomes ill and died, Elijah calls upon the name of the Lord and he is risen again. 

The pictures of the word of the living God, being provided for, tended by ravens as they were angels, made alive again by the Lord. The living God. The wrath upon the wicked. The reward for the faithful. This is one of my favorite chapters in the Old Testament.

The great story of Elijah vs the prophets of Baalim, even the prophets of the groves who ate at Queen Jezebel's table. 

God sends Elijah back to the Northern Kingdom of Israel after 3 and a half years of drought and famine. 

**Luke 4:25**
*But I tell you of a truth, many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias, when the heaven was shut up three years and six months, when great famine was throughout all the land*

Ahab, having been searching for Elijah this whole time to get the prophet to undo the curse Israel was under is off searching again for Elijah, and with him his chief steward Obadiah. 

They separate, and Elijah comes upon Obadiah who knows him well. Obadiah is a saved believer in the Lord, yet he works for the wicked king and queen.

Elijah tells Obadiah to fetch Ahab and tell him he's returned, and Obadiah fears for his life. He has been, this entire time, hiding his faith, just as he has his the prophets of the Lord in caves to keep them from Jezebel. 

Rather than standing up to evil, preaching against Baal and sin, to bring Israel back to the Lord, they've been shut up in caves and Obadiah's paranoia at the possibility of Elijah ghosting him shows the level of fear of man, and not the fear of the Lord he claims to have. 

This is similar to the way many Christians today hide their faith and fear tribulation and persecution more than they fear God. God may have used those hundred prophets to bring about revival. But they hid rather than face death. 

**Matthew 10:28**
*And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.*

But Elijah assures Obadiah he will speak to the king that day, and when they return Ahab accuses Elijah of being responsible for the famine. Elijah corrects the wicked king, that it is he and his father's sin that brought it about. And Elijah challenged Ahab to being all Israel together and the prophets of Baal, and meet him at Mt Carmel. 

There Elijah challenged the people of Israel; *How long halt ye between two opinions? if the Lord be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him.*

Then, as now, people generally are unwilling to commit to faith. They go along to get along and put off the choice of salvation or damnation if they can, usually to their own destruction. 

The purpose of the word of the Lord is to bring people the choice and force them to decide; do they want to accept the truth? Eternal life in Christ Jesus, admitting they are sinners deserving death and taking the gracious gift of God? Or do they want to reject God and be given up, and given over. Twice-dead.

There are saved people in the world. There are slightly fewer reprobates (although that number seems to be growing). There is a vast majority of those who are caught between, often and in indecision. Soul-winning, giving the gospel to the unbelievers forces them to make this choice. And many receive it gladly. But others, it's the final straw before they decide they do not wish to retain God in their knowledge. And it's too late, reprobate. 

Elijah is putting this same decision in the hands of the people. 

And as a sign, Elijah calls for two pyres to be set up, two altars, with bullocks upon each as sacrifice. He challenges the 450 priests of Baal to call down fire from their god, to burn up the sacrifice. 

And these priests called and called and danced and prayed and from morning until noon cried out 'O Baal, hear us!' But there was, of course, no answer.

*And it came to pass at noon, that Elijah mocked them, and said, Cry aloud: for he is a god; either he is talking, or he is pursuing, or he is in a journey, or peradventure he sleepeth, and must be awaked.*

And so until evening they intensified their futile and vain efforts, even cutting themselves as the demonic and pagan do, and of course no answer came and no fire was called down from their dead gods. 

And Elijah repaired the altar to the Lord that had been torn down, and took 12 stones for each tribe, representing the tribes of Jacob to whom the Lord had come. And he made a trench about the altar and had them fill it with water and soak the wood and upon the sacrifice. Four times he had them drench the area. 

And Elijah said; *Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel, let it be known this day that thou art God in Israel, and that I am thy servant, and that I have done all these things at thy word.*

And fire fell and consumed the burnt sacrifice, the wood and stones and dust, and evaporated the water in the trench. 

And the people who had gathered bowed falling on their faces and said "The Lord, He is the God!" 

This is a picture of the end times, and the fire from heaven and the sure return of Christ, when every knee shall bow and tongue confess that He is the living God. 

And while the people were in a fervor from this mighty sign, Elijah tells them to take and kill all the prophets of Baal, and they do, at the broom Kishon.

Elijah, having proved his point in an epic fashion by the mighty hand of the Lord, turned to King Ahab and says; *Get thee up, eat and drink; for there is a sound of abundance of rain.*

Elijah then takes himself, and goes up Mt Carmel, and waits. Sending a servant 7 times to go look towards the sea. And it came to pass on the 7th time there raised a cloud from the sea. At that, Elijah sends a message to Ahab to hurry and get home that the rain not stop him. And a great rain fell as the king returned to Jezreel. Elijah running to the entrance by the hand of the Lord, beating the King and his chariots as the rains came down.

Epic story of faith and the power of God. The people witnessed a great miracle, and see the skies open up. They even slew the prophets of Baal. But as we will see, this zeal didn't extend to a revival at all. And Elijah will have more challenges before him.

Elijah shut up the heavens from rain, causing three and a half years of famine by the word of the Lord. He was fed by ravens, and by meal and oil that never ran out or spoiled. He called upon the Lord and saw the widow's son raised from the dead. 

By faith, Elijah returned to Israel and confronted the king and the 450 prophets of Baal, and by the word of the Lord called down fire from Heaven to show the children of Israel the power of the living God. They slew the prophets of Baal. And by the word of the Lord, rains came and returned to the land. 

During the challenge to the prophets of Baal, Elijah claimed to them that he alone still followed the Lord and against the 450. He met Obadiah, who kept his faith secret for fear of the king and hid prophets of God in a cave, an act of cowardice compared to mighty Elijah. 

And yet, Elijah fled. And went beyond Judah, to Horeb. Mount Sinai, where God appeared before Moses with the Law, and lived in a cave. 

The triumph that should have led to revival brought depression and fear in the prophet. He wished to end his life. 

He says: *I have been very jealous for the Lord God of hosts: for the children of Israel have forsaken thy covenant, thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword; and I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.*

In our Christian life, even after seeing the power of God on us and having great triumphs of faith, it isn't unusual to feel a sense of letdown afterwards. To have doubts. To feel alone. But the Lord works in more than us. And we are never alone. There is always a righteous remnant, and despair isn't an option even in the face of tribulation. God has use for us yet.

*And he said, Go forth, and stand upon the mount before the Lord. Ahab, upon hearing the judgment of the Lord, humbled himself before God. Fasting in sackcloth, going forth softly, in humility, hoping that the Lord would repent. 

And God does soften His judgement against Ahab, telling Elijah that while this evil will befall his sons, and that wicked Jezebel, He will forestall His wrath during Ahab's time. 

Ahab had multiple warnings to get right. He still wasn't a saved believer, but he feared the Lord enough to humble himself when it looked as though he was finished. His acts of humility were sufficient to delay judgment, but not prevent it. 

If our leaders were humbled in such a manner. If perhaps the Lord spared their life from an assassin, and they felt compelled to rend their clothes and humble themselves and turn towards God for mercy, perhaps the nation they lead would be prolonged and the inevitable judgment of God put off. 

But sadly, these days, the leaders will not humble themselves and instead turn towards their false gods and worship abominations. Leading their people to sin. 

God's judgment is fierce. And it will be just when it arrives. And dogs will lick the blood of the men who brought about these abominations.

Jehoshaphat, King of Judah was a weak but godly king, walking in the ways of Asa. But Ahab of Israel was wicked all of his days, walking in the way of Jeroboam. 

When Ahab was at peace with Judah and Jehoshaphat came together with him, Ahab's thoughts turned to war. 

Ahab had peace with Syria and its king that Ahab compromised with, in defiance of God's will. But he saw opportunity in his alliance with Judah and asked Jehoshaphat if he would come with him in war against the Syrians to reclaim disputed land. Out of kinship, Jehoshaphat agrees, but wants to first seek counsel from a prophet of the Lord. 

Ahab sends for his prophets of Baal, even 400 of them, who all speak encouraging words and flattery. What Ahab wants to hear. 

A godly ruler seeks the word of God. A wicked ruler seeks to have their pride and ego stroked. 

Jehoshaphat asks if there isn't at least a prophet of the Lord to ask, and Ahab begrudgingly sends for Micaiah, whom the king says is his enemy, because he preached against Ahab and didn't hold back from delivering the word of God. 

Many leaders today surround themselves with yes men. With pastors and religious leaders who all too willingly will provide a wicked ruler with encouragement and support and claim God is with them. Using flattery and deceit, they convince these evil leaders, and themselves, that God is blessing them.  

But Micaiah comes, and while he at first just parrots the false prophets, Ahab knows the game and asks for him to speak truth. 

And the truth is that Israel will be scattered without a shepherd, because Ahab will die in battle. Further, Micaiah says that an angel of the Lord came as a lying spirit to put falsehoods in the mouths of the prophets of Baal, to feed the delusions of Ahab. To lead him to destruction. 

Ahab has Micaiah jailed until his return (a return the prophet stakes his veracity on not happening). 

And the kings set off to battle. But Ahab disguised himself, hoping to escape being the target of the Syrians. Jehoshaphat goes out to battle in his robes, unashamed. There's symbolism there, the godly king unafraid in battle to proclaim the truth of God and place his faith in Him. 

But an arrow finds Ahab anyway, and always the king and the words of the prophet are fulfilled, every Israelite returning to their homes, leaderless.

I feel very strongly that the lessons of Ahab and the other kings of Israel, who get worse and worse as they go headlong to their ultimate destruction, are being played out this week. I think we are witness to a very similar tale. 

I think God sends warning to these wicked kings, the time and again. Maybe by word of a prophet. Maybe by the near miss of death. 

And most, being wicked and prideful, seek rather the comforting words of false prophets guided by lying spirits, feeding their strong delusions.

Reading this chapter, it should stand out how similar in form and content it is to how the Gospels are written. The anointed one of God going forth and having average people come to him seeking something, and miraculously receiving it by faith. 

Parallels with Christ are there; Elijah as John the Baptist, a voice in the wilderness, Elisha as he who came after him, with twice the spirit of the Lord upon him. The sons of the prophets as disciples. Bringing the word of God to the people. 

In the first story, we find a certain woman, wife of a man of God, a believer in the Lord. Her husband's death, leaving them in debt. Her and her sons, about to be sold into bondage to pay it. 

Elisha asks what does she have, and she replies only a little oil. He tells her to go out to her neighbors and ask for empty containers, and not a few. As many as she can get, and fill them from the pot. And she does as he says, acting on her faith. She fills every vessel they have, and yet there was still more in the pot. She tells Elisha, who says go and sell them and pay her debt, and her and her sons live off what's left over. 

In scripture, oil is almost always a picture of the holy Spirit. Debt and bondage, sin and the wages of sin, which is death. 

Her husband feared the Lord. He left her with nothing but oil. The Spirit. And she takes that oil and fills the vessels of her neighbors and more. Just as we who are saved are filled with the Spirit, and we can fill others, as vessels, infinitely. It never runs out. The Spirit is enough to not only pay for our debt but to live on, forever.

As men, we should do well to leave our wives and children that inheritance. Greater than any other, the surety of the Spirit in our house, by faith in Christ Jesus.

The second story, of the Shunammite woman, a great woman the Bible says, has similar parallels. She, understanding that Elisha is a holy man of God, not only feeds him daily bread, but makes room for him in her house. Setting up a bed, chair and table, with a candlestick, in a chamber for him to come into. 

This is a clear picture of how we are to seek to place Christ, the holiest Man of God, in our hearts. She sought first the daily bread, the word of God. And by faith that comes from the word, perceive the truth of Christ, in her case that Elisha was of God. And then make room in our hearts for Christ to come into and stay. The candlestick, often a symbol of the Spirit. The light of God that shines forth from believers. 

And the woman did all this not wanting for anything in return, but the prophet through his servant asks, what does she truly desire. Just as the Spirit brings our prayers to God through Christ. 

**Romans 8:26-27**
*Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit, because he maketh intercession for the saints according to the will of God.* 

Gehazi the servant may also be as a picture of a believer, praying on behalf of another. 

The Shunammite woman longs for a son. Her husband great in years, she has been left childless. Elisha through Gehazi, hia messenger, tells her that her desire will be granted and she will bear a son, miraculously. 

Again, an echo of the angel Gabriel, a messenger of God, telling Mary of a miraculous birth. Also of Sarah, etc. God opens and closes wombs. 

And sure enough, she bears a son. And when he has grown enough to go with his father to the reaping of the harvest (another common picture of soul winning), that he said unto his father, My head, my head. They took the boy to his mother, and he died in her arms. 

She places the dead boy in the chamber she had prepared for Elisha. Again, a symbol of her own heart and the space she made for God. She asks for an ass and a rider to bring her to Elisha. From afar off, he sees her and recognizes her, but says he doesn't know why she came. God had not revealed it to him. (I find that interesting, that the humanity and lack of omniscience reminds us that he is just a man, only a picture of Christ, not actually Christ)

He sends his servant, Gehazi, to ask her if all is well, and she tells the servant yes. But when she reaches the prophet, she throws herself at her feet, lamenting her child. The pain of being given what she asked for, but losing it is likely far worse than if she'd never been given him at all. At least in that moment. You can really feel for her as a parent. 

*Did I desire a son of my lord? did I not say, Do not deceive me?* Heartbreaking.

Elisha sends his servant, saying to slow down or stop for nothing, *and lay my staff upon the face of the child.*The mother, with Elisha, follow behind. 

Gehazi comes back to meet them saying the staff did not work. Elisha himself comes into the house, finding the son dead. 

Elisha shuts the door and lays upon the child, praying to the Lord. He leaves the child and paces the house, and returns and lays upon him again and the child sneezed, 7 times (symbolic of something, seven being a number of perfection of the Lord). And so, the son was alive. 

*And he called Gehazi, and said, Call this Shunammite. So he called her. And when she was come in unto him, he said, Take up thy son. Then she went in, and fell at his feet, and bowed herself to the ground, and took up her son, and went out.*

Next, we find Elisha in Gilgal, where there is a famine in the land. He tells his servant to set a pot for pottage, to make a stew to feed the sons of the prophets, (again a term meaning believers or disciples, in my opinion).

*And one went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine, and gathered thereof wild gourds his lap full, and came and shred them into the pot of pottage: for they knew them not.*

They go to eat and realize that the gourds of the wild vine have apparently poisoned the stew. The allegory here shows how a group of saved believers, of the true vine that is Christ, welcoming in the fruit of a wild vine, can lead to death. *O thou man of God, there is death in the pot. And they could not eat thereof.*

Just as Peter warns the churches of Christ in the NT;

**2 Peter 2:1-2**
*But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction. And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of.*

But Elisha adds to the stew some meal, the ground barley that makes bread, and casts it into the pot, and makes it safe to eat again. 

Just as the word of God preached, the daily bread, can cleanse a church of the false doctrines of false teachers.

Finally, this story;

Here in **2 Kings 5**, we find the Syrian captain, Naaman, stricken with the incurable disease, leprosy. And a servant girl, captive out of Israel, tells Namaan's wife of the prophet of the Lord in Samaria, that is Israel.

With permission of his king and loaded with treasure, Naaman and servants go into the King of Israel, asking he be recovered of his leprosy. 

The king becomes upset, thinking this is a trap. How can he heal a man of something that is untreatable? The King of Syria would hold it against him, he rends his clothes in distress. 

Elisha heard of this and sends for Naaman, and when the Syrian comes to him, the prophet's servant comes to him with a message; Wash yourself in the Jordan seven times and be healed. 

At first, Naaman is offended. He expected the man of God to come and lay hands and make a show and heal him there in the spot. He questions why he just go to the Jordon, when Syrian rivers are superior in his mind, and more convenient. 

But his servants convince him to try, and he does as the prophet said, and is healed. Cleaned of the leprosy.

He returns to Elisha, and confesses that now he believes there is no other God in all the earth, but in Israel. And he offers the treasure he has brought to the prophet. 

Elisha refuses, in the name of the Lord. 

Namaan asks then for two burdens of earth, soil from Israel, that he would make sacrifices of burnt offerings only to the Lord. As he had previously believed the waters of the rivers were different in Syria, now he assumes the mounds of Israeli dirt would matter in the sacrifice to God. 

He also asks for pardon, for Elisha's blessing, that when he returned to Syria, that when he went in to the house of Rimmon, a temple to idols, and bow himself down, that the Lord forgive him. He is indicating that while he believes that the Lord is the only true God, he would still go before idols and bow down before them, because of custom and what others might think. 

Asking for permission, and the Lord's blessing to be unfaithful to the Lord he proclaimed, Elisha offers nothing, but says "Go in peace." 

Whether Naaman actually believed on the Lord is doubtful. He seemed caught up in the moment and the miracle that had occurred, and yet still carnal. Seeing the water as important, rather than following the word of God. Seeing the soil as different. Pledging with one hand to worship only the Lord, and at the other admit he would continue in the false religion of his people. 

In many ways, this is the experience many have when given the Gospel. They are resistant to the truth, show doubt and disdain when told there is only one way to salvation, faith in Christ Jesus. They may taste of the Heavenly gifts as the Spirit works in them to help bring them to the truth. They may even confess that this IS the truth, and they promise they will do whatever it takes to convince God, the person who gave them the gospel, other Christians. 

But in the end, they are already thinking about the ways they will back out of their promise. They are already back to their old beliefs before the words of the promise had come out of their mouths. They never accepted the truth in their hearts. 

They are like the seed sown on the pathway in the parables of the Sower;

*Behold, a sower went forth to sow; And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up*.

*When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side.*

An all too common occurrence.

Some get confused by Elisha's telling him to go in peace, that by this he was blessing Namaan's request to pardon his sin of returning to the worship of his false gods. But really, he doesn't acknowledge it, and politely sends him on his way. 

It may also be why he refused any of the rewards. Not just for keeping himself from filthy lucre, but that it wasn't a sincere conversion and Naaman may well have taken the wrong idea, that he could buy God's favor. 

But we see covetousness and greed strike Elisha's servant Gehazi, who rides after and makes up a story to get some of that silver and clothing for himself. He then lies to Elisha when he returns, but the Lord reveals to the prophet the truth. And so, fittingly, Gehazi is stricken with leprosy, and cursed to his entire lineage.

There's also a lesson here for saved Christians. Those who are the rocky soil, who receive the truth of the word with gladness and hope, but because they have no root in themselves, with her and die without producing fruit. 

It is possible to receive the gospel and believe unto salvation and yet return to the same old life. Healed, washed, clean and reborn the way the Syrian Captain was, and yet living in the old flesh doing the same old things. Seeking pardon for not living the way you should, knowing that you've been forgiven. 

Of course, if good works and sanctification came automatically with salvation, the New Testament wouldn't be filled with encouragement from the apostles to do good works. To pursue sanctification by walking in the spirit rather than in the flesh. To feed the new man rather than the old. 

It's also why we are to disciple those that we help lead to Christ. Or to be edifying and supportive in the lives of those who we come across. Encouraging them to walk in the Spirit. 

There are quite a few professing Christians and even entire denominations that teach that works come automatically, and without evidence of a changed life, we should doubt the salvation of someone. 

While faith without works is dead, not being profitable to others, and we are justified before men by our good works, we should be careful to be understanding rather than judgmental. To encourage rather than condemn. 

We have all been as Naaman, excited about the Lord and turning back towards the things that we were trusting in before. We should have some Grace and understanding for people who aren't where we are in our spiritual walk. Not to condone sin. But to not be confrontationally judgmental. Elijah could have lectured Naaman. But he told him to go in peace. 

I think there's a lot that can be taken from that.

Here in **2 Kings 6**, we find another series of acts of Elisha, the prophet of God. Similar to the structure of the Gospels and Acts of the Apostles, they are stories that provide a window into the faith of the man who had double the measure of the Spirit as the great Elijah. 

While 2 Kings paints a picture of a man of great faith, it is careful to also let us know he is just a man, and that it is God that guides and protects him.

Here, he and his disciples, at their behest, set off to the banks of the Jordan to build a dwelling for them, as their current place in Carmel isn't big enough. I take this to mean that the prophet had gathered a good number of the sons of the prophets. 

They ask if they may, and he agrees. They ask him to come and he does. 

While felling trees for beams, the iron ax head of one of the men falls off into the waters. Seemingly lost. Because the tool has been borrowed, the man is upset, being responsible for another's property. 

But Elisha simply asks where, and breaking off a stick, casts it into the stream, and the iron floats to the surface. The iron did swim. 

With God, all things are possible. With faith enough, even iron did swim. The casual way Elisha trusted in the Lord, is a testament to his great faith. 

As Jesus spoke to the Apostles;

*Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you.*

The amount of faith needed to receive Christ and be saved is infinitesimal. The Apostles were unable to cast out a certain demon in a man, yet Jesus said it was a lack of faith. That the faith the size of a tiny mustard seed could move mountain. Elisha demonstrates this kind of faith, and is an example to us. 

When the King of Syria sets a trap for the King of Israel, Elisha having had it revealed to him, warns the king, saving him multiple times. 

The Syrian King, frustrated by the failure of his ambush, suspects a traitor in his court had been tipping off the King of Israel. But his men explain that it is Elisha, who knows even the things whispered in his bed chamber. (I wonder how they know, unless there be spies in the other kings house, telling them!)

And so the Syrian King sends his army to get Elisha. And surrounds the city he is in with a multitude of troops. 

Panicked, Elisha's servant goes to the prophet in fear, asking what shall they do against such an array. 

Elisha calmly tells him to not be afraid, for those with them are many more. Elisha prays, asking the Lord to open the servant's eyes to see, and the young man looks and all around him are horses and chariots of fire, surrounding the prophet. 

We should remember this in times of distress. If we are walking in the Spirit and doing the work of the Lord, we should fear no man. 

And as Elisha prayed to open the young servant's eyes, he prays for blindness to fall on the Syrian host. 

And, they being blind to it, are led by Elisha into the very heart of Samaria, delivered unto the king. 

The King of Israel asks for permission to gleefully slay them, but the prophet says not so. They are captives. Feed them and give them drink and send them to their master. And so they do, and peace comes between the kingdoms for a time.

So another tale of Elisha, the siege of Samaria by the Syrians. A host of Syrians lay encamped about the city, to starve the king out. And the people were so desperate for food they boiled the heads of asses, and ate the dung of the birds. Even boiling their own children to eat, as one grieving mother tells the King. She was tricked into offering her own child with the promise of another woman to then cook her own. 

We cannot imagine such tribulation and hunger. We are blessed beyond measure. And still we complain. 

We have food in abundance, clothing, shelter. Relative peace and security. 

We are free to worship God, to attend church, to read the Bible, free to give the gospel to the lost...All things denied Christians for hundreds of years. Things that could be a death sentence in the past. Yet how many people claiming Christ do them? How many exercise the liberty we have?

One of the reasons Israel was so often afflicted was, that when they knew God, *they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish hearts were darkened.* 

They turned to the worship of idols and worse. They held the truth of God in unrighteousness. 

But first, they took for granted the blessings of the liberty they had from the Lord. 

As longsuffering and merciful as God is, the Lord's patience runs out. With individuals, and with a nation. 

How many Christians spend their time complaining about how bad they have it, how fearful they are about the state of things, and yet do not pray everyday in thanksgiving, glorifying God for what they have?

How many neglect their Bible? How many foresake the assembly? How many make excuses as to why they don't have to go to church, they don't have to live separated lives, they don't have to win souls and be a light? 

And the excuses always are ridiculous. "There are no good churches! No good pastors! The Bible is hard to read! It's easier to listen to a podcast or to watch YouTube debates!" Itching ears, taking every rationalization they are fed, while rejecting the word preached, and complaining all the while. 

America may end up as Samaria. Under siege and eventually overrun. But today we have unprecedented freedoms to turn to the Lord and to make an impact with His light so shining. 

We don't have to wait until it's too late because of fear.

And so, as bad as it is, the King sends one of his lords to fetch Elisha, blaming the prophet of the Lord for their troubles. Seeking his head for their misery. For the testimony of the word of the Lord.

This is, in my opinion, the real fear that drives some Christians to reject our role in this world. They are afraid of the backlash that comes from rebuking the wicked by God's word. The tribulation that may come from standing firm against sin and wickedness. Being a light against those that love darkness. 

They don't want people to think they are a peculiar person. They don't want people to think they are "judgemental." They don't want people to point out their own sin, and call them out as hypocrites, because they are comfortable in their sin. They become codependent with the world. 

But Elisha knows that regardless of what the reaction may be, God's will be done. So, he tells the messenger that by that same time the following day, the famine will be ended. That barley and flour will be so plentiful, that they will sell for a shekel at the gate. 

The lord sent by the king mocks this, asking if the Lord will open windows in heaven to make it so. Elisha says that while he will see this come to pass, he won't himself eat thereof. 

And so, God in the night scares off the hosts of Syria, thinking they hear hoofs of an army approach. They run where none pursued, leaving behind their fully provisioned camp. 

Some beggars, with leprosy, waiting by the gate, decide to go to the Syrian camp to seek food, and find the camp abandoned. They spoil some things for themselves, but think better of not telling anyone inside the city. So they go and tell the King. 

The King, fearful of a trap, sends out scouts and they return with the news, and the people of the city trample the lord Elisha had prophesied against, in their haste to gather the spoils. And so it came to pass, just as the prophet had said.

One of the biggest hurdles to overcome in doing the right thing, is that if you begin, you know you will have to continue. 

If you begin reading the Bible every day, you're admitting that you should. And if you know that you should, you know it's wrong if you don't. And now you are without excuse. 

If you haven't been to church in a while, and you go once, you are admitting you should be going regularly, and now you don't have an excuse. 

If you haven't been living a separated life, as blameless as you can, and you try to clean it up, and get rid of worldly things in your life, you will have to continue in it. 

If you begin to testify for the gospel, people who know you will judge all those sins they've witnessed you do. And now you're forced to show genuine faith and a change. 

This can be terrifying. It makes us make rationalizations. Or empty promises and vows to "do better tomorrow." While living for today. 

But we are to be doers of the word, not hearers only. We are supposed to let our light shine. 

A prophet is not without honor, except in his home country. We will have family and friends who aren't Christian who will roll their eyes. Who will feel threatened by your newfound dedication to the Lord. Who will look for chinks in the whole armour of God you try to put on. 

You will fail sometimes. It's ok. God's mercies are new every morning. 

Yes, you will be making yourself obligated to doing the right thing by acknowledging it is the right thing. That is the Spirit working in you. Accept it. Accept people will be put off by the change. Accept some will make fun of you, mockers. It's ok. 

Because this tribulation is nothing compared to eternity. God will bless you in this life and the next.

Here in **2 Kings 9**, we are given at last the fulfillment of the task given Elijah against Ahab, where God sent him to anoint Hazael over Syria, Jehu over Israel and Elisha as his successor in **1** **Kings 19:15-18**.

Because Ahab had humbled himself before the Lord at the prophesying of Elijah, God had forestalled His judgment, but now it was come due upon Ahab's son and against that wicked Jezebel. 

Elisha sends his disciple to the front in the war against Syria by the northern and southern kingdoms, and annoints Jehu, telling him the Lord has chosen him as king over Israel. And that he is the instrument of God's judgment against Jordan and Ahaziah, king over Judah. 

Jehu rides furiously with his host to the King's residence in Jezreel, and spying his approach, Joram sends messengers to ask if it be peace, and Jehu turns both sent to his side, as they fall in behind him. 

Finally, they can tell by his manner that it is Jehu, captain of the men approaching, and so the two kings ride out against him, ironically (or providentially) meeting at the portion of Naboth the Jezereelite, whom Jezebel had murdered to procure his vineyard for Ahab. 

*And it came to pass, when Joram saw Jehu, that he said, Is it peace, Jehu? And he answered, What peace, so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts are so many?*

And Jordan fled, but an arrow from Jehu fell him, straight through his heart. They cast his body in the field of Naboth, to be eaten by the field if the air as the Lord had spoke. 

Ahaziah, King of Judah flees, but Jehu smites him as well. He continues, wounded to Meggido, dying there and was taken to Jerusalem to be buried with David and his fathers. 

Jehu then sets off to the city, and there Jezebel paints her face and readies her hair and looked out a window to see. She cries out an accusation against Jehu, comparing him to the ill-fated Zimri, who ruled for 7 days after his coup against Elah. 

Jehu calls out to the others inside the keep with her, and asks who is on his side. And a couple of eunuchs took and threw her down from her window, and horses trod on her blood underfoot. 

Jehu sends to have her buried, but only a portion remained of her corpse, the rest eaten of dogs as God had cursed. *The carcase of Jezebel shall be as dung upon the face of the field in the portion of Jezreel...*what a fitting and terrible fate.

God's judgments are true, and will come. Turning from wicked ways may bring God to repent of the evil He would do, but the chastisements will come, eventually. For rulers, for nations, for His sons and daughters who have backslidden and ignored His chastening. Eventually, for the whole unbelieving world.

One of the most epic chapters of **2 Kings**, the story of Jehu and his consolidation of power and carrying out the command of the Lord by the prophet Elisha, utterly destroying the house of Ahab and killing all the servants of Baal. 

For his faithfulness in this task, the Lord promises Israel will be reigned over by his sons to the 4th generation. But due to his leaving the golden calves of Jeroboam, where Israel was made to sin before God, worshiping them in His name, God afflicted the nation with the armies of Syria, under Hazael (who was anointed as well to do just that).

Jehu had great zeal for the Lord, and was ruthless in his execution of it. When the throne was his, he had to deal with securing it from an heir to Ahab, who had 70 sons. Rather than waiting or riding himself, he wrote to the men entrusted with their care challenging them to rise up against him. When they pledge loyalty out of fear, he immediately calls them on it, demanding the heads of all 70 sons. And they deliver. 

He has the heads piled at the gates, and says to the people who may have judged him as an usurper for slaying the king of Israel (and Judah); 

*Ye be righteous: behold, I conspired against my master, and slew him: but who slew all these?*

The power of doing mighty works for God lay in the number of others who will do likewise at your example. The number of folks that will follow your lead and do their part and great things are accomplished for the furtherance of Christ. 

Being able, when persecuted and accused for your faith and your witness, to point at results greater than anything you've personally achieved, and say "Who slew all these?" is a powerful rebuke to those who hate Christ, and seek to oppose the Lord.

Then the brethren of Ahaziah, the King of Judah whom Jehu had also slain, came riding to "pay their respects" to the family of Ahab and Jezebel, as it were. They likely came for vengeance, and the very act was disrespectful to Jehu as king. He has the 42 men taken alive, cast into a pit and slaughters them there, together.

Then he meets with Jehonadab the Kenite, son of Rechab. The Rechabites, mentioned in Jeremiah, are non-Israelites who lived among them as nomads, never owning land, planting vineyards or drinking wine. Fierce followers of the Lord. 

Jehu, seeking his approval and support meets with Jehonadab and shaking hands in peace, invites him into his chariot, saying; *Come with me, and see my zeal for the Lord.*

They then set out and slew all the men loyal to Ahab, and those of his seed, according to the saying of the Lord, which he spake to Elijah.

We, as Christians, like to think of ourselves as Jehu in this moment, and with other believers, show our zeal. I know I have been fired up for the Lord and eager to do His bidding and to show that zeal to others. It is a line of scripture that always has my heart stirring and gets me pumped up. 

I think we can learn a lesson from this to not allow our zeal to burn bright and fade away, as it did for Jehu to some extent. In his zeal, he did the things the Lord set before him with gusto. But long term, the Bible says;

*But Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the Lord God of Israel with all his heart: for he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam, which made Israel to sin.* 

Sometimes, especially for new Christians, that initial zeal can be lost and faded over time. We are better to stoke our zeal for the Lord as a fire, and keep it going as warm embers for our entire life, than burn out quickly and fade like Jehu.

But the flame of Jehu's zeal is awesome, none the less. To rid the land of Baal, Jehu calls an assembly, telling the priest and followers of Baal to gather in their temple for a feast. He makes out as if he is with them, and they all gladly come to curry favor with the new king. 

There he has the assembly of Baal look for any followers of the Lord snuck in among them. Then gives them special clothing, vestments for Baal (all the easier for the soldiers outside to recognize them). Then, as they sacrifice their false god, he orders his men to slaughter them. 

They do, and break down the houses of Baal, destroying the images and idols. Turning their temple Into an outhouse. 

*Thus Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel.*

This story always gladdens my heart and makes me long for the day we break down the idols and drive the false priests of the Roman church and its harlot daughters out of our land.

**2 Kings 12** provides more detail of Jehoash, King of Judah, who the Bible says reigned rightly in the sight of the Lord while being guided by Jehoiada, the high priest that had raised him. 

He reigned for 40 years, brake down the house of Baal and destroyed the idols, as we read in chapter 11. But we see that many of the people of Judah still worshipped in the high places and burnt incense there. 

And Jehoash orders the priests to use the money they received from dedications, from extra donations given by men, (Corban as the NT calls it) and money they acquired themselves outside of tithes and offerings, and use that money to help them repair the Temple. 

They do not see to the repairs themselves and their own money they don't use for it, and so Jehoash orders them to not receive the money any longer. 

The impression is that they were to fundraise and rather than dedicate that money to the repairs, they spent it in other ways. It doesn't indicate if it was misappropriation (although they did not do as the King commanded so, it would be regardless). But the system didn't work as intended. 

But Jehoiada creates a donation box, and set it at the entrance, and by and by it is filled with money. This money was gathered and used for the hire of workmen who repaired the Temple. None of the extra money was used to increase the treasure of the house of the Lord, only to upkeep. And the men who did the work and the priests that paid them did so honorably and honestly. 

I think this is a story of the best intentions of the King, but a lack of wisdom in how to carry it out. Where his chief advisor, the high priest Jehoiada's plan works to achieve the same end, illustrating the King's need for that guidance. 

Because, *Jehoash did that which was right in the sight of the Lord all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him.*

And when the King of Syria, Hazael, set his face to go up to Jerusalem to make war, King Jehoash took all of the wealth of his house that was dedicated to the Lord, hallowed things of his fathers and his own, and even of the Temple, and sent it as ransom to Hazael, who accepted it and left Jerusalem alone. 

Again, the wisdom of such a thing is questionable. Giving that which was the Lord's to save him, rather than trusting in the Lord to deliver them from their enemies. A shortsighted lack of faith. The next event is his assassination at the hands of his servants, and it seems to be a consequence of his poor decisions after no longer having the priest to guide him. 

And so, as 2 Kings turns to the Southern Kingdom, we see Amaziah, his son, take the throne.

Here in **2 Kings 13**, we are back in the Northern Kingdom of Israel, and Jehoahaz the son of Jehu. The Lord had promised Jehu his sons would reign to the 4th generation, and this promise is kept here in this chapter, as we are also told of Jehoahaz' son, Joash and his son, Jeroboam, all taking the throne. It is a speed run through the lineage, and more is told of their reigns in **Chronicles**. 

During this time, God was using Syria to punish Israel for their continued sin, worshiping idols in His name, and Baal in the groves and high places. Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.

At some point, despite the evil he had done, *Jehoahaz besought the Lord, and the Lord hearkened unto him*. And the Lord provided a savior to Israel, allowing them some relief. 

Jehoahaz visits the dying Elisha, who gives to him a bow and arrow, and tells him to smite the ground with it. Jehoahaz smites the ground three times, and Elisha says that it would have been better had he done it more, but now God will deliver victory against the Syrians three times, and as we see, He does. Syria still will ultimately destroy Israel, but not as yet. God for the sake of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob forestalls their final judgement. But Israel are still in great tribulation, forced to live in tents as their fathers did. No longer tied to the land by inheritance. 

Hazeal of Syria died, and his son Benhadad rules in his stead and continued the affliction of Israel.

Elisha's death occurs in this chapter, and a miracle concerning the prophet; Moabites invade and while burying a man, they spied a band coming, a s so they cast the dead man into the sepulchre of Elisha, and when he was lowered into the tomb, he touched the prophet's bones and revived. 

This one short verse is used, primarily by the Orthodox Church, but by many Roman Catholics as well, to justify their veneration and worship of corpses, skulls and bones. Relics, they say, of "holy men," the "saints." They claim the bones have power, that there is Spirit still invested in them, and that this power can be transferred to those that touch them, pray to them, and worship them in rites and rituals. 

This pagan cult of relics, worshiping death, serving the dead things of the flesh, is wicked as Hell. As Proverbs says; *all they that hate me love death.* 

They store the skeletal remains, usually of unknown origin but with grandiose claims or being Apostles, certain saints, in special places. Temples of death. In glass cases to be paraded about, being served. Miracles are attributed to these abominations. Forgeries abound. 

But Scripture gives no such accounting. A miracle occurred. The how and the why aren't given. Elisha isn't exhumed and carted around to temples. No Israelites lined up to seek to be healed by the relics of a finger bone or skull. 

No instruction is given by the inspiration of God to do anything of the sort. In fact, we are told repeatedly by the word of God that to do so is unclean. It's gross.

Here in **2 Kings 14**, we are given more history of the Kings of Israel and Judah, and see the first open war between the kingdoms, when Amaziah of Judah and Jehoash of Israel met in battle, Judah losing to their brothers, and Jerusalem sacked. 

The Bible says that Amaziah did right in the eyes of the Lord, but did not have the heart of David. He kept Baal worship out of Judah as his father did, but allowed the high places and sacrifices there to continue. 

He did right by not slaying the sons of the servants who had murdered his father, killing only the assassins themselves. 

*The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor the children be put to death for the fathers; but every man shall be put to death for his own sin.*

A reminder that the concept of "original sin," the false idea that we are born condemned by the son of Adam, rather than having his same sinful nature, is unbiblical and goes against the teachings of God. 

Amaziah went against Edom and had success. This prompted his challenge to Jehoash in Israel, who taunted his challenge saying that he was a thistle compared to his mighty cedar. 

Jehoash did evil in the sight of the Lord, and so too his son Jeroboam who was crowned after his death. But the prophet Jonah, son of Amittai spoke to him the word of God, that he expand and shore up the territory of Israel due to the affliction He saw in the land. He used the wicked king to be a deliverer for the people, while the lukewarm king of Judah, who did that which was right but wasn't sold out for the Lord, was not as successful in ruling. He was overthrown by a seditious plot, as was his father. And like him, his son was placed on the throne.

A key element to the stories of the kings of Judah is their unwillingness to drive all the sin from the land. They may break down the house of Baal and destroy the images and slay the priests, but they never turn to the high places. They leave sin in the land. 

While Israel continues its slide towards destruction and promoting a false religion, they have varying success and failures, afflictions and victories, as the will of God found necessary. 

But Judah, who are as a saved Christian, trusting the Lord and getting right on major sin, never fully commit. And God chastens them for it. 

We can take that lesson and apply it to our own lives as saved believers. We should seek to have a heart like David's, and not be lukewarm in our walk, but strive to remove the high places in our hearts.

Wicked King Ahaz, of Judah, who took the gods of the high places and passed his son through the fire, and brought the gods and altar of the Assyrians to the house of the Lord in Jerusalem.

Had his fathers rid Judah of the high places, and kept to the faith of their fathers, would Ahaz had the opportunity or desire to be tempted away to heathenism?

As with the Philippian jailer and Cornelius, often the lead of the father, the patriarch, brings whole households to the Lord. Other times, even the most righteous men have wicked sons. It is no guarantee. 

But if you walk in the paths God provided us, and raise up your child in the way they should go, and remove the high places in your heart, keeping your house, your kingdom, unspotted from the world, you increase the odds that your children will do the same. 

A sincere man who is a believer, who walks in the ways of righteousness, and loves his wife and children with the same love as God shows us; longsuffering, kind, merciful but uncompromising on what is right, firm but fair, as a doer of the law, who visits the widow in their affliction and is a good judge to the fatherless, will more likely have children who do.

Some Christian men make the mistake of being iron fisted and provoking their children to wrath, and think that is the way to rule their household. They fear the world and its influence so much that they believe the only way to protect their children from it is as a tyrant, trying to control everything they do. Their fear shows their children a lack of faith, and it can often drive them away from the Lord. 

We can raise our kids rightly, not sparing the rod of correction, chastening them betimes, training them up in the way they should go, while also showing them the unconditional love and mercy of the Father. Being an example of the same tender mercies God showed us in our salvation. 

Some men think that is weakness. God is not weak when He does this for us. Don't think it weak to follow His example.

**2 Kings 20**
