Here in **2 Kings 20**, the final tales of good King Hezekiah of Judah. First, we find the King near death. The prophet Isaiah comes and tells him to get his things in order, for the word of the Lord says he will surely die. 

Now we know from his introduction in chapter 18 that Hezekiah did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord, and walked in His ways. So hearing of his pending untimely death, he turned in prayer to the Lord. 

He reminded God of his faithfulness and his living according to God's precepts, and asks to be spared this fate, in tears. 

And before Isaiah had gone out of the courtyard, God repents and grants Hezekiah 15 more years. That after 3 days, when he is clean, he shall go up to the house of the Lord. (This seems like a picture of Christ, and the healing power of the Spirit to me).

And Hezekiah asks for a sign, to know that what Isaiah speaks is true, and he offers that the Lord can make the shadow of the sundial move forward 10 degrees, or backwards 10. Hezekiah asks for the sub to move backwards in the sky, being a more sure sign of God's might, and it does. 

And the Lord promises;

*I will deliver thee and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria; and I will defend this city for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake.*

Note again, it isn't for the Jews and it isn't for Hezekiah that the Lord preserved Jerusalem. But for His own sake and the covenant He made with David, that is Christ.

Hezekiah asked for a sign that the word of God spoken of Isaiah was true. Paul writes in **1 Corinthians 1**:**22-24**;

*For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom: but we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; but unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God.*

In the Old Testament, the Hebrews often asked for a sign, and were given them. Sometimes, God offered a sign that they may know His word was true. But we have the Spirit testifying within us, and the more sure words of prophecy of the Bible. 

In our life, when we are praying to God to deliver us from bad things, illness, family members in trouble, whatever, we are reassured by the Spirit confirming the word of God and His promises to us. That according to His will, He is faithful to deliver us. This is sign enough. 

But often we need more. As the tearful father said to Jesus, asking Him to bring back his daughter unto him, *Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.* Or as the apostles said to Christ, *Lord, Increase our faith.*

We can ask God for reassurance. We can ask for things we've hoped for, and see the work of the Spirit bringing it about. Increasing our faith. Helping our unbelief. It doesn't mean we doubt our salvation, or that God can't deliver. It just means we are human, and the flesh fears. 

This is why it is important to be in good standing with the Father, as Hezekiah was. Able to go before God to ask of Him what we need. By walking 3the Spirit and being right with the things of God, our faith is made stronger, and our trust in him when we are weak will come more naturally. 

But when we are in sin, and ashamed, and walk in the flesh, our doubts and fears increase. Our faith that God will save us falters, knowing we don't deserve His mercy. 

Thankfully, He is faithful to us, that if we turn to Him, and confess our sins, He will forgive us. **1 John 1:5-9** 

*This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. If we say that we have fellowship with him, and walk in darkness, we lie, and do not the truth: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.*

**1 John 5:13-15** 
*These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God. And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us: And if we know that he hear us, whatsoever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we desired of him.*

So, like Hezekiah, let us walk in the light that we may have confidence in the Lord to deliver us from our troubles.

But a story of an Old Testament saint wouldn't be complete without an example of their sin. For all have sinned and come short of the glory of God. And Hezekiah was no different. 

The king of Babylon sends his regards, having heard of hezekiah's illness. And the recovered Hezekiah entertains the servants of the king. The Bible doesn't tell us that Hezekiah praised the Lord for his recovery, but rather showed them all of the riches of his kingdom, the city, his household and in the Temple.  

His sin is pride. Boasting of his riches while just a short while before he was on his deathbed. 

This is possibly the most common thing that I have experienced myself and witnessed in others; a great triumph of the Lord acting miraculously in our lives, followed by a low point where we forget the trouble we were in, and grow comfortable, taking it for granted. 

It is so easy for sin to creep in when this happens. 

One of the ways to avoid it is to not only go to God in our troubles and with supplications, but to praise the Lord for when He acts mightily in our lives. Bragging on him rather than ourselves. Staying humble. 

Because of Hezekiah's sin, Isaiah comes to him and tells him that God has judged and that all of the treasures he had shown off to Babylon would be carried away there. And that his son s will be eunuchs to their King.

Hezekiah accepts the rebuke and the judgment. And is thankful that it won't be in his day. But that small comfort isn't worth the moment of sin. 

Judah will soon learn a lesson in humility. And while God won't destroy them yet, because of his own interests and his promise to David, they will be made desolate for 70 years.

Josiah becomes King of Judah, and does that which is right in the eyes of the Lord. He seeks the truth and is given it, when the scribe and priest find a copy of the Law, the word of God, and deliver it to him. The young king reads it and rends his clothes knowing the sin of their fathers, and the people not harkening to all that which was written. 

He seeks to know God's will, and enquires of a prophetess who tells them that God will judge Judah harshly, with desolation, but that because of the tender heart of the King, and Josiah's humble and faithful reaction to hearing the word of God and believing it, judgment is spared for the length of his reign. 

The story of King Josiah is a picture of the coming of Christ. Where some were seeking truth, hearts meet for repentance, and the Word of God came among them, and they believed, and because of that faith, are spared the wrath of God. 

This applies to the 1st century Jews who accepted Christ, and the desolation of Jerusalem in 70AD. 

It also applies to believers in general, who hear the word of God with tender hearts and humble spirits, and are delivered from the wrath that will pour out in the world at Christ's return.

We are here in **2 Kings 23**, and the reign of Josiah, King of Judah. A godly man, who sought the Lord and, when finding the law of God and reading the covenant that had been ignored for generations, uses his power as king to set things right; to honor the covenant of the Lord. 

He orders that all, great and small, come to the temple and he reads the entire book of the law to the people, and standing by the King's pillar, makes a covenant with God to walk in His commandments, keeping His statutes with all their heart and soul. He leads a revival. 

Now the pillar he stood by, the same as that which other kings had, I believe is a picture of Christ. The promise of Him, shown to us as that unmoving pillar of the king whereby Josiah stands firmly in the word of God. 

And Josiah's zeal for the Lord is excellent. 

He destroys all of the groves, altars, high places, images, idols, and other abominations to false gods, not only throughout Judah, but even into the territory of Israel, whereby Jeroboam had led Israel to sin. 

He destroys that altar and the image where the prophet of old had come and preached against the first king of divided Israel, foretelling of this day, which we covered [here](https://t.me/HouseOfWews2/14487).

He destroys the houses of the sodomites, kills the evil priests and tears down the places where children were sacrificed by passing them through the fire. And at each place, the king not only grinds them to dust, but scatters their ashes and desecrated the places with the ashes of dead men's bones. 

When we read the list of places, and see that not only evil kings, but "good kings," such as Solomon, had put up these abominations. That the worship of false gods had permeated nearly everything, including the temple and the gates of the city. 

A little leaven had leavened the whole lump. But Josiah purges it with fire.

*Notwithstanding the Lord turned not from the fierceness of his great wrath, wherewith his anger was kindled against Judah, because of all the provocations that Manasseh had provoked him withal. And the Lord said, I will remove Judah also out of my sight, as I have removed Israel, and will cast off this city Jerusalem which I have chosen, and the house of which I said, My name shall be there.*

The revival and zeal for the Lord shown by King Josiah led God to grant his reign a measure of peace and delayed their judgement against them. But it did not prevent God's wrath from being poured out eventually. 

And Josiah knew by the prophecy given to him that the judgment was inevitable. But he still did that which was right and was tearful and full of regret for the evil done in the land by his fathers and the people. 

Contrast that with when Hezekiah said unto Isaiah, who had given the same warning; *Good is the word of the Lord which thou hast spoken. And he said, Is it not good, if peace and truth be in my days?*

Hezekiah, a good king as well who did fear the Lord, accepted the judgment and was glad it wasn't in his day, but did not utterly purge the land as Josiah did. He was relieved that the wrath was held back, and that his children would suffer the consequences rather than him. 

This mentality is common among what is called the "baby boomer" generation, many of whom recognizing that the consequences for their sin would lead to judgment, took comfort in the fact that they wouldn't be here to see it. And it is no wonder that the false doctrine of a pre-tribulation rapture was so appealing to them. 

They rested in the delusion that while the nation may be going to Hell in a hand basket, and that judgment was coming, that they didn't need to worry. They would be spared any trouble when it "got really bad." They didn't make any effort to turn back to the Lord with zeal and lead a revival in hopes of turning back God's wrath or buying more time. They said *Is it not good, if peace and truth be in my days?*

Then you see another generation come, who like Josiah, look to the word of God and understand that the sodomites and the idols and the failure to walk in the statutes of the Lord is the cause of the judgment, and as righteous as God's indignation against us is, we still have a duty to follow His commandments, even if it means facing great tribulation. To lament the wickedness done and to preach and act against it. And to proclaim the word of God and His righteousness to the world. In season or out of season. 

It is a different attitude, and one that the old guard of Christians often resent and look down upon, because it convicts them for their inaction, or leads them to special pleading, saying "I tried ...it's not my fault."

I would rather have the spirit of Josiah rending his clothes and seeking after the Lord than of Hezekiah's acquiescence and pride in his earthly wealth.

The nature of revival, of proclaiming the truth of God to all men, to soul-winning and contending for the faith, and challenging false ways and compromise, is that it forces people to choose. 

We often talk of God's constant winnowing, the separation of the wheat from the chaf, which is shown throughout the Bible, but the truth is, God is constantly giving men a choice. He is offering us the truth and life, and placing the choice on our hearts. 

**Deuteronomy 30:15-20**
*See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil; In that I command thee this day to love the Lord thy God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments and his statutes and his judgments, that thou mayest live and multiply: and the Lord thy God shall bless thee in the land whither thou goest to possess it. But if thine heart turn away, so that thou wilt not hear, but shalt be drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them. **Joshua 24:15** 
*And if it seem evil unto you to serve the Lord, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.*

Forcing people to make this choice is the purpose of revival. It is the fruit of preaching the word and going out to win souls. It forces people to choose. 

Some will hear the word and be converted unto eternal life. But many will reject Christ and decide to harden their hearts and hold the truth in unrighteousness. 

The revival led by King Josiah was shortlived. When he died in battle, his sons were made king, first Jehoahaz, who was then carried away to Egypt, and then Eliakim aka Jehoiakim. Both did evil in the sight of the Lord. In our study of **Jeremiah**, we covered these kings and the wickedness of Judah in their day, when Babylon came and made Jerusalem a desolation, fulfilling the word of God. They did evil in the sight of the Lord and willfully and knowingly turned to the sins of their fathers and the abominations that they did. 

The Lord giving Judah one last chance to know the truth, to have it read to them by Josiah, and acted upon by his hand, meant that while many believed unto righteousness, most chose death. 

So that when God's wrath came upon them, they were without excuse. 

Soul-winning is what we are called to do, but the more we do it, the more the gospel is proclaimed to every creature, and gone out to all the world, the more people will become reprobate. Even our own families. 

At some point, the fullness of the Gentiles will come in. Everyone who will be saved will be, and the rest will choose to worship the beast and take his mark, and condemn themselves. 

Our job is to go work the harvest. To force the issue. To make people decide if they choose life or death.

**Luke 12:51-53**
*Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division: For from henceforth there shall be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three. The father shall be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother in law against her daughter in law, and the daughter in law against her mother in law.*

This idea of division is confusing for some, but it is something that I think saved Christians understand by the Spirit, even if they don't intellectually. 

We all have had loved ones, family, friends, who we have shared the gospel with and given the good news to, but we hesitate to push the issue. To bring them to make a decision. To force them to either accept or reject the truth that's saved us. The grace that we stand on. 

Sometimes, it's embarrassment at our own sins being evident to those who know us best. Fear of being exposed as a hypocrite.

But often, it is the understanding that pushing the issue may push them away. That in trying to save them, we could lose them. And that nagging feeling that if we do, we lose them forever and that they will condemn themselves. 

Christians are often so afraid that our loved ones will perish and be damned, but at the same time are scared we could be the cause of it. We love them more than the truth of Christ and our indecision and fear of making them choose comes from that. And the spiritual discernment to know it may be their final decision, reprobating themselves.

**1 Chronicles 17** finds David at his peak as King of Israel. He has power, a capital, great palaces and all from the anointing of the Lord. He sits with Nathan the prophet, and inquires about building a temple for God that He may no longer be in tents. 

And just as in the same story found in **2 Samuel 7**, God speaking through Nathan tells David that he shall not build the temple, but makes instead a covenant with David that his son will, and that the son of David will rule forever. This is a clear picture of Christ. 

The intended audience for the chapter were men of Israel returning from the captivity of Judah by Babylon, and God's mention of redeeming their fathers from Egypt was particularly fitting for them, as was the reassurance that the kingdom was blessed by God through David's son. That a Temple of God would be built. A house, just as the exiled were returned to rebuild. 

But the same covenant is clearly speaking of Jesus, the house He shall build, the redemption He would pay for. That Jesus would be as a son to the Father. And rule and reign forever. 

It is a beautiful passage, and you gain understanding of why when in the gospels people call Jesus the "son of David" there is a messianic meaning behind it.

Repent ye; for the Kingdom of heaven is at hand. 

Repent means to change your mind, to accept new information as true and have a change of heart, a conversion.

As we near the end of **1 Chronicles**, we see the account of David, having assembled the people, all of whom he'd assigned roles and drawn lots for responsibilities, to give them the plan for the resting place for the ark, and a footstool upon the earth for the Lord. That his son Solomon had been chosen of God to do this thing, to build the temple, and the details and design which were given David by the Spirit. 

Again, the audience of the author are the Jews returning from captivity centuries later, who would rebuild the temple, that it serve as a picture of the risen Christ. That it be there, in Jerusalem when Jesus came, to serve its purpose of sacrifice and ceremony until that reformation came; the resurrection of the Christ.

I recently was giving the gospel to someone who said, "I understand God loves us, and that His Son, Jesus was born and died and rose again for us, but I struggle with the question; Why?" Not as in why did God do this, which we know is because He so loved us. But why in this manner?

I think one of the reasons is that man by our nature we know sin requires a sacrifice for atonement. 

Of course every animal sacrificed from Adam and Eve and God showing them the way, through righteous Abel, to Noah disembarking from the ark, to Abraham with Melchizedek, to Moses and Arron and the Levitical priests, were pictures given by God of the actual sacrifice to come. The Lamb slain before the foundation of the world. And they who trusted in the Christ to come were saved by that faith. But without some means of understanding, it was difficult for them to form faith. Thus the process laid out in the law. 

But for the other nations called, after the crucifixion and resurrection, the one sacrifice made for all time, for all sin, by Jesus' blood, man needed to understand it clearly. And so we place trust in His word. Faith being the evidence of things not seen, which comes from hearing His word. There needed to be witnesses. It had to happen here, in this world that others would believe, sight unseen. 

As Jesus says to Thomas, *blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.*

Without the prophets and scriptures promising Christ, the sacrifice of Christ, and without the witnesses to the resurrection testifying of Christ, I think man would not believe God wanted to forgive them. Without the gospel preached, a witness, exactly as it stands:

Here in **1 Chronicles 29**, the final chapter, we come to the transition of power between King David and his son Solomon. David has, in obedience to the Lord, organized the Kingdom, set up the leaders of men and the chain of command in the various roles and responsibilities. He has given Solomon the plans for the house of God, the pattern given by the Spirit, and laid up treasure and provisions to see it built. 

And the people all willingly gave treasure to build up the house of the Lord and to do His work. Free will offerings. 

David calls them to prayer and to bless the Lord God of Israel, to give Him all glory and honor. David's prayer reminds us that whatever we give to the service of God is His to begin with. 

Tithing, the practice of giving the first of the flock, the tenth of the wealth and harvest, etc...these are commands in the Old Testament, that we honor today in the New. 

But the free will offerings here are a reminder that all we have *cometh of Thine hand, and is all Thine own.* Not just 10%, pretax income, itemized and listed on our taxes. All of it. Everything we have is His because it is by His grace we have it at all. 

For all things come of God. And when we give, it is of God's own. 

When we approach giving towards the church, or to help the brethren, or missions and church plants and soul winning trips...whatever it may be, give cheerfully, willingly. 

Because riches and honor come from God. It is His power to make us great, and blessed by whatever riches He provides. We can't take it with us; there are none abiding. 

So give joyfully, knowing it's not yours but the Lord's. And rejoice in it, praising Him in thanksgiving, that you have abundance wherewithal to give.

In **1 Kings 3** we see Solomon settling in as King of Israel, making peace with the Pharaoh of Egypt through marriage to his daughter, while building his palace and the Temple of the Lord in Jerusalem. 

We are told that the people sacrificed in high places because there was no house of the Lord for central worship as had been when the Ark and the Tabernacle were in one location, together. David had brought the Ark to Jerusalem, while Zadok the priest was in charge over the Tabernacle in Gibeon, apparently a high place, according to the account in **2 Chronicles 1**. 

And while we have association with Baal worship in high places, and the existence of them was no God's plan for a central place of worship, in this strange in-between time, it wouldn't be outrageous for Solomon, who loved the Lord and kept David's statutes, to sacrifice at Gibeon to the Lord God of Israel. 

And Solomon does, and offers a thousand burnt offerings upon the altar of the Tabernacle out of love for God. 

And God graciously speaks to Solomon by dream, and tells the new king to ask what God shall give him. 

Solomon says *Thou hast shewed unto thy servant David my father great mercy, according as he walked before thee in truth, and in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart with thee; and thou hast kept for him this great kindness, that thou hast given him a son to sit on his throne, as it is this day.*

Solomon wisely begins his petition by recognizing how God blessed his father, David. The great mercy the living God showed him, and the great kindness of giving David an heir to sit upon the throne. 

As the father of saved children, I can tell you this kindness is awesome, and the mercy of God that we may know our children are co-heirs with Christ to the Kingdom is one of the greatest gifts God can bestow on a parent. 

Solomon continues, wisely recognizing his youth and inexperience as he takes the throne given to him as God's anointed, king over a great number of people. And so Solomon asks for an understanding heart to judge God's people, strong discernment between good and bad. 

This pleased the Lord, and because Solomon did not ask foolishly or selfishly, God says *Behold, I have done according to thy words: lo, I have given thee a wise and an understanding heart*. The wisest man to ever live. 

The question then arises, was this gift given to Solomon at this moment, where his eyes opened and he gained this wisdom supernaturally? Or, given his upbringing by David, and his love for the Lord and his desire to walk in the ways of his father and the word of God, had Solomon been shaped by God from birth to be such a King? 

When Solomon is given an opportunity to ask of God anything, and he was wise enough to give glory to God first and ask for right judgment to rule wisely, was he already displaying that wisdom that had been given him by the Lord? 

Because Solomon asked rightly, God says He will not only bless him with wisdom, but riches and honor, elevating him above all kings during his reign. 

God also repeats His promise, one that stands for Christians today; *And if thou wilt walk in my ways, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as thy father David did walk, then I will lengthen thy days.*

And so, we are told the famous story of an example of the wisdom of Solomon; the cutting of the baby in half. This is such an extraordinary tale, that even secular and worldly traditions of wisdom recognize it and teach it throughout the world. 

Two harlots, and both give birth to sons within days of each other. And the one accidentally kills her own baby, smothering it in its sleep. She steals the other woman's son in the night and gives to her the dead child. 

They come before the King to judge and he discerned the matter by presenting a horrific choice; cutting the infant that each woman be given half. 

The woman who objects and says rather let the other woman keep it, is clearly the real mother, while the one who agrees to "split the baby" is revealed to be the imposter. 

This wisdom established the understanding throughout Israel that God had blessed their King. and gained Solomon the people's respect. Fame that would soon spread to the rest of the world.

"According to the first-century Romano-Jewish scholar Josephus' book Antiquities of the Jews, **Jachin** (Hebrew יָכִין yakin "He/it will establish") stood on the right on the portico of Solomon's Temple, while **Boaz** (Hebrew בֹּעַז boʿaz "In him/it [is] strength") stood on the left, and the two were made by a Canaanite craftsman named Hiram."

The pillars stood outside the entrance, free standing. One to the North the other the South, in the East-facing entrance. East to catch the rising sun.

Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the Temple is dripping with doctrine. Of the glory of God and the promises of salvation, the covenants with David, and with Israel. 

The King begins recounting that God's glory is hid by the thick darkness, the cloud that protects the people from being consumed by His majesty, but Solomon has built this house for a dwelling place. 

Blessing the Lord God of Israel, loyal and true, keeping the promises made to David by His word. That He has chosen Jerusalem to place His name, and in David, a King to rule. The promise of Christ Jesus.

Solomon, on his knees, kneeling upon a brazen scaffold, hands outstretched to the heavens before the congregation, says *O Lord God of Israel, there is no God like thee in the heaven, nor in the earth; which keepest covenant, and shewest mercy unto thy servants, that walk before thee with all their hearts*. 

We who are the Israel of God, believers, are His servants. We receive these same blessings of our faithful God. His kept promises and mercy adding to our faith, and our faith leading to our obedience in Him. 

Solomon acknowledges that the Lord God of Israel cannot be contained by a dwelling place, not of a temple made by hands, but prays instead that God's eyes be on this house he's built, that He in His grace grant prayers and supplication made within the Temple. To the people of Israel and to the stranger who comes to worship. That all nations be blessed in Him. 

He prays for forgiveness for future generations, who may by sin be chastened by the Lord, that if they turn again to Him, that the Lord forgive them and bring them again into the land. Or to heal the land from pestilence and blight. 

He prays that God favors their armies when they set out to do His will, to return them from captivity when they repent, and that His mercies extend to the people who pray towards the land, the city, the Temple, the house which has been built for His holy name.

Of course this is relevant to us, who as saved believers are the temple of God. He has placed His name in us, and His great mercies and blessings extend towards us, in the name of Jesus. The land we turn towards is that better country, the Kingdom of Heaven. Our King, the king of kings, the Son of David upon His throne forever. 

If we sin, *for there is no man that sinneth not*, He will forgive. We are His priests, clothed with salvation. His promise, His Word, the ark of strength in our hearts. 

Let us rejoice in goodness. Amen

**2 Chronicles 9** tells a digest form of the reign of King Solomon, describing the heights of his kingdom. Famed for wisdom, brought riches by other kings and queens, the boundaries of Israel expanded to their largest, and held in peace. 

It tells of 666 talents of gold brought to Solomon per year. And tribute made by kings seeking his presence and to hear his wisdom, as the Queen of Sheba had. The vessels of silver and gold, and horses and spices, year after year. The great ivory throne that he has built, as his judgment seat. The ships of Tarshish brining treasure from far lands.

We have read in **1 Kings** the story of Solomon, good and bad. His wives by which he sinned. His son, doomed to rule a divided kingdom. But here, we are given the description of a king and a kingdom that are a picture of the millennial Kingdom of the Lord Christ Jesus. 

As the author says, the rest of the acts of Solomon are found elsewhere. In long lost books that the inspired book of **Chronicles** is drawn from. In **Kings**. But the purpose of this retelling, like the previous chapters, is to give inspiration to the returning captives and to provide saved Christians insights and examples, in our own way leaving the captivity of Babylon by our salvation in Christ. 

Solomon's wisdom and judgment were a good report throughout the world. By his faith and putting God first, others sought him out to learn how and why he was so blessed, and glory was given to the Lord by his example. 

We know Solomon wasn't perfect. He had flaws. But by honoring God, honoring his father, by seeking to do right for others, he became a beacon drawing others to God.

*Happy are thy men, and happy are these thy servants, which stand continually before thee, and hear thy wisdom. Blessed be the Lord thy God, which delighted in thee to set thee on his throne, to be king for the Lord thy God: because thy God loved Israel, to establish them for ever, therefore made he thee king over them, to do judgment and justice*.

This statement by the Queen of Sheba can also be seen as a prayer to the Lord God the Father about His holy Son. 

Happy are His servants, blessed is the Lord our God. The Israel of God established forever. Amen.

The term "Jew" will begin to be used as a designation for those residing in Judah, including Benjamin, Levi and those who fled to Jerusalem, wishing to serve the Lord God only. *Ought ye not to know that the Lord God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David for ever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt?*

The Lord is with the armies of Abijah, and they slay 500K Israelites, routing them and taking Bethel and other lands from the North.

Here in **2 Chronicles 18**, we find King Jehosaphat, whose reign in Judah has been blessed by God, and who has walked as David walked, pleasing to the Lord, Yoking himself to wicked King Ahab of the northern Kingdom of Israel. 

This retelling of the story found in **1 Kings 22** retains the facts of the matter, Jehosaphat visiting Samaria, the feast given by Ahab, the proposal to retake Ramothgilead from the Syrians. The false prophets given the lying spirit of the Lord. Righteous Jehosaphat asking that they inquire of a true prophet of God. 

Micaiah the prophet is called for, whom Ahab despised. He speaks the word of God and tells Ahab he will die in the battle, the men scattered and going home to their tents for lack of a leader. And of course, all this comes to pass. 

But here, in **2 Chronicles**, and the perspective of how blessed and faithful Jehosaphat is, his alliance with the wicked Ahab is surprising. Especially his willingness to commit to going to war with the prophecy of Micaiah, knowing it is a doomed endeavor. 

How often in our Christian life do we find ourselves in a similar situation? Where maybe we seek peace, or not to offend, or a fruitful partnership with someone who is unsaved, and wicked. And in our desire to please men, join them in things that the word of God has told us are wrong. 

Jehosaphat, wearing his kingly robes at Ahab's suggestion, becomes the target of the Syrians. If not for calling out to the Lord, he would have been slain then and there. 

The wicked taking advantage of mistaken loyalty to save their own skin is one of the biggest risks of finding yourself in the position of being allied with them. 

Meanwhile, Ahab disguised himself, as if to fool God. So, a random arrow fired by a certain man finds him, and slays him. 

But Jehosaphat, who walked righteously, spread the word of God, removed the sodomites and high places and groves, and who had prospered in all things, does suffer a decline. 

We are given this information in **I Kings 22:48**, after the death of Ahab;

*Jehoshaphat made ships of Tharshish to go to Ophir for gold: but they went not; for the ships were broken at Eziongeber.*

This was a significant thing Solomon had done to increase his wealth and power, but Jehosaphat fails, his ships wrecked. Is it the fruit of his alliance? Maybe. It could just be the way things go. But we shouldn't risk being unequally yoked with the wicked.

The child-king, Joash began to reign at the age of 7, but was under the council of the high priest, Jehoiada. And all the days of Jehoiada, the Bible tells us, Joash did that which was right in the sight of the Lord. 

But, as we will see, once the influence of Jehoiada was gone, after his death, Joash allowed idols and groves and wickedness to flourish in Judah. 

**2 Chronicles 24** gives a slightly different view than what is given in **2 Kings 12**, regarding the collection for the restoration of the Temple, and added context to the story. 

I notice we are told that Jehoiada took a second wife, and immediately afterwards, Joash orders the collection to restore the house of "your God." The King chastises the priests and his vizier, Jehoiada for their not making haste in doing as he commanded. 

This story, and the context of some recent events, set me of mind about the relationship between father figures and sons, of the flesh or spiritually, and the dynamic that ofttimes plays out. 

Nothing in the Bible is accidental, coincidental or incidental. Joash is riding the faith and judgment of his spiritual father, Jehoiada. He is walking in the ways because his mentor is. 

When Jehoiada takes another wife for himself, Joash makes a demand for a great work to be undertaken, and then complains that it isn't being done fast enough to his liking. 

How often do we see the sons or daughters of a Christian man, who have been kept holy by their father's holiness, kept in subjection, and seeing a crack in their father's character (for all have fallen short), grow to resent them. Grow to hate them. 

In that resentment and hate, their own sinful desires find an outlet, a justification. And they often will set an impossible standard, or a subjective measurement to meet for the authority figure, in an arbitrary way, just so they can claim a moral high-ground from which to rebel. 

Here, Joash demands a great work to ("your") God. Was it objectively a good thing? Probably. Did it come from prayer and seeking God first? There is no indication. 

Joash has created a way to outwardly show how righteous he is, while using it to claim Jehoiada and the priests are falling short of it. 

This is as a rebellious son, wanting to justify their own sin and unrighteousness by tearing down the reputation of the man who they have decided is a hypocrite, because that man reminds them daily of their own shortcomings. 

They feel judged continuously, because they feel guilty. And rather than look to themselves and get right with God, they tear down the moral authority in their life. 

And once that authority is removed from them, they sink further and further into sin. 

Many such cases.

A lesson for fathers here, too. You cannot exert your own righteousness and salvation onto your children. Individuals have free will. We aren't given to micromanage our children, but to;

*Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it*.

We should not spare the rod. We should raise our children to fear the Lord, and be an example to them. When we fall short, demonstrate the mercy of God on us, and keep the same longsuffering mercy God shows us, and apply it to them. 

*And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.*

But we shouldn't try to carry their salvation on ourselves, that they never learn and build their own relationship with God. 

Joash did that which was right in the sight of God while under Jehoiada's influence. But it sounds like he was never saved. If he was, the King allowed his own resentment for Jehoiada to fester, and then to justify being backslidden. 

Either way, it is a lesson in leadership.

Ahaz reigned for 16 years, and did much that was wicked in the eyes of the Lord. When Hezekiah is anointed King, he immediately turns to the word of God as given to David, through Nathan the prophet, and David's seers, and reinstituted the Temple worship according to the Law of Moses.

Hezekiah recognizes the tribulation their people had suffered under the rule of Ahaz, and their own whoredoms with Baal. 

*And all the congregation worshipped, and the singers sang, and the trumpeters sounded: and all this continued until the burnt offering was finished.*

The sacrifices are so great, the Levites who served the priests were called to help in administering the offerings;

But the priests were too few, so that they could not flay all the burnt offerings: wherefore their brethren the Levites did help them, till the work was ended, and until the other priests had sanctified themselves: for the Levites were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests.

This indicates that the sons of Aaron, who were the priests tasked with the slaughter of the offerings, were not as zealous to sanctify themselves as the rest of the Levites. That there were not a few who just didn't care enough to get right. 

Here you have a young king, leading a revival by turning to the word of God, and some pushback or reluctance by the priesthood is indicated. 

Sometimes older Christians in lukewarm or dying churches resist the zeal of the young who come into the congregation. Even the pastor and deacons may resist the sudden change in attitudes that young Christians can bring to an assembly. 

But they should be as the loyal priests and Levites, eager to sanctify themselves and to do the work of the Lord. Even those saints who aren't used to evangelizing, or who have little to no experience with soul-winning, have to step up and join in the service of the Gospel. 

An injection of youth into a church is a reason to celebrate. Even the most prayerful and spiritual group of elders need foot soldiers to do the work of the Lord.

*33 And Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the chiefest of the sepulchres of the sons of David: and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem did him honour at his death. And Manasseh his son reigned in his stead.*

Here in **2 Chronicles 32**, and we have the last chronicles of the King, Hezekiah. Sennacherib, a captain of Assyria has come to lay siege against Judah and her walled cities having already begun its conquest of Israel. 

Knowing the hosts of the enemy are going to surround Jerusalem, compassing it about, Hezekiah has his men stop the flow of water to the fountains without the city. 

He has done great public works projects, and throughout his reign in Chronicles, we see how his diligently seeking the Lord has blessed him with civil engineering marvels (later we see he turned a river to bring water closer to the city). 

So his order to shut up the fountains so that *Why should the kings of Assyria come, and find much water?*

When Sennacherib comes, he immediately begins to profane and blaspheme God. 

The parallel I see to the Reprobate Doctrine, that those who do not wish to retain God in their knowledge and blaspheme and speak of the Lord God of all creation as if he were like other gods, weak and ineffectual and not to be trusted or relied on, have the waters of Life shut up from them. 

While all others are told by Jesus to come and drink freely, reprobates come to spoil that which is God's and to do harm to his people, because they have been denied partaking in the water of Life.

And while under siege, and railing and ranting by word and epistle, taunting God, Sennacherib, like the beast surrounds Jerusalem with his armies. 

And King Hezekiah cries out to heaven for deliverance with faith in the Lord. 

And the Lord strikes down the armies slaughtering the mightiest men of valor among them and sending the Assyrian General home in disgrace. So much so that his own children slay him. 

There's echoes of the end times there but also of the promise that God makes to us. If we are steadfast and true he will deliver us from the evil that the sons of Belial seek to do to us. Amen.

The book of Ezra begins with the proclamation of Cyrus, returning the Jews to Jerusalem in fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy, and the order to rebuild the house of God. 

As king of Persia, Cyrus says he is given his power by the Lord God of heaven, and that the Lord has charged him, a foreign potentate, with the reconstruction of the temple. 

As we know from Haggai and Zechariah, the work on the temple would not be completed while he was king. But the treasure sent to prepare the temple was impressive. When the Lord says in **Haggai 2:8** *The silver is mine, and the gold is mine,* He is not only saying that all riches in the world are His, but specifically the treasure given for this purpose, which languished until Zerubbabel and Joshua heard the prophets and finished the job.  

But here, at the beginning of the end of exile, the Jews; Judah, Benjamin and Levites, gladly returned to the city, with the treasure of the Lord.

The account of **Ezra 2** is till looking back at the time of the return, to establish some things needed to be understood for his story. The return from captivity first under Cyrus the great, and then under Darius I, when Zerubbabel and Joshua and the others returned to Jerusalem. The genealogy of the Levites who returned is given here. 

The timeline from Haggai and Zechariah to Esther, then to Ezra, and Nehemiah spans several decades within the Persian Empire's rule over the Jews. Haggai and Zechariah prophesied around 520 BC during the reign of Darius I, focusing on the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem. 

Approximately 40-50 years later, around 483-473 BC, the events of Esther unfolded under Ahasuerus (likely Xerxes I), who reigned from 486 to 465 BC. 

Following Xerxes I's death, his son Artaxerxes I ascended the throne around 465 BC. Ezra's mission to Jerusalem occurred around 458 BC, and Nehemiah's efforts to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem began around 445 BC, both under Artaxerxes I's rule.

So we have skipped forward around 60 years in time from Zechariah to Ezra. 

We see Zerubbabel and Joshua (Jeshua) mentioned. Nehemiah mentioned here is likely not the same as the Governor of Judah who ruled after Ezra's time. 

Just as the Mordecai mentioned in **Ezra 2:2** as part of the list of exiles who returned to Jerusalem around 538-520 BC, during the reign of Cyrus the Great, 65+ years before the events of Esther, make it highly unlikely he is the same guy. 

It is possible that Ezra is giving their names, or at least Nehemiah's, as a shorthand way to say his people returned then. 

The Nehemiah in **Ezra 2:2** would have been part of the initial return and rebuilding efforts, whereas the later Nehemiah was a high-ranking official in the Persian court before being appointed governor to oversee the reconstruction of Jerusalem's walls.

But it's more likely that these men shared a common name.  
 
We are given a genealogy for multiple clans of the Levites and the understanding that those who could not provide a patriarchal lineage were rejected as polluted, and put away from the preisthood. It is funny then that today, Jews Mark their lineage by mother, not father. A matrilineal line due to their rampant mixing, fornicating and adultery. The inverse of their supposed father's law. 

We are given their list of holdings they returned with, and the wealth they gave freely as an offering to the service of God. So we see the priests, Levites, the singers and porters and the Nethinims listed. What a great choir of 400 people singing Psalms and hymns!

I had to look up what Nethinims meant. "The Nethinim (or Nethinims in older King James translations) were a group of temple servants in ancient Israel, meaning "given ones" or "those set apart". Primarily of foreign descent and assigned to the Levites, they performed menial, practical tasks like cutting wood and carrying water for the Tabernacle and later the Temple."

They were likely either of mixed Gibionites or Midianite decent, used as slaves to the Levites under Solomon, their children returning in service as well.

In **Ezra 5**, the governor Tatnai and his allies had written to Darius I, king of Persia, seeking to stop the building up of Jerusalem and the restoration of the Temple, which had begun under Cyrus, and was now being done in earnest by Zerubbabel, after the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah. 

Here, in **Ezra 6**, we see that Darius seeks to understand the matter, and finds the scroll of Cyrus's proclamation. The return of the treasures looted from the house of God by Nebuchadnezzar, and the gift of stones and timber ordered by the former king. 

Darius not only endorses the construction and decrees it is good, but calls on God to curse those who oppose it, and demands that Tatnai and the others pay a tribute in sacrifices to the effort, that the Jews may offer unto God and pray for their king and his sons. 

When the enemies of the people of God sought to derail His will, they not only failed, but were made to aid the effort. 

It may be a reach, but it seems to me to be a picture of what would come when the Jews sought to stop Jesus, to destroy Him, and instead brought the sacrifice that fulfilled God's will for man. And Jesus, the Temple was raised again on the third day, just as 3 years after the construction started, in the 3rd year of Darius, the new temple was complete. 

And like Zerubbabel, Joshua the high priest, and all the children of Israel, the priests, Levites and the rest in captivity kept the Passover with joy and the rebuilt temple, as we rejoice over the Passover Lamb, which is Christ.

Here in **Ezra 8**, he recounts the genealogy of those that came down to Jerusalem from Babylon, carrying the treasure for the house of God. 

It lists the key patriarchs of the lead families, each with significant roles. Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, secured a priestly covenant through zeal. Ithamar, Aaron’s son, upheld temple duties. David, the iconic king, represents royal and messianic legacy. Shechaniah, meaning "YHWH dwells," ties to divine presence. Parosh ("flea") led a resilient clan. Pahath-moab ("ruler of Moab") suggests foreign integration. Joab ("YHWH is father") was a chief warrior for David's mighty men. Along with the others, each are given a pedigree to note the continuity of things, going back to Jacob, Moses and Aaron, and David. 

The integration of Moabites and others after the captivity, into the ranks of "Jews," is something that is often contested, and will come into play here in **Ezra 9** and **10**, but it's interesting.

Ezra says that he refused armed escort from the king, relying on God to protect them. He proclaimed a fast of 3 days, as they prepared to make their way across the Jordan, asking the Lord to watch over them. 

They are traveling with an incredible amount of wealth and treasure. The offer wasn't unreasonable. But Ezra had spoken to the king saying The hand of God would protect them. 

It is like the old cliche about the person trapped in flood waters, refusing rescue boats and helicopters because the Lord would save him. Maybe the offer itself came from God. 

Not everything in the Bible is proscriptive, and in Ezra it is often just his description of events. Their faith saw them through and God did deliver them, but we shouldn't always refuse help when that help may be the means God chose to protect us. 

It's like when Satan is tempting Jesus in the wilderness. 

**Matthew 4:5-7**
*Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple, And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone. Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.*

There is a fine line between faith and knowledge that God will watch out for us, and tempting God by putting ourselves in the position where He has to. Between courage and faith and testing the Lord. 

I think Ezra fell just on the good side of faith vs tempting God. It was God's will and plan that they rebuild His house and the situation was providentially blessed. However, it may not always be the wisest course. 

They arrive in Jerusalem and the sum of the treasure is weighed, and offering is made for them by the priests. Their mission accomplished. Furthering the people and the house of God.

**2 Corinthians 6:14**
*Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?*

Ezra, having returned to Jerusalem with the treasures to aid in the building of the walls of the city, and the establishment of God's law in the rebuilt temple, faces a crisis when he sees that the Levites among the land have taken strange and outlandish women for their wives. 

He calls in prayer, recalling the words of God that Israel, upon entering Canaan would not give their daughters to the sons of the heathens, nor take their daughters in marriage. 

He reasons that, given God's grace in allowing the restoration and the support of kings, and the end to captivity, this affinity with abominations cannot stand. That it would be the final straw, and God would destroy them utterly, leaving not a remnant behind. He says to God, we cannot stand before you in their trespasses. 

Worse, the mixed marriages, the "holy seed of Israel" joining with these heathen nations had led to the men doing accord to the abominations of the Canaanites. 

Just as the sons of God, those of the line of Seth, Enos, believers who called upon the name of God, mixing with the daughters of man, those unbelieving and from Cain, led to the wickedness and abominations that caused God to repent of creating man. Sending the flood that only Noah, perfect in his generations, and his sons and wives escaped. 

Just as today, we are told not to be unequally yoked to non-believers, not just in marriage but in all spiritual enterprises. 

But is the sin here the mixed marriages by ethnicity or spiritually, where the women bring the men to commit idolatry and abominations? The way that Balaam caught the Israelites at Baalpeor. 

There are 4 outlandish women (Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba—referred to as "the wife of Uriah") in the lineage of Christ. God showed grace to these mixed marriages, clearly. He used their offspring in the human genealogy of Christ. No greater honor could be given any woman. But these women had faith, making the difference.  

That God uses our mistakes and weaknesses to His benefit and to do His will, is a lesson found throughout scripture. A sovereign Lord that doesn't simply micromanage everything, but actually allows free will, time and chance within all of His creation to determine things, and ultimately, He uses all those things for His will regardless of how they seem to us.

Having said that, many will teach that the Bible clearly paints mixed marriages as a sin. That beyond the spiritual things, being unequally yoked with unbelieving spouses, that the physical nations, races, should not marry. 

Others point to Moses and the Ethiopian woman he married, and say that it is fine. That Miriam's leprosy given as a curse by God when her and Aaron took the opportunity to undermine Moses, shows that God hates racism or something. 

But Miriam's sin was rebellion. Not "racism."

In my opinion, it is less than ideal, but not always a sin. That God would prefer a nation of believers that kept marriage among themselves. That the natural consequence of mixed races are generally negative, especially when both parents are outside of the faith, and doubly so when one spouse is a believer and the other is not. 

He gave us the nations and bounds and habitations thereof. Every tongue and kindred can come to salvation by faith. There is no difference, Jew or Greek. But there are nations in Heaven, the Bible says. On earth, it matters. 

Mixed marriages are how the Assyrian empire destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel. How they became Samaritans over time. Being bred out of existence by miscegenation is a judgment of God against a nation. 

So, in my opinion, it is taught against, it is unwise, ibut it is also not the end of the world if both are saved believers and they raise their children to be. 

But if one isn't a believer and the other is, that sin is compounded by it being a mixed-race relationship. Especially as we see from Eve to Solomon, and even these Levites, that being spiritually mixed always takes men's hearts from God and into sin through their wives.

Just to be clear, I think pastors should ALWAYS preach against spiritually mixed marriages. To tell young people in no uncertain terms that they shouldn't even date an unsaved person, especially from unsaved families that practice a different religion. 

I think they should counsel against ethnically and racially mixed marriages, even between believers. That it's generally not a good thing, 
personally and for your nation. And if done out of the wrong spirit, it is wicked. Fetishism. To spite parents. To chase the exotic. To force the issue when you lack the faith that God will provide you the appropriate partner. Self-loathing. These are all common and sinful motives behind the act. 

But, sometimes people do what people do. And they do it out of genuine love and things happen. So we should show grace to those in such a relationship, when they are brothers and sisters in Christ. 

If this seems like a compromise to some, I don't know what would please you. If this seems harsh and racist to others, I don't care.

Ultimately, Ezra's concerns are both racial and spiritual. He is going to make his case in the next chapter for how this problem can be resolved. 

And depending upon your viewpoint, depending on your discernment.... Your opinions might differ from his.

Malachi writes, *For the Lord, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away*, and Jesus clearly teaches that the idea of divorce is not God's, but man's. 

**Matthew 19:8**
*He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.*

Divorce was never in God's plan for marriage. The children of Israel may have been commanded to not intermarry with the heathen, but He never commanded them to divorce. 

Ezra's emotional breakdown over the issue did not lead to God telling him to order this. A man, responding to Ezra came up with the idea. And Ezra agreed and the people went along with it. 

113 men are assumed to have been unequally yoked, based on the list and names. (I didn't count it, I looked it up). They spent a considerable amount of time doing it. Ending with sacrifice for their sins. 

But was this God's will? Wouldn't the more prudent course of action be to do to the men who had taken strange wives as they would have done to those that didn't come down to Jerusalem to vote in the matter?

*And that whosoever would not come within three days, according to the counsel of the princes and the elders, all his substance should be forfeited, and himself separated from the congregation of those that had been carried away.*

These men could have been removed from office, having disqualified themselves. The way a pastor or Deacon would be if they divorced or committed adultery. 

Two wrongs don't always make a right. There should have been grave consequences for their disobedience, but not at the expense of the institution God ordained.

In Neamiah, we will see shortly that he faced a similar problem with one specific priest. And he doesn't order the priest's divorce, he removes him from office. 

I think Ezra was overcome and overwhelmed by the tough choice he had to make, and when the man Shechaniah the son of Jehiel came up with the idea of putting the wives away, so that the men who transgressed could eat their cake and have it too, Ezra pounced on it because it was the easier path. 

When we are faced with a hard choice because of our sins, and decisions of what to do about it will require self-sacrifice and dealing with unpleasant repercussions, we should wait on God's will. Do the hard things. Not latch on to man's compromise and easy way out. 

It is hard to put someone out of church, but it is God's prescription for certain situations. 

It can be hard living with a spouse who doesn't treat you right. God says stick it out. 

We should patiently accept the consequences of our actions. That would show true remorse and humility before God. Not doing the easy thing and then crediting yourself for it.

We are in **Nehemiah 1**, which continues the narrative of the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and it picks up roughly 13 years after the end of Ezra. Nearly 100yrs after Haggai and Zechariah. 

And we are told that the city's walls and gate remain in ruin, still fire scorched from the original invasion by Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonian empire. 

Nehemiah, the cup bearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I, in the 10th year of his reign, laments the languished reconstruction. That now, after many divine starts and human stops, Jerusalem still is not walled. 

He recounts the instructions of Moses, that if the people who call themselves the children of Israel failed to keep God's commandments, and chase after other gods, they would be scattered to the ends of the earth. 

But if they turn back again to Him, repenting towards the God of their fathers, He will bless them and gather them again. 

Nehemiah's prayer is often used by dispensationalists, saying "See, this proves that God will always gather His people!" 

But, alas, this is the final time. The city God chose to place His name needs to be ready for the coming of the Messiah. The people have been unable and unwilling to repent. Only a remnant remain faithful. 

In a few centuries, Jerusalem will be under Roman control which will act as a means to protect and preserve the city until Jesus' birth. Doing what the Jews failed to do all this time. 

Also, we see Nehemiah lay out the condition for this gathering, that the people turn back to the Lord and obey Him. That includes being ready for the coming of Christ, with hearts ready. That if they believed Moses and the prophets, they would be prepared for Him. 

Modern Israel was not the result of Jews coming to repentance, and turning towards God the Father by embracing His Son. It was the result of pride, and satanic forces. They are cut off in unbelief, their covenant faded away. 

As Jesus cried;  *O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!*

*Behold, your house is left unto you desolate. For I say unto you, Ye shall not see me henceforth, till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.*

Nehemiah recounts how he came to be in the king of Persia's presence, as cupbearer. Bringing wine to the king. And his sad countenance at the condition of his fathers' home, Jerusalem, still not finished rebuilding. 

The king inquires about the matter, and he agrees to give Nehemiah a time to go an do the work, letters of passage and of support to show the governors beyond the river, that they prepare timber for beams and provide materials. 

Unlike Ezra, Nehemiah travels with captains and horsemen.

*When Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, heard of it, it grieved them exceedingly that there was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel.*

But Nehemiah continues to the city, and the gates are consumed with fire, collapsed to the point he has to enter on foot. He goes out and examines the gates and the walls without announcing himself, and afterwards he goes to the Jews and says *let us build up the wall of Jerusalem that we be no more a reproach.* 

Hearing his encouragement and that the hand of God was upon him and this goal, they rose up to join him. 

Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite and Geshem the Arabian scoff at Nehemiah's mission. But the cupbearer tells them they have no portion in Jerusalem. 

*The God of heaven, he will prosper us; therefore we his servants will arise and build.*

Christians today have a mandate from the King of kings, Christ Jesus, to build up heavenly Jerusalem. And He will prosper us when we do. 

But as Peter writes, *Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts.*..

When we seek to do the works of the Lord, we will face acorn and ridicule, often from those close to us. But they have no portion or memorial in Jerusalem. We should be ready laborers and remind ourselves of this. That we please God and not men. And do the work He has commanded us to do.

All hands on deck is how we should approach the local church. If you have a talent or skill or even time, you should pitch in. The gifts you have are of God, designed to edify the church in the same way these men edified the walls of Jerusalem.

Nehemiah bears the end of the construction of the walls and gates and his enemies still seek to destroy him. 

When they realize they cannot lure him out, they threaten to defame him that the authorities of the King of Persia will come and destroy him for rebellion. But he isn't tricked and he calls them out on their lies. 

Then they seek to have him violate the sanctity of the temple in fear, sinning. Again, his faith is in the Lord and he refuses and continues the work to completion. 

Then the nobles of Jerusalem, who are in league with Tobiah, and intermarrying with his family begin to tell Nehemiah what a good guy he is, and to convince Nehemiah while at the same time Tobiah is sending him threatening messages. 

These are common tactics of the enemies of God. Truck, threaten, betray, seek to have you sin, tell lies about you, flatter you, and get those with influence in your world to turn on you, while they try and get the powers that be against you. 

The Jews did it to Christ. He says, because they hated Him first, they'll do the same to us. 

But Nehemiah continues to the end, doing what God commands. Faithful that it will work out for good. 

He doesn't waste time exchanging railing for railing or fighting with them. He just does the work of the Lord. 

This is all we can do. Trust God. Don't fear.

The final chapter of Nehemiah's account of the restoration of the walls in Jerusalem, and the continued efforts to cleanse the priesthood and the people of outside influence. 

Nehemiah writes of how, when the law of Moses was read and the truth that Ammonites and Moabites were forbidden from joining the congregation forever, by God, that the people removed them, wives and children, from the priesthood and the church. 

But now, years later it's still a problem for a holy people, separated unto God, but having mixed multitudes in their midst. Unequally yoked to non-believers. 

Tobiah was a prominent Ammonite official who vehemently opposed Nehemiah's efforts to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem and was a bitter adversary of the Jewish people. Despite this, the high priest Eliashib, who was related to Tobiah by marriage, inappropriately prepared a large room in the Temple courts for Tobiah's use. The room was storage for sacrifice and holy things, so to give it to an Ammonite, especially one who opposed the man of God, was especially galling to Nehemiah. 

He threw the items out, cast out the Ammonite, and had the temple priests cleanse the space. 

He notes that intermarriage was rampant. Mixed children unable to speak the Jewish tongue. Merchants of foreign people came and sold on the sabbath. And so the Jews worked themselves on the day of rest. 

Outside influence was leading the people to sin. 

Comparing it to Solomon, the wisest and greatest king of Israel, who was undone and led to sin by foreign wives, Nehemiah not only preaches against mixed marriages, but assaults men into agreeing to not give their daughters to foreigners. He shuts the city gates on the sabbath and appoints his own sons to keep guard. 

When the merchants set up shop outside the city walls, he threatens them until they never come back. 

Nehemiah cleans the city and people of outside influence, driving the ungodly from among them. And he prays God to remember this good he did. 

It is shoveling against the tide sometimes, to hold standards and expectations of God, among a stubborn and rebellious people. As a pastor or a father in a Christian home, it can seem endless, the number of times the people go out into sin always seems greater than the rebukes and restoration done to undo the last. 

A constant struggle against the world and the god of this world. And the lust of the eyes, the pride of life. To keep the people who you have charge over pure and separated unto God. 

Let alone ourselves. 

But it is important to be constantly diligent. 

Just as Moses saw the Israelites rise up to play, and to worship an idol, being gone just 40 days, and so soon removed from bondage in Egypt, Nehemiah is gone a short time and the city of Jerusalem has descended into sin. 

People forget the bondage and cruelty of their unregenerate pre-Christian life. They quickly forget chastisements. They soon return like a dog to its vomit. Like a pig to the mire. 

It takes constant vigilance, preaching and hard leadership to maintain even a bare minimum of standards. 

But it is a good work. And something Christian men should commit themselves to.

Beginning the book of Esther, we find it is set during the time period between Ezra and Neamiah, under the rule of Xerxes, here rendered Ahasuerus in the Hebrew. The king of the Persian empire, where the Medes still has influence. And his empire is great encompassing lands from India to Ethiopia. Including obviously, the Kingdom of Judah. 

And 3 years into his reign, he orders a feast that lasts nearly half a year. And in that feast he orders the queen to appear. And she, having a feast of her own refuses. 

This presents a problem. The princes of the empire say to the king that her disobedience will be copied by other wives throughout the land. And that he must remove her from office and strip her of her titles. The King agrees. A new Queen will be found. 

Obviously, the concept of a wife submitting to their husband is biblically sound. From Eve having her desire be that of Adam, through the New Testament teachings on marriage, it is given that a wife should submit to her husband. 

As in much of the book of Esther, We are presented with two wrongs. Not one. Vashti should have taken heed and appeared. Her desire to stay at her own feast that she threw where she was the head of the show, led to her being made an example throughout the empire. 

But,  Ahasuerus' example of a drunken feast where obsequious princes gathered, was a poor one to set for the kingdom as well. And it was more his embarrassment in front of his friends than doing the right thing that led to his proclamation. 

In a similar way to the Book of Judges, we are called upon to use discernment when reading Esther. We will see that God is not in it, literally. God isn't mentioned. And so, we are given circumstances and situations to judge. And so we shall.

So Esther, and really Mordecai her uncle, had gotten vengeance on Haman and his family, because of the wrath Haman had towards Mordecai's insolence. 

And now the King gives to them Haman's property and inheritance, And gives Mordecai haman's position in the Kingdom. Even allowing him the ring that seals the proclamations and that he could write them in the king's name. 

Esther asks the king to reverse the earlier order given to Haman for the destruction of the Jews throughout the empire. But because a king's proclamation cannot be reversed, he simply has them write a new one that gives the Jews the full backing of the government to kill all the people that would kill them, even the women and children of their families. 

How that would be determined? What were the criteria for determining that someone would have come against them? It doesn't say. 

I've heard it preached that they were just given the right to self-defense and that on that day people did rise up and try to kill them. But the text says that the people not only didn't rise up to try to kill them but converted to be Jews out of fear of the Jews. 

Not fear of God.

The final chapter of Esther, and we see the origins of the Jewish observance of Purim. On the day Haman had hoped to wipe out the Jews, the Jews had gained power instead and used it to mass murder their enemies. 

The rulers of the provinces of the empire, their military and officers of the King helped the Jews to find and kill those that they said hated them. Mordechai was given greater power. 

The king reports to Esther that Haman's sons were killed and 500 in the palace, and unknown number in the rest of the Kingdom, and the King asks his wife if she's satisfied. 

She isn't. 

They hung the sons they slew on trees. They extended the slaughter another day. They killed 300 more in Shushan. They killed another 75,000 throughout the empire, though they did not take the spoils. 

And the Jews declared it would be a feast day. Mordechai made it official. Because Haman had sought to cast lots on the Jews, Pur, they called the feast Purim.

Again, nothing of God. They made their own holy day and feast, celebrating the slaughter they had. 

They did what was right in their own eyes, and proved that Haman was right to see them as a threat. Even if he went about it the wrong way. 

There are no heroes. It's a history of something that happened. God wanted us to know.

The Book of Job begins with the introduction of a man in the land of Uz, the titular character; Job. Uz, from the biblical clues appears to be a fertile plane in the Arabian peninsula, near where Edom would be. The time frame, many believe, is during the era of the patriarchs; Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

It would be good to note that, Abraham, or Abram, was a Chaldean, a nation who are mentioned here in this chapter located in what is modern Iraq. Where the seat of Babylonian power would be. And he was called out from the city of Ur there, to go unto Hebron by God. 

And, as mentioned throughout his story and his sons', there were people in this post flood era who feared the Lord, and offered sacrifices unto him. 

Of course we know about Melchizedek, King of Salem, and high priest, and the tenth of the spoils offered by Abram to Melchizedek. Many consider him to be a pre-incarnate appearance of Jesus. 

All this to say that the idea of the worship of God originating with Abraham, and only his seed after the flesh, is incorrect. There were many following the flood and the dispersion of nations out from Babel, that called upon the name of the Lord for salvation, and sought to offer the blood as a picture of their faith in Him, as we see Job does for himself and his family. 

One of the conceits of modern Zionism and dispensationalism holds that only the sons of Israel after the flesh were special, and that they invented monotheism. But throughout the Bible we find people who were not of that line, and not given to idols and false gods. It's important to understand that salvation has always been by grace alone through faith in the Lord, calling upon his name. And that salvation was always offered to all people. 

We will see in Exodus the mixed multitudes that followed Israel into the wilderness from Egypt. We will see high priests of other nations that fear the Lord. There will be people like Ruth and Rahab and others who have the faith. 

The distinction for Israel was that they were given the oracles of God. That they had the prophets and the word of God delivered directly to them, and given the law of the Lord that they may be perfect, complete, and a light unto the Gentiles. The other nations. Calling all men to repentance. 

But we see the greatest man on Earth at this moment, according to God, who feared Him, eschewing evil, offering sacrifices to sanctify himself and his family. Without the law. Without the temple. Without a priesthood. Without the oracles of God, knowing by the faith of his fathers what was expected.

And so we find Job, faithfully keeping the sanctification of sacrifices for himself and his children, and he has been blessed beyond measure by God. 

10 children, seven sons and three daughters. Incredible wealth and cattle and livestock. Great land and a great house. And all his adult children successful in that they were established in their own homes to have their own feasts. Having established all of this, the Bible shifts focus to the throne of God in Heaven.

*Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan came also among them.* 

I've covered this multiple times in other studies, but the sons of God here refers to the spirits of those saved by faith in Christ. The same as the sons of God in **Genesis 6** being the children of obedience, through Seth. Because the only way to become A son of God, is by faith in THE Son of God. 

So, not to belabor the point, but at no time has God called angels His sons. And further evidence of this is in the text itself, in verse 6. Satan came also among them. 

Satan is an angel. A rebellious angel, a cherub. Perhaps a prominent angel but, an angel nonetheless. And he came among them, as a separate entity than them. Not as one of them. 

And God asks him where he's been, and he says going to and fro in the earth and walking up and down in it.

Thematically, as prose, this setup creates tension in the reader. I'll probably say this multiple times throughout this study, but the Book of Job is the finest example of literature ever written. 

While its exact date of composition isn't known, it likely found its final form during the Babylonian captivity. 

Shortly thereafter, in the Hellenistic world, the Greek drama became a literary style. Acted out by people, to tell a story either from a monologue or a soliloquy or a troupe of performers. 

Because we are gifted with the King James version, and it's eloquent prose in what many would say is Shakespearean English, it's easy to picture the Book of Job as a play. And it is possible to perform, and many have. And it is greater than all of the plays the Bard penned. 

Isn't it interesting that it was put to pen under the inspiration of God, separate from and before the Greek tragedies and comedies that the world now considers classic literature?

“Naked came I… naked shall I return thither” – “Thither” or shām in the Hebrew means, “to that place." Clearly Job doesn't mean the womb. The return is to what then? What is thither? The grave? "Sheol" and nothingness? 

We're going to see that Job's faith is redemption through the Lord. Not that empty meaning that many give in their Old Testament interpretations. 

Either way, Job sees life as lease, not ownership, that all is from God, Who is blessed forever. It's humbling and something we should always keep in mind. Life is a vapor.
