He poetically compares the digging for hidden treasure to those that can find the grave. 

He is miserable. 

But he has not sinned against God with his lips.

Job 4 will begin a dialogue between Job and the three friends who came to him to mourn. 

The first to reply to Job's plaintive cry, cursing the day he was born, is Eliphaz the Temanite, of Teman, a city in Edom. (**Genesis 36:11, 15; Jeremiah 49:7, 20; Ezekiel 25:13**). His initial argument is made in chapters 4 and 5, and offers a view of "retribution theology," the idea of karma in God's doings. That sin is the cause of suffering, and that you get what you deserve. 

Job’s friends defend retribution theology rigorously, and it is difficult to disagree with many of the points made, from a human perspective. Much of it sounds right in our minds. So, before we dive deeper into the text, we should keep in mind the end of the matter, where (spoilers), God addresses the men and what they say. 

**Job 42:7-9**
*And it was so, that after the Lord had spoken these words unto Job, the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath. Therefore take unto you now seven bullocks and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and offer up for yourselves a burnt offering; and my servant Job shall pray for you: for him will I accept: lest I deal with you after your folly, in that ye have not spoken of me the thing which is right, like my servant Job. So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went, and did according as the Lord commanded them: the Lord also accepted Job.*

The friends of Job, (and later, the young accuser Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite), are given opportunity to make multiple philosophical and theological points regarding the nature of God, His justice and their natural suspicion of those who suffer as being sinners, and worse, that those that suffer worse than they do must be greater sinners than they are. 

This line of thought is just as common today as it was then, and is human nature. But not God's. And while there is general wisdom to be found in their arguments, the application they choose to make is wrong. 

As we go, it is good to keep this in mind, especially when we read something that seems perfectly reasonable to us, and may reflect our own views that we may have held against others in our life. It should cause self-reflection.

So, to recap: Job, devastated by the loss of his children, wealth and health, and wishing he was never born, while yet not sinning against God or cursing Him, sits in ash, scraping his sore-covered flesh, in agony. 

He had been blessed by these three well meaning friends, who traveled afar, and patiently, in love, sat mourning in silence for a week. But with the silence broken by Job's lamentation, Eliphaz the Temanite now speaks up. 

He starts by asking that, if they attempt to talk with him, will it offend Job? And then immediately, before Job can answer, Eliphaz gives himself permission by saying "Who can withhold themselves from speaking?"

We have all likely, at one time or another been on the receiving or delivering end of this. "I know you're going through a lot, so I don't want to offend you, but I can't help myself..."

As well intentioned as this sentiment can be, what follows it rarely is a help to the person hearing it. Ultimately, the motivation behind it is self-centered and doesn't come from sympathy for the aggrieved, but out of an impatient empathy, where the friend sees it from their detached view, and thinks their opinions and musing can fix what's broken, or even just make the person stop complaining. 

Many times, after having given our two-cents, we can feel comfortable washing our hands of any obligation to be bothered by a friend's burdens. "Well, if they'd just listen to reason...Oh well, I tried."

Better to have remained silent than to do this.

Eliphaz the Temanite barrels along right into it. He begins by pointing out the example Lot has been for many, that his faith and council have helped those in troubled times. Strengthening the weak. But...it is never good to follow a compliment with a "but," but now that it has come upon Job, he faints and is troubled. 

Rather than encouraging Job to embrace the same strength and hope that he gave others, Eliphaz uses this good quality of his friend as an indictment. As an accusation of weakness. 

I would doubt that any of the people Job had encouraged had gone through anything even remotely touching the tribulation that he found himself in. But even so, rather than repaying the favor and encouraging Job, Eliphaz makes an accusation out of it. 

*Is not this thy fear, thy confidence, thy hope, and the uprightness of thy ways?*

He says, isn't your religion, your trust in God, your piety and righteousness, shouldn't that all be enough to console you? If all of that was sufficient for Job to preach to others in their moments of doubt and pain, why isn't it enough for him? 

And rather than waiting for a reply to his condescending "tough love," Eliphaz answers his own question in the least charitable way possible; by accusing Job of hidden sin. 

*Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?*

This is the crux of his argument, That Job deserves what has happened to him. That he is reaping what he has sown. 

Eliphaz uses the truth that God's wrath is revealed from Heaven against the ungodly, to say that this is evidence enough that so great a temptation has befallen Job, because his piety was vanity, and hid the truth of his sin.

"What goes around comes around," even when true, is the last thing we should say to another when we're trying to comfort them. Especially considering the grace God has extended to us. 

 In **Luke 13**, Jesus answers his disciples, who suggest that recent tragedies that happened to others was a direct result of their sin, that it was karma, by asking "*Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things?*" Jesus says, nay, and that something evil can happen to anyone by chance, but if men don't repent, everyone will likewise perish. Stuff happens. The rain falls on the just and the unjust alike.

A similar question is asked in **John 9:1-3**
*And as Jesus passed by, he saw a man which was blind from his birth. And his disciples asked him, saying, Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind? Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.*

The Truth is we cannot assume by someone suffering that they deserved it for some secret sin that we imagine they did. It may be comforting to us to think that we're safe from such tragedies, because of our innate goodness in contrast to this wretched sinner. 

But we are all deserving of death and hell, and it is by the grace of God that we yet live.

Eliphaz continues, letting us know of a vision that he had just before sleep, of a spirit he thinks he glimpsed and a voice he heard, that asked:

*Shall mortal man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker? Behold, he put no trust in his servants; and his angels he charged with folly: How much less in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, which are crushed before the moth?*

His private interpretation, his own inner musings that he paints as a spiritual vision, posits that since man is obviously not as holy as God, and if even the Angels were punished for their rebellion, how much more man is under judgment for our wickedness, men, whose life is but a vapor and to dust we return, crushed as easily as the moth.

And it is true that God reserved punishment for the angels *which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day..*

**2 Peter 2:4** 
*For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment*.

And in **Hebrews 2:6-7** (paraphrasing **Psalm 8:5**) *What is man, that thou art mindful of him? or the son of man that thou visitest him? Thou madest him a little lower than the angels...*

Again, Eliphaz uses true things to make false points.  

And because it is true that God punishes the wicked, that he spared not the angels that kept not their estate but sinned, and that all men die, and their bodies decay and their excellency goes away. And it happens to the wise and those without wisdom alike. 

**Ecclesiastes 9:2**
*All things come alike to all: there is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked; to the good and to the clean, and to the unclean; to him that sacrificeth, and to him that sacrificeth not: as is the good, so is the sinner; and he that sweareth, as he that feareth an oath.*

Many times the greatest lies are based on a misrepresentation or misapplication of the greatest truths.

Eliphaz's monologue continues, directly from chapter 4, and he continues to paint a picture blaming Job for his own suffering. Implying secret sin that has led him to his current condition. 

He says to call upon the righteous, and see if any man would answer him. Some Catholics use this verse as a proof text for praying to saints. Because they will strip verses from context, and ignore that God completely rebukes everything that is said by Job's friends. 

But Eliphaz is not encouraging Job to pray to the dead, but to appeal to the stories of the righteous to find if any ever suffered as he did, If any holy one had ever been down so low. 

He then begins to list off parables, about the foolish being cursed, their children killed, their harvest spoiled, their things taken by thieves. He says that this trouble doesn't come up out of nowhere, but that men are born into trouble and that it comes up like sparks flying out of a fire. As embers. That the destruction that comes naturally follows the life of a foolish man. 

He advises his friend to seek God and to commit his cause to God Who is mighty and punishes the wicked. But saveth the poor. 

He then gives the proverb that a man should be happy when God corrects him and to not despise the chastening of the Almighty.  

**Proverbs 3:11**
*My son, despise not the chastening of the LORD; neither be weary of his correction*.

So he is quoting scripture, and some of what he is saying is true. But he's misapplying it by assuming that that is the cause of his friends misery. 

And worse, he mentions children being crushed at the gate, knowing that Job's own sons and daughters were killed by a collapsing house. He insensitively talks about having his things spoiled and stolen. 

He's clearly indicating that he believes Job acted foolishly in some way and deserved everything he got. And in his own judgment he thinks he's giving good advice. 

It's something we should be aware of because, far too often we judge a matter by its appearance. And we have a ready verse to give. And we pride ourselves in it when we should be comforting the afflicted. Not forgiving sin, not excusing it, but when we don't know the circumstances or the situation, or even more, we know the person is honorable and upright in their ways, we shouldn't assume or presume to lecture. 

But you can tell Eliphaz really thought he was cooking here, giving these great words of wisdom to a man laying in ash, with a shaved head for mourning, scraping the oozing sores on his flesh. 

Telling him to hear it now and know that it's for thy own good, is the last thing Job needs to hear.

Job begins his reply to Eliphaz's accusations of sin being the cause of Job's woe. That he must have deserved it, and so he has to get right with God and stop complaining. Job is overcome by his faithless friend's words. 

He says his grief is heavier than the sands in the sea, and if measured against his lamentation, his words would be swallowed up by it. That while the poisoned arrows and terrors of God be in him and against him, Eliphaz chose to lecture Job instead of pitying him.

Job asks rhetorical and obvious questions, saying that Eliphaz's argument is as obvious as these sayings. A fed animal doesn't bray and flavorless food needs seasoning and the white of an egg is flavorless, and the accusations and advice Eliphaz gave are just as unnecessary to say.

They may be true, but they are obvious truths that Job is already well aware of. They aren't great insights, and they do nothing to help him in his grief. 

He still longs for death, and Job begs God to take him, and call him home. That he should find comfort, let God not spare him. 

Here, Job gives his confession of faith, his trust in the Holy One, Christ Jesus. He is his strength and his hope. If his end is heaven, why prolong his life? His faith built upon a rock, His ready help in Job, His wisdom is present, still. 

And so, Eliphaz's rebuke stings, rather than the comfort of pity, and Job points out this is sin, and turns the accusation back upon Eliphaz, that his erstwhile friend has forsaken the fear of God by his callousness. 

That his brother has dealt deceitfully, and gives an allegory of a brook, a small stream that freezes cold in the winter, undrinkable, only to vanish in the heat, dried up. It's a stinging rebuke. 

The brook, like his expected compassion from a brother is like its waters, t*he troops of Tema looked, the companies of Sheba waited for them.* The water is gone, and they are left without the expected relief. 

Job accuses Eliphaz further, saying his holier than thou act comes from fear. If Job, who Eliphaz knows has been faithful and a good council, in the Lord, has been cast down so low, what could that mean for him? 

Job says, did I ask you for anything? Money? Deliverance? Redemption from captivity? He didn't ask for Eliphaz's opinion either. 

He continues to upbraid his friend, saying if Eliphaz has something to teach Job that he doesn't already know, Job would listen. He would gladly accept understanding, but Eliphaz's argument is insulting. Job asks what exactly is he reproving by it? 

Job asks did Eliphaz think he was reproving a shallow argument of the desperate. Job had wailed in his sorrow, he didn't curse God or sin with his lips. So what exactly did Eliphaz think he was rebuking? 

Job says it is as attacking the fatherless, as digging a pit for his friend to fall into. Iniquity and betrayal. 

He says, "look at me," and asks if he's lying. If there is sin in his speech. Is he saying anything against God? Job's righteousness is in it. It is sorrow that compasses him about.

Job’s longing for death is not despair but a plea for release into the only comfort he still trusts: God’s final summons. “Let Him not spare me” is not suicidal rage; it is the confidence that his end is with the Holy One. Even here, in the furnace, Job confesses the rock beneath his feet, Christ Jesus, his strength and hope. The rebuke of Eliphaz therefore wounds doubly: it is not merely unfeeling; it is faithless. To kick a brother when he is down is to forsake the fear of God. 

The presence of faith in Job's response to this unspeakable tragedy has been consistent. The vain theology of karma that Eliphaz offers is predicated on the idea that Job deserves what's happened, while Job in his heart knows his trust is in the Holy One, his Redeemer. 

It is similar to the struggle Paul felt, as he wrote to the Philippians from his bondage in Rome, potential death by execution, certain.

**Philippians 1:20-24** 
*According to my earnest expectation and my hope, that in nothing I shall be ashamed, but that with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death. It can be tempting in trials for a believer to long to be called home. But, better to redeem the time while we are here. God's perfect timing is His, not ours.

Many argue that Jesus wasn't known in the Old Testament, that salvation by faith didn't exist. That it is an anachronism to see Jesus in Job, and *the Holy One*. 

There is no anachronism when we see Christ in in the Old Testament. It is entirely about Him. 

He is the Lamb slain before the foundation of the world. The same Word who was with God and was God, Who walked in the furnace with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. 

He was the Rock in the wilderness.

Job’s cry a few chapters from now, “I know that my Redeemer liveth” being about Christ is not an anachronism or a theological reach; it is an inspired revelation.

When Job clings to the Holy One as his strength and hope beyond death, he is laying hold of the same eternal Christ who is the substance of every shadow, the end of every type, the answer to every promise.

The Old Testament saints were saved by the same faith, looking to the same Savior, the same redemption, if through a veil that has now been torn.

In the Old Testament, We see that the cultural tradition of a hireling is to be taken on for the course of 3 years, and paid out a reward at the end in addition to his wages and room and board.

He asks for that blessed pardon, for the forgiveness and death, that he would die that night in the flesh so that he doesn't have to live as a burden and in vanity and in weariness.

*He teareth me in his wrath, who hateth me: he gnasheth upon me with his teeth; mine enemy sharpeneth his eyes upon me. He laments, crying out that his friends scorn him even as he calls out to God.

*O that one might plead for a man with God, as a man pleadeth for his neighbour!*

An indictment of the three, but also an appeal to Christ the mighty councilor.

Where Zophar the Naamathite kept his argument to generally true sayings, only hinting at Job's supposed guilt being the cause of his suffering, Eliphaz the Temanite, in his final outburst, lays charge to Job. 

He accuses him of great wickedness and infinite iniquity. Breaking pledges, and the arms of the fatherless. It seems as though the railing accusations come from a resentment of Job's well-known perfection in his faith. The righteous living that made God point him out to Satan to begin with. 

Eliphaz claims that God is not pleased by well doing, and doesn't care if man makes his ways perfect, complete and mature.

The leaven of the Pharisees is the fruit of works based salvation. Hypocrisy drives feelings of being holier than others. But it also leads to envy of those more obviously righteous than the adherent. And so they love to tear these people down and delight in their shortcomings. 

People who trust in their own works of righteousness live in a sweet spot where they have to be less sinful than the next person. And so they have to resent anyone who upsets this equation by being better than they are.

The secret of God, I believe is the gospel. The mystery of salvation to those that believe God and it is counted for righteousness. The Almighty was with him, Job was blessed with children and prosperity and had the respect of the men at the gate. 

This is the patriarchal rule of the day. The men of means and power sat in the street of the city and heard matters, and offered wisdom. They judged. 

The young men feared Job, the elders gave him deference. Even the princes, the governors of the city gave him his due. They listened and watched what Job would say and do. His influence was such, that he had everyone's respect and attention.

Because he clothed himself in righteousness and wore judgment like a crown. 

This should be the goal of all Christian men. To have this mind in them as it was in Christ, to start with the Lord, and to lead others in His wisdom, for His purpose and other's profit.

The world has made arrested development into a virtue. Being unserious as a way to comport yourself. This retards the growth of a Christian man. 

We see it in ourselves, certainly. An immaturity that must be tamed and brought under control. It's fine to joke and laugh, but in its place. Sobriety and gravity are what we should strive for, coupled with grace and mercy for those who have no one to deliver them.

Job comes to the conclusion of his final defense. Having stipulated all that the friends had said about God's judgement against the ungodly, and having given a list of all the ways Job had proven himself over the years, and having admitted that his reputation is now in tatters among those young and bitter men (a backhanded insult to the quality of his friends character), Job now ends his words by again listing what he has tried to do, and what the judgment would be had he not. 

He says, I try to do this, and if I didn't then yeah, I deserve punishment. But these are the things I have done. 

Job made a vow to his own eyes, to not look at a woman with lust. 

He says that the inheritance of the wicked is destruction. Punishment. God sees everything, so if he has done anything vain or deceitful, then let the Lord do his worst. 

Let him sow and not reap the harvest. Let others eat it. If he's committed adultery, coveting his neighbor's wife, then let his own wife be a harlot. 

He treated his servants well, took care of the widow, the fatherless, the poor, and if he hadn't, he asks, *What then shall I do when God riseth up? and when he visiteth, what shall I answer him?* 

That day of judgement, the day of the Lord, is coming for all men. How will we answer for our iniquity? 

Job asks how he could harm others when the same God fashioned them both in their mothers' womb. 

For from his youth, he says he has been as a father to the fatherless and has guided the widow, taking care of her. 

This reminds me of the rich young man who asked Jesus what he must do to be saved, and who claimed he had done all these things from his youth. The difference between him and Job being that Job first acknowledged God. The rich young man didn't see God sitting in front of him.

But Job's wisdom came from his fear of God and the destruction and wrath to come. So he doesn't trust in himself or in gold or his wealth. He trusted in the Lord and fed the stranger and took care of the poor. Cursing no one. Helping everyone. 

He says, if he had done all these bad things being assumed, and had not done the good the Lord expects of us, if he had sins of commission and omission, then he would admit them. If they were written, he would wear the book of his sins upon his head as a crown. He would accept the punishment of God and the derision of men. 

And so in all things Job maintained his fear of God, and spoke not in sin. He maintained his integrity and did not curse God. 

He just wants to know, why?

One of the things that we should take away from Job is his attitude towards service. Putting others first.

A lot of people seem to think that Jesus introduced all of these concepts of loving your neighbor, and caring for the poor in the New Testament. But again and again we see that this is how God wants us to be. 

He took no pleasure in the blood of bulls and goats. He called people to mercy and judgment. To have discernment. To be so grateful for the things that we have that we have no problem sharing them with others. That we put others profit before ourselves. 

Especially when it comes to the fatherless, the widow, the poor and feeble-minded.

He is angry at Job's friends, who accused Job but didn't answer him when he defended himself. 

He says "I am young, and you are *very* old." Starting off with a false humility, claiming to respect his elders, that he held off from giving his opinion until they were done, but now he must share his opinions. 

He was chomping at the bit to tell his elders off, who are very old (not just older). 

Elihu is rash, while counting himself reserved. He is rude, while claiming to be patient and respectful. He is a picture of impertinent youth. 

Four times we are told Elihu is angry, and three times he tells the men that he is going to give his opinion. An opinion no one asked for. 

Young men, do not be as Elihu. He waited on the elders, it's true, but not out of respect or seeking after wisdom, but to bide his time so he could give his opinion. He is a special boy. 

He wants Job to know, God thrust him down. He wants the friends (who didn't hesitate to accuse Job), to know they are weak and afraid to say it. To condemn Job utterly. 

He describes his need to unload his opinion as wine fermented in a sealed cask, the gases exploding the seams. 
*For I am full of the matter.* He cannot wait to tell them what he thinks. 

He rationalizes and spiritualizes his rashness, by saying he won't give flattering titles to them, won't show them respect they are due, because his maker, the Lord, wouldn't like it. Convenient!

The pride and arrogance of youth is what he is actually filled with. How often do we see this in chatrooms and even in churches? 

Young men with no experience, babes in Christ, convinced they know more than their elders. Who can't wait to tell them their opinions, because the older people just don't get it, in their eyes. 

As we will see, Elihu actually offers little to the conversation. It really is just his pride. 

If you are like Elihu, if you jump in to give your opinion thinking your newfound wisdom and knowledge, repeating things you recently heard, thinking you are blowing minds, stop. Consider him, and this lesson. You aren't a special boy, and you have limited understanding. Have real humility, not the fake kind Elihu shows here.

Elihu is the "Someone's wrong on the Internet! I will stay up all night to make sure they know!" Meme. 

Don't be Elihu.

Elihu, having spent all of the previous chapter telling Job that he's heard all of the conversation, and is going to speak his opinion on the matter, and how much he is looking forward to give it, then spends another 7 verses prattling on about how he is going to speak, and Job better listen up.

He gives his own recap of Job's points, he says I have heard the voice of your words, saying "I am clean, without transgression, I am innocent." This is more than Job actually said. Elihu begins to pontificate about how God actually speaks to men in dreams,  and describes the outcome of old age as punishment to humble man. 

God speaks to us by inspired words, and prophets. Clear teachings. 

**Hebrews 1:1-2**
*God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds*

Dreams may be involved, but Elihu's understanding is overly spiritual and limited, and his idea of old age being a humbling curse is a conceit based on his relative youth. How he sees his elders.

Elihu sees himself as the messenger of God in v23. And that all this was God's way of giving Job Elihu's wisdom. Of bringing him the truth of God through Elihu, to spare Job from the pit, from death. To be enlightened. 

It is an absurdly grandiose view of himself. *Hold thy peace, and I shall teach thee wisdom.* Quiet Boomer, let me tell you how it is!

Paul's instructions to Timothy, address his young protege's age;

**1 Timothy 4:12**
*Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.*

This isn't a command to elders to give any special honor to Timothy, to the young. It's a warning to Timothy to be an example by his behavior, that no man would see him and hold his limited years against him. To not be like Elihu. 

Young Christian men should keep this in mind. That if you want to gain respect of the elders in your life, let it be by your spirit, charity and purity, not puffed up vain words.

Elihu's point about God speaking through dreams and visions or through pain and affliction to turn people from pride and the pit isn't entirely wrong theologically (Scripture elsewhere affirms God can use suffering redemptively **Psalm 119:67, 71; Hebrews 12:5–11).** But applying it directly to Job's case assumes the suffering is for specific sin or pride, which the book's prologue shows isn't the full story. Job's trials stem from a heavenly challenge, not personal wrongdoing. But Elihu's unable to hold enough grace and empathy to relate to Job in charity. In faith. 

Young (or any) believers gain influence through quiet godliness, love, and purity, not puffed-up words that lack empathy for profound grief. Job's story shows that suffering often defies neat explanations, and the wisest response is often humble presence rather than overconfident correction.

Everyone else's misfortune isn't an opportunity to show how smart or wise or spiritual you are. No one profits from that. It leads to men despising your youth, not establishing you as more wise than they are

I also want to point out that all the build up Elihu uses before he starts to speak directly, all his "I am going to speak, and words will come off my tongue and my lips will move and I will breathe, so listen up!" set up, and even the arrogant end to the chapter....

*Mark well, O Job, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I will speak.*
 *If thou hast anything to say, answer me: speak, for I desire to justify thee. If not, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I shall teach thee wisdom.*

...where Elihu tells Job to hold his peace....unless he has something to say, shows the lack of conviction and confidence that betrays his own brashness. 

Elihu is super confident, and you better listen up, unless you don't want to. He knows he is over his head, and these slips show an insight into his character that adds depth to the story and character in a purely literary sense. Job is such an awesome study on people and how we can tend to be.

This is also a very common tactic online, especially with young theology bros. They learn the proof texts and apologetics for their presuppositions, and can only apply them to certain expected responses. *A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject.*

The Lord continues to speak to Job out of the whirlwind. Job, His servant, seeks to know why he has been afflicted. But God challenges him to see the things that His providence delivers. The grand scheme. The big picture. 

That for all the wisdom the Lord has given man, and the ability of man to apply it for their lives, there is so much more that is beyond our control, but not His. 

God asks Job to consider the wild goats, the wild ass, the unicorn - which isn't a one horned mythical beast, but the wild oxen, the strong bull or aurochs as it was known, the ostrich or the horse. The hawk and the eagle. 

Man doesn't control or understand the time of the goat, when they calve. Unlike the tame goats, they, without any aid or midwifery, bring forth their kids in sorrow, and cast them out to fend for themselves. And God provides. 

The wild ass is free. God has given it liberty in the wilderness, and a stubborn rebellion against being controlled by men. He searches the mountains for his food, and while it doesn't starve, it isn't fed as a tamed donkey would be. 

The unicorn, or wild bull, doesn't serve man, or tread out the corn. It doesn't reside in a stable. It can't be trusted with the work of the tamed oxen. But it lives. 

God gives goodly wings to the peacock, which cannot fly. And wings and feathers to the ostrich, which not only cannot fly, but runs in the wilderness, dropping her eggs to be hatched in the sand and sun. Not protected in a nest, but exposed to being crushed or broken and eaten. And yet, they don't go extinct. God provides, even as He withheld wisdom and understanding to the big dumb bird, giving her speed to outrun man, even on horseback. 

The ways and whys of creation don't always make sense to man, and are often well out of our control, and yet it continues on, in His ways. 

Like the beasts, man is a wild thing, marrying, and bringing forth children. Stubborn and strong willed. Even at liberty, prone to wander, God provides. 

The rain that brought forth green vegetation in the wilderness, and it becomes the food the wild beasts survive on. 

The horse, whose strength man has harnessed, did not gain its strength from men. It can be startled by a grasshopper, but charge into battle, the noise of armed men, and the shield and spear rattling against him, the trumpet sounding as it rides headlong towards death. 

The hawk flies towards the south, soaring in the warm winds, without our instruction. The eagle nests in the castles of mountains, and seeks prey afar off. Not by will of man. Her chicks go where corpses lay, and feast. 

In all this, man is helpless. It is all the providence of God. 

But we are like these same beasts. We go about our lives, having children that will grow and go off. Stubborn to instruction, refusing to be driven where we should go. Forsaking the blessings of being a servant to God, in exchange for His mercies and bare sustenance in the wilderness. 

All things exist as He made them. And the systems in place for a reason. 

Man, who is frightened of thunder and who can't be trusted to do what's right, who runs after war, who abanons their own kin to the wastes of life, who feeds on the dead, our wisdom is not sufficient to explain our nature, or how it mirrors those wild beasts we can't comprehend. But to God, and to His point of view, it is all in order.

God's speech from the whirlwind is a humbling reminder of divine providence over creation, far beyond human control or full comprehension. **Job 39** portrays wild creatures thriving under God's care, even in ways that seem precarious or counterintuitive to us, underscoring His sovereignty while highlighting our own limitations and rebellious tendencies. Like these wild creatures, we often wander in stubborn liberty, forsaking full submission, yet God sustains us in mercy.

We behave in ways that should result in our extinction. And yet, God's mercies are extended to us in ways we don't even notice or comprehend.

In all these, suffering, danger, apparent neglect, and death are woven into the fabric of life, yet the creatures flourish under God's hand. None of it is explained to them. None of it is micromanaged by man. And none of it indicates that God has abandoned His creation. 

Job is asking "why?" But God is showing him "Who." By enlarging Job's view of God, and the order He created, He is answering Job, just not in the way Job intended.

**Psalms 1**

*1  Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.*

*2  But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.*

*3  And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.*

*4  The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away.*

*5  Therefore the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.*

*6  For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish.*

The book of Psalms, songs sung by the congregation, musicians and singers, in the called out assembly. 

Most are attributed to King David, whose playing of the harp soothe his predecessor, King Saul, and while **Psalm 1** isn't clearly introduced as David's, it follows his patterns of praise and doctrine, and generally is believed to be his. But more importantly, they are of the Spirit, like all scripture, and profitable for learning and reproof. 

And much like the poetic wisdom of Solomon, we find the gospel of Christ throughout. 

Verse 1 opens with a standard refrain found in **Psalms**; the blessedness of the man, and the understanding that it is by God's grace and mercy all blessings flow, Whose promises are sure. 

Here, the promise to bless those who do not listen to the ungodly, the wisdom of this world. Blessing those who do not go the way of sinners, or the scorners. 

In many ways, the Psalms reflect the wisdom of the Lord found in Proverbs, and give an insight to the mind and heart of the King, a man after God's own heart. 

David contrasts the ungodly sinners and scorners with the man who delights in the law of God. Who meditates upon the word day and night. This too is a frequent theme found in **Psalms**, and it shows the importance of scripture, and its role in the Christian life. 

Too often we see those opposed to Christ attacking the inerrant, inspired and preserved word of God. As Satan tempted Eve in the garden, saying "Yea, hath God said?" enemies of God attack His word, because it is the easiest way to cast doubt, or to put false doctrine, vain traditions and damnable heresy in place of the rock which Jesus tells us to build upon; these sayings of His. 

Even so-called professing Christian sects and denominations, that make their history, mythology and traditions the focal point of their faith will downplay and minimize the importance of scripture, mocking Bible believing Christians for making it the sole authority in our faith and practices. 

But what sayeth the scripture? Those that walk in the Spirit, seeking the blessings of God, meditate in His word day and night. By doing so, we become as a tree planted by the river, constantly fed and nourished. Bearing fruit for God. Not withering and being cut off, as the unfruitful. Prospering in all our ways.

**Psalm 6** continues the prayer and plea theme, with David now up all night with sweat and tears and crying out to the Lord for mercy and for the destruction of his enemies. 

Appealing to the mercies of the Lord, to not rebuke us in anger, to not chasten us while He is hot and fiery in His wrath, is wisdom that all Christians should take heed of. 

When we sin, when we have been goaded into a reaction by the temptations in our lives, our first instinct should be to ask God to forgive us. 

The Devil knows our weaknesses. Our enemies know what buttons to push. How to frustrate us and to get us to react. We are weak. We need God to heal us. 

David is crying out that his body and soul are vexed and he is in real pain, and only the Lord can heal him. 

Before anything else, the Psalmist has prioritized calling out to God, humbling himself spiritually, physically and mentally, admitting fault and decency on God. This should be our starting position in prayer. 

Praise, humility, mercy, then judgment.

Jesus taught us to pray; lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. To bring an end to the tests and trials, and deliver us from the evil set against us.

Many of us may use prayer as a means of complaining, to gripe to God for whatever trouble there is in our life, and to whine about it being unfair that we are suffering at all. I think all Christians can fall into that during our despair. But the problem with this is it lacks the self-reflection and humility, and acknowledgement that we are to blame for many of our own problems. Begging for forgiveness, and forgiving others, recognizing our sin before God, and then asking for relief from His chastening puts the matter right in our heart. 

And so, settling this, David transitions to judgment, asking how long will the Lord allow David's enemies to vex him? How long will the trials and temptations continue?

One of the effective means of prayer taught in Psalms, and reinforced by Jesus, is importunity. Persistent prayer. David will frequently ask the Lord to deliver his enemies and ask how long must he suffer the affliction in his life. There is nothing wrong with persistently going to God and asking for His resolution to the matter to come quickly. 

**Luke 18:1–8**
*And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint; Saying, There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: And there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary. And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me. And the Lord said, Hear what the unjust judge saith. And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?*

We should not be afraid to bother the Lord with long-standing issues, be it health, or work, or enemies or anything else. Praying for resolution of a matter, while understanding that His will be done, and resigning yourself for whatever the end of the matter is, is crucial in the Christian prayer life. 

And often, settling it in your heart to be glad with whatever God has given you in terms of an answer will lead to Him blessing you with yet a better alternative or outcome. 

I have personally experienced this. I have witnessed it in others. Persistent prayer and genuine gratitude for whatever His will is, can often work miracles and bring the Lord to not only give you mercy, but shower you with His grace.

*Return, O LORD, deliver my soul: oh save me for thy mercies’ sake. For in death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?*

Here, David appeals to the promise of God to save us. To remind God of His word shows you actually know it, and trust in it. I think this is pleasing to the Lord.

He means the physical death here, but it has the same application spiritually. How are we to praise Him, if we are dead? How can we show the world His mercies if His promises aren't kept. 

I wonder how many appeals to the throne David sat though, that showed him this pattern of petition. 

Letting God know how weary it has become, how the vexation has worn you down, is also an effective means of working it through yourself. 

David says he is weary with his groaning. He's sick of hearing his own laments. It's all he thinks about, and it is destroying him. The desperate plea to God appeals to His love for us. 

He finishes this Psalm as he has others, letting his enemies know his faith in the Lord is unwavering and his confidence in God is strong. 

No matter how weary we are, no matter how long we are vexed, no matter how long our temptations, we know we have already overcome in Christ. 

The Lord has heard our plea. He promised, and so we know He has. He will receive our prayers. Our enemies will know He is with us, when we keep these models of prayer in mind, and humble ourselves to God's will. He will not make us ashamed.

**Psalm 9** continues the prayerful praise of the Lord, the call for His righteous judgment, destruction of enemies, rebuke of the heathen, and the eternal salvation to come. 

The first of the two great commandments, *Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind*, is reflected in the praise and worship of David's song. Praising God with our whole heart, acknowledging all His wonderful and marvelous works, rejoicing in them. 

Note, David is beset by enemies, his cause is right, yet many are against him, he is oppressed, and yet, David begins with praise and rejoicing. 

It's been said before, but Jesus does not take away our burdens and cares, He simply makes those burdens light. His yoke is easy. When we are buffeted by the cares and worries of this world, we should stop and praise God for all He has done. 

Gratitude and praise should be in the front of our minds and love for Him in our hearts, because in the end, His grace, His saving us is sufficient. We are on the winning side. We have overcome the world in Jesus. So sing praise to His name, *O Thou most High.* 

*When mine enemies are turned back*, not if, but when, when they are destroyed by His presence, it is because His enemies are ours. 

**Matthew 5:43–44**
*Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy. But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you*

We are called to love our personal enemies. David had multiple opportunities to kill Saul, yet he spared him, and appealed to the King in love. 

But those that oppress the righteous, and the wicked full of iniquity, God will judge. And we can absolutely pray imprecatory prayers against them, that God will repay. That His vengeance be done, knowing that in the end, there is no escape for the wicked. Their cities will burn, their line will be cut off, there will be no memory of them, and their soul will be in flames of eternal torment. 

What little we can do in our wrath? Better to rejoice in the wrath of God, knowing He will handle it. 

His throne is established forever in righteousness. He will judge. He will take up the cause of the poor and oppressed. Even in great tribulation, it shall be cut short for the elects' sake. 

Because we have placed our trust in His holy name, the Lord Jesus, Who will not forsake those that seek Him. He hears the cry of the humble.

There are so many problems we will have in our life, as men on the earth, and persecutions and attacks added on top of them for believers, if we do the works of God. If we serve Him, we will see trouble. 

How often do we experience or witness the attacks of the devil on believers who turn to God, and do His work? 

I was talking with a younger sister in Christ who just won someone to the Lord, and how awesome that was. Within a few days, she was being afflicted from all sides by multiple travails and trials. 

It was good to be able to give her this perspective. To know to patiently endure it, and see her faith grow. To turn to trusting the Lord to see her through it, and to love on those around her so that they will see her light so shine, that they'll praise God in Heaven. That the unsaved might be persuaded by her chaste conversation. Her behavior in the face of adversity. 

David's story is a wonderful example of how we should view things. His Psalms help sharpen that focus on God when we are really going through it. 

We can humbly ask God for His mercy, and know that He who has lifted us up from the gates of death will save us, while the heathen and enemies of God will be snared by their own sin and turned into Hell. Amen

Brief note on "Higgaion. Selah." 

Higgaion is a Hebrew word that means 'meditation,' or something like it, and seems to be a cue for a musical break, heavy harp, where the singers and congregation considered the words just said. It is used just a couple of times in the Psalms. 

Selah, which is used much more frequently, seems to serve as a pause, perhaps for a musical bridge. 

The definitions are somewhat educated guess, and opinion. I feel that 'selah' is a bit of a 'think about that,' and 'amen' combined. But I am not a musician, and it may seem more of a way to bring the music back around to those that are. 

I think it is more important to look at what's being said, and not get caught up in the pedantic. Selah.

**Acts 17:22–31**
*Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars’ hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious. For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you. God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands; Neither is worshipped with men’s hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things; And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation; That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring. Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man’s device. The cry of David against the heathen, that those who don't believe in the power of the Lord be destroyed, is turned into a warning by Paul to the heathen of Athens. The time of God winking at their pagan idolatry is over. The judgment is here, because in Christ there is no excuse. 

God was made flesh, died for all men and rose again. That assurance is sure, and every man must come to repentance, trusting on the name of Jesus.

**Psalm 10** acts as a pair to **Psalm 9**, and a meditation on the wicked, against who David is seeking God's judgment. 

David opens the Psalm feeling like God's delay in judgment is His hiding Himself, standing afar off, allowing it to continue. We may all feel this way at times. We know God hears us, we have experienced His mercy and blessings and seen His wrath revealed from Heaven, that no man has any excuse to not fear Him...yet, His perfect timing can make us impatient. Even as the saints in Heaven, martyred in tribulation cry out;

Obviously, the wrath of God pours out soon after, His vengeance is sure. We can trust it will come. But it is hard for our human minds to wait. 

The wicked, through pride, do not seek God. They boast of their wicked desires, and bless those that join in their covetousness. They persecute the poor with their evil devices. Set snares and nets, dig pits, and scheme mischief against the fatherless and the poor. Their iniquity knows no limit. 

While their murder and violence is obvious, some of the ways of their deceit is less so. 

*He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den: he lieth in wait to catch the poor: he doth catch the poor, when he draweth him into his net.*

The subtle ways of the wicked, the nets they spread, are not only to blatantly rob the poor of whatever meager wealth they have, but to trap them in temptation. 

They are the drug dealers, booze peddlers, pimps and whoremongers, pornographers, bookies running gambling parlors, scam artists with get rich quick schemes...all of the ways, big and small that evil men seek to take advantage of those who are struggling, who have no father to guide them, who are desperate to escape their poverty, who are not strong in faith and so are easily caught up in vice. 

The description of these men in verse 9 echos the description of their father, the devil. 

**1 Peter 5:8**
*Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.*

These men are as the devil, seeking to take men into their maw, and to bring the righteous to falling, that the adversary can accuse the brethren before God. 

David, praying to spur action against these men, reminds God of their pride and arrogant way, dismissing any thought of God making recompense against them. They say that He will not require it, He won't make them pay the wages of their sin. That they mock God, so they deserve swift and immediate recompense. 

David often uses these formulas for the Psalms, praising God, reminding Him Who He is, what He's promised, who the enemy are, what the Lord has done against them in the past, what they deserve now, faith in what He will do to them in the future. 

Because, God is the judge to the fatherless and defender of the oppressed.

The reoccurring theme of the Lord defending the widow, the fatherless and the poor, and our role in carrying out righteous judgment for them, is probably the most talked about doctrine outside of Who God is, and the doctrines of salvation in Christ. 

More than anything else, we are to clothe and feed the truly needy, to make sure people don't take advantage of those who have no one to defend them. No husband, no father. To do unto the least of these, and in doing so, doing it for Jesus. 

**James 1:27**
*Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.*

This is the ultimate expression of our faith. The outward practice God expects. Self-sacrifice for others, not the selfish sacrifice of the works-based religions of the world. 

**Hosea 6:6**
*For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings*

All the penance and "Eucharist" sacrifices, and all the other rites and rituals men do to get the Lord to be pleased with them are vain. God wants us to exercise mercy and judgment. 

**Proverbs 21:3** 
*To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.*

Jesus, reading Isaiah, gives us the mission statement for Christians;

Luke 4:18–19
*The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.*

Amen

**Psalms 11**
*In the LORD put I my trust: how say ye to my soul, Flee as a bird to your mountain?*

*2 For, lo, the wicked bend their bow, they make ready their arrow upon the string, that they may privily shoot at the upright in heart.*

*3 If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?*

*4 The LORD is in his holy temple, the LORD’s throne is in heaven: his eyes behold, his eyelids try, the children of men.*

*5 The LORD trieth the righteous: but the wicked and him that loveth violence his soul hateth.*

*6 Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone, and an horrible tempest: this shall be the portion of their cup.*

*7 For the righteous LORD loveth righteousness; his countenance doth behold the upright.*

**Psalm 11** is a short song addressing a doubtful disputation of an unknown interlocer, someone who may say our faith in the Lord is insufficient to save us from our enemies. 

Our trust is in the Lord. We have no need to fear. To flee. Especially in the end times this Psalm's dual-fulfillment of prophecy, portends. 

I think of all the fairweather Christians who spend their days in fear, prepping to flee to the mountains in the Tribulation. Who plan to flee as a bird to their mountain. 

The wicked seek to shoot their arrows at the hearts of the upright, even now. In the Tribulation, they won't need to do it privily, but will openly seek the lives of the children of God. 

David asks, rhetorically, *If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?*

If the Lord isn't true to save us, if the foundation of our faith is destroyed, we would of all men be most miserable. 

**1 Corinthians 15:13–17**
*But if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen: And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain. Yea, and we are found false witnesses of God; because we have testified of God that he raised up Christ: whom he raised not up, if so be that the dead rise not. For if the dead rise not, then is not Christ raised: And if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins.*

Because there is no other foundation upon which we may trust;

**1 Corinthians 3:11**
*For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.*

Knowing this sure foundation, and knowing He is risen, we can place our trust in Him. 

We know with certainty the Lord is in His holy Temple, the Lord is on His throne. We know He is the omnipotent judge of men. 

He tries, or tests the righteous to increase our faith. He hates the wicked and the violent, and shall rain down His wrath upon them. This is the portion of their cup. This is a promise of God. 

**Revelation 14:10–11**
*The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.*

But the righteous are before the face of the Lord, always.

I want to take the opportunity here, with such a short and concise Psalm, to deal with the way many modern "theologians" approach the Old Testament, and the Psalms in particular. 

When I read and react to the text, all I see is Jesus, the gospel, and the clear and present application of worship in our lives, and the prophetic nature, which clearly is reflected in New Testament end times scripture. 

Nearly every Psalm is an uplifting song of praise, worship and trust, with the warnings against the wicked and promises of deliverance from their evil, and God's wrath upon them. 

Meanwhile, most studies become hyper fixated on the context David wrote them in, the situation he was facing. Often totally invented by the author (or parroting an earlier study of another man).

Seeking to be wise, they become fools. They want to impress the reader with how clever they are and how their "knowledge of the Hebrew" and extrabiblical sources puts them above the normal believer, who may read the plain text and see themselves, and the future promises of God, as the primary application today. 

A typical example;

"Actually, Psalm 11 is best understood as David’s response to well-meaning but fearful advisers during a time of personal danger, most likely when political enemies or rebellious forces threatened the stability of his rule. The opening dialogue (“Flee as a bird to your mountain”) reflects counsel to seek temporary physical safety amid apparent societal collapse, while David’s reply anchors his confidence in Yahweh’s unchanging character: the Lord remains in His holy temple and on His heavenly throne, testing the righteous and preparing judgment for the wicked. This likely was written during one of the many crises King David faced.   Notably, the Hebrew of verse 3—kî haššātôṯ yēhārēsûn (“for the foundations are being destroyed”)—employs a rare plural form of šātâ that some scholars conjecture may allude to the subterranean pillars of cosmic order rather than mere institutional collapse, thereby elevating the crisis from the merely political to the ontological; yet even this linguistic subtlety serves primarily to underscore David’s immediate existential plight rather than any distant eschatological horizon."

These men miss the forest for the trees, and create this sterile and unrelatable version of the word, buried under jargon, and with little to no edification or doctrine. 

I don't claim to ever exhaust the full meaning and layers of the text in my morning studies. God's word is deep and there are passages that carry a meaning and purpose today, and then read later, convey something totally different. Where the Spirit leads. But when a study becomes an exercise in dazzling the reader with theology, vain philosophy, jargon and concepts that come more from linguistics, semantics and traditions, than the Spirit, I recommend they be avoided.

**Psalms 12**
*Help, LORD; for the godly man ceaseth; for the faithful fail from among the children of men.*

*2 They speak vanity every one with his neighbour: with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak.*

*3 The LORD shall cut off all flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things:*

*4 Who have said, With our tongue will we prevail; our lips are our own: who is lord over us?*

*5 For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD; I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him.*

*6 The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.*

*7 Thou shalt keep them, O LORD, thou shalt preserve them from this generation for ever.*

*8 The wicked walk on every side, when the vilest men are exalted.*

**Psalm 12** opens with the most plaintive cry, yet. Calling upon the Lord, "Help." 

That simple prayer, asking for help during our trials, is perhaps the most often prayed. 

"Help, Lord" because the circumstances have led to humble ourselves before Him. Our admission of weakness allows God to be our strength, and glorifies Him that deserves all glory. 

Even the erstwhile atheist, the fool who says in their heart, "there is no God," cries out for help from the deity they profess doesn't exist. 

We often will ask someone we give the gospel to, have you ever called out to the Lord for help? Because of health, or the health of another. Cry out in fear, because of a crisis or an emergency need has left them no other way to turn, except towards the Lord and His mercy. Or something as simple as a job, or test. Nearly all will say "Yes" if they're being honest. 

From there, it becomes easier to lead them to the truth that they need to call upon the name of the Lord specifically to save them, eternally. To receive forgiveness of sin and everlasting life. 

If man struggles with the things of this world on his own, how much more do we need help for the spiritual things of God? 

Have you cried out to the Lord? Have you come before God, unable to go on, let alone articulate the need you are petitioning, beyond a simple "Help?" 

Have you called upon the Lord for salvation?

David's plea for help, like many of the Psalms, comes from the vexation of spirit in dealing with the wicked of this world. That in a world where believers, Christians, are called to be separated and holy as He is holy, the fallen world full of the iniquity of man troubles us. It is the lot, no pun intended, of the believer.

**2 Peter 2:6–9**
*And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly; And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: (For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;) The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished*

This is a feeling we can all relate to, if you walk in the Spirit. 

The vexation is not just bearing witness to the unlawful deeds of the wicked, but in *hearing* them as well. 

David says they speak vanity to each other, and flatter, and with a double-heart, speak lies. They pridefully boast. It is the wickedness of words that sees David cry out. 

**Matthew 12:34–37**
*O generation of vipers, how can ye, being evil, speak good things? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh. A good man out of the good treasure of the heart bringeth forth good things: and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth evil things. But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment. For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.*

Jesus shows us that words are the window to the heart of a man. An evil heart brings forth evil words, and it is those words that condemn them. 

**Matthew 15:10–11**
*And he called the multitude, and said unto them, Hear, and understand: Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man.*

This understanding, that it wasn't the ritual washings and dietary laws, cleaning the outside of the cup -but the heart, and what proceeds out from it though the mouth, that makes a man unclean, is often neglected by Christians, today. But one of the most repeated commands in scripture is to watch what you say. 

Proverbs is full of advice to remain silent, to not speak like the fool or the froward. To speak truth in all things. To refrain from vain, useless speech. 

But the wicked refuse to hear God's word and follow His way. Men *Who have said, With our tongue will we prevail; our lips are our own: who is lord over us?*

Of course, by admitting they have power over their own tongue, they condemn themselves.

James, the half-brother of Christ, writes in his epistle, about the importance of controlling your tongue. 

**James 3:2–8**
*For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body. Behold, we put bits in the horses’ mouths, that they may obey us; and we turn about their whole body. Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth. Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth! And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity: so is the tongue among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell. For every kind of beasts, and of birds, and of serpents, and of things in the sea, is tamed, and hath been tamed of mankind: But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.*

Controlling your speech will go far in controlling your body. We talk ourselves into a multitude of sins. We give cause for the enemies of Christ to blaspheme by our publicly spoken words, far more than our sins done in secret. 

When we curse, profane and use vulgarity, when we lie and double-deal. When we oppress and offend others. When we puff up with vain words and flattering lips. We defile the whole body by that tiny member, the tongue.

*For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD; I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him.*

This is a promise from God Himself. These are His words. 

**2 Peter 1:20–21**
*Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.*

The psalmist was moved by the holy Ghost to pen the words of the Lord. His promises are our sure foundation. His word settled forever in Heaven. Jesus is the Word made flesh. The promise fulfilled. 

Faith cometh by hearing the word of God. Those that hear and do the things the Lord says are built upon a rock. We live by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. All scripture is given by inspiration of God. It is the source of all our knowledge and understanding. His precepts give us understanding. We are told to meditate in His word day and night. To bind His words upon our heart. His words are powerful;

**Hebrews 1:1–3**
*God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds; Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high*

The word which we preach is the power to save men's souls to all who trust His word:

**Ephesians 1:12–14**
*That we should be to the praise of his glory, who first trusted in Christ. In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory.*

And so, the preservation of God's word for all generations is a divine role. God supernaturally has revealed His word to man in sundry times and diverse manners, and He keeps His word pure. 

*The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times. Thou shalt keep them, O LORD, thou shalt preserve them from this generation for ever.*

If man needs every word of God to live, as much as bread, man needs access to every word He has given us. 

The blessing of having a consolidated, complete, incorruptible source, an every-word Bible, cannot be overstated. The King James Bible is the every-word source, in English, without error. 

The 6 earlier English attempts, like a refiner's fire. We have the purified silver of the Authorized version. We can know the Lord has preserved His word. We can trust and build upon that sure foundation.

**Psalms 13**
*How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?*

*2 How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?*

*5 But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation.*

*6 I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me.*

Psalm 13 beautifully captures a very real feeling of the Christian life, the impatient waiting for God's perfect timing, turning into an acknowledgement that He has dealt bountifully with us. 

It can be easy to slip into despair when facing trials. It can be easy for us as humans, weak in the flesh, to see the enemy seemingly triumph. To pray and wait upon the Lord, but feel like He may have forgotten you in regards to your trouble. 

We've discussed the idea that even as martyred saints in Heaven, this impatient call for the Lord to hurry and fulfill His judgment, occurs. How much more can this take hold in our finite flesh? 

As Peter reminds us;

**2 Peter 3:8–9**
*But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance*.

God calls upon His faithful to wait. And in that waiting, there is promise as well.

**Isaiah 40:31**
*But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.*

In our patience, God gives us added strength. It is part of a ladder of virtue in the Christian life, elevating us to godliness. 

**2 Peter 1:5–8**
*And beside this, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness; And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity. For if these things be in you, and abound, they make you that ye shall neither be barren nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.*

In the end, our prayers for God to act, and reminders that He has promised to tend to our welfare, and bring us peace from our enemies must inevitably lead to our recognition of His mercies and blessings. Of His salvation. 

Because, as we call out to Him, it is impossible to not remember the very reason we are trusting in Him, beginning with eternal life granted through Jesus. And with the heavenly perspective of God's grace, it is incredibly difficult to continue in complaint. *Because he hath dealt bountifully with* us. We've already received more than we could ever deserve.

**2 Corinthians 12:7–11**
*And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ’s sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong. I am become a fool in glorying; ye have compelled me: for I ought to have been commended of you: for in nothing am I behind the very chiefest apostles, though I be nothing.*

It's also good to remember that, if a prayer remains "unanswered" by our measure, it very well may be answered in His. That His grace is sufficient. We've already been spared, hell and deaf, and given the glory of eternal life in Christ. 

Remember the Israelites, who when delivered out of Egypt and bondage, complained incessantly in the wilderness. They complained about a lack of water. They complained about the daunting task of taking the land, despite God promising to drive the inhabitants out before them. They believed the bad spies report, and ignored Joshua and Caleb. They complained about mana, and they complained about quail. And God had to constantly remind them that He had delivered them in the first place. 

Sometimes if we feel the need to complain to God, we should remember that he's delivered us in the first place. That His grace is sufficient. Reminding ourselves of what we're going through currently is nothing in comparison to the abundance we've already received. 

**Romans 8:14–18**
*For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God. For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God: And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. Keeping that eternal perspective gives us faith in the Lord's of ability to deliver us. The suffering of this present time is nothing. Life is but a vapor. 

So, having persistent prayer and letting God know how you feel while waiting for His perfect timing to occur is fine. But keep that perspective in mind. And understand that patience builds godliness. And everything to His glory, amen.

The opening 3 verses of **Psalm 14** stand as the definitive and true statements of the doctrine that all men have sinned and falled short of the glory of God. Quoted in part by Paul in **Romans 3:10–12**
*As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one: There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one*.

It serves as a universal appeal to the need for the gospel, and the reconciliation of fallen men with a holy God. There is none good but God. All have gone astray. 

The opening verse is an even deeper truth, showing the self-deception that leads fools to claim there is no God. They may say this, but ultimately every man knows that God is, and the judge of all things. 

Like the scribes and Pharisees that Jesus preaches against in **Matthew 23**, these fools, the workers of iniquity, devour the poor. They eat up the people as bread.

He is the salvation come out of Zion, and at His coming, Jesus brings all the risen saints, death and Hell defeated.

This is our future, rejoice.

The Christian life is one of separation. Of leaving behind the things of this world, and the wickedness men do, separated unto His gospel, and proclaiming His truth. 

Epistles in the New Testament show us examples of godly living. Admonishments against the behavior that the lost may do, but we should strive to reject even the company of those that behave as the heathen. 

**1 Corinthians 5:11**
*But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.*

*Again, think ye that we excuse ourselves unto you? we speak before God in Christ: but we do all things, dearly beloved, for your edifying. Here, David gives a similar refrain. Against backbiting, talking behind someone's back, railing and gossiping. Against evil done to your neighbor.
