**Psalms 17**
*Hear the right, O LORD, attend unto my cry, give ear unto my prayer, that goeth not out of feigned lips.*

*2 Let my sentence come forth from thy presence; let thine eyes behold the things that are equal.*

*3 Thou hast proved mine heart; thou hast visited me in the night; thou hast tried me, and shalt find nothing; I am purposed that my mouth shall not transgress.*

*4 Concerning the works of men, by the word of thy lips I have kept me from the paths of the destroyer.*

*5 Hold up my goings in thy paths, that my footsteps slip not.*

*6 I have called upon thee, for thou wilt hear me, O God: incline thine ear unto me, and hear my speech.*

*7 Shew thy marvellous lovingkindness, O thou that savest by thy right hand them which put their trust in thee from those that rise up against them.*

*8 Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings,*

*9 From the wicked that oppress me, from my deadly enemies, who compass me about.*

*10 They are inclosed in their own fat: with their mouth they speak proudly.*

*11 They have now compassed us in our steps: they have set their eyes bowing down to the earth;*

*12 Like as a lion that is greedy of his prey, and as it were a young lion lurking in secret places.*

*13 Arise, O LORD, disappoint him, cast him down: deliver my soul from the wicked, which is thy sword:*

*14 From men which are thy hand, O LORD, from men of the world, which have their portion in this life, and whose belly thou fillest with thy hid treasure: they are full of children, and leave the rest of their substance to their babes.*

*15 As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness.*

**Psalm 17** again shows us the model of importunity in prayer. 

Importunity is a noun that means asking for something over and over again in a strong, pushy, or annoying way. It is the act of persistent begging or making urgent demands that wear people down. David utilizes this in Psalms to great effect. Pursuing an answer from the throne of God, with repeated supplication. 

It may seem contrary to the fear of the Lord and humility before Him, but scripture shows it is effective. Jesus taught us this as well. 

**Luke 18:1–8**
*And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint; Saying, There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: And there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary. And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me. And the Lord said, Hear what the unjust judge saith. And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?*

We often find ourselves in difficult situations, where we have not because we ask not. We also tend to move on, rather than "bother God" with whatever it is we need of Him.  

Praying without ceasing, staying strong in prayer because we are weak, this is pleasing to the Lord. So we should pray without fainting, and in doing so, exercise our faith that should Christ return in our time, He finds that faith upon the earth. 

Notice too, that the woman before the unjust judge is pleading for vengeance against her adversary, just as David is here in this psalm. Just as the martyred under the throne in Heaven plead with God for His wrath to pour out. 

Imprecatory prayers are Biblical. Acknowledging God's ownership of vengeance, while suffering for His sake, is an act of great faith. And as we have seen previously in **Psalms,** patience is a virtue that leads us to godliness. 

Importunity in prayer, and imprecatory prayer feels wrong to many. I have seen supposed Christian teachers make the claim that there is no room for this in the New Testament. But they are a mighty tool in our arsenal of faith.

The psalmist calls for the Lord's judgment, that His sentence be given against the wicked. But it is foolish to cry out for God's perfect justice to be administered, while you yourself are guilty. 

It is like a thief going to the police because his partners robbed him of his share of their stolen things. Of a drug dealer complaining about being ripped off in a deal gone wrong. 

And so, David wisely shows us the pattern of praying imprecatory prayers includes self-examination and willingness for God to judge him the same way he is judging others. 

*Thou hast proved mine heart; thou hast visited me in the night; thou hast tried me, and shalt find nothing; I am purposed that my mouth shall not transgress.*

David credits God's word to keep him from the *paths of the destroyer.* A key doctrine, that it is God's word that we judge ourselves and others by, not our own feelings or desires. We judge righteously when we allow God to tell us good from evil. 

David then calls for the Lord to hold up his goings, to keep him on the right path. 

So we see that it isn't simply cursing your enemies and expecting God to overlook your sin. But praying for God's judgement, knowing He is just and seeking His confirmation that you are blameless in the matter. Also, praising Him for keeping you from sin in the first place. 

All glory goes to God. 

Having the faith to be judged fairly by God, knowing that because of God you have walked in His ways, but accepting any fault of your own that He may find...this humility should be at the heart of your prayer life.

Continuing in **Psalms 17**, we see that David's importunity comes from his faith in God to hear those who call upon Him. That we may go boldly before the throne of grace, because He has shown us that He listens to our cries. The initial call for salvation in the Lord's name gives us the hope that He listens to us for far less important matters, such as our suffering in this life. 

The Lord's lovingkindness is already apparent to those that put their trust in Him, that have been saved by His strong right-hand. Christ Jesus. We know that our Savior is at the right hand of the Father. The New Testament is clear on this. But David is writing hundreds of years earlier, showing that Old Testament saints knew and understood the concept, even if they didn't have the full revelation and details. 

*Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings, From the wicked that oppress me, from my deadly enemies, who compass me about.*

Keep me, o Lord. It is His power that keeps the children of God under His protection and secure in His promises. We shall not fear, because we are under His mighty wing, as a mother hen keeps her chicks. 

Jesus laments the unfaithful Jews for refusing to be gathered thus. 

**Matthew 23:37–39**
*O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not! **Psalm 18** is one of the first long-form songs of David, and it reflects his own experience with the Lord, his trust in God, and deliverance from his enemies, while weaving together prophetic views of Jesus, the doctrines of salvation, the end times wrath and Kingdom of God. 

Ultimately, the Psalm gives us understanding of Who the Lord is and why He is worthy of our trust, today. 

The Lord is our strength. Our rock. Our fortress. Our deliverer. Our strength. Trustworthy. Our buckler, the horn of our salvation, our high tower. He is worthy to be praised. He is merciful to those that are merciful. Upright in all His ways to those that walk in them. Pure to the pure and froward to the froward.

His way is perfect, His word is tried and trusted, and the strength and shield of those that place that trust in Him. 

*For who is God save the LORD? or who is a rock save our God?*

There is no other rock than the Lord. There is no other name given but Jesus. He is the fulfillment of the word, the word made flesh, the promise of God come down from Heaven. The Christ. And He liveth. 

The shield of salvation is given, by the right-hand of God. His gentleness has made those who trust Him great. 

*The LORD liveth; and blessed be my rock; and let the God of my salvation be exalted.*

The Lord is praised among the heathen. The strangers hear and obey. The people who were not a people are come, and are subdued under the throne of David, to his Seed. To His anointed, evermore. 

The enemies of David, like the enemies of Christ, are crushed before them by the fiery and fierce judgment of God. Rains of fire and brimstone, hail and lightenings, leading the wicked to cry out, and hide themselves from His fury. And ultimately be destroyed by His coming. 

The Lord then is a rewarder of those that trust in Him, who diligently seek Him. Who follow His ways and obey His statutes. He will reward us for the righteousness we have shown, and the recompense for our cleanliness in His sight. The righteousness of Christ imputed on His children. The gold, silver and precious stones we build upon that foundation. 

He lifts us up, strengthening us to do great deeds in His name. He fills us with His light. 

He hears our cries. He comes to our aid. He destroys the wicked for our sake, in the anger kindled by their sin against Him and their treatment of His children. 

*Therefore will I give thanks unto thee, O LORD, among the heathen, and sing praises unto thy name.* Amen

Songs of deliverance and praise, with the appearance of the Lord as a consuming fire, yet displaying tender mercies to His beloved, those that place their trust in Him, and who call upon the Lord, are found throughout the book of Psalms. 

The reassurance to believers that what God has done for David will be done for us, His name and word are worthy, and are to be trusted. The picture of salvation and judgment. All are detailed repeatedly, just as much as songs of despair and pleas for God's intervention. But both styles of song contain thanksgiving and praise for His grace and mercy, and all the blessings He has already provided those that love Him. 

Taken as a whole, Psalms gives us the complete picture of the Christian life. They give us a model of prayer and praise that fits every stage of our growth and development, while also dripping with doctrine, teaching us the truth of God.

**Psalm 19** is fairly short, yet packed with doctrine, teaching the purpose of creation, the testimony of God to all creatures, the picture of Christ, and the establishment of the law of the Lord in nature itself, that there is no excuse, while the believer is given constant reminders of His judgements. 

**Romans 1:18–20**
*For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness; Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them. For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse*

The heavens declare the glory of God. Looking upon the night sky we see His precision and power. And as the day follows day and night follows night, each with the passing of the sun and the stars, we are given evidence of His might. 

The things of creation speak without words, that all man may understand. They don't need a language. They don't need to be explained. Man sees the passage of time, seasons, years, decades even, in heavenly bodies. 

The vain hypothetical of a savage on a remote island, never hearing the gospel, is undone by the understanding that all nature is a parable and a testament of God, showing men truth. 

The boldness of the sun breaking forth in the morning is as the risen Christ, returning in glory, a picture of the Creator Who is blessed forever, amen. 

Nature teaches us God's law. His ways. 

**1 Corinthians 11:14**
*Doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him?*

His wrath is revealed against those who sin, even without the oracles of God documenting His commandments. The Spirit showing mankind the results of their transgressions. The understanding that murder, adultery, lying, stealing, all of these things that do harm to your neighbor and are a shame before God, are known. 

**Romans 2:11–16**
*For there is no respect of persons with God. For as many as have sinned without law shall also perish without law: and as many as have sinned in the law shall be judged by the law; (For not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified. For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves: Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another;) In the day when God shall judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ according to my gospel.*

Man can see the law of God, know it written in their hearts, watch the outcome of their behavior and the wrath upon those who sin, and know they are guilty before the consuming fire which is God. 

How much more are we who have His statutes and commandments by the oracles of God? 

**Romans 3:1–2**
*What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision? Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God.*

The advantage given Israel, and held by the Jews in Paul's day, is now given to the world. That everyone may know His word. 

*The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.*

If the day declares His righteousness and the night His knowledge, and the very nature of things speaks to His wrath, then the oracles of God give us the hope of His mercy. God is a rewarder to those that diligently seek Him. 

The fear of the Lord is clean, and known to all men. The fool may say in their heart there is no God, but the wise fear Him, even if they don't know scripture. 

The truth is more desirable than gold, sweeter than honey. Its pursuit is its own reward, spurring us to seek Him. The warnings and rewards, motivation to learn His ways. 

And, in that knowledge, we find His word, and from that word, salvation.

In Him we are cleansed from our iniquity. In Him we are conformed to His image, kept back from presumptuous sin. Made upright. His righteousness imputed on us that we may be transformed. To be our strength and the Lord our Redeemer.

We are blessed to have the knowledge of the truth before us. His inspired and preserved word, that we may know Him. And God does not leave those without the oracles lacking. 

But for the children of God, creation gives us reassurance and opportunities to worship Him for His might and glory. To have reminders that He loves us. 

To every seed we sow that comes to fruition. To every shooting star, or bird in flight, or wave crashing on the shore, we are able to look at the Lord in awe. Babies born to the death of the elderly, spring following winter, the setting sun and darkest night...all creation is a parable to those with ears to hear and eyes to see. 

To know God loves us. And His mercy upon us is evidence to others seeking truth. The light in us shines that others may see and glorify God. 

We are to be as the firmament, as the rising sun and the crashing wave. His children are meant to teach the heathen who seeks the Lord, as much as anything in creation. Because we are new creatures in Christ, brought forth as a testimony to God's greatness. 

*Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer.* Amen

**Psalm 20** is yet another song of praise and worship for the salvation that is in Christ Jesus. 

The name of the God of Jacob. The Lord that strengthens us out of Zion. The one offering forever, the burnt sacrifice. Christ Jesus. 

The love of God has been granted to us in his grace, and his counsel is wisdom; trust in the Lord. 

We will rejoice in the salvation given to us in the name of our God. We will set up banners in His holy name. He is Christ Jesus, and God hears all our petitions, lifted up in His name. 

The Lord saves His anointed. He did not leave his soul to see corruption. His anointed was not left in hell. The saving strength of His right hand. Christ Jesus. 

Some trust in the power of this world, their own strength, their own works. And they will be brought down low. He will say depart from me. I never knew you. 

But to those of us who trust in the name of the Lord, our God, we are risen and made to stand upright. In Christ Jesus. 

Save, Lord. In the name of the King of Kings and the Lord of lords, Christ Jesus.

*Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.*

This verse is often quoted, and has inspired generations of believers. But in practice it can be difficult. We often seek reassurance from our material, wealth and position. 

David, writing this. Psalm with dual purpose (at least), the prophetic imagery of Christ Jesus and the surety of his salvation, but also as an intercessional prayer before a battle against a well-armed and equipped foe. 

David's showing us that it is better to trust in the Lord than all the horses and chariots in the world. That in our battles, even if we are seemingly overmatched by our enemy, we are still victorious in God. 

What a comfort. What a blessing. That we can stand fast, and be sure of our deliverance. That we can trust in the Lord in all things, because we've first trusted in Him, our eternal security. 

When we are weak we are made strong. God uses us to confound the wise. We have already overcome in Christ. And we should rejoice in our salvation.

*Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?* 

In the 9th hour, Jesus cried out from the cross the words of the Psalm, the opening line of a song of desperation, penned by David centuries earlier. 

An event recorded twice in the gospels:

**Matthew 27:46**
*And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?*

**Mark 15:34**
*And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?*

The man Christ Jesus, after a day of betrayal, abuse, beaten beyond human recognition, scourged, shamed and mocked, cursed, hung on the tree, and become sin for all mankind, acknowledging in death that, by taking on all of the sin in all of creation, He is, in that moment, no longer looked upon by the Father Whom He has been with, and a part of, since everlasting. 

The prophetic words of the Psalm, Christ's words echoed through time to the psalmist, words Jesus Himself knew from before the foundation of the world, conveying the heartbreaking moments before the perfect and holy Lord would willingly give His life that we may live. 

Jesus cried out in Aramaic, the daily language of the people, the language He grew up in life speaking, conveying His humanity in that moment. 

The Hebrew words, long sung by Israel in the congregation, translated, and again, interpreted into Greek, and given to us in English, never losing a scintilla of power. Given to us as the blessed hope, an example of the endurance and steadfastness we should look to:

**Hebrews 12:2-3** 
*Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds*.

Jesus, our scapegoat, receiving our sin in atonement, without the camp. Taking them utterly away. Not as the blood of bulls and goats, offered yearly for sanctification by the High Priest of the Tabernacle, but once and for all, shed for man. And He, as THE High Priest, entered into the Heavenly Tabernacle, and applied His own precious blood upon the mercy seat in Heaven. 

No greater love than this has ever been shed towards us, that God became flesh, and lived among us, sinless and perfect, that He might drink of this cup. Going to the cross that we might live. 

The tragic nature of these words reveals the depth of the love of God. That while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

**Psalm 22** continues from its powerful open, to convey the desperation that Jesus' flesh must have felt in that moment, which is felt by everyone of us at times in our life. Certainly, it was David's own state of mind when the Spirit led him to compose it. 

That we cry out to God, and feel like He is far from us. That He doesn't hear. That He may have abandoned us to our plight. 

But there is always the hope of faith, and trust in the holy God, Who has kept His promises and delivers those who trust in Him. 

The promises made to the fathers, kept. He heard the cries in Egypt, and brought them out of the land. He heard their cries during the time in the wilderness. He delivered their children to the promised land. He heard them in the days of judges, where their own sin brought them low, sending men to raise them up and bring them out of evil.

Those that trusted Him were not confounded. 

**Hebrews 12:1**
*Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us*

We know that God is good, and cannot lie. And so our deliverance is assured, even when our flesh is weak and we feel abandoned. 

The almighty God's consistent faithfulness in keeping his word to those he foreknew, gives us confidence and strength. These things were written for our admonition. That we may know Him as a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him. 

**Romans 15:4**
*For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.*

We are given that knowledge of the past that we might have the surety of the future.

The prophetic nature of the God-inspired Psalm of David continues, showing the children of Israel the truth of Christ, through a glass darkly. In David's personal pain, we see a shadow of the suffering of Jesus, a reproach of men, despised of the people, laughed to scorn. 

**Matthew 27:39–43**
*And they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads, And saying, Thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days, save thyself. If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross. Likewise also the chief priests mocking him, with the scribes and elders, said, He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he will have him: for he said, I am the Son of God.*

Compassed about by bulls, by dogs, men like lions, surrounded by the Roman soldiers doing the work of the Jews, piercing Jesus' hands and feet with nails. Splayed out upon the cross, His joints distended and twisted to support the weight of His body. The sinking feeling of death settling in His guts, as He struggled to breathe. His bones in sharp relief to His stretched out skin.

Crying out for water, Jesus is given vinegar to drink, raised up on hyssop, a bitter gall that could not quench His overwhelming thirst. The soldiers then parted His garments by lot:

**Matthew 27:34–35**
*They gave him vinegar to drink mingled with gall: and when he had tasted thereof, he would not drink. And they crucified him, and parted his garments, casting lots: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, They parted my garments among them, and upon my vesture did they cast lots.*

The desperation and loneliness, the mental anguish Jesus suffered on the cross, He had also carried with Him for 33 years. Understanding the suffering that awaited Him at Calvary, knowing His anointed part in the great redemptive plan, while at all points being touched by the infirmity of the flesh, and tempted as we are. His prayers at Gethsemane, Son to the Father, that if it were possible to take this cup from Him, please let it be so. But steadfast to do the will of the Father, even knowing the physical and emotional pain He would endure. These stanzas in this psalm tragically capture it all, before transitioning to the joyful hope found in every tribulation those who love God can take comfort in:

**Romans 8:28**
*And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.*

Psalm 22 continues. The desperate plea of the condemned man, compassed by dogs, scorned and ridiculed, pierced and heartbroken, feeling abandoned by God, turns to a prayer of certain hope. 

We know God has delivered every promise He has made. He has heard the cries of His people and, in due season, saved them. 

We may persist in our prayers, reminding God, and ourselves, of His faithfulness, as we ask for more immediate relief. His perfect timing may not be ours, but at our weakest He shows His strength.

*Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog. Save me from the lion’s mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns.*

From the proverbial horns of a dilemma, from the immediate threat, we call upon the name of the Lord. Not only the saved, His darling, but the lost often find His strength in their time of trial. Foxhole converts.

The Potter often moves the clay in such a way, that we finally see our shortcomings and impotency, and need His hand to lift us up, that we may be what He has planned for us to become. 

If even Jesus Christ was to be made a reproach and murdered by bloody men in a wicked act, that we may know eternal life, as the risen and triumphant Son of God, then our trials are an opportunity to overcome by His power and to give the Lord the glory. 

*I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee.*

In the midst of tribulation, we shall praise Him. That is the mind of a mature Christian. It is difficult to see, sometimes, and we may feel isolated, alone, but in our most desperate hour, we praise Him. We declare His holy name to our brethren, in the congregation we hold up His excellence. 

(It may not be a primary (or even secondary) application of this psalm, but it strikes me that we cannot lift up our voice in praise to the congregation, to declare His name unto the brethren, if we avoid church. If we forsake the assembly. Go to church!)

*Ye that fear the LORD, praise him; all ye the seed of Jacob, glorify him; and fear him, all ye the seed of Israel.*

The praise and glory and fear of the Lord comes from knowledge of the doctrines of God. The understanding of His ways, the past performance of His promise, the teachings of the fathers through the inspired and preserved word of God. 

Faith cometh by hearing.

In the midst of the congregation, among those that fear the Lord and sing His glory, blessing God and His holy name, we are not only given the opportunity to give testimony of what He has done for us, but hear what He has done for others. To learn doctrine and see that He has heard those who call out to Him.

We can know, as Elijah on the mountain, alone, that there are a remnant of believers. 

**Romans 11:3–4**
*Lord, they have killed thy prophets, and digged down thine altars; and I am left alone, and they seek my life. But what saith the answer of God unto him? I have reserved to myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to the image of Baal.*

We have fellowship in our gatherings with the brethren. We have understanding from preaching and support of prayer, and the opportunity to worship God with those who have gone through what we have. To edify those going through things we have endured. 

**Hebrews 10:23–25**
*Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;) And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.*

That communal exhortation is invaluable to a believer in tribulation. Going through a personal trial. Hearing the victory Jesus has given others provides the strength to go on. 

To know the meek shall eat and be satisfied, seeking the Lord and finding Him, unto eternal life.

**John 6:35–37**
*And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst. But I said unto you, That ye also have seen me, and believe not. All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.*

This is the meat we eat, and are satisfied, never to hunger again. Complete in Christ, and having eternal life.

The truth of this gospel goes out to the ends of the world. And every knee shall bow. *For the kingdom is the LORD’s: and he is the governor among the nations.*

Ultimately, our hope rests on the truth that what God has promised to deliver, He will. And the present suffering pales in comparison for what will come. 

**Romans 8:18**
*For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.*

*A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation. They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this.*

Our suffering is cause to praise the Lord to the brethren, to being others to the knowledge of Christ, to proclaim His power and promise, and to partake in the spreading of His gospel to all people, that every tongue shall confess that He hath done this. 

Amen

**Psalms 23**
*The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.*

*2 He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.*

*3 He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.*

*4 Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.*

*5 Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over.*

*6 Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.*

**Psalm 23** is perhaps the second most famous passage of scripture, behind **John 3:16**, and like it, contains the gospel promise, the good news of the Lord towards believers. 

The world knows the Psalm because it has become the standard go to, in fiction and in real life, recited at funerals by priests and reverends, in every religion that claims the name of Christ. Sadly, for most, the departed have no idea that the promises are not automatic, and aren't achieved by their works, their character or how "good" they are. They are by faith in the Good Shepherd, alone. 

Of course, Jesus is that shepherd. 

**John 10:11** 
*I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep*.

He gave His life that we may be forgiven, and rose again that we may have eternal life. He did this for those that follow Him, and who have been entrusted to Him by the Father. Believers are His flock. 

And because He is our shepherd, we shall not want. 

What an amazing promise, which God Who cannot lie has given us. We shall not want. He provides all things:

**Philippians 4:19**
*But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus.*

Not riches as this world judges, necessarily, but all our needs are met by Him by Christ Jesus. 

**2 Peter 1:3**
*According as his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue.*

You may feel financially burdened, or pressed by health concerns. You might be struggling in your faith, to live by trust in God to deliver. But ultimately, the truth is that all we need, everything that pertains to life and godliness, is given freely, that we may have life and more abundantly in His name. 

The green pastures and still waters are generally equated to Heaven in the way the world uses **Psalm 23**, and certainly, what little we know of Paradise is the peace of being in the presence of the Lord. But this stillness is a promise of this life, for a believer. 

**Philippians 4:7**
*And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.*

Our burdens aren't removed, but the yoke of carrying them is made light by His grace. Because in the end, whatever we are going through will be for our good. 

**Romans 8:28**
*And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.*

We are renewed in Him, and regenerated by the Spirit in faith, our soul restored. We are led in His ways, and shown the truth from His word, for His name's sake. In Jesus we are made whole, and by His power revealed in us, by His word, we are shown the deeper things of God. 

*Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.* 

This allegory is considered death itself by the secular world, but note the imagery of a shadow. The Bible says a shadow is not the very image of the things that cast it. 

We may be in a low point in our lives, a valley, and maybe even feel the shadow of death on our flesh as we endure this season in our lives, but the strength to fear no evil, to glory in our tribulation, comes from knowing the good Shepherd is with us. His rod and staff, our comfort. 

The rod of correction, the staff that guides us as we go astray. His protection, our safety. Knowing He laid down His life for us. That He will seek and save His lost sheep, and bring us home by His power.

What the unsaved world uses as a false comfort in death should be a comfort in this life for saved believers.

The table He has set for us, the bounty of His blessings, the deliverance from those who seek to destroy us, that they may know we fear the Lord, and glorify Him, is in this life. In the presence of our enemies. 

Yes, there is the idea of a feast set for us in the end times prophecy, a wedding feast for the Bridegroom. Served by Christ Jesus:

**Isaiah 25:6**
*And in this mountain shall the Lord of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined.*

**Luke 12:37**
*Blessed are those servants, whom the lord when he cometh shall find watching: verily I say unto you, that he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them.*

...but the primary application in **Psalm 23** is the peace found in this life. At this time. Our cup runneth over with His grace, even now. The table has been set in Heaven, but the bounty we are given starts the moment you call upon His name in faith. 

The final verse places this context firmly in the "now" of the believer:

*Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.*

Goodness and mercy follow us, today. We can rest assured that He has delivered us, and be blessed in this life, knowing we have eternity with Him in the next. 

We shall fear no evil, because we have eternal life and shall never perish. We will dwell in the house of the Lord forever, so rejoice even in perils and trials. Rest in the green pastures by the still waters. We have a good Shepherd Who loves us. Amen

*The earth is the LORD’s, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.*

*2 For he hath founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods.*

*3 Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?*

*4 He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully.*

*5 He shall receive the blessing from the LORD, and righteousness from the God of his salvation.*

*6 This is the generation of them that seek him, that seek thy face, O Jacob. Selah.*

*7 Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in.*

*8 Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle.*

*9 Lift up your heads, O ye gates; even lift them up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in.*

*10 Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory. Selah.*

**Psalm 24** is a meditation on the truth of the Christ, the Lord, King of Hosts. Creator of all things, and the truth of the way of righteousness for those that trust in Him.

The gospel message of the Psalms, sung in the Temple, performed by the chief musicians and the congregation is the inspired doctrines of God, and the focus is entirely Jesus. 

They may have looked through a glass darkly, but the concepts of Christ are hammered home, in verse after verse, chorus and stanzas of praise for the name of God, the Holy One, the Lord. 

Here in the 24th Psalm, David asks *Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?*

Those with clean hands and pure hearts, who hasn't put their trust in vanity or lying lips, but who trusted the God of their salvation. 

*He shall receive the blessing from the LORD, and righteousness from the God of his salvation.*

We are made clean of our sins, our hearts purified by the imputed righteousness of God. We receive these blessings by grace through faith, and access to the Kingdom, not by our own righteousness but by submitting to the righteousness that is God's. 

**Romans 4:5–8**
*But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, Saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.*

There are false religions that deny the imputation of righteousness by faith in Christ. They say that imputation is not taught in scripture. This is a lie.

**2 Corinthians 5:21**
*For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.*

Our righteousness is as a filthy rag, our works could never justify us before a holy and perfect God. But these men believing vanity, and swearing deceitfully, teach that man needs to establish their own righteousness through works of the law, and many are misled by this lie. 

**Romans 10:2–4**
*For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge. For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.*

Roman Catholicsm rejects the idea that we are made righteous by receiving righteousness from the God of our salvation. The Council of Trent (Canon 11 on Justification) anathematized the idea that people are justified “by the sole imputation of the justice of Christ, or by the sole remission of sins” and that righteousness is "infused" by works, sacraments and "grace transforming a person," so that their own righteousness is established, rather than submitting to the righteousness of God. 

But let God be true, and every man a liar. The generation of them that seek His face shall not be ashamed. All who come to the saving knowledge of Christ are made pure, in Him. Righteous, in Him. 

**Titus 3:5–7**

In the original Hebrew, David used the format of an "alphabetic acrostic psalm," where stanzas begin with consecutive letters, to act as an mnemonic device, and form of poetry, that David uses multiple times in Psalms. 

This stylized form of writing is "lost" in translation, some textual critics may say, but the strained gnat of it all makes them miss the power of what we have in English. 

The repeated calls to trust the Lord, seek forgiveness, humbly petition and wait with patience is all beautifully expressed in Psalm 25 as we read it here. The prose of the Authorized English loses nothing to the power of God's word. 

So, while it is interesting to note the format, and discuss the ways it was used (here, imperfectly with missing and skipped letters) it isn't necessary for the truth to prick our hearts and give us comfort.

However, recognizing **Psalm 25** as an attempted alphabetic acrostic in the original Hebrew, intended to run through the 22 letters of the alphabet, does give us the opportunity to see something of ourselves in it. 

In this Psalm, the alphabetic pattern is incomplete, the letter *vav* is missing, *resh* appears twice, and the final verse falls outside the sequence. The broken acrostic still carries the psalm’s prayer, and focuses on the Lord's mercy and power. 

Could the broken format look to the broken-hearted sinner, imperfectly calling upon a perfect God? Could it be that by breaking the expected  format, David shows the same brokenness of spirit we have in this life as we wait upon the redemption of Christ in the end? 

I don't know. But it sounds good. Selah.

**Matthew 7:1–2**
*Judge not, that ye be not judged. For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.*

Jesus' words are often twisted by others to mean a Christian should never judge another person, no matter how wicked they are or what sins they do. But, we know the warning is against hypocrisy, not right judgment. 

**Psalm 26** gives us a picture of what Jesus is actually teaching, where David asks the Lord to judge him by his doings, according to his faith, in comparison to the wicked around him. 

The understanding of proper judgement is key to good Christian living. It allows us to be separated, to be holy as God is holy, to put away the filth of the flesh and walk in the Spirit. To seek to be a disciplined servant of the Lord. 

We walk in integrity, and trust in the Lord alone, that we shall not slide. Firmly on His rock, not backsliding to live as the world does. 

It is not an automatic transformation. We are sanctified by the Spirit by the inward man, the new man, but our flesh is still prone to lusts of the eyes and the pride of life and we can stumble and fall. 

But if we seek the judgment of God, asking Him to try us and see that our heart is right, we are opening ourselves to correction and refinement, to better be used by God. 

Walking in His truth, keeping ourselves pure and humble, seeing others in the way God does, with grace and mercy and lovingkindness, we can make our case to the Lord, and compare ourselves to the wicked without the leaven of the Pharisees, hypocrisy. 

David lists the things he has not done, to separate himself towards God. 

He has not sat with vain persons, false believers. He has not had ecumenical fellowship with the dissemblers, the false prophets who teach lies. He has avoided the congregation of evil doers. The bitter fruit of the false religions of this world. He has not yoked with unbelievers. 

Instead, knowing he is innocent of these things, and sanctified, he is able to come before the altar of the Lord. To gather with the assembly of God's people. To walk into church without the burden of unresolved sin, with a good conscience towards God. 

He doesn't do this to be haughty, or to puff up himself in comparison to the wicked, but that he may proclaim the goodness of the Lord in the midst of the congregation, without hypocrisy. 

Meekly seeking God's judgment in our lives that we may be a better testimony is a good thing. Judgment that leads to repentance and forgiveness of others, that we may love the habitation of His house, that we may know how to behave in the church, as a pillar and foundation of truth, is a good thing. 

Asking the Lord to remember us, that we aren't caught up in His judgment of the wicked, but rather walk in our integrity, waiting for His redemption out of His wrath, seeking His mercy in our obedience. 

*My foot standeth in an even place: in the congregations will I bless the LORD.*

This should be our guiding principle. To rightly judge, beginning with ourselves that we may purge ourselves, be separated unto the Lord that we may boldly proclaim His mercy and bless the Lord in the congregation. Amen.

**Romans 4:6–8**
*Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, Saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.*

This positional standing of righteousness before God, despite our sins, through His imputed righteousness is made possible, through the Holy Spirit, by the renewal, the regeneration, the quickening of our spirit. The new man within us. Blessed is the man *in whose spirit there is no guile.* 

We are given the Spirit of truth, that we may acknowledge our sin, knowing that we are forgiven of all sin, first, not by works but by faith.

Rioting in the daytime and being kept up at night by our conscience, being convicted in the Spirit, gives way to the peace that passes understanding, through the forgiveness that is given to us by God's mercy and grace.

While it isn't entirely wrong to take the words transgression, sin and iniquity, and use them interchangeably, they do carry subtle differences in their meaning. 

Transgression is the wilful rebellion against the truth of God and His commands. The transgression of Adam, for example, having one law to obey, and choosing of their own volition (even as Eve was deceived, Adam most assuredly knew better), deciding to be disobedient. 

Sin, which the Bible says is the transgression of the Law, also carries with it the idea of missing the mark, falling short. 

**Romans 3:23**
*For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God*

We aren't able, in the flesh, to hit the mark, the target being the perfect holiness of God. Only Jesus Christ did.

**2 Corinthians 5:21**
*For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.*

Iniquity comes from the Hebrew word, *Avon*, meaning to twist, bend, or distort. The perverted and crooked nature of fallen man. The bent toward evil, the guilt that stays with us, and the perverted character that drives the outward actions. It is the *guile* or deceit mentioned in verse 2.

Our natural tendencies towards willful rebellion, to sin, and to lie to ourselves and others, including God, about the evil that we do. Excusing ourselves with lies. 

Taken together, the blessed assurance that our transgressions, sins and iniquities are eternally forgiven demonstrates the mercy and grace of our Lord towards His children, through the suffering of Jesus. 

**Isaiah 53:5–6**
*But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.*

He suffered these things for our iniquity and transgressions, that we may be purged. That His righteousness be imputed on our ledger, even as His blood blots away our sins. 

Our transgressions are forgiven, our sin is covered, our iniquity will not be added to our account, because we are justified in Christ.

This accounting is a spiritual gift, applied to the ledger that in judgment, we are found not guilty by God. 

(Some call this Penal Substitutionary Atonement, the idea that Jesus paid the price of the debt we owe, so that we do not have to receive the wages of sin. Many reject this idea. Whatever you want to call it, it is undeniable that Christ suffered that those who trust on Him, won't)

On the cross, Jesus carried away our rebellion, covered our failures with His blood, and cleared the ledger of our crooked nature by imputing His own perfect righteousness to us. Past, present and future. That we may be made the righteousness of God.

In the physical Tabernacle and the Temple of Solomon, there were no chairs. A priest could never sit down because his job was never done. The blood of bulls and goats only provided a temporary cover for the *remembrance of sins made again every year*, meaning the priest had to stay on his feet, continuously working, because he could never truly take away sins. 

But then we see Jesus, the author and most importantly, the finisher of our faith, sits down, on the right hand of the Father. 

**Hebrews 10:12–14**
*But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God; From henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool. For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.*

**Psalm 35** is a model of prayer that carries with it both the plea for deliverance, and imprecatory, or negative prayers against enemies who seek our hurt. 

In David's case, we understand that he was falsely accused, had enemies trying to literally kill him and destroy him. 

We may not have the threat against our lives, but we can relate. 

The Lord is our Judge of judges. We go boldly before the throne of grace, asking anything, that we may plead our cause. Asking God to get involved in our lives, to fight our fights. 

We have such an awesome advocate in Christ Jesus and a Father Whose mercy and judgement is righteous and true. It is foolishness not to go before Him in prayer, knowing that He seeks our prosperity. Not the riches and accumulations of things, as the false teachers preach, but our overall benefit and success spiritually, that we may do His will. 

So, of course when we have enemies in this life that seek our hurt, it would be natural that we get God involved. 

*Draw out also the spear, and stop the way against them that persecute me*. That is to form a flank before us, a hedge of protection, like a wall of men, spear extended. A host to shield us from the advances against us. To show us and comfort us with the truth that He is our salvation. 

Let our enemies be confounded and confused. Let them be scattered as the chaff. Let the angel of the Lord be our guardian. His children have guardian angels;

**Hebrews 1:14**
*Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?*

We can call upon Him to give them direction to not only shield us, but it persecute them that seek to do us harm. 

But we shouldn't misunderstand that these ministering spirits are ours to control, or to plea to them. Many pray directly to angels, or archangels, which is wicked. 

**Revelation 22:8–9**
*And I John saw these things, and heard them. And when I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which shewed me these things. Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of them which keep the sayings of this book: worship God.*

We pray, as David did, to the Living God. He directs His hosts. 

The Bible says that false teachers will mislead people into worshiping angels. 

**Colossians 2:18**
*Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind*.

Pray directly to God in all things. Pray for Him to dispatch His angels to defend us and attack our enemies, as David demonstrates here.

Like David, our enemies may seek to trap us, secretly. Digging pits for us to fall into, snares to catch us, to spoil us, taking what is ours, even if it is simply our reputation, and in doing so, ruin our testimony to others. 

If the seek to ruin us in secret, then let the Lord's destruction come upon them without warning. Let their plans come to nothing and better still, catch them up in their own devices. 

*And my soul shall be joyful in the LORD: it shall rejoice in his salvation.*

But, what about *love thy enemies*? 

Notice that David is pleading for their destruction, not only for their acts against him, but because of their false witness and betrayal. 

They rewarded his good with evil. 

When they were sick, he humbled himself in prayer and fasting. He sought intercession for them with the Lord. He shows them love. 

This is what we are to do, what Jesus asked of us. 

**Matthew 5:44**
*But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you*

This seems contradictory, but it's not. When they are weak, or in need, we are to love them. To pray for their healing and to give to them the charity we wish they'd show us. 

We may win them as brothers, or heap hot coals on their heads by our kindness. 

But we do not have any obligations to pray they succeed in the evil they do, and while we should not seek vengeance ourselves, we can leave it to the Judge of all to take up our cause and dispatch justice against them. 

If we behave as a friend or brother, and mourn with them as their mother, and they still choose to persecute us? That's on them. They can rejoice in our pain, gather together to our hurt, but the Lord will see and repay. 

*With hypocritical mockers in feasts, they gnashed upon me with their teeth.*

They may make a feast of our lives, inviting other wicked men to join them, until they seemingly turn the whole world against us, yet we have the Lord. 

**Romans 8:31**
*What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us?*

Pleading with the Lord to not tarry, to come quickly to our aid, with the knowledge that we will sing His praises for His salvation, is a key piece of prayer. 

We have discussed importunity in prayer, asking God again and again to please help us in our time of need. When we are past the point of what we think we can stand, to give us relief. 

We have nothing to give but our love and praise in exchange. 

Some try to bargain with God, usually when we pray amiss, seeking our will rather than His. "I'll go to church more, I will read my Bible more." I will stop this sin or that. We offer sacrifices of our own time or effort or even money. 

But that's not what God seeks. Those are things that are the least we could do, even as unprofitable servants. 

What we do have is praise for His power and His strength. And He is due all the glory. 

*I will give thee thanks in the great congregation: I will praise thee among much people.*

When we bargain with God for what we want, when we add our efforts and barter for His, we give ourselves a means to boast. We can fool ourselves into thinking our works played a part in the outcome. We begin to forget how helpless we were, and how God deserves all the glory. We begin to see our efforts as the reason God "owed it to me" rather than His love and righteousness. 

And so, we may keep asking God for His intervention, and we may remind Him that our gratitude will be expressed to His worship and to show others His strength and power. 

But avoid bargaining or anything that shares the glory with Almighty God. Trust that He loves you and will, in His due time, make whatever it is you are going through to be handled to our good and His will. 

**Romans 8:28**
*And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.*

Pray that our enemies be confounded. That those that do not fear the Lord come to see the bitter end of the wicked. Let man see His wrath on the unrighteous. Let the praise and rejoicing of His people reveal the mercy of God from Heaven. 

*Let them shout for joy, and be glad, that favour my righteous cause: yea, let them say continually, Let the LORD be magnified, which hath pleasure in the prosperity of his servant. And my tongue shall speak of thy righteousness and of thy praise all the day long.* Amen

Paul writes in **Philippians 4:6**
*Be careful for nothing*... We are commanded not to fear and anxiety over potential persecution is a sin. We are told here to *fret not because of evildoers*. 

The courage we are expected to show as Christians isn't based on our own efforts or strength, it is based on the power of our God. And consider the next stanza of the opening verse, *neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity.*

We will see that they have their rewards, our inheritance is to be preserved in this life from hunger and taken care of with our basic needs. The meek shall inherit the earth, while the workers of iniquity shall be destroyed and their seed cut off. 

We may understand that evil loses in the end, and we have already overcome the world. Faith in this truth should lift us up. 

But more, these two concepts go together in a physiological truth. God has built us in a way that makes our gratitude for what we have the source for being less anxious. 

This isn't just a "Hey, don't worry and don't envy the wicked, it's gonna work out" platitude. 

Science shows that gratitude, being satisfied and thankful for what you have decreases activity in the amygdala, which is the part of the brain that triggers fear, panic, and stress. It moves our bodies away from the fearful "fight-or-flight" mode and into the "rest-and-digest" mode. 

It is impossible for those that are truly grateful to God for their station in life, their economic conditions, the blessings He has given us, and the protection of His mighty hand, to fret. To feel anxiety. To fear. 

Practicing thankfulness boosts dopamine and serotonin, which naturally lower stress hormones like cortisol.

Our brain struggles to focus on threat-detection (anxiety) and present-moment safety (gratitude) at the same time.

**Philippians 4:6** continues, ...*but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.* 

Science once again catches up with the truth God has given us in His word. 

And so, when we are commanded to not be envious of evildoers, and given reasons to be thankful, God is giving us the means to not fret. 

Gratitude for all He does, being satisfied and knowing how to be abased and abound, naturally makes us less anxious. To fear not.

Continuing in **Psalm 37**, God promises that the wicked shall be cut down like grass, while those that trust in the Lord and do good shall dwell in the land and be fed.

People are judged by faith. Nations are judged by Christians' works.

**Genesis 4:13**

David, who in **Psalm 32** sang of the blessedness of the man whose sins are forgiven, covered and not imputed against them, is now singing of the wounds, failing strength, bitter loneliness as a result of his actions. Abandoned and betrayed.

The difference between worldly sorrow that works death versus godly sorrow that works repentance to salvation, being delivered from the scourging, the ancillary consequences and from the scorners and those that plot mischief, taking advantage of our broken and contrite state.

*I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit.*

James, the brother of Christ, writes of the importance of this in his epistle.

God has blessed us with the conviction of the Spirit, that even in the miry pit, we heard Him, and see with our eyes the mighty God, being converted and healed. Calling upon the name of the Lord. 

**Romans 10:13**
*For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.*

Continuing in **Psalm 40**, rejoicing that God has given men ears to hear the truth, and the glory to God for His protection and comfort, we are called to spread this word, proclaiming it to all men. 

We are delighted to do His will. His law written in our hearts. 

**Romans 7:22**
*For I delight in the law of God after the inward man*

Even as our flesh may be prone to wonder, the outward man waging war against the spirit, we can know His righteous paths, and preach them among the beloved believers. Declaring His faithfulness and the salvation of the Lord to all who will hear. Singing His praises, letting His light shine through us, magnifying His glory. Proclaiming His great Gospel.

Having acknowledged all He has done for us, and encouraging ourselves and others to turn to Him for salvation through the blessing of the Lord, David's Psalm turns introspective. He confesses the sin that has beset him, and compasses him about with the repercussions of it. 

*Withhold not thou thy tender mercies from me, O LORD: let thy lovingkindness and thy truth continually preserve me. For innumerable evils have compassed me about: mine iniquities have taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up; they are more than the hairs of mine head: therefore my heart faileth me.*

Just as David and Paul write of having the law written in their heart, and delighting in His word, they both lament the sinful flesh that requires a Savior.

*O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin.*

That God use us to shame those that wish to do us evil, to His glory. 

Praise, thanksgiving, confession, deliverance, and destruction of those who hold the truth in unrighteousness. This is a model of prayer. That His will be done on earth as it is in Heaven. 

And in the end, the joy of His salvation overwhelming us with gratitude and praise, that such a holy and Almighty God takes heed of our prayers and notices us. Loving us so much, while we are yet sinners. Thinking of us. Providing for us. Delivering us. 

*Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: let such as love thy salvation say continually, The LORD be magnified. But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me: thou art my help and my deliverer; make no tarrying, O my God.* Amen
