In **Ecclesiastes 1**, Solomon established his underlying idea, that all of life is vain, meaningless, full of travails, trials and hardships, that every life is full of tribulation, a cycle of never-ending labor. Now, the preacher begins to expound. 

He starts chapter 2 by explaining how he, to test all things, gave in to the pleasures of the heart; mirth, laughter. Wine and merrymaking. Partying, as we would say today. And he found it wanting. 

He continued in wisdom, while allowing himself folly, testing all things to see what was good that man should do. A scientific approach that rationalizes sin in the name of gained knowledge. Solomon, a King gifted with supernatural wisdom sought pleasures for a season, to prove wisdom. Yet, this approach to life is honestly all too typical for man. 

We sow our wild oats. We all have our time of life where we question the wisdom of our parents, the law and ways of God, the judgment of our conscience, to see what good can be found in the ways of the world. And, for most of us, we grow out of it. God's chastening and the reality of the wages of sin, bringing us back from folly, to see these things as vain. Ineffectual and worthless.

Wisdom teaches better, but folly is doing what you know you shouldn't, and expecting a better result than doing the right thing. Reality is a harsh tutor, and when it comes to the party lifestyle, you don't have to be the wisest man ever to live to see it is folly. 

Yet many fools continue to chase after mirth, drunken merrymaking, long after it has cost them everything and brutally affected the lives of those around them.

Solomon then talks of the great works he undertook, to redeem the time in more constructive ways. Building houses, planting vineyards, gardens and orchards and every kind of budding fruit trees. He made pools of water to irrigate his great gardens. 

He had many servants, even generational, born in his house, all to staff his households and agricultural enterprises. He owned much cattle, great and small, livestock more than any other before him. 

The accumulation of wealth, the peculiar treasures of kings, unique offerings and crafts made of precious stones. He gathered unto himself silver and gold in abundance. 

The description of Solomon's possessions, the magnitude of his wealth, seem at first blush to be beyond our ability to understand or relate to. But, within these pursuits we should find familiarity. 

We all seek to build out our home. We plant our gardens, both literally and metaphorically, utilizing what we have to build something more. We all have projects and plans we devote time and resources to. We may lack servants and palaces and peculiar riches, but we all strive to have more. 

Solomon used his position to have multiple singers, male and female, musicians and the delight of music to entertain him. Again, we may see this and think, "he is a king, of course he can command this, I can't relate." But today, even the most poor among us has instant access to the greatest singers and musicians of the past century, to listen to the delights of the sons of men greater than even Solomon at his height could ever hear. 

The Preacher says *So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me.*

And in that wisdom, these pursuits, as cyclical and vain as they were, did produce joy. He says he *withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced in all my labour: and this was my portion of all my labour.* The brief moments of joy all of this brought him, he considered his reward. 

But, beyond the temporary rejoicing, he perceived the underlying problem; death. 

Looking at all he worked for, all he gained, and the fruit of that labor, and he sees the same end as the mirth and laughter. 

...*behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.*

All the things that man could do, under the Sun, had been done before. Even by a King who could do more, and more abundantly than any other man, and it was all in vain, without lasting meaning. Even his son, Rehoboam would be unable to achieve anything new; Solomon had exhausted the most extreme versions of all that existed and was known to man under the Sun. But his wisdom remained;

*Then I saw that wisdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness. The wise man's eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all.* Death.

The end comes for the fool and the wise alike. And the depressin*g* notion came to him, thinking, *As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me; and why was I then more wise? Then I said in my heart, that this also is vanity.*

What good is wisdom, if like the pleasures and labors of life, it all ends in vanity? What good is the pursuit of discernment and knowledge, to know the ways of the world and gather wisdom from experiencing all that life has to offer, if in the end it dies with you, as the folly of a fool dies with him?

If this is all that life has, if the meaning of it is to toil, travail, and then die, then all is vanity and vexation of spirit. Solomon says he hated the vanity of life, hated all his worthless labor, which in the end would be left to an heir who may or may not value it, who may or may not be wise, or a fool, and squander whatever inheritance there may be. The projects and planning and pleasures, and treasure and toil, all are vanity.

The works of wisdom and in knowledge and equity, fair dealings and not being a respecter of persons, the wisdom we saw again and again in **Proverbs**, is the same portion as those that did not pursue wisdom. *This also is vanity and a great evil.*

*This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God.*

The Preacher is building a case, and the answer to vanity and vexation of spirit, and we see here the first hint of what the answer is, by the grace of God towards the just.

Solomon reasons, *If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years be many, and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he.*

**Ecclesiastes 7** is the true beginning of the culmination of the Preacher's sermon, where the wisdom gained by observation of all things under the Sun, and the ways of man and God, leads Solomon to many conclusions regarding life. 

It is deep, and full of truth that is both particular to King Solomon, and broadly applicable to all people.

In chapter 6, Solomon compared the relative benefit of the stillborn over the man of toil, who lived long and labored much, but enjoyed none of the fruits of his hands. This was to add to his argument that the blessings of God towards us, that while we are cursed through Adam to travails, God's mercy is that we get to enjoy the results. 

He made the case that it is better to walk upright, and gain increase through the blessings of God, than to seek wealth greedily. To be wise rather than a fool. Because ultimately, the sluggard and the foolish gain little, and see what little they have given to others. 

Here, in chapter 7, Solomon posits a different argument; that the end is better than the beginning. That the day of death, for some, is better than their birth. That *a good name is better than precious ointment.* People will remember you in a better light than the fool. 

He says, *It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart.*

Our time with death better prepares us for life. We can appreciate the mirth and feasting all the more, having an appreciation for the end that comes to all of us. Sorrow heals us, more than vain laughter. The wise go into the house of mourning, giving comfort to the broken hearted, and taking from the truth of death, seek more of God and eternity. 

The fool seeks pleasure, and forgoes the pain that brings experience. They sing songs of shallow happiness, like the crackling of thorns, green briars used to kindle, and their laughter is vexing to the wise.

*Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad; and a gift destroyeth the heart.* 

This aside, noting that under stress and oppression a wise man may be driven to madness and in wrath, commit sin, or by bribery, brought to do wrong, sets up a subtle transition. 

Testing his thesis, the idea that the end is better than the beginning, Solomon notes the human limits of wisdom and righteousness. Things which may make it appear that all things under the Sun grow progressively worse. 

The proverb of v9-10 warns against the tendency to see things this way; *Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools.* *Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this.*

This tendency, especially among the righteous who walk in the ways of God as much as lies within them, is a snare. It leads to sin that we are all guilty of at times. 

"Make America Great, Again," and calls to RETVRN! and other appeals to the "better days" of the past prey upon the inclination to see the former days as better, especially given the evil we see all around us. For we all feel like Lot at times. 

**2 Peter 2:7-8**
*And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: (For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;)*

But coveting the past takes us away from doing what we are supposed to in the present. 

There is no political solution to a spiritual problem. Revival is a continuous process. The need for revival is never greater than now. No matter when "now" is. 

To enquirer wisely, it is better to ask God to straighten that which He has made crooked. To seek God to make the hardships given to teach us wisdom worthwhile. Rather than curse that things are the way they are, which is vanity. 

If we seek His wisdom from adversity, we gain. We gain understanding and, by our diligence in tribulation, wealth. And both serve as an inheritance to our children, a defense, Solomon writes. It is profitable to our future to redeem the time in the present, rather than getting angry about a past we cannot change. 

The excellency of knowledge is the wisdom that giveth life. This is what we should consider. Giving to our children the understanding of God. 

Solomon reiterates the understanding that we should rejoice in the good days, for the prosperity God grants, while also considering that God gives adversity as well, and for our own good. He sets the two against each other, that we find nothing after Him.

Continuing in **Ecclesiastes 7**, where Solomon the Preacher has built upon the truth that the toil and tribulation of life is vain and vexing, his observation that despite this, God has blessed men to enjoy the fruits of that labor. He has shown that it is better to be reminded of the short span man's life is, that death comes for us all, wise or fool, rich or poor. 

That, despite the seeming vanity of life, the pointlessness of endless striving, that the blessing of God makes it bearable and that this blessing comes on the righteous and the wise, while the foolish and froward, greedy and lazy see their efforts come to nothing in the end. 

And so, picking up in v15, the Preacher concedes that he has seen the wicked prosper and the righteous perish. That there are other factors that determine the outcome. That the just man may see a short life, while the unrighteous may prolong their time under the Sun. 

But generally speaking, the just and wise are blessed more than the fool and the wicked.

From this he argues temperance, and against self-righteous displays of piety, or becoming self-important in your wisdom. Why tempt God? And don't be wicked or foolish, because again, God will repay. 

It isn't the appearance that brings life, but the genuine fear of God. The key understanding is sincere and humble respect for the Lord. The rest takes care of itself.

The strength of wisdom is true, and can be relied on, but the truth of the matter is we all fall short. For all have sinned. 

v20 *For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not.*

This wisdom is the foundation of the gospel. We are all sinners before a holy God. So even in appearance of righteousness, we have sin. Even in the strength of wisdom, we've all done foolishly. Thus, what the Lord decides is just, is just. 

It is hypocrisy to think more of ourselves than we should. An honest inventory, examining ourselves as we are instructed to do, reveals that we too have fallen short. 

We have cursed others. We have held hatred in our hearts. We have dealt unfairly, the iniquity we see in the wicked has had a home in our hearts. 

Fear of God humbles us to know our own heart. Acknowledging this truth of ourselves, the course of the wicked and the just, revealed by the wrath of God from heaven, and His mercy and longsuffering towards us, we should humbly seek His grace.

Finishing up on **Ecclesiastes 7**, the Preacher explains that, even as he proved his argument from wisdom, and sought understanding, there are still things he fails to know.

That man's labors are endless, the travails of life grinding, that death comes for us all. He has learned that God blesses man to enjoy what we have, but that seeking much increase leads to more trouble. Not necessarily more blessings. 

He has found that the lazy, unjust and wicked receive His wrath in due time, but even the just man may come to an early end, while the wicked continues on. That the lessons learned in mourning, the inevitable death of all men, are more valuable than the mirth and enjoyment of our labors. 

He has sought wisdom and been given understanding from God that all have sinned and fallen short of His glory. That even as we judge the fool and the iniquity of others, waiting for their recompense and fall, we have our own account of sin. That judgement comes for us all.

The preaching of Solomon continues. He has considered all things under the sun, mirth and madness. Labor and travail.  The vanity of life. 

He has sought the wisdom of God, and come away with fear, that the ways of the Lord are past finding out. That the only thing that makes a life of vanity worthwhile are those things God has blessed us with. 

The righteous and the wise and their works are of God. Our understanding comes from Him. We who walk in faith are in His hands.

But the fact of death is inevitable, and to every man the same event comes. To the righteous and clean, to the wicked and unclean. *As is the good, so is the sinner.* 

Only God is good, as Jesus tells us. And so any righteousness we have is His. Ours is as filthy rags, the Bible says. Our works that aren't built upon Christ are wood, hay and stubble. Fit to be burned and remembered no more. Only the silver, gold and precious stones, refined by fire, will remain. 

Solomon laments this truth. That the wickedness and evil of a man's heart dies with him. That *the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten.*

The things that last, are from God. Our children will live out their life of vanity. The inheritance we leave them will eventually be gone and forgotten. 

But the good works done for the Lord will last, and be rewarded. And those works, especially leading others to Christ, will ripple throughout time. 

The Bible says in **Hebrews 9:27** 
*And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment.*

The righteous and the wicked alike are judged by a holy and just God. 

**Romans 14:12**
*So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.*

For the unsaved, this judgment occurs at the great White Throne of God, where the dead are judged against the books of the law, and cast into the lake of fire, which is the second death. But for the saved, clothed in the righteousness of Christ, we are judged by Jesus, for reward. 

**1 Corinthians 3:10-15**
*According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon. After we die, there is no more chance to get right. No more opportunities to seek the grace of God. No more works we can do to earn reward. No more memory of our life's wood, hay and stubble. Our love, hatred and envy will perish. There is no more portion to be blessed with for our labors. 

So live your life to the fullest with eternity in mind. Life is but a vapor, our time is short. Redeem the time. Set your heart on the treasure above. 

 *Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart; for God now accepteth thy works. Let thy garments be always white; and let thy head lack no ointment.*

Solomon's preaching on the vanity of life leads us inevitably to consider the works done for the Lord, which are never in vain. 

**1 Corinthians 15:58**
 *Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.*

We have to understand that the preacher is appealing to the life of man, which is short and brutal. But spiritually, those that are wise fear the Lord. And those works that we do have lasting impact. And the rewards we receive, they are blessings from God. 

We only know love because He so loved us. 

**1 John 4:7-8** 
*Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God.He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.*

We know a wife is a gift from God. We know the fruit of our labors in being able to enjoy it comes from Him. We know the sweet things of life, to eat, drink and be merry, is of God. 

All good things are of God. And it's okay to enjoy those things. They are a gift. They are examples of His grace. 

*Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which he hath given thee under the sun, all the days of thy vanity: for that is thy portion in this life, and in thy labour which thou takest under the sun. Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.*

The Preacher, having established the goodness of the portion we receive in this life, that it is from God and should be enjoyed, continues to bring sobering truth to the purpose of life.

*The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.*

There are things beyond our control. The swift and strong do not always persevere. Wealth and sustenance don't always go to the wise and understanding. Skill isn't a guarantee. Time and chance, opportunity and luck, play a role in the outcome. Just as the traps and snares of men catch the unlucky fish or fowl, a man may be taken out before his time. He may lose everything including his life to chance. Bad luck. It rains on the just and unjust alike. 

He gives a parable of a little city with few men delivered out of the hand of a great king and his siege of it by the wisdom of a poor man, forgotten afterwards despite it. Wisdom is ultimately despised, despite being greater than strength. People remember the mighty men and often remember foolish men, far after the memory of the wise has faded. 

Wisdom is better than weapons of war, and yet men place their trust in chariots and swords. A lowly wise man may save a city, but a single sinner can destroy more than the wise saves. 

The impact we have in this life may not reflect in our monetary situation, or our glory among men, or in lasting memory after we die. Time and chance may take us out. But better to be wise than not, either way. Wisdom is its own reward and the desire of the Lord for us. Fear Him and in all thy ways acknowledge Him, and He shall direct thy paths.

Chapter 10 sees a familiar format, where the wise Preacher goes down some rabbit-trails with proverbs. We've obviously seen some scattered throughout the book, and so it isn't surprising. Holy men moved by the Spirit gave utterance to truth, because the word of God *is* truth. 

Vs 1, continues from the final verse of **Ecclesiastes 9:18**, that wisdom is better than weapons, but one sinner destroys much good. Here, Solomon compares how one dead fly ruins a sweet savoy ointment, the same as a little folly ruins a wise man's reputation. 

Recall **Ecclesiastes 7:1** *A good name is better than precious ointment.*..

It is difficult to build a good reputation, it takes time, understanding; walking in the fear of the Lord. And it can all be thrown away by one act of sin. Think of all the great preachers brought low by their sin. (And as children of God, when we sin in secret without repentance, one of the ways God will chasten you is to make sure your sin is found out)

David, a man after God's own heart, sinned greatly in secret, but Nathan reminded him that the Lord knew, and so David suffered for his sin. 

We always talk about Solomon's wisdom, but temper it with the understanding that he was backslidden and allowed his strange wives to worship false gods. Of course He knew better and believed the truth, but he succumbed to the same temptation as Adam. Pleasing the wife, rather than God. 

It is a sobering reminder that our heart is in our hands. Wise man's heart is in his right, but the fool's is in treachery, in his left. And a wise man can become a fool in a single act. 

And when a fool walks in his way, his folly will always reveal itself to others. In deed or in word, it becomes obvious that they are fools. 

Vs 4, he transitions to a Biblical truth, that if a ruler comes against you, justly or unjustly, it is better to yield than to flee or fight. We see it time and again, the greatest example being Jesus of course. But the apostles who willingly went to judgment to further the cause of Christ, even in death. We see it in the Old Testament where Jeremiah warns the people of Judah to stay put and trust the Lord. Those that fled to Egypt were slain in the way. Those that rebelled were put down. We see the example of Daniel and his friends, Joseph in Egypt, 

David while being pursued by Saul, had opportunity to kill the king, and refused and continued to appeal to his reason. 

Vs5-7 Solomon recalls an evil he has witnessed where rulers give honor to fools, and treat servants as princes. While we are not to be respecters of persons, we shouldn't give dignity to full of foolishness or rebellion. 

Tying vs 4 with 5-7, I can't help but think of Mordechai from the book of **Esther**. Where rather than yield to the king's prince, Haman, he continued to disrespect him...even as the plot to kill the Jews was known to him. 

Jesus says in **Matthew 5:25**
*Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison.*

We are to give honor and tribute to whom it is due. The entire affair that led to the slaughter of 75,000 people could have been avoided by simply and meekly apologizing, and bowing. 

And the King put Mordecai on a horse, and rewarded him, despite his unwillingness to yield to authority. Haman reacted with evil, but there are no good guys in the story. 

Vs 8 and 9 reflect the understanding that we saw in **Proverbs**; that treachery and iniquity will come back to bite you. It echoes the proverbs against moving landmarks, or setting traps for others, that God's justice will see to it that you will receive the recompense for the evil you do to others. 

He then compares wisdom to the sharpening of a blade, noting the dull blade makes work harder. Wisdom sharpens, making work easier. And we can make each other wiser, sharper, with advice and counsel. 

**Proverbs 27:17**
*Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.*

Of course the sharpest sword is the word of God.

**Hebrews 4:12**
*For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.*

For wisdom and spiritual things, there is no greater tool than the Bible.

**Ecclesiastes 10** continues with Solomon's proverbs against the fool. He repeats the theme from his broader book of Proverbs. That a fool's lips, his words, lead to his own destruction. They begin with foolish nonsense and end in *mischievous madness.* The further from obeying wisdom a fool gets, the greater their distance from God's path, we see that their folly becomes insanity. 

We witness this today, where the foolishness and abomination of allowing sodomites led to they/them pronouns and transvestites being held up as role models. When there is no bulwark of truth from fear of the Lord, then evil runs rampant. 

The fool is full of words, bold predictions based on their own inane blabbering, while they don't consider the likely consequences of their actions. If a normal man is already blind to the future, who can tell the fool? The humility to know you can't control the future is lost to him. 

Even the work of the fool is tiresome. They don't have common sense. The city would have broad ways towards it and normal people have a clear understanding of how to get there. These fools can't see the obvious path before them. We have cruder terms about not knowing one body part from another.

The Preacher preaches woe to the land ruled by children, where judgment is deferred for their own bellies, their own selfish interests. But, being under a king raised to rule, who understands judgment, is a blessing. Where the leadership delays their own gratification to do right by the people, and feasts for strength, not drunkenness. 

*By much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through*. It takes work to maintain anything. Especially a home or other building. But it is the laziness of man that sees it decay. 

*A feast is made for laughter, and wine maketh merry: but money answereth all things.* The appropriate thing for the appropriate thing, but at the end of the day it is money that solves the problem, moves the man, satisfies an accuser, and gets things done. 

Finally, Solomon warns against gossip and backbiting, especially against the king. "A little bird told me..." The things we think we say in secret and in confidence have a way of getting back to those we are cursing in secret. Even in our own thoughts. 

The rabbit trails of King Solomon's sermon continue into chapter 11, as he comes to the end of his preaching on the vanity and vexation of life. The benefit of Wisdom, and seeking the blessings of God.

The Preacher, Solomon, is beginning to wrap up his homily. He has built his case, that while life is vain, and full of vexing things, toil and tribulation, that God blesses us to enjoy the fruits of our labor. And that God blesses the wise and prudent more than the wicked and fools. 

The chapter begins with an appeal to generosity. Casting your bread on the waters. Giving liberally to others, and guarding against an uncertain future. It will return to you in like measure. And you can't take it with you. Who knows what tomorrow may bring?

Whatever will be will be. If the clouds bring rain, or a tree falls in the forest with no one to see, it still is what it is. And so is life. Natural events occur without our ability to predict or change. 

**James 4:13-15**

We should then make the most of it, and God willing, enjoy the blessings He provides with thanksgiving. Hospitality. Generosity. Charity towards all, regardless of the conditions we find ourselves in. 

Don't wait for a perfect opportunity to do right and live well. *He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.* Take what you are given and act. 

We don't understand the miracle of life, the ways of God, let alone the ideal circumstances for our best laid plans. Remember, time and chance happen to us all. Death comes for us all.

Spiritually, this includes the seed that is the word, and laying up treasure in Heaven. Be ready at any opportunity to give the gospel. 

**Isaiah 55:11**
*So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.*

The light is sweet. We glory in the sun. The warmth of Summer. The time of sowing. The joy of our lives is like a sunny day. It is welcome and refreshing, but we should remember the darkness, the Preacher says; *for they shall be many.*

In every life, there are periods of darkness. There are more winter days, and cloudy days than there are joyous ones. *All that cometh is vanity*. 

Keeping this perspective in mind makes the sunny, joyous days more precious. We tend to lose sight of this perspective, especially in our youth. When time seems abundant and the promise of tomorrow makes the cares of today seem insignificant. 

Solomon says to the young; enjoy it now. Be cheerful. Let your heart be merry, and walk in your ways, but, he cautions, know that for all that we do, God will bring us to judgment. 

Youth is vanity. It is fleeting, like beauty on a woman or the warm sunny days of Summer. 

What we sow comes back to us. Be it charity or God's word, or our sin. The blessings of God upon us is all that makes the vanity of life worthwhile. 

*Therefore remove sorrow from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh: for childhood and youth are vanity.*

Before the day of the Lord.

The preacher is wise. The wisest man in history, filled with the Spirit of God to know things and the time and treasure to consider all the ways of man under the Sun. **Hebrews 9:27**
*And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment*

*For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known and come abroad.*

Vanity, vanity, all is vanity. But faith in the Lord, fearing Him only and keeping His ways and wisdom, in all our ways acknowledging Him that He may direct our paths...this is the secret to life. 

As Jesus says in **John 10:10** *...I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.*

With this, the sermon ends. The matter is settled. Life is a gift from God, and an abundant life is in service of Him. The true meaning of it all is to give Him glory. Our purpose is to be known of Him that we may know Christ. 

Amen

**Song of Solomon 1**
*1  The song of songs, which is Solomon’s.*

*2  Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine.*

*3  Because of the savour of thy good ointments thy name is as ointment poured forth, therefore do the virgins love thee.*

*4  Draw me, we will run after thee: the king hath brought me into his chambers: we will be glad and rejoice in thee, we will remember thy love more than wine: the upright love thee.*

*5  I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon.*

*6  Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me: my mother’s children were angry with me; they made me the keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept.*

*7  Tell me, O thou whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest, where thou makest thy flock to rest at noon: for why should I be as one that turneth aside by the flocks of thy companions?*

*8  If thou know not, O thou fairest among women, go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock, and feed thy kids beside the shepherds’ tents.*

*9  I have compared thee, O my love, to a company of horses in Pharaoh’s chariots.*

*10  Thy cheeks are comely with rows of jewels, thy neck with chains of gold.*

*11  We will make thee borders of gold with studs of silver.*

*12  While the king sitteth at his table, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof.*

*13  A bundle of myrrh is my well-beloved unto me; he shall lie all night betwixt my breasts.*

*14  My beloved is unto me as a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi.*

*15  Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; thou hast doves’ eyes.*

*16  Behold, thou art fair, my beloved, yea, pleasant: also our bed is green.*

*17  The beams of our house are cedar, and our rafters of fir.*

We are in the penultimate book of the Bible for the purposes of my goal to write out studies of every book of the Bible. Only Song of Songs and Psalms remain. 

Here in the first chapter of Solomon's ode to his love, we can observe why it is in scripture; the clear allegory of Christ and His beloved, the saved. 

The poetic language used, going back and forth between the woman and the man, is beautiful prose in itself. Begging for kisses from one whose love is better than wine. Whose savour is as good ointments. 

The use of ointment and fine, perfumed oils as a representation of the Spirit, is found throughout the Bible. Her saying that even the king's name is as an ointment poured forth, that the virgins, or the innocent ladies in wait, do love him. Just as the righteous in Christ love even the name of Jesus. 

She says to draw them, the damsels, to call them. And they will run after him. Just as the Spirit calls us, as a sweet savour to those that seek Him, calls us, and we willingly respond. *We will be glad and rejoice in thee, we will remember thy love more than wine: the upright love thee.*

The upright, like virgin, indicates the quality of the saved. We are the righteousness of God. We have Jesus imputed righteousness upon us and a new man within, making us as virgins in His eyes. The forgiveness of the Father. We are upright because He is upright, and we are His. 

 *I am black, but comely*...the woman isn't referring to race here, but the darkness of her skin from the sun. Her mother's children were angry with her, forcing her to keep their vineyards and to feed the sheep. 

But the blackness is also sin, what it does to our heart. And the daughters are unbelieving Israel. They who persecuted the prophets and would crucify Christ. The world hates believers, because of His love for us. That despite our sin and being made their servants to do the work of the field, He so loves us. 

The bride, having spoken of her love, and having told the daughters of Jerusalem her unworthiness, and having sought to find the king, hears back from him. 

She seeks out his flocks, to be with him, and Solomon responds to her in verse 8. *If thou know not, O thou fairest among women, go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock, and feed thy kids beside the shepherds’ tents.*

He praises her, after her own shameful confession. She calls herself black from the work of being a servant. He calls her most fair among women. This is how Christ views His own.

Solomon says, follow the footsteps of the flock. Find the shepherds. We are Jesus' sheep. He is our Good Shepherd. We may find Him where the other sheep are, and follow in their footsteps that we may know Him. 

Solomon goes on to describe his beloved in epic terms, and the chorus of the daughters of Jerusalem tells of how they will dress her in fine jewels and ornaments of fine gold and silver as the King's desire. Where before the children of Israel had despised her, the fair daughters of Jerusalem follow the lead of the King, and honor who he has chosen. 

Verse 12 sees the woman at the King's table. In his court. The spiced wine calls him. She compares her attraction to him as the pleasant smell of myrrh, and her desire is for him to lay upon her bosom all night. 

He is like a cluster of henna flowers, or *camphire*, alluring, heavily scented clusters of small white and yellow flowers used as perfume. 

She longs for him, his eyes like a doves. Their bed green. The beams cedar and rafters fir. The finest materials build their house, and she wishes to live with him forever.

**Song of Solomon 2**
*1  I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys.*

*2  As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.*

*3  As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.*

*4  He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.*

*5  Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love.*

*6  His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.*

*7  I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.*

*8  The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills.*

*9  My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice.*

*10  My beloved spake, and said unto me, Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away.*

*11  For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone;*

*12  The flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our land;*

*13  The fig tree putteth forth her green figs, and the vines with the tender grape give a good smell. Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away.*

*14  O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.*

*15  Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes.*

*16  My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.*

*17  Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, turn, my beloved, and be thou like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bether*.

Chapter 2 contains a poetic back and forth dialogue between the woman and the man, the rose of Sharon and her beloved, an apple tree among the trees of the wood. He compares other women to thorns, but she is a lily, a beautiful flower among them.

The woman delights in his shade, his protection, and in his fruit, which is sweet to her taste. He calls her to his banquet, under the banner of love. 

Again, we see the gospel. He is the tree of life, over a precious flower among the thorns. Invited to the banquet house of the Lord. The wedding supper of the Lamb. 

She is overcome by his love, she longs for him as we long for Jesus, and His embrace in that great day of redemption. 

 *I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.*

The timing of the Lord's return is at God's pleasure. Just as she waits for her love to awake, we patiently wait for Him to return. 

The roes, the hinds of the field are the wild deer that play in the pastures and roam the hills and mountains. 

She hears the voice of her beloved, and compares him to the roebuck leaping and skipping on mountains and hills. She sees him through the lattice of the window, just beyond her walls, and he speaks to her, calling her to rise up and come with him. 

This pictures the return of Christ, gathering the elect from the four corners of the world. Jesus descends with a shout. We who are His hear His voice, and Rise up, and come away with Him. 

*For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone;* it is spring. The rains fall and the flowers burst forth, and a time of peace is at hand. The signs of the season are showing. The fig tree puts forth her green figs. 

**Matthew 24:32–33**
*Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When his branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is nigh: So likewise ye, when ye shall see all these things, know that it is near, even at the doors.*

She begs to see her love, he is among the clefts of the rock, the stairs of the mountains, as a dove, his face is upon those that take shelter from His wrath there. They fear him. But she longs to see him. 

**Revelation 6:15–17**
*And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?*

*Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes.* The wrath is upon these "little foxes," the wicked, those that spoil and corrupt the tender grapes. The wicked that seek to destroy the believers, especially during the great tribulation. 

Her certainty of their love, that he is hers and she is his, even as he waits for his time, reflects the eternal security we have as believers in Christ. Waiting patiently for His return, when the day breaks and the shadows flee the light.

**Song of Solomon 3**
*1  By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.*

*2  I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.*

*3  The watchmen that go about the city found me: to whom I said, Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?*

*4  It was but a little that I passed from them, but I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me.*

*5  I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.*

*6  Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all powders of the merchant?*

*7  Behold his bed, which is Solomon’s; threescore valiant men are about it, of the valiant of Israel.*

*8  They all hold swords, being expert in war: every man hath his sword upon his thigh because of fear in the night.*

*9  King Solomon made himself a chariot of the wood of Lebanon.*

*10  He made the pillars thereof of silver, the bottom thereof of gold, the covering of it of purple, the midst thereof being paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem.*

*11  Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals, and in the day of the gladness of his heart.*

Chapter 3 begins with the woman waking to a desolate bed, unable to find her beloved. Seeking him, she desperately searches in the night, throughout the city streets. She repeats the refrain that she *sought him, but I found him not.* 

She then encounters the night watch, and enquires of them if they had seen *him, whom my soul loveth.*

This passage beautifully reflects the death of Christ, picturing the panicked feeling of believers at His death, and at the empty tomb. The watchmen, the religious leaders who crucified Him, unable to give an answer, but then, in her search, she finds him. *Him whom my soul loveth.* 

And she holds him and will not let him go, bringing him into her mother's house, even to the bed chamber she was conceived in. As Jesus comes into us, and is held in the most intimate chamber of our hearts. 

For the second time in the song, the chorus in verse 5, also found in chapter 2:7 is repeated:

*I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please*. 

It is repeated again in chapter 8, and the verse is used as transition in the structure of the song. 

While it may picture the current time, where we wait for our beloved, the Lord Jesus to return, it also serves as an oath, asking the daughters of Jerusalem to swear by the roes and hinds, the graceful and skittish deer of the land, to not stir the Beloved too early. To let him sleep as late as he pleases. 

The immediate application speaks to the delicate nature of love, especially in its earliest stages, where you almost feel a surreal and magical experience and are afraid it could burst like a bubble at any time. You don't want to lose that joyous state. You don't want it to be disturbed, like the gazelles of the mountains startled at a sudden movement or sound. 

She has found her beloved and taken him into her heart, and wants that joy of her salvation to last. 

The chorus serves to transition the narrative to an epic description of the King, and his entourage, emerging from the wilderness like pillars of smoke, an endless caravan. Perfumed and decked out in fine clothes for the wedding. 

This pictures the return of Christ, after the wrath, on a white horse with ten thousands of His saints, wearing their wedding clothes, prepared for the marriage supper of the Lamb. 

The bed of the King, his chariot, surrounded by threescore valiant men, the valiant of Israel. The soldiers with swords at their hip, like the prophets armed with the word of God. 

King Solomon's chariot, made of the finest wood, decked in silver and gold, covered in royal purple, and as it goes, *paved with love*, *for the daughters of Jerusalem*. This is the interior of the royal chariot, embroidery made by the daughters of the land with love, the inner bed, where the King and his bride would recline. 

The purity of God in the silver pillars, His grace, the gold that surrounds us. The purple of His majesty as Lord, and the interior, the soft comfort of His love for us. 

The bride of the song calls out for the daughters of Zion, Jerusalem, to go out and welcome the King. To examine his wedding crown, to celebrate the betrothal and his gladness. The tradition of the people is that the mother of the bridegroom crafts a crown to celebrate the nuptials. Not a crown of royalty, but of love. 

In **Revelation 19:12**, as Christ rides forth to claim ultimate victory and gather His people, the text says, *on his head were many crowns*. 

The crowns of Christ at His triumphant arrival to meet the descending New Jerusalem, adorned as a bride, are the diadem of His love for His beloved, just as Solomon's love for his bride. 

As John writes in *Revelation 21:2*: 
*And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.*

The allegory and picture of the King of Kings arriving at His wedding feast, at the culmination of history, to usher in His millennial Kingdom, reflected in the prophetic love song written by Solomon.

**Song of Solomon 4**
*1  Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; thou hast doves’ eyes within thy locks: thy hair is as a flock of goats, that appear from mount Gilead.*

*2  Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep that are even shorn, which came up from the washing; whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them.*

*3  Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, and thy speech is comely: thy temples are like a piece of a pomegranate within thy locks.*

*4  Thy neck is like the tower of David builded for an armoury, whereon there hang a thousand bucklers, all shields of mighty men.*

*5  Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins, which feed among the lilies.*

*6  Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, I will get me to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense.*

*7  Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.*

*8  Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions’ dens, from the mountains of the leopards.*

*9  Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck.*

*10  How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices!*

*11  Thy lips, O my spouse, drop as the honeycomb: honey and milk are under thy tongue; and the smell of thy garments is like the smell of Lebanon.*

*12  A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed.*

*13  Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard,*

*14  Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:*

*15  A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon.*

*16  Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out. Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits.*

Chapter 4 opens with an ode to the beloved bride by her lover, the bridegroom. When he looks upon her he sees her fair beauty, her eyes as doves', her hair as the flocks of wild mountain goats. Picturing her black, flowing locks as the long, black, silky hair the goats have. When a herd of these dark goats grazes and moves down a steep mountain from a distance, the flowing movement creates a visual illusion of cascading hair. 

He compares her teeth to the whitest of sheep, shorn and clean and notes there are none missing, a rarity to be sure in the ancient world. 

Her lips, red as scarlet thread and her speech comely. Her temples and neck and breasts and scent, perfect and without blemish. 

*Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.*

The poetic nature of the song, romanticizing the couples love, could be seen as hyperbole. The aura of beauty that comes with infatuation. The perfection we see when we are caught up in our love for the other. 

But, as a spiritual allegory, we see the woman, who works the field and vineyard, black skinned, is without blemish when the King looks upon her. Just as we who are saved and sanctified by faith in Christ are pure when the Lord looks upon us. Clothed in righteousness. No sin imputed upon our new man. 

**2 Corinthians 5:21**
*For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.*

He has made us without blemish;

**Colossians 1:21–22**
*And you, that were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight*

Solomon's King sings passionately about his beloved; *How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse!* A sister of Israel, his spouse through their betrothal and marriage. 

This is also how Jesus sees us, His beloved. We are His brothers and sisters, and spouse as a collective. Made one within the body of Christ. 

**Matthew 12:50**
*For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother*.

His idealized view of us, despite our sin and despite our falling short of the glory of God, comes entirely by His love for us. That while we were sinners, Christ died for us. That He justifies the ungodly. That the Spirit quickens and seals us unto redemption. 

So when Solomon compares his love to an inclosed garden, walled off, a spring shut up, barred from use by others. A fountain sealed, carrying the seal of the King, and so kept pure from pollution. In this allegory we see the promise of eternal security in Christ. We are eternally His. 

The fruits of the garden are orchards, even pomegranates, and pleasant fruits, and flowers and spices used in ointments and perfume. Spikenard, the precious Himalayan plant, used to anoint Christ;

**Mark 14:3**
*And being in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head.*

The odors of her garden are pleasing. Precious to the King.  Just as our fruit, our good works in Christ, are pleasing to Him. 

*A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon*. He views us and the works we do for Him the same way, and we issue forth the living waters of the Spirit when we walk in His ways. 

The chapter ends shifting to the beloved woman, the bride, calling upon her lord to enter her garden, *that the spices thereof may flow out.* Spiritually, calling upon the name of the Lord, that one may be saved, that God may eat His pleasant fruits.

**Song of Solomon 5**
*1  I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk: eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved.*

*2  I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.*

*3  I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?*

*4  My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my bowels were moved for him.*

*5  I rose up to open to my beloved; and my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with sweet smelling myrrh, upon the handles of the lock.*

*6  I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.*

*7  The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me.*

*8  I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.*

*9  What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women? what is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us?*

*10  My beloved is white and ruddy, the chiefest among ten thousand.*

*11  His head is as the most fine gold, his locks are bushy, and black as a raven.*

*12  His eyes are as the eyes of doves by the rivers of waters, washed with milk, and fitly set.*

*13  His cheeks are as a bed of spices, as sweet flowers: his lips like lilies, dropping sweet smelling myrrh.*

*14  His hands are as gold rings set with the beryl: his belly is as bright ivory overlaid with sapphires.*

*15  His legs are as pillars of marble, set upon sockets of fine gold: his countenance is as Lebanon, excellent as the cedars.*

*16  His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.*

Chapter 5 opens with the aftermath of the close of the previous chapter, which ended with the woman calling upon her bridegroom, her lord. 

The spiritual moment of acceptance and humility, asking Him for salvation. Opening yourself to be intimately known of God. 

Verse 1 gives the bridegroom's POV. Having entered the garden, come unto his dearest sister, his spouse, gathered the spices and ointments of myrrh, eaten the sweet of the honeycomb, drunk the wine and milk, and calling those at the wedding feast, and his bride, to eat and drink, abundantly. 

**Revelation 22:17**
*And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.*

This picture of salvation, the immediate joy and celebration, the call to get your fill of an abundance of the sweet and precious food and anointing oils, wine and milk, to drink abundantly, is God's call to us to now walk in His Spirit. To take full advantage of the relationship His children have with the Father in Christ, the true King. The Shepherd. The Bridegroom. Not a thief, but our Savior. 

**John 10:10**
*The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.*

We are called to walk in the Spirit and receive the fruit thereof;

**Galatians 5:22–25**
*But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. And they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit.*

This initial feeling of having come to a feast and being overwhelmed with the love of God towards us, His blessings and rest, is marvelous. But we may tire and sleep in that contentment. 

The bride sleeps, but her heart wakes. She hears a knock. A voice. It is her beloved, calling to her to let him in. He asks her to open to him, *my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled*. He has come, his hair wet with the dew of the night to see her. 

He is Christ come to give His bride a blessing, but she doesn't leap to open the door. 

She makes excuses; *I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?* Rather than hear His voice and do His will, that we may be blessed, a believer may see their contentment and undefiled spirit as a bed to rest upon. When God asks so little of us whom He has saved, to open when He knocks, will we respond? 

**Revelation 3:20**
*Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.*

In the Christian life, God gives us works to do. Poor to be fed. A gospel to be preached. Divine appointments to be kept. His burden is light. He wants so little from us, yet in our own selfish interests, we make excuses. Taking for granted all He has given us. 

And, even as the beloved reaches his hand in through the door, making that extra effort to stir his bride, God will try and overcome our hesitation, moving in our lives. 

His effort stirs her. She rises but too late. She feels the sweet smelling myrrh, the holiness of Christ, upon the lock. But, He has withdrawn. 

When we don't respond to God's callings, and hesitate to do His will, He will give us a taste of life without Him. He will lift His hedge of protection. He will let us suffer consequences He has spared us from. He will chasten every son. 

The bride's soul fails, knowing she did wrong and desperately she seeks her beloved, in the very manner she once sought him. Wandering in the dark streets, calling for him. Trying to find her own way. 

This time, the watchmen find her and persecute her. The smote her and wound her and remove her veil of purity. She suffers for her love's sake. 

The watchmen who could not tell her the way to her love in chapter 3, now treat her wickedly.

This could be false teachers, those religious leaders who were not able to give her the gospel, now kicking her when she's down, to try and spoil her faith. 

We may backslide. We may become complacent. We may try to avoid doing His work. We may ignore His calling and then, when tribulation comes, look for Him where He is not, seeking answers. And we may be subject to tribulation, to remind us that we need Him, to remind us we are His. 

Just as Jonah was brought to Nineveh in the whale. Just as the church in Jerusalem, ordained to spread the gospel to the four corners of the world, stayed in Judea until the persecution against them scattered many. Just like Paul's repeated attempts to win his countrymen led him again and again to Jerusalem, finally being brought out and delivered to Rome in chains. 

It's hard to kick against the pricks. 

And so beaten and bloody, the bride charges an oath to the daughters of Jerusalem; *if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.*

To our modern years this sounds bad, but what's being said is that she is sick from love, overwhelmed by her feelings. Lovesick for her beloved. 

Despite persecution, she will not renounce him. Despite tribulation for his sake, she still longs for him. And she tells others who may be seeking him to give him her message of love.

The daughters of Jerusalem answer her refrain;

*What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women? what is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us?*

She has been backslidden, treated horribly by the authorities, bloody, aiming to destroy her remaining faith and strip away her public testimony (the veil), and yet her love is true. 

The daughters cannot understand what makes her beloved so special, above all others, that she would still call to him after all she's suffered. 

Unsaved people who see Christians suffer for Christ and still preach His love, often are baffled, but sometimes are moved. When the churches have been persecuted, traditionally we have seen exponential growth. Men are persuaded to willingly go to their death for the cause of Christ, and this testimony brings others to the faith. 

Why is your beloved more than others? Why is your God over the gods of men?

And she answers.

He is white, with purity, sinless. Divine. Ruddy, a red complexion picturing the humanity of Jesus and blood shed for us. The chiefest among ten those, the Lord of hosts. King of kings. 

Crowned of gold, sovereign above all. His locks, eternally young, everlasting. His eyes, full of grace and compassion for His beloved. 

Kissing His cheeks, like a bed of spices. Sweet flowers. His kiss, soft like the petals of the lily, dripping with precious oils. His love and our love for Him. 

The strength of His hands, the purity of His works, the gold and precious stones of all that He does. The inward parts of Christ are strong and pure as ivory, with heavenly blue sapphires the eternal Godhead in Him.

She affirms her faith; *I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine: he feedeth among the lilie*s, and then the narrator shifts again to the King. 

He praises his beloved, comparing her beauty to Tirzah, a city known for its natural beauty, and even as Jerusalem, ready for war, filled with bannermen, armies ready to march. 

He is overwhelmed with her beauty, repeating the verses poetically comparing her hair and teeth to goats and sheep as the lyrics from chapter 4. 

He numbers her among 60 queens and 80 concubines and countless virgins, a royal harem, and says she alone is above them all. Undefiled. The choice daughter, whom all the other women blessed and praised. Beloved above them all. 

Verse 10, the daughters of Jerusalem, the very courtesans the King compared his beloved to, sing her praises. 

*Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?*

We are His beloved. We are the light of the world. We shine forth to all nations, calling them to Christ. Provoking them to envy, that they may seek to be His bride. 

The woman sings in verse 11, that she has gone down to her beloved's garden. To see the fruit of the garden, and if the vine flourished, Jesus is the true vine. She's returned to His rest, as quickly as the chariots, to her beloved, upon seeing the bounty of his garden. 

The daughters encourage her, *Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee.* And her beloved asks them *What will ye see in the Shulamite? As it were the company of two armies.* A refrain answered in the next chapter.

It is worth noting that the woman of the Song of Solomon is often referred to as the "*Shulamite* Woman" based on verse 13. 

There are conflicting theories as to what that means; is it a region, a nation, a family name? Some believe it is a feminine form of Solomon. The evidence for any of these ideas is scant, and I have purposefully refrained from calling the woman a Shulamite because, in my opinion, in the end it doesn't matter to understand the context and subtext of the Song. 

You may disagree, and that's ok.

*Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved?* 

They see the love-changed woman, who was the girl they had watched grow.

Beginning in **Isaiah 1**, the major prophecy set in pre-captivity Judea, the Southern Kingdom, Isaiah preached in the 8th century BC, in a similar timeframe as the minor prophets and Kings and Chronicles we have recently covered, and so the themes are familiar. 

Israel is gone astray, into adultery with foreign gods, idols, and wickedness. Blood of the innocent shed, the poor defrauded, the widow uncared-for. The sickness of the rulers, even in Judah, has corrupted the Temple as well. God is displeased, and is warning of His coming judgment. 

Here, in Isaiah, God is pleading with the people, *Let us reason together*. The Lord has made it clear, from Moses to their present that if they walked in His commandments, they would be His people, and He would be their Lord and the land would be theirs and be blessed.

The prophet Isaiah continues his preaching against Judah, and the judgment of the Lord that is already upon them. 

The Lord has taken from them the stay, or that is the stores of food and water. There is famine and drought. 

Further there is a lack of leadership in the land, a lack of righteous judges and men of honor. A lack of prophets and wise elders. In their place are children. And because of this, the children rise up against their elders, and dishonor their fathers, and promote the base, that is the morally wicked. The perverts and sodomites. 

No one reputable wants to lead, because the nation is ruined and fallen. 

These are signs of a nation already under judgment. We often mistake these things as a reason we will eventually be judged, but the Lord is clear they are the results of already being judged. 

*The shew of their countenance doth witness against them; and they declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not. Woe unto their soul! for they have rewarded evil unto themselves.*

I believe this is the expression and affectations that sodomites and other reprobates all seem to have. That weak mouth and wide, whites of their eyes showing. The lispy voice. The cruel smirk. The proud look of those who have rewarded themselves for evil. 

But the Lord wants His children to know they will be blessed, even in the collapse around them, that the righteous will eat of the fruit of their doings. And the wicked shall receive their reward. 

But the people of the nation are led by children and women, and being brought to error and sin. The shame of a nation, which no longer has righteous men to rule over them, having had them taken away in judgment.

Moreover, the Lord says, His judgment is upon Judah for the behavior of her daughters, the women of the land being haughty, proud, not meek and gentle but wearing opulent clothing and jewelry, rings in their fingers, jewels in their nose, bells on their toes. Carrying themselves like they are special, mincing or gliding along. 

God says they will receive scabs upon their heads, baldness, and be smitten with stink and burning, STDs and worse. They will be made to wear sackcloth, and they will mourn in the streets for their men, slain by the sword. 

While the primary blame for the fall of a nation into judgment is upon the men who abdicate their roles and responsibilities, and chase pleasure and sin, defrauding the poor and afflicting the weak, the women play a part in it as well. 

Their lack of virtue, and pursuit of vanity bring about their own judgment against them. God hates a haughty spirit. This is why Christian women are called to modesty and meekness.

**Isaiah 5** gives us a clear glimpse into the judgment of God and how He sees Israel, and especially Judah. The length and breadth of His vision, being able to see all things from beginning to end. 

People today act as if they understand the long view of time, and they really have no idea. 

The Lord planted a vineyard, the root and the vine. Israel was given everything, a hedge of protection, a tower of strength, and yet it didn't produce the fine fruits expected.

**Deuteronomy 32:32-33**
*For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and of the fields of Gomorrah: their grapes are grapes of gall, their clusters are bitter: Their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps*.

And it shall be trodden down. 

The Lord called forth the armies of the other nations to come and destroy it. The people drunk on wine and strong drink, oblivious to the destruction. The oracles of God ignored.

*That say, Let him make speed, and hasten his work, that we may see it: and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw nigh and come, that we may know it!*

*Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil...Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight! ...Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink: Which justify the wicked for reward, and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him!*

Some use **Isaiah 25:6** to justify drinking alcohol. 

Wines of the lees, that is juice of the grape left with the dregs, seed and skins, unfiltered, to develop a deeper taste and sparkling, indicates to them wines of today that are left in their lees; champagne, moscato and others. 

These style wines are lower in alcohol, generally, and consumed for their taste more than their ability to get someone drunk, but they do contain alcohol. 

But does every wine that is left in their lees for flavor, ferment? 

The Hebrew word *shemer* refers to the dregs or lees, and it generally is used in a negative context, comparing nations to unfiltered wine. 

**Jeremiah 48:11-12**
*Moab hath been at ease from his youth, and he hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither hath he gone into captivity: therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed. Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will send unto him wanderers, that shall cause him to wander, and shall empty his vessels, and break their bottles.*

The lack of tribulation, of wars and captivity, of the nation of Moab, God says, means they are like unrefined wine, left in their lees. Settled with the dregs. This is a negative quality. 

Compare this to **Isaiah 25:6**, which says we will drink wines on the lees *well refined.*

The refining, the filtering, is the difference. Alcoholic wine, left in its lees, was filtered before drinking. But wines filtered from their lees before fermentation, and frequently filtered or refined, was significantly weaker and the alcohol content negligible.

Plutarch, who lived between 46 and 120 A.D. said, "Wine is rendered feeble in strength when it is frequently filtered. The strength or spirit thus being excluded, the wine neither inflames the brain nor infests the mind and passions, and is much more pleasant to drink." 

Pliny the Elder (23-79AD) wrote, "The most useful wine was all its force or strength broken by the filter."

This process, a well refined wine left in its lees, produced a weak, good tasting juice. Pleasant to drink, a drink of kings. 

Just as the fat and marrow of meat was desirable, highly refined, despirited wine was as well. 

The Lord of hosts will make unto all people a feast. Amen.

*This is the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner.*

*Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner, And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed.*

There is no other foundation upon which man can built that doesn't come to naught, but Jesus. And we build up on that rock, precept by precept. Here a little, there a little. Until we are raised to judgment, and eternal life. 

**Matthew 7:24**

Amen

Now the destruction of the Lord, His wrath, is like a farmer who plows his field, turning over the soil, so that he may plant seed, and harvest fruit. They beat the shafts of the plants with a rod to loosen the seeds. 

The Lord teaches them these things, and like all of creation, as a parable for His ways. 

*This also cometh forth from the Lord of hosts, which is wonderful in counsel, and excellent in working*.

What a wonderful thing to know we are instructed by all creation to better know the Lord God. That His percepts are found in all of nature, that man have no excuse. 

Rejoice when the field is broken up, and plowed under. That the seeds may rise and live again, and bring forth fruit.

Isaiah, preaching against the city of David, that city Jerusalem, here called Ariel, or the lion of God, and again saying the wisdom of the leaders and prophets will be rendered useless. Unable to understand the vision of the Lord, as a book sealed up to the wise and not understood by the unlearned.

The promise of the coming of Jesus, that the blind will see and the dead hear His word and the meek and poor shall rejoice in Him, the Holy One of Israel.

*So that none of the remnant of Judah, which are gone into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, shall escape or remain, that they should return into the land of Judah, to the which they have a desire to return to dwell there: for none shall return but such as shall escape.*

The prophetic warning to Judah, that when their time of tribulation came, the captivity to Babylon, not to flee to or trust in Egypt to save them, was fulfilled in Jeremiah's day. 

He also warned them, referring back to the prophets, beginning with Isaiah. God, knowing what they would do, warns against it. And you know those in Jerusalem who believed the word of God did not flee, and be destroyed in the way. 

The dual fulfillment here is also clear, the Holy One of Israel, the Lord Christ Jesus at His second coming and the wrath that pours out from His lips, the fire of Tophet, a name for Hell, is lit from the brimstone from His mouth, that kindles it. 

Egypt is a representation of the world, our pre-Christian life of sin, under the yoke of the law, slaves to sin. As the Bible says again and again of the Israelites being led by Moses, that in their freedom they would long to return to the bondage of Egypt out of fear or inconvenience.

This is written for our admonition, that we who are His children don't turn again to the world and to sin when we face tribulation. That trusting in Egypt is death. 

We all come out of Egypt. We all are baptized in the crossing, and sojourn in the wilderness, awaiting the promised land.

*21 But they held their peace, and answered him not a word: for the king's commandment was, saying, Answer him not.*

*22 Then came Eliakim, the son of Hilkiah, that was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah, the son of Asaph, the recorder, to Hezekiah with their clothes rent, and told him the words of Rabshakeh.*

Here in **Isaiah 36** we have the third telling of this historical event, where the captain of the Assyrian horde has come down through Samaria, along the Jordan, from Lachish, the city of Dan in the north, unto the plains before Jerusalem in the South. 

Hezekiah is king over Judah, and while not a good king in the tradition of David, but he has trusted the Lord, preached by Isaiah, with his illness and been healed, being granted 15 years to his life by God. He had taken down altars to the false gods, in high places. And here the city is under siege. 

The Assyrian Rabshakeh, speaking in Hebrew, calls out to the King's advisors on the wall, telling them of the futility of their position and asking *What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?*

What a question, and one our adversaries in the world, mockers and scoffers and those seeking us harm may ask. One our spiritual adversary, Satan, may corner us into answering. 

Rabshakeh says who will you trust? Egypt, a broken reed, nothing one could put their confidence in. For us, God uses Egypt as an example of the bondage to sin and the world. 

Or do you trust in the Lord? But notice it isn't the Lord God, but his natural man understanding of what God is, and what religion of the believers looks like. 

*But if thou say to me, We trust in the Lord our God: is it not he, whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah hath taken away, and said to Judah and to Jerusalem, Ye shall worship before this altar?*

The false religion of worshipping God in high places and idols and altars, which the world sees vs our worship in our hearts, at the Temple of God's choosing. Hezekiah had done right, and Rabshakeh is mocking it. 

The world sees the Roman Catholic Church, or any of its splinters this way, as the true religion of Christianity. If we reject those trappings, they think we weaken God, or doubt our faith. 

We see this all the time, when the world makes fun of "Pastor Bob" with a strip mall church. The world respects the high places, the ornate temples made of hands. They don't fear the god of these places, but they understand it, the carnality of elegant churches, idols, altars. 

To the world, trusting the Lord humbly, and in weakness is foolish. But to us, strength.
