**Isaiah 39**
*At that time Merodachbaladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah: for he had heard that he had been sick, and was recovered.*

*2 And Hezekiah was glad of them, and shewed them the house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices, and the precious ointment, and all the house of his armour, and all that was found in his treasures: there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not.*

*3 Then came Isaiah the prophet unto king Hezekiah, and said unto him, What said these men? and from whence came they unto thee? And Hezekiah said, They are come from a far country unto me, even from Babylon.*

*4 Then said he, What have they seen in thine house? And Hezekiah answered, All that is in mine house have they seen: there is nothing among my treasures that I have not shewed them.*

*5 Then said Isaiah to Hezekiah, Hear the word of the Lord of hosts:*

*6 Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the Lord.*

*7 And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.*

*8 Then said Hezekiah to Isaiah, Good is the word of the Lord which thou hast spoken. He said moreover, For there shall be peace and truth in my days.*

Hezekiah, who had expressed so much faith and appreciation in God's mercy, saving him from death and granting him 15 years longer to live, crashes out when the envoys from Babylon visit him to congratulate him for his miraculous recovery. 

And instead of praising God and giving Him all glory and honor for it, shows them instead his wealth and treasure. 

This is a cautionary tale for Christians. At the moments of our Christian walk, where God has blessed us, and we have been humbled enough to seek the truth, and given opportunity to serve Him, is often the moment we fall the hardest. 

Spiritual triumph, wounded by pride. Our blessings are to give us opportunities to praise and sanctify the Lord to others who don't know His grace and mercy. And yet we not only hesitate to give Him the glory, we often take credit for ourselves. 

This will, as we know, come back to harm Judah, as their wealth will be remembered and covered by Babylon as its empire grows. Isaiah prophesies their captivity and Hezekiah's sons serving the Babylonian king.

Yet, Hezekiah takes the wrong lesson from this warning, taking comfort that the worst will be for future generations, and not his to deal with. 

How familiar this is for us today. How our fathers fell to sin and pride, squandering the blessings of God, and leaving their children to deal with the inevitable consequences? That is why, even when we backslide, even when we let our pride get the better of us, and we do that which is wrong in the sight of God, that we turn again to Him in humility, seeking forgiveness. 

There are some mistakes we make, and sins we commit, that have long lasting repercussions. An act of fornication that results in a baby, or a disease. A marriage broken by adultery. A drunken night ending in death.

Hezekiah had his pride become a cause for his children to be slaves and his nation made desolate, and he took selfish solace in the fact it wouldn't affect him. What a wicked thing. 

Put others, especially your children, above yourself and when you err, turn to the Lord for forgiveness least your sins rebound in future generations.

This again calls forward to the events described in **Revelation 21**, which I posted yesterday. The New Jerusalem that depends from Heaven, decked as a bride. 

People often talk about the wedding of the church to Christ. I know it's used as parable a couple times, but the actual feast is here and the bride that golden city, where Christ will reign forever. 

We've seen it again and again in the Chronicles and Kings, and from the prophets, that the only reason Judah wasn't destroyed like Sodom, like Israel, was the promise to David, that the Christ promised to Abraham would come from the King's lineage. And, every time, to keep Jerusalem as the place God chose to place His name. As the spot where Jesus would be offered. And where He would triumphantly reign. 

It was never the Jews. They were beneficiaries of God's plan. They were not His plan, themselves. 

And when the city was made desolate by the captivity, the exile to Babylon. And, in the Great Tribulation, when the abomination of desolation is made, when many would say that Jerusalem is "Forsaken," that it will not be. That Christ's redeemed will flock to Jerusalem, a crown of glory. A royal diadem. The symbol of His power.

What unbelieving Jews and Muslims do there doesn't matter. If a so-called 3rd temple is built, it won't be God's. If the Man of Perdition lays siege and slaughters the Jews in days of vengeance, and sits in the place of God declaring himself God, it won't matter. Because it is the Lord's and He will repay. It will be as a crown to Him. A holy bride. Amen.

Zedekiah did that which was evil in the eyes of the Lord, according to all that Jehoiakim had done. Through the anger of the Lord it came to pass in Jerusalem and Judah, till he had cast them out from his presence, that Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

The Lord sends Babylon against Judah to punish them for their transgressions, and Zedekiah and the people harden their hearts and rebel against Nebuchadnezzar rather than repent towards God. And the Lord's wrath comes upon them, and they are besieged. For a year and a half Jerusalem are starved out by the Chaldean horde surrounding them. 

They die of famine and pestilence and war. Just as the unbelieving are slaughtered by the horsemen. 

The city is torn down, not one stone remaining upon another. They are made desolate. Empty. 

The king and his men flee to the wilderness and are captured. Zedekiah brought before the king for judgment. His seed is sniffed out before his eyes, and then he is blinded. Blind unto his death. 

Just as the Jews who rebelled against God were blinded, those who believed not on the Lord Jesus Christ. Blind and imprisoned until their death. Cut off. 

Then Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard carried away certain of the poor, the residue of the people. A remnant. 

The rest fell away, fell to the king of Babylon. The multitude. A falling away. 

But there was a remnant saved, and left behind to be vinedressers and husbandmen, tasked with bringing in the harvest. The increase of which belongs to the lord set over them. Just as Christians are, to bring forth fruit. After their kind. Servants of the Lord. 

The pillars of the temple were taken away. Broken down. Carried off to Babylon. Just as believers are the pillars of the temple of God, the body of Christ that is the church of believers. Just as we who are alive and remain will be broken by the antichrist when he makes war on the saints. Just as the abomination that maketh desolate will break the pillars, the saints. 

And the cauldrons and bowls and spoons and sniffers and all the vessels of brass wherewith they ministered. The holy vessels, used to minister, the same are saved Christians. Vessels of the Lord fitted for His purpose. Taken away. The refined silver. The brass. The pillars. This is the great tribulation and the martyrdom of the saints. 

And the 7 kings who set up Zedekiah, and his scribe, and the guards and all the ministers of the false king. A picture of the Beast and his prophet and the seven horns that give him his power...they are smote by the King set over them by God. 

But there are carried away a remnant who live. Who are brought out of great tribulation to serve the king. And the king of Babylon (at this time Evilmeridach), suffered not to leave Jehoiachin in prison, and lifted up Jehoiachin, to sit at his right hand. To be king of kings. Where he would eat bread every day of his life. Just as God the Father has lifted up His Son, the Lord Jesus.

There are so many parallels here and I am not doing it justice. But I needed to write it out so I have a better outline of study. The details found here are repeated in **Jeremiah 39**, **2 Kings 25** and **2 Chronicles 36**. God really wants us to see what happened to Zedekiah and the Jews at the hands of His servant Nebuchadnezzar. 

Taken in conjunction with Daniel, and especially **Matthew 24**, first and second **Thessilonians**, and **Revelation**, we see that when Jesus says all the prophets gave witness, we can understand better the way of the Lord. 

Also, study out the idea that we are the servants of God. The husbandmen and vinedressers. The pillars of the body of Christ. The temple of God. The holy vessels fitted to His purpose. It was to be like Jeremiah, and boldly go into the city, before the kings and scribes, and the people, and preach the word of God.

Beginning in the book of the prophet Jeremiah, who lived in the southern Kingdom of Judah, roughly 600 years before Christ, and after the destruction of the northern Kingdom of Israel by the Assyrians. 

He was active during the time of King Josiah, who sought to return Judah to the right ways of the Lord, and had engaged in repairing the Temple, as well as tearing down the altars, groves and high places of Baal worship. **(2 Kings 22-23)**

Jeremiah preached reformation and repentance towards the Lord as the King sought the same, seeking to make right what had been done by his grandfather Mannaseh. 

During the renovation of the Temple Josiah was presented with a copy of the Law. And having it read, came to understand by faith what God wanted of His people. And while the efforts of Josiah and the prophets, including Jeremiah, kept the wrath of God at bay, ultimately it only delayed His punishment against this wicked people who had turned from Him. Babylon would invade and destroy them shortly after Josiah was killed in battle with Egypt at Megiddo, and his successors were exceedingly wicked. 

And so Jeremiah preached, unwillingly at first but with the word of God upon him, the prophet would witness the fall of the Temple and captivity of unfaithful Judah.

God reveals to Jeremiah that He will use the armies from the North to come against Jerusalem, and tells Jeremiah that He will protect him as he preaches against the whoredoms of the Jews, who had turned to false gods. 

The Lord reminds Jeremiah of the history of the people, taken from out of Egypt to be a holy nation. That Israel went after God in the wilderness, and how He brought them to the promised land, and the bounty and blessings He bestowed on them. And yet they made His heritage an abomination. 

The people, the kings and priests did not seek the Lord, forsaking **Him that is the fountain of living waters,** to turn to empty manmade cisterns of dead idols. Passing their children through the fire to Baal. 

They turned from faith in the Lord, the Christ to come. The fountain of living waters as Jesus describes Himself. This is the faith that saves, in all ages. Calling upon the name of the Lord. 

The word of God upon Jeremiah, He says; *Yet I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed: how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?*

The vineyard imagery, describing Israel as the vine God planted, is used throughout the NT to describe the final rejection of the Jews, who had become a strange vine, not producing fruit, cut off and burned as another people were grafted in. 

The destruction of his nation for their unfaithfulness to the Lord that Jeremiah witnessed is very relevant to any nation that calls itself by His name. We are witness to a similar time, with the same punishment due for our wickedness and deliverance available, by turning back to Christ.

God says; *For I spake not unto your fathers, nor commanded them in that day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices: but this thing I commanded them, saying, Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and ye shall be my people: and walk ye in all the ways that I have commanded you, that it may be well unto you.*

This is the only dispensation that there ever has been. The dispensation of grace offered by God through faith, unto adoption, and by love unto obedience of His commandments.

They were given after the promise that if they believed on the Lord, He'd be their God and they'd be His people.

Faith cometh by hearing and hearing by the word of God. OT and NT.

*22 Are there any among the vanities of the Gentiles that can cause rain? or can the heavens give showers? art not thou he, O Lord our God? therefore we will wait upon thee: for thou hast made all these things.*

Now we're there in chapter 14 of Jeremiah and we see a continuation of what has become the pattern over the past few chapters, that Jeremiah is beseeching the Lord for mercy for his people while the Lord preaches through Jeremiah to them about their sin. And especially the judgment that has come upon them. 

As it goes, we see Jeremiah becoming more desperate in pleading the case for the children of Israel. And we see God has hardened His heart against them. He is promising that they shall die by famine and by sword and be carried away captive into a strange land. God's mind is set upon this judgment and His wrath is upon them. 

In chapter 14, we see Jeremiah begging not to do this to the people who call themselves by his name, Who are his people. And God says don't even bother praying for them. They can't make burnt offerings or fast enough for Him to repent. Reprobate, silver shellman call them because the Lord has given up on them. 

Again, the parallels to today are striking. And again, we should remind ourselves that in all times and places there have been Jeremiah's. And there have been people who have done wickedly and received the just wrath of God. 

Part of the  reason for the book of Jeremiah and lamentations that follow is to help set us in the right frame of mind and understanding when tribulation comes to our nations. When the wickedness of our people leads us to destruction. That we can be at peace with it even as we preach hard against it. Hoping that our people turn back to the Lord. 

Much like Job and understanding how God deals with us as individuals, Even we who are righteous in His name. 

But also like Job. It is easy to empathize and feel the emotion as they go through their trials and tribulations. The frustration of it. But it's humbling to understand that God's will is not our will. And God's point of view is outside of time and perfect while we see through a glass darkly. Our faith should be bolstered by reading this because we know how it turned out in the end. And we know how Israel was delivered by Christ and the resurrection promised in the scriptures by a God who cannot lie. And so we should take comfort in that as the people who call ourselves by His name. As we await a better country.

I've said it before and perhaps not often enough, but if you believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and are walking the best you can in the spirit, and you still find yourself fearful and angry all the time, no love for others, snapping at them, constantly frustrated and wrathful... Then there's something wrong with your Christian walk. Is something you need to get right with God about. 

We talk with Him, as we stay in his word and in prayer, and God uses us for his purpose, You should find your faith increasing and the peace that passes all understanding coming upon you. You should find yourself a lot less afraid of the things of this world. And you should find yourself having more patience and long suffering for others, especially as tribulation works in your life and you see God bringing you out of it. 

Whatever is troubling you, He is there to help you. 

*Persecutions, afflictions, which came unto me at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra; what persecutions I endured: but out of them all the Lord delivered me. Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.*

...*And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.*

...*These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.*

So if you find yourself discouraged and afraid. Remember this. See comfort in books like Jeremiah and Job. Consider the sufferings of Paul and how, at the end, He had been abandoned by most of the people he had helped bring to Christ. But yet he was of good cheer. 

*For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God.*

We should also mention that you see Jeremiah preaching through this whole ordeal as Israel slips into its eventual captivity, and he is no doubt getting people saved. He has better equipped those who trust in the Lord for what is coming by, reconciling them to the Father through the Son. 

And that is what we are compelled to do. It's why we are to spread the gospel and go soul winning. Out among the highways and hedges. Compelling people to come to the Lord. It is why we have the Great Commission. 

This world is fallen and the god of this world holds men's hearts sway. And while we should standfast preaching against sin and holding to His word, we should do so understanding that we won't reach everyone or even enough that their oblations will prevent the wrath that is to come. That the land itself wants to spew out people who allow innocent blood to be shed with no recompense from the guilty.

**Jeremiah 18** begins a shift in the narrative structure, where for the past several chapters Jeremiah had made some effort to plead with God to not be too hard on Judah, and God explaining that they've condemned their own selves with their fornication, going after false gods. Not heeding the word of God from the prophets but following the vain jangling from the false prophets telling the people that they were fine and judgment wasn't coming. That they were at peace with God. Even as they burned incense to idols and baked cakes to the "queen of heaven."

But chapter 18 begins with God sending Jeremiah to observe a potter, who is spinning the wheel to turn clay into a vessel. And, seeing the potter discard a bowl that didn't turn out right, to make another that would. 

While many take the potter analogy and make it about us as individuals, because God does shape us to be fitted for His purpose, the primary application here, and in **Romans 9**, is about nations, specifically the physical nation of Israel. The descendants of Abraham. 

*O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the Lord. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel. At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it*.

As Paul writes, nearly 8 centuries later;

*Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour? What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction: And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory*.

We see that the context remains the same. The destruction of the Jews serves God's purpose, that His wrath be manifest, but also His glory in those raised up in His mercy, the Gentiles. 

God's judgment against Egypt and Pharaoh allowed His mercy to be seen in the children of Israel. His destruction of the northern kingdom, as a warning to Judah in the south. Judah's destruction by the Babylonians that Jeremiah is preaching will allow God to be glorified in their eventual return. The final destruction of the Jews in their rejection of Christ opens the door to the Gentiles to be graft in. 

God uses the judgment against nations to bring about the glory of His mercy to those that believe. His wrath revealed from heaven allows His mercy and grace to be manifest in those He will be saved in His son.

Short chapter, but powerful. The Lord shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs. One very good, the other evil and inedible, and He tells the prophet that the very good figs are the remnant that was carried away in captivity to Nebuchadnezzar. He promised that the tribulation of this is to turn their heart towards God, and they will be returned to Jerusalem filled with zeal. 

But the rotten figs represent the wicked of Judah, who will be scattered and bred out of existence, killed by the sword or by pestilence. To be a proverb and a byword for other nations, "see how they have fallen." 

Both the saved remnant and the reprobates reveal the glory of God. In His mercy and deliverance from the worst of conditions, to a restored Jerusalem and His wrath against the ungodly who hold the truth in unrighteousness. 

The same holds true today. 

As **Romans 1:16-20** lays out;

 *For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith.*

In **Jeremiah 25** we see that the prophet has been preaching the word of God for 23 years, and he was not alone. Zephaniah and Habakkuk, and eventually Daniel and Ezekiel (after captivity began), are Jeremiah's contemporaries. The prophets of God trying to make strait the paths of Judah, while God uses His "servant," Babylon as the rod to lead them back to Him. 

In chapter 25 we see the preaching of destruction and desolation of Judah laid out;

*Moreover I will take from them the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the candle.*

But, the Lord says through Jeremiah that His wrath will also come to the other nations of the region, utterly destroying them as well. Babylon as an empire serving as God's tool to pour out His wrath. And Judah will be captive 70 years, saith the Lord.

But God also tells us that this desolation and destruction will come to all nations. That God will recompense them according to their deeds. God judges nations by works, even as He offers salvation to individuals by faith. 

And so God gives the prophet an understanding that the wine of His fury will be poured out against them all. Both literally the nations of Egypt and Uz and Moab and Edom and the rest, and as we read on, God swears His vengeance on every nation, in that great and terrible day of the Lord. 

Even as Isaiah preached. And as the revelation of Jesus Christ gave to John about the future nation with the spirit of Babylon upon it, whose destruction parallels with the destruction of Jerusalem in Jeremiah's day:

*And the light of a candle shall shine no more at all in thee; and the voice of the bridegroom and of the bride shall be heard no more at all in thee*.

Even as all hope for God's repentance is lost and Jerusalem and the other mighty nations of the time cannot escape the judgment that's upon them, God gives the hope that His wrath against His people will be short lived, and He will eventually turn that wrath against Babylon, the nation that has its spirit upon it in the end times.

There is some confusion about what Babylon in Revelation refers to. We see through a glass darkly. But some will claim Jerusalem is end times Babylon based on the similarities between those verses in **Jeremiah 25** and **Revelation 18**. 

However we see in **Revelation 16** that this is not the case;

*17 And the seventh angel poured out his vial into the air; and there came a great voice out of the temple of heaven, from the throne, saying, It is done.*

*18 And there were voices, and thunders, and lightnings; and there was a great earthquake, such as was not since men were upon the earth, so mighty an earthquake, and so great.*

*19 And the great city was divided into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell: and great Babylon came in remembrance before God, to give unto her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath.*

If we note the order of things, that great city, Jerusalem, is divided in thirds by the catastrophic world-wide earthquake that fells all the great cities, and then God turns to Babylon specifically for destruction. 

And it is fitting and proper that God bookends His wrath, bringing the utter destruction and desolation against Babylon that they had brought against Jerusalem. Poetic justice as it were. 

In my mind, the spirit of Babylon is upon the United States, and the empire that extends across Europe and in other White nations, Canada, Australia, New Zealand. The Idolatry and profane fornication of a people claiming to be of God, yet wicked in every way. Used to destroy other wicked nations by God, and yet still facing His ultimate judgment just as the original Babylon.

In **Jeremiah 35**, the prophet receives the word of God, telling him to bring the sons of the Rechabites into the temple and to offer them juice of the vine, or wine. The Rechabites were a nomadic people within Judah, who are not of the Hebrews, but rather as the Bedouins, herders who lived in tents and refrained from agriculture and landholding by practice and custom. As strangers in the land, perpetually, they obeyed the law of their father to abstain from drinking all but water, not settling down and owning land, not building permanent structures and planting vineyards, that they may keep the words of Jonadab the son of Rechab and live many days in the land where they be strangers. 

(Getting this out of the way; Because fermented wine, or strong drink, was prohibited of the Levites in the performance of their duties, it certainly wouldn't be allowed within the temple. Wine in the Bible generally refers to the fresh or preserved non-alcoholic juice of a fruit, typically grapes, unless specified as fermented. This isn't a chapter about consuming alcohol, so I don't want to get bogged down in that argument)

According to Jonadab, the proscription against wine is part of the larger point made to his sons; not to become tied down to a place and enjoy the comforts that end up tying a people to a land. Nomadic shepherds, like Abraham and Jacob were, lived in tents and dwelt in the wilderness where the grasses and water were free, and grazing moved with the seasons. A taste for wine, which was expensive and a treat compared to the water that the Rechabites drank exclusively, and the father of this people saw it as a temptation that would inevitably lead to the erasure of his clan and their way of life. 

Many times the law of our fathers is like this; stipulations made to ensure a continuity of their offspring in the ways that seem good and right, to secure a future for their children. 

It is important to note this wasn't a command of God. Owning a vineyard and drinking juice isn't a sin. It isn't a call to separation or of a vow to God, like the Nazarites, who for a season lived lives deprived of comfort, including not consuming grapes, or their juice. It was just the ways of their father that they obeyed as sons, even unto generations. 

God uses their example to illustrate how the children of Israel were in disobedience to their Father, the Lord God.

In **Jeremiah 36**, the word of the Lord comes upon the prophet telling him to write the words of prophecy God had given him in a scroll, and to have the word of God read in the temple and to the people of Jerusalem. With the aid of a scribe named Baruch, he does just that. And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.*

The people who heard the word of God through Jeremiah believed in vain that their performative acts of penance and fasting would offset the sin in their hearts, their trust in idols, their adoption of the customs of the heathen. Their sin and degeneracy. They needed to repent, to think again, to know God's judgment is real and there is only one way, God's way. And all the beating of their chest and sackcloth and ashes, fasting and outward signs of religion couldn't save them.

And this ties into the renewed theme of the week; repentance. 

The thing most people "repent of" isn't their sins. Most people know sin is bad and hate it and don't like themselves for it. These Jews in Jerusalem for the fast knew in their hearts they were in sin, just as people do today. They have a conscience and the Spirit convicting them, least they be reprobate. 

What people most often repent of are the false beliefs they have about God. About His  judgment. About their own righteousness or how they can escape punishment for their sins. 

"Oh I thought idols would save me." 
"I thought the law would save me." 
"I thought maybe hell wasn't real." 
"I didn't know my works weren't enough."

It's literally what they are being called to repentance from in NT scripture. The Jews thinking by their being Abraham's seed they were going to inherit the kingdom no matter what. That they could achieve their own righteousness by works of the law and keeping the traditions of men. That the Kingdom of Heaven was theirs on this earth. That the Messiah would be political. A man of war. That circumcision availed them. 

The Greeks believed their dead idols and false gods, that they superstitiously bowed to and served, would save them. That God wasn't real. They worshipped the created more than the Creator who is blessed forever, amen. 

Jews and Greeks alike didn't believe Jesus was the Christ. They sought a sign, and wisdom. But the power to be saved was in the word of God. The Gospel preached and believed. Repentance from dead works and vain traditions and towards God. Reconsidering the way to the Kingdom of Heaven, and believing. 

Just as in Jeremiah's day. Just as it is today.

In **Jeremiah 37**, we see the king and his princes, those in power besieged by Babylon. They had not harkened to the Lord and did not listen to the wisdom of the word of God, preached by the prophet Jeremiah. But in their calamity they sought him to pray for their salvation from the Chaldean horde. 

In a like manner, many men will wait until the foxhole is being shelled to ask God for deliverance. To protect their lives. Even as they reject His word, and salvation of their souls. They shout out "Oh my God!" with no faith. They want to eat their cake and have it too. 

But God again and again tells us that He calls early, and often. That wisdom is crying out her voice in the streets.

That, as a mother hen, the Lord seeks to gather us as she would chicks under her wing, but they would not listen. And they slew the prophets and did what they wanted, and so when destruction is due, God laughs at their calamity. 

Salvation, be it the individual soul liberty of those justified in Christ, or the physical salvation of a nation, is not extended indefinitely. God is longsuffering. He is mercy and His grace abounds. But He is clear. There comes a time for both people and nations, where His patience runs out and He scourges with a rod of iron. His wrath is kindled. Too late, reprobate. 

This has application in the saved Christian's life as well. He wants to form us into vessels fit for His use, that we may bring forth fruit after our kind. But if we resist Him and live for ourselves not heeding His word, separating ourselves to the Gospel, becoming backslidden, being reproached again and again and ignoring it, God will eventually destroy you. Punishment will be more severe for us than the wicked who prosper. Or taking us home earlier than maybe we would have been. 

At some point it is too late, even for the saved.

And so when the armies of Egypt offer the Judeans a false hope, and scare off the Babylonians, the rulers turn on Jeremiah and shut him up in prison at Jonathan the scribes house. Rather than considering the years he spent preaching the word of God, telling them Babylon was going to come against them while their own false prophets preached "peace and safety," they seek to blame him for his prophesying that Babylon would return. They had turned to him for prayer in their hour of need, but when they had a false hope, they turned against him again. 

Most of us have witnessed this. People in our lives who are only receptive to the word so long as they face tribulation, and then the moment they see relief, discarding everything preached to them. 

But the king was fearful, and sought the word of the Lord, only to again return the prophet to prison when he preached destruction, howbeit with some added comfort, for fear of the Lord.

I should note, the cycle of turning to the Lord in tribulation, only to gain the prosperity of fools, the good times and blessings that may come in relief, but then in that prosperity, turning back to sin and not listening to the word of God, is something that afflicts many Christians. It has me. 

I have had periods of my life where, walking in the spirit during rough times, and being delivered and given blessings and grace, get comfortable and forget what brought me low to begin with. Sliding back to old ways that had brought me troubles to begin with. To forget the Lord and His deliverance. 

This is why it is vitally important for a Christian to not wait until there's trouble in their life to take their walk seriously. To turn to the Lord in praise and thanksgiving when times are good. To humble yourself and understand that all blessings and tribulation are of God and work for good to those who love Him. To seek His wisdom early. To be constant in prayer and in His word. To do all things in Him. That His will be done. 

Life's ups and downs become less volatile and the waters calm.

The fear of the Jews. The Jews who sought to kill Jeremiah. The Jews who carry the blood of all the prophets from Abel to Zachariah. A to Z. Who'd slain the Lord Jesus and who are contrary to all men. 

Jeremiah, who had preached destruction by the Babylonians, prophesying what had now come to pass, now was relaying the word of the Lord from prison, during the siege of Jerusalem, to surrender and live. 

In their fear and pride, the princes of the city, the high ranking politicians and clergy, sought Jeremiah's life for demoralizing the people, surrounded and without much food already. They took the prophet and threw him in a pit full of mire, where he sank into the muck, left to starve and die. 

But a believer, an Ethiopian eunuch serving in Zedekiah's court, interestingly enough, brought the matter to the king's attention. And so the king, who we have seen, was a double-minded man, who feared the Lord but also feared his men and the judgment of the people, sent to retrieve Jeremiah. 30 men working with makeshift straps of fabric, were needed to pull him from the mire. And the king comes to him for private council. 

He promised the prophet he can speak freely. That he won't have him put to death. But, he pleads, tell him the word of the Lord. 

*Then said Jeremiah unto Zedekiah, Thus saith the Lord, the God of hosts, the God of Israel; If thou wilt assuredly go forth unto the king of Babylon's princes, then thy soul shall live, and this city shall not be burned with fire; and thou shalt live, and thine house: But if thou wilt not go forth to the king of Babylon's princes, then shall this city be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and thou shalt not escape out of their hand.*

Surrender and live. Fight and die. 

And in his fear of the Jews, and in his his pride, the king refuses. He fears the captured Jews will mock him for obeying the word of God. 

Jeremiah again tells him he has a simple choice. Obey and trust in the word of the Lord or all that he fears will come true. The princes of Babylon will have him in derision. The women will even mock him, as if Zedekiah were trapped in mire as Jeremiah had been. 

But fearful and double-minded, the king returns Jeremiah to his original prison in the court of Johnathan, and swears him to secrecy. And there the prophet remained until Babylon had taken the city.

This story has so many applications. In the lives of saved believers, we often are mocked and ridiculed for preaching the word of God and telling those in sin that they're wrong. And when these unsaved come to the supposed leaders of churches and denominations, and say "tell this Christian to shut up," essentially, they comply. 

They say that we have to be loving. We can't preach against sin. Against the wicked. Against sodomites and Jews. That we can't tell people the judgment of God against those who sin and those who are haters of God. That we may offend them. They will even say things like Billy Graham or various Popes; "Jews. Muslims and Hindus who are sincere will find Heaven," knowing the Bible says the only path to the Father is through the Son. 

And so much of it comes from fear of the Jews. How much dispensationalism and Zionism is preached by pastors who know better, for fear of the Jews? Fear of lost funding. Fear of being called names by the ADL? Fear of being persecuted? 

Even in our own lives, we may have relatives if people in our church who tell us to cool it with the antisemetism. Stop speaking out against abominations. To reign in our hatred of every false way. 

These same types will also wet-blanket soul winning and evangelizing the Gospel. They may even call giving the Gospel to Jews a hate crime. 

For fear of the Jews. 

But we know that by following the word of God and fearing only Him, we will be delivered. Even in death, we are delivered. So we speak boldly. We give the Gospel to every creature. We stand against evil and we defend that which is good. Even if it means we are mocked. Because we know the mockers will get their reward. 

2 Peter 3:3-4
Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts, And saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation.

We know the Lord is not slack concerning his promise. We know the mockers will be destroyed. That we shall overcome and be delivered by our Lord Jesus Christ.

King Zedekiah's fear and double-mindedness, and his equivocating between fear of the Lord and fear of man, honestly reminds me so much of supposed leaders like Donald Trump. Who talk tough, but always keeps it vague enough where he has wiggle room. Where he laments that others don't stand up and do things that he himself only hints at. Where he feigns piousness, while the fear of the Jews has him embracing evil publicly, to be seen as all things to all people, while standing for nothing. 

Trump isn't the only coward like king Zedekiah. All our politicians are craven. All fear the Jews more than the Lord. All fear what men can do to the flesh rather than He who can destroy the soul. 

It is why we shouldn't be caught up in waiting for a leader to come to save us. Like the people of Jerusalem who thought the Pharaoh's armies from Egypt would save them from the Chaldeans, but the respite was short lived. And Jerusalem fell anyway. 

We need to set our minds on Christ. Be led of God through the Spirit. Harkening to the word of God.

As God had said through the prophet, so it was. 

And then a particular Jew, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, using trickery, took matters into his own hands and murdered Gedaliah, the governor, and also killed collaborators and those that came down from Samaria, formerly Israel, with gifts. 

And though the rebels were chased from the land and slain, Ishmael escaped to the Ammonites. 

And the people, for fear of the Chaldeans who may seek to punish them for Ishmael's treachery, fled to Egypt.

These things happened and were written that we can see the nature of God and man. We often cannot see how the will of God is better than our own flawed understanding of how things should be. And when we take matters into our own hands to "fix" it, we make things worse, and turn to sin.

**1 Peter 4:17**
*For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God: and if it first begin at us, what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God?*

Having been made desolate, spoiled. Many dead, more led away to captivity, and now, having the governor placed over them slain by one of their own, the remnant of Judah left in Jerusalem are desperate and full of fear. And in fear of destruction, they turn to Jeremiah, claiming to seek God's will for them in the calamity that's ensued. 

They say they want God to show them the way wherein they may walk. The thing they may do, to escape destruction. They know the word of the Lord is with Jeremiah, who had for years and years preached the coming destruction, despite stocks and smiting, being jailed and left to die in mire. And all he prophesized has come to pass. 

And they swear to the Lord that good or evil, they shall do as God tells them. 

This is the way so many of us are, unsaved or saved. Those who come to inquire of the Lord, "What must we do to be saved?" Or those who are children of God, and yet not walking after His will. 

They come to calamity, they see destruction ahead. They know they need to harken unto the word of God. They even will go to the godly to inquire, "What may we do?" swearing to obey. But in their hearts, they've already decided on Egypt; to sin. 

These men of Judah are told to trust in the Lord. To stay in the land, to not fear Nebuchadnezzar. To trust the Lord, that He *is with you to save you, and deliver you from his hand*. 

God promises them peace, mercy, to be returned to their own land. If they believe the word of God, they shall be saved. Note they didn't have to do anything other than believe that He would deliver them. That God repented of His wrath, if they simply obey His word. They didn't have to go anywhere. Do anything. Just believe. 

But God knows the heart of man, and He knew they hadn't asked Jeremiah to hear the truth, but to be told what they wanted to hear. That it was ok to flee to Egypt. 

That they should take it up on them to save themselves. 

The Lord promises them that if they don't believe on Him that delivers the faithful, they will be destroyed. That in Egypt, they will die by the sword and famine and pestilence. That they would become an execration, a reproach, a curse. That people would use their fate as a warning to all those who do not obey the good news given by the word of God. 

Unsaved people today will inquire of us, asking what they must do to be saved. And most will hear the gospel and refuse to obey it. They will seek their own works as justification. Or flee back to sin, as these Jews fled to Egypt, ignoring the warning of their destruction. 

And some saved Christians, who believed the gospel and know the word of God is true, that He is faithful, will still fall into sin and in tribulation, refuse to standfast in the faith, but as the house of God, turn from Him disobeying His word, to their destruction.

As Peter asks us; If God will destroy those who are His, chastening every son He receives, if His judgment begins in His own house, against His people, what will He do to those who don't obey the Gospel?

As we near the end of the Book of Jeremiah, we see the prophecy against Babylon, which soon would be crushed by the Medes, establishing the Medo-Persian Empire. Cyrus the Great will eventually restore the remnant of Judah to their land, after the 70 years of captivity, and the 2nd Temple will be built. 

But the Lord used Babylon to crush the rebellion of the Jews against Him. To winnow the wheat from the chaf, just as He will the armies of the Beast in the days of vengeance. In this prophecy, we see dual imagery being used; predictions of the soon to come fall of that great Golden empire, but also of the end times. Of the Lord Jesus and the final destruction of that spirit of Babylon, which works even today. And the promise of eternal peace for God's people, the saints who believed on His word. Because God will have justice for the blood of the innocent, the prophets and if the saints that were all slain upon the earth.

The symbology of these chapters and how they tie in to Daniel and Ezekiel and Revelation is deep. She who is upon many waters. The cup that makes the rulers of the earth drunk. The fornication of idols and false gods. The innocent babes who had been passed through the fire to Baal being part of the army of Christ. The harvest time soon to come. Babylon without foundation or cornerstone, while the Kingdom of Heaven is founded upon the Rock that is Christ. The mountains falling on them as Zion rises.

*The portion of Jacob is not like them; for he is the former of all things: and Israel is the rod of his inheritance: the Lord of hosts is his name.*

The glory of Christ made manifest.

The final chapter of Jeremiah, and what seems to be a recap of events already covered here, and in 2 Kings. The book of **Lamentations** is the poetic book of Jeremiah the "weeping prophet." In it, the desolation of Jerusalem and the sins of the people of Judah, as well as the goodness of God, are described in poetic language. The passages progress from this dismal and dismayed beginning to a bitter understanding of their predicament. 

Much like the progression Jeremiah has in the early chapters of his main book, where he goes from protest and prayer for the salvation of his people, to grave acceptance and faith in the right judgments of the Lord. 

The psalms contained in the 4 short chapters are a comfort in themselves to me when facing tribulation. Things could be much worse. And also a reminder of God's wrath against the ungodly.

How often could we say that our signs are many and hearts faint? 

But unlike Judah, we have a comforter that's with us at all times; the holy Spirit. To know we've never been abandoned or left to our enemies, for the presence of the Lord, the living God, dwells within us. 

As Jesus tells us in **John 14**:

*Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also.*

*Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also; and greater works than these shall he do; because I go unto my Father. And whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If ye shall ask any thing in my name, I will do it. If ye love me, keep my commandments. And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you. I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you.*

So in tribulation, rejoice. We have not been left as Jerusalem. We have a comforter, if we believe on Jesus, trusting His word. And as we walk in Him, so too does the Spirit indwelling us. Jesus promises us He will not leave us comfortless.

One of the major themes of the prophets, aside from the promise of deliverance in the promise of the Lord, is the judgment of God upon those who chase after other gods. Who commit fornication with them, metaphorically. The whoredoms of the people, who He consistently compares to a woman caught in adultery, whose lovers have abandoned her in her downfall. That she is like a woman exposed, naked to the world, ashamed.

The Lord is longsuffering and merciful, His patience and grace are abundant and His love for us who are His is unending. But those who fall away to apostasy, Idolatry, faith in strange gods, while still calling themselves His, provokes Him to wrath. God's name is jealousy. 

So, in our times where the largest sects calling themselves "Christian," are decked in scarlet and purple, clad in gold and jewels, and bowing and serving idols, putting faith in the creation over the Creator, lighting candles and incense to the "queen of heaven," it stirs God to wrath. 

The abominations of the heathen, the shedding of innocent blood, violence, sexual perversions...all of these the Lord hates, but it is that adultery of those harlots that really stirs Him to wrath.

With this perspective, the woman taken in adultery story from the Gospels, takes on added context: 

**John 8:3-11**
*And the scribes and Pharisees brought unto him a woman taken in adultery; and when they had set her in the midst, They say unto him, Master, this woman was taken in adultery, in the very act. Now Moses in the law commanded us, that such should be stoned: but what sayest thou?* 

*This they said, tempting him, that they might have to accuse him. But Jesus stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground, as though he heard them not. So when they continued asking him, he lifted up himself, and said unto them, He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her. And again he stooped down, and wrote on the ground. And they which heard it, being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last: and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst. When Jesus had lifted up himself, and saw none but the woman, he said unto her, Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee? She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.*

Now the scribes sought to test Jesus and make Him choose; either keep the law as they saw it, and stone the woman angering the Romans, or speak against the law, angering the Jews. 

But as we know, Jesus simply said *'He that is without sin among you, cast the first stone.*" 

The truth was they didn't bring her before Him in good faith, they didn't bring the man she had supposedly committed this crime unto death with, that he may face the same justice. But their real sin was their own adultery against God. The hypocrisy wasn't so much in their judgement of the woman, but in their unfaithfulness to the Lord. 

And then Jesus, having shown them their own adulterous hearts, tells the woman to go and sin no more. Which spiritually, in that context of whoredoms against God, is a call to repentance towards Christ. (not a call to sinless perfection and works salvation)

**Lamentations** chapter 2, like chapter 1 and 4, is 22 verses, because these poems are written in an acrostic format, where each verse is started by a letter in the alphabet, in this case the 22 letters of the Hebrew language. Verse 3, as we will see, is 66 verses, because it uses the same format, but repeats 3 lines per letter. 

It is interesting that God's poetry loses nothing in their beauty being translated to English, the poems and Psalms not relying on a meter or rhyme. 

And of course, these poems of lamentation are Jeremiah's weeping over the destruction of Judah by the Babylonians, but clearly by the hand of God. 

The first chapter describing Jerusalem as a widow and an adulterous, left desolate and friendless. The second, a daughter left without hope, covered in a cloud in his anger, and cast down from previous highs, brought low by His wrath. 

The prophet describes how the Lord has torn down their habitations, their walls and strongholds, their temple and altars, kings and princes, priests and prophets. Taken everything from them. That their children beg for wine (juice) and bread in hunger. 

*The Lord was as an enemy*, He bent his bow against them as an enemy. His wrath was upon them as He violently took away their Tabernacle, cast off the altar, ended the law, the sacrifices...taken from them everything. Only a remnant saved, carried away to a far kingdom. All by the hand of God. 

*The young and the old lie on the ground in the streets: my virgins and my young men are fallen by the sword; thou hast slain them in the day of thine anger; thou hast killed, and not pitied. Thou hast called as in a solemn day my terrors round about, so that in the day of the Lord's anger none escaped nor remained: those that I have swaddled and brought up hath mine enemy consumed.*

This it will be in the day of the Lord. The same will happen to the nations of the world. Their temples and kings will be cut off. Their strongholds, even the very mountains they flee to, will be struck down. And the streets will be littered with the bodies of the young and old. None will escape the anger of the Lord except those carried away to His kingdom, His servants, on that great and terrible day.

**Lamentations 3** is one of the most beautiful and heartfelt poetic works of the Bible, which is saying a lot considering the beauty of the Psalms. 

But in the Spirit Jeremiah captures so many things relevant to the life of a believer; the misery of being mired in sin, having God against us, as His enemy, pictures of the suffering of Christ for our sins, salvation by calling upon His name, the humility and faith gained in tribulation, and the imprecatory prayer against those who rise against us, and the prayers for our deliverance from their hands. 

It is an emotional rollercoaster, where for 20 verses we are left in the worst state of man, with images of Jesus' suffering used to describe this lowly state. The gall, the derision, the turning of the other cheek when struck. Bearing the yoke. Being cut off, prayers unheard;

*Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?*

Powerful understanding that as we were, (or are yet) unregenerate sinners, we have the rod against us, being provoked by the Spirit towards repentance, and as low as we feel, Christ Jesus paid a far worse penalty, for our sins not His. And in this remembrance, is our blessed hope:

*My soul hath them still in remembrance, and is humbled in me. This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness. The Lord is my portion, saith my soul; therefore will I hope in him. The Lord is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him. It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord.*

And in this hope, we call upon the name of the Lord, and are filled with the Spirit of His promises. We are assured of our lives being redeemed in Him. His mercies and compassion new every morning. We are called to pick up our cross every day, so if we stumble and backslide, if we turn to the left or the right, God is merciful in calling us back to the straight paths. Regardless of the temptations and tribulations that beset us. 

Even though, as the weeping prophet progresses through the verse; we remember our pain and our adversaries. We have been humbled and understand our own iniquities. We know we are only redeemed in His name. By the blood of Christ. But still, we tearfully know the suffering of life and the cares of the world. **Lamentations** chapter 4 continues the series of acrostic poems by the prophet Jeremiah, lamenting or mourning the desolation of Judah and destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians physically, but under the wrath of God. 

And as we have seen, the weeping prophet uses allegory to paint a picture of the evil he has witnessed. The horrors he prophesied come to pass. 

The sons of Zion are like the spoiled gold if the temple, turned to earthen clay pots. Basically worthless. 

The mammals of the sea, likely seals or small whales, that give suck to their pups, but the daughters of Jerusalem have become like ostriches that abandon their eggs in the wilderness. The babies' tongues are stuck to the roof of their mouths for hunger. There is no bread for the children. Rich men who fared sumptuously are eating dung. 

Jeremiah writes that the destruction of Sodom wasn't as brutal and horrific as Jerusalem, because at least it was quick and complete. Here the starving draws out their suffering.

This under the vow of the Nazarites, who would be by clean living for a short period, be considered the peak of good health, now are sunken and gaunt. 

The women have cooked the flesh of their own children for want of food. 

And this is all because of the wrath of God, who is long suffering and merciful and quick to repent of evil against His people when they repent towards Him. And yet, they were left destroyed and desolate. Spoiled and carried away to captivity. 

Jeremiah calls out the false prophets who shed the blood of the innocent to defend their heresies. Blind guides, as Christ called them, here wandering the streets, polluted in blood of the dead. Unclean. 

The Lord no longer regarding them, just as He no longer regarded Israel after the flesh in **Hebrews 8:9**;

*Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers In the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; Because they continued not in my covenant, And I regarded them not, saith the Lord.*

And the prophet is left weeping at the dismay that has come upon the daughter of Zion.

The final stanzas of lamentations for includes a prophecy against Edom. As we will see in Ezekiel and Obadiah, Eden was destroyed because they rejoiced and mocked the destruction of Israel. We can develop that further later when it comes, but it is something to keep in mind that the brother of Israel faced God's wrath, Just as the final chapters of Jeremiah detailed the destruction of Egypt and the surrounding nations and ultimately Babylon. 

God judges nations based on their works. Even as he judges individuals based on their faith. It's an important distinction to keep in mind as we rightly divide the word of God.

Poor Ezekiel. 

God commands Ezekiel to perform symbolic acts to foreshadow the judgment on Jerusalem and Judah. He is instructed to draw Jerusalem on a clay tablet and stage a siege against it with a wall, battering rams, and camps, representing the city’s impending destruction. Ezekiel is told to lie on his left side for 390 days to bear Israel’s iniquity and on his right side for 40 days for Judah’s sins, each day symbolizing a year of punishment. 

God also commands him to eat a meager ration of bread made from mixed grains and pulse (beans and lentils), baked over dung, to signify the scarcity and defilement of food that the starving people will endure during the siege. Originally, human dung, but to appease Ezekiel, God allows him to use cow dung. Hardly better, but apt given the situation. 

These acts serve as a powerful sign to the Jews of God’s judgment for their disobedience.

The 390 years align with the capture of Judah by the Syrian "king of the North," the Seleucid empire, which would see Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the figure of the antichrist, that vile man, take power in the region. 

The Lord asks much of the prophet. We should be grateful we are given such a light yoke.

**Ezekiel 10** describes a vivid and wild vision of God's glory departing from the temple in Jerusalem. Ezekiel sees the cherubim, angelic beings with four faces and wings, accompanied by wheels full of eyes, moving in unison with the divine presence. 

The glory of the Lord, depicted as a radiant cloud, rises from the cherubim and moves to the temple's threshold, signifying God’s judgment and withdrawal from an unfaithful people. He was no longer present in the Temple. 

The man clothed in linen is instructed to take burning coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city, destroying it with fire. 

Ezekiel says these living creatures, or the beasts in Heaven from revelation, are the same as his first visions, in case there were any doubt. I do not think we can process with our human minds the sights of these things. The Lord pulled away a veil and showed them to the prophet, and he is trying his best in the Spirit to make us understand the glory of what he saw. 

Jerusalem being made desolate is the point, however. There in the 6th year of Babylonian captivity, destruction has come to them for their wicked abominations.

**Ezekiel 14** opens with elders of Israel coming before the prophet to hear him, but the Lord speaks to Ezekiel, saying that they have idols in their hearts and the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face. They have coveted other things before the Lord God. They are unjust and filled with their sins. 

And so the Lord says they should be told to repent, and turn from their idols, turn away their faces from abominations. Otherwise, when anyone, Israelites and strangers in the land, seek a prophet, He will set His face against them. And the prophets will lie to them. And the Lord God says He is the means of deceiving them by the words of that prophet. In other words, He will give them strong delusion, that they believe a lie. 

**2 Thessalonians 2:11-12**
*And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie: that they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness*

The Lord also says that the false prophet will be as punished as these idolatrous men, and all become a proverb and a byword, that Israel turns back towards God.

Then the Lord gives Ezekiel His word, that when God sets out to destroy a land as wicked as Israel, that even if *Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it,* He would only save them themselves from it. 

The illustration that 3 renown righteous men would not be sufficient to save a nation that had backslidden to the point of Judah in this day. No children. No remnant. Only the righteous men themselves. 

This establishes a few things that we may know from other scripture. One that, as Abraham argued with the Lord concerning Sodom and Gomorrah, that the presence of the righteous is generally sufficient to stave off judgement, at least for a time. We are the salt of the earth. We preserve the world unto judgment, but eventually it isn't sufficient and God's wrath comes due. 

Second, when this judgment comes, only the saved are spared. Only those made righteous by faith in the blood are not appointed to wrath. 

Third, it is interesting that Daniel, a contemporary of Ezekiel has, by this time, been noticed of God. It isn't clear that Ezekiel himself may know of Daniel, although the youth was made a president of the Babylonian empire early in captivity. But the Lord knows, and knowing we'd know, he is held up as an example. 

Finally, there is a tendency of God's mercy, that when it isn't a final judgment, when it serves His needs, He will save the family of the righteous from that judgment. As 8 were saved by the righteousness of Noah. As Lot's wife (almost!) and his daughters are saved from Sodom. As the remnant of sons and daughters mentioned here in **Exikiel 14**.

In **Ezekiel 16**, Jerusalem is personified as a woman whom God rescued, adorned, and entered into a covenant with (verses 6–14), akin to a marriage. 

However, her persistent idolatry and unfaithfulness (v15–34) provoke God’s judgment, described in terms of punishment and abandonment (v 35–43). The chapter reads as a writ of divorce. God breaking up with her, in a spiritual metaphor. 

When God found her, she (Judah specifically here, but Israel generally), they were as the Canaanites. Worse, they were abandoned. Alone. Again this isn't literal and genetic, but their spiritual condition. Abram was a Chaldean. Jacob was a Hebrew, as Abraham lived in Hebron. 

There was intermarriage with the Canaanites, but the analogy is not about lineage but beliefs and idolatry. 

When God lays out their abominations, giving the fine clothing, incense and worship to strange gods that was meant for Him, and murdered rhe children He gave them it is adultery and worse than the abominations of Samaria (Israel) or even Sodom. 

The idea that what they did was worse than Sodom and her daughters, the like cities around them, is a theme. The worst place imaginable, and yet unfaithful Judah is worse:

**Isaiah 1:9**
*Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.*

**Matthew 11:24** 
*But I say unto you, That it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment, than for thee.*

They despised their oath. They broke the covenant. They behaved like their sisters, humanity that didn't know better or didn't have the privilege that He had bestowed upon them. The line of David. The glory of Solomon. The oracles of God, the Temple, the blessing and the promise. And so God is righteous to divorce them. 

But, despite this condemnation, the Lord leaves room for hope. Christ is coming. And not only would Judah be restored, but her "sisters," the Gentiles. That He will establish His covenant, and we shall know He is the Lord.

This parable, a riddle posed to the people of Jerusalem, is difficult to follow, but God gives the answers.

A great eagle (representing the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar) comes to Lebanon (symbolizing Jerusalem), takes the highest branch of a cedar (the king of Judah, Jehoiachin), and carries it to a land of merchants (Babylon). 
 
The eagle then takes “seed of the land” (Zedekiah, a new king from the royal line) and plants it in fertile soil by abundant waters, where it grows into a low, spreading vine (Judah under Zedekiah’s rule, dependent on Babylon). 

Another great eagle (representing Egypt) appears, and the vine (Zedekiah) turns toward it, seeking support, despite being planted in good soil. This symbolizes Zedekiah’s rebellion against Babylon by seeking an alliance with Egypt.

And so, the Lord asks, can they prosper? 

By turning to Egypt and asking for horses and men to push out the Babylonian rule, they insult God and seek to mollify His judgment. So no, they will not prosper. It's vain.

And so, Egypt’s help will fail Judah. Babylon will overpower Jerusalem because Zedekiah despised his oath and covenant with Nebuchadnezzar. An oath made in the Lord's name. 

**2 Chronicles 36:13**
*And he also rebelled against king Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God: but he stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart from turning unto the Lord God of Israel.* 

This betrayal and violation of the covenant means that nothing that follows will prosper. But the Lord Himself has another covenant, made with David, for a Messiah. 

And so, God turns the parable to Himself as the eagle, and that He will plant a cutting on Zion, cropped off the top of that cedar, representing David's lineage. A goodly cedar shall bring forth boughs, many branches bearing fruit. And under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing, the saved from many nations, and in His shadow shall we dwell. 

He shall exalt the low tree, being down the high tree, dry up the green tree (unbelieving Jews) and make the dry tree flourish, the faithful Gentiles. 

*I the Lord have spoken and have done it.* Centuries before the physical birth of Jesus, it is already done. Amen

This prophecy of Exikiel is an often cited chapter regarding the doctrine of "original sin," which it clearly teaches against. But it is also cited by workies as to why turning from sin is part of salvation. But as always, we need to look at the context. 

First, the parable among the children of Israel in Judah, that the fathers ate sour grapes, but the children's teeth are on edge, has to be understood. And it is something many of us are guilty of saying. 

The judgment against the people had come, and Babylon was bringing them into captivity, and slaying many. So the younger generation was blaming the sins of the older generation for their troubles. That their fathers had eaten the sour grapes but they were the ones with the taste in their mouth. That God's judgment was unfair, and they were being punished for the sins of the father. 

We often blame Boomers for ruining the country they inherited, and it is true. They set up high places and committed adultery and violence and rejected the God of their fathers. But many who complain the loudest about this are themselves living the same way, or worse. 

Revival is on us, today and our present generation. As it says in verse 14, *Now, lo, if he beget a son, that seeth all his father's sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like*...he shall surely live. 

It is up to us to get right, regardless of the hole dug by our parents. This is true regardless of the age we live in. And if we haven't, there's always time for turning from our own sins, and walking in righteousness, through Christ. 

The Lord has no pleasure in the deaths of the wicked, but rejoices in those who turn to Him and live. 

The word of the Lord shuts down the idea of original sin condemning us. The sins and the righteousness of each generation are their own. A man isn't judged by the sins of their father or his righteousness, but by theirs. And vice versa. 

We aren't condemned by Adam's sin, but by our own. We have his nature, being sons. But we all make our own way. 

But the Lord challenged the people saying He is unfair, because in fact they did as their fathers.

As for the use of this to teach "repent of your sins" for salvation, we understand that this is in the context of a nation being judged. While God's judgment is upon the wicked, and His mercy is upon those that walk in His ways, the wrath upon a people is based on their nation's sin. He will spare the righteous from His wrath. That's a promise.

It's important in understanding this particular prophecy of God that this is not about salvation, it is about life on this earth, and soul in this sense means the person. Spirit and body together form a soul. 

Now with that understanding, let us consider the opening verse. *What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge?* 

The saying refers to the idea that the children of Israel are claiming that God is judging unfairly by punishing them for what their parents did. What their immediate forefathers got up to. That they ate sour grapes but it's the children whose teeth are on edge. 

It's important to keep this chapter of Ezekiel in mind when we're looking at the boomer question. God judges us fairly on this earth, saved or unsaved. We may suffer from the sins of a father, but our own inequities are what we are punished with. 

Just as a just man may have an unjust son, so too can an unjust man have a just son. It is the keeping of the statutes and doctrines of God that prolongs ones life and brings blessings to it. It is being mired in sin that brings ruin and physical death, regardless of your faith in Christ. 

If anything you're chastised even more so as a child of God. 

So while it is well and good to point out the sins of the father, that we may learn from them and not do them, we can't blame our troubles on God punishing us for our father's sake. It's entirely up to us to forge ahead in a righteous life.

Basically, people need to understand; *the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.* 

You have no one to blame but yourself. No matter how wicked your father or mother may have been, your life on this earth, and eternal life to come is entirely up to us.

The word of the Lord gives a scathing sermon against the whoredoms of Israel and Judah. Where some prophecy is more obscure, parables and dark sayings, this is plain and undeniable in its meaning. God is very specific as to what it is all about. The adultery of His people. 

The fornication in Egypt, that He took them out from. And the adultery of Samaria with Assyria. And the whoredoms of Judah with Babylon, Assyria and Egypt. 

Their blood is upon them. The wrath abiding to the uttermost. What else is there to say? The judgment is come for their idolatry and lewdness and the blood upon their heads. Their defilement of the holy city and the Tabernacle. 

*And ye shall know I am the Lord God*.

The current debates over the role of modern Israel, Zionism and dispensationalism in Christianity rests on the idea that the Jews are and always have been God's chosen people. His elect by the law and the covenant. That He would always bless Israel. 

The false understanding many professing Christians have is that in the Old Testament, Jews were the heroes of the story. That while they had their faults, God never rejected them, and in the New Testament, other than some of their leaders, they still were God's chosen, and so someday, all physical Israel would be saved. 

It is impossible to read the prophets and come away with the idea that the Jews are generally the good guys. They were always a stiff-necked rebellious people who needed to be punished to do right, and even then rarely repented. 

Full of complaints. Full of formication and adultery. From Egypt through Babylonian captivity, and beyond. They were continually cursed and spoken against by the word of God.

As in the previous chapter, **Ezekiel 26** contains prophecy against another nation, not Israel and Judah. Here, it is the Phoenician land of Tyre, their city of Zidon, in Palestine. The coasts of the Mediterranean. 

A Semitic people, a great seafaring empire of trade, and who, at many times throughout the history of Israel, were friends and allies. It is likely that there were many believers among them. They helped build Solomon's temple, and provided great ships to increase the king's wealth. 

In many ways, Tyre serves as a picture of the believing Gentiles of the early Christians, the pillars Jesus builds His church of. Like cedars of Lebanon. And like the gathering of wealth from abroad to bring home to Zion. 

But here, centuries later as Babylon rises in power, Tyre falls to the wrath of God. 

Their sin, like the other nations mentioned in chapter 25, include mocking the fate of Judah, its desolation and captivity. Of seeking to take advantage and loot and pillage what's left in Judea. 

As we see in the other prophets, God's word of judgement was given repeatedly to them, that they had no excuse. 

We should also note that, while God held Jerusalem and the line of David, His chosen place and lineage to bring about the Christ, the Messiah, He did not focus all of His attentions only on Israel. He is the God of all nations. His will was always that all men come unto Him. 

Israel itself was meant to be a beacon of light unto the nations. A peculiar people. A royal priesthood. But their failure led to our gain, amen. Ultimately, the covenant with Israel was done away with, and only the new and better testament remains. Salvation in the blood of Jesus. Amen.

Continuing the prophecies against the nations in proximity to Judah, we have in **Ezekiel 29** two against the kingdom of Egypt. 

The first prophecy, in the 10th year, 10th month, 12th day (around 587 BC), was given during the siege of Jerusalem, before its fall in 586 BC (the 11th year by the prophets reckoning, which uses the reign of King Zedekiah as a starting point). This is when Egypt was still a potential player in the region, promising aid to Judah against Babylon. 

God's anger at the Jews who turned to Egypt for help is found throughout the prophets, particularly Jeremiah. 

Because Egypt represents the old, unsaved life of Christians, under bondage to sin, we can draw an application here to not turn to the world for help when we are in trouble, but to turn only the the Lord. 

God says Egypt is like a staff of a reed, the hollow and weak grass that grows by a river. Especially the Nile. That Israel leaned on for support, but it buckles immediately and they bruise their shoulder and put them in the ground. 

We should look at the world's solutions to our problems the same way. Weak and insufficient, knocking us on our butts when we rely on them.

 
The second prophecy is made 16 years later, (571 BC) and comes after Nebuchadnezzar’s prolonged siege of Tyre (circa 585–572 BC), which was costly and yielded little reward, as Tyre’s island fortress was difficult to conquer, although it destroyed Tyre's power. This later prophecy clarifies that Egypt would be given to Nebuchadnezzar as a “wage” for his efforts against Tyre. 

The word of God said that Egypt would be scattered and taken into captivity for 40 years, (echoing the 40 years Israel spent in the wilderness) and when it gathered again, it would never be as powerful. This way, when Cyrus gives the go-ahead to the Jews to rebuild Jerusalem, there's no temptation to lean again on Egypt. 

In your Christian walk, this sort of thing may happen, where the supports you have among friends, family, alcohol and drugs, old habits and lifestyles, even hobbies and activities, may be taken from you for a season, long enough to not be available to you for support or shelter, and if they ever come back around, their weakness is obvious. You cannot count on them. It is the Lord only we can depend on. Amen.

We see in the prophets that there was a timeline given, specific events and kingdoms would come to be exactly as God said. That we may know He is the Lord. 

Nations that God said would never recover, didn't. Egypt was never a power again. Assyria was gone. Babylon never rebuilt. Etc...

In that process, we also see how events put in motion the very things that led to the future prophecy of Medo-Persians, Alexander the Great, the Hellenistic and Ptolemy kingdoms, and ultimately Rome for the time of Christ. 

The fulfillment of Ezekiel’s prophecies, with Babylon and later Persia, weakening key Middle Eastern and African nations, created favorable conditions for Alexander’s rapid conquests by reducing any resistance.

This, in turn, set the stage for Rome by leaving a fragmented, Hellenistic world that Rome could easily conquer and absorb. 

While Ezekiel’s focus is divine judgment, the historical outcomes align with the prophesied decline of these nations, directly shaping the things yet to come. 

It isn't just God calling His shots, it is how God uses all things to His will. Stepping back and seeing the overall picture, measured in centuries, it is hard not to see, that we may **know** that He is the Lord.
