**Ezekiel 33** contains a lot of doctrine, and is one of the most often cited chapters of the prophet. Due to time and density, I will break it down over a few days. 

The Parable of the Watchman is told in verses 1-9, and the idea of being a watchman, warning for danger is given, a trope used earlier in **Ezekiel 3**;

If you recall, God appoints Ezekiel as a watchman for the house of Israel, instructing him to warn the people of God’s judgment. If Ezekiel warns the wicked and they do not turn, their blood is on their own heads. If he fails to warn them, their blood is on his hands. 

**Ezekiel 3:17**
*Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me*.

Here, in **Ezekiel 33**, the word of the Lord establishes this be understood to all the watchmen appointed to warn of the impending judgment, coming in the form of Babylon. The sword which is coming against Judah for her sin. 

A good watchman sounds the trumpet, notifying the people of danger, and should they not heed it, the watchman is free from their blood.

But if the watchman doesn't sound the horn, he carries the blood of all those he could have warned. 

In the days of siege warfare and raids, this was serious stuff. And again, in OT days, quite literal. 

In the New Testament we are given these parables and stories for our own admonition and to teach us spiritual things, as Paul's application in **Acts** shows us, warning others about death and Hell, the coming judgment, removes their blood from our heads. 

Soul-winning, or rather soul warning, is a responsibility for all saved Christians. That whenever we have the opportunity, we should be sounding the alarm. Blowing the trumpet. Warning others of the danger of an unregenerate life. Paul says he has done this, and is pure of the blood of all men. 

When we miss opportunity to warn others, to share the gospel, we are like the watchman who fails to sound the alarm. Derelict Christians. And those who we could have warned and didn't, God says *his blood will I require at the watchman's hand*. 

When we go out into the highways and hedges to compel others to come to the Lord, or tell our friends and family about eternal life and damnation, we cannot force them to accept the invitation. That is between the Spirit and them. 

But we can and must warn them.

I know it weighs heavy on my heart the number of people I have passed on giving the gospel too. The regret of hearing someone you know died, that you never warned. Feeling that blood on your head. I think every Christian, even babes in Christ, have had this feeling. 

"Oh, how I wish I had warned them!" is a common lament. 

How much more then should we feel that burden when we don't go soul-winning? When given a church, an opportunity to door knock, and we don't go?

It's one thing to wake to a fire in your own house, and warn your family to flee. But if you passed the home of strangers, and saw a fire spreading, wouldn't you bang on the door to get them to evacuate? 

Or would you pass on by, leaving them to burn? 

We cannot reach everyone. It would be difficult to quit our jobs, abandon our family and make evangelizing the world out only purpose. But everyone can spare a few hours a week to go soul-winning. 

If you aren't part of a church, join one, even if it is for this sole purpose. 

Organized door knocking is more profitable, and having a place to send the souls won to be taught all things and be baptized is crucial. 

If you go to church, and they don't have soul-winning, ask the pastor to start a program. Offer to organize it. There are faithful people who would make excellent watchmen, sitting on the sidelines for lack of a program. 

Warn souls. Be pure of the blood of all men.

Reading through Ezekiel 36 and 37, and remembering that Hal Lindsey used these chapters as the basis for his hyper dispensationalist Zionist writings in the 1970s. He had a very popular book that absolutely tainted the discussion around end times Bible prophecy, even after his predictions failed to occur. 

Hal Lindsey, in *The Late Great Planet Earth* (1970) and later works, made several specific end-times predictions that failed to materialize. He suggested the rapture might occur in 1988, 40 years after Israel’s 1948 founding, based on his reading of **Matthew 24:34**, but no such event happened. He predicted the Soviet Union, as “Gog” from **Ezekiel 38-39**, would invade Israel, which never occurred before the USSR’s 1991 collapse. 

Lindsey also linked the European Economic Community, a precursor to the EU, to a revived Roman Empire led by the Antichrist, but the EEC’s evolution into the EU didn’t align with his vision. Because the eec had at one time, 10 Nations, he claimed it was the ten horns found in Revelation. 

He foresaw a 200-million-man Chinese army attacking Israel (**Revelation 9:16**), which never materialized, and a rebuilt Jerusalem Temple, which remains unconstructed. 

These unfulfilled predictions, tied to 1970s geopolitical fears, drew criticism for their speculative nature and weakened Lindsey’s credibility among some evangelicals. The popularity of the book, which sold over 30 million copies, cemented many of the key ideas into the public consciousness.

A lot of people get confused about Gog and Magog. There is a lot of eschetology and charts and predictions about who these are and what it means in current times.

During the 1940s to 1990s, various theories emerged about the identities of Gog and Magog, often reflecting the geopolitical climate of the time. 

In the 1940s, some Christians  associated Gog and Magog with Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan, tying them to their roles as aggressors in World War II. 

From the 1950s through the 1980s, it became popular in evangelical circles to identify Gog as the Soviet Union and Magog as its satellite states or China, driven by Cold War fears of communism. 

In the 1980s, Ronald Reagan and New Christian Right leaders specifically linked Gog to the Soviet Union, emphasizing its communistic and atheistic nature.

 Following the Soviet Union's collapse in the 1990s, some speculated Gog and Magog could represent Russia and allies like Iran, influenced by Middle Eastern conflicts. 

By the late 1990s, George W. Bush connected Gog to Iraq, citing biblical prophecy especially post-9/11. 

These interpretations consistently mapped biblical figures onto contemporary geopolitical rivals, ignoring the timing given in scripture. 

They would conflate the battle of Armageddon that comes at the return of Christ on the day of the Lord, at the beginning of wrath and before the Millennium, with the events described here, which occurs afterwards. 

Handy to blame your current enemies as the enemies of God. But it isn't cut and dry and it is not possible to prove who makes up the final army of Satan when we're are always more than 1,000 years away from it happening.

Of course this confusion and political opportunism in end times Bible prophecy gained more and more traction with the adoption of dispensationalism and Zionism, post 1948. Where the Jews being given Israel by the UN was seen as the fulfillment of the dry bones prophecy (it wasn't). 

Then they would just conflate Armageddon and Gog and Magog and make whoever the Jews were against into these armies of the beast.

As we enter the final chapters of Ezekiel, 40-48, we are given one last prophetic vision of the Lord, and again, as in earlier prophecies, an angelic being is given as a tour guide of sorts to the man of God. 

Ezekiel’s visions are often revealed by divine messengers delivering profound messages about judgment and restoration. In **Ezekiel 1:4-28**, he encounters the four cherubim, radiant beings with four faces (man, lion, ox, eagle), wings, and wheels. They show him God’s glory on the throne. In **Ezekiel 8:1-16**, the fiery, amber-skinned figure shows the prophet God’s glory in the temple in Jerusalem, and the corruption of the temple, exposing the abomination of idols, Tammuz worship, and sun worship. In **Ezekiel 10:1-22**, the cherubim reappear, moving with God’s glory as He departs the temple, confirming the withdrawal of divine presence due to the abominations and sin of the Jews. 

Finally, in **Ezekiel 40:1-47**, a bronze-like man with a measuring rod and line appears to show Ezekiel a detailed vision of a new temple, and a vision of future restoration. 

**Recall Ezekiel 8:1-3;**

*Then I beheld, and lo a likeness as the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins even downward, fire; and from his loins even upward, as the appearance of brightness, as the colour of amber. And he put forth the form of an hand, and took me by a lock of mine head; and the spirit lifted me up between the earth and the heaven, and brought me in the visions of God to Jerusalem, to the door of the inner gate that looketh toward the north; where was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provoketh to jealousy. And, behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there, according to the vision that I saw in the plain.*

Here, he writes *behold, there was a man, whose appearance was like the appearance of brass, with a line of flax in his hand, and a measuring reed; and he stood in the gate.*

Similar, but not identical descriptions. 

Also, the concept of the reed and measure is repeated in John's encounter in **Revelation 11:1-2**;

*And there was given me a reed like unto a rod: and the angel stood, saying, Rise, and measure the temple of God, and the altar, and them that worship therein. But the court which is without the temple leave out, and measure it not; for it is given unto the Gentiles: and the holy city shall they tread under foot forty and two months*.

The text does not explicitly state that John completes the act of measuring nor does the Bible record the dimensions of the measurements if he had. But in **Ezekiel 40** onward, the bronze-like man meticulously measures the temple with highly detailed dimensions of the temple. 

The being measures the temple's walls, gates, courts, chambers, and pillars. He gives the layout of each, along with the purpose for many of the inner chambers described. His reed is 6 cubits long, with each cubit being roughly 18 inches plus 1 handspan (6 inches), making a cubit 24 inches. Thus, the reed is 6 cubits or 144 inches, so approximately 12 feet. 

Solomon’s Temple **(1 Kings 6)** was 60 cubits long, 20 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high. Each cubit is 18 inches, so the temple was 90 feet long, 30 feet wide, and 45 feet high.

Ezekiel’s Temple is described as 100 cubits long, 100 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high. Each cubit is 24 inches, so the temple was 200 feet long, 200 feet wide, and 60 feet high. Much, much larger footprint. 

Ezekiel’s vision includes a vast outer area (about 5100 feet square), far exceeding Solomon’s Temple courts. 

Contrast this with the 2nd Temple of Ezra and Nehemiah’s Temple, which was 60 cubits long, 60 cubits wide, and 60 cubits high. Each cubit is 18 inches, so the temple was 90 feet long, 90 feet wide, and 90 feet high.

This discrepancy is important to keep in mind when trying to discern what Ezekiel's vision is describing. Obviously both the 1st and 2nd Temples were built on Mt Moriah, the site of Abraham's aborted sacrifice of Isaac.

The site of the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, which David purchased and made sacrifice to end the plague on his people for his sin of counting them. Where Solomon built his temple.

Today, it is called the Temple Mount, and is much disputed between the Muslims and Jews, as it is the site of a mosque. 

But the relevant thing to understand is that, despite the destruction and clearing of the land by the Romans, the site isn't sufficiently large enough to fit Ezekiel's temple. 

Ezekiel’s temple complex (1000 x 1000 feet) would fit within the Temple Mount’s dimensions (1600 x 900 feet), occupying less than half its area of roughly 35 acres. However, the complex’s vast outer area (500 reeds square, approximately 5100 feet square or 1 mile square) is too large for the current Temple Mount, suggesting a significant topographical change, like a supernaturally elevated Mount Zion, would be needed to accommodate its building.

All this math to say, the main theories about what exactly Ezekiel is being shown here, could possibly be correct, but none completely line up with other scripture, history and current topographical reality, in a neat and clear way. 

Could this be a command for the 2nd Temple that fell short? Zerubbabel’s temple, smaller in footprint and lacking the expansive courts of Ezekiel’s vision, didn’t match the grand design. This could reflect practical limitations—limited resources, a smaller population, or Persian oversight—falling short of God’s ideal blueprint.

Some Jewish traditions suggest the returned exiles’ efforts were a partial fulfillment, constrained by their circumstances. For all have fallen short of the glory of God. 

This theory is especially plausible given the timing of the prophecy. Ezekiel’s temple vision occurs in the 25th year of his exile, around 573 BC, counting from his deportation in 597 BC with King Jehoiachin. 

Jeremiah’s prophecy predicts a 70-year exile for Judah, starting with the first Babylonian siege in 605 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar took captives like Daniel. By 573 BC, this marks roughly the 33rd year of Jeremiah’s 70-year timeline. Nearly the halfway point of the captivity. 

Also, the description of the sacrifices and the continued elevation of the Levitical line of the sons of Zadok (rather than Aaron, a change made by Solomon in **1 Kings 2**) as the high priests, marks it as of the time of the 2nd Temple. 

It would be counter to the New Testament that we are under to have a priestly caste and animal sacrifices in a temple that, as we will see, has the presence of God within. 

But again, the problem is that if this was the expectation of God's perfect plan that the Jews returning from captivity failed to achieve, it wouldn't fit on the very site that was given. Assuming cubits are consistent. 

There are other theories we can explore as this continues. But again, we see through a glass darkly and we should be open to the idea that some things we just don't know.

*But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, then should no place have been sought for the second. For finding fault with them, he saith, Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah*

The moral law and commandments, which are still in effect today in the NT, were a schoolmaster to lead us to Christ for salvation. Same then as today. Even the law written in our hearts, for the Gentiles without the advantage of the oracles of God. All have sinned and fallen short, so we need a spiritual redeemer. 

But the laws of sanctification and reconciliation for the physical nation were not only doable, but God gave pretty explicit instructions on how to maintain it, which some of the time -  during the period of the Wilderness, the entry into the promised land, here and there during the time of Judges and Kings, they managed to keep. And had God's blessings upon them. 

Israel was meant to be a light unto the world. Showing all nations that if they did these things and sought after God, they would be blessed as well. Eventually, it would lead to the culmination of the time of Christ, the BRANCH, The Lord, the King of Kings, coming to establish all of the end times promises of the Kingdom given to the people. In the city He chose to place His name. In the line of David as promised. 

And they would not. 

So, when Jesus did come, the leaders of the Jews were unable to deliver a people meet for repentance. They, being teachers of the Law were blind guides, thinking that whatever promises they had, were deserved being "Abraham's seed." That their added rituals and Pharisaical cleansings meant they deserved both the spiritual salvation and the restoration of their earthly kingdom. 

And rather than being ready for the Kingdom, they were instead cut off and cast out. 

**Matthew 8:11-12**
*And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven. But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.*

This is why they expected a conquering Christ and an earthly kingdom. This is why they placed more value in the carnal and forgot the spiritual things of God, like mercy and judgment. Their entitled attitudes, after so long a period of judgment and chastisement against Israel by God to get them to get right, was the result of hardened hearts and stuff necks. 

And so they killed Christ and His death and blood entered us into a new testament, a better covenant. With better promises. Not a physical nation of the law and circumcision of the flesh, but a spiritual nation and a people circumcised of the heart. 

And with the fading away of the Mosaic covenant, there was a necessary change made to the law. 

**Hebrews 7:12**
*For the priesthood being changed, there is made of necessity a change also of the law.*

The end to the Levitical priesthood of Aaron or Zadok, an end to sacrifices and diverse washings and Sabbaths and carnal ordinances. All these things satisfied in Jesus. 

But the end of the Old Testament also meant the elimination of certain aspects of the end times prophecies. Not all, but some. 

Just as the children of Israel who left Egypt and were promised Canaan, yet died in the wilderness, just as Saul was given **two** chances to be part of the lineage of Christ (once from his own anointment, and a second chance through his daughter Mical and David), just as all the other people who had a promise made that they lost by their own actions. 

**1 Samuel 13:13-14**
*And Samuel said to Saul, Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the Lord thy God, which he commanded thee: for now would the Lord have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever. But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the Lord hath commanded him to be captain over his people, because thou hast not kept that which the Lord commanded thee.*

Just as David would have built the first Temple, but his actions ended that, and Solomon built it instead. 

These missed opportunities didn't make God a liar when He promised them. But He rightly withdrew them when those the promises were made to didn't keep up their end.

All this to say that the 5th theory of Ezekiel's Temple is that it is a picture of a promise for an end-times that will now never be. That God was promising the Jews in captivity a chance to make things right. That by His grace and mercy and longsuffering, He was telling them of the glory of the Kingdom of God that He had in mind for them IF they turned back and were faithful. 

An alternate ending of things that, though He knew wouldn't come, God was graciously offering Israel, one last time. 

And so Jesus came not to judge the world, which He would have had they listened, but to offer salvation. 

**John 12:47**
*And if any man hear my words, and believe not, I judge him not: for I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.*

God continued to see His will done, by other means. Because, despite the Calvinist protests, we are given free will, yet our God is not weak and beggarly as Calvin's having to micromanage everything to reach a conclusion He desires. The Lord can let all creation do as all creatures will, and regardless of our choices, still will His Kingdom come. 

And so, Ezekiel's Temple will never be. It was an offer that isn't. Not because of a flaw with God, but with the people.

An alternate universe, where **Ezekiel 40-48** serves as **Revelation**. It's the most glaring example of what could have been in the Old Testament end-times prophecy. An achievable promise, rejected by those it was promised to.

And so the implications of this Theory are broad and deep. It would apply to just about every covenant promise made with conditions to the people of Israel in the Old Testament and any differences between Old Testament prophecy of end times and New. 

Ezekiel's Battle of Gog and Magog has some different aspects to it than Revelation's. They still happen, As described by John from the Revelation given him, and the difference is what could have been versus what will be now that the Old Testament is done away with. Necessary changes. 

The millennial Kingdom references in Old Testament prophecy very slightly from what we are clearly taught in the new New Testament. 

All of the little nuances and seeming contradictions and places where people trying to rightly divide the word of God are jamming Square pegs into round holes to make the prophecies we are given in the New Testament fit with the promises given in the Old. 

One of the evils of dispensationalism is that it has so badly blinded everyone, but even we who reject it are so used to dealing with everything on their terms. What if that's just a huge mistake. What if we need to scrap everything that comes out of Darby and Schofield and dispensationalism entirely, and take a new view of the Old Testament through the lens of the New?

Honestly, this might be the most important post of my Bible study. It reframes quite a bit of uncertainty that I've had that I've had and a bunch of pieces are clicking into place because of the implications. Trying to keep this frame of reference going forward while simultaneously looking back and applying it is going to be a challenge but I think it's the right thing to do. I think it's how we rightly divide the word. 

That the only difference of dispensations doesn't revolve around salvation which was always by grace through faith, but two major dispensations of how things would have gone or will go.

And of course the practical application for Christians today that we should take away from this is that concept of missed opportunities. Of promises made by God that we just miss out on because of our own choices. Ways that we could be used by God and blessed by God, and anointings to His purpose, what could have been... All undone by sin and stubbornness and self-will. 

And even if we have made mistakes in our past that could have made things turn out different had we done the right thing, there's still reconciliation with God because we are saved. There are still opportunities that He has for us because he can use anyone for His purpose. If we turn from our wicked ways, and walk in His paths, and hold His judgments, we can be restored and do great works for the Lord.

I realize that almost no one is going to read all of this however I highly recommend that you do. If you have problems differentiating the seeming contradictions of the Old Testament and the New Testament and why things were the way they were and what changed and all of that this study is going to help you.

The Temple of Ezekiel prophecy continues, with the laying down of the law; the customs and ordinances that would be observed in this Temple, the House of the Lord. 

The East Gate remains closed, but the inner gate of the courtyard that faces it would be opened on the Sabbaths and holy days. The prince, who would enter in by the porch would be by the pillar, and give his offerings, and worship there. 

The people would enter either by the North Gate or the South Gate, but we're not allowed to leave by the way they came in. 

This is a picture of our spiritual state upon entering into the house of God. We shouldn't leave the same as we came in. It should change us, by the hearing of the word and the worship of the Lord.

There are further instructions for the places of boiling and baking and slaying the sacrifices the people bring. All a picture of the lamb. If things had been different, and Jesus hadn't been killed, these sanctification rituals would have continued. But in His sacrifice, we are cleansed by the Spirit. A better covenant.

Here in the final chapter of Ezekiel, we are given a division of land in the city, its suburbs and a grid roughly 50 miles by 20, as an oblation, or a holy section for the Levites, priests of Zadok, and a portion for the prince and the Temple. 

The land is divided systematically among the twelve tribes, with a central holy portion for the sanctuary. The chapter begins by assigning land to seven tribes north of the holy oblation, from the northern border of the land and decending southward. Dan, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh and Ephraim (Joseph's double portion), Ruben and Judah which borders the holy oblation. 

These stacked portions are as wide as the land reserved for the city, roughly 50miles. Their height is not clear but seems to be an equal division. Perhaps this is an idealized, God-designed Israel. Just as He alotted the tribes in the wilderness, He does so here in a way less spread out and uneven than the lots cast when Joshua divided the land. 

South of the oblation, the holy area, are plots for the remaining tribes, Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulon, and Gad. 

The dimensions are given but other than a quick calculation, I don't know exactly. But it is orderly and symmetrical, and logical. 

The size of the the overall area is significantly smaller than the New Jerusalem that comes down from Heaven in **Revelation 21**. 

*And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain, and shewed me that great city, the holy Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God, Having the glory of God: and her light was like unto a stone most precious, even like a jasper stone, clear as crystal; And had a wall great and high, and had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written thereon, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel: On the east three gates; on the north three gates; on the south three gates; and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. And he that talked with me had a golden reed to measure the city, and the gates thereof, and the wall thereof. And the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth: and he measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand furlongs. The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal. And he measured the wall thereof, an hundred and forty and four cubits, according to the measure of a man, that is, of the angel.*

This city is significantly larger, and a cube. But it contains the same 12 gates, each named for a tribe of Israel. 

Again, Ezekiel's Temple seems to be an idealized design, but to be made with human hands whereas the heavenly city is made by God, and its glory and size and treasure is infinitely greater.

This design and God's plans for man can be debated, but the fact that God has greater things in store for us than we can ever imagine, if we simply obey Him and His commandments, and seek to do His will. 

We have all fallen short. We won't love Him as we should until the resurrection. We won't be perfect until then. But we can be useful and conform to the will of the Lord that we may be used by Him. Separate. In order. Not of confusion and the chaos that our sinful lives create. 

The more we walk with God and spend time with Jesus, we should be changed. We should understand the promises He has made us, out of the abundance of Christ's love and mercy, requires sacrifice and commitment. That we not quench the Spirit, or deny His influence. Not feeding the flesh. 

I fail at it daily, but God's mercies are fresh each morning. So we should pick up our cross and seek to be followers of Him, doers of the law not hearers only. 

Only God knows the secret things He has in store for us when we do. Amen

And with it much of the vessels of Solomon's temple, brought to Shinar, and the house of Nebuchadnezzar's god. This will be important later, after the captivity ends under Cyrus of the Persians. 

And among the captives, those of David's lineage, of Judah, were brought into the service of the king as eunuchs. In hopes the highborn would have better intellect and ability to learn the Babylonian tongue, Chaldean, as well as its learning and ways, to better serve the king. 

We meet *Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah*, and they are given Chaldean names; *Daniel the name of Belteshazzar; and to Hananiah, of Shadrach; and to Mishael, of Meshach; and to Azariah, of Abednego*.

(I still call the three Rack, Shack and Benny. Old habits die hard)

In a show of magnanimity, the king allows the eunuchs to eat of his meat and drink, the food apparently offered to his god. With the intent that they grow to be nourished enough to stand before the king and serve him. 

But Daniel asks the prince of the eunuchs, his overseer, if rather than defile themselves with the meat and drink offered to idols, if he and the three others may eat pulse, that is lentils. 

Daniel, meek and faithful, doesn't rebel against the authority in his life, and yet doesn't compromise his faith and love of God. He instead asks permission. 

When the prince of the eunuchs explains that it would get him in trouble if they seem to be less healthy than those who ate the king's portion, Daniel offers him a compromise; feed them 10 days and try them. If they aren't any worse for it, then honor this request. 

Many people today hate the idea of submitting to authority. They want to riot in the daytime, and seek to use their faith to justify their rebellion. 

They say they won't pay taxes, despite Jesus saying to render unto Caesar. Despite clear commands to render duty and honor and tribute to those set above us by God. Men refusing to submit to any authority. Refusing to join a church and submit themselves to a pastor. Who slack off at work, and constantly disrespecting their bosses. 

This encourages the feminism that tells wives to rebel against husbands, and children against parents. Ultimately, it is rebellion against God. 

The Bible says  *For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry*.

But what if authority over you asks you to do something that would offend God? Daniel shows us how it is done. 

Meekly asking to be tried, the overseer agrees and after 10 days the four are healthier looking than all the other eunuchs. Daniel honored the authority in his life and pleased God. An example for us to follow.

And so after the 3 years of preparation, the king brought the eunuchs in and found none as excellent as Daniel and the others. 10 times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm. And so now Daniel as well as Rack, Shack and Benny, in are on good terms with the King. And Daniel will continue as an advisor over the next several monarchs. In a position to do Godly things for the Lord in an ungodly place.

This is why it's so important for us to be a good witness in the world. If we have secular jobs we have to let the light of God shine through us. As we will see later on it will lead to great things for the Lord. But it starts with obedience and humility.

Before I begin, I want to recognize that Daniel's prayer, blessing the Lord our God should be ours as well. Our God is an awesome God. 

I've written about it before, especially in the prophets, that the prophecies of the Bible are so precise, prescient and perfect, that it is impossible to believe anything other than an omniscient God could have made them known. 

The Old Testament is for our admonition, to instruct us in the ways of righteousness and make known the mystery of the gospel. That faith comes from hearing the word of God. 

How can you not see **Daniel 2** as evidence of things unseen? The substance of things hoped for? How can it be read, and from our vantage point, and not lead one to fall to their knees and worship the living God who made his future, our past, known to Daniel? 

And then, knowing this, how can you hear the promises of God in Christ, eternal life, the resurrection of the dead and His everlasting Kingdom and not trust that they are true? 

*So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.*

Now **Daniel 2** is a familiar story. King Nebuchadnezzar has a dream that troubles him, and he cannot recall what it was, but seeks someone to tell him the dream and its meaning. 

And all the wizards and wise men of Chaldea cannot do this impossible task. The king orders that all his advisors be put to death for their inability to do this, including Daniel and his friends, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah (Rack, Shack and Benny).

But Daniel stays the hand of the man, Arioch the king's captain, by asking him to give Daniel time, and a promise that the Jewish eunuch could find out the kings dream and interpretation. 

And in prayer the matter is made known to him by God. And he brings it to Nebuchadnezzar. 

That the king dreamed of an idol, a collosal image. Head of gold, chest and two arms of silver, belly and thighs of brass, legs of iron and feet, iron mixed with clay. 

And the interpretation thereof, 

The Head of Gold: Babylonian Empire   
 
The Chest and Arms of Silver: Medo-Persian Empire   
 
The Belly and Thighs of Brass (Bronze): Greek Empire (Macedonian, under Alexander the Great)   
 
Legs of Iron, the Roman Empire

Feet of Iron and Clay: the Roman Empire divided, and then scattered among the nations. 

This is the history that came to pass. 

And then we see Jesus. The stone cut from the mountain, without hands. The stone the builders rejected. The foundation upon which is built the everlasting Kingdom. Destroying the kingdoms of men.

**Daniel 4**, written in Aramaic from the hand of king Nebuchadnezzar, in the form of a proclamation to the whole world, tells of the king's final arc, these past 4 chapters, towards accepting the Lord God, the most high. 

In a way, the first 4 chapters of Daniel are Nebuchadnezzar's story as much as Daniel's. 

We see from the beginning of the captivity, throughout the other prophets like Jeremiah, that the king is called God's servant. That the Lord uses him to bring desolation to Jerusalem and refine the people of Judah as of fire. Preparing the way for Christ to come 500 years later. 

But in this arc we see there's more. Nebuchadnezzar is convinced by the wisdom and excellent spirit of Daniel, the miracle of the firey furnace, and here by the humbling by God against his pride, and confesses that He is above all, even the mightiest king. 

His testimony, that Daniel had given him the interpretation of the dream, full knowledge of what God had judged against him, and the opportunity on his own to get right, to break off his sins by righteousness and showing mercy to the poor. To get saved and live according to God's word. He ignored it, and after a year of God's long-suffering, the curse fell upon him. 

This proclamation went out to every nation. Nebuchadnezzar willingly told the world about the seven years of humiliation he was given by God. To live in the fields like a beast. Without his faculties or riches. Lost to madness. Restored at God's command after the 7 years, humbled and a new man. 

In it, we see how merciful God truly is. How in ways big and small, through the Spirit, he tries to bring men to repentance. That even the mighty and the most based have ministering spirits over us. That God will give us room to repent, time to get right on our own. And He will humble the proud to show them their error. 

God would that none perish. But it falls on us to respond to Him. 

I imagine that this testimony, and the truth of God's power and judgment, brought many outside of the captive Jews to believe. Add to this the scattered remnant of Israel, and the seeds for those Gentiles, the nations of men to believe on Christ when the time came, was all part of God's plan. 

Everything working towards Christ and the new testament.

One last point; God chastens whom He would, scourging every son. Too many Christians get comfortable in the blessings and protection God provides us. Like Nebuchadnezzar, we not only take things for granted, but begin to pridefully take credit for the things in our life that are by the grace of God. 

He heard God's word and forgot all about it. He became prideful and paid for it. 

I think mental illness is often from God, making us deal with the cognitive dissonance of our lies and self-deception and the truth of His word. 

Don't be surprised if you continue down the road, backslidden, to have this type of punishment. I have both observed it and experienced a fraction of it. Don't let it happen to you!

Some time has passed, and Nebuchadnezzar's son, Belshazzar has taken the throne of Babylon. And we find him using the vessels of the temple of God, taken in the captivity, to drink wine and praise images and idols. They were *gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone.* Some Catholics will deny that they do this very thing by claiming they aren't carved images, but we see here every type of idol, from carved to hewn to cast. All abominations in God's eye.

And so part of the hand of God appears to the king and writes upon the wall. 

The king cannot understand it, but is struck with terror. Knees knocking, he calls for the wise men of the kingdom to interpret for him. Of course, they cannot. But the queen recalls Daniel and what he had done for Nebuchadnezzar, his excellent spirit, being filled with the spirit of God. 

They call for him, the king promising to give him power as the 3rd over the kingdom, a chain of gold etc. But Daniel says he doesn't need riches and power, he will do it for nothing. 

Daniel reminds Belshazzar how his father came to know the true and living God. Not serving dead idols, but being convinced by his 7 years of madness that there is one God, the most high. Who gives us our next breath. Who sets up and tears down who He will. 

Belshazzar, Daniel says, has forgotten the lesson that was hard taught to his father, and in pride had done a wicked thing. So, the writing on the wall spelled his doom. 

Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin. God had numbered his kingdom and finished it. It has been judged and found wanting. The kingdom will be divided and given to the Medes and the Persians. Just as the great image in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, the chest and arms of silver. 

Daniel is rewarded according to what the king had said. But it was too late. That night, Belshazzar was slain.

As children, we should honor our parents, regardless of their own failings. One of the chief ways we can console ourselves if they are lacking is to learn from their mistakes. To see God's wrath upon them, the misery of their lives or their repentance unto God, and take wisdom from it.

One of the messages of the sermon on the mount, in fact it's primary theme, is achieving excellence. Going above and beyond the bare minimum, striving for perfection, which means being complete. Whole. 

That if we think it's enough to not commit adultery, it isn't, for even the thought of adultery is sin. Even hate in your heart is murder. If someone compels you to walk a mile with them, go two. If they take you coat, give them your cloak. Loving your enemies, not just the brethren. Going the extra mile, excelling, being perfect. 

We see in Daniel that he had the spirit of excellence within him. He was blameless in his work. He did more, meekly and humbly, in God's name, serving Him. And it paid dividends with blessings from God and promotion over others. This of course led to their resentment, but they couldn't find anything to accuse Daniel of, except for his faith. And they had to trick the king into signing a law to persecute Daniel for that faith. 

This is what we should all strive for. Make them come at us for our faith having nothing else with which to attack you. Being blameless and excellent. Working diligently on everything you do. Going that extra mile. Heaping coals on your enemies by praying for them and meekly and honestly dealing with all. Giving tribute to whom tribute is due. Rendering custom. 

Make those that hate and resent you for your faith persecute you for it. Make it the only thing they can lay charge to you with. 

And when you are thrown in the lions den, or put in the firey furnace, put you in bonds like Paul, or whatever else they use to attack your faith, believe that God will deliver you.

Here in **Daniel 6**, the Medo-Persian empire has assumed power over what was Babylon, and Daniel exceeded all men beside the king, because of his faith and excellent spirit. 

And the princes and wise men under him plotted to have him lose the favor of king Darius. Tricking the king into signing an immutable law; for 30 days all who petition God or men rather than the king would be thrown in a lion's den. 

Of course they knew Daniel was faithful in prayer, praying to God three times a day on his knees, towards Jerusalem. 

Caught in prayer, they take him to the king, who despite not wanting to harm Daniel, is caught by his own decree. Daniel is thrown in, and the king prays that God protect him, and was up all night fasting and weeping for Daniel. 

In the morning, Darius sought after Daniel at the mouth of the den, and Daniel is alive. The angel of the Lord had protected him. For innocence was found in him. 

The king rejoiced, sentencing those that plotted against Daniel, and their families, to die the death they had sought for him. 

King Darius then wrote to all people and nations, in every language praising God. That Daniel's God is the living God, steadfast and true. Fear Him. His Kingdom shall never be destroyed but His dominion lasts forever. 

This now is the second king of a mighty empire that has declared the glory of God because of Daniel's faith.

The prophecy that came upon Daniel in chapter 9 carries with it multiple applications, both present at his time, in the 1st century with Christ, and in the end times.

Great arguments have been made among Christians and those who profess to be as to the exact meaning of Gabriel's revelation to Daniel. 

Was it meaning the destruction of the temple that would be built? Daniel has figured out the 70 years of captivity and desolation of Jerusalem that God foretold Jeremiah was drawing near. And after the captivity, they would return to the city God chose, and build it. 

Was it referring to the end times? When the beast tramples Jerusalem underfoot, before the second coming of Christ? All of this? 

As I read it, the thing that I focused on wasn't the mystery of these things, and their meaning, but instead the faith of Daniel and his humility before the Lord. 

He read the word of God and believing it to be true, began to plea for mercy, with a contrite heart before God. 

Daniel reads the curse in the law of Moses, and acknowledges that the Lord has justly judged against Israel and Judah. That their predicament is of their own making. Their own trespass against the Lord. He confesses this sin, and says not of their righteousness, but by His mercy, Lord save us. 

Daniel's prayer should be the main focus of this chapter. As Gabriel says, "thou art greatly beloved." 

Daniel, we are told repeatedly, had an excellent spirit. He had great faith and humility. He prayed multiple times a day. He sought peace with others. He trusted in the Lord, and served the authority God put in his life with humility, always doing his best. 

And here, reading the words of Jeremiah and understanding them in the Spirit and knowing the promises of God given his people, centuries before, he turns to God in supplication and meekness, seeking forgiveness and mercy. Not for himself but for his people. 

What a model Daniel is for us. Especially in these last days. The spiritual applications to take from Daniel should exceed whatever timing and charts and arguments over what he was told. 

We may have different opinions, may think this applies to the 3.5yrs of tribulation (I do), or whatever pre-trib promises the dispensationalists might take from it. 

But if we all held to the spirit of Daniel, and prayed like him and served like him and sought to be pleasing to God, even in a wicked kingdom, even as we are in spiritual Babylon, those things would work themselves out. But we would be pleasing to God. 

And our people would be delivered, just as He promises.

I have to also point to the prophecy of Jesus' first coming. It is wild how God gave Daniel this vision of the "seventy weeks," laying out a timeline that points right to Jesus. Gabriel tells Daniel about 490 years—seventy weeks of years—starting from the decree to rebuild Jerusalem (around 457 BC, give or take, with Artaxerxes’ decree). Fast forward 69 of those weeks (483 years), and you land in the time of Jesus’ ministry, around 27-30 AD. 

The Messiah is "cut off" being the crucifixion. God dropped a prophecy hundreds of years earlier, nailing the timing of His Son’s arrival and sacrifice.

Like in Isaiah and Jeremiah, God was saying, “I’ve got this all planned out, and I’m showing you I’m in control.”

The precision blows my mind—centuries before Jesus walked the earth, God gave Daniel the timing, and it played out just as He said. 

Some folks debate the exact dates or lean into a future fulfillment, but seeing those 69 weeks line up with Christ’s coming? That’s the power of God’s Word shining through. It’s a reminder that when God speaks, it’s as good as done.

Daniel Chapter 11: A Prophetic Overview (533 B.C. - 164 B.C.)

Daniel receives this prophecy in the third year of Cyrus (Cyrus the Great, ~536 B.C.), delivered by an angel who strengthened Darius the Mede (~539 B.C.) in his first year (v. 1).

The chapter outlines historical events from the Persian Empire through the Greek kingdoms, focusing on conflicts between the *King of the North* (Seleucid Empire) and the *King of the South* (Ptolemaic Empire), leading to Antiochus Epiphanes’ actions, foreshadowing end-times events.

Verse-by-Verse Summary:

- v. 1: The angel recalls supporting Darius the Mede (~539 B.C.) during his reign’s start.

- v. 2: After Cyrus (Cyrus the Great, ~559–530 B.C.), three kings arise: Cambyses II (~530–522 B.C.), Darius I (~522–486 B.C.), and Ahasuerus (Xerxes I, ~486–465 B.C.), the richest, who attacks Greece, leading to battles like Thermopylae (~480 B.C.).

- v. 3-4: Alexander the Great (~336–323 B.C.) conquers widely but dies young, his empire splitting among four generals: Ptolemy (Egypt), Seleucus (Mesopotamia), Lysimachus (Asia Minor), and Cassander (Greece) (~323 B.C.).

- v. 5: Ptolemy I Soter (~323–283 B.C.), King of the South (Egypt), grows strong, but Seleucus I Nicator (~311–281 B.C.), King of the North (Mesopotamia), becomes stronger.

- v. 6: Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II Philadelphus (~283–246 B.C.), marries Antiochus II Theos (~261–246 B.C.) to form an alliance (~252 B.C.), but the deal fails after Ptolemy’s death, and Berenice is abandoned.

- v. 7-8: Ptolemy III Euergetes (~246–222 B.C.), a relative of Berenice, invades the North, defeats Seleucus II Callinicus (~246–225 B.C.), and returns to Egypt with captives and treasures (~241 B.C.).

- v. 9-10: Ptolemy III returns home, but Seleucus II’s sons, Seleucus III Ceraunus (~225–223 B.C.) and Antiochus III the Great (~223–187 B.C.), assemble forces to retaliate.

- v. 11-12: Ptolemy IV Philopator (~221–204 B.C.) defeats Antiochus III (~219 B.C.), but his prideful victory doesn’t strengthen him.

- v. 13-15: Antiochus III returns with a larger army, allies with others against Ptolemy V Epiphanes (~204–180 B.C.), and captures fortified cities (~200 B.C.).

- v. 14: Jewish opportunists try to exploit the conflict for gain but fail (~200 B.C.).

- v. 16: Antiochus III defeats Ptolemy V and occupies Israel, harming it (~198 B.C.).

- v. 17: Antiochus III sends his daughter, Cleopatra I (~193–176 B.C.), to marry Ptolemy V (~192 B.C.), but she sides with Egypt, thwarting his plan.

- v. 18-19: Antiochus III wins naval battles but is defeated by a Roman prince (Scipio Asiaticus, ~190 B.C.), returns home, and dies (~187 B.C.).

- v. 20: Seleucus IV Philopator (~187–175 B.C.) focuses on taxation but dies mysteriously, not in battle (~175 B.C.).

- v. 21-22: Antiochus IV Epiphanes (~175–164 B.C.), a vile person, seizes power through flattery, defeats opponents, and kills the high priest (Onias III, ~171 B.C.), the “prince of the covenant.”

- v. 23-24: Antiochus IV makes deceptive alliances, gains strength, and uses occult practices to conquer strongholds (~170 B.C.).

- v. 25-26: Antiochus IV defeats Ptolemy VI Philometor (~170–164 B.C.) in battle, aided by betrayal within Egypt (~169 B.C.).

- v. 27: Antiochus IV and Ptolemy VI negotiate deceitfully, but their plans fail (~169 B.C.).

- v. 28: Antiochus IV returns home, plotting against Israel’s religion (~168 B.C.).

- v. 29-30: Antiochus IV’s second campaign against Egypt is halted by Roman ships (Popilius Laenas, ~168 B.C.), and he turns his anger on Israel, allying with apostate Jews.

- v. 31: Antiochus IV and apostate Jews desecrate the temple, stop sacrifices, and set up a statue of Zeus, the “abomination that maketh desolate” (~168 B.C.).

- v. 32: Antiochus IV empowers apostate Jews, but faithful Jews resist and perform exploits (~168 B.C.).

- v. 33-35: Faithful Jews teach others but face persecution, martyrdom, and trials, receiving some help (~168–164 B.C.).

- v. 36-37: Antiochus IV exalts himself above all gods, possibly as a sodomite, rejecting traditional deities (~168 B.C.).

- v. 38-39: Antiochus IV worships an impersonal “god of forces,” promoting it with riches and dividing land for gain (~168 B.C.).

- v. 40-43: Antiochus IV defeats Ptolemy VI again, conquers Egypt, Libya, and Ethiopia, but spares Edom, Moab, and Ammon (~167 B.C.).

- v. 44-45: Antiochus IV, disturbed by eastern and northern news, sets up his palace in Israel between the seas, but dies without human hand (~164 B.C.).

Antiochus IV Epiphanes (c. 215–164 BC), a Seleucid king, is generally accepted as the "vile person" found in **Daniel 11**. Antiochus IV obtains his kingdom by flatteries, reflecting his usurpation through cunning. His military campaigns, particularly against Egypt, match his invasions of the Ptolemaic kingdom, marked by deceit and temporary alliances. The reference to defiling the sanctuary corresponds to his temple desecration in Jerusalem, and his self-exaltation, declaring himself as God, is echoed in his epithet "Epiphanes" (meaning "God Manifest"). His *fierce countenance* and understanding of *dark sentences* fit his reputation for ruthless ambition and strategic manipulation.

He ruled Syria from 175 BC until his death. Born as Mithridates, he adopted the name Antiochus upon ascending the throne. He was a son of Antiochus III the Great and gained power after his brother Seleucus IV’s assassination, seizing the throne from the rightful heir, Demetrius I. 

Known for his ambition and erratic behavior, he sought to expand Seleucid influence, campaigning against Egypt and imposing Hellenistic culture on Judea, which sparked the Maccabean Revolt. His desecration of the Jerusalem Temple, banning Jewish practices, and setting up an altar to Zeus cemented his notoriety.
 
Historical records, including 1 Maccabees and Josephus, claim that in 167 BC, he desecrated the temple by erecting an altar to Zeus Olympios, where sacrifices, including pigs, were offered, as part of his campaign to enforce Hellenistic, or Greek, worship. While he claimed divine status for himself, Zeus was the "god of forces" he brought on Jerusalem. The god of his fathers, Apollo, was traditionally revered as the divine patron of the Seleucid dynasty, symbolizing royal legitimacy, and in doing so, he rejected the god of his fathers. 

The Seleucid Empire remained formally independent until 63 BC, when Roman general Pompey the Great annexed Syria as a Roman province after defeating the last Seleucid rulers, effectively ending Seleucid sovereignty and placing Judea, Galilee and Samaria under Roman authority. 

And this was why, in Jesus' day, Rome ruled, but Greek was the lingua franca of their region.

*And at that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people: and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time thy people shall be delivered, every one that shall be found written in the book.*

Finishing with **Daniel 12**, the messenger of God which has revealed so much to the prophet, leaves Daniel with an assurance of salvation and resurrection. 

He says that Michael, the archangel who stands for the people of God, Israel, believers throughout time, who leads the charge at the beginning of sorrows to cast out Satan and his 3rd of angels from heaven, stands up. And tribulation begins. But, he says, the people will be delivered, every one found written in the book. The book of life. 

Many will say that the tribulation and the deliverance by Christ's return, is for the Jews. That Christians will have been raptured before any of this happens, before the first trump. At the beginning of sorrows. Pre-tribulation. But those found in the book of life, who have not been blotted out, absolutely includes we who are saved. It contains the names of the faithful from all time. 

And in v2 we find the promise of the resurrection; that some, the saved, shall come to everlasting life and others, the damned, to everlasting shame and contempt. 

And we who are given eternal life are also rewarded for our works, especially in winning others to Jesus. Turning people to righteousness in Christ. 

Then he tells Daniel to shut up the words, seal the book. That many will come and knowledge increased, but this prophecy is for the time of the end. 

As Daniel is told to shut up the book and seal it by the man in linen, the angel he'd been speaking to, looks and sees two other angels, one on each bank of the river. This is similar to what happens to John in **Revelation 10:1-7**

*And I saw another mighty angel come down from heaven, clothed with a cloud: and a rainbow was upon his head, and his face was as it were the sun, and his feet as pillars of fire: And he had in his hand a little book open: and he set his right foot upon the sea, and his left foot on the earth, And cried with a loud voice, as when a lion roareth: and when he had cried, seven thunders uttered their voices. And when the seven thunders had uttered their voices, I was about to write: and I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Seal up those things which the seven thunders uttered, and write them not. And the angel which I saw stand upon the sea and upon the earth lifted up his hand to heaven, And sware by him that liveth for ever and ever, who created heaven, and the things that therein are, and the earth, and the things that therein are, and the sea, and the things which are therein, that there should be time no longer: But in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he shall begin to sound, the mystery of God should be finished, as he hath declared to his servants the prophets.*

I sometimes wonder if Daniel and John are both witness to the same event, without seeing one another. Different human perspectives. Both angels swear by He Who liveth forever and ever that the things they say will be, and similarly both prophet and apostle hear to seal these things up until the appropriate time. 

But as for Daniel, he is told of the time, times an half, the 3.5 years when all things will be finished. Just as John writes if the end of time itself, and the finished work of God has come.

Daniel says he doesn't understand this, O my Lord, what shall be the end of these things? 

He is told to go his own way, the word sealed up, but again reassuring Daniel (and us), that many will be purified, made white, and tried, tested. That the wicked will continue to be wicked, but the wise shall understand. 

Similar to Revelation, where repeatedly we see the saved in Christ dressed in white, purified by the blood. And those who are purified will be tried. The tribulation. All who would live godly in Christ Jesus are tried. 

He again restates the signs, that from the time the daily sacrifice cases and is taken away, and the abomination that maketh desolate set up, there shall be 1,290 days. 

And blessed is he that waiteth and come to the 1,335 days. 

I think Jesus is paraphrasing this passage from Daniel in His Olivette Discourse, when He says;

*When ye therefore shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, stand in the holy place, (whoso readeth, let him understand:)*

The wise shall understand. And when Jesus says *he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved*, it is the same promise that he that waiteth to the end will be blessed. 

The chapter ends with another promise of the resurrection, that Daniel will rest and then stand in his lot at the end of days. May we all take comfort in that promise. Amen

**Timeline of Days in Daniel 7 - 12**

**I. Daniel 8:13-14 – Vision of the Sanctuary Cleansing**

**Daniel 8:13-14**
*Then I heard one saint speaking, and another saint said unto that certain saint which spake, How long shall be the vision concerning the daily sacrifice, and the transgression of desolation, to give both the sanctuary and the host to be trodden under foot? And he said unto me, Unto two thousand and three hundred days; then shall the sanctuary be cleansed.*

**II. Daniel 12:11-12 – Specific Time Periods**

**Daniel 12:11-12**
*And from the time that the daily sacrifice shall be taken away, and the abomination that maketh desolate set up, there shall be a thousand two hundred and ninety days. Blessed is he that waiteth, and cometh to the thousand three hundred and five and thirty days.* 

**III. Timeframe Breakdown**

**Total Period: 7 Years**

**Daniel 9:27**
*And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease…*
- The "week" equals 7 prophetic years, calculated as 2,520 days (7 x 360-day lunar year+a “leap month" of 30 days).

**First Half: 3.5 Years (Tribulation of the Saints, 1,260 Days)**

**Daniel 7:25**
*And he shall speak great words against the most High, and shall wear out the saints of the most High, and think to change times and laws: and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and the dividing of time.*
 - This period of 1,260 days (3.5 x 360) represents the tribulation where the saints face persecution.

**Midpoint: Abomination of Desolation**

**Daniel 9:27**
*…and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease, and for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate…*
 - Occurs at the 1,260-day mark, splitting the 7 years.

**Second Half: 3.5 Years (Great Tribulation, 1,260 Days + 30 Days)**

**Daniel 7:25**
*…a time and times and the dividing of time.*
 - Extends to 1,290 days: Daniel 12:11 And from the time that the daily sacrifice shall be taken away, and the abomination that maketh desolate set up, there shall be a thousand two hundred and ninety days.
 - Extra 30 Days: The 1,290 days include the 1,260 days of the second half plus an additional 30 days, likely an intercalary month in the Jewish lunar calendar to align the 360-day prophetic years with the solar calendar, ensuring proper timing of events.

**Additional 45 Days (Great Tribulation Concludes)**

**Daniel 12:12**
*Blessed is he that waiteth, and cometh to the thousand three hundred and five and thirty days.*
 - The 1,335 days extend 45 days beyond the 1,290 days (1,335 - 1,290 = 45).
 - Total 75 Days: The 30 days (1,290 - 1,260) plus 45 days (1,335 - 1,290) form a 75-day period of intensified great tribulation, overlapping the second half’s end, concluding key events.

**Wrath of God: 3.5 Years (Post-1,335 Days)**
The remaining time after the 1,335 days (approximately 1,260 days, calculated as 2,520 total days minus 1,260 tribulation days and 75 great tribulation days) aligns with the period of God’s wrath, following the conclusion of the great tribulation.

**Hosea 1**
*The word of the Lord that came unto Hosea, the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel.*

*2 The beginning of the word of the Lord by Hosea. And the Lord said to Hosea, Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the Lord.*

*3 So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim; which conceived, and bare him a son.*

*4 And the Lord said unto him, Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel.*

*5 And it shall come to pass at that day, that I will break the bow of Israel, in the valley of Jezreel.*

*6 And she conceived again, and bare a daughter. And God said unto him, Call her name Loruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away.*

*7 But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and will save them by the Lord their God, and will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by battle, by horses, nor by horsemen.*

*8 Now when she had weaned Loruhamah, she conceived, and bare a son.*

*9 Then said God, Call his name Loammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.*

*10 Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered; and it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God.*

*11 Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head, and they shall come up out of the land: for great shall be the day of Jezreel.*

Poor Hosea, the prophet with the burden of the Lord to make his very life a living parable against Israel. To marry a whore, representing the whoredoms of Israel, chasing after false gods. 

To have a son, named after the place, Jezreel, where Jehu slew the house of Ahab. Where blood would be avenged by the Lord to end the kingdom of Israel. 

Then to have a daughter, Loruhamah, meaning that God's mercy was no longer upon the northern kingdom. That God would destroy them utterly. 

The word of the Lord does make an exception for the southern kingdom of Judah, prophetically telling of Jesus Christ. That there would come up on them salvation, not physically. Not as by armies and horses. 

Then a son, Loammi, *for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.* This judgment is devastating, and another nail in the coffin of dispensationalism. 

But even in this prophecy of destruction, the promise of the Israel of God found in Christ. That it would be said to the innumerable saints in Christ, *Ye are the sons of the living God.*

*Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head, and they shall come up out of the land*.

Great shall be the day of Jezreel. 

Jezreel means "He sows" in Hebrew. It was also the most fertile valley in the land. With the gospel of Christ, and Him crucified, the word of God, the seed of salvation, has been sown throughout the world. 

The time of harvest has come; 

**Matthew 9:37-38**
*Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few; Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.*

And eventually the fullness of the Gentiles will come, and the last reaping of those in Christ. 

**Revelation 14:15-16**
*And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to him that sat on the cloud, Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe. And he that sat on the cloud thrust in his sickle on the earth; and the earth was reaped.*

We are called to be husbandmen of God's great harvest. To sow and water and reap. Let us labor in this, as good and faithful servants. That we may not be ashamed at His coming, but rejoicing, bringing in the sheaves.

The Lord compares them again to an unfaithful wife, who has run off with different lovers, who credits the wealth and plenty they have to these strange gods. And now He would strip them bare, leaving the nation desolate because of them.

Blotting out the names of the false lords, the gods of the heathen, that only one name under Heaven be praised.

**Hosea 3**
*Then said the Lord unto me, Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the Lord toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods, and love flagons of wine.*

*2 So I bought her to me for fifteen pieces of silver, and for an homer of barley, and an half homer of barley:*

*3 And I said unto her, Thou shalt abide for me many days; thou shalt not play the harlot, and thou shalt not be for another man: so will I also be for thee.*

*4 For the children of Israel shall abide many days without a king, and without a prince, and without a sacrifice, and without an image, and without an ephod, and without teraphim:*

*5 Afterward shall the children of Israel return, and seek the Lord their God, and David their king; and shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the latter days.*

Here again, the Lord instructed the prophet to play the cuckold, to love a woman as a friend who is an adulteress, just as Israel played the harlot to their God. 

The Lord is that man, the people wickedly left His protection and provision for wine and idols, as an unfaithful wife. 

Hosea purchases the service of a whore for a pittance, (15 pieces of silver is half the 30 that is the price of a servant, a measure and a half of barley, barely enough for bread), but with the expectation of faithfulness, to represent the desolation that is to come upon Israel and Judah. A time where the plenty of God is taken away. No king, no sacrifice, no priestly duties, no image to bow to. And yet He wants them to know by this preaching that the Lord expects them to suffer through this loss and still maintain their faithfulness to Him. Something they weren't able to do in plenty, now do in tribulation. 

But why? Because of the promise of the Lord, that in the latter end of things, they will seek the Lord their God and David their king, being Christ Jesus, and receive His goodness once again.

We are all given the choice. He would rather we come to him by His mercy and gratitude for the blessings of His love upon us. But absent that, our coming to Him in hard times for the blessed promise of His goodness in Christ is worthy too. 

Or we can continue in drunkenness and idolatry, and the desolation and famine that comes with sin. Continuing in death.

The Lord says that if they don't wish to retain Him in their knowledge, they will perish for that lack of knowledge. If the priests won't reprove and rebuke sin, then they are in common cause with it. Let their sins consume them. God won't even scourge them for backsliding. Perfect is the judgment of God

*16 Then the men feared the Lord exceedingly, and offered a sacrifice unto the Lord, and made vows.*

During the reign of King Jeroboam II of Israel, many prophets were turned towards the northern kingdom to preach the word of God, and the southern kingdom, then under the rule of Uzziah. Amos was a contemporary of Jonah. They preached repentance towards the truth of God, in the face of sin in the land and fearsome threats of their neighbors, primarily at this time against the Assyrians. 

So when Jonah is called by God to go preach in Nineveh, a city in the heart of Assyria, to warn them of their pending destruction, Jonah refuses the Lord. 

Jonah is faithful and fearful of God. He is a saved believer, who has understanding of God's wrath and power. Yet he risks running away to avoid preaching to the heathen as the burden of the Lord came upon him. 

While Jonah may have feared for his safety, going among the heathen who had warred against Israel and Judah, as we will see, he simply did not wish to give his enemies the chance to hear the truth and avoid God's wrath. 

And we all know the story. He sets out for Spain, the exact opposite direction. Hiring passage on a ship. And the storm comes up on them, and the men of the vessel vainly call upon their false gods, before determining that Jonah was the source of their tribulation. And that the God he had testified to them was responsible for the tempest. Ultimately, Jonah offers his life for theirs, and they reluctantly cast him overboard where he is swallowed by a great fish, prepared by God for this purpose. And Jonah spends three days and nights in its belly. 

We are also all familiar with the picture of Christ in Jonah. 

**Matthew 12:38-41**
*Then certain of the scribes and of the Pharisees answered, saying, Master, we would see a sign from thee. But he answered and said unto them, An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas: For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: because they repented at the preaching of Jonas; and, behold, a greater than Jonas is here.*

Christ being greater than Jonah, or any other man, is obvious (although not to the Jews seeking after a sign). But the picture of the Son perfectly obeying the will of the Father, even unto death, that His enemies be given a chance at repentance towards the truth of the gospel contrasts starkly with the prophet who did all he could to avoid it.

It is funny how, despite Jonah not wanting to preach the Lord to the heathen, he still manages to get the men of Joppa to believe on the Lord God. He is literally the worst prophet and yet God uses him mightily. 

Often Christians are reluctant to preach the word to others. We bury our talent of silver. We put our light under a bushel. We flee to Tarshish, running to the things of this world seeking to avoid our responsibility. And even in our dereliction, God uses us to proclaim His truth. How much more so if we let Him shape us into worthy vessels? 

We shouldn't need to be swallowed up by a whale to be dragged back to where we need to be to do God's will. But if that's what it takes, He won't hesitate. 

It is hard to kick against the pricks, as Jesus said to Saul on the road to Damascus. The Bible says to know to do good and to do it not is a sin. 

Make this new year the year you dedicate yourself to doing the will of the Lord. To soul-winning and preaching His word, even to your enemies. To stop running away. 

Don't make God send the storm.

Poor Jonah, used mightily by God and miserable in his anger. Still hoping Nineveh be destroyed, praying for it. Willing to sit and wait for its destruction, while knowing and acknowledging the Lord is merciful and longsuffering, even to Assyrians who are enemies of Israel at this time. 

Stubborn to the end, telling God he'd rather die angry than get a good spirit, and see things the way the Lord sees them. 

And God prepares a gourd, as He had a great fish, and it grows in a night and gives Jonah shade for a day. And He prepared a worm to wither it in the night, killing it. And God prepared a fierce East wind, a cloudless sky from it, and Jonah fainted from the sun, wishing he could die. 

God asks again if Jonah's anger is serving him well; *Doest thou well to be angry for the gourd?* And stubborn Jonah says it is well with him to be angry, even unto death. The prophet seething. 

God shows him that he has pity for the plight of a gourd, which Jonah had no hand in making, but took the shade from, and yet none for a city of 120,000. 

God made the gourd and made the men (and much cattle), and it was His mercy to give. Showing the people right from wrong through His word, preached by Jonah. It's a tough lesson. There's no indication that Jonah learned it. He may have been angry unto death at this. A poor spirit throughout. And yet the Lord showed the same mercy and longsuffering to him as the Ninevites.

Continuing the prophets, Micah is preaching in the time before the destruction of Israel and the desolation and captivity of Judah, *in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah*.

His burden of the Lord, the word come upon him, is very specific and clear. He lists places in Samaria and Judah, their sins and the destruction that's due them. 

It is amazing how the Lord sent so many prophets, even those not mentioned in scripture, with the same warnings against their idols, graven images, false religion and worship of foreign gods, fornication, murder...and it largely went unheeded. Just like modern times. 

And as with modern times, the prophets also brought the hope of salvation in the heir of God, the glory of Israel, the Messiah, Christ Jesus. 

Then, as now we are to preach the whole word of God, rebuking sin, spelling out the wrath that is to come, while showing the redemption possible for individuals who believe on the Lord. The promise of the Father to deliver us through His Son. The Word of God made flesh. 

All the prophets gave witness, speaking by the word of God. That word became flesh. The promise kept just as surely as the promise to destroy  Israel and the high places and groves and walled cities came true. Amen.

Continuing a thought from the study of Hosea; Christ could be preached to unbelievers through the book of Micah, just as Jesus was preached to the Ethiopian Eunuch by Phillip, using **Isaiah 53**. Micah, like the other prophets, preached judgment for sin, the holiness of God, the truth of His mercy and His Messiah, and redemption by faith in His word, and a call to sanctification and separation for us once saved. 

We are blessed to have the clear Gospels, but you can see how there were always a righteous remnant. 7,000 who hadn't bowed the knee to Baal. How the Old Testament was entirely about Jesus and salvation has always been by faith, calling upon the name of the Lord.

The Bible is not only about the grace and mercy God extends towards sinners in Christ, and the promises of forgiveness and redemption, but it is a book of judgments against evildoers. It is evidence of God's wrath against the workers of iniquity, and His promise to those who are meek and humble that their oppressors will surely be punished by an almighty Lord.

**Micah 6** sees the prophet giving to the people of Israel the testimony of the Lord, Who is making His case to the world against those who had been His people. 

And even as Balaam could not but speak the words God gave him to speak, the prophet Micah rings out the charges against his countrymen. 

The Lord reminds them of His grace towards them, leading them out of Egypt, delivering them through the wilderness into the land they now possess (though not for long).

He reminds them of Balaam being unable to curse them, at Balak the Moabite's hire. The righteousness of God is evident in the righteousness of the people. *How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed? or how shall I defy, whom the Lord hath not defied?* 

But even so, the council of Balaam was that if you wanted to curse the children of Israel, Balak had to make them sin against the Lord. And so Moab sent her daughters to commit whoredoms with fornication and bringing idols and false gods among them, until God sent a plague to smites His people, they had brought a curse on themselves. 

The Lord reiterates His often stated position that it isn't the blood of rams and goats that pleases Him, but faith and mercy and judgement. To do justly and walk humbly with God. 

The blood offerings were a picture of Christ. Not the means of salvation themselves. What good are dead works if they aren't given in faith? Trappings of religion rather than pure religion, undefiled;
