Habakkuk was a prophet and contemporary of Jeremiah, preaching during the time leading up to and during the Babylonian captivity. He begins by saying the *burden* which he did see. Just as in Jeremiah we see that the prophets called being given the word of God *the burden of the Lord.* 

**Jeremiah 23:36-40** mocks the false prophets who continually claim the burden of the Lord. 

But Habakkuk sincerely carries this burden, beginning with his  crying out to the Lord in anger and frustration at the state of Judah in his day. 

There is violence, strife, contention and spoiling or thefts, the law isn't being enforced and corruption keeps right judgment from being made. The wicked are prospering and are protected by the government while the righteous are victimized. 

Sounds familiar.

In verse 5, God begins to respond. The Lord says He will work a wonder in the prophet's days, rising up the Chaldeans, the Babylonian empire, and they will invade Judah and possess it. 

God says they are terrible and mighty, even their horses like leopards fiercer than wolves. That their armies will gather up Judah to captivity, scoff at their kings, and the cities will be destroyed by them. 

God also gives Habakkuk the prophecy that the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, shall take credit for this wonder God wrought against Judah. 

*Then shall his mind change, and he shall pass over, and offend, imputing this his power unto his god.*

(This is fulfilled in **Daniel 4**, another study for another day)

Habakkuk replies, respectfully but a bit incredulous. 

*Art thou not from everlasting, O Lord my God, mine Holy One? we shall not die. O Lord, thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O mighty God, thou hast established them for correction. Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?*

He asks how God could use the wicked Nebuchadnezzar and the heathen Chaldeans to destroy Judah, that as bad as it is, they are still more righteous than Babylon. They make men no more than fish to be caught in nets, slaying nations, and then worship the net rather than the Almighty God who established them. Worshiping the creature more than the Creator. 

*Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous.Shall they therefore empty their net, and not spare continually to slay the nations?*

He asks, what about their judgment? 

It is so familiar to us, today, and likely this story resonated with believers throughout Biblical history. We decry our own nation falling from grace to judgment. We call out to God to deliver us, to punish the wicked, and set right the sins in the land. A Christian nation that has fallen away. 

But when God rises up the heathen, the wicked, the Muslim and the Jew and the pagans of India and the godless of China, and we are beset from all sides by the worst, whom God has raised up, we ask how can this be that *the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?*

But God will explain that while He may use the wicked to judge the more righteous, they too will face His judgement.

**Habakkuk 2** continues the prophet's dialogue with God and the burden places on him by the Lord. Habakkuk compares his waiting for the word as a watchman on a tower. 

Having asked God why, as evil as Judah is, that wicked Babylon would be used to destroy them. He awaits his reproval, and the Lord answered him, telling him to record what He said, in plain words that they may be read and understood, to be preached and affect the hearer. 

The Lord says the vision He is granting Habakkuk may take a while to come to fruition, but it surely will. 

The Lord begins describing Nebuchadnezzar, ruler of the Babylonian empire, both specifically and generally as a nation. This is a very common device used by God throughout the prophets. The empire can be the King, the capital city, the empire itself, or its people. 

He begins, *Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith*.

Contrasting Nebuchadnezzar and his pride with the just, who live by faith places an understanding that for all his power and standing, he is not as the just, the righteousness of believers, humbled to receive God by faith. 

He drinks, and is proud, and never satisfied, constantly expanding his empire as Hell enlarges, and like death, can't be satisfied. The picture of Nebuchadnezzar's unquenchable desire for more lands to conquer and spoil being like Hell, in that it is continually growing to fit more and more taken into captivity by it, or as consistent and relentless as death, never being satisfied, never being full, is both poetic and insightful to his character, and doctrine. Death and Hell are as an empire ruining nations. But Jesus is victorious over it and delivers us from the captivity. 

And the people, as the saints in Heaven cry out for God's wrath, seek justice and judgment against Babylon, saying *Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long?*

God promises their vengeance will come from Him; *Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee; because of men's blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein*.

*For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.*

Again, as dual fulfillment, this is a prophecy against Babylon and its king, and of the end times. God will repay. Vengeance is His. The whole world will know His glory and righteousness, and woe be unto them that face His wrath. Amen

*Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that puttest thy bottle to him, and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness! Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the Lord's right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory*

This is an allegory for the sins of Babylon, and sound doctrine on drunkenness and the warped and perverse results of it.

Its neighbors, the nations it takes over and the abominations of false gods they introduce to the captives are compared to alcohol being given to take advantage of another. 

Similar to the Great Whore, Mystery Babylon; 

*And the woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet colour, and decked with gold and precious stones and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand full of abominations and filthiness of her fornication...with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication, and the inhabitants of the earth have been made drunk with the wine of her fornication.*

But, it also is a stark reminder of what alcohol does to people, and the disgusting things that come about from it. 

God promises that for this sin, or leading others to drunkenness that they may be taken advantage of, Nebuchadnezzar's own nakedness will be revealed instead. His own shame and humiliation will be exposed. 

When we read **Daniel 4**, we will see this.

Finally, Habakkuk receives this gem;

*What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols? Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach! Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it. But the Lord is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.*

The truth of idolatry is its vanity. The idea that man can make a god of his own hands. That there is even a fraction of divinity and power in them is foolishness. 

And the people who today bow and serve idols, kneeling and offering prayers to them, lighting candles and incense and telling themselves that these lifeless statutes and carvings and molten images are a representation of the holy or divine are just as foolish as the maker of heaven images described here by the Lord. 

God is in His temple, sitting on His throne. Our God lives, and is not found in anything created by man's hands or in temples made of stone. The earth is His footstool. All creation is a testament to His power.

The final chapter of the prophet Habakkuk is a song, written in the Spirit, apparently upon a stringed instrument for the chief singer to sing. A *Shigionoth* may be the name of that instrument. It is also thought to be a style of prayerful song, but the Bible defines itself, and the closing verse indicates it was an instrument used to write this prayerful song.

Habakkuk writes of his fear of the word of the Lord he received, of the judgment against wicked Judah by the hands of the Chaldeans, and the judgment that will come upon Nebuchadnezzar and Babylon after they are used by the Lord for this purpose. 

The prophet asks that in the midst of the years, during this time, that in His wrath God remembers His mercy. 

He recounts that God came up from the South, from Tenant and mount Paran, in the wilderness where the children of Israel came, up towards the promised land. That His glory filled the heavens and the earth full of His praise, His brightness as the light. This is the Lord that was with them, the fathers in the wilderness who entered into the promised land as His people, and He their God. 

*He had horns coming out of His hand*...horns being leaders in the Bible, God sets up captains and kings over people and takes them down. He sent pestilence and fire before them, and drove the nations of Canaanites asunder. The mountains scattered and hills did bow, the great nations that were there before Israel. 

He asks, *Was the Lord displeased against the rivers? was thine anger against the rivers? was thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation?* 

We know that His wrath was against the people and their abominations. But the prophet is poetically saying that even the mountains and rivers were affected by the fury of God's wrath. Even the oceans deep, and the sun and moon stood still;

Joshua 10:13
*And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, Until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. Is not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day.*

The prophet sings that God marched through the land in indignation and thresh the heathen in anger, while being the salvation and deliverer for His children, and *even for salvation with thine anointed*, a mention of Christ to whom all prophets gave witness. 

It is important to remember this, that the promise of salvation in His anointed, (Christ means anointed one, Messiah) was the faith of the Israelites in the wilderness, and of the saved throughout the Old Testament. 

Habakkuk describes how the Lord destroyed the rulers and delivered the land to them in violence and wrath. And then he says his lips quivered and he trembled and rottenness entered his bones knowing that the same wrathful vengeance was coming against Judah in his day. That the Lord would be doing to them what He did to the people before them.

*Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation.*

Even so, in this time of tribulation and even in the desolation he describes, Habakkuk says he will find joy in the God of his salvation. He will rest in the day if trouble. 

This is a great illustration of the way we, as saved believers, should approach the Great Tribulation should it come in our day, or even individual troubles we may have. In the midst of days, the Lord remembers His mercy. We have rest. We find joy in the God of our salvation. 

We would do well to remember this. 

*The Lord God is my strength*. Amen.

Because those in Jerusalem did not obey the voice of God, receive their correction and turn to the Lord, He promises to destroy the city. 

Because of the oppression there, the corrupt princes, the leaders of the city who judged unrighteously, their corruption like ravening lions and wolves, greedily making prey of the people. Not even stopping to gnaw the bones.

We look for much and it comes to little and we wonder why. *Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house* and turn on the 80" 4K, gorging yourself with pizza and wings and beer.

Zechariah begins with the prophet receiving the word of God, telling him to preach to the people that the Lord wants reconciliation with them. That if they turn to Him, He will restore them. To not be as their fathers, stiff-necked and rebellious, and who didn't harken to Him. 

Here, at the end of the 70 year exile and captivity, Zechariah's message mirrors Haggai. Zechariah and Haggai were contemporary prophets ministering around 520 BC, during the second year of Darius I of Persia, when the Jewish exiles had returned from Babylon to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple. Haggai’s primary message was to urge the people to resume work on the temple, which had stalled due to opposition and apathy. Zechariah’s visions, including those of the red horses and four carpenters, were similarly meant to encourage the people by affirming God’s presence, judgment on their enemies, and His commitment to restore Jerusalem.

The Lord reminds them that their fathers and their prophets are dead. But His word and statutes remain. That the Lord of hosts had done to them according to their ways. They got what they deserve.

A short time later, Zechariah is given a vision, a man riding a red horse, standing among myrtle trees, with other horses with him, red horses, red speckled with white and pure white. 

The angel tells the prophet that he will explain, and as he does, the man among the trees, the Lord of hosts Himself, says that these are they whom the Lord hath sent to walk the earth, to and fro. These answer to the Lord saying they have walked their routes and they found the earth to be still and at rest. 

There are a few interpretations of this, and what the horses represent. I will tell you mine. That the red are judgment and wrath, war. The speckled are wrath tempered with mercy. The white, the mercy of the Lord upon the people. Their role, to travel about ready to exact judgment on nations. Their report, everything at that moment was at peace. I could be wrong. 

The. The angel guiding Zechariah asks the man, the Lord of hosts, (pre-incarnate Christ Jesus? I think so. A theophany), he asks "How long wily though not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah?" Noting the 70 years they've been desolate. 

*And the Lord answered the angel that talked with me with good words and comfortable words.*

And the angel instructs the prophet; *Cry thou, saying, Thus saith the Lord of hosts; I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy.* 

That He is displeased with the heathen who are at peace, given their role in the desolation and captivity of Judah. That the Lord returns to Jerusalem with mercies, that His house will be rebuilt. That prosperity will spread out from Jerusalem, and the Lord shall comfort Zion, and shall choose Jerusalem. As earlier prophets spoke, the city where the Lord chose to place His name. 

Then Zechariah receives another vision, seeing four horns, those nations whose rulers scattered Judah, Israel and Jerusalem. Assyria, Babylonians, Persians and Egypt (in my opinion). And that there were 4 carpenters who come to fray these horns, to cause them terror and to be cast out. 

Again, there's speculation as to who these four are, or what it means that four builders come and restore Jerusalem. I think the simplest explanation are the 4 figures we are given who are responsible for the restoration of the Temple and the practices among the people. Zerubbable and Joshua the high priest, also contemporaries of the prophets, but also Ezra and Neamiah. Zerubbabel and Joshua (520 BC),  Ezra (458 BC) and Nehemiah (445 BC) came later.

This makes sense to me. But again, I could be wrong.

Through 7, 8 and Matthew 9, we see Jesus attracting multitudes, yet He deals with the individuals He meets. The miracles bring crowds, but the focus is on those few who in faith call upon Jesus to heal them. 

The man with palsy taken to Christ by his friends, all full of faith, is told his faith has brought him forgiveness of his sin. Jesus physically heals him as well, but note the order of things. 

We're given a simple and short story of the calling of Matthew, a publican. A tax collector for the empire. Called, he goes. 

Jesus meets with sinners to give them the good news, to bring them to righteousness, turning towards God and believing on Him. 

These miracles and His preaching have the Pharisees and scribes besides themselves. 

The whole need not a physician.

Jesus uses cloth being mended and skins, containing grape juice to be preserved as a parable. For the unworn cloth will rend the rip further, and the old, cracked and weakened bottles will burst with unpreserved and fermented juice it produces. 

Jesus then brings the daughter of a certain local ruler back to life, the rulers faith overcoming the scoffers gathered at her death, who doubt the power of Christ. 

And as Jesus fame grew for the miracles, even more crowds turned out for Him. Blind men beg to be healed, and they are. And despite His seeking to keep some of these miracles a secret, His fame grows and the multitudes come. His compassion for these lost sheep is touching. God would that all men come to salvation. He laments how few laborers there are to harvest the many who are seeking Him. This is as true today as then. The harvest is plentiful, we are called to go out and bring the increase to God. 

When casting out a devil, we see the bitter Pharisees accusing Jesus of doing it in the devil's name. Matthew 18 is a lesson in humility and forgiveness. The humble nature of a child and the debt incurred by trespass, and the good king who has forgiven all, and yet some ungrateful men cannot bring themselves to show a hint of the grace that's been extended to us.

The apostles ask Jesus, "who is greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven?" Jesus points to a child, an innocent who oblivious to the law, and unable to offend, humble and without pride, represents those who have been brought low by the truth of the Gospel, and fearing the Father, accepting His grace, just as a child is dependent and helpless before their father. 

To be converted, to repent, is to accept His will, to obey the Gospel, to accept we deserve death and humbly cry for mercy, and in His grace, the Father gives it to us, redeemed by Christ, forgiven all debt incurred by our sin. 

Jesus continues this lesson when Peter asks how often should we forgive a brother. The law says 3 times, he doubles it and again and asks is 7 times enough?

Jesus replies, 70 times 7, indicating an order of magnitude greater than the letter of the law. To essentially always forgive those seeking it. 

And, spinning off of this, Jesus teaches how to ask for forgiveness ourselves, and what to do if a so-called brother refuses. That we ask in private, then before witnesses, as pertaining to God's law, and then, if he refuses still, to put him out and treat him as an unregenerate sinner. A publican. A heathen. Because lack of forgiveness and grace is a sign of an unsaved heart. 

He tells the parable of the unforgiven servant, who beseeching the king to be forgiven a massive debt, then refuses to release a fellow servant a relatively minor one. 

This lack of grace means he didn't humbly partake in the same from the king, and undeserving, is cast into prison for torment. 

And so it is for all men. The Bible says Jesus paid the debt for all men. Those who seek that forgiveness in truth and reconciliation of grace will by nature show grace upon those who have wronged them. Not perfectly, we may need reminders, we may need the presence of witnesses to our stubborn pride to see our error. But holding a grudge against one who has sincerely asked to be forgiven is evidence of pride and arrogance, and a sign one has no understanding of the humility of receiving grace from God for our own trespass. 

It is a humbling feeling to know you are in the hands of the Living God, and deserve death and Hell, and yet, He forgives. The prideful cannot understand because they cannot admit to themselves their own debt. They can't receive His mercy, because they think it unfair or overcharged, or worse, doesn't exist. 

To them is forgiveness denied and the full price extracted. 

But we forgive as we have been forgiven. We understand that there but for the grace of God go I. Even if we sometimes need a reminder to. 

And our forgiveness should be as longsuffering and loving as that which was shown to us. 

If you are holding a grudge against someone, and cannot let it go, you aren't right with God. If you're truly saved, you know the feeling of grace, extended to you. Forgive. 

And if you can't understand grace, and hold on to your grievance, you will find yourself before the strait gate unable to enter. Like a camel entering the eye of a needle, unable to pass. 

Let go and humble yourself to God in Jesus name, and receive His grace. Amen.

Another chapter of Matthew, another multitude seeking Jesus to heal them, another instance of the Pharisees come to trip up or trick Jesus into saying something they could use against him, and another time Jesus, using scripture that they *should know,* makes fools of them. 

They ask about divorce, which under Roman law was allowed for any reason at any time, and simply required one party to leave a marriage. Jewish law, given under Moses set certain conditions to be met, and obligations to be had. 

It is often this conflict between Roman law and Jewish tradition that the Pharisees sought to exploit, making Jesus say something that would either put Him in trouble with the government or to offend the people and give them cause to rebuke. 

And just as He does in other instances, Jesus uses the word of God to show that they offer a false choice, that God's way is perfect and without error, placing the shame of rebuke upon them. 

Again we see the mistaken impression that the Pharisees were legalistic and strict, when in reality, they sought loopholes from God's law and Jesus teaches a stricter interpretation. The false idea that Jesus came to liberalize the law rather than liberate us from the law is part and parcel to the works crowd's self-righteous theology.

And so Jesus reminds the Pharisees that Moses compromise on divorce came from the failures and weaknesses of men, not a contradiction of God's intent, that what he joined together no man can tear us under. That divorce is adultery. That other than putting away a betrothed before the consummation due to her or her parents lying about her chastity, that she had fornicated, there was no sufficient reason to not marry the woman to whom you'd pledged yourself, and cleaved unto. 

In cases of premarital fornication, the male partner was meant to pay a dowry and make her his wife, having taken her honor. Note that fornication, a grievous sin, has remedy under God's perfect law that satisfies all parties involved, while discouraging the practice. Whereas adultery is met with a death sentence, it's being a crime.

And Jesus perfect understanding of the law, for he was the word made flesh, once again turned away the Pharisees in their temptation of Him.

Faced with the truth of this doctrine, and the gravity of the concept of marriage, some of his disciples questioned whether or not marriage as it's laid out under God's law is profitable to a man. The responsibilities and obligations outweighing The virtue and benefit. But Jesus corrects them, that while there are eunuchs, or today we might say incels, who have been gilded from birth, or by man, or to achieve the kingdom of heaven without temptation of the flesh, there are still those who marry which is the norm and his instruction is to them.

I will say God wishes us to mary, become one flesh, and be fruitful and multiply. For the law of God is Not grievous to those that love Him.

And again, as in previous chapters, the crowds that have gathered to see Jesus bring their children before Him to be blessed. And again Jesus compares the humility of a child to what is necessary to enter the kingdom of heaven, to received salvation. To suffer the children and despise them not, for their angels are before God always. And that offending one of these little ones, that is spoiling them from being able to receive the Gospel or misleading them to some other truth, or abusing them into reprobation - is a great sin that is punished in Hell exceedingly. That it's better to tie a millstone around your neck and cast yourself into the ocean if you are a "MAP," for example, for at least you'll avoid a worse damnation than that which already awaits.

Next we see another telling of the Rich Young Man who claims righteousness by the law, saying that he has obeyed all the commandments since his youth, but what more must he do to be saved?

He calls Jesus good master, in an act of flattery that Jesus turns around on him handing him a softball on a tee. If only God is good why call me good, Jesus asks. He's taking the compliment and giving a subtle opportunity for the Rich Young Man to say "Because thou art God," which of course will not say, it having been an insincere platitude.

Running through the list of commandments, Jesus asks if he follows them all to which the Rich Young Man assures him that he has his whole life, but when Jesus suggests he sell all that he have giving up everything to follow Him, which would give action to his claim of righteousness, the Rich Young Man balks and departs. 

It's this pride and arrogance that Jesus is preaching against throughout the past few chapters. It is more difficult for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of Heaven than it is for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, because they're carrying that pride with them, their love of the material wealth that they've accumulated, their self-righteousness in thinking that they have adhered to the whole of the law, not just by letter but in spirit, when in truth they're as much a sinner as the beggar, who in faith, inherits the kingdom of God through Christ Jesus. 

Had he recognized Jesus as Christ, the son of God, and truly sought the kingdom of Heaven by faith, he would have abandoned his riches and followed Christ, when asked, and in that faith, been saved.

We see then that the disciples were amazed at this doctrine, questioning then who can inherit the kingdom of God, if that is the level of adherence to the law one would need to achieve.

Jesus answers "With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible."

Again, we are saved by grace through faith, a gift of God, through the blood of His Son, Christ Jesus. 

It is impossible for us to achieve any righteousness sufficient through our works. You cannot repent of enough sin to enter into the kingdom of Heaven. No amount of self-righteous acts can ever be sufficient.

Finally we see peter, always ready to ask a question whether it is prudent or not, asking what reward then do they have, having already renounced all of their worldly goods to follow Him, having already received an inheritance in the kingdom of God for their faith that He was the Christ. And Jesus responds that they will have seats of judgment, over the 12 tribes of Israel in his kingdom when it comes. And that all who forsake or lose anything in his name, suffering tribulation, or division from family and friends, being maligned for our faith, persecuted, led to martyrdom even, that these will rule over the Kingdom of Heaven with him. 

So many Christians today seek to avoid tribulation, when it's that very tribulation that gives us rewards in heaven. They do fruitless works of self-righteousness, a thinking that by them they will achieve salvation. Meanwhile it is the meek, and the humble who inherit the kingdom of heaven, the poor in spirit. And they who suffering tribulation, keep the faith holding on knowing that a reward not made of hands, but of God, awaits them.

The Gospels shows that even among Christ's staunchest followers, there was competition between some of the Apostles. Who will be greater in the Kingdom of Heaven? What reward will they receive for their devotion? Even John telling of the footrace he won with Peter to Christ's empty tomb. This continued even after the day of Pentecost, and the contentions between Peter and Paul. 

These human traits of pride and expectation are laid bare by God in His word, just as the great men of the OT, patriarchs, prophets and kings, are all shown to be flawed humans. Prone to sin. Often prideful. Sometimes foolish. The Apostles are no different, and suffer more for comparison to Jesus, who is perfect, the only truly perfect man in scripture, being God in the flesh. 

It is fascinating from a literary sense, how consistently and fully fleshed out most of those who appear in the Bible are, as characters. And the spiritual aspect, a constant reminder of who we are, and who God uses for His purposes on Earth. 

It is encouraging and yet humbling that these great men and women, human, do mighty works and yet are as weak as we are. Great in faith, but with moments of doubt. Great in the spirit of righteousness, but still sinners and weak in the flesh. Serving as examples, like Peter often does, with his well intentioned rock-headedness. 

In chapter 18, they asked who would be greatest in the Kingdom, to which Jesus used a humble child to illustrate the humility that it would require. 

A similar dispute occurs both in Luke 9 and Luke 22, where the Apostles are said to have had *strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest.*

Here, in Matthew 20, is the direct continuation of the end of 19, where Jesus had just illustrated the problem with the self-righteous and rich with humbling themselves sufficiently to enter into the Kingdom of Heaven, unable to accept the simple salvation of faith, and unwilling to give up everything in this life, for the eternal. 

Peter had asked what will their reward be, having done just that. Walking away from their profession, their income, their families, wives and children to follow Jesus. And Jesus taught them they have their reward, but cautions them to remember the lesson of humility, suffering the children, and many that are first shall be last in His kingdom. 

And so we are here in Matthew 20, and Jesus tells His disciples a parable. Of a man, hiring hands for the harvest, where each is given the agreed upon wage, a penny for a day's work. Those that labored from the start, and even those who labored but a short time. And the longest among them grumbled that they should receive the same reward.

But entrance to the Kingdom of Heaven is the reward itself, agreed upon in faith, and contentions of who will be greatest therein is up to the judgment of God the Father, and our own judgment of our own works does not give us the right to question this. 

Believing Jews in the newly forming churches saw themselves as "first," the Gentiles, "last." Often prideful and puffed-up Christians, having been born to believers and raised in a church will look down on babes in Christ, coming from a sinful past and yet to get right in all things. 

Those who volunteer at church, and attend 3 times a week. Who carry all the chairs and make the largest pot luck. Who show for soul winning times, and go on mission trips, spreading the Gospel, but not out of humility of being a servant. Not out of satisfaction of being least, and thus, doing all things from that meek humility of the recognition of their retched state, but instead out of striving and contention. Pride.

Good works done, and some reward had, for certain, when the fire burns away the wood, hay and stubble, some diamonds will surely remain. But yet, how much the greater their reward if they had become like unto children? Had been ministers to others. Willing and happy servants? 

This is the lesson Jesus tries to teach His disciples, and was preparing them to see Him live out, in Jerusalem.

Now the sons of Zebedee, James and John (whom Jesus nicknames 'Boanerges,' which means "Sons of Thunder” (**Mark 3:17**) were part of His core inner circle, along with Peter. They witnessed the transfiguration on the mount. James was the first to follow Christ's example of being willing to die for Him, and was first of them to be martyred. John, living the longest, writing His gospel, the revelation of Jesus, and passing from old age, the only one of the original 12 to do so. Truly they were great men of God.

Here, in this context of the last and the first, the martyrs and servants, those who lose everything to gain Christ, and His impending sacrifice, that their mother comes asking, "*Grant that these my two sons may sit, the one on thy right hand, and the other on the left, in thy kingdom.*" And Jesus replies that she doesn't understand what she is asking for them. That to obtain such position isn't His to give, but the price is higher than perhaps a mother could ever grieve for their sons. 

"*Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of, and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?*" Jesus asks them, signifying the manner of death that awaited Him. And, the Bible says, they replied, "*We are able*."

Perhaps it is out of mercy that God only held one brother to that fate, and used the other for some of His greatest work on earth, writing the definitive Gospel of faith that unbelievers should know salvation, and revealing to John the manner of the end of the world, in his old age. 

James however wasn't spared. One wonders if his mother was alive to see it, and if she made peace, knowing finally what it was she had asked.

Now this exchange causes the other 10 to strive with the 2 brothers. Jesus pleas with them to not engage in that kind of dispute over who is greater.

He says that the princes of this world exercise authority by who is greater, who has the most, commands the most. But that in His kingdom it isn't so. 

"*Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant: Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many*."

This still applies today. Jesus did not come here to bring peace, but division. Separation. Among family. Among friends. From wealth and personal comfort. That we will see tribulations and persecution. And to be hated by man for His name. 

The promise is that *every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold.* That tribulation in this world is glory in the next. That being meek, poor in spirit, but great in faith, willing to suffer that others may gain, is how we are to live, and great is the reward for those of us who may. 

To be servants. To wash the feet of others. To be ministers. Not puffed up. But as like unto a child. To show mercy for others, not being proud of our own righteousness but a reflection of Christ's. 

And as they pass two blind beggars, persistent in their faith, Jesus has mercy upon them, and they are given their sight. 

The blind made to see. 

If you, like I, struggle occasionally on this lesson, how to be humble. How not to resent our status, position, wealth and comfort. How to live for Christ as a minister to the weak, with no expectations for added reward, but happy with the gift of eternal life we have hope on, listening to the Spirit with the new man inside, pray. Pray and worship, persistently. Asking Jesus to be able to see.

Approaching the finish of His work on earth, Jesus arrives in Jerusalem, meekly riding an ass, triumphantly received by the people, all in accordance with scripture. The prophets who spoke of Him signifying Jesus was the Christ. The people hailed Him with hosannas, "*This is Jesus the prophet of Nazareth of Galilee"* and calling Him the son of David, indicating they saw Him as heir to the kingdom. 

And He again chased the moneychangers out of His Father's house, who had made the house of worship into one of merchandise. And again, the Scribes and Pharisees, high priests of the temple, were threatened by His presence and sought to do evil towards Jesus. 

And hearing the throng of children in the temple, witness to Jesus' miraculous teaching and healing, crying out "Hosanna to the son of David!" the Bible says these supposed "men of God" were sore displeased. They confront Jesus, questioning if He hears what they are shouting out, hoping to trap Him in a blasphemy. Jesus instead replies, again with scripture, **Psalms 8:2,** giving the vipers nothing to accuse Him of, but God's word.

Matthew continues the narrative the next day, with Jesus returning to the temple, hungry. (A reminder that in all things, Jesus was fully human as well as fully God, and aware of our condition).

Approaching a fig tree, barren of fruit, Jesus says "let no fruit grow on thee, henceforth and forever," and the tree withered on the spot. This is both literal and allegory for the Jews who were to reject Him. 

The Apostles seeing this sign, marveled. And Jesus teaches them, had they faith enough they could do this and more. That they could move mountains. That all things asked of in prayer can be delivered unto us, we simply must have faith enough. 

*All things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive.*

This is a promise from God Himself, in the flesh. Don't treat it lightly or as some kind of daily affirmation, but as literally true. Grow in faith, living faith to faith, building upon it, and witness it in your own life. God is not slack concerning His promises.

Next Jesus is again tempted by the Pharisees, asking "*By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority?"* And again, Jesus confounds them by asking them to answer by what authority do they say came John the Baptist. 

*If we shall say, From heaven; he will say unto us, Why did ye not then believe him? But if we shall say, Of men; we fear the people; for all hold John as a prophet. And they answered Jesus, and said, We cannot tell. And he said unto them, Neither tell I you by what authority I do these things.*

Then Jesus questions them by way of a parable. A certain man with two sons, orders them to work his vineyard. One refuses, but changes his mind and goes to work. The other days yes, but doesn't do it. Which did the the will of the father? 

They rightly say the first, not seeing the meaning and Jesus readily gives it to them, but good. 

*Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you. We see again, Biblical repentance is a turning towards belief in what God tells us is His will. Faith in His word. Jesus tells these self-righteousness holy men that the worst sinners who believed John that the kingdom of God was at hand are the first son, and they the second, claiming they do the will of the Father but did it not, not believing him who He sent.

We have begun the series of chapters in Matthew, (starting in 21 which we covered yesterday, and continuing in 22-25), of nonstop preaching by Jesus. In parables, in scriptures, in harsh rebuke, and revelation, leading up to His crucifixion. Where the scribes, lawyers, Pharisees and Sadducees come to tempt Jesus, to test His doctrine and find fault with Him, that they may accuse Him. But having not understanding of the word, they each fail to Christ's perfect understanding, as the word made flesh. 

Today's reading opens with Jesus continuing in parables to convict the so-called holy men of Jerusalem for their dereliction and disobedience to God. He has described them as the son who agreed to work the fields for their father, but did not go. To being the husbandmen of the vineyard, who rather than giving of the fruits of the harvest to the lord,  beat and slay his servants, and betray and kill his son in an attempt to steal his inheritance and deny their lord his increase. Jesus has revealed to the crowd, hailing Him as a prophet of God, the hypocrisy of their religious leaders, and if it were not for fear of that crowd, the high preists would have seized Jesus there at the temple. 

Jesus now boldly preaches on the Kingdom of Heaven, His Father's Kingdom, likening it unto a wedding feast for the Son. 

And the King sends forth servants to bid all to come to the wedding, and none would. 

He instructs his servants to tell all that that they bid to the feast that the work is done, the meal is ready, the meat slain and prepared, and so come, and yet those bidden scoff and make light of it, and returned to their merchandise, to their money, to their land and material goods and wealth. And some took the King's servants, treated them spitefully and murdered them. 

And so the King in his wrath sends armies to destroy the people whom he had invited. Whom he had assured all was ready. Who refused to believe him and come. Who killed those who came to invite them. He destroyed them utterly. 

And now, still requiring guests for the feast prepared, to share in the work the King had done, he tells his servants to go out, to the highways, throughout the land, and as many as they find, bid to the feast. 

God had promised this wedding, this celebration of His righteousness and love, His creation, to mankind from Adam, and was rejected by most. He gave a select people the details, written in His law and spoken to of the prophets that they may be a light to the nations, bringing the world to the feast. And they rejected His word and slew His prophets. 

And so, God destroying them, sends His servants to bid all to salvation. Both bad and good. Whomever will come. 

And as the parable continues, the King sees a guest arrive, without a garment fit for the feast. In his own filthy rags, his own righteousness, representing those who believe they can enter the Kingdom by their own works. The King has him bound and removed, cast into the outer darkness. The lake of fire that is the fate of all who do not have the spotless white garment given to believers by the lamb of God. The imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ which covers all our sin.

For many are called, but few are chosen, for they rejected the invitation. Didn't believe the report. Didn't arrive dressed for the feast.

Make no mistake, as servants of God, this is our role. 

We are the sons who do labor in the field for the harvest. We are the loyal husbandmen, tending the Lord's vineyard, and bringing to Him the fruit of the harvest. We are the servants bidding all to come to the wedding feast of the Son. 

We are commanded to win souls to Christ. To go out along the highways, and as many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage. Both bad and good. That they may attend in the raiment fit for a wedding feast.

“*He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.”*

Our role as those obedient to the Gospel is to go out to give the same Gospel that saved us to every creature, and compel them to come in, that God's house may be filled.

Often the focus here is mistakenly on Jesus saying to render unto Caesar what is Caesar's, which is true. We should, as much as possible, live peaceably with all men, giving tribute to whom tribute is due, custom to whom custom is due. Materialistic things are the provence of the world.

Regardless of how we get to the point of repentance, of taking the truth we hear and believing it, in our heart, turning towards God. 

Not of sin, though godly sorrow for sin may lead us there. Not of any works, or deeds of the law. Not of our sincere, careful, vehement desire to make right what we've done wrong in godly sorrow. These may work us to the change of heart and towards faith, but they aren't requirements for salvation, which is to believe on Jesus Christ, that He was raised from the dead. 

Some call upon the name of the Lord while in tribulation, being beset by the wicked and surrounded by enemies. In desperation, stricken by poor health, or in mourning for a loved one. By example of the righteous being kind and compassionate to them in their hour of need. Of being fed and clothed by believers, when they had nothing and hungered. Of seeing God's light magnified in the kindness and charity, mercy and faith of we who believe. 

The Bible tells us of many circumstance that brings a sinner to repentance towards God. It is not always of guilt and shame. Making it so excludes many from receiving the Gospel, and the prominence of this doctrine, making repentance of sin the way to be born again, places the onus of salvation, of being justified, upon the would-be believers to clean up their act. It implies that this is the means of salvation, their ability to do the works of the law. It becomes works salvation, either before the fact, or after, to show "genuine repentance," to maintain salvation, or as proof it was real. 

To both backslidden believers and the unregenerate sinner who had already 'cleaned up their life,' and had genuine sorrow and repented of their sins, but not believed on Christ, it places a stumbling block. 

It is a wicked heresy for this very reason. And that is why Satan pushes it so hard.

I think one of the stumbling blocks for those who have come to repentance via their genuine sorrow for sins, those that hit bottom, so to speak, seeing their lives and relationships destroyed by their own selfish and destructive behavior, and having a rocky path to making things right, is that there are resentments for those who come to the faith by other means. 

There are many who are raised Christian, in godly homes, and can't even tell you when they believed. 

There are many who, when they heard the truth, accepted it. Absent trauma or drama, and yet saved. 

There are those who had long ago cleaned up their act, dealt with their addictions, or put away the anger and hurt at being victimized, say by abuse, physical, sexual or emotional. That turned over a new leaf, and yet only believed on the Gospel years after. 


And there are those, caught in the jaws of addiction, struggling to get out, long after repenting of what led them there, but unable to break free, who are comforted by a believer, and asking them, are given the Gospel and while yet, still sinners, in a moment of clarity, believe.

People who crawled through whatever hell on earth to come to salvation, by sorrow for their sin, can look at these disparate cases, and others like them, and think "that person is not really saved, like I am." 

And the promotion of the idea that we must repent of our sins to be saved feeds that resentment, and can make a repentant heart grow bitter over time.

This resentment is similar to the workers who labored all day for the same penny that those late arrivals collected in the parable Jesus tells in Matthew 20. It's sort of the inverse reaction of the good son in the parable of the prodigal son. 

It's this attitude that leads to holier than thou fruit inspectors, judging others salvation by their works, being a respecter of persons regarding testimonials, etc.

Before heading in to Matthew chapter 23, it's a good idea to consider how hypocrisy flourishes from the idea of salvation by repentance from sin, rather than repentance towards God and faith in Christ. 

By placing the emphasis on what was turned from, rather than the testimony of what is turned to, what the changing of mind has wrought through faith, it creates an almost inevitable form of a caste system within a church. Of respecters of persons, who in hypocrisy see themselves as *more saved* than others. 

Just as the apostles asking Jesus of whose sin was responsible for the man blind from birth, or those questioning him about the men killed by Pilate, are those who had a wall fall on them killing them, the tendency and inclination to place the path to righteousness some take over the experience of others is the same form of hypocrisy which Jesus warns us against.

For all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. For all were perishing before repenting to believe on Christ. For all are deserving of hell, and none are justified by their works of the law. 

We are all in the same boat and there but for the grace of God go each and every one of us. Regardless of how relatively easy we came to salvation, and regardless of how we struggle to pick up our cross daily and follow him.

And losing sight of that leads to our focusing on the mote of our neighbor's eye. Of neglecting the beam in our own. Of judging in hypocrisy the Christian walk of others, while neglecting to work out our own salvation in fear and trembling. 

This is one reason why I dislike so-called testimonial preaching. Not the testimony of Jesus Christ and the saving power of faith, but the long winded testimonials, almost reveling in past sin, showing you just how down low someone was before receiving the gospel, almost a point of pride of how much they had to dig themselves out to get to where others are mercifully, by the grace of God. 

And I have been in churches where this becomes almost a competition of sorts. And where people blessed to have been born into a Godly family, and whose sowing of wild oats was almost incidental, making it out to be that they were low down wretched creatures, by way of showing just how really super duper saved they are, through their "struggle." Who haven't been blessed by God's grace and mercy, are embarrassed by it, for the glory that is heaped upon those with a testimony of a life of sin, turned around. 


This is yet another reason why Satan has painstakingly and methodically brainwashed everyone into adding "...of sin" to repentance. It's another way this becomes toxic in even good churches, with the right Gospel. 

We should not glory in the fact that those more sinful than we were saved. We should glory in God that he would save any of us. We were all equally damned. We all had to turn to believe the same thing to gain life. One sin or millions. A degenerate life in the swinehurd, for a life of ease and comfort of our father's estate. 

For all have fallen short of the glory of God and deserve death and Hell. 

But God has sent his servants to invite us to his Son's wedding feast, both good and bad, called to repentance. Amen

Matthew 25 continues the Olivette Discourse between Jesus and His disciples, where in the previous chapter He had laid out much of end times prophecy, and His warning and instruction to be watchful and mindful, like a good servant keeping the house while the Lord was away, so as to not be taken unawares at His return. And so, by way of parable, Jesus expounds on this doctrine. 

The first, the parable of the 10 virgins, 5 wise, 5 foolish, awaiting the bridegroom, with their lamps. The 5 wise have lamps filled with oil, the 5 fools never bothered, and caught unawares are shut out of the marriage. And in their pleading the Lord says, "Verily I say unto you, I know you not." 

The oil is the Holy Spirit, the lamps, our hearts. The foolish virgins, the unsaved who, knowing full well of the bridegroom's pending return were lazy, slumbering.

At His return, the foolish virgins beg the wise for some of their oil, for shared righteousness, but it is not the wise's to give or share. Each must get their own from Christ. And so, the foolish were locked out in the darkness, wailing. 

There are many calling themselves Christian who never received the oil, never accepted the Spirit, and tarried and slept while the master is away. Like the virgins, they may well have lived chaste lives, turning from sin, present in the chambers, but never coming to the truth and repentance to be saved. 

They believed they could purchase the oil, and return. Be given another chance. But once the wedding feast starts, it's too late.

The next is the parable of the good and faithful servants, and the unprofitable one. In this familiar story, Jesus tells us of a wealth man, gone on a journey, leaving to each of his servants his goods to watch over. Divided according to their ability. Given talents according to their talent. 

The one who received 5 talents doubled it, and he who received 2 did the same. But the one to whom the lord offered one, took it and buried it and had no use of it at all. 

When the master returns, after a long time Jesus emphasizes, each gives an account. The 2 servants who have used what was given unto them to increase the master's wealth, and are rewarded for their efforts. 

To each, he says "*Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord."*

Note that to both is given the same reward, though what each is made ruler over may differ. Jesus uses the same wording for both in this teaching of the Kingdom of Heaven for a reason. While we may be given responsibility based on our talents, our salvation, entering I to the joy of the Lord is the same. And so, while one may do great things for the Lord and be given greater responsibility in the Kingdom, and another given less, but just as faithful, is given less responsibility, both are entered into the Kingdom. Both are given to the joy of the Lord having accepted the responsibility while He was away. 

And to the unprofitable servant, who didn't take the responsibility, but despised it. Who the lord expected little of. He just buried it until the return, not even joining in where the work of others may have given increase to what he was left. He is an unsaved person who knowing of Jesus, thought wickedly of Him, and didn't accept the gift of salvation, not even to just be partaker of the joy of the Lord. 

The unprofitable servant gives his excuse; "*Lord, I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed*."

It is important to remember that in scripture, what a man might say, especially one representative of the unsaved, isn't necessarily true. That while the narration of the Bible is truth, the words uttered by characters aren't always. Jesus is not a cruel master. We see this in the parable where he takes into account our ability, and asks little of us considering. He rewards generously those good and faithful to Him. 

So the unprofitable servant claims it was fear of an unjust Lord that led him to squander and reject that which was given him. 

And the Lord says if that were true, and you actually thought that of me, you'd have at least tried out of fear. 

Many who refuse to believe claiming the worst of God, that He is unjust, and takes what isn't His to take, don't actually follow through on their fear. For if they believed it, they'd have done their duty out of that fear. 

God prefers we accept the gift, the salvation He offers and to make the most of what's given us, out of love and loyalty to Him. But He isn't opposed to it being received in fear for His wrath.

The promise of God through Christ Jesus is the reward for the faithful servant, and the eternal punishment of those who reject Him.

*For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath. And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.*

This is the offer made in the testimony of God, His word.

Some use these parables to teach that you can lose your salvation. That the foolish virgins and the unprofitable servant were saved, and having been sinful or disobedient, had lost their shot at Heaven. But there is nothing to this, for ALL are called. We all, every person, has been given the truth, written in our hearts, through creation, and have no excuse. God will that none perish. Every name is in the book of life until it's blotted out. When one dies, or is given over to reprobation or, in the end, refuses to repent and believe when the day of the Lord is come, it's too late. They are damned to eternal fire. To eternal torment. 

The foolish virgins and unprofitable servant believed falsely, and what had been given them, the chance to enter into the joy of the Lord, is taken from them. Salvation cannot be lost, only refused.

Consider, had the five foolish virgins filled their lamps with oil at the first, they may still have slumbered and been lazy regarding their waiting for his return, but they still would have had that oil, the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, and still would have entered into the wedding with the five wise virgins.

Similarly, Jesus says that had the unprofitable servant simply thrown in the one talent of silver giving him, his own salvation, with others seeking to increase the harvest, he would have still entered into the joy of the Lord, the Kingdom of Heaven.

The Bible says in **Romans 4:5**
*But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.*

And while I would rather have great rewards in the kingdom, being given responsibility over much, or even responsibility over little, the goal is to be present at the bridegroom's wedding feast, to enter into the joy of the Lord.

Far too many reject the gift. Bury it in the ground and don't even use it for themselves, let alone accept it and bring increase to the Father, honoring the Son.

Rounding out the chapter, Jesus gives us a summation of the end, that He will gather His sheep unto Him, and the goats, the unbelieving, be cast into Hell. 

Christ's rationale, that those who are His extended charity to the needy brethren, and by this, perhaps unwittingly as it is painted by Him, did so unto Him;

*Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me...Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.*

Again, works-based heresy puts it that it's these acts of charity, which is the love shown others as a reflection of the light of God, the grace He's shown us magnified by our works is the means of entering into the Kingdom, rather than the way by which our faith is shown. How we are separated from the goats as His sheep. As the Bible says in **James 1**;

*Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.*

Religion is the practice of our faith. This is how it is lived. 

And note that the sheep didn't even consider the gain, that it was truly Jesus being helped rather than a stranger. It was just what they did. As Paul reminds us; *Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares*.

And to the goats, Jesus says; *Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me.* The significance of their not having charity in their hearts from God's grace is reflected in their spiritual condition.

Finally, there is a wicked doctrine that circulates among the unsaved, pushed by vipers that there is no Kingdom of Heaven, that our reward and inheritance is of the earth, and that there is no Hell, that the damned do not face eternal torment and burning for their sin. Many pushing this false doctrine claim Jesus never spoke of either, and that Hell and the grave are the same. 

Some use corrupt versions of the Bible to claim foolish things such as Sheol being different than Hades, that "Abraham's bosom" is a place rather than a body part, a paradise inside or along side Hell. They use semantics and concordances, pedantic reasoning and ignore the actual text and context regarding both. It has been a snare and a stumbling block for many. 

Some see the idea of eternal punishment as 'unjust,' and like the unprofitable servant, accuse God of being unjustified in His condemnation. Others will paint believers as the offenders, offering up an "unfair" God, when, in their mind, God is love and so he "wouldn't subject people to eternal torment just for not believing in Jesus." 

They may even trot out the old "what about the savage in the jungle, hmm? Is *that* fair??" chestnut. 

All of this is natural man foolishness as both the promise of Heaven and eternal life, along with Hell and eternal torment are given throughout scripture, and as just **Matthew 25** demonstrates. 

Jesus says the Kingdom of Heaven is like the wedding of the bridegroom, to which the 5 wise virgins are let in to, the door shut to the fools, whom the bridegroom says he never knew. He doesn't say the millennial reign on earth. He doesn't say the New Earth of revelation. He consistently says the Kingdom is of Heaven. It is our promise and reward, both now after our physical death, (*to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord*) and our inheritance in the resurrection. 

But what of Hell? Is it simply being shut out of Heaven? Again, in **Matthew 25** Jesus tells us details of the unbelievers' fate. 

Of the unprofitable servant, He says "*cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."* This is a formula used throughout Matthew by Jesus to describe Hell. Wailing and gnashing of teeth. Torment and agony. But is 'outer darkness' Hell? 

**Revelation 14** says of the damned; *The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.*

Tormented with fire and brimstone, the smoke of their torment ascending forever and ever. Sounds like Hell. 

As an aside, some wishy-washy Christians will claim that Hell is actually just the "separation from Jesus," when here we see the burning torment of the damned is done *in* His presence. 

**Revelation 20** tells us;
*the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever...And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death. And whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.*

Further, **Revelation 21**; *But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.* 

And **Revelation 22**, after telling of those who have overcome are within the Holy City, that *without are dogs, and sorcerers, and whoremongers, and murderers, and idolaters, and whosoever loveth and maketh a lie.*

Back in **Matthew 25**, Jesus says "*Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels....And these shall go away into everlasting punishment.*" 

Everlasting fire. Everlasting punishment. But to the righteous, life eternal. 

This is the biblical teaching on Hell. It's a real place, in the pit of the earth for now, and later cast into the outer darkness, the lake of fire, after the physical world is destroyed, after the millennium has ended and the White Throne Judgment of the unrighteous is done.  

So do not be fooled. Hell is very real, and God is not slack regarding His promises. He is perfectly righteous and holy. And if He says throughout His word that eternal torment, punishment, burning, is what awaits those not clothed in the righteousness of Jesus then you can believe it is true.

**Mark 3** sets the same pattern we've seen in the other Gospels, of Jesus healing or teaching and the Jews who oppose God trying to use the occasion to be rid of Him. Here, Christ heals a man's withered hand on the Sabbath. As we have just read in **Mark 2**, Jesus continues to make this point, that it is lawful to do good on a sabbath. That Sabbaths were made for men, not men for the Sabbath. He is the Sabbath. 

Failing to lay hands on Him, Jesus makes His way to the sea, and multitudes came to see Him from all about the region, so much so He asks a boat be ready to help Him depart, should the crowd be too much. He heals the multitudes, and gains more who flock to see the wonders, and glory God, and some unto believing on Him as the son of God by faith. This is important, as He reprimands the unclean spirits He casts out to silence their proclamation that Jesus is Christ, the Son of God. 

We see that then, after retreating to the sea, Jesus then goes to the mountains, continuing to preach to the masses following Him. He formally ordains the 12 Apostles to preach and heal in His stead, so as to minister to the crowds that have gathered. 

And because people from all over Galilee, Judea, and beyond have come to see Him, and the proximity of Nazareth to Capernaum, where much of Christ's ministry had been, His family, mother and half-brothers and friends He grew up become concerned, not knowing who Jesus truly is. They thought Him crazy. But the scribes accused Him of being from Satan, and the Holy Ghost by which He cast out these demons, they label an unclean spirit. A blasphemy He warns is unforgivable, and is a way to reprobation and damnation. 

As Jesus says a house divided cannot stand, as if Satan turned on his own. How can Satan cast out Satan?

And all sins of men will be forgiven. This is important. A penitent believer will be forgiven all manner of sins, but the blasphemy of the Holy Ghost and deliberately changing God's word (Rev 22).

These are direct causes of reprobation that most Christians will accept. The will also concede death without believing is final, and damned. But they often struggle with the idea that some, not wishing to retain God in their knowledge are turned over by Him to a reprobate mind. A rejected mind. Hearts hardened. Conscience seared. Twice-dead. **Unable** to come to the knowledge of the truth. This is the case for many of these Pharisees and scribes. Such was the case for many in the Old Testament, Cain and Pharoah for example. It continues to be the case today. 

And because people confuse reprobation, a spiritual state of man, finally rejected of God, and the unnatural lusts and sins committed by reprobates, they argue, that if all sins be forgiven, then there is no such thing as "too late, reprobate." This puts the sodomite cart before the horse. 

Unnatural sin is not the cause of reprobation, but a symptom that it's occured. It is important to get that right. It's never about the sin itself, but the state of a man's heart towards God. Belief unto salvation. Unbelief and vain beliefs of the unsaved which can be overcome with the word and repented of unto faith, or rejection of belief to the point God gives up, stops shining the light. In Mark 4 we see another parallel passage, this time with [Matthew 13](https://t.me/HouseOfWews2/5194) which we studied a few weeks ago. (it's repeated in **Luke 8** as well, which God willing we shall see soon)

The parable of the sower is another instance of the nature of creation existing that Jesus, the word of God though whom all things were created, may use it as example to explain the heavenly things of God. The physical to understand the spiritual. 

For we who are saved, the greater lesson is how we rightly divide the word, understanding that His words are spirit. That His words are eternal life, and what that means. That creation speaks the word of God for those with ears to hear and eyes to see. Who aren't without deep roots, who aren't choked out by thorns. That we may be fertile soil and bring forth fruit after our kind, 100 fold. 

*And he said unto them, Unto you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God: but unto them that are without, all these things are done in parables: That seeing they may see, and not perceive; and hearing they may hear, and not understand; lest at any time they should be converted, and their sins should be forgiven them*.

Jesus used clearly discerned pictures of the natural, the physical, to help us understand the spiritual, the unseen, that we who are seeking God's truth or who have received the quickening of our spirit may receive faith, which the Bible says *is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.*

He uses the seen to give us insight to the unseen. This is what I was getting at [yesterday](https://t.me/HouseOfWews2/6127). 

But to the carnally minded all things are physical, literal. Materialists see Jesus parables as Nicodemus did; taken to absurd levels or autistic literalism and missing the actual spiritual application. 

This is what the Bible means by "*the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned."*

The natural man is earthly. They rely on the wisdom of man. They lean unto their own understanding. They are those by the wayside where the word is sown and *Satan cometh immediately, and taketh* it away. 

And as we see in the parable of the sower, as Jesus explains, there are saved Christians who are the stoney ground. They hear the word and believe, but having nothing to take hold of, being unprofitable, without a church, without reading their Bible, without seeking to learn the deeper things of God, *and so endure but for a time: afterward, when affliction or persecution ariseth for the word's sake, immediately they are offended.* 

There are Christians who hear the word and are saved, but are among thorns, the cares of the world. They allow covetousness and lust to choke them out, and become unable to bear fruit. To get more people saved by their example. Unprofitable to God or to others. 

We should seek to grow roots, deep in fertile soil which is God's word and His ways that we may win souls to Christ and bring in the harvest for the Lord.

The lesson of why Jesus uses parables, and the true nature of creation to serve as that parable is given us that we may receive more. That having been given eternal life, and having been made alive in the spirit, we may be given yet more. 

It's the opposite of gnosticism, where the secrets are revealed by measures, and final "enlightenment" kept hidden until one archives the ability to see. 

The Bible way is that we seeking enlightenment are given it immediately, if we believe God's word. Then our knowledge grows the more we receive it, freely given. The light put on a candlestick, not hidden under a bushel. 

It's not hid from those who ask. It's freely given *with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you: and unto you that hear shall more be given.*

It's up to you if you be stoney ground. It's up to you if you allow thorns to choke you out. It's up to you if you be fertile soil. What you ask for is what you're given, to those that hear. 

*For he that hath, to him shall be given: and he that hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he hath.*

He that hath not, those without ears to hear, those by the wayside, they are given the chance to receive the word. The seed is sown in their hearts. But even this is taken away eventually. God doesn't shine His light on all men forever. The Spirit tries for a time, but if you don't want to hear the truth, if the seed can't spring up on your hardened heart, compacted like the well-worn soil of the pathway by the wayside, He will take His light away to shine on more fertile hearts. Then it is too late.

*So is the kingdom of God.*

Jesus uses all these things of His own creation to make simple the ways of God to us. 

And a man sows seed, which grows after its kind, blade, and ear and fruit. He doesn't make it grow, it just does, and when it is ripe for the harvest he brings in the bounty. 

And so is the Kingdom of Heaven. The seed is the word, Jesus tells us, and it will *spring and grow up, he knoweth not how.* Meaning God, represented as the farmer doesn't dictate to the seed that it germinate, that it sprout, when it should flower and bud, that it bear fruit. Only that it will as it will, and in due season be ready for harvest. 

Obviously God knows *how,* but the point is He doesn't determine which seed sprouts, or the nature of how it grows. 

It's a rebuke of Calvinism, but it is meant to give us understanding of the Kingdom and our role in it. Both as the sowers and the sheaves. How Heaven grows. 

*And he said, Whereunto shall we liken the kingdom of God? or with what comparison shall we compare it?*

We are privy to these lessons. We are not given the parable only, for those with ears to hear, but given their meaning. Nothing hid. And scripture gives us the meaning that we who believe may gain deeper understanding. 

Heaven is like a mustard seed, tiny but that grows massive trees, with branches spanning out, each branching further. We are the branches sprung out from the seed. We can trace our lineage in terms of believers who led others to Christ, who led still others, who eventually were those who brought us to salvation. Like a family tree, stretching back to the seed that was sown. 

 *For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ. For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit.*
*For the body is not one member, but many.* **(1 Corinthians 12)**

*My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father's hand.*

*I and my Father are one.*

If you have been one of those who felt lost and hopeless because you were told God only saves the righteous, and that if you become Christian, you have to be perfect or face Hell, understand that this is not what the Bible teaches. As we have seen so often in the Gospel of Mark, each chapter seems to have a casting out of devils, a purging of unclean spirits, or a physical healing by faith, and here we get both. 

Jesus having left the Western shores of Galilee, arrives in the east near Decropolis, the 10 cities. Here he meets the man possessed by a legion of unclean spirits, which had left him wild, among the death of the tombs in the local graveyard. Cutting himself. Unable to be restrained by normal means. A danger to himself and others. 

Many such cases today. 

The man possessed by legion, overtaken by the unclean spirits falls in worship, that is kneeling before Jesus, and the devils beg for mercy. 

It's important to note that this is what worship means in the Bible. Not some sort of special feeling or praise, that is subtly different than veneration. It means to fall to your knees before someone or something. 

The devils were obviously not worshiping Christ as believers, but because He is the Son of God, and they fear Him. 

They ask that they may be cast into a herd of swine and Jesus agrees. The swine then, 2000 of them, run off the cliffs into the sea. The healed man, grateful, seeks to follow Christ but instead, Jesus calls on him to return to his friends to share the power of God that he may be glorified. 

The miracle also causes consternation among the Gentiles of the city, and they beg Christ to leave them, and He does. 

Returning to the other side of the sea, throngs wait on Jesus, to be healed and to hear Him preach. 

A woman with a blood disease, in faith touches Jesus garment and her faith and His virtue heal her. Just as we are healed by our faith in His righteousness, spiritually. 

And in one of the most touching stories of faith and the mercy of Christ, Jesus resurrects the young girl for the faith of her father, Jairus. A leader in the synagogue, knowledgeable of scripture, and desperate for his beloved daughter. Jesus takes mercy on her, and says in Aramaic, *Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise.* 

The mercy of Christ and His love for us makes me cry. Especially as a father. And again faith has made her whole. It is such a wonder and a blessing to know He holds such love for us. Amen.

There is so much narrative packed into **Mark 6**, it really is dense with both stories of Christ and the meaning of His ministry for us as believers. 

Even Jesus found it hard to testify among His own. Those who knew Him best, sinless as He is, and yet doubted. His own half brothers and sisters.

For many Christians who become born again as adults, to families that aren't believers, we know this feel. A prophet is not received by his own. Not even Christ. 


Faith that begets faith. The Lord provides. The sending out of the 12 to the highways and hedges. 

The fear of Herod's guilty conscience, the fate of John the Baptist, and the surmising by the people to who Jesus is.

How many of us have hardened hearts?

The repudiation of following what is the tradition of men, worshiping God in vain, continues. Jesus Christ in condemning the hypocrisy of the Pharisees gives us insight to all who are like them, leaving the commandments of God to embrace the traditions of man, and lose their way. It is what is in our hearts, our old man's mind of the flesh that wars with the new man created of the Spirit within us. The key is to walk with the Spirit, in God's word and in prayer, that the heart be filled with His righteousness and not our own sinful flesh. It doesn't stop us sinning but it makes it less out of our control, giving it over to Christ.
