The Apostles, deapite having understanding, witnessing the feeding of 5000, the 4000, with a handful of loaves and a couple of fishes, filling all men up, and like the grace of God, with an abundance left over, stumble like the blind man with his partial sight restored. Missing the truth of it, though knowing Jesus was Christ. 

This was why Jesus cautioned those He healed to say nothing of it to others. Both to protect them that were healed from the adversaries, the Pharisees and Sadducees and scribes, and to show signs and wonders that His sheep may see and believe, but not proclaiming them to those of that wicked generation, seeking after a sign, evidence of who Jesus is, while missing the signs all around them.  

*That seeing they may see, and not perceive; and hearing they may hear, and not understand; lest at any time they should be converted, and their sins should be forgiven them.*

Jesus' exasperated sigh at the inability of His own closest disciples not understanding precisely who He is, and protesting what He must do on the cross that the glory of God be made manifest is something many Christians today feel when talking to those who call Jesus "Lord, Lord" and then proceed to talk of their works. Who call themselves by His name, Christians, and yet cannot see the truth when presented to them. 

Who, sensing the light and seeing the movement, yet see men as trees, walking. Unable to discern the shapes of things. Missing the signs of the times. Not comprehending the wonders shown in Christ. 

And as Jesus says, *Get thee behind me, Satan: for thou savourest not the things that be of God, but the things that be of men.*

They savor the thing of man, not the things of God. 

And so they remain blind to the full truth. Their faith is in vain. 

*For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge. For they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.*

When believers are faced with those full of zeal for the Lord, but going about to establish their own righteousness rather than the imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ, we sigh in exasperation and ask, "are ye hearts still hardened?" 

If Jesus felt that way, who being God is longsuffering and patient, it is understandable that we too can reach that point when dealing with the heresies and false understanding that so many have today.

Don't get down. Don't become bitter and wrathful. I speak to myself as much as the few who may read this. Be edified by the love Jesus showed in continuing to reveal the truth to those that genuinely were seeking it. The lost who hear His voice. 

It can be frustrating, but don't give up. You may be the water that brings a seed to fruit someday.

And if you are still savoring the things of man over God, if you're still seeing things unclearly. If you haven't put your full faith and trust in the Lord Jesus Christ to provide you with his righteousness, lacking your own and having no way for you to obtain it yourself, then believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and confess him with your mouth and be saved. Given eternal life. Becoming an heir to the kingdom of God.

Because if you're trusting in your works even for a fraction of your salvation, no matter how much you say to him "Lord, Lord," He never knew you. And you will perish. Repent that He may open your eyes with His amazing Grace.

Jesus continues to prepare the Apostles for what is to come. His death, and by which manner, and His resurrection into power and glory. 

We are given an account of the transfiguration of Christ before Peter, James and John. With the spirit of Moses and Elijah beside Him, Jesus in His full glory, and the voice of the Father from Heaven, as if from a cloud, "This is my beloved Son: hear him." Such will He be at His return. 

We get another example of Peter, the stone, stumbling over what to say. 

*Let us make three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias. For he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid.*

It's easy to mock Peter and his continual struggle for understanding, but he represents us in the Gospels. Faithful and seeking understanding. We've all be as Peter before the word of God. 

Then we are privy to the Apostles asking Jesus about a contention with the scribes, who doubting Christ has come claim that "Elias must come first." That they claim to know the prophets and that the conditions have not been met for the Messiah to come. 

Of course Jesus corrects them. *Elias verily cometh first, and restoreth all things; and how it is written of the Son of man, that he must suffer many things, and be set at nought. But I say unto you, That Elias is indeed come, and they have done unto him whatsoever they listed, as it is written of him.* This speaking of John the Baptist, and his manner of death, the same as the prophets of old. The scribes, not believing miss the signs, a recurring theme of Mark and the Gospels.

Next we are told of the casting out of the dumb spirit. How the Apostles and disciples were unable to heal the son brought by his father who, in his pain and in need, calls upon the name of the Lord, in faith and praying for still more faith, that his son may be healed. Jesus has mercy and heals the son, who is struck dead by the departure of the devil within him. And Jesus raises him up immediately, restored. 

*If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth.* 

This is what we must always keep in mind. It will guide you through anything, fearlessly. In peace. 

The Bible says "*Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus*."

Amen.

We come to Jesus's teaching in Capernaum to the Apostles. 

He asked them what they had been swabbling about between themselves and they reply embarrassed, over which of them shall be first among them. A very human thing, stemming from pride. 

And Jesus famously answers, but the first shall be last and the last shall be first. Many misunderstand this, and create confusing feel-good doctrines, but as Mark chapter 9 gives us the full teaching, we can understand that it is in service to the least that we become the first. It's serving those in Jesus name who are weaker, children, the poor, the widow. Pure religion undefiled. It is in that service that willingness to be last, to be least, to be humble servants, that elevates our status in the Kingdom of Heaven. That gives honor and Glory to God. 

Jesus uses a helpless innocent, a child, as a picture of what this means. That the things we do for the least among Us elevate us.  To  do without for others, meekly abasing ourselves for others benefit. 

And using the same child, Jesus transitions to those that rather than serving, offend. Offense in the Bible in this context, refers to obstacles to faith, things taking you away from the word. Stumbling blocks. 

And of those who rather than serve the week, the innocent, the children rather seek to offend them, that is hurt them in a way that brings them from the faith, Jesus says it is better that they kill themselves. That they would be better off tying a millstone around their neck and throwing themselves into the ocean then to bring a fence, to place a stumbling block, to traumatize a child with their own wickedness. Groomers and pedophiles, sodomites and the wicked of this world are better off killing themselves early then racking up offenses, in its other meaning. Because the fires of hell that awaits them will burn hotter for them for this.

Just as the last shall be first, elevated in the kingdom of heaven and rewarded for their service to the least among Us, so too will the punishment of eternal Hell be that much worse for those who offend the same.

These fools who deny the perfect justice of God to teach damnable heresy with pride and arrogance, are literally an offense, a stumbling block to those who are seeking the truth. 

For if there is no hell then there is no punishment for our transgressions that we need to be saved from. If there is only oblivion and the grave, there's nothing to escape. 

*Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell?*

He says sinners will be *cast into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched,* *cast into hell fire.*

The first section of **Mark 10** deals with a common theme of the Gospels, the Jews attempt to trap Jesus with gotcha questions, believing they were more clever than the Son of God. Here it is Pharisees tempting Jesus with a question regarding divorce, and again we see by its nature and their response to His question back that the myth that Pharisees we're "too strict" regarding the law, and that Christ was some liberal hippy is absurd. 

The Pharisees suggest Moses' allowance for putting away a betrothed for fornication was carte blanche for divorce, and superceded the law. Jesus corrects them of that notion. 

It was the hardness of your hearts, He says. That the lack of forgiveness and understanding regarding God's law led to making an exception, but that all who divorced and remarried are guilty of adultery. Both man and wife. By using the word of God, scripture, Jesus shut up the tempters. 

Divorce is ugly. It destroys whole nations. It creates the idea for many that marriage is based on what's good or convenient for the individual man or woman, rather than an instrument of God. We are His. All we have is His, we are but stewards on this earth. And marriage, the blessing of a husband or wife, is no different. And the vows to God He holds us to. 

But by cheapening the concept and making it culturally accepted to divorce, first for cause, which leads inevitably to no-fault divorce, Satan puts enmity between the sexes and gets us to violate God's law. 

(Full disclosure, I am divorced and remarried (to a widow, so she's good) but this makes me an adulterer. It doesn't matter the circumstances. It doesn't matter the excuse. It is this because Jesus says it is and so we know it is true. But, thankfully we are forgiven in Jesus)

First he gets us to justify divorce. And by this he makes a generation of us adulterers. Then fornication and living in sin, cohabitation becomes normalized because if divorce is not only allowed but considered inevitable, what's the point of marriage?

And if marriage can be dissolved at any time, and we are going to be considered adulterers anyway, why wait? And so adultery becomes normalized. 

And if divorce harms children, and divorces inevitable, then why have them in the first place? And if it's up to us and our convenience, marriage being just an arrangement for man, rather than a gift from God, why not treat having children the same. And so birth control, abortion become the norm.

And Satan keeps accusing.

And if the children feel that they are a burden rather than a blessing, and if life is so cheap and that it can be murdered in the womb, and if none of it matters and parents have no responsibility for their own children, then predators are loose upon them. And to the story of the rich young man, presented in **Mark 10** and as we also read in parallel passage of **Matthew 19**, a few weeks ago. 

In Mark we see it in slightly different light, as the young man comes off more sincere in this telling, but is identical in result and reason for it. 

He begins by flattering Jesus as "good master," and tempting him, Jesus asks why he's called Him good when there is no one good but God. 

This truth is important, because it is both a rhetorical question Jesus is using to give the young rich man the opportunity to understand that Jesus is God, for He is good. But also serves to set up the exchange to follow. That there is none righteous by the deeds of the law. There is none that does good. All have fallen short of the glory of God. But as we see, this young man misses both points and asks his original question, "what must I do to gain eternal life?" And he asks this sitting next to the way, the truth and the light, maintaining that he has observed all the commandments of the law since the days of his youth. 

He is sitting next to the sinless perfection of Christ, claiming to be 'good.' Jesus, looking upon him with love as it says here in Mark, tells him then, if this is true, "sell all your possessions, give up everything to the poor, and follow me." 

And the rich young man declined and goes his own way. 

People delude themselves regarding their own righteousness. We consider ourselves more righteous than we are, especially in comparison to other people who we are certain are far worse sinners. And the more possessions we have, the more material wealth, the more we can dilute ourselves into thinking that to have such blessings God must favor us. That we must be doing something right. We develop a pride, a comfort in the material, and neglecting the spiritual, are trapped by our riches. 

We have to come to Jesus as little children, who own nothing, are full of trust and wonder, innocent and fearful of God knowing that we're sinners. In contrast, the Rich Young Man comes with a pride and arrogance, and unable to come to the truth about himself or Christ Jesus.

*Children, how hard is it for them that trust in riches to enter into the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God. And they were astonished out of measure, saying among themselves, Who then can be saved? And Jesus looking upon them saith, With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible.*

It is impossible for man to be righteous. But with God all things are possible. If you're trusting in anything of this world, you are like a camel trying to pass through the eye of a needle.

Given as contrast to the rich young man, we learn of blind Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, who sat by the highway side begging.  

A man with nothing, and further blind of sight. 

The rich young man having everything, and being able to look Jesus directly in the eye and not see Him for who He was, compared to a blind beggar, Bartimaeus, who lacking sight, has faith enough to truly see, crying out repeatedly "*Thou son of David, have mercy on me*."

And when Jesus showed mercy on him, asking what he'd have Him do, he replied "Lord, that I might receive my sight." And healing the blind beggar Bartimaeus, Jesus says "Go thy way, thou faith has made thee whole." 

But unlike the young man earlier, Bartimaeus, having already obtained eternal life, his faith having made him whole, having called upon the name of the Lord for mercy, leaves what little he has to follow Jesus. (Which is why we know his name)

One man, relying on his own righteousness, unable to see that the Son of David, the Son of man, the Son of God, the Christ, sat beside him. And unable to part with the things of this world, to be healed, to follow Christ, he departs unsaved and damned.

The other, Bartimaeus, is a picture of salvation. Coming as beggars to call upon the Lord for mercy and to be healed, having faith that He is as He promised. And having been healed, and stripped of our cares for this world, become followers of Christ. 

It is a presentation of faith vs works. Of physical sight and spiritual blindness. Of following Christ in faith vs trusting in your self, and going your own way.

One more thing regarding **Mark 10**; There is a false doctrine claimed by works-n1gg3rs, taken from the story of the rich young man. 

They will say something along the lines of, "Jesus tells him he has to leave everything pick up his cross and follow Jesus, and that he gained eternal life if he did. This means we have to do works. We have to follow all of The commandments just as this man did, and we have to sell everything we own, and be willing to give it all to the poor and follow Jesus or else you're not saved."

They ignore the blind bagger Bartimaeus, and all of those Jesus heels throughout the Gospels, who having been healed by their faith in Jesus go their own way. Jesus literally tells Bartimaeus that, but the now healed man unlike most of those who are saved, who were healed, who had faith on the Lord Jesus Christ, decides to literally leave everything, and follow Christ.

We should follow christ. We should care nothing for the things of this world, beyond their ability to help others. We should pick up our cross daily and be willing to suffer for the truth. We should obey the commandments to the best of our human ability. But the only requirement to be healed is faith.

Would that we all leave everything we have to follow Jesus, but he doesn't expect us to. He would like us to, some of us are called to, but we are free to go on our way and still be healed. 

Don't allow a natural man misunderstanding of a partial chapter and a handful of verses mislead you as to what is required for salvation. Don't be like that rich young man who trusted in his own righteousness and couldn't humble himself to Christ and ask to be healed. Who was spiritually blind, too blind to understand that the gift of eternal life was sitting there next to him if he but had faith.

*And Jesus answered and said, Verily I say unto you, There is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my sake, and the gospel's, But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life.*

This follows the rich young man, who bidden to leave his material wealth and follow Jesus, declines, even though the potential for eternal life presents itself, (for this was what he was asking on, and Jesus knowing his heart so tested him)

And here Jesus makes a promise, as Lord. He says those that have sacrificed of this world for His sake and the furtherance of the Gospel shall receive 100 fold on this earth.  Gaining houses, family, children and lands, and of course the gift of eternal life in the next world. 

Some twisted vipers take this to a covetous and greedy place, pushing a prosperity false gospel. That God will make you a millionaire of you do good works. But this is not what Jesus says.

The chapter opens with Mark's telling of what is popularly known as Palm Sunday, though it occured on a Saturday. The Jerusalem crowd hailing Jesus, riding on the colt of an ass as in prophecy, as he arrives for the Passover, of which He will be the sacrifice. 

The colt is there where He said, and they allow the disciples to take it, as He said. Because everything in this world is God's and His to use for His glory. 

Then we have a telling of the fruitless fig tree. Jesus, seeking fruit finds none and curses the tree that it will produce no fruit forever after, and the tree is withered and destroyed from its root. 

*No man eat fruit of thee hereafter for ever... And in the morning, as they passed by, they saw the fig tree dried up from the roots. And Peter calling to remembrance saith unto him, Master, behold, the fig tree which thou cursedst is withered away.*

It is not "replacement theology," it is the taking away of the Kingdom for failing to provide fruit, not bringing souls meet for repentance unto salvation. For rejecting the stone, cut without hands, laid as the cornerstone before the foundation of the world. 

For the "God's not done with the Jews!" false doctrine, this story is twisted, because a plain reading is perfectly understandable. We see more in **Matthew 23;**

*And when he saw a fig tree in the way, he came to it, and found nothing thereon, but leaves only, and said unto it, Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever. And presently the fig tree withered away.*

This is a literal story that holds obvious symbolism regarding the Jews, here at the end of Christ's earthly ministry. Fruit, as always in the Gospel, means saved believers, those faithful to God and saved by His promise, in His Son, Jesus. 

It's reminiscent of a parable in **Luke 13:6-9**;

*He spake also this parable; A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard; and he came and sought fruit thereon, and found none.Then said he unto the dresser of his vineyard, Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground? And he answering said unto him, Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it: And if it bear fruit, well: and if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down.*

The tree is Judah. The Lord, God the Father, the dresser, Jesus Christ. His earthly ministry, to the lost sheep of Israel was the final attempt to produce fruit of that tree. And having no more fruit, it was cut down and destroyed. 

God's word is clear, it is forever that the tree is destroyed. It is cut down. It is cast into the fire. Never to bloom again. 

The dispensationalist lies are built on denying scripture.

*Jesus went into the temple, and began to cast out them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves;*

*And would not suffer that any man should carry any vessel through the temple. And he taught, saying unto them, Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves.*

Mark 11 tells us of the second clearing of the moneychangers in the temple, something Jesus did at the beginning of His ministry, and here in its final week. 

Eaten up by His zeal, and full of wrath at the Jews making merchandise out of His Father's house, Jesus drives them out and flips tables, and this is seen by many as the final straw for the Pharisees and scribes. They now affirm that they seek to kill Him. He has disrupted their graft. Their filthy lucre.

*Have faith in God.*

*For verily I say unto you, That whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; and shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe that those things which he saith shall come to pass; he shall have whatsoever he saith. Therefore I say unto you, What things soever ye desire, when ye pray, believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them.*

This is not simply an affirmation to put on Instagram. It's not just a "hang in there, God provides" pick me up for a daily inspirational devotion. 

It is a promise from God. All He asks is your forgiveness for others as He has forgiven you. To not hold grudges. To let things that aren't important in this life, and keep you from earning the rewards of the next, to let them go. 

*When ye stand praying, forgive, if ye have ought against any: that your Father also which is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses. But if ye do not forgive, neither will your Father which is in heaven forgive your trespasses.*

Now, all our sin is forgiven and forgotten in Christ Jesus, at judgment. All believers are in the Book of Life, and so saved. 

But on earth, God still punishes the disobedient believers, His chastisement falls on those He loves. 

*For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not?*

*But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons.*

And we are to confess our sins to God asking for forgiveness;

*If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness*.

But how can we humble ourselves to ask for forgiveness for disobeying God when we hold back forgiveness from those who've wronged us? Forgive our trespasses as we forgive others is part of the model for prayer Jesus provides. 

Lack of forgiveness is a burden. In the same measure we give mercy and extend grace, the Bible says, is what we receive. 

Be mindful of this, and in faith unfeigned, without the burdens of hate and a lack of grace, go boldly before God with your needs. And the Lord God, who cannot lie, promises He will provide.

Finally we see the murderous Jews attempting to tempt Jesus into saying something they may use to justify His death, and once again, Jesus silences them by their own hypocrisy. 

This is the proper way to deal with such matters. Not reacting and railing, but trusting in God, being blameless and allowing their own internal contradictions and corruption to hamstring your enemies. Using scripture when needed. Forcing them to persecute you directly for His name's sake and for the word. 

When we spiral in anger and get drawn into debate, all we do is give them the hook to hang us with. Instead, Jesus shows us how petty and foolish they are, exposing them. 

This lesson in meekness as strength is often lost by believers. It's good to be constantly reminded of throughout the Gospels.

Not persecution that seems overwhelming. Not betrayals by family and friends, or hatred of us for His name. 

These things will always occur. They must be. 

But when we see the abomination of desolation stand where it ought not, we should know the day of the Lord is nigh. 

Jesus warns that all who may be in Judea should flee, shifting His focus from 'ye' to 'they.' That those present there shouldn't even take time to grab their coat. This is described in the parallel passage of **Luke 21** as "the days of Vengeance" and it is my belief, comparing scripture with Mark, Luke and Matthew 24, that the vengeance is upon the Jews for their role in setting up the beast to put the abomination of desolation in the midst of Jerusalem. The antichrist turning on them and destroying them. Either way, it's yet another sign when it comes upon them. 

And *Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled.* 

There is a lot of speculation as to what this means, but it seems pretty cut and dry. Jerusalem was trodden down by Rome, an empire of Gentiles, and it remains so, under Jews who say they are but are not. They that are in Judea. Until the harvest. Until the fullness of the Gentiles has come. When the increase is gathered, the sheaves brought in. The day of the Lord is the harvest. 

With all biblical end times prophecy there is dual fulfillment, and as we see frequently throughout the Bible, things that fit prophecy are but a picture of the thing to come. But even understanding this, I still see this as fairly straightforward prophecy, given the frequent analogies of the harvest. The fullness of the season. 

*And there shall be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars; and upon the earth distress of nations, with perplexity; the sea and the waves roaring; Men's hearts failing them for fear, and for looking after those things which are coming on the earth: for the powers of heaven shall be shaken.*

And Jesus says this is when you know for sure that His coming is soon. There are those who say that the resurrection is passed, or that we are already in the millennial reign. The Sun and Moon darkening is the consistent signal the day of the Lord is here throughout the Old Testament prophecy and the New. This has not happened. And what follows certainly has never happened. The triumphant return of Jesus in the clouds, visible to all men. 

*And then shall they see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory.*
*And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh.*

This is the sign. This is how you know for sure. This is the Great Tribulation such as never has been, followed by Sun and Moon darkening, and Christ's return and the gathering of the elect. The fullness of the Gentiles come in.

And so this is the parable of the fig tree. This is the sign that it's soon. *So likewise ye, when ye see these things come to pass, know ye that the kingdom of God is nigh at hand.*

*Verily I say unto you, This generation shall not pass away, till all be fulfilled.*

This last verse confuses many. They ignore that this generation refers to the people alive and present when these things come to pass, and instead say that Jesus was speaking directly to the apostles in front of Him and their generation. 

It's this confusion and other deliberate distortions of these scriptures that dispensationalists seize on to change the plain meaning of the Olivette discourse regarding the end times. They make it more complicated than it is, and trust those they are misleading won't understand the scripture. Exactly what Christ gave warning to beware.

Continuing in **Mark 13**;

*And except that the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh should be saved: but for the elect's sake, whom he hath chosen, he hath shortened the days.*

*And then if any man shall say to you, Lo, here is Christ; or, lo, he is there; believe him not:  For false Christs and false prophets shall rise, and shall shew signs and wonders, to seduce, if it were possible, even the elect. But take ye heed: behold, I have foretold you all things.*

Jesus says again, don't be fooled. *Behold, I have foretold you all things.* 

And so, knowing these things he has foretold us, and keeping His warnings in mind, we can know when His day is near, for He gives us the signs and the timing. 

..*In those days, after that tribulation, the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, And the stars of heaven shall fall, and the powers that are in heaven shall be shaken. And then shall they see the Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of heaven.*

In those days. AFTER the tribulation. The return. The rapture. The promise of eternal life given in the day of redemption, the Great Day of the Lord come at last! Amen.

And so, knowing all this, and understanding what to look out for and what to be wary against, what shall we do? Christ tells us.


*But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father. Take ye heed, watch and pray: for ye know not when the time is.*

*For the Son of Man is as a man taking a far journey, who left his house, and gave authority to his servants, and to every man his work, and commanded the porter to watch. Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning; Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping. And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.*

Watch. Be prepared. Be sober and vigilant. Not carried away by the cares of this world. Not in fear of the tribulation of this world. Not fooled by false prophets. 

We are to watch and be good stewards who sow increase for the Lord. Be like the virgins prepared for the bridegroom, who filled their lamps with oil. Be like a servant left with 10 talents of silver, who increased his master's treasure. 

Watch and be ready, that on that great day Jesus greats you saying "well done my trusty servants. Well done."

Here we have Mark's version of events leading to the crucifixion of Jesus. Like most of Mark, it is condensed but packed with narrative and meaning. 

Like some of Mark's Gospel, details change slightly from the other three, though all of it is there. The difference in timing and point of view, but the testimony the same. Unlike those who came to bear false witness against Christ before the high priests. 

We see the familiar anointing by the woman with the precious oils. Hear of Judas' decision to betray Him because of it. See the last supper feast, Jesus breaking the bread and blessing the wine, saying He won't drink the new wine, fresh juice of the vine, again until He drinks it in the Kingdom of God. And while Jesus says the bread represents His body, broken on the cross, and the wine, the blood to be shed of the new testament, He clearly doesn't believe it is literally His blood, or else why say that? 

Christianity is not a cannibal cult.

Jesus goes to pray, exceedingly sorrowful at His fate, but resigned to it. Peter and the others sleep when they should be on watch. Peter swears he would die with Jesus, but He tells Peter of his future denials, knowing all things that must happen. 
Judas betrayal with a kiss. The ear of one of the guards cut off. The disciples scatter. 

He is arrested. A detail found only in Mark, a boy wrapped in a linen blanket appears and the guards go to grab him, but he runs off naked. It is an odd account but most believe that a young Mark is that boy, his mother's house being in Jerusalem (**Acts 12:12**).

Next we see the false accusations, but Jesus condemned by the truth that He is the Christ. I believe this is important, that they did not turn Jesus over to be crucified for false claims and lies, but they murdered the Son of God for the truth that He was Christ. 

In the garden, 3 times Peter swears he will stay with Jesus unto death. Jesus tells him to watch and pray that he be not tempted. Yet three times Peter is found sleeping. Peter denies Jesus 3 times when called out, breaking that vow. 

Had he stayed awake, watching, praying, perhaps Peter then would have had the courage to not deny Christ and honor his vows. In the previous chapter, Jesus warns us the same as Peter, to keep watch for Him. To be vigilant and sober and ready for persecution that will inevitably come for those who standfast in His name as we await Jesus return. To pray for the strength to suffer without fear. 

And most of us, like Peter, read that admonition in Mark 13, and vow to God in ourselves that we will surely be vigilant, and never back down or deny Him, even unto death. Just as Peter does in the garden. 

And just like Peter, many Christians, if not all, have periods in their lives where we fall asleep, spiritually. Where we are accused by the unsaved in Jesus' name, and deny Him. Where our vows of vigilance and devotion are forgotten and abandoned. And when we are reminded of Jesus's words, we fall to our knees weeping, like Peter, understanding how unworthy we are of Christ. 

So, let us learn the lesson of Peter, to stay awake and in prayer that we may not fail when tempted, that we remain vigilant for His return. That we won't deny Him when troubles come because we love Him that the world hates.

1 Peter 2:18-25

*Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward.*

*For this is thankworthy, if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully.*

*For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.*

*For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth: Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously: Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.*

*For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.*

Peter, aware of his own falling short, encourages us to understanding that to suffer for God with good conscience, taking it patiently as Jesus exemplified, we shall be found acceptable to God. 

Peter makes a distinction here, that if we be punished for our own wrong doing and accept the punishment, we aren't doing anything to glory of. That's just expected. It's bare minimum. 

But how often do we fail even this, and find ourselves facing true accusations or the consequences for our sin, and yet rail against our accusers or lash out at our punishment? This when we are guilty, let alone when we are innocent. 

Peter says Christ's suffering, *when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously* even though Jesus was blameless. Without sin. And in His patience suffered for us, carrying ours. 

Jesus is our example; *For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.*

This dichotomy of the believer, knowing the sacrifice and given the gift of eternal life anyway through God's unearned grace, through faith in Jesus, often make commitments to turn from sin. To sacrifice our comfort, wealth and possessions, even relationships, to show our love for Jesus. Vows made, despite the Bible's warnings. Good intentions, often gone astray. 

We slip. We backslide. We feed the old man, neglecting the new. We have the Spirit inside of us, God's word before us and Jesus by our side, ready to carry us. And yet, for all this advantage, we turn back towards the world. 

But, the Bible says if we walk in the word daily. In prayer and supplication. Growing faith on top of faith. Building on the foundation laid by Jesus, we won't be as easily tempted. We won't fail when tested. And we will not fall into sin to be accused of, and rightly punished for, but rather suffer patiently for Jesus'name, and in doing so, be pleasing to God. 

So we are called to pick up our cross daily. To *be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.*

And so we begin the Gospel according to Luke, the physician who journeyed with the apostle Paul, and was companion to evangelists throughout the churches. This (and the book of Acts), written as letters to "Theophilus." The identity of whom is subject to debate, but the term means "friend of God," and may be a general salutation to the saved, given the context; a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us...*That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.*

Luke begins his recitation of events, not with genealogies of Mary and Joseph as Mark or Matthew, or the divine origins of Christ as God the way John does, but tells us the tale of John the Baptist's miraculous birth to Zecharias and Elizabeth. 

Here we see their lineage is of Levi and or Aaron, the tribe of the priests of the temple. Zecharias (Zachariah) of the order of Abijiah, the course of Abia in the Greek. When David was king he divided up the sons of Levi into various orders or courses, that they be born into tasks within the temple. 

The course of Abia was responsible for maintaining the altar of incense. It was at this task that Zacharias was visited by the angel of the Lord, Gabriel, who brought God's promise that their prayers for a child would be answered as they were barren and in their old age. That they shall have a son and name him John, who will be a prophet making way for the coming of the Lord, that *the children of Israel shall he turn to the Lord their God. And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.* 

John was given the ministry to bring the children of Israel to turn to God, to repent. 

This is the meaning of repentance, to turn towards something. To turn the hearts of the fathers towards their children, to turn the disobedient towards the wisdom of the just. To make a people mete for repentance. To make them ready for Jesus Christ that they might believe. When John is in the wilderness calling the people to repent, this is what it means. 

Zacharias expresses doubt, and is struck dumb by the angel for unbelief, until the time of this birth be fulfilled. 

Elizabeth becomes pregnant with John, and glorifies God for His mercy that He take away her reproach among men. Her embarrassment at being without child. She hides her condition for 5 months. 

At the 6th, Gabriel appears unto Mary. A lowly virgin living in Galilee, in the city of Nazareth, in an area outside of Judea, formerly of the northern kingdom. Samaria. And we are told she is betrothed to Joseph, a descendant of David. 

*Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women.*

He tells her that she will bear a son, and name him Jesus. That He will be the heir promised of David who will be called *the Son of the Highest* and *the Lord God.* That He will rule forever, in a kingdom without end. 

Mary asks how can this be, seeing she knows not man. 

*And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.*

And to shore up her faith, Gabriel tells her of her cousin Elizabeth and her miraculous pregnancy. *For with God nothing shall be impossible.*

This is important to note. Mary, as well as Zacharias and Elizabeth, all are blessed by God. Full glory and honor is given Him by Whom all things are possible. Zacharias and Elizabeth, we are told, were righteous in their faith and perfect in their ways. Not without sin (doubting the angel of the Lord is a sin), but chosen to be blessed for their faith. So too was Mary.

She gives consent to God to be used by Him in this manner, saying she is His handmaid, a servant. She believes God's word and is blessed with His promise. Just as the patriarchs and prophets were. Not because she was "sinless" or righteous on her own, but because she had faith and it was counted on for righteousness.

We learn that Mary spent the remainder of Elizabeth's term with her, and departed. John is born and so named, as the angel instructed Zacharias. 

When people who know them hear this, they question why. And when mute Zacharias writes in faith that his son's name is John, he is freed from the curse and able to speak again. And the Holy Ghost comes upon him, and he gives praise to God almighty, prophesying in His name;

*Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people, And hath raised up an horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David; As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, which have been since the world began: That we should be saved from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us; To perform the mercy promised to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant; The oath which he sware to our father Abraham, That he would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear, In holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life. And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways; To give knowledge of salvation unto his people by the remission of their sins, Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.*

This is the promise of the Lord given witness by all the prophets. Don't miss this. Zacharias is showing, in the Spirit, how all is being fulfilled. With the mercy of God is with them. That his son shall prepare His way. To give knowledge of salvation, by the remission of sins. A light. A guide. Showing the way of peace. Because in sin, man is at enmity with God. But in Christ, God is offering peace on earth, goodwill towards man. 

This is what was promised Abraham. Moses. David. All the prophets, up to and including John. Jesus is come.

I would note that the gospel of Luke is the most thorough regarding the nativity of Jesus. It's what Linus quotes from in the Charlie Brown Christmas special. It's often what we think of and read from at Christmas time. And as Luke writes, this is a *declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us.* 

And so we should notice what is absent. Those things which are not commonly believed among the first century Christians to whom this gospel is addressed. 

There is no mention of the immaculate conception of Mary. There is no indication she was born without sin. While she exclaims in the Spirit that future generations shall call her blessed, it isn't because of a special quality of her's, but by the works of God to whom she's a servant. Mary does the will of God through faith, and in faith is blessed among women to be chosen to bear the incarnation of Christ Jesus. This is the grace that God bestows upon her for her faith. For her willingness to believe. 

Just like the Old Testament saints, Mary believed and it was counted upon her for righteousness. She was saved by faith alone and chosen because of that faith. 

The Bible says that without faith we cannot please God. Mary could not please God without faith. Zacharias and Elizabeth could not please God without faith. None of them could be righteous absent their belief that God has provided them remission of sins in his mercy. Given the gift of salvation from His grace. 

Removing this concept from the gospel, those that worship Mary missed the entire point and so they cannot understand God's mercy and they cannot receive God's grace.

**Luke 2** brings us to familiar ground with the recounting of the nativity of Jesus. Every man in the modern world has heard the details of this story, even if they choose not to believe them. 

How all the world was taxed by Caesar, and returning to the city of David, where Joseph's lineage came from, Mary gave birth, laying Jesus in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn. 

That shepherds keeping watch over their flocks witness the angels of the Lord heralding His arrival. That God was extending peace, goodwill towards man. Tidings of great joy, which shall be to all the people. (All the people, not some, not chosen, all)

*For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord*.

The shepherds gather to witness that which the angels told them, and they spread the word throughout the countryside. Early evangelists, and those they preached to wondered at what they were told. 

And Mary pondered these things in her heart. 

After eight days, as was fitting the old covenant still in effect until the day of His resurrection, they took Jesus to the temple to be circumcised and be presented to the Lord. A sacrifice made of two turtledoves. 

Simeon, who we are told was just by his faith in the coming Christ had the Holy Ghost upon him, and he came by His prompting to see the child, being told that before his death he would witness the Lord's Christ. He blessed the child and glorifys God, saying 

*For mine eyes have seen thy salvation,*
*Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people; A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel.*

The promise of the expected Christ was the faith that saved those who came before Jesus incarnation. Just as faith in His perfect work saves now. Trusting God's word, His promises and covenants. It has always been the sole means of salvation. 

And again, the promise is to all people. 

And again, Mary wonders at these things as Simeon in the Spirit prophesies that Jesus will fall and rise, and that it will be as if a sword pierces her soul, as the spear pierces His side. 

They encounter Anna, a prophetess whonin her old age as a widow, works in the temple for God. In the instant she saw the baby, she gave thanks to God and went and told all those who in faith looking forward to the redemption that the Messiah was here. 

*And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him.*

Jesus, being fully man and fully God, was born as we are. He grew as we do. He waxed in spirit and filled with wisdom, meaning He grew into these things. 

When we see the story of a young Jesus who tarries behind in the temple after going with His family to celebrate the feast of Passover, it is often portrayed as Jesus instructing the scribes there. But the Bible tells us that Jesus was seeking knowledge and understanding from them. 

Yes He was fully God, but in the flesh, He was tempted, tested, in all things as we are, being fully man as well. 

He waxed in spirit. He filled in wisdom. He grew physically and in knowledge.

*And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions. And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers.*

He astonished them with His ability to understand, but He sought to gain wisdom and knowledge. He was about His Father's business. 

Some believe he came out of the womb with the full knowledge of everything, and had the whole word of God memorized in His heart, being the author of it. But this story found only in Luke paints a picture of a child who had to grow into a man as we do. And while He was perfect in His ways and without sin, that didn't mean He didn't hunger, thirst or have to devote Himself to learn scripture, just as we do. Jesus' did the will of His Father as an example to us. And God calls upon us to hear His word, question the meaning, learn His statutes, and commit His word to our hearts. Things that take discipline and faith, of which Jesus was the ultimate example. 

And again, Mary took these things and remembered them, trying to understand just what it meant, that Jesus was Christ.

*For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.*

The implications of this are important to consider. That Jesus as man had to, at every step of His life, choose to do the will of the Father, putting that above His own will and the weaknesses of the flesh He resided in. 

Jesus had to choose to be without sin, though He suffered in the flesh. He chose to learn the word of God as a man would. Devote His time and energy to pleasing His heavenly Father and honoring His earthly parents. Not letting discomfort, cold, hunger, thirst, frustrations, humiliation, or any other thing being Him to sin. Yes the grace of God was upon Him. But we who are saved have a similar grace, but still sin. 

He grew, He waxed in the Spirit. He grew in knowledge and wisdom, one day at a time, choosing at every opportunity to do the will of Him Who sent Him, so that He could call us to do the same. In that grace. In that love. Amen.

I was just struck with a realization about the irony of those who call Christianity "cucked," and who attempt to discredit the writings of the Apostle Paul based on his Epistles regarding the behavior of Christians, especially relative to the powers that be. To the government. Being subject to those who have power over us, given by God. To, as much as possible, live at peace with all men. Romans 13, etc. 

The irony being that Paul was subject to constant persecution, was stoned to death at one point, had to be snuck out of cities in baskets least the mobs led by Jews tear him apart, and who wrote a majority of his epistles from chains. Literally bound for preaching the word of God and the gospel of Christ crucified. 

We are instructed by the Bible to not riot in the daytime or take vengeance for ourselves. To render custom to who is due custom and tribute to who is due tribute. Pastors to subject themselves to Jesus, servants to their masters, husbands to loving their wives as Christ loves His brethren, wives to be subject to their husbands and children to honor their parents. To render unto Caesar that which is Caesars. To pay our taxes and obey the laws so long as they do not contradict the authority of the Lord and His word. 

To have faith that God will save us from tribulation and persecution. To allow God to exact vengeance for us. To glory in our persecution for His name's sake. This isn't being "cucked," it's literally the only way we win. 

And Paul, who wrote much of this from a jail cell, under house arrest, bound to a centurion by chains 24 hours a day for the cause of Christ, saw no contradiction in any of that. 

As long as you're preaching the word of God, you shouldn't worry about things like hate crime laws or censorship, or any other persecution led by the Jews. Glory in your affliction and speak the truth. 

In Acts, Peter, James, Paul and others are openly condemned and set up on for vocally pointing out that the Jews were antichrists who killed Christ Jesus. Stephen was martyred for "hate speech" against the Jews. 

These meek and humble servants, who turned the world upsidedown with their preaching, drew a line in the sand. 

They turned the other cheek, loved their enemies, heaping coals upon the heads of those who hated them by their charity and humble conversation. Living peaceably. 

But when it came to the preaching of the word and the truth of those who hate Christ, they boldly spoke out, despite threats of jail, and even unto death. 

Would that we are blessed by God with so strong a faith.

Here in Luke chapter 3, we find his goal, stated in the opening of his Gospel to "*set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us*," being met, giving precise details to the time in which John the Baptist, followed by Jesus, began their ministry. Luke establishes who was in charge, and where, pinpointing for readers the time and place of this happening, with familiar figures of their recent past; *That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.*

And so we find John, born roughly 6 months ahead of Jesus, has fufifiled the prophecy given his father by Gabriel, to be the answer to the prophecy given Isaiah; the voice in the wilderness making straight the paths of the Lord. 

In the times before modernity, when the lords and kings would travel abroad, often in caravans, taking weeks or months to get where they were going, a group of their servants would run ahead, both to herald their lord's passing to prepare those in the path chosen to receive their king, and to make certain the road was clear. That the way was smooth. Harbingers and workmen. 

So too, Christ the Lord was coming and the paths were to be made straight for Him. 

In scripture, we often see the idea of walking in God's statutes, following His wisdom, being righteous by obeying His sayings, is compared to walking a path. Turning neither to the left not right. But following the narrow way of the Lord. 

John, the harbinger of the Lord is sent by God to spiritually make straight the paths, to bring the people to repentance, turning towards His Son. Baptizing those who believed, a picture of Christ's crucifixion, burial and resurrection, and a symbol of their being washed clean by the remission of sins. Preparing them that shall see the salvation of God among them. Exhorting those who were saved to now do the works meet for repentance. Charity. Proper living. Changed as those who are free from the wrath should live. 

John is filled with the Holy Ghost, as promised, and speaks boldly and with authority the words of God. He is the first prophet of the Lord to have the Holy Ghost upon him in 400 years. His hard preaching against sin and of the word of God, scripture, draws people from all over the region.

We see the lands mentioned by ruler, and it encompasses all of Judea, up into Samaria and the provinces from the sea and in and around Jordan, and it is from these places that multitudes come to hear John preach and to be baptized. 

In **Matthew 3** we see that this draws attention of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and that the preaching he does, also shown in **Luke 3**, is an indictment of the Jews, especially their religious leaders. 

*O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance: And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.*

John speaking in the Spirit says that if they are truly there repentant of their false ways, show the fruit of it. Especially the religious leaders who have not the fruits, the souls prepared to repent towards God. They've failed the people. They have rested on the fact that they are God's "chosen." They haven't prepared anyone for the salvation to come. 

This generation of vipers has believed that by the nature of their lineage they would be saved. This is the same mistaken idea behind dispensationalism and the "God's not done with the Jews!" mentality among so many misguided and judaized Christians today. 

But John repudiates the idea of special treatment for the Jews. He says God could raise up Israelites from rocks if He so choosed. They aren't special boys. And they certainly aren't living in a manner that shows God-fearing reverence for Him and His laws.

The people ask themselves if he is the Christ, and he responds that one greater than him comes, who he isn't fit to untie His shoes. That the savior to come will not baptize with water, but with the Holy Ghost, and with fire, burning the chaff and gathering the wheat. 

And so, Jesus comes to be baptized, to do the will of His Father. 

*And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased.*

Amen.

But John's preaching against sin, especially of the political and religious leaders of that day, leads him to conflict with Herod, who had taken his brother's wife, among other evils, and so John is locked up in prison. 

It is at this time where Jesus, being around 30 years of age, begins His earthly ministry.

Luke, having established the time and circumstances surrounding these events, then gives his version of the generations of Jesus, going from his stepfather Joseph's lineage. Perfect in his generations, all the way back to Adam, who we are reminded, was begat of God. 

Being the son of Joseph, even adopted, places Jesus in line for the throne of David, fulfilling the prophets sayings that there will be a King from the root of Jesse, a descendant of David, who would rule and reign forever. The Son of David. 

To the more secular, this places Jesus in line to be an earthly king. To make the Christ the physical deliverer of Israel. But to those called by the Spirit, and given understanding of scripture, the savior of their souls and heir to the Heavenly Kingdom. The Son of God.

It is these two sonships that Jesus was born into. Fully God. Fully man. And the conflict in the hearts of those who hear of Him, even those who directly saw Him walk among them performing miracles and preaching on the Kingdom of God, would set the stage for His ministry.

John the Baptist is in the wilderness, preaching to the masses of people from all around Judea and the surrounding countries, who have come to hear the word of God preached, under the power of the Holy Ghost. 

Many repent and believe and are baptized in expectation of the Christ. But they, as babes, don't know what to do, now that they are saved. What does this mean in practice? How is it applied in their lives. John says that dead trees will be hewn down and burned. Like the vipers of the Pharisees and Sadducees who do not produce any fruit, they're not bringing people to turn towards God. They aren't doing works of charity. As Jesus will later preach, they are hypocrites and worse. But those who by hearing the word of God come to faith, not wanting to be as the vipers, the fruitless, pricked in their conscience by the word, not wanting to be hewn down, they ask "What shall we do?" 

And to the publicans, who were tax collectors, a group known for their overcharging, abusing their office and taking bribes, he says take no more than you're appointed to, basically to be honest in your dealings. Don't lie. Don't behave as the vipers, hypocrites and unbelievers. Love others the way you want to be loved. The way you trust in Christ to love you.

At home, do you love your spouse as Christ loves the church? Jealously and putting their well being before your own? Honoring your parents? Not coveting your neighbors possessions? 

Are you a blessing to your community? To your church family? To strangers? Are you a light that shines, magnifying God's love for you that others may come to ask you why you're full of love and hope?

Luke chapter 4 picks up with Jesus after His baptism in the Jordan and by the Holy Spirit, having been proclaimed by the Father "His Son, in whom Im well pleased."

The Gospel says, Jesus was led of the Spirit to the wilderness, and there to fast and be tempted by Satan, 40 days. It is often overlooked that the three instances given here and in the other Gospels are not the only tests of the devil Jesus suffered. He was tempted 40 days. 

Jesus hungered. He thirst. He was weary. He was alone. Without shelter. Cold at night. Hot in the sun of the day. In all ways tempted as we are. But without sin.

And Jesus was led of the Spirit to this temptation, He was not given a pass, was not brought to the temple in Jerusalem to preach the Gospel to an adoring throng of people. He was brought to desolate places where the prince of this world would tempt Him. 

Satan, the accuser of the brethren, seeking to corrupt the Christ, and derail God's plan of salvation for the world, tested and tried Jesus that he may go before the Father and say, "your Son is not worthy to be a sacrifice. He is not without blemish." But Jesus withstood Satan, and in doing so, gave us the pattern for dealing with temptation in our lives. 

**1 Corinthians 10:13**
*There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.*

The Bible says Jesus was tempted as we are. Knows our infirmities and understanding, shows mercy on us. We are not given more than we can handle. If we reject Satan, God will provide us a way. 

That way is found in what Jesus used to resist Satan. The word of God. 

So understanding that Jesus did not have some special means to supernaturally avoid succumbing to sin, it wasn't His divine nature that saved His human flesh from falling, but His doing His Father's will, and clinging to the word. 

Jesus was hungry and weak, and the devil said to turn a stone to bread. A temptation of the flesh. To satisfy the immediate need to please ourselves physically. 

And Jesus replied *It is written, That man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.* 

Note His use of "it is written." That man loves not by bread. Not by the needs of the flesh. That there is more to this than satisfying our physical desires but that we live by *every word of God*. 

He quotes scripture to put of the devil from Him. Every word of God is all we need to live. (The presupposition is that, in order to be true, we have access to every word of God. Thus the preservation of His word). This having double meaning, as the manna in the desert was a picture of Christ, Jesus who is the bread of life come down from Heaven, and He is the Word of God made flesh, through whom eternal life is given to all who believe. 

And Jesus, using God's word, rebukes Satan. 

Then, tempting Jesus with power, Satan offers Him the thrones of this world, of whom Satan is god. Given power to influence kings and regents. The spirits that bring wickedness to high places. Overseeing the principalities of the rulers of the darkness of this world. By supernatural means, he takes Jesus to the top of a mountain and shows Him all the lands of man in the world. The devil says to Jesus, worship me and I will give you an earthly kingdom, ultimate power. 

And Jesus, again citing scripture rejects him; *for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.* And again the power of the knowledge of God's word saves Jesus from temptation. 

Finally, frustrated, Satan places Jesus upon the spire of the temple in Jerusalem. Hundreds of feet in the air. And says to jump, because the scriptures say that God the Father would not suffer to see even His foot dash against the rocks. That God would send angels to stop Jesus from even stubbing His toe, so surely they would catch Him. 

*And Jesus answering said unto him, It is said, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.*

Again, using scripture, Jesus turns aside Satan and his temptations.

And the devil departs having failed to stand against the word of God. In Matthew we read; *Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.* 

By faith of this Jesus endured, that God the Father would provide. That He loved Him and was true. Not slack in His promise. By turning to scripture, Jesus resisted sin, and was rewarded for His trust. 

This is the pattern for our lives. The path we follow, led by Christ. When the Spirit leads us into the wilderness. When we are weak, and tired and hungry. When we are in peril, as Jesus upon the steeples of the Temple. When we are at our lowest physically and mentally, Satan will come to tempt us. And when he does, we can know that none of what he offers us to sin, none of the temporary satisfactions of the flesh, are beyond our means to resist as long as we turn to God, stay in His word, and have faith that our needs will be met by Him Who loves us.

It is our daily walk with God that protects us. We ask Him to provide our daily bread, not just physical need for food, but spiritually, studying the word of God. We start our day in prayer, taking to God, and reading His word that His will be made known to us. His promises made clear that we may grow in faith. This is how we resist temptation. This is how we keep Satan at bay. 

We are weak in the flesh, but if we feed the spirit, the "new man," as Paul describes it, that quickened spirit that is the surety of our eternal life, we shall overcome as Jesus has overcome. 

And when we walk after the flesh, and neglect our prayers and our reading of the word, and we get caught up in the cares of this world, the way Satan caught up Jesus to the top of that mountain, to the heights of the temple, and we fear, and lust, feel wrath, covet and put ourselves at risk tempting God, and have not the means to escape though God has given them to us. His word; The pattern made by Christ to follow.

It should be mentioned that before beginning His earthly ministry, Jesus sought to purify himself with prayer and fasting. Legitimate fasting, denying Himself not personal taste and treats, preference and privilege, but actually sacrificing physical necessity that He may focus on the things of God. The word. In prayer and supplication. 

How can those who deny that we have "every word of God" and that don't read it daily, allowing other men to be an intermediary, how can they resist temptation? If their prayers are to other men, not boldly going before God the Father with supplication?

They can't. 

That's why they often seek worldly power. It's why they fast and pray to be seen of men, and not locked away as God commands. Not going into the wilderness but proclaiming their "sacrifice" to the world. It's why they tempt God.

We will see later in this chapter that Jesus again quotes scripture to the people and we should note that already in the past 3 chapters, and all through the book, the scriptures are referenced constantly. The law and Psalms and words of the prophets. 

Because, *All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.*

Man lives *by every word of God.* 

Biblical fundamentalism. That God's word is the only and final authority. All we need for doctrine that we may be perfect, whole, complete. 

It was good enough for Jesus in the desert against Satan. It is good enough for us today who follow Him.

Picking up where we left off in Luke 4 yesterday, we find Jesus at the start of His earthly ministry. Having just been baptized and anointed by the Spirit, and proclaimed by the Father as His Son, and having fasted, prayed and withstanding the devil in the wilderness for 40 days, the Bible says Jesus was full of the power of the Spirit, and returned to Gis home province of Galilee, where He taught in the synagogues of God, gaining fame and renown throughout the area. 

We see that Jesus ministry begins in the remnant of the Northern Kingdom of Israel, outside of Judea, but preaching to the lost sheep of Israel. In these times, synagogues were the local churches of those who worshipped God. Where they would go, not only weekly on the Sabbath but throughout the week, to hear God's word read from scriptures, to pray and to learn about God's word. The Temple in Jerusalem was for feasts and sacrifices and pilgrims, but the communities abroad had independent, fundamentalist gatherings, or churches that people attended. 

**Psalms 74:8**
*They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land.*

Note the Bible says there was a time synagogues were of God. It wasn't until after Christ where the unrepentant Jews were made a synagogue of Satan by the Lord, rejected. Reprobate. 

And Luke tells us that going to these houses of worship was Jesus's custom. It was His routine. Oh to be like Jesus and make going to church to read, hear and learn the word of God as part of our custom. To be our routine. 

And of course, just as churches are today, the synagogues were likely hit or miss in regards to what they taught, how they acted, if they produced fruit meet for repentance, if they were ice cold or lukewarm or red hot for the Lord. I am sure Jesus Christ Himself sat through boring sermons, by dull preachers who were wrong on doctrine, in congregations of people who were sinners and hypocrites or holier than thous. But it was Jesus's custom. And so, to begin His work, Jesus went to church. We should too.

Now having established somewhat of a following throughout Galilee, Jesus returns to Nazareth, the town He grew up in. Where He lived as a child with Mary and Joseph, His half brothers and sisters. Where He developed the habit of going to synagogue. He returns full of the Spirit, and is called to read, and He preaches the prophecy of Christ from **Isaiah 61:1-2**
*The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound; To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn;*

**John 3:17**
*For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved.*

For those who doubt that Jesus ever proclaimed Himself to be the Christ, here He is saying precisely that. From the beginning. In no uncertain terms. 

And the crowd becomes incredulous. "Is this not the Son of Joseph?" They knew Him, watched Him grow, saw Him in synagogue. 

In response we are given the first record of Jesus preaching in Luke;

*Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself: whatsoever we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in thy country. And he said, Verily I say unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country.*

In **Mark 6**, we get more detail of this part; *A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house.*

Basically, those who know us best, whose familiarity has them over comfortable in their understanding. Many Christians can relate to this, where after being born again we try to share the good news with relatives or friends, and they, knowing us intimately, scoff. "You? I saw you that one time..." Or even just see us as the child they watched grow and can't accept that you've got something to offer them in your youth. It's why it can be difficult for a Christian to get members of his own family saved. 

And so, being rejected of His hometown crowd, Jesus doubles down and preaches even harder, using scripture. He says, citing **1 Kings 17**, you remember Elijah, how he was rejected and shut up the heavens that it didn't rain for 3 and a half years? That in Israel was great famine? The Spirit led the prophet to a Gentile widow in the land of Zidon who, along with her son was about to die of hunger, having only one meager meal left between them. God sent Elijah there because of her faith. In the story she offers the food to the prophet in faith, even though it was all she had. And God works a miracle where they are all fed and sustained with what little she had until the time of famine was over. 

Jesus says, I bet there were many widows starving in Israel. But it was a Gentile woman who He saved. 

Then, Jesus mentions **2 Kings** 5, and the prophet Elisha, where a Syrian, the captain of the hosts of the army of the king, suffered leprosy. Jesus says that many lepers were in Israel in the time, but it was this Gentile that God sent His prophet to heal. 

That the prophets were rejected of their own, and so the healing power of God, His blessings and promises went to others. To Gentiles. 

**John 1:11**
*He came unto his own, and his own received him not.*

Jesus spitting fire, using scripture, He rebukes and reproaches His countrymen for their rejection of the word of God, the Gospel of truth He's brought to them, in a prefigure of the rejection He would face of the Jews at large, and prophesying God's turn to the Gentiles that would receive Him. And in a like manner, the crowd engaged at their own sin being pointed out, gathered to kill Jesus. They bring Him to the top of a hill, looking to cast Him off headlong.
But Jesus, as He will do throughout His ministry after crowds of Jews offended by His hard preaching turn on Him, supernaturally passed by out of the crowd. His time having not yet come.

Afterwards, we are told, Jesus *came down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and taught them on the sabbath days. And they were astonished at his doctrine: for his word was with power.*

It was more fruitful here. And while He could not perform miracles in Nazareth by their lack of faith, here Jesus begins to heal multitudes.

Luke being a physician focuses often on the healing power of Christ during his Gospel. 

A man possessed by an unclean devil is exercised, the demon recognizing Jesus as the Christ. *Let us alone; what have we to do with thee, thou Jesus of Nazareth? art thou come to destroy us? I know thee who thou art; the Holy One of God.*

And the people are amazed; *with authority and power he commandeth the unclean spirits, and they come out.*

Luke tells us that Jesus heals Simon's mother, rebuking the fever she had, and being healed, she set about serving them food. 

Because of these miracles, a multitude brought their sick or possessed loved ones to be healed. *And devils also came out of many, crying out, and saying, Thou art Christ the Son of God. And he rebuking them suffered them not to speak: for they knew that he was Christ.* His time not yet come, and relying on the people to repent by faith, seen by the signs and hearing of the word, Jesus repeatedly tells the unclean spirits to be silent about who He is. 

And even when Jesus had left the city for the wilderness, to travel to other places with the word, the people followed Him. He gently reproaches them that He must go to others too. And so, His ministry grows throughout the land of Galilee.
