Acts 5 picks up immediately following the last verses of 4, where the gathered believers of the assembly had just praised God in Jesus name, and been filled with the Holy Ghost to preach the scriptures boldly. They had all things in common, meaning they shared possessions as needed, forsaking materialism to edify the church and do great things for the Lord. One disciple, Barnabas had just sold property and donated the sum to the church at Jerusalem. Likely to praise and blessings. And so we meet a married couple, Ananias and Sapphira.

Ananias and Sapphira, in the context of seeing Barnabas coveted his praise and honor in the church, and having land themselves to sell, sold it for a sum, but presented to the Apostles a lesser amount, keeping a portion of the proceeds for themselves while saying they gave all of it to the church.

Peter, by the Holy Ghost calls out Ananias, who is present before them presenting the gift. Peter says he knows that it's not the full total, and asks why lie to the Holy Ghost about it considering they weren't required to sell the land at all, or to give any of the money to the church. They had every right to give a portion, as it was theirs to give. 

But the lying for praise and to be favored among the congregation is the problem, and confronted, Ananias collapses dead at Peter's feet. 

The brothers bury him, and a few hours later, as they are putting him in the ground along comes the wife, Sapphira.

Peter gives her a chance to be truthful, and she sticks to the story her and her husband had concocted. Peter, again in the Spirit curses her to the same fate of her husband, striking her dead. The gathered now know Ananias' death wasn't just happenstance, but that the couple has been punished by God.

Were Ananias and Sapphira saved? Didn't they just feel the presence of the Holy Ghost when the church prayed the chapter before? The Bible says in Acts 4 that the entire church was of one heart and one soul. They were of that church. I think the implication is clear they were. 

But their being in Heaven when they die, justified by faith and Jesus' imputed righteousness didn't keep them from sinning, nor did it stop God from punishing them with their lives. 

Many of the religion of works, who maintain that you must repent of sinning to be saved, and claim that the Gospel of Christ, salvation by faith in grace, is a "license to sin." And so, being fruit inspectors, take this story as evidence they were not believers. But what it shows is that God chastises His own for our iniquity. He takes the rod to His children when they sin. The Bible says He scourges His adopted sons and daughters. Even unto death. We saved are held to a higher standard than the unsaved, and we are punished here in this earth, sometimes more so than the unsaved, who are not God's children. This is why we should walk in the word, live for God, take up the cross and follow Jesus. Honoring our heavenly Father, which brings blessings upon blessings. 

It is an amazing gift to be given a chance by God to bless others, to help people. To give freely what we have to others in the church in need. But our own pride and greed can often stop us from receiving the blessings, and instead lead us to chastisement in our sin.

Now we see that for the believers, this made them fearful but more determined to serve the Lord but others it a frightened to the point with a dare not join the church. These could be a mix of people saved and unsaved, who's seeing how tight a ship God is running through the apostles with the Holy Spirit, but still living a car in a life in their sin, we're afraid and In their fear were forsaking the assembly. But others unsaved in the general population, hearing this group of believers preaching the word boldly with one mind and soul, and seeing the power of their testimony, we're eager to believe and join them.

And of course, this brings them into conflict with the Jews again.

It wouldn't be a new testament scripture without mentioning the evil of the Jews. 

The Sadducees taking the place of the Pharisees as the big bad of Acts stems mainly from the disciples preaching in a resurrected Christ's name. And primarily from the true accusations that they killed Jesus. 

It's the same today, as we see groups like the ADL calling this biblical truth that they killed the Son of God "anti-semitism."

This preaching, laying the blame squarely on the shoulders of the Jews of Jerusalem for killing Christ is what the early Acts of the Apostles references to repentance refers to. 

Peter and John and the others, tell The gather Jews listening to them at the temple that they may have acted out of ignorance but now is the time to repent and believe on the Lord Jesus Christ for the remission of their sin. 

And the high priests and officials, knowing their guilt, sought to imprison and threaten the disciples into silence.

So we see when all of the disciples are imprisoned at the temple for preaching the truth of the Gospel and the healings being done by the Apostles (whom Jesus had anointed to have the power to lay hands when He had originally sent them out), and the multitudes being saved because of it all.

An angel of the Lord comes and frees them. One of many jailbreaks in the book of Acts. They're told to redouble their efforts and continue preaching boldly, and they do. 

To the consternation of the Jews.

So we see the problem as the Sadducees see it; *ye have filled Jerusalem with your doctrine, and intend to bring this man's blood upon us.*

And so *Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.* Peter again preaches the Gospel and indicts the Jews for Christ's death. 

Now we are introduced to a Pharisee on the council named Gamaliel. He is the same who Paul would later say taught him before his conversion. 

Gamaliel warns the council to just ignore the disciples, and names a couple of previous false messiahs they'd seen. That if they aren't of God it will come to naught. He warns the Sadducees, who are essentially religious atheists, that if they are of God then any effort to harm the disciples will not work. 

Still, they ordered them beaten and released, threatened not to speak in the name of Jesus. 

Often Christians will not boldly talk in Jesus name. They will talk about higher powers and a vague God, rather than proclaiming Jesus. It is from the same fear, I think, that the Jews sought to instill in the disciples. 

This persecution leads them to rejoice. And they take it as a sign they are doing Jesus' work, who had preached that they would be persecuted for His name's sake. 

We are similarly called. If you aren't facing personal persecution, it may well be because you aren't boldly proclaiming what you believe, or who your faith is placed in.

Now Act 6 opens with a problem for the early church at Jerusalem. The Apostles, disciples and converts, of one mind and soul, *daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ.* And to the congregation they added thousands, both Jew and Greek. 

Now we know the role of the church assembly is to teach and preach the Gospel of Jesus to the unsaved, the things of God and His doctrines from scripture to the edification of the saved, and to minister to the least among them, especially widows indeed. 

And even in this, the purest church with the purest doctrine, full of saved believers, full of the Holy Ghost, witness to signs and wonders by those whom had the power anointed unto them by Jesus through the Holy Ghost, people remained prone to sin, being of the flesh. They were respecters of persons. These saved Judeans favored their own in the ministering of the poor sisters of the faith, the Grecians. 

Faced with this issue, the 12 gathered the disciples, those dedicated daily to the word and the work, and had from among them 7 chosen to serve the needs of maintaining the larger church and its ministry to the poor members.  This is the establishment of the biblical office of decon. 

We see here in verse 3 some of the qualifications for decon; *men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom.* This is expounded upon in **1 Timothy 3:**

*8 Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre;*

*9 Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.*

*10 And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.*

*11 Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things.*

*12 Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well.*

*13 For they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.*

The Apostles and other disciples appointing them deacons, maintain their position as pastors and evangelists, *to be continually in prayer and in the ministry of the word.*  

It is important to understand that these are the only two offices given in the Bible, and that the deacons work for the church and answer to the pastor, not the other way around. We see also that this office is key in allowing the church to grow, that freed of the mundane daily tasks as the deacons serve full time to take care of matters, the numbers grew and multiplied.

In this election of deacons, we meet several key members of the early ministry, chiefly Stephen, *a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost.* We see that in addition to his duties, he maintained his soul winning, teaching and working signs among the Jews to bring them to Christ. 

Stephen being so effective that certain sects of the Jews in synagogue, Hellenistic freed slaves, returned to Jerusalem from where they'd been captive, disputing with Stephen and his doctrines of Jesus Christ. 

Unable to counter his preaching and pure doctrine, they instead get men to falsely accused him of blasphemy. 

By getting a mob worked up by these lies, they drag Stephen before the council. We see from their railing accusation that they are twisting Jesus prophecy of the temple destruction, and misleading about the law, which continues fulfilled in Christ, and the doing away of the carnal ordinances, sacrifices and diverse washings. 

We leave this short chapter in a cliff hanger, as they look upon innocent Stephen, with a face like an angel....

So forgive me for almost skipping chapter 8, because it is a good one. 

We see Saul again, fresh from being the coat holder for the Jews who stoned Stephen to death, and are told he consented of that evil. The Bible says being a partaker in another man's sin is as bad as commiting it ourselves. Saul, in his ignorance embraces the persecution of the believers in Jerusalem and in all of Judea, zealously thinking he is doing it for God, that the saints were blasphemous doing what they did in Jesus' name. 

We see once again that in persecution, all things work together for good to them that love God, and God in their affliction uses the scattering to bring the truth of the Gospel out of Jerusalem and into the whole world. 

Phillip, one of the deacons selected with Stephen and whom the Apostles laid hands on, filling him with the gifts of the Holy Ghost goes to Samaria, the capital of the province that was once the Northern Kingdom of Israel, before God used the Syrians to wipe them out. There, there are a mix of followers of the Hebrew religious practices, who followed scripture and knew of Christ to come, and unbelievers from every background. It was this mixed race mess that caused the Jews to look down on Samaritans, despite their cultural and racial similarities and origin. 

Phillip has tremendous success in getting Samaritans saved, through his preaching and the miracles of healing and casting out devils through the power of the Holy Ghost imparted to him by the Apostles and the laying on of hands. 

We meet Simon, AKA Simon the sorcerer, a charlatan who had great fame in the land, but who did trick people into believing he had some power from God. But his paltry parlor tricks were nothing compared to the truth of the word and the power of God moving through Philip, and as the masses believed on Christ, Simon too became saved, born again in faith and even joining Philip in his ministries.

When the Apostles hear of the great things of God Philip was doing among the Samaritans, they went up to see and give the gift of the Holy Ghost upon the believers that they may continue to grow the church there and bring people to salvation. 

It is important to understand the difference between the quickening and indwelling of the Spirit upon belief and salvation, and the doctrine of laying on of hands. All believers were born again and had the Spirit inside them with the new man created at the time of their salvation, but the gifts of the Holy Ghost, in the Old Testament sense of having Him come over one and grant them power, was something that the Apostles were granted by Jesus, and given unto them to share as needed to the glory of God.

Simon seeing their ability to imbue others with this great power, and perhaps missing the glory he had in the past, coveted it, and sought to pay Peter and John for the same gift earning a harsh rebuke from Peter, telling Simon to get his heart right with God. He tells Simon to repent of this wickedness and pray for forgiveness. 

Many grace-mixing works heretics point to this, one of the few times "repent" is followed by anything close to "of sins" as proof text for their false doctrine, but in doing so they omit that Simon was already saved. He believed on Jesus already. He did something wicked, but his repentance isn't for righteousness but as a believer who has sinned. 

And showing the conviction of his salvation, Simon accepts the rebuke and repents. Often you will see unbelievers, even those who claim Christ, bristle at correction. As the Bible says they despise it. But Simon, to his credit learns and grows from it.

Now Philip is called by the Lord to go to the desert of Gaza, and being obedient, he goes. He is called to do a great thing because he had shown God his commitment. The more we do for God the more He gives us to do, and so Philip gets this opportunity to show us how soul winning is done. 

We meet the Ethiopian eunuch, who we are told was the queen of Ethiopia treasurer, and that she and he were followers of the Hebrew religion, or what the modern form of Pharisees it has taken.

Acts 9 tells the story of Saul/Paul's 'seeing the light' on the road to Damascus. He had gone from a student of the Pharisees taught by the high priest Gamaliel, to a participant in the martyrdom of Stephen, to becoming a zealous persecutor of the church in Jerusalem, to the point where the disciples were scattered abroad.

Now, seeking to further put down what he saw as a blasphemous uprising, he asked permission to go and arrest Jews in another nation, Syria. With that license, he set off on the journey only to be struck blind by the appearance unto him of Jesus Himself. 

Saul, astonished and fearful responds to Jesus' rebuke, asking "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?"

And, Saul blindly asks "Who art thou Lord?" Jesus identifies Himself, and repeats the charge against Saul of persecuting Him, through His church. 

Jesus tells him it is "hard for thee to kick against the pricks." A idiom of the time, referring to the pricked stick used to steer an ox in the field. It means that the more you fight it, the harder it's going to be, as an ox who kicked against the prick would only further imbed the sharp ends. (Modern versions omit this verse because they are written by reprobates who take away from the word of God). 

Blinded and desperate, Paul asks what he must do, and Jesus directs him to Damascus, where he will be told. In Damascus, a disciple Ananias is given a vision by the Lord to go to Saul, and give him the truth of the Gospel, laying hands on him that he might be gifted by the Holy Ghost to be a great man of God, preaching to kings and spreading the Gospel to the Gentiles. 

Naturally, Ananias protests. This is Saul who has been breathing threats and slaughter against believers. Who had a warrant to arrest them in the city. Now Jesus was asking him to go, in faith and visit him, that he might see. 

Three days without sight, fasting, without drink, Saul was praying to God for answers, visited with a vision of Ananias coming and healing him. 

Here we see that while Jesus appeared and struck Saul blind, He doesn't give Saul the answer to what he must do, but rather a man must go to him and bring him to Christ. 

We are called upon by God to bring people the truth. It is from faith to faith, by hearing the word of God from saved Christians, that brings them to salvation. Jesus could have told Paul in that vision, but that's not how it works. We are the laborers who sow, water and harvest. It is an awesome responsibility. One too many of us shirk, under far less threat and danger than Ananias here. 

He was called to go into the den of those who sought to arrest or kill him, on faith he obeys and brings perhaps the most influential Christian in history, to the Lord. If he can do that, we can give the Gospel to a coworker, friend or neighbor, with only the threat of being mocked or rejected standing in our way. 

So, it is with that understanding and faith that Ananias goes to his enemy, and heals him, and Saul, now Paul, able to see, believes and is baptized in Jesus' name.

Paul himself tells the story again in Acts 22, with a bit more detail, which we will see. But his conversion, seeing the light, being once blind but now seeing, becomes the chief analogy for Christians being born again.

Paul, being a brilliant student of the law and coming to understand all things in Christ, and filled with the boldness of the Holy Ghost, begins immediately preaching the truth of Jesus in every synagogues, and immediately we see the pattern repeat, that those who oppose Christ and hate the truth began plotting to kill him. 

And the multitudes grew, the various independent churches through the Levant were edified by his preaching, multiplying believers. God working through the man who had persecuted them the most, to win souls to Christ.

Paul visits the churches he's planted along the journey, as he returns to Jerusalem. 

We get a side note about the the couple meeting Apollos, a Jew who was saved by faith knowing the preaching of John the Baptist, but not knowing Jesus had come. They tell him of Jesus and His being the Christ, and God uses Apollos, a fervent and eloquent speaker, who went to the Jews abroad with what seems to be more success than Paul, whose primary mission was to the Gentiles. Showing by scripture that Jesus was the Christ.

We later see in Paul's scathing epistle to the Corinthians that division grew in the church there between those saved by Paul and others who came to Christ by Apollos. "For while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?

Acts 21 sees the final leg of Paul's ill-fated journey to Jerusalem. For the past 3 chapters we have seen it written that it was Paul's will and desire to get to Jerusalem before Pentecost, and to celebrate in the Temple with the Jews, deliver alms to the saints at the church in Jerusalem and give the good news that the Gospel has spread out among the Gentiles, further and greater than the last Apostle could have imagined when he began. 

And in his journey we have seen strife, tumult in the cities of Asia as he went, and now we see multiple disciples in multiple cities prophesy in the Spirit that Paul should not go. But despite this, Paul remained determined. 

There are differing theories regarding this narrative. One is that Paul obstinacy in doing his own will was warned and opposed by God. This seems likely, as even the best of us get sidetracked into heeding out own desires and ignoring God, telling us not to as we think we should. Yet it remains our choice and all glory will come to God, even as we are chastised, and His will be done as all comes together for good. 

Another view is that Paul, heading to tribulation and suffering for Christ Jesus, was given warning by God so that Paul's decision was made with full awareness, in free will to better glorify God in his afflictions. 

We won't even get into the theological nonsense regarding the "permissive will of God" vs the "sovereign will of God." Theology is man trying to make God fit into their own notions of how things work, and theologians and their students are fools. Bible says it, believe it. Simple as. 

Anyway, we see Paul accepting the warnings, including of a man named Agabus, who we are told predicted the famine in the land back in Acts 11, so his gift of prophecy by the Holy Ghost is known. 

Either way, Paul is not dissuaded.

And so, Paul and Luke and the rest of his company return to Jerusalem, and straight away Paul goes to the head of the church, James, and the elders, and personally tells them of his success in the Gospel. 

But there's a problem. Those believers among the Jews who had earlier stirred up trouble regarding the practice of circumcision are again unhappy with Paul. They may be saved by faith but they see perfection and separation through the keeping of the law. 

We know from Acts and Paul's epistles that while Paul (and James, Peter and the others) all are in agreement regarding not forcing the Gentiles to take up the Mosaic laws, that they all still, as Jews celebrate the holy days and go to temple and kept the traditions. That Paul even circumcised Timothy, not as part of salvation but to show the Jews he was born of their people having a Jewish mother. 

As Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 9:20-21:
 
“And unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to them that are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain them that are under the law;To them that are without law, as without law, (being not without law to God, but under the law to Christ,) that I might gain them that are without law." 

Elsewhere he instructs, under the Spirit that these things are nothing to him, but a means to get people saved. That the carnal ordinances, diverse washings and dietary laws of the Levitical priesthood are done away with. That the sacrifices do nothing to wash away sin, that only faith in Jesus saves. 

But while the temple remained and the believing Jews maintained the old ways during this transition between the resurrection and the destruction of the temple, there was great debate among them what Christianity would look like for the Jew.

We see James reiterate their message to the Gentiles that they are not yoked to the law. But to satisfy the Jews in his church, James asks Paul to not only set their mind at ease, but to undertake a vow, shave his head and purify himself in the temple so that they are more receptive to his plea.  

(BTW verse 25 should be a nail in the coffin for the 'Hebrew Roots' nonsense)

So Paul, who sees these things as nothing if they edify the church and give glory to the Gospel of Jesus, goes along with the plan, and it almost immediately blows up when unbelieving Jews from Asia, likely at the Temple for the holy days as Paul was, spot him there. 

The Jews stir up the crowd and accuse him falsely of teaching heresy and of bringing 'unclean' Greeks to the Temple. This gets the Jews of the city into a mob, and they were going to kill Paul, beating him to death, when he's rescued and arrested by the chief captain and his guard who have to carry Paul due to the extent of injury. 

The crowd, an unruly and angry mob shouts out all manner of accusations against Paul, and trying to ascertain who he is, the captain brings him into the castle there, and Paul corrects him, in Greek, as to who he is. Taking to the stairs, Paul is allowed to address the crowd, in Hebrew, and we leave off for the next chapter to see what he says.

And despite all this, like all the prophets before him, even the Son of God, Christ Jesus, the Jews of Jerusalem seek his life for the truth offends them.

The captain of the guard orders Paul scourged to find out what he must have done to anger the people like this, hoping to gain a confession by his stripes. This will begin a series of events that leads to the Gospel being spread to the seat of power in Rome, and great glory to God.

Now in Acts 23 we find Paul already delivered to the Roman governor of the province, Felix in Caesarea, and his accusers called before Felix to hear charges against the Apostle. Having seen Paul's gift for rhetoric, Ananias the head Priest of the temple brings a ringer, the orator Tertullus.

Tertullus flatters the Roman governor and government, praising their stewardship, and claims Paul and the "sect" of Nazarenes is sowing sedition against Rome. He throws the chief captain under the bus, and bemoaning the "great violence" of the centurions, the Jew cries out in pain as he strikes.

The Governor then hears Paul's rebuttal, and Paul likewise appeals to Felix's honor as a judge, as he sets about the truth of the matter. 

He notes his business in Jerusalem was to bring alms, that he was found by certain Asian Jews while undergoing purifying in the Temple. That those same Jews aren't even present to accuse him. Paul testifies that it is his faith in the resurrection that's the real issue. 

He orders Paul held for the time being, and Paul is able to preach the Gospel to him and his wife, a Jewess named Drusilla, shaking Felix who allows Paul some liberty under guard, failing to entice a bribe from him. 

Two years pass in Paul's house arrest, and Porcius Festus takes Felix's place as governor under Nero, and to show the Jews a concession, continues to hold Paul.

This all is taking place roughly 58-60AD. The political situation in Judea and among the Jews of Samaria is getting strained and rebellion is growing. This untoward generation of unbelieving Jews is rapidly approaching its judgement, the Jewish war of 66, followed by the desolation of Jerusalem scattering the remnant of Jews of the flesh and total destruction of the temple in 70AD. It's a fascinating dynamic, and Jesus' and His apostles and believers impact on the hastening of these events is obvious. 

We need not sow sedition or take up arms or anything else but have faith in God. Turning towards Him, trusting He will judge the nation using His means for His wrath in His time. 

Often Christians get impatient with God and His long-suffering, and eager for their perception of justice, try to take vengence into their own hands. Their lack of faith and sin of fear grips them, and desperation fueled by provocation and deliberate humiliation is used by the enemy to tempt us. To have us turn away from God and towards an earthly solution. Reactionary spirals, further worsening the conditions we face. Dancing to the devil's tune. Slaves to Satan's plans. 

Tribulation and persecution is a part of the Christian life. The Bible promises us that as believers we will be hated of the world, because the world hates Him. That the greater things we do for God, the harsher the persecution. And, as we see through out the Bible, and in history, the more God's people are persecuted in His name, the more His people flourish. 

*For we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.*

And knowing this, how can we be fearful? And being fearful, how can we be a light that shines? How can we *be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you?*

Paul has been scourged repeatedly. Scared by stripes. Stoned to death and raised immediately. Chased out of countries, driven from cities. Plotted against and arrested multiple times. 

And like when he was held in a Philippian jail, singing songs and Psalms of praise to God for it. 

God has written to us to be not afraid 365 times in His word, once verse for every day of the year, and yet so many Christians live in misery and despair. They hide their light under a bushel, while the faithful shine it to beggars and princes alike.

A common lament of the believer is that their friends and family are perishing, damned without faith. The worry and stress of having that knowledge and their inability to convince them of the truth leaves many feeling impotent and frustrated. But this is all the more reason to remain steadfast. To magnify God's love for us, reflecting it to those we care about. To be the rock that they can turn to when they are troubled, and maybe coming to see the truth of the word though our example. The reason for our hope. To be *an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.*

Why would someone believe someone telling them of the peace that passes all understanding found in Christ when we are as miserable and fearful as everyone else?

Answering a question with a brother about **Romans 2** had me really rethink something that I missed, and it clarified a lot of the misunderstanding around the chapter, specifically who it is written to. 

Because of the language Paul uses, specifically at the end of the chapter, many assume he is directly addressing Jews there, despite the greetings in chapter 1 being to the church in Rome, which are Gentiles. In my study, I did what a lot of people do and just squared the circle by saying basically the church has both Jews and Greeks (which is likely true, but irrelevant to what Paul is doing).

The entire epistle is a general one, and all believers are the audience. But there is a default understanding that some of it is actually targeted to Jews, in the church, based especially on the last half of chapter 2. 

But it's not. 

Paul's not writing to Jews. He's writing a rhetorical method of argument that addresses common points made about Gentiles, then Jews, in a methodical way. 

It's part of the larger argument that he's making in the epaitle. It isn't literally him saying to the Jew the things he says, but addressing questions often raised by Jews against Christians who were preaching that Gentiles were now made accessible to the Gospel of Grace. When Paul says "O man..." is like when James says "a man may say..."

It's a method of rhetoric common in the era. Anticipating and answering objections to stipulate certain points. 

And so after establishing that Gentiles, despite being pagans and many reprobate and given over, with no excuse, given up to all unrighteousness, have access salvation in Christ, Paul continues to hammer Jewish objections to this idea. 

*Behold, thou art called a Jew, and restest in the law, and makest thy boast of God, And knowest his will, and approvest the things that are more excellent, being instructed out of the law*...This is addressed to a rhetorical Jewish opponent who would make these claims, not specifically "to Jews."

Chapter three changes to 3rd person, because it was always the arguments being made, not the audience being addressed. 

*What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision? Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God. For what if some did not believe? shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect?*

Having chapters and verse helps to quickly reference scripture, but the breaks can cause confusion when a larger point is being made. Go back and read the entire epistle in one go, and consider it's Paul, in the Spirit, making several arguments, methodically. Not telling Jews one thing and Gentiles another.

*11 And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised: that he might be the father of all them that believe, though they be not circumcised; that righteousness might be imputed unto them also:*

*12 And the father of circumcision to them who are not of the circumcision only, but who also walk in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham, which he had being yet uncircumcised.*

*13 For the promise, that he should be the heir of the world, was not to Abraham, or to his seed, through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.*

*14 For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect:*

*15 Because the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression.*

*16 Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace; to the end the promise might be sure to all the seed; not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham; who is the father of us all,*

*17 (As it is written, I have made thee a father of many nations,) before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were.*

*18 Who against hope believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to that which was spoken, So shall thy seed be.*

*19 And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sarah's womb:*

*20 He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God;*

*21 And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform.*

*22 And therefore it was imputed to him for righteousness.*

*23 Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him;*

*24 But for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead;*

*25 Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.*

What shall we say then? Paul, having concluded that all are under sin, all being unrighteous, and the grace of God given to all who believe on the Son, and that no man may be justified by the works of the law but only faith, now begins the application of this knowledge. The implications of this law of faith, given us by God. And he uses scripture and the promises to Abraham to explain the Old Testament in light of the New. 

Abraham, the physical father of the Hebrews, including the remnant of Jews from the Children of Israel in Rome, what was Abraham's experience? A story every Jew would be familiar with. 

Paul starts by saying, if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory. Abraham could brag in his works, his decades of service to God that includes willingness to sacrifice his only begotten son, but we know that there are none righteous. That boasting is excluded when we are judged by grace, as all the glory belongs to God, and the righteousness of Christ.

So Paul writes, if it were by works, Abraham could glory, boast, brag that it was due him being so righteous. But not before God, being in the flesh, a sinner. (Which we have already stipulated in chapter 3)

What then? 

Well, scripture says in **Genesis 15:6**; *And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness*. Paul quotes this and argues that if it were of works, that means God would be indebted to us. To pay us for our works. That we were owed. 

And so the reward would be not reckoned, or accounted for, by grace. Because grace is an unmerited and unearned gift or favor. Debt is deserved. Grace is undeserved. 

*But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.*

*Abraham believed God and it was counted unto him for righteousness*.

Abraham is the example Paul uses, given us in scripture as a lesson in justification by faith to God, by grace not of debt. That the glory in our salvation is God's alone. 

But what about before other men?

A man may say that faith without works is dead, being alone. That, to men, justification isn't seen of faith but by a man's works. 

**James 2:18-23**
*Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works. Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble. But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead? Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar? Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect? And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God.*

*A man may say...* The overlooked predicate for the argument James makes in his epistle, written to brethren, the saved, to encourage them to good works. A man may say that Abraham's faith was shown in his works and thus he was justified to others. 

But we know that scripture says it was faith that justified Abraham to God. 

*For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God. For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.*

By comparing scripture with scripture we see that there is no contradiction, only context. That Paul is writing of justification before God in grace, while James is writing of justification before man, by doing good works in faith. 

The rhetorical question asked by a rhetorical man, "Was not Abraham justified by works?" is answered by the holy Spirit in **Romans 4** and **Genesis 15**. Not before God, or he would have to glory. The boasting wouldn't be excluded. The law of grace would become one of debt. 

The misuse of **James 2** to teach a false gospel of works is one of the great stumbling blocks to salvation and faith. But by comparison, context and understanding we see that there is no contradiction found, anywhere in the Bible.

*Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.*

But to him that worketh not, but believes, his faith is counted for righteousness just as Abraham's. Just as all who believe. Works has nothing to do with salvation. God doesn't owe us salvation. 

Our works, no matter how good we think they are, can never offset our sin, and the wages thereof. 

When someone says their salvation or their ability to stay saved is contingent on their works, they are saying they are good enough to please God. That they are owed salvation. That the glory is theirs. That their boastings before God are justified. That they don't need grace. 

**Hebrews 11:6**
*But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.*

Their lack of faith in Christ to be the propitiation for our sin, the sole sacrifice pleasing and acceptable to God, means their works are dead. They have no grace and no works. They are incapable of pleasing God.

**Hebrews 6:1**
*Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God*

Repentance from dead works and to faith towards God. Turning from means turning towards. From trusting in our works of righteousness to faith in God. This is the foundation that is built on the rock that is Christ. 

And so, reckoned of faith, the man who does no works but believes, is saved by that faith alone. Paul quotes Davin from **Psalm 32**
*Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, Whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity, And in whose spirit there is no guile*.

The Lord will not impute sin, our ledger is clean, our transgressions forgiven. 

For what is sin?

**1 John 3:4**
*Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law.*

But we who believe not only are forgiven of sins past, but God will not impute sin to us. Our transgression is forgiven. This is a promise of God.

**Hebrews 10:17**
*And their sins and iniquities will I remember no more.*

So this is the promise made by God that if we believe on the Son, we are saved by His grace. Our sins forgiven. No sin even being imputed upon us. Whether we work or not, because work is debt not grace. 

Paul continues using Abraham's example;

*Cometh this blessedness then upon the circumcision only, or upon the uncircumcision also? for we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness. How was it then reckoned? when he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.*

Abraham did not receive the ordinance of circumcision until decades after his believing God's promise, and being saved by that faith. He was blessed with the accounting of righteousness when he did not know circumcision. So this promise, predating this rite of the Jews, means it does not only apply to the circumcised, but also to the uncircumcised. And so the promise of grace doesn't require circumcision, but faith alone. 

This point is both specific to the issue of circumcision being introduced by the Judaizers in Paul's day, but also generally speaking, that there is no rite or ordinance that is required for salvation. Not baptism. Not any ritual or keeping of tradition. No works of the law. 

*And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised: that he might be the father of all them that believe, though they be not circumcised; that righteousness might be imputed unto them also*.

Abraham as the father of all who believe, the circumcision of the spirit, the generation of believers are partakers of the promise, that the righteousness of God is imputed upon us in faith. 

*For the promise, that he should be the heir of the world, was not to Abraham, or to his seed, through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect: Because the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression.*

The promise of God that Abraham believed was that through his faith, he would be made father to many nations, and inherit the kingdom of God. This promise was made possible in Christ. 

**Galatians 3:16**
*Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ*.

Unbelieving Jews felt they were owed the kingdom by God for being Abraham's seed under the law. That the inheritance was by blood, and the promise made to them after the flesh, and not in the spirit. 

This is the basis for Zionism and the false doctrine of dispensationalism. 

But the Bible teaches the exact opposite. There is no difference between Jew and Gentile. All are under sin. It is by faith only that we are made heirs. That the seed of the promise is Christ manifest in the flesh. 

**Matthew 3:9**
*And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.*

It is not an inheritance by the law but by faith. Like Esua and Jacob, the inheritance went to the younger. It was taken from the elder, who with tears sought repentance from God, but none was found. 

**Luke 13:25-30**
*When once the master of the house is risen up, and hath shut to the door, and ye begin to stand without, and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, Lord, open unto us; and he shall answer and say unto you, I know you not whence ye are: Then shall ye begin to say, We have eaten and drunk in thy presence, and thou hast taught in our streets. But he shall say, I tell you, I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out. And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God. And, behold, there are last which shall be first, and there are first which shall be last.*

The kingdom of God was taken from the Jew in their unbelief and given to the nations of people bringing forth the fruit thereof. Who had faith. 

There is no plan for the Jews after the flesh and those teaching dispensationalism to claim there is are teaching heresy.

*Because the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression. Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace; to the end the promise might be sure to all the seed; not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham; who is the father of us all, (As it is written, I have made thee a father of many nations,) before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were.*

Because the law brings wrath, because we are all under sin, it isn't by the law we are saved. It is impossible for all have sinned. 

As James writes in the parts of his epistles ignored-by-works salvationists;

*For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.*

Remember, there are none righteous. Knowledge of the law brings wrath. But faith, the grace of God. 

We access His mercy and forgiveness through faith alone. Plus nothing, minus nothing.

And in grace we receive the promise given Abraham, and count as his seed in the spirit. Adopted into the kingdom of God. Made sons of God. Abraham is the father of us all who believe. 

 *(As it is written, I have made thee a father of many nations,) before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were.*

God, who can see all things, the future which is not to us, and yet it appears as it were to God, who quickens the dead, who breathes life into our dead spirit, and who made this eternal promise to all who believe. 

The Jew has no claim to Abraham, outside of faith. None. And to none of the promises made, for they all are fulfilled in Christ. 

If it feels like I am beating a dead horse, understand that it is God's word that stresses this over and over again, because it is the Gospel, the good news, that is the entire point of scripture. To bring us into the promise through faith and the imputed righteousness of God.

Paul continues to show that despite the unlikely nature of some of the specific promises to him made of God, the hope against hope that he father a child with Sarah in their old age, that they would through Isaac become many nations, to people more numerous than the sand of the shore, the stars of heaven. 

*And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform. And therefore it was imputed to him for righteousness.*

But was this for Abraham alone? No. 

This was written for our sake as well, that we may KNOW we have eternal life and the imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ if we believe on the promise of God. 

*Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him; But for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead; Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.*

Amen, amen, amen!

I pray to the Lord that this series continues to be a blessing to others and that my understanding grows from presenting it. That the undeniable meaning of the theology of God found in scripture changes hearts with the power of His word. Have a blessed Sunday, and remember to thank father Abraham on this father's day. 

For he is the father of all who believe. 

In Jesus name, amen

Building upon the conclusions reached in Chapter 3, we see in **Romans 4**, Paul uses scripture to flesh out the ideas and demonstrate the truth of his argument. The veil lifted, so that by the reading of Moses a believer may understand God's word. 

He begins with the understanding that Abraham was not justified by his works or by circumcision, but by his faith. Abraham believed God and it was counted for righteousness. 

And when Abraham believed, it was decades before the institution of the carnal ordinance of circumcision. A practice giving an outward sign for the continuation of the people chosen to bear Abraham's seed, which is Christ.

While **Romans 4** is frequently cited to demolish the heretical argument that we are saved in any capacity by our own works, it is primarily an argument against the Judaizers who think to themselves to say they have Abraham as their father. 

But as John the Baptist says in **Matthew 3:9**;

*And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.*

It wasn't circumcision that saved Abraham, but faith. It wasn't even his willingness to sacrifice Isaac. All the great works of faith by Abraham may be reason to glory among men, but not before God. They may be reckoned for reward out of debt, but not of grace which is freely given to those who believe, to the glory of God. 

As David wrote, Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin. Those who do no works, but have believed on Christ, that faith is counted for righteousness. 

It is an accounting. The only thing that is reckoned for forgiveness of sin and salvation from death, is faith.

And so, if this blessing came by faith and not circumcision, there is no profit in circumcision. 

And if the righteousness of Abraham came by faith, there is no profit in being able to call Abraham your father after the flesh. 

The promise of God, that through his seed all nations shall be blessed, and that seed should be made heir to the whole world, was not made to Abraham, or to his seed through the law. Meaning his physical descendants, who under the law are inheritors. 

The promise to be made heir was through the righteousness of faith. 

This excludes unconditionally any claim Jews would have on the Abrahamic covenant, except by faith in Christ. 

*For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect*

If dispensationalist Zionism were true, that by the law Jews are heirs to Abraham's promise, *then faith is made void and the promises made of none effect.* 

Saved Christians who believe that Jews are the inheritors by this promise, are like Esau, selling the promise for pottage. Despising their inheritance.

Abraham believed. And in that faith, received the inheritance, which in Christ is given to all who believe. Whether they were circumcised or uncircumcised. And the righteousness and promises of faith given Abraham was not only to him, but to all who believe the Gospel of Grace, again recounted here by Paul;

*Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him; But for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead; Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.*

This is the faith that imputed righteousness on Abraham and upon we who believe. Plus nothing and minus nothing. 

The same faith that saved Abraham saved us today, and will until the day of the Lord comes, and we are gathered unto Him. Jew or Gentile. At the great harvest of God.

So, in 4 chapters we see that there is no difference between Jew and Gentile, all are under sin, all condemned, with the law or without. 

We see that all who are saved from that condemnation are saved by faith in the blood of Christ Jesus. By believing God's promise. By the imputed righteousness of Jesus, our own sins are not counted against us. Without works. Not by the law. Not by circumcision. Not by being physical heirs of Abraham, but spiritual heirs in faith. 

There is no replacement theology, only the continuation of the covenant made to Abraham, which is to all nations. 

There was no other dispensation given. There is no future dispensation to be had.

Therefore. Therefore what?

*Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.*

As the heavenly hosts proclaimed in the hills of Bethlehem at the birth of the man Christ Jesus;

*Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.*

The peace and goodwill on earth was come from God to man. Not the peace of men not warring. Not goodwill between tribes. But the enmity of wrath in the transgressions of man made justified by the peace offering of His only begotten Son. 

We are justified by faith alone. There is nothing more noted. We have already concluded that by the works of the law no man shall be justified. We already know that by faith, Abraham became father to all who believe. We already know that the judgment of God is upon Jew and Greek alike. *Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.* 

What's more; By faith we have access into the grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. 

Believing, we are given grace, and by grace, God is given the glory for our salvation. Note, "wherein we stand." This isn't the future, this isn't a process. This is now, at the time of our repentance towards belief in Christ as our redeemer we then, at that moment, stand in grace. And rejoice. 

And we not only rejoice in the glory of God's grace that provides us with salvation through faith, because it shows the mercy and judgment and righteousness of God (which remember is one way His glory is revealed to man from Heaven), we also glory in tribulations here on earth, knowing they are a refining fire; that worketh patience, which brings experience, and experience brings hope. Hope builds faith.

*Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen*.

Hope is the sure knowledge that a thing will be that is not yet. The object of faith. Tribulation in our lives, not only persecution for our faith, but just general troubles like health, finance, whatever things common to all men, saved or unsaved, all of it gives opportunity to glorify the Lord, as it makes our faith sharper as we are brought out of it by His mercy and blessings, better for having experienced it. 

And our hope is fufifiled in the love of God, by the comforter, the Holy Ghost, which is given us, who indwells with us, quickening our spirit and leading us to that peace which passes all understanding, even in turmoil and crisis. 

Our faith in man, traditions, our own works, all will leave us ashamed at some point. But the hope we have in Christ Jesus will never bring us shame. God never lets us down.

And how do we know that God's word is good, that our hope is true? Because 

*But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us*.

That when we were still enemies, working inequities, dead in sin, God reconciled us through the death of His Son. God loved His enemies, and offered the free gift of salvation by the shedding of blood of His only begotten Son. 

Think about this, for in it is the righteousness of God. 

And if He offered us such a gift, if a righteous man gave His life for us while we were enemies, dying for us while we were dead in sin, then how much more shall He do for us whom have been reconciled to Him in faith by the death of His Son? Who stand in His grace? We shall be saved by His life in the resurrection. 

And not only so, that we shall know we will be saved out of tribulation by His resurrection and the promise of God to us likewise for eternal life, but we also joy, rejoice, in God through our Lord Jesus Christ by whom we have now received the atonement. 

Our hope is that, today we who believe are spared wrath for our sins, adopted to the promise, and that in tribulation on this earth we will be saved by God's love for His sons, because of the atonement of Christ Jesus that we holdfast to in faith. Amen

And so the law came, to Noah, to Abraham, to Moses, and by Sinai, so detailed and expanded, much more than the single commandment of the Garden, so that man had to know that the holiness of God was unattainable by their works, and that faith in His grace alone was our only hope. 

And with the law, sin abounded much the more, that God's grace may abound to His glory.

It is the free gift given by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ. The gift of His righteousness that we may be justified through Him to God. By His obedience to the end, and the death on the cross for all men, that in His resurrection we may enter into grace by faith.

And to make this point clear, Paul quotes Elijah, who was cursing Israel for their unbelief and seeking the prophet's life. God's reply to Elijah is that there was a remnant of Israel who were saved by faith, who had no bent the knee to Baal. Who were still faithful. 

By comparing his present time to Elijah's, Paul deliberately specifies that there is a remnant, just as he himself is a remnant, according to the election of grace.

*And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then it is no more grace: otherwise work is no more work.*

What then? 

Israel hath not obtained that which he seeketh for.

The rest were blinded.

That we present our bodies as a loving sacrifice, without blemish, which is our service, separated to the Gospel. Be holy that we may be better able to be of service to God. Vessels fitted for glory. Blameless. 

This isn't an appeal to hit the gym and not eat poorly. Our bodies are corruptible, and flesh is going to lead us to sin. It is about walking in the spirit that we may not fulfil the lusts of that flesh, and by example bring others to Christ. 

He writes, *be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind*, which comes from walking in the spirit. To know the will of God. Proving, testing to see what is acceptable. 

We are to remain humble, understanding that to every man of faith God has shaped to a purpose. Not all have the same gifts, the same talents, but all are members of the same body, which is Christ. None more important or less important. A similar theme Found in **1 Corinthians 12**:

*But now are they many members, yet but one body. And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you.*

And so each of us should seek to use the talents we have to edify the whole of the body of believers. 

*Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith; Or ministry, let us wait on our ministering: or he that teacheth, on teaching; Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness.*

So, to our measure, we all make perfect the will of God. And we see too, that attitude is everything.

*Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.*

Dissimulation is deceit, dishonesty regarding intent. Concealing motives. Love without dissimilation requires also to abhor, to hate, that which is evil. 

Speaking the truth in love. There is no love in manipulation or in hidden agendas. There is no love without hate.

These two tendencies of the world, to see all relationships as transactional, and so what men call love is often manipulative and controlling. Toxic. And with this toxic false love comes the lack of judgment, calling nothing evil. Tolerating all manner of corruption and perversion. "Not judging" but allowing others to do as they will and calling it good. 

It is codependency, an allowance for other's sin that we then can remain in our own. This isn't love. 

God's love is without manipulation. It is freely given. We don't have to work for it. Unconditional. To avail ourselves of it, we have to believe He so loved us He gave His only begotten Son. But His love came first, while we were yet sinners. 

And God hates evil. Many falsely say "God is love" and ignore His holy nature and the revelation of wrath against the wicked. His word telling us of abominations to Him. For example:

The wicked slogan of the prideful sodomites, "Love is Love," is simply putting evil for good, bitter for sweet.

And so, chapter 14 begins with a hypothetical situation to illustrate the point Paul is building to. 

*Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.*

This caveat  is important to understand what he is proposing; A person weak in the faith may hold themselves to a higher standard than the Bible calls for, that we being more stable in the faith may see as silly. 

Right up front Paul is warning not to use the occasion to argue with them. Especially of they are so weak of faith, or babes, that either may dig in their heels at rebuke, and add to the Gospel their opinions. Doubtful disputations, arguments about unimportant things that ultimately rest on "if you disagree you aren't saved."

Paul uses eating of meat vs vegetarians, but He also applies it to celebration of holidays, even the first day of the week as sacred. 

Other than the strong admonishment against eating meat sacrificed to idols in 1 Corinthians for example, even if you don't think the idol is anything but wood or molten metal, is clear. And the giving to us that all food is clean and good to eat, that is blessed in Christ by our thanksgiving, there is nothing that says we have to eat meat. Just as there's nothing against abstaining. 

But one weak in the faith and consumed by guilt at eating an animal, or who sees holidays as unnecessary or even wrong in their conscience, we should be patient with. We shouldn't push them to do what's wrong in their mind, to stumble. Even if you think they're fools. 

To love them, we shouldn't place stumbling blocks but rather edify them. Our job isn't to judge one another who believe and are not in open sin regarding clear teachings, over petty matters.

We are to build each other up. 

Stand fast for what's true, in love. If the Bible says it and they are against it. Correct them.

Note that Paul first praises a woman, Phebe, commending her for her great work laboring for God, spreading the Gospel and being a strength to others in the faith. She is one of many women God immortalized in scripture for their labors.

Many assume because Paul reiterates God's command that women remain silent in church, and not be pastors (a position many men couldn't qualify for either), that Paul was a misogynist or something. Both men and women lose sight of this in current year, and resentments and divisions surrounding this keep us from fulfilling the labors God has for us. 

Paul goes on to salute and praise men and women of the faith who are his fellow laborors. Helpers. Being about the business of the Father. Winning souls and edifying the saints. Paul, as always begins with greetings, and as always, is writing to the saved believers in Christ. He had helped stablish this church in Corinth back in Acts 18, and so personally had led many of the church there to Christ. If you recall he was with Priscilla and Aquila there, and that they had also found a brother, baptized by John the Baptist, Apollos, to whom they introduced Jesus as the Christ, making his faith complete. This will be important to keep in mind as we read this epistle. 

Paul greets them as saints, as are all who call upon the name of the Lord. Who are sanctified by Jesus. 

And even as they were sanctified by the testimony of Christ, Paul expresses that God's grace continue to bless them in all things, so that they receive all spiritual gifts and knowledge and wisdom. This is the prayer we should have for ourselves and others in our church and those who share our faith. That by their faith, and God's grace they receive understanding and grow in their Christian life to be made more perfect, and in doing so become better use for God. 

We see the promise of the coming of Christ, who will confirm us to the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, His second coming. The day of the resurrection and rapture. We are sealed unto judgment with a gift of eternal life that can never be lost or taken away. Jesus redeems us. God confirms us. The Spirit seals us. God is faithful.

After his greeting and the establishment or, re-establishment of the shared belief that unites those in Corinth, Paul gets to the heart of the matter in that he has heard reports of division in the church. Those who had been saved by Paul, or Apollos or Peter, and even those who had been saved during the ministry of Jesus Christ, are beginning to form schisms and divisions.

Paul is admonishing this, and points out that the baptism and who did it is incidental to the saving faith in Christ Jesus, in whose name they were baptized all. We see this a lot today, people treating what should be a unifying faith as a scene, and bickering about personalities within the scene. This is a real problem and, the denominational splits that we see in the church later all stem from it. Especially the schism that gives birth to the Roman Catholic Church 300 years later, and all of the devastation to Christianity that spun out of it.

Paul reminds them that the baptism isn't what they're there for, but to preach the gospel. Here Paul makes several doctrinal statements regarding the preaching of the Gospel that are both sublime truth, and yet obvious to those of us who are saved upon hearing it. 

That the preaching of the Cross appears to be foolish to those who are either seeking after a sign from God, or to be reasoned with into faith. As Jesus said the only sign the Jews would receive was that of Jonas, of his being in the belly of the Earth for three days and three nights to be risen again. And for the greeks, who sought a reason above all, giving them faith which is the evidence of things unseen, in lieu of logic, appears to be foolishness.

We all know people today who are constantly looking for supernatural signs from God before they can commit to believing, or physical evidence of the truth of the Bible from secular sources. Or who seek to impose their own logic on matters that are spiritual. And who stuff at the simplicity of the Gospel as it's presented, despite our knowledge of the power of God that is within it. 

Similar to the Epistle of James that we read over the weekend, Paul notes that the proud and wealthy, the powerful etc, are less likely to receive the Gospel because God uses our weaknesses to become our strength. Our humility and meekness becomes power in the hands of a believing Son of God. And what many see as foolishness, or weakness and passivity, or supposed slave mentality, is actually the wisdom of God expressed through our understanding, patience, long suffering, and the love that we show to all. 

A lot of people grapple with this even saved Christians. They seek their own vengeance, they carry the wrath that belongs to God, they grow impatient with His perfect timing. For those who are not saved by faith, these things are a snare and a stumbling block, their pride being caught in those traps.

And Paul explains to us too that this all is in service of glory to God. That none of our works, or who we know, or any other ways that man might justify himself in his own wisdom and conceit, but that all we are and all our wisdom and knowledge, sanctification and redemption, comes from God himself and so all the glory goes to him.

Second chapter of First Corinthians, Paul is still establishing a few things, making certain basic stipulations regarding the faith, before getting to his main topic of settling disputes that have come up in Corinth. 

In chapter one, he speaks to the faith they share for salvation, and the fellowship of the sons of God that they should have in that faith and Spirit, given all wisdom and understanding come from God in that Spirit. 

That unlike the Jews who ask for signs and evidence and the Greeks logic, but that God's wisdom comes from faith and meekness, that the strengths of this world are weakness, and our weakness, God's strength.

Paul continues this theme in chapter 2. Paul says he was determined when he came professing nothing of the world, but only Christ when evangelizing to them in the first place, and Him crucified. Reminding them he was with them as they heard and knew the truth and accepted it with fear. 

Paul humbly says it wasn't his oratory or logic, but the power of the word that convicted them. That word is the "hidden wisdom" of Christ Jesus, written before creation. The reference to "mystery being revealed" isn't gnosticism, but that Jesus being the Christ, "to whom all the prophets gave witness" is the mystery revealed. Christianity is an anti-gnostic religion, in that knowledge of who Christ Jesus is and what He did and why is the great mystery that is told us plainly in the Gospel. It's the entry point to the full enlightenment for the novice, not some secret kept for the adept. It's a mystery, only so far as Jesus identity, and kept only for those prior to His resurrection. *Which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.*.. (**Ephesians 3:1-6)**

Paul furthers the doctrine of understanding the word. That it is only in those quickened by the Spirit that all things of the wisdom of God are revealed through His word. 

*For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God...But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.*

The wisdom of God is available to all who believe the Gospel and stay in His word. But to those who don't believe, who can't humble themselves to admit they are sinners deserving death, that they are incapable of being  righteous enough to justify themselves through their works or repenting of sin, and that our only hope is the imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ, freely given through God's grace, God's wisdom is denied them. They can't understand scripture. They stumble over the word. They are offended, snared, trapped in their own pride. Or blinded by their own rejection of God and kept blind by Him. 

If you are a believer who has done any kind of soul winning, preaching the Gospel, or even engaged with others regarding scripture online, you will quickly see this inability to understand by the non-believer. It's often just their own reliance on the wisdom of the world that conflicts with the truth of God's word, but sometimes you see that it is a supernatural blindness. It can be disconcerting to show someone clear verse that is clearly understood, and they cannot see it, no matter how you present it or how many supporting verses you share. The spiritual blindness is real, and further proof of the power of God and His word.

Having established these truths and basic understandings, Paul has set up what will follow, and has subtly separated those people in Corinth by reminding them that hear that they have the mind of Christ and should share understanding and common wisdom, from God and His word, in the Spirit. 

Just as the Gospel is foolishness to some of the unsaved, the word of God used in correction and reproach should resonate with believers. Hard preaching against sin or heresy should click, be understood, when weighed by the saved, comparing spiritual with spiritual.

Remember, this letter to the church at Corinth is to rebuke strife and divisions regarding earthly things among spiritual brethren. Paul uses carnal, of the flesh, to refer to the things of this world that aren't spiritual. He says he can't even speak to them of spiritual things because they are yet carnal. Babes in Christ who barely can digest the milk of the word, let alone the meat, the harder things of God. His reproach is to say they are yet carnal, and he gives evidence of their arguments over who they got saved by. What minister of God planted the seed or watered that seed or harvested them unto repentance towards God is unimportant. All believers have a minister from who they heard the word, and believing the word, had faith. We are all called to be such ministers, but to God is the increase. To God is the bounty that none of the husbandmen can glory. 

And when we are in heaven, our works in this regard will be judged. And what we do will be determined by fire, as to whether or not it is wood hay and stubble, to be burned away as unimportant, or precious jewels and gold and silver with which we will be rewarded for our labor. 

Things of hay and stubble will be these unimportant worldly matters in which we might be right, or diligent in what we do, but with no real spiritual value. Nothing that adds to the glory of God or magnifies His word.

Winning souls to Christ, helping the poor and the fatherless, the widows, being doers of the word and not hearers only, those things are rewarded by God in the judgment. 

Our common foundation is Jesus Christ, and what we build upon that foundation honestly comes down to whether it gives glory to God or not. And your going to the right denomination, adhering to traditions of men, engaging in sacraments and rites, having the correct opinion about a political dispute or a question of genealogies, or the shape of the realm that we inhabit... All of that is wood, hay and stubble.

Don't get it confused, and be carnal. Seek the higher things of God comparing spiritual with spiritual, and in your discipleship put away the strife and divisions that the world serves up to us. They are snares. And they use our own pride and subjective nature as hooks to snare us on.

We lose reward that we might have expected thinking that what we did was of significance to God, but often our pride and conceits can trick us into thinking that hay and stubble are precious stones.

These are carnal.  

That's not to say that discussing it and wondering about it having fun discussions regarding it is necessarily wrong. I enjoy them. But putting them in primacy over the spiritual is foolishness and carnal.

Paul, having dispensed with the rebuke, moves on to answer questions asked pertaining to those who have taken a vow of virginity, and then marry, have they sinned? 

Paul gives a wide ranging answer, and speaks of his own situation as well as marriage in general. 

Much of this advice is given from Paul, not speaking in the Spirit and he says so repeatedly, yet its inclusion and his final judgment to say he believes he has the Spirit of God on this, tells us it's God's word.

To withhold relations with our spouses for reason other than brief periods of fasting, is defrauding our spouse. If you are going without intimacy for a brief period, agreed upon, consummate at the end least your incontinence, that is your being hornt-up, leads you to sin.

Paul, as the Apostles agreed upon in Acts, then speaks again on the circumcision issue, that it's nothing. 

Paul continues this side note, away from matters of marriage and celibacy, explaining how we must remember that regardless of our station, servant or master, we are God's, bought with a price, in Christ's blood, and so to remember, as a slave we are free in Christ. In chapter 8 of First Corinthians, Paul gets into an often misunderstood doctrine. It's regarding eating food sacrificed to idols in heathen temples and homes, but it can apply to many other things in our Christian life. Things that aren't explicitly sin, in our knowledge and understanding of both our salvation, and the liberty that's in Christ, and of God's law in our conscience, which is bulwarked by the Spirit. 

As Paul says, we who are saved should understand that there is only one living God, and that idols are dead, made by man and have no power, being graven images. But the unsaved man or a babe in Christ, still superstitious of the things of this world, may stumble or be snared by seeing our eating of the sacrifice. Knowing it's nothing but meat, and the pagan practice silly and stupid, we could, in good conscience eat the sacrifice and laugh at how silly the pagans are and give all blessing and honor to God. But if that thing done in our knowledge were to cause the weaker man to sin or not come to the faith of the one true God, we shouldn't do it. It is offensive. 

This can apply to the circumcision. Maybe to other practices not forbidden by the scriptures, or that is sinful only in intent of the heart, not in the doing for one at liberty.

I would list a few things, but in doing so I risk offending a weaker conscience. 

Ultimately, we should be mindful of others and their infirmities, and seek to build up their faith, not please ourselves.
