The sudden turn in chapter 9, to address another matter of contention among the church makes me believe we are seeing Paul's point by point replies without seeing the questions he's replying to. But we can discern the meaning as we go, based on his answers. Here, some had questioned his apostolic credentials. 

Paul makes the case that despite his not pressing the matter to not offend and to make the Gospel known, he was within rights to ask for a wage and support from the congregation. That other apostles, as is right, earn a wage for their service. A tithe of carnal things of meat and drink like the priests of the temple, in exchange for the spiritual things they bring to the believers. He notes that Peter and the others are paid enough to support a wife and yet he and Barnabas, being single, didn't ask for the same, even though they were within their rights to. 

Those whom the Lord has ordained as ministers of the word, evangelists and pastors, preach the Gospel and so should live of the Gospel. Paul says he'd rather die than any man could accuse him of doing it for his own glory. 

We know that Paul was a tentmaker by trade, and worked with Aquila and Priscilla in this during his ministry. 

Paul says he is compelled to preach the Gospel, a feeling many of us have the further we get into the word, building our faith. We will see later in this epistle that some are "addicted to the ministry of the saints." Working in the church, edifying the faithful, sharing the Gospel. Would that we all have this addiction. 

Paul makes the point that his sacrifice of doing without to service of the ministry is done willingly. That his reward from God would come only because he does it of his own free will and liberty. This is the same for all works we do. We are free in Christ from death and Hell. We are liberated from the law, being washed clean. Any work we do thereafter isn't by force or fear but love. It's a sacrifice to serve, and laborers are paid by the fruit of their labors, as God's law states. Even the oxen. 

Those working to gain or maintain salvation are working against their will, for a price, and so the reward they get is the bondage of having to be slaves to the whole of the law. It's not sacrifice, it's selfish, and they perish for it. 

Paul continues, explaining that in service to the Gospel he willingly suffers all things that it may spread, and that he may be a partaker of the glory of God. 

He compares this service to an athlete, temperate in all things, training his body for a prize, a corruptible crown of laurels, while we do it for the incorruptible crowns of life given to us as reward in Heaven. 

He tells us to run to win. To fight, not shadow boxing, but fully engaged. Keeping our bodies under subjection to be able to be blameless to others as we present ourselves as God's people, and spread His good news of grace. That we not be hypocritical and backslidden to those we seek to win to the Lord.

Paul continues his teaching to the Church at Corinth, and reminds them all that their forefathers were baptized unto Moses by the passing through the sea, and by the cloud that followed them as they wandered, the Rock that provided water, a symbol of Christ. And despite this, those saved out of Egypt were backslidden and committed wickedness, as all sin common to man tempts us all. 

They committed idolatry and idleness, with the golden calf (**Exodus 32**). They were tempted by the daughters of Moab and led to slaughter by their fornication (**Numbers 25)**. They complained of the Mana and were struck down by the fiery serpents (**Numbers 21**). They murmured and complained against Moses' leadership, and the gainsaying of Koreh was met with instant death (**Numbers 16)**.

These Israelites were faithful to leave captivity, made free by that faith, baptized of a sort, led to the promised land by a cloud and a pillar of fire, fed from the corn of Heaven, they did eat angel's food, and were given the water from the Rock, that was like the living waters of Christ. They ate of the communion the meat, and drank the common drink, and yet they fell to fornication and idolatry, and God did punish them for it, just as believers who are backslidden and castaway are punished by God. *For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.* (**Hebrews 12**).

Paul says these examples are lessons given us by God to learn His ways. God will not allow us to be tempted beyond our ability to resist, but it is up to us to resist, by the path God provides us to escape each test and temptation. 

That way of escape is found in our knowledge of the word. By how much time we spend in it. It's why Paul uses examples of scripture to reason with the Corinthians, it's why he reminds us of the lessons from God's word. 

If you are facing sin, as thorns in your heart, and you want to be rid of it, or if you are engaging your lusts of the flesh or cares for the world, you will find relief and understanding from God, being in His word. It's the truth. The closer you get to Him the more clear your path becomes and the fewer snares and stumbling blocks there be.

Now Paul having established this, gets to the heart of the matter; eating sacrifices. 

As he's already said it is nothing to a Christian, knowing that the gods they are sacrificed to are just dead stone and wood. And knowing that all things are fine for us to eat as blessings from God as long as we acknowledge that. Again all things are lawful to us, but not all things edify others.

And just as we sit in common with our Brothers and sisters in Christ and are told, by Jesus, on those occasions that when we break the bread and drink the wine we are to remember him, Paul says that by being partakers in this, we shouldn't be partakers of the meat sacrificed unto idols. That although we could do it, there are reasons why we shouldn't.

He draws the analogy between the communion of saints, the Lord's supper, symbolic act when we come together and bless the food we consume together in God's name, in remembrance of Jesus, we are like the levitical priests who partook in the sacrifice of the altars in the Old Testament. And where Christ died once for all men, the sole propitiation for our sin, we partake in the food and drink God has provided us in remembrance of him and that sacrifice.

And if we so partake, how does it look to other people whether they not be saved yet, or maybe babes in Christ, and they see us sit down at the table of idolatry to partake in those sacrifices?

And so we do not exercise our Liberty at the expense of others. We do not seek our own comfort and fortune, we should seek others. We should be pleasing to all men in service of the gospel. We should do without rather than offend.

This aspect of Christianity, that we are both free from all sin in the blood of Christ, and the knowledge that most things people think of as sin is a sin of the heart, because what goes into the mouth doesn't defile us, but what comes out. And out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. It is our intent, it's the adultery we commit in our hearts. And the knowledge of that is the Liberty we have in Christ. But it is not a license to sin. Because if what we do in our Liberty hampers another person's ability to believe or come to faith, or makes them struggle with the loss of their own flesh which turn to sin when exercised by them, then we must do without.


This is what Paul means by pleasing others. This is what loving your neighbor entails. We are to be weak to those who are weak that they might be strong.

And unlike the Jew who is contrary to all men, we are to be agreeable with all men in God. That's not going along with earthly sins and lusts of the flesh, but it's being cognizant of how our actions on matters can be a snare or a stumbling block for others.

There are many who criticize this as being a Christcuck. That it is this a good natured Christian impulse to not offend that has left us defenseless against those who would subvert and destroy us. That this is a slave mentality of sorts.

But that's not what's being said here at all. When we act agreeable to others to win them to the gospel that is not the same as accepting wickedness in our presence or going along with these abominable people when they seek our destruction. 

Being mature enough in the word to understand the distinction is one of the goals of consuming the word daily. Rightly dividing the word of God.

BTW if I wasn't clear, there is no sacramental aspect to this, no Lord's supper as it were, it's the meals we have together with other believers we're to remember Jesus, with the breaking of the bread and the drinking of the juice of the vine, or anything else that we eat together. 

The idea of a real presence, or the Hocus pocus of a transubstantiation, is neither implied nor even hinted at. When two or three are gathered together in his name Jesus is there. He's always present. Our taking the time to remember him and thank God for the food, and acknowledging Christ's sacrifice for us it's just something we should do when we gather together.

I've gone into detail about the first half of this chapter before and made my opinion about the second half known even yesterday, but chapter 11 is one of contention for a lot of people.

The first half of the chapter, regarding "coverings" and shorn and shaven heads, is about hair and hair length. 

Women are to have long hair, not cropped short. Men are to have short hair. It is a shame for a man to have long hair just as it is an abomination for him to wear that which pertainith to a woman. 

Some take this that women must wear a veil or head scarf in church. It's such a non-issue that the doctrine is again one where if a woman thinks she should, it's of not a big enough deal to argue with her. Just like the eating of meat vs herb, it's up to those of us in grace to not quibble about what in the end is nothing. The primary doctrine about men and women being made of God, and the order of who is put over whom, with God as the head, is what's important here. 

As for the second half, I point that "as often as ye eat and drink" give blessing and remembrance of Jesus. Simple as. The Corinthians appear to have some showing up when they gather who are in fornication and there for their gluttony, not in the spirit of the Lord.

How various NT churches decide to engage in a Lord's supper together is really not important, so much the spirit by which it is done. Some do it in honor of the day leading to His death burial and resurrection. Some do it weekly. Some do it every meal they have at church or at home. I tend towards that, at least in the blessing and remembrance. 

What isn't good doctrine is placing more in the physical eating and drinking than the spiritual application. Or placing it as a source for grace and salvation. The Catholic version of this and the Protestant spin offs have at their heart the wrong motives spiritually, and so eat and drink damnation unto themselves. 

As Jesus says in **John 6**, *It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.*

Those that heard and didn't understand this were offended and many disciples left from following Christ, because they took spiritual things literally, just as the Jews condemned Him for these "dark sayings."

One of the problems with replacing the spiritual application of biblical principles and examples with rites and ceremony, carnal ordinances and diverse washings, and dietary laws and restrictions, is that, as the Bible demonstrates, these sacramental ordinances become a religion unto themselves. Just as the Old Testament which was a symbol of the Christ to come, eventually devolved into the phariseitical religion practiced in Jesus day, Christian churches who put all their emphasis in these vain traditions of men, the pomp and circumstance, lose the spiritual aspect of what it represents. And in doing so run the risk of running into a damnable heresy where their ability to perform a ritual or the frequency with which they do is tied directly into their salvation.

The lesson of God's word should be for us to understand the spiritual nature of our eternal lives rather than the limited and short nature of our corruptible flesh. 

All things in creation point to the spiritual lessons and are there for our edification and learning. All ritual and levitical practices were there to point us to the spiritual meaning. Meats for the belly and belly's for the meats, but our spirit and what is in our hearts is what we take with us when our flesh dies. That's where our sin is. And that's where our salvation is in the quickening of our inner man. 

As Jesus said it's not what goes into the mouth that defiles a man, but what comes out of it. A man who's committed adultery in his heart, feels hatred to another, has sinned just as much as those who commit the act. 

It's why Jesus spoke in parables because there are those among us who cannot live in the spirit, but only in the flesh and so they cannot receive the things of God.

Paul, comparing the assembly of saints to a body, Christ as the head (both literally, as ruler and figuratively in this anatomical allusion), gives examples of the talents expressed by believers towards the edification of that body. Building up the church of believers. 

The Corinthians, who we know were prideful, set at variance over who it was that led them to Christ, tolerating fornication among them, worse than the unsaved Gentiles, eating meats given to idols, profaning the ordinance of blessing the cup and breaking the bread when they gathered, believing heresies among them, and coveting, resenting and lording over each other when it came to spiritual gifts.

To some on the fence, it may help convict them in the Spirit. 

But for the unscrupulous, those wishing to gain that prominence by the "gifts of the Holy Ghost," healing becomes an opportunity. Taking advantage of the desperate and brokenhearted. Performing flashy "miracles" of "healing," for filthy lucre's sake. To gain power over others with false hope. 

I believe that these "faith healers" are all Reprobate. I believe they are blaspheming the holy Spirit when they claim they are performing miracles by His power. I think it is as wicked as those who claim to be mediums, talking to the dead to take advantage of mourning souls. 

And it is incredibly easy to fake. Whether by the placebo effect, plants in the audience, the gullibility of the crowd. Those wanting to be part of something miraculous. 

And sometimes, it might be through devils. 

And when the frauds are exposed, it brings a bad report of the genuine power of God among the heathen. It shakes the faith of some and becomes a stumbling block to others.

Remember, that regardless of anything else if you are saved and you have been blessed by the indwelling of the holy Spirit, you have been gifted with talents by God for the purpose of ministering to others and edifying the brethren. Use them. Not for yourself, not selfishly, but with a heart right towards Christ and to serve the purpose God graciously gave them to you. Pray for opportunities to bless others with them, in your family, church and community. Diligently seek the spiritual things of God, that He can better use you for His purpose.

Paul's more excellent way, as promised in chapter 12; charity. 

That regardless of the spiritual gifts we all have, or the special gift of the Holy Ghost some in those days were blessed with, it is the unfeigned love, given for no personal gain, but genuine and selfless, that is above all else, and is a faint reflection of the love God showed us by giving His Son that we may be saved, and the love Jesus showed us while we were still sinners, to give His life for us, and taste death and Hell for our transgressions.

We usually use the basic definition of charity to mean giving something away to help others, alms. And that certainly can be a form of expression for charity, but it is not itself charity as we see in verse 3. 

Paul defines it by what it's not or what qualities it has. And its qualities are those of the love, the charity of God shown towards us, that Jesus teaches us in His sermons.

So many do so much as a form of "charity" but for selfish purpose, or taking pride or accolades for it. Storing up hay and stubble without ever gaining rewards for it, because they do it in the wrong Spirit. 

IMO, works done to "earn" or keep salvation being the most selfish of all, and the least charitable. 

This chapter also parallels with James 2, and the "faith without works is dead, being alone" lesson. It's the true meaning. We may have faith enough to move mountains, as Paul says here, but if we have not charity it profits no one. 

When the Kingdom is here and established in Christ's reign, and then when we know all things and are as an adult to a child, the mysteries all solved, charity will remain, even as all our other things we placed importance in fade.

We need to read the Bible in full context. Chapters and verses are there to make navigation of the word easier, but these are not stand alone concepts, but entire thoughts that span entire books. 

If we look back at chapter 12, we see how Paul is leading to the lesson of charity:

*That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another. And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it.*

*Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular. And God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues.*

*Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers? are all workers of miracles?*

*Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues? do all interpret? But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way*

You see the charity is caring for the others in the church, sorrow for each members' sorrow, and joy for their individual success. Not coveting the gifts each may have. Edifying one another. 

In Chapter 14 we will see that it is the gift of tongues driving much of the contention here, given its prominence in Paul's epistle. Thus if someone preaches in tongues, even with the language of angels, they become as sounding brass and tinkling cymbals, it's useless without charity. 

We can know all things in scripture, and all knowledge can be show us, and of we aren't edifying others and given to love people, it's for nothing. It's the motive not the gift.

Speaking in tongues is described in Acts as the miracle of the disciples present on Pentecost, going out to the crowds of the feast in Jerusalem, and giving the gospel to those gathered from every nation in their own tongues. Their languages. 

Judeans and Samaritans, who knew Aramaic, Greek. Hebrew, suddenly were speaking Parthian, and Mede, and Elamite, and Mesopotamian, and Phrygian, and Pamphylian, Egyptian, and Libyan and Latin, and a host of other languages, of all the scattered Israelites and others, gathered there that day. Prophesying the word of God and preaching the risen Christ.

This gift of the Holy Ghost continued in the early church, as it grew and served as a sign that brought the gospel to every nation, tongue and kindred. The God who had divided the nations and confused the languages in Babel, uniting them through the miraculous gifts of speaking in, and as we see in Corinthians, understanding or interpretation. Allowing them to be understood and to understand, that the gospel would be preached. 

Even today, absent miracles but by the same grace, the same gift is given many who are quick studies in understanding languages, and given to allow the furtherance of the Gospel, bringing many to Christ. 

The men in the church of Corinth, blessed with the more suspense gift, were puffed up, showing off, in the church. This was not only causing contention within the church, but as Paul says, gave a bad report to those without, that they were all babbling madmen. He admonishes them in Chapter 13 to seek rather Charity, the unfeigned and gracious love of others. Their profit and welfare. Their edification. Not our own. 

And in the case of being able to speak in a tongue foreign to others, it serves no one but the speaker. 

*Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal...For he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him; howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries. But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort. He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church.*

This is the sum of what Paul is teaching. He uses the idea that *even if* he were to speak in the language of angels, if no one understands it, it is useless, even to the speaker. Paul is not saying that they *are* speaking the language of angels. It is a hypothetical exaggeration given for instruction. 

That some make an entire doctrine from that goes to show that those who wrest with scripture do so to their own destruction, because in the same scripture lays the context and the truth.

Pride and wanting to seem more spiritual, more holy, more blessed by God, in the eyes of others, feeds the Pentecostal movement and its foolish doctrines of speaking in tongues, the inane babblings of fools. 

Of all the spiritual gifts, it's the easiest to fake. And when everyone present is afraid to call it out, they not only enable and encourage it, they'll even have some "interpreters" sharing the delusion and claiming they can understand the other person. 

Since it is not any recognizable language, and because the noises being made have no bearing of prophecy, because they're not preaching the word of God but their own infantile speech, edifying no one, It is in direct conflict with what Paul is teaching here in 1st Corinthians. 

It's to no one's benefit but the speaker. There's no charity in it, only pride and dishonesty.

It is always amazing to me that the strong delusion people are under when they twist a small portion of scripture to serve their heresies, manages to fool others and bring them into the same delusion. 

*But the natural man receiveth, not the spiritual  things of God for they are spiritually discerned.* And because they seek after the error of Simon the sorcerer, they don't know the spiritual things of God. They're blinded to them. 

In chapter 3, Paul had already chastened the church for being carnal in regards to these gifts; *For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal.* That's the attitude they had was not spiritual, after the manner of God. He calls them children. And not in an endearing way. And understand he's speaking to people who actually possess these gifts. People who are actually saved by the Gospel through faith by grace. How much worse are these that fake it in order to seem spiritual? How much worse are they who, not being saved, not understanding the gospel, having faith in themselves instead of faith in Christ Jesus? 

Simon, the sorcerer was saved. He took rebuke when Peter gave it. We see in the second epistle to the Corinthians that they too were corrected by Paul's letter. 

One of the signs of a saved person is their ability to be corrected from scripture, by the word of God, because the Spirit that inspired it and the Spirit that indwells us are in harmony, being one. God is not the author of confusion. But you'll find that regardless of what you show them, Pentecostals and Charismatics will refuse to repent of their belief. They will double down. They will accuse you of not being faithful for trying to pop the bubble of their delusion.

Paul continues his teaching to the Corinthians on spiritual gifts, having put in place the doctrine that we shouldn't covet and envy those who have received talents to the edification of the church that differ from ours, that all in the body serve the same head, that head being Jesus and through Him, the Father. Then making the case that being charitable, the love for others that God expressed to us, and Christ demonstrated on the cross, then we've a better gift than even those the Holy Ghost bestowed on many in this time. Specifically the ability to speak and understand foreign tongues, or languages. 

The Bible is clear that this is the meaning. Not the nonsense gibberish of the pentecostal heathen. No where in the Bible does the term "speaking in tongues" exist (unless you read one of the perverted modern versions that sow false doctrine with confusion so often). 

This gift is rather the use of those who can interpret or prophesy scripture to those who speak another tongue. 

Like the Apostles and disciples on Pentecost, who spoke the Gospel to those pilgrims from all over the world, in Jerusalem for the feast. They spoke to understanding, and it amazed the crowd and acted as a sign, bringing thousands to belief as they heard the word of God in their native language. 

Prophecy in the Bible is the preaching of scripture, and bringing the relevance of the word of God to the people. It is giving the Gospel to the unbelieving. It is teaching the law. It is relevant preaching to the building up of the church. It is the advice of proverbs taught at a mother's knee. It is the exhorting of the pulpit to the flock. 

And if any of this be done in a language none of the hearers understand, as Paul says in chapter 13, it is of *sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.*

This goes for false religion that gives entire services in a dead language. It is to no one's edification but the speaker. 

This goes for the "You must return to the Hebrew! You must return to the Greek! God's word is impossible to understand in English!" nonsense of puffed up "scholars" who take pride in their private interpretation and sowing confusion among the people to show how learned they are. 

This goes to the Ruckmanites who take the preservation of the Word in the KJV to be a further revelation that is more perfect than the Greek and Hebrew, which is nonsense. 

Paul says that if you have a gift of knowing a language that can be used for interpretation to the person being reached with the Gospel then use it, but not to show off to the believers who cannot understand it, which seems the case in Corinth. 

As Pentecost showed us, God's word is powerful in any language, and in every tongue God, who is not the author of confusion can make His word known. 

Verse 26 he wonders how it is so many in Corinth are puffed up by claims of their own doctrines and revelations and psalms, and strange tongues, etc. They apparently were many among them who, in covetousness and pride were deceitfully inventing whole doctrines and aping gifts they did not have, or bragging about gifts they were given and wasting them. 

As for tongues, today we have the inspired Word of God, preserved by the Spirit, in English in the KJV. And we should be grateful that we need no one to tell us it's lingual meaning, as every word and term is defined in itself. There is no need to appeal to a concordance or other work of an unsaved man to explain to us the plain meaning of His scripture.

Paul notes, and it appears to be an issue in Corinth, that women in the church are to remain silent, so as to no usurp the authority of their husbands, and to protect the hierarchy God created, as enumerated in Chapter 11. This is not to say women cannot prophecy at all. They are called to teach scripture to their children, to convert their unbelieving husbands with their chaste conversation. We have multiple examples of women giving the Gospel and being active in spreading the word. 

But in church, under the leadership of a man of God, the pastor, who has very specific qualifications listed in the pastoral epistles, they are to learn in silence, and in their questions to turn to their authority, their husbands or fathers, first. 

As Paul had previously mentioned, each member of the body is important to the goal of the whole, and the "more important" parts shouldn't be puffed up, as they have reliance on the "uncomely" parts that serve the same head. 

It isn't the role but the goal.

And we each have a responsibility to that larger goal, giving God the glory and increase of His harvest. And all who serve that goal shouldn't take pride in their role but humble themselves, which is the larger theme of this letter to Corinth.

Paul writes his second epistle to the church at Corinth, approximately a year following the first. As we know from Acts, his plan to go to them was derailed, slightly and instead, elders of the church went to him as he traveled, and so he writes with some apology in his greeting. That the troubles he came to in his travels that prevented him from going to them, were actually blessings. 

He acknowledges the truth of the Gospel is in them, as it is in him, and that of the hope of eternal life we also receive the comfort of God in the Holy Spirit. 

The message, that in our tribulations and troubles, we have comfort, given by God's grace, and in that comfort, the ability to give the same comfort with grace an understanding to others in need. Thus, his tribulation and that which the churches experience are a gift, that gives us consolation and salvation from trouble, that we may provide the same to others. 

He reminds them that if our faith in God is to the hope of the resurrection and eternal life, then there's nothing we can't place on God to deliver for us. 

This is the goal of a Christian life, to see not only riches and good fortune as blessings, but troubles and tribulations even unto death, as giving glory to God.

The gift of prayer for others is a gift that is repaid with thanks in prayer, towards God, "Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts." 

We are sealed unto the day of judgment, and the ernest, or the down payment on the promise of eternal life, is the Spirit living within our hearts. And so with this knowledge, the testimony of our faith living within us, we can trust in God. His promises are 'yea, yea.'

It's a beautiful introduction and sober reminder that in God, all things are possible and we needn't be troubled by anything in this world, because in Christ we have already overcome it.

The final line in chapter 1, regarding the apostle and the evangelists who have ministered to the churches throughout the region, and specifically to Corinth not being in dominion over the believers there, but helpers, because they are established and stand by their own faith as individuals. Their churches are independent as well. They may receive reproach or guiding, but it's not to dictate over them who are equal in the faith, members of the same body with Christ at its head.

Quick sidenote to this and the series of readings and studies we are undertaking; I have all but stopped noting when the Gospel of faith alone and grace alone is mentioned, because it is nearly every chapter and it is inarguable at this point for those who come here daily. Paul doesn't write to them about being stablished in their works, or ceremonies, or how willing they are to turn from their sins, but by the faith they believed shared by those who ministered unto them.

Chapter 2 continues Paul's introduction, speaking now as to why he hadn't come to them, *with a rod,* as promised in his first epistle to them, saying he decided in part to not come to them "in heaviness" to grieve them. 

As we saw in 1 Corinthians, Paul had laid into them pretty hard, especially in chapter 5 regarding one member and his wicked fornication. 

Paul says to them that he considers them his sons in Christ, having asked them to follow him as a father who brought them to the gospel, and like a father, scourging those he loves, Paul says his chastisement was necessary but he doesn't want them to mistake it for anything other than his love of them. 

He says in verse 5 that it wasn't personal. He's not doing this out of hurt feelings.

And likewise, as he's showing kindness to those he'd chastised, he says to them that they should be forgiving to those in the church that they punished as he'd called for, and they having repented, be welcomed back and comforted that they not fall back into sin.

We are never to tolerate or enable other Christians sins, especially those that lead to church discipline, but when a Christian makes a sincere turn around, we are to be gracious like God is with us, daily. Forgiveness of trespasses. 

Paul says if they've forgiven some their sin and brought them back from being backslidden, it's good enough for him, because it is good enough for Christ. 

This may be specifically the man who was sleeping with his step-mother, but it reads as a more general item. We should be happy to forgive and forget, just as eagerly as we are to condemn and rebuke. 

As a parent treats their child, which is how Paul looks at those he's won to Christ, this is an incredibly important concept to master. How we love our children, including how we discipline and forgive, is an imprint in their minds of how God works, and by showing firm hand, but loving kindness and forgiveness, the same as He shows us, we are demonstrating to them His love and grace. 

When we are resentful, angry, taking it personally and overcharging them, failing to forgive and forget, they may *be swallowed up with much sorrow.* It is how Satan gains an advantage in their lives. 

Many parents create a barter system in place of love, where everything is transactional. They may forgive but not forget, throwing past behavior at their child, holding it against them. Many parents don't even realize they are doing it. This behavior builds within a child the seeds for a works-based relationship with God, and can cause all sorts of problems in their lives. Never being "good enough." Never having healthy relationships with others. Never really understanding the charitable love and grace we have in hope through Christ Jesus. Maybe even bringing them to reprobation in the end, bitter against you and so bitter against God.

Paul shifts back to his delay of his promised visit, and talks of his going into Macedonia to give the Gospel. 

Verse 15 and 16 notes that to those who believe, the sincerely preached gospel by a saved Christian is a sweet smell, the savior of life, but to those perishing, they smell only the death that their sin is bringing them. This is the division Christ brings. This is the reason for their hating us in His name.

One aspect of spreading the Gospel that most miss, and misunderstand, is that as many receive it, even more reject it, and in doing so, eventually run the risk of reprobation. Soul winning can and does create reprobates, and that is intended by God. Every hearing is a seed sown, or watered, and could be what leads to harvest. Paul has begun this letter to Corinth far less hostile than the last. His reproach cooler. 

His reframing of the question of letters of commendation to one of the Spirit and the heart of the persons saved by his or those he sent's ministry, that the believers' own salvation and behavior are the real epistles of the authority Paul and the others have is softer, and yet more biting. 

He spins from this to the idea of the letters of the law, of the old testament, being what condemned us, knowledge of the law bringing with it sin, which the Bible defines as transgression of the law (**1 John 3:4**), but in the Spirit is Liberty, the eternal life given in the new testament. 

This becomes a major theme for Paul in other epistles, the use of the law by God as a schoolmaster, bringing us to sure knowledge of our transgressions and death from sin, and the liberty found in Christ, which is more glorious than even the hand of God engraving stone and giving it to Moses. 

The veil Moses wore to protect the Hebrews in the wilderness from the lingering glory of God reflected in his face becomes a metaphor for the veil keeping the glory of God, through Christ, from the hearts of the Jew. 

But, with the veil taken away by belief on Christ, we see the glory manifest, and in that image, have it reflect in our own faces, the way it did to Moses, but unhidden and used to show others our faith that they might believe.

Up until this point, Paul has made a conscious effort to be kinder and gentler in this second epistle to Corinth. Writing in response to a request of some sort of letters of commendation for the workers in Christ coming to collect alms from them, and set the church there right, especially after the problems they had with fornication and other sin in the assembly the year before. 

First Corinthians being harsh, 2nd is far more friendly, as Paul has laid out the reasons why the very idea of letters of approval from men towards others, giving bona fides, is foolish given they are all servants of Christ in the same faith and to the same ends of edifying the believers and spreading the gospel. 

But now, here in chapter 10, Paul turns harshly towards those who may, at this point of reading his epistle, still have doubts of him, his authority, the authority of those sent, and of the shared understanding of salvation in Christ. 

Rhetorically, he destroys them.

He says that he's come to them in meekness, like Christ, and that some may judge him as unimposing physically, compared to the boldness he showed in his first epistle. That they are judging him as if he were just some unsaved person, and not by the authority of the gifts he has received or as the father of their salvation that he was, bringing them the Gospel. 

That he could boast more of this, and not be ashamed in the boasting. He could come with a rod, and in spiritual gifts, destroy the nay sayers, despite being weak in the body and his manner of speech. 

He's telling them they are lucky he isn't coming there to crack heads, because whatever they think, he has the power to. 

He adds some cutting lines about those who measure themselves with themselves, to commend themselves being "*not wise*." Then in a stinging rebuke, cleverly worded to shoot down those unwise, reminds them again of his position in bringing them the Gospel while insinuating that the boastful seeking the letters of commendation from Paul are puffed up over what was his work. Labors of another. 

He ends reminding again it is being approved by God that matters, not of other men and certainly not of ourselves. 

It is worth reading through a couple times, out loud if you can, because the grammar is dense in places and can be confusing in print. There is no doubt the power of the Spirit is in these writings.

"White knuckle sobriety" describes one who gives up alcohol or other addiction, but doesn't seek support, preferring to go it alone, on their own plan. Lacking guidelines, guidance and accountability it generally is a recipe for relapse. The individual is just using pure willpower to stay sober. It is like they are just hanging on, waiting for the ride to end, hence "white knuckles."

As I understand it, the difference between "white knuckle" sobriety and a "dry drunk" is subtle; both are relying on themselves to maintain sobriety, but the "dry drunk" does nothing else to change the underlying behavior or causes that feed their addiction, while the white-knuckler may take steps, as near as his own understanding allows, to make some changes in their life. Some of which may be good ideas if part of a well-supported recovery, some old wives tales or misled by bad advice found online, from friends, media, self-help books, etc..., some just plain rationalizing. 

The point is that outside of proper support and absent real accountability, they are usually going to fail, often harder than they were before the futile effort. 

If I have it wrong or am missing anything, forgive me. My point isn't about addiction, but the tendency to white-knuckle when someone is looking to make a positive change in their life. 

For many Christians, or those who are seeking to be Christian, both believers and those believing in vain, they are living what can only be described as "white-knuckle Christianity." 

They may be babes in Christ, who heard the Gospel preached and believed on the Lord, but never followed up on it by finding a church, getting into the Bible, learning how to walk in the Spirit. 

They might be longtime casual Christians who once were super zealous, but as the newness wore off and the cares of the world overtook them, they backslid into old habits and even new sins.

They are white knuckling without a church. Without real life brethren to hold them accountable. Without guidance from older and more mature Christians that know them personally, and have an interest in their life.

Leading captivity captive. Freeing those in bonds only to bind that which had captured them. Jesus Christ, fulfilling the promise of God. Paul draws the parallel with **Psalm 68**, David prophesying the Christ to come and our salvation. 

**Ephesians 4** is a beautiful devotional of the love we have received and should magnify with one another. 

That as Jesus both descended into Hell for 3 days and nights, to leave captivity captive, ascending to Heaven with our liberty from death, the keys of Hell, to rule all things. 

We are all one body, joined with one faith, bought with the same price, granted the same liberty, a gift given by the same grace, sinners made righteous in Christ, quickened and sealed by the Spirit. Adopted by the Father, forever, amen.

And so with that unity of faith, in the knowledge of the Son of God, *That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive; But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ.*

And so we should walk in that truth, live the love we have received. Not as others in the world who are captive by the *vanity of their mind*. The foolish doctrines of man. The ignorance that comes from *the blindness of their heart*. Not walking as the reprobate does, *being past feeling,* given over to *lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness.*

In grace, through Jesus, we have a new man, created by the Spirit, and that Spirit convicts us in our sin, where the reprobate is past feeling, we are made all the more sensitive to God's will, a new man made with righteousness. 

And so Paul encourages we put off lying, wrath, stealing, envy, corrupt communication, that is speech that tears down rather than edifying others. Speech that puts blame on us and hinders others faith, we shouldn't engage in. 

So, with our conscience quickened, *grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.*

Note the doctrines here, that unity of faith into the body, where Christ is the head. That we are sealed by the Spirit, given eternal life, testified by the new man within us, that we may know and have confidence in our trust in God. This is the promise of salvation. 

Denominations that teach you can lose your salvation, that you must earn it, that only they can give it, that they are the head and the body, teaching the vanity of the mind and tossing their members to and fro with every changing wind of doctrine, rather than standing fast upon the unmoving rock of the Word...these false churches cannot save. They are the bondsmen, keeping people in chains.

Some take the admonition against corrupt communication to be simply not to use vulgarity, lewdness or potty talk, but while all those things *can be* the type of corrupt communication Paul's writing about, it isn't what he means. In this context, he's regarding the things we say in wrath and anger, envy, strife, backbiting, tale bearing, railing, false accusations, etc. 

Not the words used, as if a naughty word has power to corrupt, but the means and meaning of what's being said. 

Is it edifying? Does it leave you blameless to share the good news without embarrassment or hypocrisy?

That's the meaning, and while a cuss word can be something that can be corrupting in this context, it isn't always and discernment should be given. Jesus wasn't using corrupt communication when he said "Raca." When scripture says "ass," or "pisseth."  When Song of Solomon gets a little spicy. 

Overly legalistic types lose their mind at a stray vulgarity while accepting hypocrisy, backbiting and railing, being holier than thou.

Finally, consider that we are to edify, building up the body that is Christ's, *speaking the truth in love,* that they *may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ.*

Fellow believers are in various stages of this work, babes in Christ to those more sanctified by time and experience. The backslidden and the just. Those of incredible faith, born out of tribulations we can't imagine, others struggling in tribulation right now. And our own place in that journey, in our Christian walk. 

We should be cognizant of this, with the same mercy and grace and love that we have received (unmerited as we are sinners), and show the same to others where we can. Being understanding. Charitable. The true kindness, not as the world measures kindness, with wickedness, enabling and justifying evil as good, but speaking the truth of God in love.

Paul in a few short paragraphs gives God's will for us that He's adopted. It isn't asking much, considering the gift we've been given. But the flesh is weak and wars against our spirit. Still we should strive for this bare minimum.

The final chapter of Ephesians, Paul continues to build on the idea that we are not to despise government, the hierarchies put in place by God, but to honor and respect them, even when they are cruel to us. For we aren't theirs, but God's and what we do in our labors is His. 

Be it a husband, a mother, a child, a master or a servant, a king or a subject. If they aren't demanding we sin, truly sin in the despising of God, worship of idols or the blasphemy of the Spirit, and the like, we should in all good conscience work that which we can do, upright. This bothers many. 

"How can I obey and serve a cruel and ungodly master? A wicked husband? Dishonorable parents? A beast-system state?" The Bible tells us with faith, meekness, serving God and by our actions, convert the lost. 

I find that those that bristle the most at this were raised without proper fear and respect for their parents, due to whatever reason, although mostly having the rod spared or worse, used in anger, bringing their children to wrath. And as the relationship with the father goes, so to becomes their relationship with all superiors, and in the end, their relationship with God.

We should, as Christians, seek to be blameless. Be the hardest worker at your job. Be the most honest. Take the least advantage and support and uplift others, not being a respecter of persons. Diligent and happy. Having faith in God who rewards us, Paul says, *Knowing that whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord, whether he be bond or free.*

This is not weakness, but strength. For the powers that be have authority from God, be they wicked or just, those who bear the sword do it to the fear of the unrighteous.

However many works-based false teachers use the "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling" line to teach that you cannot be assured salvation, and that we must do works to be saved. *For your fellowship in the gospel from the first day until now;*

He has confidence in them, that they partake in the same grace that saved him. This is only conditioned on their having fellowship in the same Gospel he preached to them, not on their works, and with not doubt that God works in them. 

It is another case of reading the whole of scripture and comparing it with itself, saving us from bad doctrine.

Paul argues to these Gentiles, that if birth, circumcision and zeal for the law saved anyone, it would be Paul, but he counts all his own "righteousness" as dung, so that he may gain Christ. 

He warns to beware the dogs, reprobates sneaking in and judaizing churches, subverting houses, crept in unawares. Evil workers. They of the circumcision. Paul says

*3 And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel, with Clement also, and with other my fellowlabourers, whose names are in the book of life.*

*4 Rejoice in the Lord always: and again I say, Rejoice.*

*5 Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand.*

*6 Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.*

*7 And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.*

*8 Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.*

*9 Those things, which ye have both learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me, do: and the God of peace shall be with you.*

*10 But I rejoiced in the Lord greatly, that now at the last your care of me hath flourished again; wherein ye were also careful, but ye lacked opportunity.*

*11 Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.*

*12 I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.*

*13 I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.*

*14 Notwithstanding ye have well done, that ye did communicate with my affliction.*

*15 Now ye Philippians know also, that in the beginning of the gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church communicated with me as concerning giving and receiving, but ye only.*

*16 For even in Thessalonica ye sent once and again unto my necessity.*

*17 Not because I desire a gift: but I desire fruit that may abound to your account.*

*18 But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God.*

*19 But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus.*

*20 Now unto God and our Father be glory for ever and ever. Amen.*

*21 Salute every saint in Christ Jesus. The brethren which are with me greet you.*

*22 All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household.*

*23 The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.*

Paul ends what is one of the most beautifully written thank you notes of all time. Full of exhortation and doctrine, blessings and thanks. Lessons for how to live for God and be at peace in Christ. 

*Rejoice in the Lord always: and I say again rejoice.Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand. Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.*

This should be the default state of your Christian life. Joy, not worrying and fearful for the cares of this world but trusting, in prayer and supplication to the Lord, in thanksgiving for the blessings and the tribulation by which the Spirit strengthens us. Having the peace with God that comes from being Christ's. 

If your walk isn't this, if troubles of the world weigh you down to bitterness, anger, resentment, envy and strife, then know it doesn't have to be this way. Walk less in the flesh and more in the spirit. In daily prayer, scripture reading, singing songs of praise and the psalms. Knowing with confidence your blessed assurance, that *God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus.*

Think upon things of virtue, honesty, pure, true. Meditate on the law of God, and you will learn to praise Him and be content with whatever state you find yourself in. Abased or abounding. Satisfied with what you have, thankful to God that you have it. Knowing for certain in faith that you can do all things through Christ which strengthens us. Living faith to faith. 

And be fruitful, not as the world measures in wealth and status, but in souls won by your faithful service to God, reached by His word, a path lit by the light of your example.

For me, in my journey here, it was fear and concerns of this world that led me consistently to misery, anger and resentment. The Bible warns us against this inclination of man, towards faith in all things. And in the paradox of the wisdom of God, it is accepting on faith that these things don't matter, where you will see the most change. That you're willing to count for loss but gain in Christ are the areas God will bless you the most abundantly. 

Fear for family, work, relationships with others...all the trauma and drama of this world, all things work for good when you love God and trust Him, thankful regardless of outcome. Just have to let go. 

The more you do, the more you stay in the word and do what your supposed to, without worry or fear or entitled expectations of what you "deserve" the more you will find you get what you need. And the more you bring people you love to the same peace, that passes all understanding, that comes from the grace God shows His children.

Paul thanks them again for what was a care package the Philippians took it upon themselves to send him. He pours out thanks and praise to them, for thinking of him in his bondage, under house arrest in Rome. He gets in one last clever aside to show how even in duress, all things work for good. 

*All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household.* 

A sly nod to the will of God working through our tribulation to bring others to Him, even to the most powerful in an empire, even by the most lowly of us, in chains.

I've heard pastors preach sermons on Philippians that can be summed up, beautifully, that the primary message of the epistle is joy.

 Rejoicing in our salvation. The joy of knowing Jesus. The Joy with which we should live our lives. Rejoicing for the Lord. It's why it's one of my favorite books of the Bible, and hopefully that message of joy comes through in your reading of it.

*According to my earnest expectation and my hope, that in nothing I shall be ashamed, but that with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.*

*Yea, and if I be offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I joy, and rejoice with you all.*

In prison, literally chained to a centurion in Rome, uncertain of his future but caring not for his life, (for to be absent the body is to be present with the Lord) and his hope, Paul's ernest expectation, which is, by definition what faith is. What hope is. An earnest expectation, we sincerely expect this to happen, that God who cannot lie has promised our salvation and eternal life through faith in His Son Jesus Christ. And in that knowledge, that belief, Paul says whether it be his life or death, whether he sees the Philippians again or not, that he will have joy, and rejoice. 

Amen. Amen.

Here in the opening of Paul's letter to the saints at Colosse, we have one of the most eloquent descriptions of who Jesus is and our shared faith in Him.

Note again, Paul prays for God's grace, and the peace that comes from it for those reading. It is only possible to have peace by having peace with God, and that peace is only possible by being partakers of His grace. And all knowledge and wisdom of God's word comes from Him, and those sincerely seeking it. Paul wishes all this that the Colossians may continue being fruitful, sharing the faith and winning more to the body of the church, which is Christ's. Preached to every creature. 

Strengthened with His glorious power, that we may endure all things with longsuffering and patience and joy. Delivered with His blood. Redeemed by Him. Partakers of the inheritance of the light, saved from the darkness. Translated into the Kingdom of Heaven. 

(This is the biblical meaning of being translated in regards to our spiritual state, and the Kingdom. It is not the bodily assumption of our corruptible flesh, as some presume, but a change of our spirit, quickened by the Holy Ghost, made acceptable by the blood)

Jesus is the express image of God the Father, and made through Jesus, all that has been created is His, who was before all things. Who is the first fruits of the resurrection, so that He may have preeminence in even that, making peace with God through the cross, reconciling all things. 

And for us who are grounded and settled to this Gospel of reconciliation: 

*And you, that were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled. In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight.*

We who were dead in sin, enemies of God through our wicked works, made unblameable and unreproveable before God, reconciled with the Father by the Son. Our sins forever forgiven. 

And Paul made a minister unto the Gentiles, suffering in the flesh for the Gospel's sake, to edify, build up, the body which is the congregation of believers, serving the head which is Christ Jesus. Rejoicing in this suffering, Paul encourages us with this joy, that we may preach to every man and win every man to the same peace we have through grace in Christ.

Paul continues his greeting to the churches in Colosse, including a shout out to the early church in Laodicea, churches he himself didn't establish in person, as the Gospel has been preached throughout the world, faith to faith, to the Gentiles, beyond even Paul's direct ministry. 

All believers, members of the body of which Jesus is the head, united in spirit, in the joy of peace with God through grace and faith, sharing the goal of bringing increase, the harvest of fruit of righteousness, winning souls to Christ with the Gospel of reconciliation. Bringing forth fruit meet for repentance. Turning those that heard and believe towards God. 

We see in epistle after epistle, in the Acts of the apostles, in Jesus' own ministry, and His sending of disciples out, two by two into the highways and hedges. We see it in John the Baptist's preaching in the wilderness. It is faith shared and souls won. To God the increase. 

The so called holy men, vipers chastised by John and Jesus Himself, Peter and Paul, were unable to bring forth this fruit, to lead believers to Christ. 

Neither can false prophets, and yet they are here in Colosse as they were in Galatia, Ephesus, in the Judean wilderness, as Satan himself, trying to lead the churches astray, causing others to sin, and damning souls with their doctrines of works. 

It's the same play as Satan in the desert with Christ. We see it today. They beguile us with enticing words, to *spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.*

Paul is again writing to warn the churches of the Judaizers, who were demanding a return to Hebrew roots by the newly grafted Gentiles, adherence to the Law, the carnal ordinances and the circumcision of the flesh. The acts and works and vain traditions of men, dietary laws, esteeming days over others, all done away with in Christ as they were a foreshadowing of Him. 

This is told to us, over and over again, because it is Satan's main play against us. Giant red flags that should warn us of false preachers who creep in among us to lead some astray. It is the bulk of the NT outside the Gospel by which we are saved for a reason. Even moreso than instruction against sin, Paul and James and Peter and Jude write to warn the churches to avoid these doctrines of men and appeal to the flesh, and remind us we are of a spiritual circumcision.

Paul's focus shifts to now-familiar themes. If we be saved, children of light, then seek the things of Heaven. The word of God. The glory of Jesus. The resurrection to come and being raptured, caught up, into the clouds with Him in glory. 

For this cause, we should mortify our members against sin of the flesh, even as Jesus preached (later in today's Matthew study), "if an eye offend thee, pluck it out." We who are heirs keep our bodies in submission and our thoughts to what's pure, good and holy. 

Lusts of the flesh, lust, which is the longing for what's not yours, worshiping in the Idolatry of covetousness. As it is written, in **James 4**:

*From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members? Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not. Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.* 

These sins are the reason for God's wrath upon the children of disobedience to the Gospel, but we are children of the light, the shining city in the hill. The light we have inside is a reflection and magnifying of the love God shines on us, so don't hide it, but hold it high for all to see that they might be partakers with us. Putting off anger, wrath,Malice, blasphemy, filthy conversation, the behavior of the unsaved that acts as a bushel to hide our light and turn some away from the truth within us. 

We put on the new man, have honest dealings with one another ("Let your yea be yea, and your nay, nay" - also Matt 5), doing everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, in thanks to God the Father by Christ's name. 

And if we are in the new man, and we have put away the lusts of the flesh, if we mortify our members, having honest dealings with one another, edifying with songs of praise and teaching the doctrines of God in psalms, our light shining as a guide to the truth for others to follow, then what does this look like?

Wives submitting to their husbands, husbands loving their wives, children honoring their parents, fathers judging their children righteously,not in wrath, not frustrating them, but as God the Father has loved you. 

And, at work? Heartily and without malice or anger, do what you're asked, because we work for God, already rewarded with the kingdom of which we are heirs. Diligently and honestly setting out to complete what is required of you, with joy and a meek spirit and the confidence of your salvation. 

Those who do wrong will have their reward, just as you will for your faithful service. God is not a respecter of persons, and master or boss or elected leader, all alike will face His wrath for their transgressions. That's not on us to determine. It is on us to account for ourselves in all that we do, because we do it in Jesus' name.  

Many bristle at this. Be the best husband, wife, child, employee, neighbor, regardless of whatever else. Being blameless. Not dimming the reflection of the light that you walk in. *If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.*

So many struggle with this concept. Some false prophets and natural men claim that this submission to authority and the powers that be, given by God, as some sort of perversion by Paul, but we see it again in **Matthew 5**, preached by Jesus in the beatitudes. Paul, having laid out his instruction to Timothy, and his role in establishment of churches of the Ephesians, and giving some basic commands in that regard, and a warning against reprobate false prophets, moves therefore to spell out a broader doctrine that applies to all Christians. It is how to develop the men to have the temperament that will produce those fit for the office and called to that ministry, and how to edify the church, bringing in more believers. 

The first point, praying for all men, supplications, or asking of God for favor, thanksgiving for the blessings He bestows, intercessions that the Spirit may work to bring about outcomes that give glory to God. 

This is our instruction for the rulers of this world as much as the beggars, that we may live peaceably. Not given to fear or wrath. This causes many to bristle, but as much as possible we are to live peaceably and without offense, with all men, so we may in all godliness and honesty, bring others to the truth. 

*For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour; Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;*

We are to be a testimony to the truth of this. That our prayers and faith be lived out in a way that brings others to this truth. Doubt and wrath show a lack of faith and offends others from the truth. Simple as. 


The spiralling people do when it comes to the cares of this world, or their fearful outbursts show a lack of faith in the same God who they are supposed to be magnifying and giving glory to, as witness to others. 

Note that Jesus is our sole mediator for intercession with God. Not spirits of men. Not idols or preists. When we pray for others it is asking Jesus to intercede, God in His name to bless, the holy Spirit to give comfort. 

Also, the Bible says the will of God our savior that ALL MEN come to believe. It isn't a select few as Calvinism would claim, and it is our calling to help make God's will manifest. 

So men should be holy, in prayer, without fear, peaceable, without doubt and wrath. Praying for all men to come to the truth, even for the government that God may grant us peace, allowing more to be saved. 

In a similar manner, women have a role as well. Just as men who are unruly and fearful offer a bad testimony so to do women who dress immodestly, who are ostentatious in their appearance. Not only because of the obvious temptations, but as speaking to their character as Godly women. The two admonitions, one for men and one for women, have the same root context. That we show outward signs of the faith that is saved us to better bring others to salvation. 

It's often the men who are most fearful and wrathful, who have the loudest voice in pointing out to women not to dress shamefully. In this regard they are hypocrites. Women should do that which is pleasing to God, but so should men, we have an equal role in winning souls to Christ. 

Wear those rolls differ, the Bible says women aren't to teach, because, like eve, they are prone to being deceived regarding God's word. This is just the truth of it, and it is a sentiment found throughout the Epistles, and borne out by experience. This is not to excuse Adam and condemn eve, but rather just clarifying rules and natural tendencies to better demonstrate God's will. 

Paul goes on to say that it is in bearing children, and raising them up in a Godly way, that women have the greater influence than men leading the church. That they are saved, preserved and protected, by the generations of children that they bring into the world and give witness to God to, that they may be His. 

Too many cherry pick these verses and create an artificial men versus women divide. It is about roles and responsibilities, understanding there are differences between men and women. And we have different deficiencies and negative tendencies that can trip us up in our walk with God.
But we should take comfort that when we follow God's will, we have the opportunity to bring Him glory just the same.

There are two groups of people God has a special place for, and asks us to be protectors and caretakers of; widows and orphans. 

This biblical appeal actually became a means by which many fraternal orders, Masonic lodges and other less than godly organizations worked a grift. Collecting donations for the "widows and orphans fund" became a euphemism for this kind of shakedown charity by the 20th Century. The idea itself synonymous with corruption. A punchline euphemism for illegal activities hidden under the guise of charity. 

But in more recent decades, the concept, both Biblical and corrupt has all but disappeared, as the state welfare and entitlements has supplanted it. Now hardly any one, and sadly, few churches, give heed to the "pure religion" God commands us towards.

Here, in chapter 5 of first Timothy, Paul instructs the young evangelist on the proper church role and management for care of widows indeed. 

Before getting to that, and continuing the thought of chapter 4 regarding Timothy's youth, and how to minimize those who look down on being told what to do by a younger man, Paul gives instruction. Don't rebuke an elder. Treat them as fathers, younger men as brothers, young girls as sisters (with a purity), and elderly women as mothers. This applies to us all, and our fellow congregants. We are family for Christ's sake, and as such have obligation for respect, and at times, honor. 

Honor in the Bible has a financial aspect to it, that we give honor, payment, support, to our parents, is one of the main meanings behind the commandment. Giving honor to whom it is due is a point repeatedly made by God throughout the Bible, and this is the context of Paul's instructions here. 

A widow indeed is one who, having lost her husband and not having sons or nephews (which means not only her siblings' children but grandchildren, and other younger relations), that these family members must honor her with support, that she not be a burden to the church. He warns;

*But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.*

This is similar language to those facing church discipline laid out by Jesus, that they be put out from the congregation and treated as if they are unsaved. Heathens. Infidels.

As a side note, that may help with understanding these passages; just as "saved" in scripture isn't always referring to justification by faith, but often physical salvation from danger, "faith" isn't always referring to the saving faith that we need to be redeemed. Often, especially in the epistles (which are written to believers), "faith" can refer to the deeper trust in God, or being faithful to His commands and expectations, or our own responsibility to others. And in the same manner, "condemnation," "damnation," "justified,"  or even "infidel" may be being applied in the present sense, regarding how one is looked at by others, not their spiritual condition in regards to eternal life. These are important distinctions, and understanding the context of the terms when they are used will save you when some try to cherry pick verses to come to a different meaning regarding salvation.

Continuing, Paul lists more qualifiers for a widow "indeed," that she be desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day. Poor, no means of support and giving her life to the faith, essentially. Further, he goes on to say she must be over 60, blameless and devoted to ministry of the church, and the wife of one man;

..*having been the wife of one man. Well reported of for good works; if she have brought up children, if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted, if she have diligently followed every good work.*

This makes her a true widow. A widow indeed. 

Paul contrasts this with the exceptions. One who lives for pleasure rather than service is excluded, for example. And age is a factor;

*The younger widows refuse: for when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry; Having damnation, because they have cast off their first faith. And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.*

Young women, who could still remarry, shouldn't be given the honor by the church. Even if they swear they will be devoted to the ministry, and continuing in prayer, etc, Paul says they eventually will become wonton, that is, spoiled and pampered, having financial support with little to do all day but gossip and carry on, it will corrupt them, and eventually they will seek out a man to remarry, and make them abandon their first faith, that is that God will provide for them through the church that they are swearing devotion to, and leave for a husband. Damnation in this context means condemned by others for her behavior, not losing her salvation or going to Hell. 

This is all true, we witness it ourselves today, especially with welfare taking the place of charity or family support. And frequently you may see at church a godly woman, coming from divorce or a husband's death, will put herself all in to helping out to keep herself busy, and eventually get married, often to an unsaved man, or worse, a man of the church she led to adultery and divorce, and her testimony becomes an open shame. Many such cases. 

We see though out 1 Timothy, and other epistles but especially here, that the testimony to the unsaved by living blamelessly so that they may reach the lost with soul winning, is a top priority.

That they *give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully.*

Shifting gears, Paul gets back to how to handle elders of the church;

*Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine. For the scripture saith, thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.* 

*Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses.*
*Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear.*

So elders that serve the congregation faithfully should receive double honor, double payment for their efforts. Rewarded financially for their time. 

And accusations against them should be handled with respect, the same manner of which Jesus laid out, requiring witnesses and reproached privately, but publicly shamed and cast out if they don't repent. 

Far too many churches only do the first half, and then often will defer to the elder and their profession of innocence. It is sadly rare that they be openly shamed and cast out for their indiscretions and sin. Especially sexual immorality. The topic can be embarrassing for all involved, and the older man's excuses taken with more veracity than the younger girls (or boys) accusations. There is often fear of the entire congregation being smeared, and excuses and rationalizations made. This is the downfall to many churches, especially those that have drifted from biblical fundamentalism, and grown lukewarm. 

By not being respecters of persons in these matters, and worrying less about our own appearances, and more about doing what's right, an active lively church can avoid these pitfalls.

If your church has an elder or any member, for that matter, who engages in sinful activities, especially fornication, adultery, and taking advantage of their position against young ones, they need to be put out, and put out publicly, and police involved if necessary. 

There is no excuse. Jesus will remove the candlestick of a church that does this. The hedge of protection will be gone.

Paul charges these things to Timothy before God. This is a command as to how he should behave and what he must teach to the churches he is planting. It's a sacred duty. We have the same duty to our own churches, to maintain these standards and practices. To exercise pure religion, undefiled. 

He orders Timothy to not lay hands suddenly on no man. This may be an admonition against brawling, but more likely in this context, he means ordination with the Holy Ghost. 

Not to partake in another man's sin, which is great advice to us all. 

He says before you judge remember that while some good works or wrong doings may seem obvious, others come out later so basically don't make snap judgments. 

The kindly medical advice, to drink wine, (obviously meaning juice here as booze isn't good for the stomach), seems a non sequitur in the midst of being instructed not to show favoritism and be patient and reserved in judgment, but it seems apropos given the stress of the position and the weight of what's been charged to the young church planter.

The admonition to obey earthly authority, to please God and make His glory seen of man that you may give a good witness is repeated throughout the New Testament, from Jesus rendering unto Caesar, to Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2, and elsewhere. The introduction to this letter to Timothy, which Paul is writing from Rome, under house arrest, chained to a centurion day and night. We learn that Timothy got saved following his grandmother and mother to Christ, and was given the gifts of the Holy Ghost by the laying on of hands by Paul, an Apostle indeed. 

In his bonds, Paul shares that it is memories of things like Timothy's accepting of the Gospel that bring joy to him while in his predicament, and to encourage Timothy and others who may read this epistle to be of good cheer, hopeful in Christ and not ashamed of Paul's status. 

*For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.*

He goes on to embolden Timothy, not to be ashamed of the Gospel, to lean on the power of the Holy Ghost upon him. To be a partaker of the persecution Paul suffers, willingly, because it is to the glory of God and the furtherance of the Gospel. 

Paul says to Timothy that God has called them, *called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,* *But is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ*.

Note it is the predestination of Jesus Christ, not of the believer, that brings us to be used by God for His purpose, now that Christ was made manifest in Jesus, who abolished death and revealed immortality through the good news. The Gospel.

*For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.*

Blessed assurance. We hold the ernest of His promise in our quickened spirit, the Holy Ghost indwelling within. Even in his persecution and humiliation, Paul knows the victory already won. He will not be ashamed for having placed his faith in the living God.
