An epistle to Philemon, the host of a Colossian church, Paul writes from his bonds in support of Philemon's escaped slave Onesimus (or unfaithful servant, it has been debated), is an instruction on forgiveness. How we as Christians may settle scores between brothers in Christ, if not equals in station. Being peacemakers.

Onesimus apparently fled Philemon, and wound up in Paul's camp, converted to the faith by the Apostle. Philemon, his master, already a prominent Christian in the early church. 

Paul's delicate appeal to take back the servant, not only as a servant, but forgiven as a brother in Christ is a model for us to follow. He reminds the elder Christian of his debt to those ministering the Gospel which he's saved by, and asks he see it right to extend the same grace to Onesimus, who is seeking forgiveness. Paul even offers to pay whatever debt is owed, though he gets in a not-so-subtle reminder that Philemon owes even moreso, having eternal life by the word preached by Paul and his fellow laborers. 

We should also make overtures to bring brethren together, to help broker peace and forgiveness. And we should use reminders of what love Jesus Christ has for us that He gave Himself for us as sacrifice, that we may suffer a little worldly loss out of love for one another.

Onesimus brought this letter and the general epistle to the Colossians from Paul in Rome, and the preservation of Philemon and the promulgation of Colossians suggests that Philemon found it in his heart to forgive him, and welcome him as a brother in Christ.

Now having established that Jesus Christ, the Son of God seated at the right hand of the Father, is greater than the angels, greater than Moses, Abraham, David, in all ways, better than the Levites and the descendants of Aaron as the High Priest after the order of Melchisedek, Paul continues to show the superiority of Christ to the Mosaic law itself, which is a picture of His glory. That faith in Him that saves and the promises made of God for that faith, a better covenant. A new and better testament. 

Better than the commandments which condemn us, transgressions of the law being sin, better than the dead works which cannot save us and Jesus as our redeemer is a better sacrifice than all the sacrifices offered under the law. 

The entire epistle is an appeal to the superiority and primacy of Christ Jesus as our Lord, High Priest, advocate, and sole means of the cleansing of our sins, in either dispensation. Man has always been saved by grace through faith in Christ. The blood of bulls and goats never took away sins. It was not possible, the Bible says. No sacrifice other than Christ cleans the conscience. And so those who yearly sought forgiveness by sin offering rather than as a picture of their faith, fruitlessly returned year after year seeking to clean their conscience. 

A conscience, or "with knowledge," offended by sin, knowingly transgressing the law, with understanding, can only be made clean with the blood of Christ. The vail only removed by His flesh, offered for us. A better sacrifice, done once and forever. Taking on the sins of the whole world. 

Burnt offerings and sacrifice for sin gave God no pleasure, but Jesus doing the will of the Father, to become sin and die for us that all may be called and those that believe be saved, sanctified once and for all in the offering of Jesus Christ's body. In this the LORD delights. 

For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.

Practical application of this, the implications of this, that we are forgiven of all sin by this perfect sanctification, total remission, forever, is that we be freed from the burden of guilt and the fear of judgment that we may serve the living God. 

Faith in Christ is to be born again, our spirit without sin. The Holy Ghost as witness that we can let go of the sins of the past and have full assurance of forgiveness for sins of the flesh going forward. The knowledge that God so loved us, He offered His only begotten Son. The rest that is found in Christ. The true Sabbath. 

*This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, saith the Lord, I will put my laws into their hearts, and in their minds will I write them; And their sins and iniquities will I remember no more.*

*Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin....*

Most of our troubles as man come from the carrying of that burden. The heavy yoke of the conscience. The fear of judgment and death. The pangs of guilt are the Spirit, bringing us reproof of sin that we may understand the need for salvation, and pricked by the hearing of His word, come to understanding and in that knowledge, repent unto faith. 

But for some, who taste that heavenly knowledge, partake in the rebuke of the Holy Ghost, reject it. Resenting being judged. Clinging to the trauma, reveling in their sin. And they willfully sin knowing the judgment of God, rejecting Christ and being made reprobate by God. Having their conscience seared as with hot iron. 

These are the three spiritual states of man. Unsaved, saved and reprobate. And the underlying condition of fallen man comes in our conscience; be it guilty, cleansed by the blood, or seared by God for our hardened heart.

And so to those who live by faith, the burden of our sin borne on the cross by Jesus, quickened and sealed by the Spirit, made temples of God, adopted heirs, part of His priesthood, an holy people, we should have full confidence in the covenant and patience towards the day of redemption. 

We shouldn't be miserable. We shouldn't cling to guilt for sins and inequities God has forgiven and remembers no more. 

*If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.*

This is the liberty which is found in Christ. 

And so, by implication Paul encourages us;

*Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water. Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;) And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.*

If we truly believe all of these truths and have faith in our salvation, then let us as brethren encourage and edify each other, and do good works with a clean conscience. Not selfishly trying to appease an angry God, not in dead works and fruitless sacrifices of bulls and goats, but as servants to the Lord who saved us. Free from the bonds of the law. Free from death and Hell. Out of the same grace and mercy shown to us by our Father. 

It should be noted here that Paul encourages us, in the Spirit, to gather with other believers in an assembly for the purpose of building our faith and provoking each other to love and good works. Exhortation in the faith, especially as we see that day of Christ's return approaching. 

This is an appeal to go to church. Note, not for salvation, not just because it's sin not to, not because you can lose your salvation if you don't. But like all good works, to the benefit of others and a reflection of the love God has shown us in our salvation. 

Do not forsake the assembly, because by it we become more complete, more perfect and able to serve God better. And it will build your faith and patience, your knowledge of the Lord, bring blessings for your works as it brings more opportunities to serve others.

So if that is the practical application of our faith, and the understanding of our salvation in Christ, the end of sacrifices for sin, boldly going before God, serving Him and assembling together, then what is the implication for those who instead turn aside the faith and the new covenant to return to the yoke of the old?

And again, The Lord shall judge his people.*

Again, this is a warning to those who may have tasted the truth but are withdrawing themselves, influenced by the Judaizers who were afflicting believers with the doctrine of dead works. 

That if there is no reconciliation by animal sacrifice, if there never has been, and you have this knowledge of the truth in Christ but turn away back to the Old Testament, rejecting the New, you remain under the wrath of God. You have the guilt and fear of judgment upon you. Worse, the knowledge of the truth adds to that burden of guilt, how much worse God's vengeance is on those who should know better? And by the end of this epistle there can be no doubt. If they fall away from faith in Christ and refuse to repent towards God after hearing this preached, well, it's a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

But Paul offers encouragement, saying he doesn't think those he writes to are reprobate, because they demonstrated to him their faith. He exhorts them to remember the joy they found in being given the truth. He recalls their mercy to him when they saw him in bonds under the Romans. Took pity on him in his afflictions. *Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen....But without faith it is impossible to please him.*

*So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.*

Faith is trusting someone or something promised. Relying on the hope of an offer or covenant. Of belief in the unseen based on faithfulness of the one making the promise. The testimony given. Their word. 

Faith in God relies on His word being true, His promises being kept. His end of the covenant being as a rock. God, who cannot lie tells us His word, and by hearing, we believe the report. 

That is faith. 

And the just live by faith. 

It isn't a mystical force. It isn't will-to-power sorcery. If faith moves mountains, it is by the promise of God to move it, not our will but His. 

The Hall of Faith saints written about here, the recitation of those people who the scriptures tell us believed God when He made promises to them, who were made righteous by their faith and did the will of God for a reward not seen. A promise to be kept. Blessings bestowed on future generations. But their faith held on His word allowed them the opportunity to do great things for the Lord. Because one of the many promises God makes unto us is that He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek Him. Beginning with salvation. 

*For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.*

*That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.*

*For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.*

This is the first promise. Faith in this is the rock upon which Christ built His church. The Kingdom of promise that we trust in. We are dead in sin. But made righteous by faith, our spirit quickened. Given eternal life. For the just lives by faith. Literally. 

But more, once justified, we live by faith diligently seeking Him in His word. Rightly dividing His promises, and being told His will. And by faith we are blessed and rewarded. 

*Honour thy father and mother; (which is the first commandment with promise;) That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth*.

These are some of the promises made by the word of God that we may know are true:

*Verily I say unto you, There is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my sake, and the gospel's, But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life.*

Or, *He that overcometh shall inherit all things; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son.*

Just as Abraham was made a covenant, a son to Sarah delivered, and a blessing to Isaac promised. Just as Moses and David and the prophets were made promises they trusted, and were delivered by the Lord. Just as Jesus fufifiled so many of the promises made by God. So too, God has made promises to we who believe. Who please the Lord by our faith in His word. 

*How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!*

One of the promises of blessings, rewards in Heaven and on earth, comes from our command, the Great Commission, to spread the word of God, and live blameless that we may be living witness to the unseen promises, that others may find faith by hearing, see evidence of the hope we have. That they may come to call upon the name of the Lord and be partakers in the same promise. To live by faith.

Not all who hear believe. Not all who are told the word of God and see the promise of the hope we share, choose to believe. 

*For this people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed; lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and should understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.*

*But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.*

The just live by faith but those without faith, who harden their hearts and stiffen their necks and refuse to believe God's word, die because they are faithless. 

*He that believeth on the Son of God hath the witness in himself: he that believeth not God hath made him a liar; because he believeth not the record that God gave of his Son.*

Now, the expression of faith is found by obeying the will of God. By this a man's faith is justified before men. Just as the OT saints listed in **Hebrews 11** believed and their faith was counted for righteousness, and by faith their works showed to others the power of God's promises.

The pure hard preaching of Hebrews is building to a crescendo. The case made for faith in Christ Jesus, without the works of the law or traditions of man, against the temptations to backslide the way of Judaizers, but towards full faith in a better testament, nearly complete. 

The Spirit through the author, telling us the will of God and reminding the hearers of His word the excellency of His faithfulness in keeping the promises and bestowing the blessings on those who came before us.  Those just who lived by faith. The saints named from the patriarchs and prophets, and the unnamed Christians  who for their faith in the promise of Christ suffered mockery, pain and death:

...*others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection: And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment: They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented; (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.*

Many who endured in faith towards God's word, not seeing the promises but in hope knowing they would be delivered by the Lord, faithful and true. 

And so we, who carry burdens, the weight of guilt, of bitterness at correction, of the distractions and cares of this world, which can lead to envying of the unsaved and impatience with God, to sin, to the fornication of putting the pleasures of the flesh before the promise of our inheritance and the blessings to come, Paul encourages us to standfast in the faith. 

We have a race to run. A crown incorruptible to receive. The yoke of dead works and guilt for sins forgiven slowing us in our course. We must shed these things, striving for the mark set before us. 

And where we slip, where we stumble, know it is God's correction, rebuking those sons whom He loves. Bringing us reproach that we may turn from the sin or shed the burdens that slow us down. For our edification we must not despise the rod of correction given us by our Father, but take joy in that He loves us.

*Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds. Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.*

If we consider Jesus, who literally authored the word that our faith hangs on, and finished it by the work He did, the first fruits of the resurrection assuring us of His faithfulness, if we keep in mind the shame of the cross which He endured for our sin and to do the will of He who sent Him. Our struggles with sin and the weight we carry in this world is nothing. 

Cast it off least we be castaway.

So understanding this, that we need separation from this world, not to despise our promised blessings for a bowl of pottage, that we not satisfy the flesh in our short time here rather than see our hope for eternity. But, as Moses, *Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season.*

Don't be down or angry with God for His chastening, which as it happens may seem grievous, but understand it builds righteousness so that we may better serve the living God, and bring forth fruit as an example to others. 

*Wherefore lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees; And make straight paths for your feet, lest that which is lame be turned out of the way; but let it rather be healed.*

As scripture says:

*I have taught thee in the way of wisdom; I have led thee in right paths. I have taught you in the way of wisdom. I have led you in straight paths.*

And again,

*In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the LORD, and depart from evil.*

Following God's word, the hope that we believe on, we are given wisdom, our paths made straight. Not only for us but for those without, who are lame, who are perishing. That they may see God's glory reflecting from us like Moses come down from the mountain. 

Be peaceable with all men, showing holiness, the separation we are called for, that our faith obtains a good report, as it did the elders before us. 

*Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled;*

Don't allow your burdens and sin, or bitterness at correction or anything to give a bad report of the faith, that others may not be defiled and not accept the grace of God. 

We are a holy priesthood. We are heirs to a kingdom. We have hope everlasting. Act like it that others may attain the same. It is the least we can do considering what Christ did for us. 

For when it is too late for those we turned away by our bitterness and stife, our bad report and our sin, our despising our inheritance, our lack of faith, they are rejected. And there will be no place for repentance.

Therefore, we are again reminded that we aren't under the covenant of Sinai, but of Zion. We aren't like the Hebrews in the wilderness who, hearing God's voice and His commandments could not endure it and asked that God not speak directly to them any more (as much of fear of His commandments which establish death, as fear of the thunderings of God). We are of the new covenant of a Heavenly Zion, which established life, in the continued presence of the Lord. 

*But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect, And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.*

So we shouldn't be as those in the wilderness who turned from the voice of God, but instead glory in it, that He will not only shake the earth but the heavens as well. And so we serve God with grace, and reverence. God-fearing, where our faith brings good report. That we might bear fruit of those led to the straight paths we walk by His light that shines from us. 

*Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear:*

*For our God is a consuming fire.*

One of the key points throughout the book of Hebrews is that if we who are saved fall back again to the old ways, to the sin offerings and dead works, to bitterness at reproach, to neglecting our Christian walk, we bring others down with us, who have not received salvation. Who haven't yet come to the saving faith. Who may be pricked by the Spirit and hear the power of God's Word, and so taste of the heavenly calling and fall short by our example. And *thereby many be defiled.*

Especially knowing that there comes a point where their rejection of the truth and refusal to find faith in the hope we have can leave them reprobate. Either in death, or by being turned over to a reprobate mind by God. We give them cause to harden their hearts. To be dull of hearing. To not believe our report. 

Our faith alone cannot bring another to the knowledge of the truth. But our lack of faith can lead the lame to stumble, as we bring them to uneven paths, leaning on our own understanding. 

Many of us harp on the Reprobate Doctrine because it is an extremely important Biblical truth that far too many are ignorant of, or reject to lean on their own understanding or follow the wisdom of men. There is a point where it is too late for some. And once they are given up and given over, they are twice-dead. Children of Hell, fit for burning. 

But this isn't simply for the cursing of those who have been rejected by way of their hardened heart, but a grave warning to those of us who have been blessed by the faith in God's promise and redeemed in the blood of Christ.

Faith comes by hearing the word of God. 

So does reprobation. The Bible says they have the knowledge of the truth but don't wish to retain God in their knowledge. That they turn the truth of God into a lie. 

If they will harden their hearts and turn away from the truth, don't let it be that we, like David, *despised the commandment of the LORD,* and give *great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme.*

Don't let it be by our bad report. 

Rather, if they reject the truth of God and His offer of grace and mercy, let it be because by our righteous conversation. Our behavior. That they see our faith and that we walk the straight paths, and if it offends them so be it. If our separation from the things of this world and the peace we have because of the blessed hope we've attained offends them, then it's their own dull hearing and seared conscience to blame. 

This is a great responsibility.

As we begin the epistle of James, written to saved, believing Christians of the Jews, in the various churches throughout Asia Minor, scattered abroad. In our reading of Acts 15, that James determined from Paul and in agreement with Peter, to write concerning edification of the churches forming, and to denounce the works-based salvation that was creeping back in from "certain Jews," specifically of circumcision. 

*And when there had been much disputing, Peter rose up, and said unto them, Men and brethren, ye know how that a good while ago God made choice among us, that the Gentiles by my mouth should hear the word of the gospel, and believe. And God, which knoweth the hearts, bare them witness, giving them the Holy Ghost, even as he did unto us; And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith. Now therefore why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they.Then all the multitude kept silence, and gave audience to Barnabas and Paul, declaring what miracles and wonders God had wrought among the Gentiles by them. And after they had held their peace, James answered, saying, Men and brethren, hearken unto me: Simeon hath declared how God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name. And to this agree.*..

So, at the outset we understand the context, the reason for the epistles and the dispensation of doctrine which they agreed upon; salvation by faith. 

After his greeting James wastes no time. He praises them for keeping faith through troubles and testing, that this grows patience in the believer. We see this in our own lives, that where we are tried, and maintain our trust in God, our spirit grows stronger and we become more complete as Christians. "Perfect" in the Bible means complete, or whole. Not sinless, or without any flaw, but as spiritually complete as one can be while still in the flesh. A more perfect Christian life is the theme James hammers throughout.

James teaches the lesson that in faith, we may ask God for knowledge and understanding. That all wisdom comes from God is established in **Proverbs 2:6**
 
*For the LORD giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding.*

He cautions that we ask in faith, unwavering. Not half in, half out as some Christians are, believing the truth of the Gospel, but hedging their bets in the world. That a double minded man is unstable in all his ways. To be perfect and gain understanding we must commit to building up, faith on faith, while remaining humble, to not thinking you deserve God to just hand it to you. 

That lesson in humility carries on, that the poor should rejoice in gratitude for their salvation in God's grace, while the rich, in understanding that they are but dust, and with the same meekness and humility. 

He says again that the temptations and tests of this life are a blessing, that we are rewarded with the crown of life for our efforts. As Paul says in **Romans 4**, when we do His work, it is reckoned of debt, and we are paid for it by God, as His laborers. We rejoice in the free gift given by Him in grace, but receive rewards for our patience in temptation.

He warns against blaming God for our affliction, even as God blesses, He tempts no man with evil. 

James tells us that it is our lusts that lead to sin, and sin to death and tribulations come from this cycle. But the gifts that come from God are blessings, given in His grace. 

That we have the word of Truth, that is Christ Jesus, was beget of God's own will, that we may be His first fruits of the harvest. Amen 

And so, we should avoid wrath and be patient. Avoid temptation of lust for the things of this world, and receive the word, "*engrafted*" in our hearts, *which is able to save your souls.* This is not just the Gospel and spiritual righteousness, but living in the word, obeying His law written in our hearts, saves us in the physical sense from the temptations and trials James is warning against. 

Salvation, or being saved, is not always referring to the righteousness imputed on us by Jesus' blood, through faith. It often means being saved in a literal sense, as we'd use it today. 

We are admonished *to be doers of the word, and not hearers only*. Many Christians go to church, sit through Bible study, and simply never grow because they are hearers only. They think they are complete Christians for their idle listening, while doing no soul winning, no charity, having no grace for others, being respecters of persons, esteeming those with power, wealth, credentials, etc, over the poor, the ignorant, those of low estate. This theme of not being a respecter of persons is another that James is hammering home in this epistle. 

We are blessed in our deeds, being doers of the word. 

We are called to not just be loudmouth Holy Rollers, judging everyone without grace, and puffing ourselves up for attending church, listening to preaching, and the other trappings of religion, without doing that which we are called to do. To visit the fatherless and the widow in their affliction and to keep ourselves unspotted from the world. To be a perfect, a more complete Christian, we should do the good works we are made for, as those justified by faith.

So we have the themes of James' epistle; to edify the saved to do more than just accept the word, but to live it. To be humble in our own status, regardless of what it may be for we are all but grass that withers and dies. That by living in the word, we save ourselves from the temptations of the world. Avoiding wrath and lusts. That by practicing the pure religion, undefiled, we become more complete in our Christian life. And that we shouldn't hold any in higher esteem for worldly reasons, not being a respecter of persons. (That's the meaning of that, if you weren't sure)

Now in the second chapter, James builds on this theme. That how we present ourselves in favoring one man over another for earthly things, we sin. In this favoritism and judgement based on the outward appearance and status the way the unsaved do, we begin to fool ourselves about our own temptations and sin in the same way. 

He reminds that the poor of this world are often the most faithful, and are joint heirs of the kingdom with us, and just as damned without faith and God's grace as we are. That it's the rich of this world who often are our oppressors and enemies of God.

James then reasons with us, that those who keep the law for righteousness, if they offend in one point they are guilty of all. And that being a respecter of persons is sin, as it violates the "royal law," the golden rule, that we do unto others as we would do for ourselves. But we who are judged by the law of liberty, that is saved by faith in Jesus and so, our sins being covered, should not engage in this at all, but live the word that we have heard and believed. To judge with the same mercy and grace He has shown us.

Now we come to the verses that are a snare to so many, where they justify works based righteousness, despite all of the mountain of scripture that assures us we are made righteous by faith alone, through grace alone, in the perfect work of Christ Jesus. 

But, comparing scripture with scripture, and the verses in context, it's not difficult to understand, unless you're a natural man seeking to force the Bible to fit your preconceived notion, rather than letting it tell you God's. 

First, what follows is a series of rhetorical questions and reasoning logic, designed to give example to what James has already preached. And again, it is written to the brethren, the author assumes it is to those already saved, to exhort and edify, not to get them to believe. Not to save them spiritually, but to those already saved, become more complete in their Christian life. 

We do not receive doctrine from rhetorical questions or "a man may say..." reasoning, stripped of context. We get them from clear statements that do not contradict others. 

For brevity sake I have already given argument above, with verses as to why this interpretation that we must do works to be able to go to heaven and have eternal life is damnable heresy. Scroll up. I may add to it as we study through this section, but if that's not sufficient for you, your argument is with God, the Gospel as given by Jesus and then shared by the Apostles, and clear, consistent verses, given again and again from Genesis to Revelation. 

If you are trusting in your own works to get righteous or to maintain the righteousness given by God in Christ, you are damning yourself and being made debtor to the whole of the law which no one can keep perfectly. For there are none righteous no not one. Repent, and obey the Gospel.

What does it profit a man who says he has faith but doesn't do anything with it? Being a hearer of the word only, not a doer. James is continuing this theme, and as in the earlier verses, he is referring to being saved from the temptations and trials that arise from our lusts and sins. Remember, his goal is to educate believers into becoming more perfect, complete, Christians. Not to get people saved in the born again sense. Knowing the context answers the rhetorical question. Further, the example of this rhetorical question *says* he has faith. This is important. James is tying in the lesson that people generally are respecters of persons with the concept that we are to be doers of the word, as befits those who will be judged by the law of liberty. We aren't judged by our works and sin, as the debtors are. We are free in Christ. This is the context of the entire epistle. James has already told us that we earn crowns of life for our deeds. But salvation is a gift, unmerited. Grace-mixing isn't how any of it works. 

The next hypothetical in James reasoning, if someone is needy and you basically just say "thoughts and prayers!" it doesn't profit them anything. It's useless. Dead. It doesn't do anyone any good. 

Dead faith doesn't mean it doesn't exist, but that there's no life in it. Nothing to indicate it, outwardly. It's alone, profiting no one else. A dead body exists, but it just lays there. The same is the faith of a Christian who doesn't exercise it to help the fatherless and widows and the poor. See the theme? Understand the larger context?

You'll have to forgive me, as I do this, I am preparing to leave for a weekend camping trip and getting everything in the garden, the chickens, and stuff we need to pack ready as I do this Bible study. I'm going to finish off the chapter in a minute, but I have to shower

Getting back to it; next we see James continue to use rhetorical hypotheticals to reason with the believer, in this case, "a man may say..."

*Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble. But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead?*

A man may say this. What kind of man? Saved? Unsaved? A respecter of persons? Someone who could reasonably or unfairly doubt your profession of faith by your lack of visible works? You see that this is a device by which to show what someone *could say*, in order to get at the larger point. It is not directly stated doctrine. A man may say all manner of things. For example, we know devil's are not capable of coming to saving belief in Christ. Yet here it says, in this hypothetical man's argument, that they believe and tremble! 

It would take an extreme case of Nicodemus-level Asperger's to draw a doctrine that devils believe on God, as saved Christians do. And yet many draw doctrine from the very same verse! Amazing. 

James continues the argument: *Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?*

Was Abraham justified by his works before God when he was prepared to sacrifice Isaac? Well, no. In fact we know that's not the case. A fact James makes clear in the summation following;

*Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God.*

James says, you see how Abraham's works shut up the hypothetical man, judging Abraham? That his faith was made complete by his works, in regards to being justified by men. 

We know this is true, because again in Romans 4, Paul cites the same scripture James does: 

*1 What shall we say then that Abraham our father, as pertaining to the flesh, hath found?*

*2 For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God.*

*3 For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.*

*4 Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.*

*5 But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.*

*6 Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,*

*7 Saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.*

*8 Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.*

*9 Cometh this blessedness then upon the circumcision only, or upon the uncircumcision also? for we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness.*

*10 How was it then reckoned? when he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.*

*11 And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised: that he might be the father of all them that believe, though they be not circumcised; that righteousness might be imputed unto them also:*

Abraham was saved spiritually, justified before God, by his faith alone. Decades before his circumcision. Decades before bringing Issac to the altar on the same mountain in Jerusalem where Jesus would later be crucified. 

But to be justified before man, that outward sign of his faith, made his faith more perfect. There was a visible tangible act of faith, works that a man may say that they've been shown his faith.

*Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way?*

Rahab was justified to Joshua and the Hebrews by her aid of the spies, but it was her faith in leaving out that crimson thread, representing the blood of Christ, that actually saved her and her household. Her deeds help others. They profited others. She very well could have said yeah yeah I believe you, and done nothing to help them, and her faith in them would be dead, profiting others nothing.

The book of Jesus Christ's Revelation is not written to obscure. Its intent is literally the title. To reveal. Those of us saved by Christ are blessed by reading it. Hearing it. Keeping the prophecy of those things written therein, for the time is at hand. 

Written in the late first century, likely around 93AD, by the Apostle John, who  served Jesus in His earthly ministry with his brother James, who was martyred shortly after Christ's ascent. Called by Jesus "Boanerges," or the "sons of thunder," their mother asked Jesus for favor for her sons in **Matthew 20:20-28**. 

John was the apostle Jesus loved, who wrote the Gospel and epistles. 

Now, exiled to Patmos by Domitian, emperor of Rome from 81 to 96AD, for, as John writes here; "*for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ."* We know the timing and details from John's deciple, Polycarp, and early texts by historians Clement of Alexandria, Victorinus, Eusebius and Jerome. 

The timing of its writing doesn't much matter for us, blessed readers. The earthly things are incidental to spiritual. But the heresy of preterism requires the authorship to be pre-70AD, because it relies on the early writing to make the desolation of Judah by Rome, the destruction of the temple and murder and scattering of the Jews, serve as fulfilment of the prophecy.  

Other modern "scholars" cast doubt on the author's identity, deny John wrote Revelation, often claiming different people wrote the Gospel, epistles and Revelation attributed to John, however the style and description of spiritual things by the Apostle, as well as the clearly inspired truth contained put that heresy to bed sufficiently for believers. That John's peers and ancient historians testify that it was his bolsters that, but a careful reading of scripture is all we really need.

Now as to the contents; there are many, many commentaries on end times Bible prophecy, and a multitude of heresies and blasphemy surrounding it. The most employed tactic by vipers seeking to sow doubtful disputations and confusion is painting Revelation as an obscure and difficult book to understand, and focusing on the earthly signs, fitting the timing to a predetermined schedule, convenient for these false teachers to generate the most fear and confusion possible. Keeping Christians from simply reading it themselves, and instead relying on others interpretations.

We see here in chapter one that, like the rest of scripture, the focus is on Christ Jesus and the spiritual things of God. When we read any of the Bible, we should keep this our focus. Comparing spiritual things with spiritual. It greatly helps with rightly dividing the word of God. 

John writes that it comes "*from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth. Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood, And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen. Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him, and they also which pierced him: and all kindreds of the earth shall wail because of him. Even so, Amen."*

This is what it's all about. It isn't about geopolitics. It's not about which earthly nation or events we want it to be. It's not a warning to those "left behind." Revelation chapters 2 and 3 deal with "what is," in the prophetic sayings of Christ Jesus, to the angels or messengers of the churches in Asia Minor, through John the Apostle. The letters He bids John write are addressed to the individual churches, from an aspect of description representing Jesus, have compliments and criticism and warning and rebuke for the church, followed by an encouragement for those with an ear, of what it means to be saved. This pattern can be split up, to better see the doctrine being given. 

First, we recall from chapter 1 that the 7 stars are the angels of the 7 churches. The 7 candlesticks, the churches themselves. Taking away their candle in this context means the church would fail. No longer having the blessing of God. And, they all eventually did as none remains. 

This is a lesson to churches today. Some or all of what these 7 model churches are engaged in can be found in even the best churches today. The Lord Jesus is warning each and warning us. 

The message of overcoming, as I posted a study on yesterday, is the promises of Christ to the saved who stay faithful, who repent to do the things He instructs. A reminder of what awaits us as saved sons of God that we may be true. 

Jesus singles out three groups whom He hates and will judge; those who say they are Jews but are not, who are the synagogue of Satan. The Nicolaitanes. Jezebel and those she's seduced.  

So, let's break it down, missive by missive to each church.

*Unto the angel of the church of Ephesus write; These things saith he that holdeth the seven stars in his right hand, who walketh in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks;*

Jesus begins using a descriptor of Himself, from the description given by John from His vision in chapter 1. Jesus is holding the angels of the 7 churches in His hand. He is walking in this midst of their candlesticks. His message is to the Ephesians, the church founded 30 odd years before the writing of Revelation, by Paul and the other evangelists. That had fornication in their midst back in Ephesians 1. Jesus goes on to praise their good qualities;

*I know thy works, and thy labour, and thy patience, and how thou canst not bear them which are evil: and thou hast tried them which say they are apostles, and are not, and hast found them liars: And hast borne, and hast patience, and for my name's sake hast laboured, and hast not fainted.*

All good things. 

*Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love. Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.*

The Ephesians have left their first love. This is generally accepted as the spreading of the Gospel. They are working and laboring and being persecuted in Christ's name, trying false prophets who crept in unawares and rejecting them. But the first love of any church is the winning of souls to Christ. The joy of our salvation when fresh leads to our telling everyone about the good news. Churches grow from giving the Gospel. But many successful churches plateau and settle in with who they have, and get wrapped up in feasts of charity, laboring in their own community of believers while neglecting this command of Christ to preach the word to every creature. Without that, Jesus says, He will remove their candlestick. The church will die.  

*But this thou hast, that thou hatest the deeds of the Nicolaitanes, which I also hate.*

Another compliment, that the church at Ephesus hates the deeds of the Nicolaitanes. We have to discern from this limited information that they were a group either led by or claiming to be followers of someone named Nicolas. Many speculate that it refers to Nicolas the proselyte from Antioch, who was elevated to decon along with Stephen and Philip back in Acts. 

The doctrines refered to here, according to early writings and histories is that Nicolas, a pagan convert to the faith of the Jews, then accepting Jesus as the promised Christ, had the doctrine of despising the flesh, hating the material world, that he could better focus on the spiritual. The idea is given he was a just believer, but those who came after him took his views and drifted heavily into gnosticism. We can't know directly from scripture, but this seems very likely. It's also possible that gnostics took the name as a way of gaining legitimacy in the early churches, that they may creep in unawares, with damnable heresy. 

*He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.*

The first promise to those who overcome, who believe on the Lord Jesus Christ for salvation, is the gift of eternal life. The eating of the fruit of the tree of life, in the midst of the paradise of God. The location is going to come up later in Revelation, but the important thing is the knowledge that we who believe in He that has overcome will be given of it to eat. 

Recall in Genesis 3 that God banishes Adam and Eve from the Garden to prevent their eating of this tree themselves, having already eaten of the tree of knowledge of good and evil. Having sinned.

*And unto the angel of the church in Smyrna write; These things saith the first and the last, which was dead, and is alive;*

Again, addressing the church of Smyrna, as the *first and the last, which was dead and is alive*. This is Jesus. Alpha and Omega. The risen Christ. 

*I know thy works, and tribulation, and poverty, (but thou art rich) and I know the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan. Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.*

The church at Smyrna is poor, but rich in spirit. They are working for Christ and being persecuted for it by the Jews, so-called. The synagogue of Satan. 

The absolute failure of those churches that teach Zionism and dispensationalism, Hebrew roots and other Judaizing heresies to recognize precisely who Jesus is talking about here - **HINT: they call themselves Jews and meet in synagogues** - that failing is the work of Satan in them. They are enemies of God, contrary to all men, and they kill and persecute the saints, liars and antichrists. 

The tribulation they gave the early churches has never stopped.

Here, Christ encourages them that despite the tribulation of being jailed, it will be for ten days, and even if they die for His name they will be rewarded with crowns in heaven for their patience and eternal life for their faith. 

*He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death*.

Another promise to the saved; we shall not be hurt of the second death, which we will see later in Revelation refers to Hell and the lake of fire. The eternal damnation that those who have not overcome will suffer.

*And to the angel of the church in Pergamos write; These things saith he which hath the sharp sword with two edges;*

And so, to the church at Pergamum, from Jesus, the twoedged sword that proceeds out of His mouth, the word of God. 

*I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth.*

Pergamum was host to the main temple of Zeus, the altar to this false god was his "throne." Because of how strong the pagan religion was in the city, the Christians who professed the truth of the living God were subject to tribulation, harsh persecution even the martyrdom of one of their own, Antipas. These believers held fast, to declare the name of Jesus among the pagans. 

It is common to think of paganism as the religion of the wild barbarian. But the worship of dead idols in glorious temples made of marble and gold, their graven images and fancy altars, in the Hellenistic world (and today), is often the religion of the civilized. The superstitious nature of natural man leaves them wide open to attack by Satan, and his throne can be found in many advanced cultures as much as it is in the woods and huts of the savage. 

*But I have a few things against thee, because thou hast there them that hold the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed unto idols, and to commit fornication.* 

The doctrine of Balaam refers to the soothsaying false prophet from the OT, who appears in **Deuteronomy, Joshua** and **Numbers,** the son of Beor, a Mesopotamian false prophet who is seemingly familiar with the true God of Israel. He is sent for by Balak, the king of Moab to curse the Israelites who were warring against him in return for treasure. God prevents this in various ways, despite Balaam's best efforts to, he ends up blessing the Israelites. Balaam suggests finally that the Moabites could get Israel to sin, and that would bring God's disfavor on them. Specifically, he tells them to lead them to fornication with their daughters offered as whores, and then have the women lead them in their concupiscence to eating offerings to idols. 

We see the success of this in **Numbers 25**:

*And Israel abode in Shittim, and the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab. And they called the people unto the sacrifices of their gods: and the people did eat, and bowed down to their gods.*
*And Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor: and the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel. And the Lord said unto Moses, Take all the heads of the people, and hang them up before the Lord against the sun, that the fierce anger of the Lord may be turned away from Israel.*

*And Moses said unto the judges of Israel, Slay ye every one his men that were joined unto Baalpeor. And, behold, one of the children of Israel came and brought unto his brethren a Midianitish woman in the sight of Moses, and in the sight of all the congregation of the children of Israel, who were weeping before the door of the tabernacle of the congregation.*

*And when Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose up from among the congregation, and took a javelin in his hand; And he went after the man of Israel into the tent, and thrust both of them through, the man of Israel, and the woman through her belly. So the plague was stayed from the children of Israel. And those that died in the plague were twenty and four thousand.*

We see an admonition against chasing after the error of Balaam in **2 Peter 2**:

*Spots they are and blemishes, sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you; Having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin; beguiling unstable souls: an heart they have exercised with covetous practices; cursed children: Which have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray, following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness; But was rebuked for*

*his iniquity.*

Just as Balaam then, the church at Pergamos had those chasing after fornication, whores and eating the sacrifice made to idols. 

*So hast thou also them that hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitanes, which thing I hate. Repent; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will fight against them with the sword of my mouth.*

And again the Nicolaitanes appear, but unlike the Ephesians, these Pergamites have allowed these heretics in their congregation. Jesus warns that he will destroy them if they don't repent of these errors. 

*He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.*

Another promise to the saved; we will eat the hidden manna, the bread of Heaven, and receive a new name written on a white stone, a name which no man may know except he that received it. The Lord throughout the Bible has given new names unto those who have believed on Him. Jesus did it in His earthly ministry with his disciples, and this trait of God will continue, extended to the saint, we who have overcome.

*And unto the angel of the church in Thyatira write; These things saith the Son of God, who hath his eyes like unto a flame of fire, and his feet are like fine brass;*

Again, writing now to Thyatira, Jesus as described in John's vision. 

*I know thy works, and charity, and service, and faith, and thy patience, and thy works; and the last to be more than the first.*

The church at Thyatira is doing well, their works growing, the last more than the first. Patient, charitable, serving others, faithful.

*Notwithstanding I have a few things against thee, because thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols.*

But the Thyatirians have multiple problems, that all stem from allowing, suffering, a woman to teach. 

**1 Timothy 2:12**:
*But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.*

We see here exactly why this is a problem. Jezebel is joy only teaching, but in the authority she's gained over the men, has seduced them into fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols. The error of Balaam compounded by her role in their church. 

*And I gave her space to repent of her fornication; and she repented not. Behold, I will cast her into a bed, and them that commit adultery with her into great tribulation, except they repent of their deeds. And I will kill her children with death; and all the churches shall know that I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts: and I will give unto every one of you according to your works.*

By this passage, I assume Jezebel is actually a saved believer. That the sin she is in and leading others too comes from their disobeying God's word, and compounding the error, when given chance to repent and turn back towards God, she refused. Backslidden and defiant, Jesus says He will punish her and those who are with her. He chasteneth who He loves. These aren't some sort of reprobates like the Nicolaitanes, these are His servants gone astray. 

And the punishment is severe. Casting her into bed, stricken sick. Likely of STDs. And those she misled into great tribulation, until they repent. He will even kill her children that the other churches will know the error that they were in, and His power, giving to each what they deserve that others may learn from their folly. We should all heed this warning, God is longsuffering but has His limits. He will repay us by our works, here on earth, even if we have been saved from Hell. 

*But unto you I say, and unto the rest in Thyatira, as many as have not this doctrine, and which have not known the depths of Satan, as they speak; I will put upon you none other burden.*
*But that which ye have already hold fast till I come.* 

Jesus says to the rest of the congregation that haven't fallen into this wickedness to holdfast. Encouraging them that He will honor His promises to us at His return. 

*And he that overcometh, and keepeth my works unto the end, to him will I give power over the nations: And he shall rule them with a rod of iron; as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers: even as I received of my Father. And I will give him the morning star. He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches.*

We who are saved and keep to His commands, doing the works He has asked of us, we will be rewarded by ruling and reigning over the Earth with Him in the millennial Kingdom. Ruling with a rod of iron, the perfect law of God. And we will receive the morning star, the glory that is Christ Jesus. Amen.

Note, we are born into the book of life, we are blotted out by death as unbelievers, or reprobation, or unpardonable sin such as blasphemy of the Holy Ghost, knowingly adding to or taking away from the word of God or, as we will see, taking the mark of the beast. No one in the Bible is added to the book of life, only blotted out and removed having already been there. Understanding of this helps when faced with a few false doctrines. 

Jesus promise to us who are saved is that He will confess our names before our Father, our counsel, the sole mediator we need.

*And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write; These things saith he that is holy, he that is true, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth;*

Jesus addresses the church at Philadelphia. Jesus is holy and true. He has the key of David, mentioned in **Isaiah 22:22**:

*And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.*

To Him gave all the prophets witness. 

Also, don't miss this, Jesus opens the door of salvation to us as individual believers, and none may shut it. We have eternal life. It can't be lost or taken. But Christ Jesus also has the ability to shut the door, that none may open. This is reprobation, and it's a doctrine found throughout the Bible. Many find it difficult to accept or believe, but it is taught throughout scripture, clearly and with examples. Sadly today, many are offended at the concept. 

Jesus continues, praising them for their faith. Promising He's opened the door for them. Man has little strength. We cannot open that door ourselves, only His may. 

*I know thy works: behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it: for thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name. Behold, I will make them of the synagogue of Satan, which say they are Jews, and are not, but do lie; behold, I will make them to come and worship before thy feet, and to know that I have loved thee.*

The church in Philadelphia is being persecuted, like some of the others, and again it is the Jews. Jesus says they say they are Jews but are not. That they are liars. 

There are theories and interpretations as to what this means. Edomites? The Ashkenazi? Khazarians? These are earthly interpretations, with physical/genetic/ethnic implications. And they may very well be a marker that has some application. But what we know for certain, spiritually, that they who say they are Jews but are not, are spiritually Edom indeed. They are Esau, who sold their birthright, which has been taken by the Gentiles who are spiritually Jacob. 

**Romans 2:28-29**
*For he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly; neither is that circumcision, which is outward in the flesh: But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God.*

For us, it is sufficient to understand that those who reject the Son have not the Father. That those who deny Jesus is the Christ are liars, and antichrists. By focusing on the spiritual application, it becomes inarguable that they who say they are Jews are not, but are liars. Without going down rabbi holes arguing about their origins and debates about genealogies. The word of God is sharper than any arguments of man, and discerns quickly exactly why they are not Jews; for if they kept the law of Moses and believed the prophets, they would believe Jesus is who He says He is. That He is the Christ. 

But we who are spiritually His, who are inwardly circumcised of the heart, we can take solace in our tribulations caused by the wicked Jew antichrists, that they are a synagogue of Satan and Jesus will make them worship at His feet and know that He loves us, His brothers and sisters who believed on His name. Who trusted God's word. 

Every knee shall bow and every tongue confess. Amen!

Continuing to the Philadelphians;
*Because thou hast kept the word of my patience, I also will keep thee from the hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world, to try them that dwell upon the earth. Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown.*

Jesus encourages them. They are doing well. Holdfast. Faint not. And as the temptation, the test of the deceiver, comes upon the world, they who remain patient and true will be protected from the deception. Note that Jesus encourages them to maintain their works and faith that they not lose crowns. Crowns are rewards in Heaven given to believers based on our works.

They can be earned or lost. We are to be judged, every one of us, not of Heaven and Hell, but our works. Be they precious stones or wood, hay and stubble to be burned. 

**1 Corinthians 3:11-15**
*For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.*
*Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble; Every man's work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is. If any man's work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward. If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire.*

Pay close attention to this; he himself shall be saved, even if his works are burned up as not valuable to the Lord. But to each that has something that remains, to them is there a reckoning of reward. 

And again, more promises to the saved who have overcome in Christ:

*Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name. He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches.*

Amen. Amen. Amen!

*And unto the angel of the church of the Laodiceans write; These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of the creation of God;*

The Amen! Jesus is the Amen, the 'let it be' of God. Verily. True. Through whom all things were created and through whom all things are fulfilled. Unto the Laodiceans.

*I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.*

They are neither hot nor cold. They aren't doing much of anything for the Lord. A church that's lukewarm, does the bare minimum without any enthusiasm. Who haven't gone the way of dying off, apostasy, just grown cold to the truth of the word and aren't really living it. Comfortable. But this offense the Lord more than if they had just grown cold. Mailing it in is more offensive to God, and that's understandable. Many churches are this way. That is why the false doctrine of these churches representing ages claim we are living in the "Laodicean age." It's an easy comparison that allows a pastor to "rah rah" some life out of their members, but it being a false doctrine can lock congregations into complacency. "Sure the church isn't doing much, but it is the age we love in. Oh well." 

Meanwhile there are churches who are on fire for the Lord. There's always a remnant. 7000 who haven't bent the knee to Baal. And a dead or dying church can always be revived, this is the point of these messages from Christ Jesus Himself, to encourage and edify. Warn and chastise. 

But complacency is often found in comfort. 

*Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked: I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear; and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.*

Jesus is attacking that comfort. Saying they have physical wealth and are doing well, as many congregations are today, but they need to recognize they are poor; wretched and miserable. Blind to the word and naked in their sin. 

He says to buy Him gold tried in the fire, ala **1 Corinthians 3.** Spiritual wealth, that comes from good works; spreading the Gospel, winning souls, caring for the least of us. Having the white raiment that comes from believing unto salvation and that covers our nakedness before God. Anointing their eyes with the word, being doers not just hearers, that they may see. 

And Jesus' harsh criticism is leveled against these churches out of love.

*As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent. Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me*.

Whom God loves, He chasteneth. Scourging every son. But the promise of His fellowship is such that any who open themself up towards Him, He shall come in unto. 

And His final message to the saved;

*To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne. He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches.*

Again, the promise to rule and reign with Him. Just as God has established Jesus Christ's throne, so too are we made heirs to the Kingdom, serving in the house of the Lord. Amen.

We will study on **Revelation 4** tomorrow, where the narrative shifts gears and John's visions take him before the throne in Heaven, setting the stage for the next section of the prophecy which runs through chapter 11. It gets pretty wild.

**Revelation 4**

*After this I looked, and, behold, a door was opened in heaven: and the first voice which I heard was as it were of a trumpet talking with me; which said, Come up hither, and I will shew thee things which must be hereafter.*

*5 And out of the throne proceeded lightnings and thunderings and voices: and there were seven lamps of fire burning before the throne, which are the seven Spirits of God.*

*6 And before the throne there was a sea of glass like unto crystal: and in the midst of the throne, and round about the throne, were four beasts full of eyes before and behind.*

Revelation 4 begins the shift in focus from the *things that are,* the then current day churches in Asia Minor, to the *things which must be hereafter.*

Setting the scene, John, who is taken in the spirit and shown a throne in Heaven, and the radiant glory of the Lord upon His throne, and 4 creatures whose role is to give Him thanks and praise, as well as 24 elders, in seats surrounding the throne, given crowns themselves which they throw at the Lord's feet, saying "*Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honor and power"* for being creator of all things, and the reminder that it is for His pleasure that all things exist. 

Amen. 

This is a picture of Heaven. This is the throne before which we who are saved will bow and worship. Where the crowns we receive for the works worthy of reward will be cast before Jesus, the king of kings.

As to the beasts, each stationed at the 4 points of the throne, their description is similar to the vision given Ezekiel:

Some additional **Revelation 4** notes, particularly on heresy.

Pre-trib rapture dispensationalists will use the taking up of John to Heaven to claim this is the secret rapture, that not only John but all the saved, are gathered at verse 1. They have to point to this event, because the following chapter, **Revelation 5**, begins the opening of the seals and the tribulation that follows. But **Revelation 4:1**-**2** says nothing about the gathering of the elect (we will see that it is immediately after the tribulation, when the sun and moon are darkened). 

*After this I looked, and, behold, a door was opened in heaven: and the first voice which I heard was as it were of a trumpet talking with me; which said, Come up hither, and I will shew thee things which must be hereafter. And immediately I was in the spirit: and, behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one sat on the throne.*

This is not the bodily resurrection of the saved, glorified unto God and gathered on the day of redemption. It is John, alone and in the spirit. Pre-trib rapture is a foolish doctrine. 

Another heresy justified out of **Revelation 4**, the vain and repetitive prayers offered by Catholics. Jesus tells us in **Matthew 6:7**; *But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.*

Many Catholics will point to the praise given "without ceasing" by the 4 seraphim, the creatures before the throne of the Lord as a nullifying text that contradicts Jesus' instruction to us on prayer, and so repetitive speed-muttering "Hail Mary's" and the occasional "Our Father" until they become a mush of words used as an incantation to their idols they worship kneeling before them, is ok. It's preposterous. We shall praise the Lord without ceasing but that's not vain repetitions, but giving honor and glory to Christ.  In prayer here, in this life, we should follow the model of conversational praise, gratitude and petition laid out by Jesus, in the manner described. 

Another heresy is the idea that when we die bodily, that our soul sleeps or something, rather than being in the presence of the Lord as the Bible says in **2 Corinthians 5** that to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord, and we see that there are men, in Heaven, the 24 Elders for example. (They are not the only souls in Heaven as we will see moving forward in **Revelation**)

We can also dismiss the wicked heresy of gnosticism, that "matter is all evil," because we see, again, scripture has a different idea of creation, that God looked upon what He made and it was good. Here in **Revelation 4** we see it in the praise given by the elders; *for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created.*

The Lord God does not take pleasure in the wicked.

Even so, come Lord Jesus. Amen. 

This is the future to come. This is not the end but the beginning of infinity. Eternal life with God and Christ, in their presence, seeing the face of God the Father that Moses desired to see. Living and praising God in the light of their glory, forever and ever. 

These sayings are faithful and true. 

Blessed is he that keeps the sayings of the prophecy of this book. Behold, Jesus comes quickly and His reward is with Him, to every man according to his work. The Alpha and Omega. The first and the last. 

Blessed are they who do His commandments. That have overcome. That freely partake in the water of life. Who eat freely of the tree of life. 

 Cursed are they that add to or take away from the prophecy of this book. To then will be given all the plagues contained, and they are struck out of the book of life. Damned. 

Jesus, the root and offspring of David. The bright and morning star. Our savior who promises that *any* who hear His word and are athirst for truth, *whosoever will,* can come and take the water of life freely. This is His testimony. Amen.

Once again, John is cautioned by a messenger of God not to worship him as an angel, but God alone;

*See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of them which keep the sayings of this book: worship God.*

If they could reach across the great gulf fixed between Heaven and earth, the saints, including Mary, would say this same thing to those being misled into pagan idolatry and the "veneration" that is worship before images and icons representing man. 

*See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of them which keep the sayings of this book: worship God.*

So that's it. We have studied Genesis and Revelation, the beginning and the end. And we see in both that Jesus is the Alpha and Omega. He is there in the beginning, He is there in the end. The entire Bible is God's testimony of the Son, and the promise made to man, given by God's grace, to be accepted in faith. 

God, who knows the end from the beginning, has given us His revelation that we may know He loves us.
